                                                              ​7​
​Abstract​


​Antisemitism,​ ​which​​adversely​​impacts​​Jewish​​communities​​worldwide,​​manifests​​in​​various​
​forms,​ ​from​ ​verbal​ ​abuse​ ​and​ ​social​ ​discrimination​​to​​physical​​violence​​and​​even​​genocide.​
​Antisemitism​​has​​been​​documented​​in​​European​​football​​stadiums,​​where​​antisemitic​​chants,​
​symbols,​​and​​slurs​​have​​been​​directed​​at​​fans​​of​​specific​​teams.​​While​​numerous​​initiatives​​in​
​sports​​address​​issues​​of​​inequality​​and​​discrimination,​​relatively​​few​​have​​focused​​specifically​
​on​ ​combating​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Given​ ​the​ ​rise​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK,​ ​it​ ​is​​crucial​​to​​better​
​understand this societal issue and propose effective prevention measures.​


​This​ ​project​ ​followed​ ​a​ ​multi-phased​ ​approach​ ​consisting​ ​of​ ​four​ ​stages​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection.​
​The​ ​first​ ​phase​ ​involved​ ​conducting​ ​semi-structured​ ​interviews​ ​with​ ​experts​ ​skilled​ ​in​
​developing​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​programmes​ ​(n=14).​ ​Using​ ​thematic​ ​analysis,​ ​key​ ​themes​
​were​ ​identified,​ ​leading​ ​to​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​during​ ​Phase​ ​2,​
​incorporating​ ​a​ ​‘creative​ ​non-fiction’​ ​(CNF)​ ​methodological​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​use​ ​sport​ ​as​ ​a​
​medium​​for​​educating​​individuals​​about​​antisemitism.​​In​​the​​third​​phase,​​focus​​groups​​were​
​held​ ​with​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​ ​teachers,​ ​and​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​to​
​gain​ ​insight​ ​into​ ​their​ ​perspectives​ ​on​ ​the​ ​first​ ​draft​​of​​the​​initiative​​(n=25).​​Based​​on​​their​
​feedback,​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​was​ ​revised​ ​accordingly.​ ​Finally,​ ​the​ ​fourth​ ​phase​ ​involved​ ​a​ ​‘book​
​review’​​with​​experts​​in​​antisemitism​​education​​or​​Jewish​​studies​​to​​further​​refine​​and​​finalise​
​the initiative (n=6).​


​This​​project​​makes​​a​​novel​​contribution​​by​​integrating​​the​​emerging​​theory​​of​​HebCrit,​​which​
​critically​ ​examines​ ​Jewish​ ​identity​ ​and​ ​experiences,​ ​and​ ​using​ ​‘creative​ ​non-fiction’​ ​as​ ​an​
​innovative​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​develop​​the​​educational​​initiative.​​By​​leveraging​​sport​​as​​a​​platform​
​for​ ​combating​​antisemitism,​​the​​project​​offers​​a​​unique,​​narrative-driven​​strategy​​to​​engage​
​and​​educate​​young​​audiences.​​This​​approach​​not​​only​​addresses​​antisemitism​​in​​football​​but​
​also​​contributes​​to​​broader​​efforts​​to​​reduce​​discrimination​​in​​society​​through​​an​​impactful,​
​theory-informed educational programme.​




                                                              ​8​
​Chapter 1 - Introduction​


​Antisemitism,​ ​a​ ​widespread​ ​form​ ​of​ ​prejudice​ ​against​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​manifests​ ​in​
​various​ ​severe​ ​ways,​ ​including​ ​verbal​ ​abuse,​ ​social​ ​discrimination,​ ​physical​ ​violence,​ ​and​
​even​​genocide​​(Staetsky​​and​​Boyd,​​2015).​​With​​26%​​of​​the​​world’s​​population​​admitting​​they​
​harbour​ ​antisemitic​ ​views​ ​(Anti-Defamation​ ​League,​ ​2019),​ ​the​ ​scope​ ​of​ ​this​ ​problem​ ​is​
​alarming.​ ​Therefore,​ ​as​ ​antisemitism​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​rise​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​ ​Kingdom​ ​(henceforth,​
​UK),​​in​​education,​​the​​workplace​​and​​society​​more​​broadly​​(Community​​Security​​Trust​​[CST],​
​2024;​​Lessof,​​2024)​​it​​is​​crucial​​to​​deepen​​our​​understanding​​of​​this​​issue​​to​​develop​​effective​
​strategies for addressing it in the future (CST, 2023).​


​For​ ​decades,​ ​antisemitism​ ​has​ ​been​ ​a​ ​recurring​ ​issue​ ​in​ ​football​ ​stadiums​ ​across​ ​Europe​
​(Stratton,​ ​2015).​ ​It​ ​was​ ​particularly​ ​heightened​ ​during​ ​the​ ​1970s​ ​and​ ​1980s,​​as​​antisemitic​
​chants​ ​became​ ​notably​ ​prevalent​ ​in​ ​football​ ​matches​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​(Williams,​ ​Dunning​ ​and​
​Murphy,​ ​1984)​ ​as​ ​football​ ​fans​ ​frequently​ ​used​​antisemitic​​language​​and​​symbols​​in​​chants​
​directed​​at​​rival​​teams​​(Curtis,​​2019).​​These​​chants​​often​​included​​derogatory​​remarks​​about​
​Jewish​ ​community​​members​​and​​mockery​​of​​their​​beliefs​​and​​traditions​​(Poulton,​​2016).​​As​
​antisemitism​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​surge​ ​more​ ​broadly​ ​in​ ​society​ ​(CST,​ ​2024),​ ​it​ ​has​ ​also​ ​become​
​increasingly​ ​evident​ ​in​ ​football​ ​stadiums,​ ​with​ ​a​​significant​​63%​​rise​​in​​incidents​​during​​the​
​2023/2024 season (Kick It Out, 2024).​


​Bourke​ ​(2014)​ ​and​ ​Holmes​ ​(2020)​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​a​​researcher's​​positionality​​is​​shaped​​by​​their​
​personal​ ​background​ ​and​ ​academic​ ​journey.​ ​Since​ ​beginning​ ​my​ ​research​ ​journey,​ ​the​
​context​ ​surrounding​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​racism​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​and​​society​​has​​evolved​​significantly.​
​While​​racism​​has​​long​​been​​present,​​there​​has​​been​​a​​notable​​uptick​​in​​antisemitic​​incidents,​
​particularly​​during​​and​​following​​Donald​​Trump’s​​first​​term​​as​​U.S.​​President,​​and​​the​​rise​​of​
​populist​ ​and​ ​far-right​ ​parties​ ​across​ ​Europe​ ​(Beirich,​ ​2021).​ ​Antisemitism​ ​has​ ​varied​ ​over​
​time,​ ​often​ ​heightened​ ​by​ ​geopolitical​ ​tensions,​ ​particularly​ ​in​ ​relation​ ​to​ ​Israel/Palestine​
​(Freedman​ ​and​ ​Hirsh,​ ​2024;​ ​Seymour,​ ​2024).​ ​These​ ​shifts​ ​have​ ​reinforced​ ​the​​urgency​​and​
​relevance​ ​of​ ​my​ ​research,​ ​motivating​ ​me​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​how​ ​antisemitism​ ​manifests​ ​within​
​football​ ​culture​ ​and​ ​how​ ​this​ ​context​ ​influences​ ​public​ ​understanding,​ ​perception​ ​and​
​response.​


                                                           ​9​
​My​​own​​journey​​began​​with​​undergraduate​​studies​​in​​Sport​​Studies,​​followed​​by​​an​​MRes​​in​
​Sport​ ​and​ ​Exercise​​Science,​​during​​which​​I​​developed​​a​​focused​​interest​​in​​religious​​identity​
​and​​antisemitism​​in​​football.​​This​​interest​​was​​influenced​​by​​my​​Jewish​​heritage​​and​​personal​
​conversations​ ​regarding​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​among​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​supporters.​
​Through​ ​a​ ​reflexive​ ​process,​ ​I​ ​aim​ ​to​ ​acknowledge​ ​how​ ​my​ ​personal​ ​and​ ​academic​
​experiences​ ​have​​shaped​​the​​development​​of​​this​​research​​(Holmes,​​2020).​​I​​recognise​​that​
​my​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​cultural​ ​identity,​ ​particularly​ ​my​ ​Jewish​ ​heritage​ ​and​ ​earlier​
​research​ ​around​ ​the​ ​term​​‘Yid’,​​inform​​the​​lens​​through​​which​​I​​interpret​​data​​(Furlong​​and​
​Marsh,​ ​2017).​ ​This​ ​is​ ​explored​ ​in​ ​greater​ ​depth​ ​in​ ​the​ ​reflexivity​ ​(see​​p.​​102)​​and​​personal​
​reflection​​(see​​p.​​297)​​sections​​later​​in​​the​​thesis,​​where​​I​​critically​​examine​​how​​my​​identity​
​and values have influenced the research process.​


​While​​substantial​​academic​​research​​has​​been​​undertaken​​into​​race,​​religion,​​and​​ethnicity​​in​
​sport​​(Burdsey,​​2011;​​Cleland​​and​​Cashmore,​​2014),​​in​​comparison,​​there​​is​​limited​​scholarly​
​literature​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​English​​football.​​In​​British​​football,​​research​​primarily​​explores​
​how​ ​supporters​ ​of​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur,​ ​commonly​ ​referred​ ​to​ ​as​ ​Spurs,​ ​often​ ​face​
​considerable​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​from​ ​rival​ ​clubs,​ ​stemming​ ​from​ ​the​ ​club's​ ​perceived​
​association​ ​with​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​​(Poulton,​​2016;​​2020).​​Previous​​studies​​have​​begun​
​to​ ​highlight​ ​how​​antisemitism​​is​​present​​within​​English​​football​​(Back,​​Crabbe​​and​​Solomos,​
​2001;​ ​Poulton,​ ​2016;​ ​2024)​ ​and​ ​in​ ​other​ ​European​ ​countries’​ ​football​ ​fan​ ​cultures​ ​(Curtis,​
​2019; Poulton, 2020).​


​In​ ​contrast​ ​to​ ​these​ ​current​ ​studies,​ ​the​ ​ambition​ ​of​ ​this​ ​thesis​ ​is​ ​to​ ​examine​ ​the​ ​work​
​currently​​being​​conducted​​in​​sport​​to​​tackle​​antisemitism​​and​​other​​forms​​of​​discrimination,​
​with​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​of​ ​developing​ ​an​ ​initiative​ ​that​ ​could​ ​effectively​ ​address​ ​and​ ​reduce​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​football.​ ​This​ ​initiative​ ​seeks​ ​to​ ​not​ ​only​ ​raise​ ​awareness​ ​but​ ​to​ ​also​
​implement​ ​practical​ ​measures​ ​that​ ​would​ ​challenge​ ​this​ ​form​ ​of​ ​discriminatory​ ​behaviour,​
​and​ ​therefore​ ​support​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​Although​ ​progress​ ​is​ ​being​ ​made​ ​in​
​researching​​antisemitism​​in​​football,​​as​​it​​stands​​there​​are​​few​​practical​​measures​​in​​place​​in​
​England​ ​in​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport,​ ​specifically​ ​football,​ ​to​ ​actively​ ​combat​ ​and​ ​challenge​
​antisemitism.​




                                                             ​10​
​Two​​organisations​​currently​​working​​to​​address​​antisemitism​​in​​football​​are​​Chelsea​​Football​
​Club​ ​and​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out.​ ​Given​ ​that​ ​some​ ​fans​ ​of​ ​Chelsea​ ​FC​ ​have​ ​been​ ​known​ ​to​ ​display​
​antisemitic​ ​behaviours​ ​at​ ​matches,​ ​the​ ​‘Say​​No​​To​​Antisemitism’​​campaign​​was​​launched​​in​
​2018​ ​and​ ​is​ ​run​ ​and​ ​organised​ ​by​ ​Chelsea​ ​FC​ ​themselves​ ​(Chelsea​ ​FC,​ ​2018).​ ​Additionally,​
​Kick​​It​​Out​​has​​worked​​alongside​​various​​stakeholders​​to​​promote​​awareness​​and​​implement​
​strategies​​to​​combat​​discrimination​​in​​the​​sport.​​The​​organisation​​aims​​to​​challenge​​all​​forms​
​of​ ​discrimination,​ ​including​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​other​ ​faith-based​ ​prejudices,​ ​such​ ​as​
​Islamophobia.​ ​However,​​there​​is​​a​​significant​​gap​​in​​empirical​​data​​on​​the​​long-term​​impact​
​of​​these​​initiatives​​in​​reducing​​antisemitism​​in​​football.​​Chelsea​​FC​​and​​Kick​​It​​Out​​often​​rely​
​on​ ​short-term​ ​indicators​ ​like​ ​media​ ​engagement​ ​and​ ​anecdotal​ ​evidence,​ ​rather​ ​than​
​rigorous​ ​studies.​ ​This​ ​can​ ​lead​ ​to​ ​assumptions​ ​about​ ​their​ ​effectiveness​ ​without​ ​a​ ​clear​
​understanding​ ​of​ ​their​ ​true​ ​impact.​ ​To​ ​accurately​ ​assess​ ​these​ ​campaigns'​ ​success,​
​data-driven​​approaches​​are​​needed​​to​​ensure​​future​​strategies​​are​​based​​on​​solid​​evidence,​
​not​ ​assumptions.​ ​Compared​ ​to​ ​other​ ​marginalised​ ​groups,​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​population​ ​has​
​received​​relatively​​little​​attention​​in​​efforts​​to​​understand​​and​​combat​​antisemitism​​(Marcus,​
​2015),​ ​highlighting​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​completing​ ​such​ ​studies.​ ​Specifically,​ ​within​ ​sport,​
​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​wealth​ ​of​ ​initiatives​ ​being​ ​developed​ ​to​ ​reduce​ ​racism​ ​and​ ​other​ ​forms​ ​of​
​discrimination;​​nevertheless,​​it​​is​​evident​​that​​comparative​​action​​on​​antisemitism​​in​​sport​​is​
​limited (Poulton, 2020).​


​An​​analysis​​of​​the​​anti-discriminatory​​initiatives​​and​​projects​​being​​done​​in​​the​​field​​of​​sport,​
​particularly​​football,​​can​​thus​​provide​​valuable​​insights​​into​​effective​​methods​​for​​combating​
​such​​prejudices.​​Therefore,​​as​​mentioned​​above,​​in​​contrast​​to​​other​​work​​being​​conducted​
​in​ ​this​ ​field,​ ​this​ ​project​ ​provides​ ​a​ ​unique​ ​opportunity​​to​​develop​​an​​initiative​​that​​can​​be​
​used​​to​​address​​and​​decrease​​antisemitism​​in​​sport,​​particularly​​within​​football,​​by​​engaging​
​with​​experts​​in​​the​​field​​of​​sport​​and​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community.​​The​​next​​section​​of​
​this​​chapter​​addresses​​the​​research​​aim​​and​​objectives,​​which​​will​​guide​​the​​development​​of​
​this​ ​research​ ​project​ ​which​ ​underpins​ ​this​ ​thesis,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​creation​ ​of​ ​an​​initiative​​that​​has​
​potential to reduce antisemitic attitudes and behaviours in football.​




                                                            ​11​
​Study aim and research objectives​


​The​ ​aim​ ​and​ ​objectives​ ​of​ ​this​ ​project​ ​are​ ​outlined​ ​below.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​note​ ​the​
​significance​ ​of​ ​this​ ​aim​ ​and​ ​its​ ​associated​ ​objectives,​ ​as​ ​they​ ​have​ ​driven​ ​the​ ​design​ ​and​
​undertakings of this project (Doody and Bailey, 2016).​


​The overarching aim of this research project is:​


       ​To​ ​develop​ ​an​ ​evidence-based​ ​and​ ​co-created​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​focused​ ​on​
       ​eradicating​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​British​ ​Football,​ ​with​ ​input​ ​from​ ​anti-discrimination​
       ​experts and the Jewish community.​


​This​ ​research​ ​intends​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​by​ ​engaging​ ​in​ ​a​ ​collaborative​
​process​ ​that​ ​brings​ ​together​ ​the​ ​expertise​ ​of​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​ ​the​ ​lived​
​experiences​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​and​ ​insights​ ​from​ ​other​ ​key​​stakeholders​​within​​the​
​field​ ​of​​sport​​and​​football.​​By​​working​​closely​​with​​anti-discrimination​​experts,​​the​​initiative​
​will​ ​incorporate​ ​best​ ​practices​ ​and​ ​proven​ ​strategies​ ​for​ ​combating​ ​discrimination.​ ​Input​
​from​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​will​ ​be​ ​central​ ​to​ ​the​​initiative’s​​development,​​ensuring​​that​​it​
​gives​ ​voice​ ​to​ ​the​ ​community​ ​and​ ​accurately​ ​reflects​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​those​ ​affected​ ​by​
​antisemitism.​


​Alongside​ ​the​ ​main​ ​aim​ ​of​ ​this​ ​thesis,​ ​there​ ​are​ ​four​ ​research​ ​objectives.​ ​These​ ​research​
​objectives form the framework that guides and shapes the direction of this study:​


    ​1.​ ​Investigate​ ​the​ ​perspectives​ ​of​ ​key​ ​stakeholders​ ​on​ ​antisemitism,​ ​religion,​
         ​ethnicity and identity within the football and wider social context.​
    ​2.​ ​Identify​ ​and​ ​evaluate​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives​ ​in​ ​football​ ​and​ ​sport​ ​to​
         ​identify good practice on how antisemitism may be tackled.​
    ​3.​ ​Develop​ ​a​ ​theoretically-informed​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​that​ ​could​ ​be​ ​used​ ​to​
         ​decrease antisemitic behaviour in football.​
    ​4.​ ​Explore​ ​how​​key​​stakeholders​​respond​​to​​an​​original​​educational​​initiative​​that​
         ​aims to decrease antisemitism in football.​


                                                            ​12​
​Throughout​ ​this​ ​thesis,​ ​the​ ​objectives​ ​are​ ​intended​ ​to​​be​​addressed​​chronologically;​​firstly,​
​by​ ​examining​ ​current​ ​stakeholders'​ ​understanding​ ​and​ ​perspectives​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​
​other​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​faith-based​ ​discrimination,​ ​and​ ​subsequently​ ​evaluating​ ​the​ ​current​ ​work​
​being done in the field of sport to combat these issues.​


​The​ ​first​ ​objective​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​delve​ ​into​ ​the​ ​views​ ​and​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​various​ ​stakeholders,​
​including​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts​ ​in​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport,​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​how​ ​antisemitism​
​and​ ​related​ ​issues​ ​are​ ​perceived​ ​and​ ​manifested​ ​within​ ​football​ ​and​ ​broader​ ​society.​ ​By​
​examining​ ​the​ ​intersection​ ​of​ ​religion,​ ​ethnicity,​ ​and​ ​identity,​ ​the​ ​study​ ​will​ ​uncover​ ​the​
​complexities​​of​​these​​issues​​and​​how​​they​​influence​​attitudes​​and​​behaviours​​in​​the​​context​
​of​ ​football.​ ​The​​second​​objective​​focuses​​on​​conducting​​a​​comprehensive​​review​​of​​existing​
​anti-discrimination​ ​efforts​ ​in​ ​football​ ​and​ ​other​ ​sports.​ ​By​ ​evaluating​ ​the​ ​effectiveness​ ​of​
​these​​initiatives,​​the​​thesis​​identifies​​best​​practices​​and​​successful​​strategies​​that​​have​​been​
​implemented​​to​​combat​​antisemitism​​and​​similar​​forms​​of​​discrimination.​​This​​evaluation​​will​
​provide​​a​​foundation​​for​​understanding​​what​​works​​in​​the​​fight​​against​​antisemitism​​and​​how​
​these approaches can be adapted or improved.​


​By​​building​​on​​the​​data​​gained​​from​​the​​first​​two​​objectives,​​these​​findings​​in​​turn​​guide​​the​
​final​ ​two​​objectives,​​which​​develop​​an​​initiative,​​which​​could​​then​​be​​trialled​​and​​tested​​on​
​key​ ​stakeholders.​ ​The​ ​third​ ​objective​ ​involves​ ​the​ ​design​ ​of​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​programme​
​informed​ ​by​ ​relevant​ ​sociological​ ​theories,​ ​namely​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020)​ ​and​ ​critical​ ​race​
​theory​​(Delgado​​and​​Stefancic,​​2001).​​The​​initiative​​will​​be​​tailored​​to​​address​​the​​challenges​
​faced​ ​by​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​The​ ​development​ ​of​ ​this​ ​initiative​​will​​be​​grounded​​in​​the​
​empirical​ ​data​ ​findings,​​as​​addressed​​in​​the​​first​​two​​objectives.​​The​​final​​objective​​involves​
​the​ ​implementation​ ​and​ ​evaluation​ ​of​ ​the​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​developed​ ​in​ ​the​ ​third​
​objective.​ ​This​ ​stage​ ​of​ ​the​​research​​involves​​piloting​​the​​initiative​​with​​a​​selected​​group​​of​
​stakeholders​​and​​gathering​​feedback​​on​​its​​effectiveness​​and​​potential​​impact.​​The​​responses​
​of​ ​the​ ​stakeholders​ ​will​ ​be​ ​analysed​ ​to​ ​assess​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​potential​ ​for​ ​wider​
​implementation and to identify areas for improvement.​




                                                           ​13​
​The​ ​value​ ​in​ ​this​ ​research​ ​can​ ​be​ ​summarised​ ​in​ ​three​ ​main​ ​arguments.​ ​Firstly,​ ​as​
​antisemitism​ ​has​ ​been​ ​seen​ ​to​ ​be​ ​increasing​ ​in​ ​both​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​broader​ ​society,​ ​this​ ​trend​
​raises​​significant​​concerns​​for​​the​​safety​​of​​Jewish​​communities​​(Lessof,​​2024).​​Secondly,​​the​
​creation​​of​​an​​educational​​initiative​​that​​could​​be​​used​​to​​create​​positive,​​significant​​change​
​could​ ​challenge​ ​the​ ​current​ ​attitudes​ ​and​ ​behaviours​ ​that​ ​sustain​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​football.​
​Finally,​ ​giving​ ​voice​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​is​​of​​significant​​importance​​as​​it​​ensures​​that​
​their​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​perspectives​ ​are​ ​central​ ​to​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​strategies​ ​aimed​ ​at​
​combating this form of discrimination (Rubin, 2020).​


​Using​​HebCrit​​(Rubin,​​2020),​​a​​relatively​​novel​​theory,​​adds​​significant​​value​​to​​this​​research​
​as​​it​​emphasises​​the​​importance​​of​​amplifying​​the​​voices​​of​​the​​community.​​Additionally,​​due​
​to​ ​its​ ​novelty​ ​and​ ​underdeveloped​ ​exploration​​in​​academic​​literature,​​very​​limited​​research​
​has​​engaged​​with​​this​​theory,​​thereby​​enhancing​​its​​relevance​​and​​contribution​​to​​this​​study.​
​This​ ​thesis​ ​makes​ ​an​ ​original​ ​contribution​ ​to​ ​knowledge​ ​by​ ​also​ ​employing​ ​creative​
​nonfiction​ ​(henceforth,​ ​CNF)​ ​to​ ​integrate​ ​key​ ​principles​ ​of​ ​critical​ ​race​ ​theory​ ​(henceforth,​
​CRT)​ ​and​ ​more​ ​specifically,​ ​HebCrit.​ ​It​ ​gives​ ​voice​ ​to​ ​this​ ​marginalised​ ​community,​
​particularly​ ​by​ ​using​ ​narrative​ ​to​ ​highlight​ ​the​ ​unique​ ​challenges​ ​faced​ ​by​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community.​​Through​​the​​creation​​of​​a​​novel,​​this​​work​​is​​designed​​to​​educate​​individuals​​on​
​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​promote​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​Judaism.​ ​Additionally,​ ​the​ ​thesis​ ​seeks​ ​to​
​challenge​ ​existing​ ​antisemitic​ ​stereotypes​ ​and​ ​attitudes​ ​by​ ​developing​ ​an​ ​educational​
​initiative​​in​​the​​form​​of​​a​​book​​and​​resource​​pack.​​This​​initiative​​is​​intended​​to​​be​​used​​as​​a​
​tool​ ​for​ ​teaching​ ​about​ ​Judaism​ ​and​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​incorporates​ ​sport​ ​as​ ​a​ ​medium​​for​
​these discussions, due to its appeal and ability to encourage dialogue across diverse groups.​


​Thesis overview​


​This thesis is divided into eleven chapters.​


​In​ ​this​ ​first​ ​chapter​ ​(Introduction),​ ​a​ ​brief​ ​account​ ​of​ ​the​ ​background​ ​and​ ​context​ ​that​
​justified​ ​the​ ​study​ ​has​ ​been​ ​presented.​ ​Following​ ​this,​ ​a​ ​more​ ​detailed​ ​explanation​ ​of​ ​the​
​study's aim, objectives, and significance were presented.​




                                                            ​14​
​In​ ​the​ ​following​ ​chapter​ ​(Chapter​ ​2),​ ​this​ ​thesis​ ​begins​ ​with​ ​a​ ​thorough​ ​literature​ ​review,​
​critically​ ​exploring​ ​existing​ ​research​ ​and​ ​studies.​ ​The​ ​literature​ ​review​ ​serves​ ​several​
​essential​ ​purposes.​ ​Firstly,​ ​it​ ​provides​ ​insights​ ​into​ ​the​ ​evolution​ ​of​ ​antisemitism,​ ​with​
​specific​​reference​​to​​sport,​​particularly​​football.​​Due​​to​​the​​overarching​​aim​​of​​this​​thesis,​​the​
​review​ ​also​ ​assesses​ ​the​ ​effectiveness​ ​of​ ​existing​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives​ ​in​ ​sports,​
​including​ ​well-known​ ​campaigns​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Stonewall's​ ​‘Rainbow​ ​Laces’​ ​(Hansen​ ​et​ ​al.​,​​2023;​
​Magrath​ ​and​ ​Stott,​​2019)​​and​​organisations,​​such​​as​​Kick​​It​​Out​​(Kilvington​​and​​Price,​​2017;​
​Penfold​ ​and​ ​Cleland,​ ​2022),​ ​identifying​ ​both​ ​best​​practices​​and​​areas​​where​​improvements​
​are​ ​needed.​ ​This​ ​chapter​ ​also​ ​plays​ ​a​ ​vital​ ​role​ ​in​ ​introducing​ ​the​ ​sociological​ ​theoretical​
​frameworks​ ​used​ ​throughout​ ​the​ ​research​ ​to​ ​inform​ ​and​ ​shape​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​the​
​project.​​These​​key​​theories​​include​​CRT​​(Delgado​​and​​Stefancic,​​2001),​​HebCrit​​(Rubin,​​2020),​
​and​ ​the​ ​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​model​ ​(Darley​ ​and​ ​Latané,​ ​1968).​ ​Ultimately,​ ​the​​literature​
​review​ ​serves​ ​as​ ​a​ ​crucial​ ​chapter​ ​in​ ​this​ ​project,​ ​providing​ ​the​ ​necessary​ ​foundation​ ​for​
​understanding​​the​​complex​​issues​​of​​antisemitism​​in​​football​​and​​for​​guiding​​the​​subsequent​
​development of an educational initiative.​

​Next,​ ​the​ ​methodology​ ​chapter​ ​(Chapter​ ​3)​ ​provides​ ​a​ ​detailed​ ​description​ ​of​ ​the​
​philosophical​ ​underpinnings,​ ​methodological​ ​framework,​​and​​ethical​​considerations​​guiding​
​this​ ​research​ ​project.​ ​A​ ​multi-method​​approach​​was​​undertaken,​​combining​​three​​methods​
​of​ ​data​ ​collection.​ ​Therefore,​ ​each​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​constituted​ ​a​ '​phase'​ ​in​ ​the​
​project.​​Additionally,​​the​​development​​of​​an​​educational​​initiative​​through​​CNF​​marked​​four​
​pivotal phases in this research, as outlined below:​

    ​●​ ​Phase 1: Interviews with anti-discrimination experts​
    ​●​ ​Phase 2: Creation of an educational resource through CNF​
    ​●​ ​Phase 3: Focus group interviews​
    ​●​ ​Phase 4: Expert book review​

​In​​Phase​​1,​​interviews​​were​​conducted​​with​​anti-discrimination​​experts​​who​​have​​previously​
​worked​ ​on​ ​and​ ​developed​ ​initiatives​ ​to​ ​eradicate​ ​discriminatory​ ​behaviours,​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​a​
​better​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​effective​ ​strategies​ ​and​ ​practices​ ​in​ ​combating​ ​discrimination.​​The​
​data​ ​provided​ ​a​ ​foundation​ ​for​​developing​​an​​initiative​​through​​CNF​​in​​Phase​​2.​​During​​this​
​process,​​an​​initial​​draft​​of​​the​​educational​​initiative,​​in​​the​​form​​of​​a​​book,​​was​​created.​​This​


                                                            ​15​
​initiative​ ​was​ ​then​ ​evaluated​ ​in​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​through​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​interviews​ ​with​ ​three​ ​key​
​stakeholders:​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​and​ ​school​
​educators.​ ​The​ ​feedback​ ​from​ ​these​ ​interviews​ ​allowed​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​to​ ​make​ ​necessary​
​amendments​​while​​evaluating​​the​​key​​strengths​​of​​the​​initiative.​​In​​the​​final​​phase​​(Phase​​4),​
​an​ ​expert​ ​book​ ​review​ ​was​ ​conducted​ ​with​ ​individuals​ ​from​ ​organisations​ ​specifically​
​working​​on​​antisemitism​​and/or​​Jewish​​education.​​This​​review​​provided​​further​​insights​​and​
​validation for the educational initiative.​

​Chapter​​3​​begins​​with​​a​​discussion​​of​​the​​overarching​​paradigm,​​philosophical​​positions,​​and​
​key​​ethical​​considerations​​guiding​​the​​entire​​project,​​before​​leading​​into​​the​​specific​​methods​
​employed​​in​​each​​phase.​​Due​​to​​the​​multi-phased​​nature​​of​​this​​project,​​each​​phase​​has​​its​
​own,​ ​unique​ ​discussion​ ​of​ ​its​ ​methods​ ​and​ ​procedures,​ ​leading​ ​into​ ​its​ ​own​ ​results​ ​and​
​discussion chapter.​

                         ​Phase​          ​Methodology​              ​Results and discussion​
                         ​Phase 1​        ​Chapter 4​                ​Chapter 5​
                         ​Phase 2​        ​Chapter 6​
                         ​Phase 3​        ​Chapter 7​                ​Chapter 8​
                         ​Phase 4​        ​Chapter 9​                ​Chapter 10​




​Table 1.​​Overview of phases, methodology, results​​and discussion.​


​As​ ​shown​ ​in​ ​Table​ ​1,​ ​the​ ​results​ ​of​ ​each​ ​phase​ ​are​ ​covered​ ​in​ ​separate​ ​chapters,​ ​each​
​concentrating​ ​on​ ​its​ ​unique​ ​outcomes​ ​and​ ​discussions.​ ​Each​ ​chapter​ ​presents​ ​its​ ​own​
​findings​​by​​introducing​​and​​analysing​​its​​individual​​themes​​and​​sub-themes​​identified​​during​
​the analysis, followed by a discussion of each theme.​


​In​​Chapter​​11​​(Conclusion),​​the​​researcher​​embarks​​on​​a​​reflective​​journey,​​offering​​a​​chance​
​to​ ​critically​ ​assess​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process​ ​and​ ​acknowledge​ ​the​ ​project's​ ​limitations,​ ​while​
​emphasising​ ​its​ ​key​ ​significance​ ​in​ ​advancing​ ​society's​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​
​sport.​ ​The​ ​main​ ​objectives​ ​of​ ​the​ ​study​ ​are​​revisited​​to​​ensure​​that​​the​​original​​goals​​were​
​met​ ​and​ ​achieved.​ ​Additionally,​ ​the​ ​chapter​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​encountered​ ​and​


                                                           ​16​
​discusses​ ​the​ ​strategies​ ​employed​ ​to​ ​overcome​ ​them.​ ​Next,​ ​the​ ​conclusion​ ​provides​ ​a​
​summary​ ​of​ ​the​ ​research​ ​findings,​ ​before​ ​recommendations​ ​for​ ​future​ ​practice​ ​are​
​suggested. Finally, the researcher provides a short personal reflection of their PhD journey.​


​Chapter summary​

​To​ ​conclude,​ ​this​ ​introduction​ ​chapter​ ​has​ ​presented​ ​the​​background​​and​​rationale​​for​​this​
​thesis,​ ​and​ ​has​ ​reinforced​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​this​ ​study​ ​in​ ​the​ ​field​​of​​sport​​sociology.​​This​
​research​ ​intends​ ​to​ ​advance​ ​scholarly​ ​literature​ ​and​ ​make​ ​an​ ​impact​ ​within​ ​the​ ​football​
​arena​ ​by​ ​providing​ ​an​ ​initiative​ ​which​ ​can​ ​be​ ​used​ ​to​ ​potentially​ ​decrease​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​
​society,​​and​​football​​most​​specifically.​​In​​addition,​​the​​introduction​​chapter​​outlines​​the​​aim​
​and​ ​research​ ​objectives​ ​for​ ​this​ ​thesis.​ ​Finally,​ ​after​ ​signposting​ ​the​​reader​​to​​key​​chapters​
​within​ ​the​ ​thesis,​ ​the​​project​​moves​​into​​Chapter​​2,​​the​​literature​​review,​​which​​aligns​​with​
​the​​research​​aim​​and​​objectives​​by​​offering​​a​​comprehensive​​discussion​​of​​existing​​research​
​and theoretical frameworks that are crucial to addressing the study's aim.​




                                                             ​17​
​Chapter 2 - Review of literature​


​Introduction​

​Antisemitism​​remains​​a​​persistent​​issue​​in​​societies​​worldwide,​​despite​​the​​rich​​history​​and​
​contributions​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​communities.​ ​Approximately​ ​15​ ​million​ ​Jews​ ​live​ ​globally,​ ​with​
​around​ ​300,000​ ​residing​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​​Kingdom,​​making​​up​​about​​0.5%​​of​​the​​population​
​(Board​ ​of​​Deputies,​​2020;​​Census,​​2021;​​Dart,​​2021).​​The​​Jewish​​presence​​in​​the​​UK​​dates​
​back​​to​​1070,​​establishing​​it​​as​​the​​world’s​​fifth-largest​​and​​Europe’s​​second-largest​​Jewish​
​community​ ​(Boyd​ ​and​ ​Staetsky,​ ​2014;​ ​World​ ​Jewish​​Congress,​​2019).​​However,​​Jews​​have​
​often​ ​faced​ ​hostility​ ​and​ ​discrimination,​ ​particularly​ ​in​ ​the​ ​aftermath​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Holocaust,​
​during which six million Jews perished across Nazi-occupied Europe.​

​The​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​is​ ​diverse,​ ​encompassing​ ​various​ ​cultural​ ​and​ ​religious​ ​practices​
​shaped​ ​by​ ​different​ ​movements​ ​and​ ​traditions.​ ​Judaism​ ​is​ ​one​ ​of​​the​​oldest​​religions​​still​
​practised​ ​today​ ​(Epstein,​ ​2013),​ ​with​ ​followers​ ​who​ ​may​ ​adhere​ ​strictly​ ​to​ ​religious​
​commandments​ ​or​ ​identify​ ​more​ ​loosely​ ​with​ ​their​ ​faith​ ​(Kahn-Harris,​ ​2018).​ ​The​
​community​​includes​​Ashkenazi​​Jews​​from​​Eastern​​Europe,​​Sephardic​​Jews​​from​​the​​Iberian​
​Peninsula,​ ​and​ ​Mizrahi​ ​Jews​ ​from​ ​the​ ​Middle​ ​East,​ ​each​ ​bringing​ ​unique​ ​customs​ ​and​
​beliefs (De Lange, 2000; Rubin, 2020).​

​However,​ ​this​ ​diversity​ ​can​ ​also​ ​make​ ​Jewish​ ​individuals​ ​targets​ ​for​ ​antisemitism,​
​particularly​​those​​who​​are​​visibly​​identifiable​​as​​Jewish,​​such​​as​​Orthodox​​Jews.​​A​​report​​by​
​the​ ​European​ ​Union​ ​Agency​ ​for​ ​Fundamental​ ​Rights​ ​(2018)​ ​indicates​ ​that​ ​Orthodox​​Jews​
​are​​most​​susceptible​​to​​discrimination​​and​​violence,​​as​​religious​​attire​​and​​symbols,​​such​​as​
​the​​Kippah,​​increase​​their​​visibility.​​Notably,​​incidents​​of​​antisemitic​​violence​​tend​​to​​spike​
​during​ ​religious​ ​observances​ ​when​ ​more​ ​visibly​ ​Jewish​ ​individuals​ ​are​ ​present​ ​in​ ​public​
​(European​ ​Union​ ​Agency​ ​for​ ​Fundamental​ ​Rights,​ ​2018).​ ​Consequently,​ ​60%​ ​of​ ​the​ ​UK​
​Jewish​ ​community​ ​reported​ ​avoiding​ ​the​ ​display​ ​of​​Jewish​​symbols​​to​​mitigate​​the​​risk​​of​
​antisemitism​​in​​their​​daily​​lives.​​This​​heightened​​vulnerability​​to​​antisemitism​​highlights​​the​
​importance​ ​of​ ​understanding​ ​the​ ​term​ ​itself,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​its​ ​historical​ ​and​ ​contemporary​
​implications.​




                                                          ​18​
​In​​the​​following​​review​​of​​literature,​​a​​deeper​​exploration​​into​​the​​topic​​of​​antisemitism​​will​
​take​ ​place,​​beginning​​with​​a​​discussion​​of​​the​​challenges​​associated​​with​​defining​​the​​term.​
​Next,​​the​​historical​​context​​and​​evolution​​of​​antisemitic​​beliefs​​and​​actions​​over​​time​​will​​be​
​presented,​ ​followed​ ​by​ ​an​ ​examination​ ​of​ ​contemporary​ ​manifestations​ ​and​ ​societal​
​attitudes​​towards​​antisemitism​​today.​​The​​unique​​challenges​​faced​​within​​the​​realm​​of​​sports​
​will​​be​​addressed,​​including​​specific​​terms​​and​​behaviours​​that​​contribute​​to​​discrimination.​
​Alongside​​this,​​the​​transformative​​power​​that​​sport​​has​​will​​be​​discussed,​​then​​leading​​into​​a​
​discussion​ ​regarding​ ​current​ ​strategies​ ​and​ ​initiatives​ ​being​ ​used​ ​within​ ​sport,​ ​mainly​
​football,​ ​which​ ​are​ ​aimed​ ​at​ ​combating​ ​prejudice,​ ​with,​ ​at​ ​times,​ ​a​ ​specific​ ​focus​ ​on​
​antisemitism​​in​​football.​​The​​chapter​​will​​introduce​​several​​theoretical​​approaches,​​including​
​CRT,​​HebCrit,​​and​​the​​bystander​​intervention​​model.​​In​​addition​​to​​examining​​these​​theories,​
​their​​critiques​​will​​be​​analysed​​to​​emphasise​​both​​their​​strengths​​and​​weaknesses​​in​​practice.​
​Through​ ​this​ ​structure,​ ​the​ ​review​ ​of​ ​literature​ ​chapter​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​comprehensive​
​understanding​ ​of​ ​antisemitism,​ ​the​ ​ongoing​ ​efforts​ ​sports​ ​are​ ​making​ ​to​ ​combat​
​discriminatory​ ​behaviours​ ​and​ ​appropriate​ ​theoretical​ ​models​ ​which​ ​could​ ​be​ ​used​ ​to​
​address and challenge antisemitism in football.​

​Antisemitism​


​Antisemitism​ ​is​ ​a​ ​concept​ ​that​ ​has​ ​caused​ ​and​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​generate​ ​significant​
​misunderstanding​ ​(Beller,​ ​2015).​ ​As​ ​stated​ ​by​ ​Stratton​ ​(2015,​ ​p.​ ​295)​ ​“antisemitism​ ​is​ ​a​
​fraught​​term​​and​​one​​difficult​​to​​define.”​​The​​debate​​surrounding​​antisemitism​​definitions​​is​
​not​ ​merely​ ​academic​ ​(Langmuir,​ ​1996;​ ​Marcus,​ ​2013;​ ​Meer,​ ​2014);​ ​it​ ​has​ ​real-world​
​implications​​for​​combating​​hate​​crimes​​and​​protecting​​freedom​​of​​expression​​(Shanes,​​2022).​
​Therefore,​​it​​is​​crucial​​to​​provide​​an​​effective​​definition.​​The​​term​​antisemitism​​was​​coined​​in​
​1873​ ​by​ ​the​ ​German​ ​nationalist​ ​Wilhelm​ ​Marr,​ ​who​ ​claimed​ ​that​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​
​sought​ ​to​ ​overrun​ ​society​ ​and​ ​corrupt​ ​the​ ​German​ ​nation​ ​(Fine​ ​and​ ​Spencer,​ ​2017).​ ​This​
​historical​ ​perspective​ ​is​ ​significant​ ​to​ ​discuss​ ​as​ ​it​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​origins​ ​of​ ​antisemitic​
​ideology as not just a prejudice, but a tool used to encourage discrimination and hatred.​


​In​ ​contrast,​ ​contemporary​ ​definitions​ ​aim​ ​to​ ​capture​ ​the​ ​essence​ ​of​ ​this​ ​bias​ ​in​ ​simpler​
​terms.​​For​​instance,​​the​​Oxford​​Dictionary​​offers​​a​​simple​​definition,​​defining​​antisemitism​​as​



                                                           ​19​
​“discrimination​ ​against​ ​Jews”​ ​(Collins,​ ​2005,​ ​p.​ ​24).​ ​Another​ ​short,​ ​yet​ ​simple​ ​definition​
​comes​​from​​Meer​​(2014,​​p.​​8),​​who​​defines​​antisemitism​​as​​“the​​suspicion,​​dislike​​or​​hatred​
​of​ ​Jewish​ ​individuals​ ​or​ ​groups”.​ ​Although​ ​these​ ​definitions​ ​are​ ​straightforward​ ​to​
​understand,​ ​they​ ​are​ ​both​ ​limited​ ​and​ ​as​ ​Neuberger​ ​(2019)​ ​suggests,​ ​although​ ​these​
​definitions​​are​​adequate,​​they​​do​​not​​help​​us​​recognise​​and​​understand​​antisemitism​​in​​all​​its​
​numerous​ ​and​ ​diverse​ ​forms.​ ​This​ ​complexity​ ​necessitates​ ​a​ ​deeper​ ​exploration​ ​of​
​antisemitism's​ ​varied​ ​manifestations,​ ​which​ ​extend​ ​beyond​ ​simple​ ​definitions​ ​to​ ​include​
​broader societal and historical dimensions.​

​Antisemitism​ ​is​ ​a​ ​complex​ ​and​ ​multifaceted​ ​form​ ​of​ ​prejudice​ ​(Maizels,​ ​2022),​ ​making​ ​it​
​essential​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​clear​ ​examples​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​its​ ​various​ ​manifestations.​ ​Antisemitism​
​refers​ ​to​ ​negative​ ​ideas​ ​about​ ​Jews​ ​expressed​ ​through​ ​language,​ ​themes,​ ​or​ ​imagery​​(CST,​
​2013).​ ​It​​takes​​many​​forms,​​including​​beliefs​​that​​Jews​​are​​excessively​​powerful,​​wealthy,​​or​
​part​ ​of​ ​the​ ​capitalist​ ​oppressor​ ​class​ ​(Neuberger,​ ​2019;​ ​Poulton,​ ​2021).​ ​This​ ​also​ ​includes​
​myths​ ​of​ ​a​ ​global​ ​Jewish​ ​conspiracy​ ​and​ ​assertions​ ​that​ ​Jews​ ​control​ ​the​​media,​​economy,​
​government,​ ​or​ ​other​ ​societal​ ​institutions​ ​(Poulton,​ ​2020).​ ​Additionally,​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community​ ​has​ ​faced​ ​mockery​​based​​on​​physical​​appearance,​​customs,​​and​​beliefs.​​Victims​
​of​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​have​ ​endured​ ​verbal​ ​and​ ​physical​ ​attacks,​ ​both​ ​individually​ ​and​ ​as​ ​a​
​group​ ​(Boyd​ ​and​ ​Staetsky,​​2014).​​These​​examples​​help​​clarify​​what​​behaviours,​​statements,​
​and​​beliefs​​are​​deemed​​to​​be​​antisemitic,​​illustrating​​the​​nuances​​of​​the​​term​​and​​making​​it​
​easier to grasp.​

​A​​key​​discussion​​in​​academic​​and​​public​​discourse​​is​​whether​​antisemitism​​should​​be​​treated​
​as​​distinct​​from,​​or​​a​​subset​​of,​​racism.​​Yuval-Davis​​(2024)​​argues​​for​​an​​inclusive​​definition​​of​
​racism​ ​that​ ​includes​ ​antisemitism​ ​while​ ​recognising​ ​its​ ​unique​ ​features,​​such​​as​​conspiracy​
​theories;​ ​a​ ​view​ ​echoed​ ​in​ ​her​ ​earlier​ ​work​ ​(2020)​ ​linking​ ​antisemitism,​ ​Zionism,​ ​and​
​anti-racism.​ ​Fox​ ​and​ ​Toper​ ​(2021)​ ​also​ ​highlight​ ​how​ ​conspiracy​ ​theories​ ​are​ ​a​ ​key​ ​part​ ​of​
​antisemitism,​​setting​​it​​apart​​from​​other​​forms​​of​​racism​​that​​often​​focus​​more​​on​​physical​​or​
​cultural​​differences.​​McGeever​​(2022)​​adds​​that​​antisemitism​​is​​often​​overlooked​​because​​it​
​doesn’t​ ​align​ ​with​ ​dominant​ ​frameworks​ ​of​ ​racism,​ ​especially​ ​those​ ​shaped​ ​by​ ​colonial​
​histories,​ ​colour-based​ ​discrimination,​ ​and​ ​structural​ ​inequalities​ ​typically​ ​associated​ ​with​
​anti-Black​​or​​anti-Muslim​​racism.​​Arnold​​and​​Taylor​​(2019)​​make​​a​​similar​​point,​​arguing​​that​
​ignoring​​antisemitism​​in​​these​​spaces​​weakens​​the​​wider​​fight​​against​​racism.​​Together,​​these​


                                                            ​20​
​views​​show​​the​​need​​to​​include​​antisemitism​​in​​anti-racist​​work,​​while​​also​​recognising​​that​​it​
​has some unique features.​

​Nevertheless,​ ​understanding​ ​antisemitism​ ​requires​ ​awareness​ ​of​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​communities'​​attitudes​​towards​​examples​​of​​antisemitism.​​Therefore,​​in​​Boyd​​and​​Staetsky's​
​(2014)​ ​research,​ ​Jewish​ ​participants​ ​were​ ​presented​ ​with​ ​fourteen​ ​statements​ ​and​ ​were​
​asked​ ​which​ ​they​ ​considered​ ​to​ ​be​ ​antisemitic;​​80%​​believed​​that​​comments​​regarding​​the​
​Holocaust,​ ​suggesting​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​a​ ​myth​ ​or​ ​exaggerated,​ ​were​ ​thought​ ​to​ ​be​ ​antisemitic.​
​Likewise,​ ​77%​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​thought​ ​that​ ​comments​ ​stating​ ​that​ ​Jews​ ​are​
​responsible​ ​for​ ​the​ ​current​ ​economic​ ​crisis​ ​were​ ​also​ ​antisemitic.​ ​This​ ​research​​found​​that​
​attitudes​​differed​​based​​on​​age,​​location,​​and​​Jewish​​movement. The​​variation​​in​​perceptions​
​across​ ​different​ ​segments​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​complexities​ ​in​ ​defining​
​and​ ​addressing​ ​antisemitism,​ ​pointing​ ​to​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​further​ ​investigation​ ​on​ ​both​ ​an​
​individual and a structural level.​

​In​ ​2016,​ ​the​ ​International​ ​Holocaust​ ​Remembrance​ ​Alliance​ ​developed​ ​the​ ​following​
​‘non-legally​ ​binding, working’​ ​definition​ ​of​ ​antisemitism.​ ​For​ ​the​ ​purpose​ ​of​ ​this​ ​research,​
​antisemitism will be defined as the following:​


       ​“a​ ​certain​ ​perception​ ​of​ ​Jews,​ ​which​ ​may​ ​be​ ​expressed​ ​as​ ​hatred​​toward​​Jews.​
       ​Rhetorical​ ​and​ ​physical​ ​manifestations​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​are​ ​directed​ ​toward​
       ​Jewish​ ​or​ ​non-Jewish​ ​individuals​ ​and/or​ ​their​ ​property,​ ​toward​ ​Jewish​
       ​community institutions and religious facilities.” (IHRA, 2016, p.1) ​


​The​ ​rationale​ ​for​ ​this​ ​selection​ ​is​ ​that​ ​the IHRA​ ​(2016)​ ​definition​ ​is​ ​the​ ​most​ ​utilised​
​definition.​ ​The​ ​IHRA​ ​definition​ ​has​ ​been​ ​adopted​ ​in​ ​113​ ​university​ ​establishments​ ​(UJS,​
​2023),​​43​​different​​countries​​(IHRA,​​2024),​​including​​the​​United​​Kingdom,​​more​​than​​130​​UK​
​local​​councils,​​the​​police​​and​​the​​Crown​​Prosecution​​Service​​(Gould,​​2020).​​Most​​specifically,​
​in​ ​December​ ​2020,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​announced​ ​that​ ​the​​English​​Premier​​League,​​along​​with​​19​​of​​its​
​clubs​ ​implemented​ ​the​ ​IHRA​ ​definition,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​will​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​football​ ​is​ ​welcoming​ ​for​ ​all.​
​These​ ​are​ ​the​ ​most​ ​recent​ ​figures​ ​provided​ ​by​ ​the​ ​Premier​ ​League,​ ​however,​ ​in​ ​2021,​ ​the​
​English​ ​Football​​League,​​who​​represent​​72​​clubs​​beneath​​the​​Premier​​League,​​also​​adopted​



                                                             ​21​
​this​​definition​​(Gibbons,​​2021).​ ​By​​utilising​​the​​definition,​​it​​is​​hoped​​that​​clubs​​will​​be​​more​
​knowledgeable​ ​when​ ​training​ ​fans,​ ​stewards​​and​​employees​​in​​how​​to​​identify​​and​​combat​
​antisemitic abuse (​Harpin​, 2020).​


​Whilst​ ​this​ ​definition​ ​has​ ​been​ ​widely​ ​adopted,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​essential​​to​​understand​​the​​real-world​
​implications​​of​​its​​use;​​therefore,​​alongside​​the​​definition,​​there​​are​​also​​eleven​​examples​​of​
​what they deem to be antisemitic, including:​


        ​1.​ ​Calling​​for,​​aiding,​​or​​justifying​​the​​killing​​or​​harming​​of​​Jews​​in​​the​​name​​of​​a​
            ​radical ideology or an extremist view of religion.​
        ​2.​ ​Making​​mendacious,​​dehumanising,​​demonising,​​or​​stereotypical​​allegations​
            ​about​​Jews​​as​​such​​or​​the​​power​​of​​Jews​​as​​a​​collective​​—​​such​​as,​​especially​
            ​but​ ​not​ ​exclusively,​ ​the​ ​myth​ ​about​ ​a​ ​world​ ​Jewish​ ​conspiracy​ ​or​ ​of​ ​Jews​
            ​controlling the media, economy, government or other societal institutions.​
        ​3.​ ​Accusing​ ​Jews​ ​as​ ​a​ ​people​ ​of​ ​being​ ​responsible​ ​for​ ​real​ ​or​ ​imagined​
            ​wrongdoing​ ​committed​ ​by​ ​a​​single​​Jewish​​person​​or​​group,​​or​​even​​for​​acts​
            ​committed by non-Jews.​
        ​4.​ ​Denying​​the​​fact,​​scope,​​mechanisms​​(e.g.​​gas​​chambers)​​or​​intentionality​​of​
            ​the​​genocide​​of​​the​​Jewish​​people​​at​​the​​hands​​of​​National​​Socialist​​Germany​
            ​and its supporters and accomplices during World War II (the Holocaust).​
        ​5.​ ​Accusing​ ​the​ ​Jews​ ​as​ ​a​ ​people,​ ​or​ ​Israel​ ​as​ ​a​ ​state,​ ​of​ ​inventing​ ​or​
            ​exaggerating the Holocaust.​
        ​6.​ ​Accusing​ ​Jewish​ ​citizens​ ​of​ ​being​ ​more​ ​loyal​ ​to​ ​Israel,​ ​or​ ​to​ ​the​ ​alleged​
            ​priorities of Jews worldwide, than to the interests of their own nations.​
        ​7.​ ​Denying​​the​​Jewish​​people​​their​​right​​to​​self-determination,​​e.g.,​​by​​claiming​
            ​that the existence of a State of Israel is a racist endeavour.​
        ​8.​ ​Applying​ ​double​ ​standards​ ​by​ ​requiring​ ​of​ ​it​ ​a​ ​behaviour​ ​not​ ​expected​ ​or​
            ​demanded of any other democratic nation.​
        ​9.​ ​Using​ ​the​ ​symbols​ ​and​ ​images​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​classic​ ​antisemitism​ ​(e.g.,​
            ​claims of Jews killing Jesus or blood libel) to characterise Israel or Israelis.​
        ​10.​​Drawing comparisons of contemporary Israeli policy to that of the Nazis.​



                                                            ​22​
        ​11.​​Holding Jews collectively responsible for actions of the state of Israel.​


​However,​ ​despite​ ​its​ ​widespread​ ​adoption,​ ​the​ ​IHRA​ ​definition​ ​is​ ​not​ ​without​ ​controversy,​
​with​ ​critics​ ​raising​ ​concerns​ ​about​ ​its​ ​implications​ ​for​ ​free​ ​speech​ ​and​ ​political​ ​discourse​
​(Gould,​​2018).​​Additionally,​​criticisms​​of​​the​​definition​​include​​how​​it​​is​​extremely​​difficult​​to​
​examine​ ​which​ ​actions,​ ​language​ ​and​ ​discourse​ ​are​ ​captured​ ​by​ ​the​ ​term​ ​and​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​
​inconsistent,​ ​contradictory,​ ​and​ ​vaguely​ ​formulated​ ​(Deckers​ ​and​ ​Coulter,​ ​2022;​ ​Ullrich,​
​2019).​ ​Deckers​ ​and​ ​Coulter​ ​(2022)​ ​critique​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​terms​ ​‘perception’​ ​and​ ​‘may’,​
​arguing​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​imprecise​ ​and​ ​leaves​ ​questions​ ​open​ ​to​ ​whether​ ​antisemitism​ ​can​ ​be​
​expressed​ ​in​ ​different​ ​ways.​ ​Further,​ ​criticisms​ ​reflect​ ​broader​ ​concerns​ ​about​ ​how​
​antisemitism​ ​is​ ​defined​ ​and​ ​addressed,​ ​particularly​ ​in​ ​relation​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​
​conflict.​​Some​​organisations,​​such​​as​​University​​College​​London​​(UCL),​​Amnesty​​International​
​and​ ​the​ ​Labour​ ​Party,​ ​have​ ​rejected​ ​portions​ ​of​ ​the​ ​eleven​ ​examples​ ​deemed​ ​antisemitic​
​specifically​ ​in​ ​relation​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​ ​conflict.​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​the​ ​Labour​ ​Party​
​opposed​ ​two​ ​examples,​ ​numbers​ ​seven​ ​and​ ​ten,​ ​stating​ ​that​ ​these​ ​actions​ ​are​ ​not​
​antisemitic “unless there is evidence of antisemitic intent” (Sugarman, 2018, p. 1).​


​Furthermore,​​literature​​from​​Deckers​​and​​Coulter​​(2022)​​noted​​that​​while​​the​​IHRA​​definition​
​is​​well-intentioned​​in​​combating​​hatred​​against​​Jews,​​it​​may​​have​​unintended​​consequences​
​for​ ​political​ ​discourse,​ ​particularly​ ​concerning​ ​the​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​ ​conflict.​ ​Of​ ​the​ ​11​
​examples,​​six​​specifically​​focus​​on​​the​​State​​of​​Israel;​​therefore,​​the​​majority​​of​​the​​concerns​
​surrounding​ ​the​ ​definition​ ​have​ ​been​ ​made​ ​regarding​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​the​​Israeli-Palestinian​
​conflict.​​The​​Israeli-Palestinian​​conflict​​is​​a​​complex​​and​​longstanding​​dispute​​primarily​​about​
​land,​ ​opposing​ ​historical​ ​narratives​ ​and​ ​national​ ​identity​ ​between​ ​Israelis​ ​and​ ​Palestinians​
​(Moore​​and​​Guy,​​2012;​​Twite,​​2009).​​When​​conflicts​​arise​​between​​Israelis​​and​​Palestinians,​
​there​ ​tends​ ​to​ ​be​ ​an​ ​increase​ ​in​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​(Boyd​ ​and​ ​Staetsky,​ ​2015).​
​Nevertheless,​ ​some​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​the​ ​IHRA​ ​definition​ ​has​ ​been​ ​misused​ ​to​ ​label​ ​criticism​ ​of​
​Israel​​as​​antisemitic,​​while​​others​​claim​​it​​serves​​to​​protect​​Israel​​from​​international​​scrutiny​
​and​ ​accountability​ ​(Deckers​ ​and​ ​Coulter,​ ​2022;​ ​Gordon,​ ​2024).​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​Gould​ ​(2018;​
​2020)​ ​believes​ ​that​ ​they​ ​have​ ​been​ ​to​ ​be​ ​written​ ​in​ ​an​​approximate manner​​that​​could​​be​
​damaging to freedom of speech.​




                                                           ​23​
​The​ ​complexities​ ​around​ ​this​ ​issue​ ​are​ ​reflected​ ​in​ ​the​ ​IHRA​ ​definition,​ ​which​ ​asserts​ ​that​
​holding​​Jews​​collectively​​responsible​​for​​the​​actions​​of​​Israel​​is​​antisemitic.​​This​​highlights​​the​
​broader​ ​and​ ​ongoing​ ​debate​ ​about​ ​whether​ ​anti-Zionism,​ ​or​ ​criticism​ ​of​ ​Israel​ ​as​ ​a​ ​state,​
​crosses​ ​into​​antisemitism​​(Hargreaves​​and​​Staetsky,​​2020;​​Judaken,​​2023;​​Kaplan​​and​​Small,​
​2006;​ ​Staesky,​ ​2017).​ ​Scholars​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Goldberg​ ​and​ ​Durkheim​ ​(2008)​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​while​
​antisemitism​​and​​anti-Zionism​​are​​not​​synonymous,​​there​​is​​some​​overlap.​​This​​is​​particularly​
​evident​​in​​the​​concept​​of​​‘new​​antisemitism,’​​which​​scholars​​such​​as​​Klug​​(2003),​​Kaplan​​and​
​Small​ ​(2006),​ ​and​ ​Stratton​ ​(2015)​ ​describe​ ​as​ ​hostility​ ​directed​ ​at​ ​Jews​ ​based​ ​on​ ​their​
​perceived​​association​​with​​Israel.​​Given​​this​​complexity,​​it​​is​​important​​to​​recognise​​that​​not​
​all​ ​Jews​ ​identify​ ​as​ ​Zionists​ ​or​ ​see​ ​the​ ​support​ ​of​ ​Israel​ ​as​ ​central​ ​to​ ​their​ ​Jewish​ ​identity​
​(Baddiel,​ ​2021).​ ​Therefore,​ ​equating​ ​all​ ​Jews​ ​with​ ​the​ ​actions​ ​of​ ​Israel​ ​not​ ​only​ ​risks​
​reinforcing​ ​harmful​ ​stereotypes​ ​but​ ​also​ ​ignores​ ​the​ ​diversity​ ​within​ ​Jewish​ ​communities​
​worldwide.​​Although​​this​​research​​solely​​focuses​​on​​antisemitism,​​broader​​discussions​​about​
​the​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​ ​conflict​ ​and​ ​its​ ​influence​ ​on​ ​contemporary​ ​antisemitism​ ​will​ ​also​ ​be​
​addressed​​later,​​in​​connection​​with​​both​​the​​historical​​roots​​of​​antisemitism​​and​​the​​current​
​issues shaping the project's development.​

​Antisemitism: historical and contemporary events​

​Antisemitism​ ​has​ ​often​ ​been​ ​referred​ ​to​ ​as​ ​‘the​ ​longest​ ​hatred’​ ​(Beller,​ ​2015;​ ​Neuberger,​
​2019),​ ​as​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​have​ ​faced​ ​discrimination​ ​and​ ​unfair​
​misjudgement​​for​​centuries​​(Goldberg​​and​​Durkheim,​​2008).​​Bergmann​​(1992)​​suggests​​that​
​the​ ​history​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​began​ ​in​ ​biblical​ ​times,​ ​when​ ​there​ ​were​ ​only​ ​three​ ​major​
​religions,​ ​Judaism,​ ​Christianity,​ ​and​ ​Islam.​ ​Antisemitism​ ​emerged​ ​as​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​religious​
​rivalry​ ​between​ ​Christianity​ ​and​ ​Judaism.​ ​Later,​ ​in​ ​the​ ​first​ ​half​ ​of​ ​the​ ​20th​ ​century,​ ​Jews​
​were​ ​discriminated​ ​against​ ​in​​Britain​​on​​social​​and​​cultural​​levels,​​rather​​than​​political​​ones​
​(Endelman,​ ​2002).​​For​​example,​​they​​were​​denied​​access​​to​​clubs,​​shops,​​and​​schools​​(Dee,​
​2011;​​Neuberger,​​2019)​​and​​were​​discriminated​​against.​​Discrimination​​also​​occurred​​within​
​the workplace, forcing Jews to create businesses for themselves (Rubin, 2020; Weber, 1991).​


​The​ ​most​ ​significant​ ​instance​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​occurred​ ​during​ ​the​ ​Holocaust​ ​(1941-1945),​
​following​ ​Adolf​ ​Hitler's​ ​ascent​ ​to​ ​power​ ​in​ ​Germany,​ ​when​ ​six​ ​million​ ​Jews​ ​were​



                                                                 ​24​
​systematically​ ​murdered.​ ​Once​ ​in​ ​power,​ ​Hitler​ ​and​ ​the​ ​Nazis​ ​attempted​ ​to​ ​implement​
​antisemitic​ ​policies​ ​and​ ​discriminatory​ ​legislations​ ​which​ ​segregated​ ​the​ ​Jews​ ​from​ ​the​
​Germans.​​His​​laws​​forced​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community​​out​​of​​professions,​​persuading​
​the​​rest​​of​​the​​country​​to​​avoid​​buying​​into​​their​​business​​and​​started​​to​​restrict​​them​​from​
​their​ ​rights​ ​(Feldman​ ​and​ ​Seibel,​ ​2005).​ ​During​ ​World​ ​War​ ​Two,​ ​a​ ​deliberate​ ​attempt​ ​to​
​murder​ ​every​ ​Jewish​ ​person​ ​in​ ​Europe​ ​was​ ​made​ ​by​ ​Hitler​ ​and​ ​Nazi​​Germany​​(Finkelstein,​
​2003;​ ​Prager​ ​and​ ​Telushkin,​ ​2016).​ ​Although​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​population​ ​of​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​was​ ​largely​
​unaffected​ ​by​ ​the​ ​Holocaust,​ ​Hitler’s​ ​beliefs​ ​continued​ ​to​ ​influence​ ​some​ ​individuals'​
​attitudes,​​encouraging​​lingering​​hostility​​toward​​the​​Jewish​​community​​in​​the​​UK.​​Therefore,​
​in​ ​the​ ​first​ ​half​ ​of​ ​the​ ​twentieth​ ​century,​ ​Jews​ ​undoubtedly​ ​still​ ​encountered​ ​antisemitic​
​intolerance and bigotry due to the Holocaust (Boyd and Staetsky, 2014).​


​Laqueur​ ​(2006,​ ​p.​ ​207)​​states​​that​​“antisemitism​​is​​a​​historical​​topic,​​but​​because​​it​​has​​not​
​yet​​ended,​​it​​is​​not​​solely​​of​​historical​​interest”,​​highlighting​​that​​while​​antisemitism​​has​​deep​
​historical​ ​roots,​ ​discriminatory​ ​behaviours​ ​and​ ​actions​ ​against​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​
​continue​ ​to​ ​persist​ ​today.​ ​Recent​ ​research​ ​from​ ​the​ ​Anti-Defamation​ ​League​ ​(2019)​ ​found​
​that​​antisemitism​​is​​seen​​on​​a​​worldwide​​level,​​with​​26%​​of​​the​​world’s​​population​​admitting​
​they​​harbour​​antisemitic​​views.​​In​​the​​US,​​Jewish​​people​​are​​considered​​the​​largest​​group​​of​
​religious​ ​hate-crime​ ​victims​ ​(Federal​ ​Bureau​ ​of​ ​Investigation,​ ​2019).​ ​Boyd​ ​and​ ​Staetsky​
​(2015)​​recognise​​that​​in​​other​​European​​countries,​​including​​Germany,​​Hungary​​and​​Poland,​
​antisemitic​​abuse​​and​​attacks​​are​​more​​common​​and​​are​​usually​​significantly​​worse​​than​​the​
​UK. ​​Research​​by​​the​​European​​Union​​Agency​​for​​Fundamental​​Rights​​(2018)​​found​​that​​89%​
​of​​Jewish​​populations​​in​​the​​EU​​felt​​that​​antisemitism​​had​​increased​​over​​the​​past​​five​​years,​
​and​ ​85%​ ​believe​ ​it​ ​is​ ​a​ ​serious​ ​problem.​ ​Additionally,​ ​with​ ​25%​ ​of​ ​Europeans​ ​holding​
​antisemitic​ ​attitudes​ ​(Anti-Defamation​ ​League,​ ​2019),​ ​it​ ​is​ ​clear​ ​that​​antisemitism​​is​​still​​an​
​issue, impacting the lives of the Jewish community today.​


​Focusing​​on​​Britain,​​research​​shows​​that​​a​​quarter​​of​​the​​British​​population​​admit​​to​​holding​
​antisemitic​ ​thoughts​ ​(May,​ ​2017;​ ​Sherwood,​ ​2019).​ ​Additionally,​​75%​​of​​the​​population​​are​
​concerned​​that​​antisemitism​​is​​either​​a​​very​​big​​problem​​or​​a​​fairly​​big​​problem,​​while​​88%​​of​
​Jewish​ ​respondents​ ​believe​ ​that​​antisemitism​​has​​increased​​in​​the​​past​​five​​years​​in​​the​​UK​
​(European​ ​Union​ ​Agency​ ​for​ ​Fundamental​ ​Rights,​ ​2018).​ ​In​ ​2019,​ ​the​ ​CST,​ ​an​ ​organisation​


                                                           ​25​
​whose​ ​work​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​tackle​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​to​ ​protect​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​found​​that​
​with​ ​1,813​ ​reports​ ​of​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse,​ ​they​ ​had​ ​the​ ​most​ ​reported​ ​incidents​ ​of​
​antisemitism​​(CST,​​2020).​​However,​​these​​figures​​continued​​to​​rise​​as​​in​​2024,​​the​​CST​​(2024)​
​reported​​1,978​​antisemitic​​instances​​across​​the​​UK​​in​​the​​first​​six​​months​​of​​the​​year;​​which​
​is​​its​​highest​​January-to-June​​total​​ever​​reported.​​It​​should​​be​​considered​​that​​although​​this​
​figure​​is​​the​​highest​​it​​has​​been,​​it​​may​​be​​due​​to​​the​​population​​being​​more​​knowledgeable​
​on​​how​​to​​report​​such​​crimes.​​Nevertheless,​​the​​most​​recent​​figure​​reflects​​a​​significant​​spike​
​in​ ​antisemitic​ ​incidents,​ ​particularly​ ​following​ ​the​ ​attacks​ ​in​ ​Israel​ ​on​ ​October​ ​7th​ ​2023,​
​which​ ​heightened​ ​existing​ ​tensions​ ​and​ ​led​ ​to​ ​a​ ​surge​ ​in​ ​hate​ ​crimes​ ​against​ ​Jewish​
​communities across the UK.​


​Furthermore,​​Boyd​​and​​Staesky​​(2015)​​express​​that​​spikes​​in​​antisemitic​​incidents​​within​​the​
​UK​ ​usually​ ​arise​ ​when​ ​conflicts​ ​occur​ ​in​ ​Israel,​ ​this​ ​may​ ​be​ ​as​ ​Jews​ ​are​ ​perceived​ ​to​ ​be​
​representatives​ ​of​ ​Israel​ ​(CST, ​2018​;​ ​Stratton,​ ​2015).​ ​Jacobs​ ​et​ ​al​.​ ​(2011)​ ​explored​ ​the​
​correlation​​between​​Israel-Palestine​​conflicts​​and​​the​​rise​​in​​antisemitic​​incidents​​in​​Belgium.​
​Research​ ​found​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​increase​ ​in​ ​antisemitic​ ​incidents​ ​when​ ​conflicts​ ​occur,​
​supporting​​the​​belief​​that​​antisemitism​​is​​influenced​​by​​political​​events​​related​​to​​Israel.​​Caro​
​(2015,​ ​p.​ ​304)​ ​supports​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that​ ​“antisemitism​ ​appears​ ​related​ ​largely,​ ​though​ ​not​
​exclusively,​ ​with​ ​the​ ​Israeli​ ​Palestinian​ ​conflict,​ ​showing​ ​that​ ​much​ ​of​ ​the​ ​antisemitic​
​incidents​ ​recorded​ ​in​ ​the​ ​last​ ​decade​ ​and​ ​a​ ​half​ ​are​ ​linked​ ​to​ ​the​​Palestinian​​cause”.​​Most​
​recently​ ​in​ ​2021,​ ​the​ ​CST​ ​(2021)​ ​discovered​​a​​500%​​spike​​in​​antisemitic​​incidents​​in​​the​​UK​
​between​ ​the​ ​8th​ ​and​ ​18th​ ​of​ ​May,​ ​when​ ​violence​ ​between​ ​Israelis​ ​and​ ​Palestinians​
​increased.​​Likewise,​​the​​CST​​(2024)​​reported​​that​​since​​October​​7th​​2023,​​incidents​​between​
​then and September 2024 were the highest they had reported in a 12-month period.​

​Supporting​ ​research​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​when​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​military​ ​operation​ ​involving​
​Israel,​​and​​when​​conflicts​​are​​greater​​in​​the​​Middle​​East,​​antisemitic​​abuse​​has​​been​​seen​​to​
​increase​ ​(CST,​​2018;​​UK​​Parliament,​​2023).​​This​​correlation​​between​​geopolitical​​events​​and​
​antisemitic​​incidents​​underscores​​the​​intricate​​relationship​​between​​global​​conflicts​​and​​local​
​expressions​ ​of​ ​prejudice,​ ​warranting​​further​​exploration.​​It​​has​​been​​recognised​​by​​Stratton​
​(2015),​ ​Jacobs​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2011)​ ​and​ ​the​ ​CST​ ​(2018)​ ​that​ ​the​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​ ​conflict​ ​has​ ​a​
​significant​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​antisemitic​​incidents,​​the​​relationship​​between​​the​​two​​has​​been​​well​


                                                             ​26​
​discussed​​by​​scholars,​​including​​Beattie​​(2016),​​Kaplan​​and​​Small​​(2006)​​and​​Staetsky​​(2017).​
​Whilst​​the​​focus​​of​​this​​project​​is​​on​​antisemitism​​within​​Britain,​​it​​has​​been​​noted​​that​​there​
​is​ ​a​ ​positive​ ​correlation​ ​between​ ​the​​Israeli-Palestinian​​conflict​​and​​antisemitism​​which​​can​
​have​​influencing​​factors​​(Boyd​​and​​Staetsky,​​2015).​​Ultimately,​​understanding​​antisemitism​​in​
​its​​modern​​forms​​requires​​navigating​​the​​complex​​intersections​​of​​politics,​​historical​​context,​
​and​​the​​evolving​​nature​​of​​discrimination.​​In​​relation​​to​​this​​research,​​it​​is​​also​​important​​to​
​note​ ​that​ ​the​ ​recent​ ​rise​ ​(since​ ​October​ ​7th,​ ​2023)​ ​in​ ​conflict​ ​between​ ​Israelis​ ​and​
​Palestinians,​ ​had​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​the​ ​final​ ​stages​ ​of​ ​this​ ​project,​ ​which​ ​will​ ​be​
​discussed in detail later on in Chapter 9.​

​Debates​ ​about​ ​antisemitism​ ​within​ ​mainstream​ ​political​ ​parties​ ​became​ ​a​ ​central​ ​focus​ ​of​
​political​​discourse​​in​​Britain​​(Gidley,​​McGeever​​and​​Feldman,​​2020;​​Hargreaves​​and​​Staetsky,​
​2020).​ ​Surges​ ​in​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​may​ ​have​ ​been​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​​contemporary​​issues​​such​​as​
​antisemitic​​allegations​​and​​claims​​within​​the​​Labour​​Party​​(CST,​​2020;​​Rich,​​2016).​​Reports​​of​
​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​from​ ​the​ ​CST​ ​(2020)​ ​found​ ​that​ ​224​ ​of​ ​the​ ​1,805​ ​cases​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​
​were​ ​related​ ​to​​the​​Labour​​Party.​​In​​May​​2019,​​the​​Equality​​and​​Human​​Rights​​Commission​
​(EHRC)​​launched​​an​​investigation​​into​​unlawful​​acts​​of​​antisemitism,​​including​​discrimination​
​and​ ​harassment,​ ​within​ ​the​ ​Labour​ ​Party​ ​during​ ​Jeremy​ ​Corbyn's​ ​leadership​ ​(BBC,​ ​2020a).​
​The​ ​investigation​ ​was​ ​prompted​ ​by​ ​rising​ ​public​ ​apprehension​ ​concerning​ ​antisemitism​
​within​​the​​Labour​​Party,​​alongside​​official​​complaints​​received​​by​​the​​EHRC​​(2020).​​This​​led​​to​
​high​ ​profile​ ​suspensions​ ​within​ ​the​ ​Labour​ ​Party​ ​for​ ​antisemitic​ ​comments​ ​and​ ​allegations​
​(BBC,​ ​2020a). Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​EHRC​ ​(2020)​ ​report​ ​highlighted​ ​that​ ​an​ ​earlier​ ​inquiry,​ ​in​
​2016,​ ​found​ ​significant​​faults​​in​​the​​Labour​​Party’s​​handling​​of​​antisemitism​​within​​the​​past​
​four years.​


​Corbyn's​ ​management​ ​of​ ​the​ ​issue​ ​was​ ​characterised​ ​by​ ​inadequate​ ​understanding​ ​and​
​ineffective​​party​​management​​principles​​(Shaw,​​2021).​​His​​response​​relied​​heavily​​on​​denial,​
​evading​ ​responsibility,​ ​and​ ​reducing​ ​offensiveness,​ ​while​ ​struggling​ ​with​ ​corrective​ ​action​
​and​​reluctantly​​offering​​apologies​​(Heppell,​​2021).​​The​​crisis​​led​​to​​widespread​​criticism,​​with​
​up​ ​to​ ​85%​ ​of​ ​British​ ​Jews​ ​perceiving​ ​Corbyn​ ​as​ ​antisemitic​ ​by​ ​2018​ ​(Rich,​ ​2018).​ ​Debates​
​surfaced​ ​in​ ​the​ ​controversy​ ​around​ ​antisemitism​​in​​the​​Labour​​Party​​under​​Jeremy​​Corbyn.​
​While​ ​the​ ​EHRC​ ​(2020)​ ​reported​ ​failures​ ​in​ ​the​ ​party’s​ ​handling​ ​of​ ​antisemitism,​ ​scholars​


                                                            ​27​
​such​ ​as​ ​Philo​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2019),​ ​Winstanley​ ​(2023)​ ​and​ ​Lerman​ ​(2022)​ ​argue​​that​​the​​crisis​​was​
​politically​ ​exaggerated​ ​and​ ​often​ ​conflated​ ​with​ ​criticism​ ​of​ ​Israel.​ ​These​ ​discussions​
​reinforce​​the​​complexity​​of​​defining​​and​​addressing​​antisemitism​​within​​broader​​struggles​​for​
​social​ ​justice.​ ​Subsequently,​ ​in​ ​2020,​ ​Jeremy​ ​Corbyn,​ ​who​ ​served​ ​as​ ​Leader​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Labour​
​Party,​​was​​suspended​​from​​the​​party​​because​​of​​serious​​failings​​in​​leadership,​​including​​how​
​he​ ​responded​ ​to​ ​reports​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​within​ ​the​ ​party.​ ​In​ ​contrast,​​Keir​​Starmer,​​took​​a​
​firmer​ ​stance​ ​to​ ​address​ ​these​ ​issues​ ​(Massey,​ ​2020).​ ​Starmer​ ​implemented​ ​reforms​ ​to​
​restore​ ​trust​ ​and​ ​demonstrate​ ​zero​ ​tolerance​ ​for​ ​antisemitism​ ​within​ ​the​ ​party.​ ​This​
​included,​ ​establishing​ ​an​ ​independent​ ​complaints​ ​process,​ ​enhancing​ ​transparency​ ​in​
​handling​​allegations,​​and​​taking​​disciplinary​​action​​against​​members​​accused​​of​​antisemitism.​
​These developments are critical to understanding the broader political context in the UK.​


​It​​is​​evident​​that​​antisemitism​​is​​a​​worldwide​​issue​​and​​as​​highlighted​​by​​the​​European​​Union​
​Agency​ ​for​ ​Fundamental​ ​Rights​ ​(2018)​ ​it​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​be​ ​an​ ​ongoing​ ​problem​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK.​
​Staetsky​​and​​Boyd​​(2015)​​argue​​that​​people​​do​​not​​know​​how​​to​​challenge​​antisemitism​​and​
​believe​ ​that​ ​if​ ​there​ ​was​ ​greater​ ​clarity​ ​on​ ​this​ ​topic,​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​
​would​​hopefully​​feel​​safer​​within​​their​​environment.​​Subsequently,​​there​​is​​a​​requirement​​to​
​decrease​ ​and​ ​diminish​ ​antisemitic​ ​behaviours​ ​in​ ​society.​ ​Zannettou​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2020)​ ​highlight​
​that organisations within the UK have been working to tackle antisemitism for decades.​


​Organisations​ ​within​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​include​ ​the​ ​Board​ ​of​ ​Deputies​ ​of​ ​British​ ​Jews,​ ​who​ ​are​ ​the​
​representatives​ ​of​ ​the​ ​British​ ​Jewish​​community.​​They​​provide​​data​​and​​collect​​information​
​regarding​ ​and​ ​concerning​ ​the​ ​community.​ ​Secondly,​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​Leadership​ ​Council,​
​represents​​the​​Jewish​​charities​​and​​organisations​​within​​the​​UK.​​Furthermore,​​the​​Campaign​
​Against​ ​Antisemitism​ ​(CAA),​ ​The​ ​Holocaust​ ​Educational​ ​Trust​ ​and​ ​the​ ​CST​ ​are​ ​other​
​organisations​​working​​publicly​​to​​decrease​​antisemitism​​in​​society,​​who​​have​​been​​recording​
​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​statistics​ ​in​ ​Britain​ ​since​ ​1984.​ ​The​ ​Campaign​ ​Against​ ​Antisemitism​ ​is​ ​a​
​charity​​led​​by​​volunteers,​​who​​are dedicated​​to​​uncovering​​and​​responding​​to​​antisemitism.​
​The​ ​Holocaust​ ​Educational​ ​Trust​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​individuals​ ​on​ ​the​ ​Holocaust​ ​and​ ​its​
​relevance​ ​in​​today’s​​society,​​by​​working​​alongside​​schools,​​colleges​​and​​communities​​across​
​the​ ​UK.​ ​Finally,​ ​the​ ​CST​ ​is​ ​a​​charity​​that​​works​​to​​guard​​British​​Jews​​from​​antisemitism​​and​
​related​​dangers.​​Overall,​​it​​can​​be​​seen​​that​​there​​is​​a​​selection​​of​​organisations​​and​​charities​


                                                           ​28​
​within​ ​the​ ​UK,​ ​focusing​ ​predominantly​ ​on​ ​working​ ​to​ ​tackle​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​decrease​
​discrimination​ ​within​ ​the​ ​Jewish​​community.​​However,​​although​​organisations​​and​​charities​
​are​ ​continuously​ ​working​ ​to​ ​challenge​ ​this​ ​issue,​ ​antisemitism​ ​still​​persists​​and​​as​​previous​
​statistics​​have​​shown​​it​​continues​​to​​rise​​when​​contemporary​​issues​​arise.​​Furthermore,​​data​
​from​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​(2024)​ ​has​ ​demonstrated​ ​a​ ​positive​ ​correlation​ ​between​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​
​broader​ ​society​ ​and​ ​its​ ​presence​ ​in​ ​football​ ​stadiums.​ ​Therefore,​ ​given​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​of​ ​this​
​project, the discussion will now shift to examining antisemitism within football.​


​Antisemitism in football​


​Antisemitism​​has​​been​​witnessed​​in​​football​​stadiums​​all​​over​​Europe​​for​​decades​​(Stratton,​
​2015).​​Antisemitic​​language​​and​​symbols​​were​​often​​chanted​​by​​football​​clubs​​towards​​their​
​rivals​ ​(Curtis,​ ​2019).​ ​It​ ​was​ ​not​ ​until​ ​the​ ​1970s​ ​and​ ​1980s​ ​that​ ​antisemitic​ ​chants​ ​became​
​more​ ​frequent​ ​and​ ​commonplace​ ​at​ ​football​ ​matches​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​(Williams,​ ​Dunning,​ ​and​
​Murphy,​​1984),​​which​​often​​involved​​insulting​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​alongside​
​mocking​ ​their​ ​beliefs​ ​and​ ​customs​ ​(Poulton,​ ​2016).​ ​In​ ​2015,​ ​Verhoeven​ ​stated​ ​that​
​antisemitism​​at​​football​​matches​​had​​decreased​​since​​the​​late​​1990s,​​with​​fewer​​physical​​and​
​verbal​ ​attacks​ ​occurring​ ​at​ ​matches.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​studies​ ​by​ ​Curtis​ ​(2019),​​Poulton​​(2013;​
​2016;​ ​2020;​ ​2024)​ ​and​ ​Stratton​ ​(2015)​ ​have​ ​highlighted​ ​that​ ​it​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​affect​ ​other​
​countries’ football fan cultures, including the Netherlands, Germany and Poland.​


​Antisemitic​​abuse​​is​​commonly​​seen​​in​​the​​Netherlands;​​most​​specifically,​​AFC​​Ajax​​receives​​a​
​significant​ ​amount​ ​of​ ​abuse​ ​from​ ​opposing​ ​fans​ ​(Curtis,​ ​2019;​ ​Gans,​ ​2014;​ ​Poulton,​ ​2020;​
​Seijbel,​ ​van​ ​Sterkenburg​ ​and​ ​Oonk,​ ​2022;​ ​Stratton,​ ​2015).​ ​Opposing​ ​fans​ ​can​ ​be​ ​heard​
​chanting​ ​distasteful​ ​songs​ ​directed​ ​towards​ ​AFC​ ​Ajax,​ ​including:​ ​“Hamas,​ ​Hamas,​ ​all​ ​Jews​
​should​​be​​gassed”,​​“We​​are​​going​​Jew-hunting”​​and​​“‘My​​father​​was​​in​​the​​commandos,​​my​
​mother​ ​was​ ​in​ ​the​ ​SS,​ ​together​ ​they​ ​burned​ ​Jews,​ ​as​ ​Jews​ ​burn​ ​the​ ​best”​ ​(Curtis,​ ​2019;​
​Verhoeven,​ ​2015,​ ​p.​ ​13;​ ​Seijbel​ ​et​ ​al​.,​ ​2022).​ ​Furthermore,​ ​in​ ​2017,​ ​opposing​ ​teams​ ​used​
​pictures​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​children,​ ​who​ ​were​ ​killed​ ​in​ ​the​ ​Holocaust​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​Anne​ ​Frank,​ ​to​
​provoke​​Ajax​​fans​​(JTA,​​2017).​​The​​club​​has​​a​​perceived​​‘Jewishness’​​because​​of​​having​​Jewish​
​fans​ ​who​ ​travelled​ ​from​ ​the​ ​nearby​ ​Jewish​ ​district,​​Jodenbuurt.​​Jodenbuurt​​is​​located​​near​
​the​ ​centre​ ​of​ ​Amsterdam,​ ​and​ ​with​ ​AFC​ ​Ajax​ ​stadium​ ​near​ ​the​ ​city’s​ ​edge,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​an​ ​easy​


                                                             ​29​
​location​ ​to​ ​travel​ ​to​ ​via​ ​tram​ ​(Gans,​ ​2014).​ ​In​ ​an​ ​attempt​ ​to​ ​decrease​ ​the​ ​antisemitic​
​chanting,​​AFC​​Ajax​​adopted​​the​​term​​‘Superjoden’,​​the​​‘Super​​Jews’,​​and​​have​​used​​it​​within​
​their​​songs​​and​​chants​​(Seijbel​​et​​al​.,​​2022).​​Verhoeven​​(2015)​​notes​​a​​significant​​decrease​​in​
​antisemitic​​chanting​​at​​AFC​​Ajax​​since​​the​​1990s,​​a​​trend​​that​​is​​further​​supported​​by​​Seijbel​
​et​​al.'s​​(2022)​​research.​​Their​​study,​​which​​explored​​the​​impact​​of​​the​​Covid-19​​pandemic​​on​
​online​ ​antisemitic​ ​discourse,​ ​found​ ​a​ ​notable​ ​decline​ ​in​ ​such​ ​discourse​ ​between​ ​2019​ ​and​
​2020,​ ​reinforcing​ ​Verhoeven's​ ​earlier​ ​findings.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​Masters​ ​and​​Coppack’s​​(2019)​
​report​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​at​ ​AFC​ ​Ajax​ ​matches​ ​is​​still​​prevalent​​and​​they​​raise​
​their​​concerns​​that​​may​​begin​​to​​rise​​again,​​with​​vandalism​​and​​verbal​​abuse​​becoming​​more​
​evident at matches.​


​Before​​the​​Second​​World​​War,​​Bayern​​Munich,​​a​​German​​football​​club,​​were​​recognised​​as​​a​
​‘Jewish’​ ​team;​ ​they​ ​had​ ​both​ ​a​ ​Jewish​ ​president​ ​and​ ​a​​Jewish​​manager​​(Honigstein,​​2012).​
​Nevertheless,​ ​after​ ​the​ ​war​ ​the​ ​club’s​ ​Jewish​ ​identity​ ​was​ ​forgotten.​ ​Nevertheless,​
​antisemitic​ ​chants​ ​and​ ​symbols​ ​have​ ​been​ ​seen​ ​at​ ​many​ ​matches​ ​(Verhoeven,​ ​2015).​
​Beginning​ ​in​ ​the​ ​1990s,​ ​antisemitic​ ​chanting​ ​on​ ​a​ ​weekly​ ​basis​ ​was​ ​not​ ​uncommon​ ​in​
​Germany,​​right-wing​​extremist​​groups​​believed​​that​​football​​matches​​were​​the​​ideal​​place​​to​
​display​ ​their​ ​controversial​ ​antisemitic​ ​behaviour,​ ​as​ ​they​ ​were​ ​able​ ​to​ ​voice​ ​their​ ​opinion​
​much​ ​easier​ ​than​​any​​other​​social​​domain.​​Unfortunately,​​they​​also​​found​​it​​to​​be​​the​​ideal​
​place​​to​​recruit​​extremist​​supporters​​(Curtis,​​2019).​​Graffiti​​containing​​images​​of​​swastikas,​​a​
​symbol​​that​​provokes​​instant​​repulsion​​due​​to​​its​​appropriation​​by​​the​​Nazis,​​and​​references​
​to​ ​gas​ ​chambers,​ ​have​ ​been​ ​seen​ ​at​ ​matches​ ​(Curtis,​ ​2019).​ ​This​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​is​
​suggestive​ ​of​ ​Germany’s​ ​previous​ ​history,​ ​making​​it​​explicit​​that​​Jews​​were​​not​​welcome​​at​
​matches (Curtis, 2019).​


​Assaulting​ ​opposing​ ​teams​ ​by​ ​using​ ​derogatory​ ​language​ ​alongside​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Jew’​ ​and​
​graffitiing​​distasteful​​images​​and​​swastikas,​​has​​been​​a​​recurring​​issue​​in​​Polish​​football​​since​
​the​ ​1970s​ ​(Cole,​ ​2020).​ ​Likewise,​ ​supporters​ ​have​ ​been​ ​seen​ ​displaying​ ​banners​ ​with​
​distasteful​ ​Jewish​ ​stereotypes,​ ​including​ ​portraits​ ​with​ ​long​ ​noses,​ ​an​ ​ethnic and racial​
​stereotype​​(Curtis,​​2019).​​KS​​Cracovia​​is​​a​​Polish​​team,​​who​​like​​AFC​​Ajax​​have​​been​​labelled​
​as​​a​​‘Jewish​​football’​​club​​(Cole,​​2020).​​Additionally,​​Widzew​​Lodz​​is​​a​​‘Jewish’​​club​​(Stratton,​
​2015).​ ​Both​ ​teams​ ​have​ ​been​ ​known​ ​to​ ​receive​ ​antisemitic​ ​hatred​ ​due​ ​to​ ​this​​connection.​


                                                           ​30​
​Nevertheless,​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​football​ ​is​ ​merely​ ​a​ ​reflection​ ​of​ ​society​ ​in​ ​Poland.​ ​Evidence​
​highlights​ ​that​ ​officials​ ​are​ ​more​ ​likely​ ​to​ ​tolerate​ ​antisemitic​ ​behaviours​ ​in​ ​Poland​ ​in​
​comparison​​to​​the​​abuse​​in​​Germany,​​the​​Netherlands​​and​​the​​United​​Kingdom​​(ADL,​​2020;​
​Masters​ ​and​ ​Coppack,​ ​2014).​ ​Unfortunately,​ ​the​ ​‘Never​ ​Again’​ ​Association,​​an​​organisation​
​dedicated​ ​to​ ​combating​ ​racism​ ​and​ ​antisemitism,​ ​believes​ ​that​ ​Polish​ ​football​ ​crowds​ ​are​
​unwilling​ ​to​ ​address​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​stadiums,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​has​​become​​an​​accepted​​part​​of​​Polish​
​societal discourses.​


​The​ ​book​ ​‘​Football​ ​and​ ​Discrimination:​ ​Antisemitism​ ​and​ ​Beyond’​,​ ​edited​ ​by​ ​Brunssen​ ​and​
​Schüler-Springorum​ ​(2021),​ ​is​ ​dedicated​​to​​examining​​the​​widespread​​issue​​of​​antisemitism​
​in​ ​European​ ​football.​ ​Through​ ​a​ ​series​ ​of​ ​European​ ​case​ ​studies,​ ​the​ ​book​ ​delves​ ​into​ ​the​
​historical​​and​​contemporary​​manifestations​​of​​antisemitism​​within​​football​​cultures.​​Oswald​
​(2021)​ ​investigates​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Judenklub’​ ​[Jewish​ ​club],​ ​used​ ​during​ ​the​ ​interwar​ ​period​ ​to​
​label​ ​football​ ​teams,​ ​often​ ​without​ ​any​ ​actual​ ​Jewish​ ​affiliation,​ ​highlighting​ ​how​ ​this​
​designation​ ​was​ ​primarily​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​rivalry​ ​and​ ​discrimination.​ ​Burski​ ​and​ ​Woźniak​ ​(2021)​
​discuss​ ​Polish​ ​football,​ ​where​ ​despite​ ​the​ ​absence​ ​of​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​Jewish​ ​population,​
​antisemitic​ ​rhetoric​ ​persists,​ ​fuelled​ ​by​ ​stereotypes​ ​and​ ​chants.​ ​Schubert​ ​(2021)​ ​examines​
​German​ ​football’s​​rising​​antisemitism​​from​​the​​1980s​​onward,​​with​​neo-Nazi​​influences​​and​
​hateful​ ​fan​ ​behaviour​ ​in​ ​stadiums.​ ​Brunssen​ ​(2021)​ ​explores​​how​​RB​​Leipzig’s​​unpopularity​
​evokes​​antisemitic​​stereotypes,​​despite​​the​​club's​​lack​​of​​Jewish​​ties,​​illustrating​​how​​football​
​rivalries​ ​can​ ​weaponise​ ​such​ ​prejudices.​ ​In​ ​the​ ​Dutch​ ​context,​ ​Verhoeven​ ​and​ ​Wagenaar​
​(2021)​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​Ajax,​ ​showing​ ​how​ ​its​ ​fans’​ ​self-identification​ ​as​ ​‘Joden’​ ​[Jews]​ ​invites​
​Holocaust-related​ ​abuse​ ​from​ ​rivals.​ ​Collectively,​ ​these​ ​chapters​ ​reveal​ ​the​ ​deep-rooted​
​connections​ ​between​ ​football,​ ​collective​ ​identity,​ ​and​ ​antisemitism,​ ​shedding​ ​light​ ​on​ ​how​
​these​​prejudices​​are​​expressed,​​sustained,​​and​​at​​times,​​contested​​across​​European​​football​
​cultures.​


​Within​ ​this​ ​book,​ ​Poulton​ ​(2021)​​begins​​by​​discussing​​antisemitism​​in​​the​​context​​of​​British​
​football,​​mentioning​​how​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​supporters,​​who​​call​​themselves​​the​​‘Yid​​Army’,​
​face​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​that​ ​is​​often​​disguised​​as​​banter.​​Poulton's​​(2016;​​2021;​​2023;​​2024)​
​extensive​ ​research​ ​on​ ​this​ ​issue,​ ​particularly​ ​at​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur,​ ​combined​ ​with​ ​other​
​studies,​​have​​identified​​the​​persistence​​of​​antisemitism​​in​​English​​football​​(Back​​et​​al​.,​​2001;​


                                                            ​31​
​Curtis,​ ​2019;​ ​Dart​ ​and​ ​Long,​ ​2021).​ ​This​ ​body​ ​of​ ​work​ ​highlights​ ​how​ ​deeply​ ​ingrained​
​antisemitism​ ​remains​ ​within​ ​British​ ​football​ ​culture.​ ​Curtis​ ​(2019)​ ​recognises​ ​that​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​football​ ​differs,​ ​depending​ ​on​ ​the​ ​country.​ ​Numerous​ ​scholars,​ ​including​
​Curtis​ ​(2019),​ ​Stratton​ ​(2015)​ ​and​ ​Verhoeven​ ​(2015)​ ​have​ ​highlighted​ ​that​ ​antisemitism​ ​is​
​prevalent​ ​in​ ​the​ ​football​ ​arena,​ ​however,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​recognise​ ​their​ ​differences​ ​in​
​levels​ ​of​ ​intensity​ ​and​ ​also​ ​in​ ​approaching​ ​the​ ​subject.​ ​Markovits​ ​and​ ​Rensmann​ ​(2010)​
​recognise​​that​​football​​stadiums​​function​​as​​political​​battlefields,​​and​​that​​in​​some​​countries,​
​including​ ​Poland,​ ​antisemitism​​at​​football​​matches​​is​​a​​reflection​​of​​society.​​However,​​some​
​may​​argue​​that​​in​​other​​countries,​​including​​Britain,​​it​​is​​more​​‘football-related​​banter’​​used​
​to​​wind​​up​​the​​opposition​​(Poulton,​​2023).​​Stratton​​(2015)​​suggests​​that​​although​​these​​clubs​
​accept​​their​​identification​​as​​‘Jewish’​​clubs,​​antisemitism​​at​​football​​matches​​has​​been​​known​
​to​ ​make​ ​fans,​ ​both​ ​gentile​ ​and​ ​Jew,​ ​feel​ ​uncomfortable​ ​and​ ​those​ ​who​ ​are​ ​Jewish,​
​unwelcome.​ ​Therefore,​ ​this​ ​thesis​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​football,​ ​focusing​ ​most​
​specifically within the context of British football and Tottenham Hotspur.​


​Antisemitism in British football​


​In​​1935,​​antisemitic​​abuse​​occurred​​at​​White​​Hart​​Lane​​on​​December​​4th,​​also​​known​​as​​“the​
​day​​the​​swastika​​flew​​over​​White​​Hart​​Lane.”​​England​​and​​Germany​​were​​playing​​a​​match​​at​
​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​stadium,​ ​which​ ​at​ ​the​ ​time​ ​was​ ​known​ ​for​ ​being​ ​home​ ​to​ ​many​​Jews.​
​Before​​kick-off,​​the​​German​​team​​gave​​a​​Nazi,​​Heil​​Hitler​​Salute​​and​​a​​flag​​with​​a​​swastika​​was​
​flown​ ​over​ ​the​ ​stadium.​ ​Fortunately,​ ​the​ ​flag​ ​did​ ​not​ ​fly​ ​for​ ​long,​ ​as​ ​a​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​
​supporter,​​named​​Ernie​​Wooley,​​climbed​​up​​the​​gutters​​of​​the​​West​​Stand​​and​​removed​​the​
​flag; unfairly, Wooley was arrested (Curtis, 2019).​


​More​ ​recently,​ ​in​ ​2014,​ ​Boyd​ ​and​ ​Staetsky​ ​(2014)​​found​​that​​6%​​of​​antisemitic​​incidents​​in​
​the​ ​UK​ ​are​ ​witnessed​ ​at​ ​sporting​ ​events,​ ​highlighting​ ​that​ ​within​ ​sport,​ ​antisemitism​ ​is​
​prevalent​​in​​our​​present​​society.​​In​​British​​football,​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​supporters​​receive​​a​
​significant​ ​amount​ ​of​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​from​ ​opposing​ ​clubs​ ​due​ ​to​ ​the​ ​club’s​ ​perceived​
​‘Jewish’​ ​heritage​ ​(Kershaw,​ ​2019;​ ​Poulton​ ​and​ ​Durell,​ ​2016;​ ​Poulton,​ ​2016;​ ​2020;​ ​2024).​
​Harris​ ​(2016)​ ​recognises​ ​that​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​and​ ​their​ ​link​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​religion​ ​has​
​caused​​much​​discussion​​and​​controversy.​ ​Research​​by​​Lunn​​(2023)​​explored​​this​​complicated​


                                                              ​32​
​and​ ​often​ ​uneasy​ ​relationship​ ​between​ ​Tottenham​​Hotspur,​​the​​Jewish​​community​​and​​the​
​antisemitism​ ​that​ ​often​ ​occurs​ ​at​ ​football​ ​matches.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​as​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​this​
​association,​ ​like​ ​AFC​ ​Ajax,​ ​opposing​ ​fans​ ​have​ ​been​ ​heard​ ​making​ ​references​ ​to​ ​the​
​Holocaust​​and​​imitating​​the​​gas​​chambers,​​by​​making​​hissing​​noises​​(Poulton,​​2024;​​Poulton​
​and​​Durell,​​2016).​​Poulton’s​​(2020)​​research​​states​​that​​there​​are​​spikes​​in​​antisemitic​​abuse​
​whenever​ ​Tottenham​ ​plays​ ​a​ ​London​ ​Club.​ ​Poulton​ ​and​ ​Durell​ ​(2016)​ ​highlight​ ​three​ ​main​
​reasons​ ​why​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​have​ ​been​ ​labelled​ ​a​ ​‘Jewish’​ ​club.​ ​This​ ​includes,​
​demographics​ ​of​ ​the​ ​fans,​ ​religious​ ​identities​ ​of​ ​current​​and​​previous​​shareholders,​​and/or​
​the​ ​nickname​ ​that​ ​the​ ​fans​ ​identify​ ​with,​ ​‘Yid’,​ ​a​ ​Jewish​ ​ethnonym,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​later​
​abbreviated​ ​by​ ​the​ ​Nazis​ ​and​ ​is​ ​now​ ​recognised​ ​as​ ​race​ ​hate​ ​term​ ​used​ ​by​ ​antisemites​
​(Poulton and Durell, 2016; Poulton, 2016).​


​It​​has​​been​​estimated​​by​​Boyd​​and​​Staetsky​​(2014)​​that​​two-thirds​​of​​all​​Jews​​in​​the​​UK​​live​​in​
​Greater​ ​London.​ ​Given​ ​this,​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​typically​ ​support​ ​football​
​clubs​ ​located​ ​in​ ​London​ ​(Cloake​ ​and​ ​Fisher,​ ​2016).​ ​In​ ​the​ ​early​ ​20th​ ​century,​ ​when​ ​many​
​Eastern​​European​​Jews​​who​​were​​escaping​​from​​Russia​​came​​to​​Britain,​​they​​would​​settle​​in​
​the​​East​​End​​(Curtis,​​2019;​​Lipman,​​1990).​​In​​Tottenham,​​there​​was​​plenty​​of​​unskilled​​work​
​in​ ​the​ ​industrial​​sites​​and​​many​​businesses​​in​​the​​area​​were​​owned​​by​​Jews.​​Therefore,​​the​
​Jewish​​community​​who​​were​​in​​search​​of​​both​​a​​job​​and​​a​​home,​​started​​to​​make​​their​​home​
​in​ ​Tottenham.​ ​Due​ ​to​ ​this,​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​number​ ​of​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​fans​ ​were​ ​Jewish​
​(Clavane,​​2012).​​Cloake​​and​​Fisher​​(2016)​​argue​​that​​in​​the​​1920s,​​almost​​all​​Jewish​​football​
​supporters​ ​were​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​fans,​ ​and​ ​throughout​ ​history​ ​they​ ​have​ ​continued​ ​to​
​attract​​many​​more​​Jewish​​supporters​​(Cloake​​and​​Fisher,​​2016).​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​Stadium,​
​which​​was​​formerly​​known​​as​​White​​Hart​​Lane,​​is​​located​​near​​the​​Jewish​​communities​​with​
​a​​large​​population​​of​​Orthodox​​Jews.​​The​​Torah​​prohibits​​lighting​​a​​fire​​on​​the​​Sabbath,​​and​
​since​ ​driving​ ​a​ ​car​ ​involves​ ​burning​ ​fuel,​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​are​ ​thus​
​prohibited​​from​​driving​​to​​football​​matches​​on​​Saturdays.​​Therefore,​​for​​those​​who​​could​​not​
​drive​ ​or​ ​get​ ​public​ ​transport​ ​on​ ​the​ ​Sabbath,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​easy​ ​to​ ​get​ ​to​ ​Tottenham​ ​matches​
​(Godden, 2017).​


​Currently,​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​Football​​Club​​has​​not​​released​​an​​official​​count​​of​​how​​many​​of​
​its​ ​fans​ ​are​ ​Jewish​ ​or​ ​practise​ ​Judaism.​ ​However,​ ​a​ ​2014​ ​report​ ​by​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​


                                                           ​33​
​revealed​ ​that​ ​9.97%​ ​of​ ​its​ ​season​ ​ticket​ ​holders​ ​are​ ​Jewish.​ ​Additionally,​ ​a​ ​later​ ​study​ ​by​
​Cloake​​and​​Fisher​​(2016)​​estimated​​that​​approximately​​5%​​of​​the​​club's​​members​​identify​​as​
​Jewish.​ ​With​ ​just​ ​0.5%​ ​of​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​population​ ​being​ ​Jewish​ ​(Board​ ​of​ ​Deputies,​ ​2020),​ ​this​
​figure​ ​indicates​ ​that​ ​Jewish​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​supporters​ ​outnumber​ ​the​ ​general​
​population.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​if​ ​the​ ​majority​ ​of​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​fans​ ​are​ ​not​ ​Jewish,​ ​it​ ​is​
​unclear​ ​why​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​is​ ​considered​ ​a​ ​‘Jewish’​ ​football​ ​club.​ ​Another​ ​reason​ ​the​
​club​​is​​affiliated​​with​​the​​Jewish​​community​​is​​that​​it​​has​​former​​and​​current​​Jewish​​owners,​
​chairman​​and​​stakeholders​​(Poulton,​​2016).​​According​​to​​Cloake​​and​​Fisher​​(2016)​​and​​Curtis​
​(2019),​ ​it​ ​includes​ ​chairman​ ​Irving​ ​Scholar,​​who​​served​​from​​1982​​to​​1991,​​and​​Alan​​Sugar,​
​who​ ​served​ ​from​​1991​​to​​2001.​​They​​also​​point​​out​​that​​the​​current​​chairman,​​Daniel​​Levy,​
​has held the position since 2001, and the current owners are both Jewish.​


​The word ‘Yid’ in British football​


​The​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​originated​​from​​Yiddish,​​the​​traditional​​language​​of​​Ashkenazi​​Jews,​​and​​was​
​initially​​used​​in​​a​​non-derogatory​​way​​to​​mean​​‘Jew.’​​It​​was​​historically​​employed​​as​​a​​term​​of​
​endearment​ ​and​ ​familiarity​ ​within​​the​​Jewish​​community​​(Poulton,​​2013).​​Yiddish​​itself​​has​
​long​​been​​a​​vibrant​​and​​integral​​part​​of​​Jewish​​culture​​and​​identity.​​However,​​the​​term​​‘Yid’​
​has​ ​evolved​ ​over​ ​time​ ​and​ ​can​ ​have​ ​different​ ​connotations.​ ​While​ ​it​ ​is​​not​​offensive​​when​
​used​ ​correctly​ ​by​ ​Yiddish​ ​speakers,​ ​its​ ​interpretation​ ​changes​ ​when​ ​used​ ​by​ ​non-Jews.​ ​In​
​English,​ ​the​ ​term​ ​is​ ​often​ ​considered​ ​a​ ​derogatory​ ​epithet,​ ​especially​ ​when​ ​employed​ ​by​
​antisemites (Cloake and Fisher, 2016).​


​The​​Nazis​​abbreviated​​the​​word​​‘Yiddish’​​to​​‘Yid’​​using​​it​​in​​a​​derogatory​​way​​(Poulton,​​2016)​
​and​​it​​was​​used​​by​​the​​fascists,​​far-right​​political​​groups​​in​​the​​1930s​​(BBC,​​2020b).​​Now​​the​
​term​ ​has​ ​offensive​ ​origins​ ​to​ ​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​and​​it​​is​​considered​​to​​be​
​antisemitic.​ ​It​ ​has​ ​been​ ​argued​ ​that​ ​the​ ​term​ ​is​ ​equivalent​ ​to​ ​the​​race​​hate​​words​​‘nigger’​
