​and​ ​‘paki’​ ​(Clavane,​ ​2012).​ ​Ofcom​ ​(2012)​ ​explored​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​discriminatory​ ​language​ ​by​
​questioning​ ​248​ ​participants,​ ​from​ ​around​ ​the​ ​UK,​ ​on​ ​their​ ​attitudes​ ​towards​ ​potentially​
​offensive​ ​language.​ ​They​ ​found​ ​that​ ​words​ ​which​ ​discriminate​ ​on​ ​religious​ ​grounds​ ​have​
​been​​considered​​generally​​offensive,​​whereas​​those​​words​​associated​​with​​race,​​are​​the​​most​
​unacceptable words overall. Therefore, some may not consider the term ‘Yid’ as offensive.​


                                                             ​34​
​The​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​has,​ ​however,​ ​become​ ​controversial​ ​in​ ​Britain,​ ​as​ ​Tottenham​
​Hotspur​​fans​​have​​reclaimed​​the​​word​​and​​have​​been​​seen​​singing​​and​​chanting​​the​​word​​at​
​matches.​ ​The​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​has​ ​regularly​ ​been​ ​used​ ​against​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​in​ ​an​
​offensive​ ​manner,​ ​and​ ​subsequently​ ​has​ ​been​ ​chanted​ ​towards​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​due​​to​
​their​ ​perceived​ ​‘Jewishness’​ ​(Poulton​ ​and​ ​Durell,​ ​2016).​ ​Opposing​ ​fans​​have​​been​​heard​​to​
​chant​ ​the​ ​word​ ​in​ ​phrases​ ​such​ ​as,​ '​We've​ ​got​ ​Cesc​ ​Fabregas,​ ​you​ ​Yids​ ​are​ ​scared​ ​of​ ​gas'​
​(Kessel,​ ​2007).​ ​Furthermore,​ ​fans​ ​use​ ​the​ ​word​ ​amongst​ ​negative​ ​intensifiers,​ ​for​ ​example​
​‘dirty’​ ​or​ ​‘fucking’,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​most​ ​likely​ ​used​ ​to​ ​cause​ ​offence,​ ​and​ ​would​ ​be​ ​considered​
​antisemitic​ ​(Poulton,​ ​2016).​ ​Therefore,​​Tottenham​​fans,​​both​​gentile​​and​​Jews,​​adopted​​the​
​term​​‘Yid’,​​and​​have​​used​​it​​since​​the​​1970s​​as​​a​​fan​​club​​name​​to​​deflect​​the​​abuse​​(Poulton,​
​2016;​​Stratton,​​2015).​​They​​may​​also​​refer​​to​​themselves​​as​​‘ The​​Yid​​Army’​​and​​‘ The​​Yiddos’​
​(Tottenham​​Hotspur,​​2014).​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​fans​​have​​also​​embedded​​the​​term​​into​​their​
​own songs and chants, which is sung at matches, including (Verhoeven, 2015):​


         ​“We sang it in France,​
         ​We sang it in Spain,​
         ​We sing in the sun and we sing in the rain,​
         ​They've tried to stop us and look what it did,​
         ​Cos the thing I love most is being a Yid!​
         ​Being a Yid, Being a Yid,​
         ​The thing I love most is being a Yid!”​


​Although​​this​​term​​is​​derogatory,​​the​​fans​​use​​it​​as​​a​​sign​​of​​pride​​and​​endearment​​to​​deflect​
​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​(Lunn,​ ​2023;​ ​Poulton,​ ​2016).​ ​Similarly,​ ​in​ ​society​ ​we​​see​​oppressive​​slurs​
​such​ ​as​ ​‘queer’​ ​and​ ​‘nigga’,​ ​which​ ​have​ ​been​ ​previously​ ​used​ ​within​ ​society​ ​as​ ​a​ ​form​ ​of​
​abuse​ ​but​ ​have​ ​been​ ​embraced​ ​and​ ​appropriated​ ​by​ ​the​ ​targeted​ ​group​ ​(Coles,​ ​2016;​
​Popa-Wyatt,​ ​2020).​ ​Like​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​and​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​​word​​‘Yid’,​​these​​terms​​are​
​words​ ​that​ ​a​ ​minority​ ​group​ ​has​ ​self-labelled​ ​and​ ​identified​ ​with​ ​to​ ​take​ ​control​ ​over​ ​the​
​terms​​used.​​Furthermore,​​fans​​state​​that​​they​​use​​the​​term​​as​​a​​badge​​of​​honour,​​and​​it​​gives​
​them​​a​​sense​​of​​belonging.​​In​​2014,​​39%​​of​​non-Jewish​​and​​29%​​of​​Jewish​​fans​​felt​​that​​the​
​word was part of Tottenham Hotspur’s heritage and identity (Tottenham Hotspur, 2014).​


                                                             ​35​
         ​"A​ ​space​​where​​ethnic​​identity​​has​​connected,​​even​​become​​intertwined,​​with​
         ​national​ ​identity;​ ​an​ ​arena​ ​where​ ​Jews​​have​​fought​​the​​notion​​that​​they​​were​
         ​invaders​​who​​needed​​to​​be​​fended​​off,​​newcomers​​who​​did​​not​​belong."​​Cloake​
         ​and Fisher (2016, p.1)​


​Clavane​ ​(2012)​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​recognise​​that​​they,​​as​​a​​collective,​​are​​a​
​diverse​​group​​of​​individuals​​and​​regardless​​of​​this,​​they​​will​​ensure​​that​​football​​matches​​are​
​a​ ​place​ ​where​​the​​Jewish​​community​​feels​​welcome.​​Furthermore,​​research​​by​​Lunn​​(2023)​
​and​​Poulton​​and​​Durell​​(2016)​​found​​that​​fans​​believe​​that​​it​​is​​essential​​and​​necessary​​to​​use​
​it to deflect antisemitic hatred they receive from opposing fans.​


​Given​ ​its​ ​origins,​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​and​ ​its​ ​usage​ ​has​ ​become​ ​a​ ​controversial​ ​topic,​​which​​has​
​caused​ ​much​ ​discussion​ ​amongst​ ​football​ ​supporters,​ ​Jewish​ ​Organisations,​ ​including​ ​the​
​CST,​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​Leadership​ ​Council​ ​and​ ​the​ ​World​ ​Jewish​ ​Congress​ ​(Welch,​ ​2019)​ ​and​
​sporting​ ​professionals​ ​(Sky​ ​Sports​ ​Football,​ ​2019).​ ​Although​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​​and​​its​​usage​​at​
​football​​matches​​has​​been​​discussed​​plenty​​within​​the​​media,​​discussion​​amongst​​academics​
​is​ ​limited​ ​(Lunn,​ ​2018;​ ​2023;​ ​Poulton​ ​and​ ​Durell,​ ​2016;​ ​Poulton,​ ​2013;​ ​2016;​ ​Wilczyńska,​
​2022).​ ​Adding​ ​to​ ​the​ ​controversy,​ ​in​ ​2020​ ​an​ ​alternative​ ​definition​ ​for​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​was​
​added​ ​to​ ​the Oxford​ ​English​ ​Dictionary,​ ​stating​ ​that​ ​term​ ​meant​​‘supporter​​of​​or​​player​​for​
​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur’,​ ​in​ ​which​ ​the​ ​club​ ​has​ ​responded​ ​saying​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​misleading​ ​(BBC,​
​2020b).​


​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​football​ ​club​ ​undertook​ ​two​ ​consultations​ ​with​ ​their​ ​fans:​​one​​in​​2014​
​and​ ​one​ ​in​ ​2019.​ ​Both​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​phrase​ ​‘Yid’​ ​in​ ​its​ ​context​ ​to​ ​Tottenham​
​Hotspur.​ ​In​ ​2014,​ ​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​released​​a​​statement​​detailing​​the​​results​​of​​their​​fan​
​consultation​​on​​the​​use​​of​​the​​term​​‘Yid’.​​Data​​showed​​that​​67%​​of​​fans​​regularly​​chanted​​the​
​word​ ​at​ ​football​ ​matches.​ ​Overall,​ ​74%​ ​of​ ​non-Jewish​ ​respondents​ ​and​ ​73%​ ​of​ ​Jewish​
​respondents​ ​were​ ​generally​ ​in​ ​favour​ ​of​ ​using​ ​the​ ​word.​ ​Although​ ​the​ ​report​ ​did​ ​not​
​highlight​​why​​fans​​are​​in​​favour​​of​​using​​the​​term,​​literature​​by​​Poulton​​and​​Durell​​(2016)​​and​
​Lunn​ ​(2018;​ ​2023),​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​fans​ ​use​ ​the​ ​term​​to​​deflect​​antisemitic​​abuse​​and​​wear​
​the​ ​term​ ​as​ ​a​ ​badge​ ​of​ ​honour.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​12%​ ​of​ ​non-Jewish​ ​respondents​ ​and​ ​18%​​of​


                                                              ​36​
​Jewish​ ​respondents​ ​were​ ​against​ ​using​ ​the​ ​term​ ​with​ ​4%​ ​of​ ​non-Jewish​ ​fans​ ​and​ ​6%​ ​of​
​Jewish​ ​fans​ ​saying​ ​that​ ​they​ ​were​ ​uncomfortable​ ​with​ ​it.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​13%​ ​of​ ​the​
​non-Jewish​ ​fans​ ​thought​ ​that​​if​​others​​found​​the​​term​​offensive,​​then​​it​​should​​be​​dropped​
​(Tottenham​ ​Hotspur,​ ​2014).​ ​Nevertheless​ ​in​ ​2019,​ ​only​ ​33%​ ​of​ ​respondents​ ​use​ ​the​ ​word​
​‘Yid’​ ​regularly​ ​in​ ​a​ ​footballing​ ​context,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​a​ ​dramatic​ ​decrease​ ​since​ ​the​ ​2014​
​consultation​ ​and​ ​25%​ ​of​ ​respondents​ ​will​ ​not​ ​chant​ ​it​ ​at​ ​football​ ​matches.​ ​However,​ ​12%​
​would​ ​use​ ​the​ ​term​ ​outside​ ​of​ ​football.​ ​Results​ ​also​ ​found​ ​that​ ​nearly​ ​half​ ​of​ ​the​
​respondents​​would​​rather​​the​​fans​​chant​​the​​word​​less​​or​​stop​​using​​it​​(Tottenham​​Hotspur,​
​2019).​ ​Although​ ​there​ ​is​ ​no​​qualitative​​data​​to​​suggest​​the​​decrease​​in​​numbers,​​this​​could​
​be​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​increased​ ​media​ ​attention​ ​regarding​ ​its​ ​usage​ ​or​ ​fans​ ​have​ ​become​ ​more​
​educated regarding the origins of the term.​


​Both​​consultations​​conducted​​by​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​(2014;​​2019)​​have​​given​​an​​insight​​into​
​fans’​ ​opinions​ ​on​​the​​use​​of​​the​​phrase​​‘yid’.​​However,​​this​​data​​was​​collected​​via​​an​​online​
​survey,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​sent​ ​to​ ​all​ ​the​ ​‘One​ ​Hotspur’​ ​season​ ​ticket​ ​holders​ ​and​ ​members.​ ​As​
​highlighted​​by​​Salmons​​(2014),​​online​​mediums​​are​​not​​as​​easily​​accessible​​to​​all,​​and​​some​
​individuals​ ​might​ ​not​ ​be​ ​competent​ ​enough​ ​to​ ​use​ ​online​ ​platforms;​ ​this​ ​could​ ​affect​ ​the​
​validity​​of​​their​​study.​​When​​discussing​​the​​use​​of​​the​​term​​‘Yid’,​​it​​should​​be​​recognised​​that​
​the​ ​older​ ​generation​ ​may​ ​find​ ​the​ ​term​ ​more​ ​offensive,​ ​given​ ​that​ ​they​ ​may​ ​have​ ​lost​
​immediate​ ​family​ ​members​​to​​the​​Holocaust.​​However,​​these​​perspectives​​may​​not​​be​​fully​
​reflected​ ​if​ ​access​ ​to​ ​online​ ​platforms​ ​is​ ​more​ ​limited​ ​among​ ​older​ ​individuals.​ ​Likewise,​
​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​gave​​fans​​only​​twelve​​days​​to​​complete​​the​​survey,​​which​​could​​limit​​the​
​results.​ ​In​ ​2014,​ ​they​ ​received​ ​11,500​ ​completed​ ​consultations​ ​and​ ​in​ ​2019,​ ​they​​received​
​just​​over​​23,000​​responses.​​The​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​Supporters​​Trust​​(2019)​​states​​that​​there​
​are​ ​roughly​ ​42,000​ ​season​ ​ticket​ ​holders,​ ​8,000​ ​premium​​members,​​and​​over​​100,000​​One​
​Hotspur​ ​members.​ ​Given​ ​that​ ​this​ ​questionnaire​ ​would​ ​have​ ​been​ ​sent​ ​out​ ​to​ ​roughly​
​150,000​ ​fans,​ ​it​ ​could​ ​be​ ​argued​ ​that​ ​7%​ ​response​ ​is​ ​not​ ​representative​ ​of​ ​the​ ​whole​ ​fan​
​base​​and,​​subsequently,​​may​​lack​​validity.​​To​​gain​​a​​greater​​sample​​size,​​the​​club​​could​​have​
​given​ ​supporters​ ​a​ ​greater​ ​amount​ ​of​ ​time​ ​to​ ​complete​ ​it​ ​and​ ​advertise​ ​it​ ​on​ ​their​ ​social​
​media platforms.​




                                                             ​37​
​Some​ ​individuals​ ​and​ ​organisations​ ​have​ ​expressed​ ​concern​ ​about​ ​the​ ​reclamation​ ​of​ ​the​
​term,​ ​including​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​​Jewish​​community​​and​​Jewish​​football​​supporters,​​and​​the​
​World​​Jewish​​Congress,​​the​​Board​​of​​Deputies,​​CST​​and​​the​​Jewish​​Leadership​​Council​​(JLC),​
​who​ ​have​ ​asked​ ​Tottenham​ ​fans​ ​to​ ​stop​ ​using​ ​it​​(Welch,​​2019).​​The​​argument​​is​​that​​using​
​the​ ​term​ ​causes​ ​trouble​ ​and​ ​upset,​ ​and​ ​that​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​fans​ ​have​ ​no​ ​right​ ​to​
​appropriate​ ​it,​ ​regardless​ ​of​ ​whether​ ​it​ ​is​ ​being​ ​used​ ​in​ ​an​ ​antisemitic​ ​manner​ ​or​ ​not.​
​Likewise,​​they​​believe​​it​​encourages​​antisemitic​​behaviour​​from​​antisemites.​​In​​2019,​​94%​​of​
​fans​ ​recognised​ ​that​ ​the​ ​word​ ​can​ ​be​ ​considered​ ​a​ ​racist​ ​term,​ ​however,​ ​supporters​ ​have​
​argued​​that​​there​​should​​be​​a​​greater​​emphasis​​on​​the​​antisemitic​​abuse​​from​​opposing​​fans,​
​rather​​than​​punishing​​those​​who​​use​​it.​​They​​argue​​that​​if​​opposing​​teams​​were​​not​​chanting​
​antisemitic hate, they would not need to reclaim the term.​


​This​​research​​project​​builds​​upon​​the​​work​​of​​Dr​​Emma​​Poulton,​​who​​has​​conducted​​a​​wealth​
​of​ ​research​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​English​ ​football​ ​and​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​​‘Yid’​​at​​Tottenham​
​Hotspur​ ​matches.​ ​Whilst​ ​providing​ ​an​ ​insight​ ​and​ ​historical​ ​background​ ​to​ ​the​ ​uses​ ​of​​the​
​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​and​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​English​ ​football,​ ​Poulton​ ​and​ ​Durell’s​ ​(2016)​ ​initial​ ​piece​ ​of​
​research,​ ​analysed​ ​data​ ​from​ ​two​ ​unofficial​ ​Tottenham​ ​fan​ ​message​ ​boards​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​the​
​reactions​ ​to​ ​the​ ​‘Y​ ​Word’​ ​campaign,​ ​which​ ​promoted​ ​a​ ​‘zero​ ​tolerance’​​policy​​approach​​to​
​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’.​ ​They​​found​​that​​fans​​had​​a​​sense​​of​​pride​​in​​using​​the​​term​​‘Yid’,​
​whilst​ ​stressing​ ​the​ ​significance​ ​of​ ​the​ ​context​​in​​which​​the​​term​​is​​used,​​claiming​​that​​it​​is​
​more​​acceptable​​at​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​because​​it​​is​​used​​as​​a​​‘badge​​of​​honour’​​and​​to​​‘take​
​away the power of the word’.​


​In​ ​addition,​ ​she​ ​has​ ​aided​ ​academics​ ​in​ ​better​ ​comprehending​ ​the​ ​complex​ ​nature​ ​of​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​the​ ​sport​ ​(Poulton,​​2016).​​By​​using​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​as​​a​​case​​study,​​she​
​illustrates​ ​the​ ​various​ ​usage​ ​and​ ​connotations​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​and​ ​then​ ​proposes​ ​a​
​continuum​ ​that​ ​can​ ​be​ ​utilised​ ​as​ ​an​ ​analytical​ ​framework​ ​to​ ​better​ ​comprehend​
​antisemitism.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​she​ ​examined​ ​policies​ ​and​ ​campaigns​ ​aimed​ ​at​ ​reducing​
​antisemitism​​during​​football​​games​​(Poulton,​​2016).​​By​​gaining​​data​​from​​a​​critical​​review​​of​
​campaign​ ​initiatives​ ​and​ ​eight​ ​interviews​ ​with​ ​elite​ ​stakeholders,​ ​she​ ​discovered​ ​that​
​antisemitism​ ​had​ ​sporadic​ ​salience​ ​in​ ​comparison​ ​to​ ​anti-racism​ ​campaigns​ ​in​ ​general,​
​indicating​ ​a​ ​lack​ ​of​ ​dedication​ ​and​ ​knowledge.​ ​This​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​a​ ​more​


                                                             ​38​
​consistent​ ​and​ ​cohesive​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​combating​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​football.​ ​Her​ ​most​ ​recent​
​piece​ ​of​​work​​from​​2024​​entailed​​life-story​​interviews​​with​​39​​football​​supporters,​​whereby​
​the​ ​conversations​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​within​ ​English​ ​men's​ ​football​
​supporter​​culture.​​She​​found​​that​​Jewish​​football​​supporters​​experienced​​more​​antisemitism​
​within​​their​​football​​culture​​compared​​to​​wider​​society​​and​​that​​they​​tended​​to​​downplay​​or​
​dismiss​ ​antisemitism​ ​as​ ​‘banter’​ ​that​ ​exists​ ​in​ ​English​ ​football​ ​supporter​ ​culture,​ ​in​ ​an​
​attempt to lessen the impact of the hate they experienced.​


​This​​project​​will​​build​​upon​​Poulton’s​​research​​and​​add​​to​​scholarly​​literature​​by​​developing​
​an​​initiative​​with​​the​​aim​​of​​decreasing​​antisemitic​​attitudes.​​Furthermore,​​it​​will​​look​​deeper​
​into​ ​the​ ​strategies​ ​employed​ ​by​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts​ ​to​ ​address​ ​various​ ​forms​ ​of​
​prejudice,​ ​utilising​ ​this​ ​knowledge​ ​to​ ​inform​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​design.​ ​Lastly,​ ​it​ ​will​ ​employ​ ​a​
​range​ ​of​ ​sociological​ ​theories,​ ​including​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020),​ ​to​ ​support​ ​and​ ​analyse​​the​
​research findings.​


​The intersection of rivalry and discrimination in football​


​While​​the​​use​​of​​antisemitic​​language​​is​​widely​​recognised​​as​​harmful,​​it​​is​​often​​employed​​at​
​football​ ​matches​ ​to​ ​provoke​ ​rival​ ​fans​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​to​ ​express​ ​genuine​ ​discriminatory​
​intentions​ ​(Poulton,​ ​2020;​​2024).​​This​​contrasts​​with​​more​​overt​​forms​​of​​antisemitic​​abuse​
​that​​may​​be​​seen​​in​​countries​​like​​Poland​​or​​Germany.​​Sporting​​rivalries​​frequently​​arise​​due​
​to​ ​differences​ ​in​ ​ethnicity,​ ​religion,​ ​politics,​ ​nationality,​ ​and​ ​class​ ​(Curtis,​ ​2019).​ ​Northern​
​Irish​ ​football​ ​provides​ ​a​ ​notable​ ​example,​ ​where​ ​religious​ ​and​ ​political​ ​divisions​ ​have​ ​long​
​shaped​ ​the​ ​sport.​ ​Most​ ​teams​ ​in​ ​Northern​ ​Ireland​ ​are​ ​historically​ ​associated​ ​with​
​Protestantism,​ ​while​ ​Derry​ ​City​ ​Football​ ​Club,​ ​identifying​ ​as​ ​Catholic,​ ​represented​ ​the​
​minority​ ​(Cronin,​ ​2010).​ ​Due​ ​to​ ​escalating​ ​tensions​ ​and​ ​violence,​ ​Derry​ ​City​ ​resigned​​from​
​the​​Northern​​Ireland​​Football​​League​​in​​1972​​(Bairner​​and​​Shirlow,​​2000).​​Similarly,​​sectarian​
​divisions​ ​characterise​ ​football​ ​in​ ​Scotland,​ ​particularly​ ​between​ ​Rangers​ ​Football​ ​Club,​
​identified​ ​as​ ​Protestant,​ ​and​ ​Celtic​​Football​​Club,​​associated​​with​​Catholicism​​(Deuchar​​and​
​Holligan,​​2010;​​Murray,​​1984).​​Beyond​​religion,​​the​​rivalry​​between​​these​​teams​​also​​reflects​
​differences​​in​​national,​​political,​​and​​cultural​​identities​​(May,​​2015).​​Football​​often​​provides​​a​




                                                              ​39​
​platform​ ​for​ ​the​ ​expression​ ​of​​such​​identities,​​resulting​​in​​protests​​and​​violence​​at​​matches​
​(Boyle, 2017; Dickson, Jennings and Koop, 2016; Murray, 1984).​

​A​ ​well-known​ ​football​ ​rivalry​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​is​ ​the​ ​North​ ​London​ ​Derby​ ​between​ ​Tottenham​
​Hotspur​​and​​Arsenal.​​Due​​to​​their​​proximity,​​tensions​​between​​these​​clubs​​are​​strong,​​often​
​leading​ ​to​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​directed​ ​at​ ​Tottenham​ ​supporters​ ​from​ ​rival​ ​teams​ ​such​ ​as​
​Arsenal,​​West​​Ham,​​and​​Chelsea​​(Curtis,​​2019).​​Aston​​Villa​​has​​also​​been​​identified​​as​​a​​club​
​where​ ​hate​ ​crimes,​ ​including​ ​antisemitic​ ​incidents,​ ​were​ ​frequently​ ​reported​ ​during​ ​the​
​2019/2020​ ​season,​ ​with​ ​one​ ​in​ ​every​ ​ten​ ​matches​ ​involving​ ​such​ ​incidents​ ​(de​ ​Menezes,​
​2020).​ ​Opposing​ ​fans​ ​have​​been​​heard​​chanting​​phrases​​such​​as​​“Spurs​​are​​on​​their​​way​​to​
​Auschwitz,”​​and​​making​​references​​to​​gas​​chambers​​and​​Hitler,​​demonstrating​​the​​persistent​
​presence​ ​of​ ​antisemitic​ ​language​ ​in​ ​these​ ​contexts​ ​(Kessel,​ ​2007;​ ​Winner,​ ​2019).​ ​Although​
​these​​chants​​are​​most​​often​​heard​​from​​local​​rivals,​​clubs​​outside​​of​​London​​have​​also​​been​
​involved​​in​​such​​behaviour,​​like​​Southampton,​​who​​have​​similarly​​been​​documented​​chanting​
​antisemitic​​slogans​​toward​​Tottenham​​Hotspur,​​using​​disturbing​​references​​to​​the​​Holocaust​
​(Greenslade, 2019).​

​Interestingly,​​in​​the​​1930s,​​Arsenal​​also​​attracted​​a​​large​​Jewish​​fanbase​​and​​had​​many​​Jewish​
​investors​ ​and​ ​stakeholders​ ​(Clavane,​ ​2012;​ ​Stratton,​ ​2015).​ ​Some​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​Tottenham​
​Hotspur​​no​​longer​​has​​a​​disproportionately​​large​​Jewish​​following​​compared​​to​​other​​London​
​clubs.​​This​​raises​​questions​​as​​to​​why​​clubs​​with​​significant​​Jewish​​connections​​would​​engage​
​in​​antisemitic​​behaviour,​​especially​​considering​​that​​members​​of​​their​​own​​communities​​may​
​find​ ​such​ ​actions​ ​offensive.​ ​Rivalries​ ​between​ ​football​ ​clubs​ ​are​ ​common​ ​and​ ​can​ ​lead​ ​to​
​hostility​​and​​undesirable​​behaviour,​​including​​verbal​​and​​physical​​abuse,​​rioting,​​and​​violence​
​(Curtis,​ ​2019).​ ​Offensive​ ​and​ ​discriminatory​ ​language​ ​is​ ​often​ ​normalised​ ​as​ ​a​ ​means​ ​of​
​taunting​ ​opposing​ ​teams,​ ​with​ ​Poulton​ ​(2021)​ ​making​ ​specific​ ​reference​ ​to​ ​antisemitism.​
​Similarly,​ ​in​ ​her​ ​2024​ ​research,​ ​Poulton​ ​found​ ​that​ ​Jewish​ ​football​ ​supporters​ ​tended​ ​to​
​downplay​​or​​dismiss​​antisemitism​​as​​‘banter’​​that​​exists​​in​​English​​football​​supporter​​culture.​
​Therefore,​ ​some​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​antisemitic​​rhetoric​​in​​football​​may​​be​​used​​to​​assert​​collective​
​identity and express rivalry rather than actual prejudice.​

​However,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​acknowledge​ ​that​ ​antisemitic​ ​incidents​ ​at​ ​football​ ​matches​
​typically​ ​involve​ ​only​ ​a​ ​minority​ ​of​ ​supporters.​ ​Many​​fans​​do​​not​​participate​​in​​or​​condone​


                                                          ​40​
​such​ ​behaviour,​ ​and​ ​not​ ​all​ ​who​ ​engage​ ​in​ ​these​ ​chants​ ​necessarily​ ​harbour​ ​genuine​
​antisemitic​ ​beliefs​ ​(Curtis,​ ​2019;​ ​Poulton,​ ​2016).​ ​While​ ​some​ ​fans​ ​may​ ​defend​ ​their​
​comments​ ​as​ ​‘banter’​ ​and​ ​claim​ ​that​ ​no​ ​harm​ ​is​ ​intended​​(Poulton,​​2024),​​antisemitism​​in​
​any​​form​​is​​unacceptable.​​Such​​remarks​​can​​cause​​significant​​distress​​and​​upset,​​not​​only​​to​
​Jewish people but also to others within society.​

​As​ ​this​ ​project​ ​intends​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​an​ ​initiative​ ​to​ ​reduce​ ​antisemitism​​in​​football,​​the​​next​
​passage​ ​introduces​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives​ ​in​ ​sports,​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​tackle​ ​and​ ​reduce​
​discrimination​ ​in​ ​sport,​ ​whilst​ ​creating​ ​a​ ​more​ ​equal,​ ​diverse,​ ​and​ ​inclusive​ ​environment.​
​Before​ ​discussing​ ​these​ ​initiatives,​ ​it's​ ​important​ ​to​ ​define​ ​discrimination.​ ​Link​ ​and​ ​Phelan​
​(2001,​ ​p.​ ​367)​ ​describe​ ​discrimination​ ​as​ ​“distinguishing​ ​between​ ​human​ ​differences,​
​conferring​ ​negative​ ​value​ ​on​ ​some​ ​types​ ​of​ ​difference,​ ​and​ ​treating​ ​people​ ​unjustly​ ​as​ ​a​
​result​​by​​drawing​​on​​social​​and​​economic​​power.”​​Discrimination​​occurs​​when​​individuals​​or​
​groups​ ​are​ ​treated​ ​unfairly​ ​based​​on​​identity​​markers​​such​​as​​skin​​colour,​​gender,​​sexuality,​
​or​ ​disability​ ​(Kilvington​ ​and​ ​Price,​ ​2018a).​ ​Additional​ ​markers​​include​​religious​​attire​​(Peek,​
​2005),​ ​accents​ ​and​ ​names​ ​(Kiely,​ ​Bechhofer,​ ​Stewart​ ​and​ ​McCrone,​ ​2001),​ ​which​ ​form​
​integral​ ​parts​ ​of​ ​a​ ​person’s​ ​identity​ ​(Cumper​ ​and​ ​Lewis,​ ​2018).​ ​Sadly,​ ​these​ ​markers​ ​often​
​make​ ​individuals​ ​vulnerable​ ​to​ ​discrimination.​ ​Discrimination​ ​is​ ​a​ ​persistent​ ​issue​ ​in​ ​sport,​
​requiring​ ​effective​ ​responses​ ​from​ ​organisations​ ​(MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin,​ ​2018).​ ​Therefore,​
​the next section will critically evaluate measures aimed at combating discrimination in sport.​

​The role of sports in shaping attitudes toward discrimination​

​There​ ​are​ ​often​ ​claims​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​a​ ​powerful​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​fostering​ ​unity,​ ​tolerance,​ ​and​
​understanding​ ​(Marivoet,​ ​2014).​ ​As​ ​Kidd​ ​(2008)​ ​notes,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​the​ ​unique​ ​ability​ ​to​ ​bring​
​people​ ​together​ ​at​ ​both​ ​local​ ​and​ ​international​ ​levels,​ ​transcending​ ​boundaries​ ​of​ ​race,​
​gender,​​age,​​sexual​​orientation,​​and​​religion​​(Hartmann,​​2000;​​MacIntosh​​and​​Martin,​​2018).​
​A​ ​clear​ ​example​ ​of​ ​this​ ​is​ ​cricket's​ ​role​ ​in​ ​promoting​ ​peace​​between​​India​​and​​Pakistan,​​as​
​highlighted​ ​by​ ​Shahid​​(2015),​​illustrating​​sport's​​capacity​​to​​contribute​​to​​reconciliation​​and​
​social​ ​change.​ ​By​ ​emphasising​ ​shared​ ​values​ ​and​ ​common​ ​goals,​ ​sport​ ​can​ ​bridge​ ​cultural​
​and ethnic divides (United Nations, 2003).​




                                                            ​41​
​Sport’s​ ​inclusive​ ​nature​ ​allows​ ​people​ ​from​ ​diverse​ ​backgrounds​ ​to​​participate​​and​​engage​
​(Schaillée,​ ​Haudenhuyse​ ​and​ ​Bradt,​ ​2019).​ ​Beyond​ ​participation,​ ​sport​ ​has​ ​the​
​transformative​ ​power,​ ​helping​ ​to​ ​address​ ​a​ ​wide​ ​range​​of​​societal​​challenges.​​This​​includes​
​promoting​​gender​​equity​​(Higgins​​and​​Randell,​​2007),​​reducing​​gang​​violence​​(McMahon​​and​
​Belur,​​2013),​​and​​fostering​​inclusion​​for​​individuals​​with​​disabilities​​(Kiuppis,​​2016).​​Due​​to​​its​
​competitive​ ​nature​ ​and​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​teamwork,​ ​sport​ ​provides​ ​a​​unique​​platform​​to​​engage​​in​
​meaningful​ ​discussions​ ​around​ ​inequality​ ​and​ ​how​ ​to​ ​combat​ ​it​ ​(MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin,​
​2018).​ ​From​ ​grassroots​ ​initiatives​ ​to​​international​​events,​​sport​​plays​​a​​vital​​role​​in​​building​
​peaceful, inclusive communities (Giulianotti, 2011).​

​Despite​​these​​positive​​outcomes,​​Anderson​​and​​White​​(2017)​​caution​​that​​sport​​is​​not​​always​
​beneficial​ ​for​ ​social​ ​change.​ ​Issues​ ​like​ ​women’s​ ​oppression,​ ​homophobia,​ ​and​ ​the​
​normalisation​​of​​violence,​​particularly​​in​​sports​​such​​as​​boxing​​and​​American​​football,​​which​
​pose​ ​serious​ ​health​ ​risks,​ ​are​ ​significant​ ​concerns.​ ​Moreover,​ ​Wood​ ​(2013)​ ​points​​out​​that​
​sport​​can​​also​​provide​​a​​platform​​for​​negative​​behaviours,​​including​​hostility​​and​​aggression.​
​Discrimination​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​be​ ​a​ ​major​ ​issue,​ ​affecting​ ​participants​​and​​spectators​​alike​​on​
​the​ ​basis​ ​of​ ​race,​ ​gender,​ ​sexual​ ​orientation,​ ​disability,​ ​and​ ​religion,​ ​which​ ​creates​ ​an​
​unwelcoming​ ​environment​ ​and​ ​discourages​ ​participation​ ​(Waldron,​ ​2016).​ ​Racism​
​(Farrington​ ​et​ ​al​.,​ ​2017),​ ​transphobia​ ​(Hargie,​ ​Mitchell​ ​and​ ​Somerville,​ ​2017),​ ​and​ ​ableism​
​(Brittain,​ ​Biscaia​ ​and​ ​Gérard,​ ​2020)​ ​are​ ​amongst​ ​a​ ​range​ ​of​ ​issues​ ​still​ ​prevalent​ ​in​ ​sport,​
​prompting the development of initiatives to raise awareness.​

​Kilvington​ ​and​ ​Price​ ​(2018a)​ ​emphasise​ ​that​ ​discrimination​ ​occurs​ ​on​ ​multiple​ ​levels​ ​and​
​must​ ​be​ ​addressed​ ​accordingly.​ ​With​ ​this​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​the​ ​past​ ​three​ ​decades​ ​have​ ​seen​ ​the​
​development​ ​of​ ​numerous​ ​initiatives​ ​aimed​ ​at​ ​making​ ​sport,​ ​particularly​ ​football,​ ​more​
​inclusive​ ​(Magrath​ ​and​ ​Stott,​ ​2019).​ ​Magrath​ ​and​ ​Stott​ ​(2019,​ ​p.​ ​19)​ ​note​ ​that​
​“anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives​ ​have​ ​been​ ​part​ ​of​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​change​ ​in​ ​English​ ​football,”​
​highlighting​ ​their​ ​potential​ ​effectiveness​ ​when​ ​properly​ ​implemented.​ ​They​ ​discuss​ ​the​
​impact​ ​of​ ​initiatives​ ​and​ ​organisations,​ ​such​ ​as​​Kick​​It​​Out,​​Stonewall​​and​​Show​​Racism​​the​
​Red​​Card,​​on​​changing​​attitudes​​among​​fans,​​players,​​and​​clubs,​​reflecting​​a​​broader​​societal​
​shift​ ​towards​ ​greater​ ​acceptance​ ​and​ ​equality​ ​within​ ​football.​ ​Key​ ​institutions​ ​involved​ ​in​
​these​ ​efforts​ ​include​ ​nation-states,​ ​NGOs,​ ​intergovernmental​ ​organisations,​ ​international​
​sport​​federations,​​and​​grassroots​​community​​groups​​(Giulianotti,​​2011).​​However,​​Kilvington​


                                                             ​42​
​and​​Price​​(2018a)​​argue​​that​​despite​​the​​development​​of​​campaigns​​aimed​​at​​educating​​and​
​raising​​awareness​​about​​various​​forms​​of​​discrimination,​​it​​remains​​a​​deeply​​ingrained​​issue​
​within sport.​

​This​ ​section​ ​will​ ​examine​ ​various​ ​types​ ​of​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives,​ ​assessing​ ​their​
​successes​ ​and​ ​challenges​ ​through​ ​an​ ​analysis​​of​​both​​current​​and​​historical​​programmes​​in​
​the​ ​realm​ ​of​ ​sport.​ ​The​ ​research​ ​identifies​ ​four​ ​distinct​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​initiatives:​ ​symbolic​
​gestures,​ ​educational​ ​programmes,​ ​media​ ​campaigns,​ ​and​ ​community​ ​integration​ ​efforts.​
​The​ ​subsequent​ ​discussion​ ​will​ ​be​ ​organised​ ​accordingly​ ​into​ ​four​ ​sub-themes,​ ​each​
​highlighting one of these distinct types of anti-discrimination initiatives.​

​Symbolic anti-discrimination initiatives​


​Sport​ ​serves​ ​as​ ​a​ ​powerful​ ​medium​ ​for​ ​promoting​ ​campaigns​ ​aimed​ ​at​ ​reducing​
​discrimination,​ ​both​ ​within​ ​sport​ ​itself​ ​and​ ​in​ ​broader​ ​society​ ​(Carrington,​ ​2010).​ ​Boykoff​
​(2017)​ ​highlights​ ​how​ ​sport​ ​can​ ​positively​ ​influence​ ​politics​ ​and​ ​society,​ ​leading​ ​to​​various​
​symbolic​​campaigns​​designed​​to​​combat​​prejudice.​​One​​notable​​example​​is​​the​​‘Black​​Power’​
​salute​ ​by​​Tommie​​Smith​​and​​John​​Carlos​​during​​the​​1968​​Olympics,​​where​​they​​raised​​their​
​gloved​​fists​​to​​protest​​poverty,​​injustice,​​and​​inequality​​(Boykoff,​​2017).​​O'Bonsawin​​(2015,​​p.​
​203)​ ​describes​ ​this​ ​moment​ ​as​ ​“a​ ​well-defined,​ ​self-conscious,​ ​culturally​ ​oriented,​ ​and​
​collectively​​driven​​attempt​​to​​use​​sport​​as​​a​​medium​​for​​political​​and​​racial​​protest.”​​Despite​
​facing​ ​dismissal​ ​from​ ​the​ ​Olympics​ ​and​ ​backlash​ ​from​ ​the​ ​media,​ ​this​ ​act​ ​of​ ​defiance​ ​has​
​become​ ​one​ ​of​ ​the​ ​most​ ​memorable​ ​images​ ​in​ ​sports​ ​history​ ​(Smith,​​2011).​​In​​addition​​to​
​this​ ​historical​ ​example,​​contemporary​​initiatives​​illustrate​​how​​sport​​can​​advocate​​for​​social​
​justice.​ ​These​ ​include​ ​taking​ ​a​ ​knee​ ​in​ ​support​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Black​ ​Lives​​Matter​​(BLM)​​movement​
​(Hylton,​ ​2021),​ ​the​ ​Stonewall​ ​Rainbow​ ​Laces​ ​campaign​ ​promoting​​inclusivity​​for​​the​​LGBT+​
​community​ ​(Hansen​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2023;​ ​Magrath​ ​and​ ​Stott,​ ​2019),​ ​and​ ​the​ ​‘No​​Room​​for​​Racism’​
​badges​ ​worn​ ​by​ ​Premier​ ​League​ ​players​ ​to​ ​show​ ​their​ ​commitment​ ​to​ ​combating​ ​racism​
​(Premier​ ​League,​ ​2020).​ ​These​ ​examples​ ​demonstrate​ ​that​ ​sports​ ​can​ ​be​ ​an​ ​influential​
​platform for raising awareness and promoting positive change in society.​


​Similar​​to​​Smith​​and​​Carlos,​​Colin​​Kaepernick​​used​​his​​platform​​in​​sport​​to​​highlight​​the​​unfair​
​mistreatment​​of​​people​​of​​colour​​in​​the​​US.​​The​​concept​​of​​‘taking​​a​​knee’​​began​​in​​2016​​by​


                                                           ​43​
​Kaepernick​ ​who​ ​was​ ​protesting​​for​​fairer​​treatment​​of​​Black​​Americans.​​‘ Taking​​a​​knee’​​is​​a​
​silent​ ​and​ ​peaceful​ ​means​ ​of​ ​protesting​ ​against the​ ​unfair​ ​abuse​ ​and​ ​social​ ​injustices​ ​the​
​African-American​ ​community​ ​receive​ ​(Walker,​ ​Taylor​ ​and​ ​Chansky,​ ​2021).​ ​His​ ​campaign​
​began​​in​​the​​USA,​​whereby​​he​​knelt​​during​​the​​national​​anthem,​​and​​was​​of​​major​​discussion​
​and​ ​controversy​ ​in​ ​the​ ​states.​ ​NFL​​athletes,​​including​​high​​school​​players​​began​​kneeling​​at​
​matches​ ​to​ ​utilise​ ​their​ ​platform​ ​for​ ​social​ ​activism​ ​(McNeal,​ ​2017).​ ​Trimbur​ ​(2019)​ ​states​
​that​​in​​today’s​​society,​​‘taking​​a​​knee’​​has​​been​​used​​as​​a​​symbol​​of​​challenging​​racism.​​The​
​symbolic​ ​action​ ​of​ ​kneeling​ ​became​ ​a​ ​global​ ​concept​ ​in​ ​2020,​ ​when​ ​George​ ​Floyd,​ ​an​
​African-American​ ​was​ ​killed​ ​whilst​ ​being​ ​arrested​ ​for​ ​allegedly​ ​using​ ​a​ ​counterfeit​ ​bill.​
​Protests​ ​began​ ​in​ ​the​ ​USA​ ​and​ ​eventually​ ​spread​ ​across​ ​the​ ​borders​ ​and​ ​into​ ​multiple​
​continents,​ ​including​ ​the​​UK​​(Barrie,​​2020).​​Furthermore,​​athletes​​worldwide​​took​​the​​knee​
​before​​matches,​​igniting​​a​​new​​wave​​of​​athlete​​activism​​and​​demonstrating​​their​​support​​for​
​anti-racism​​(Walker,​​Taylor​​and​​Chansky,​​2021).​​‘ Taking​​the​​knee’​​serves​​as​​a​​significant​​social​
​and​ ​political​ ​statement​ ​that​ ​signifies​ ​a​ ​stand​​against​​racism,​​extending​​beyond​​sports​​to​​all​
​aspects​​of​​society​​(Dixon,​​Cashmore​​and​​Cleland,​​2023).​​While​​some​​view​​it​​as​​an​​important​
​statement,​ ​others​ ​question​ ​its​ ​effectiveness.​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​whilst​ ​England​ ​Captain,​ ​Harry​
​Kane,​ ​believed​ ​that​ ​‘taking​ ​a​​knee'​​is​​a​​vital​​symbol​​which​​can​​educate​​young​​children​​on​​a​
​global​ ​scale​ ​(BBC​ ​Sport,​ ​2020a),​ ​Les​ ​Ferdinand,​ ​Director​ ​of​ ​Queens​ ​Park​ ​Rangers​ ​Football​
​Club,​​highlighted​​that​​the​​original​​early​​impact​​of​​‘taking​​a​​knee’​​has​​been​​diluted,​​and​​that​
​its message has now been lost (Kershaw, 2020).​


​Another​ ​symbolic​ ​initiative​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​football​ ​is​ ​the​ ​wearing​ ​of​​‘No​​Room​​for​​Racism'​​badges​
​organised​ ​by​ ​Premier​ ​League​ ​to​ ​show​ ​that​ ​officials​ ​and​ ​players​ ​are​ ​supporting​ ​the​ ​fight​
​against​ ​racial​ ​abuse​ ​and​ ​discrimination​ ​throughout​ ​the​ ​2020/21​ ​season​ ​(Premier​ ​League,​
​2020).​ ​Players​ ​and​ ​officials​ ​wore​ ​badges​​throughout​​the​​season,​​continuously​​showing​​fans​
​that​ ​the​ ​Premier​ ​League​ ​are​ ​fully​​committed​​to​​tackling​​the​​issue​​of​​racism.​​They​​believe​​it​
​will​ ​encourage​ ​fans,​ ​and​ ​watchers​ ​to​ ​change​ ​their​ ​behaviour​ ​and​ ​report​ ​acts​ ​of​ ​racism​
​(Premier​ ​League,​ ​2020).​ ​Likewise,​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​produced​ ​t-shirts​ ​for​ ​players​ ​to​ ​wear​ ​to​
​advertise​​and​​show​​support​​for​​their​​campaign,​​in​​hope​​that​​it​​would​​reduce​​discrimination.​
​Although​ ​this​ ​does​ ​make​ ​viewers​ ​and​ ​supporters​ ​more​ ​knowledgeable​​of​​the​​organisation,​
​Raheem​​Sterling​​emphasises​​that​​it’s​​not​​making​​a​​big​​enough​​impact:​​“a​​few​​times​​they​​get​
​us​ ​to​ ​wear​ ​a​ ​t-shirt,​ ​but​ ​it’s​ ​not​ ​enough”​ ​(Poulton,​ ​2020,​ ​p.​ ​7).​ ​Furthermore,​ ​Crystal​


                                                           ​44​
​Palace’s player, Wilfried​ ​Zaha, said​ ​"The​ ​whole​ ​kneeling​ ​down​ ​-​ ​why​ ​must​ ​I​ ​kneel​ ​down​​for​
​you​​to​​show​​that​​we​​matter?​​Why​​must​​I​​even​​wear​​Black​​Lives​​Matter​​on​​the​​back​​of​​my​​top​
​to​ ​show​ ​you​ ​that​ ​we​ ​matter?​ ​This​ ​is​ ​all​ ​degrading​ ​stuff”​​(Netherton,​​2021,​​p.​​1).​​As​​Zaha's​
​comments​​show,​​members​​of​​marginalised​​groups​​can​​find​​symbolic​​actions​​demeaning​​and​
​insulting.​ ​Symbolic​ ​acts,​ ​according​ ​to​ ​players​ ​and​ ​staff,​ ​are​​inadequate​​and,​​as​​a​​result,​​are​
​not considered the best tool for combating discriminatory conduct.​


​As​ ​Hylton​ ​(2010)​ ​states​ ​anti-racism​ ​initiatives​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​are​ ​often​ ​responses​ ​to​ ​high​ ​profile​
​incidents.​ ​When​ ​the​ ​death​ ​of​ ​teenager​ ​Stephen​ ​Lawrence​ ​occurred​ ​in​ ​1993,​ ​sporting​
​authorities​ ​were​ ​pressured​ ​to​ ​act​ ​accordingly​ ​and​ ​show​​that​​they​​were​​publicly​​supporting​
​and​ ​responding​ ​to​ ​the​ ​issue​ ​of​ ​racism​ ​(Cleland​ ​and​ ​Cashmore,​ ​2014).​ ​Attempts​​to​​support​
​racism​ ​should​ ​be​ ​ongoing,​ ​not​ ​only​ ​when​ ​a​ ​high-profile​ ​case​ ​occurs.​ ​Subsequently,​ ​it​ ​has​
​been​​argued​​by​​Taylor​​(2018)​​that​​not enough is​​being​​done​​by​​organisations​​to​​tackle​​racism​
​and​ ​racist​ ​abuse​ ​in​ ​sport.​ ​Additionally,​ ​Hylton​ ​(2018)​ ​believes​ ​that​ ​the​ ​reactive​ ​and​
​historically​​uninformed​​approach​​taken​​by​​some​​organisations,​​such​​as​​the​​FA​​and​​FIFA,​​limits​
​the​ ​effectiveness​ ​of​ ​combating​ ​their​ ​own​ ​institutional​ ​racism.​ ​Athletes​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Ferdinand,​
​Zaha,​ ​and​ ​Sterling​ ​are​ ​among​ ​those​​who​​recognise​​that​​symbolic​​initiatives​​will​​not​​make​​a​
​significant​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​global​ ​issues​ ​such​ ​as​ ​racism.​ ​Overall,​ ​the​ ​effectiveness​ ​of​ ​symbolic​
​anti-racism initiatives has been questioned.​


​‘Kick​ ​It​ ​Out’,​ ​previously​ ​known​ ​as​ ​‘Let’s​ ​Kick​ ​Racism​ ​Out​​of​​Football’​​(Bennett​​and​​Jonsson,​
​2017)​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​eliminate​ ​all​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination,​​including​​racism​​and​​homophobia,​​and​
​support​​inclusive​​practice​​within​​sport.​​It​​has​​been​​described​​as​​being​​“widely​​recognised​​as​
​English​ ​football's​ ​leading​ ​equality​ ​and​ ​inclusion​ ​organisation​ ​and​ ​is​ ​active​ ​at​ ​every​ ​level​​of​
​football”​ ​(Penfold​ ​and​ ​Cleland,​​2022,​​p.176).​​To​​tackle​​discrimination,​​the​​organisation​​uses​
​symbolic,​​media-based​​and​​educational​​initiatives.​​Kick​​It​​Out​​is​​operated​​autonomously​​but​
​is​ ​largely​ ​financed​ ​by​ ​the​​Premier​​League,​​the​​FA​​and​​the​​PFA;​​in​​2017,​​they​​receive​​a​​total​
​annual​​income​​of​​£811,000​​(Kilvington​​and​​Price,​​2017).​​However,​​more​​recent​​figures​​show​
​that​​they​​received​​£2,147,307​​in​​the​​financial​​year​​of​​2023​​(Charity​​Commission​​for​​England​

​and​​Wales,​​2023).​ ​Considering​​the​​Premier​​League​​clubs​​make​​annual​​revenues​​of​​over​​£3.6​

​billion,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​FA​ ​have​ ​invested​ ​over​ ​£125​ ​million​ ​into​ ​football​ ​during​ ​the​ ​2016/2017​



                                                             ​45​
​season,​ ​authors​ ​and​ ​scholars,​ ​including​ ​Kilvington​ ​and​ ​Price​ ​(2017),​ ​Bennett​ ​and​ ​Jonsson​
​(2017)​​and​​Taylor​​(2018),​​argue​​that​​an​​increase​​in​​funding​​could​​be​​given,​​as​​this​​funding​​is​
​not​​enough​​to​​tackle​​the​​greater​​issue​​of​​discrimination​​within​​football.​​Furthermore,​​in​​2021​
​Sky​ ​confirmed​ ​that​ ​they​ ​will​ ​be​ ​forming​ ​a​ ​partnership​ ​with​ ​Kick​ ​It​​Out​​to​​help​​fight​​racism​
​and​ ​discrimination.​ ​Over​ ​the​ ​next​ ​three​ ​years,​ ​they​ ​will​ ​give​ ​funds​ ​of​ ​£3​ ​million​ ​to​​ensure​
​that​​reporting​​incidents​​of​​discrimination​​becomes​​easier​​for​​football​​fans.​​The​​£3​​million​​will​
​be a combination of both cash and ‘value in kind support’ (Sky Sport, 2021).​


​Given​​the​​popularity​​and​​success​​of​​football​​a​​greater​​fund​​could​​be​​given​​to​​support​​racism​
​in​​football,​​it​​raises​​the​​question​​of​​how​​seriously​​the​​governing​​bodies​​of​​football​​are​​taking​
​the​ ​issue​ ​of​ ​protecting​ ​both​​fans​​and​​players​​from​​discrimination.​​As​​recognised​​by​​Cleland​
​and​​Cashmore​​(2016)​​and​​Garland​​and​​Rowe​​(1999),​​Kick​​It​​Out​​has​​had​​positive​​impacts​​on​
​discrimination,​ ​mainly​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​racism,​ ​within​ ​football.​ ​Although​ ​their​ ​efforts​ ​do​ ​not​ ​go​
​unnoticed​​and​​they​​are​​heading​​in​​the​​right​​direction,​​they​​have​​been​​criticised​​for​​not​​doing​
​enough​ ​(Bennett​ ​and​ ​Jonsson,​ ​2017).​ ​Back​ ​et​ ​al​ ​(2001)​ ​argues​ ​that​ ​the​ ​FA’s​ ​actions​ ​in​
​contributing​ ​to​ ​combating​ ​racism​ ​have​ ​little​ ​impact​ ​and​ ​that​ ​instead,​ ​their​ ​attempts​ ​were​
​merely for public image rather than to tackle the issues at hand.​


​Penfold​​and​​Cleland​​(2022),​​who​​highlight​​that​​English​​football​​authorities​​should​​boost​​their​
​support​​for​​anti-racism​​organisations,​​most​​notably​​Kick​​it​​Out,​​also​​emphasised​​the​​need​​for​
​stronger​​funding​​for​​Kick​​It​​Out.​​Their​​research​​explored,​​through​​the​​use​​of​​online​​surveys,​
​football​​fans​​perceptions​​of​​Kick​​It​​Out​​and​​the​​impact​​it​​has​​within​​the​​field​​of​​football.​​902​
​participants​ ​took​ ​part​ ​in​ ​the​ ​survey,​ ​of​ ​which​ ​96%​​of​​them​​identified​​as​​White.​​83%​​of​​the​
​fans​ ​believed​ ​that​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​had​ ​only​ ​been​ ​moderately​ ​effective​ ​in​ ​challenging​​racism.​​In​
​addition,​​Penfold​​and​​Cleland​​(2022)​​found​​that​​there​​was​​a​​lack​​of​​fan​​engagement​​with​​Kick​
​It​ ​Out,​ ​in​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​lacking​ ​interaction​ ​with​ ​the​​fans.​​Finally,​​fans​​felt​​that​​the​
​club​ ​lacked​ ​resources​​and​​authority​​to​​address​​such​​issues,​​and​​69%​​of​​fans​​felt​​that​​Kick​​It​
​Out​​needed​​to​​change​​the​​way​​they​​are​​challenging​​racism.​ ​In​​agreement​​with​​the​​fans​​was,​
​the​​chair​​of​​Kick​​It​​Out,​​Sanjay​​Bhandari​​believes​​"We​​all​​need​​to​​do​​more,​​and​​we​​all​​need​​to​
​take a stand against discrimination” (BBC Sport, 2020b).​




                                                                ​46​
​Switching​​focus​​to​​the​​issue​​of​​LGBT+​​rights,​​symbolic​​initiatives​​have​​also​​been​​evident.​​The​
​Stonewall​ ​Rainbow​ ​Laces​ ​campaign​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​improve​ ​LGBT+​ ​inclusion​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​support​
​athletes​ ​who​ ​may​ ​feel​ ​pressured​ ​to​ ​express​ ​their​ ​sexuality​ ​(Lawley,​ ​2019).​ ​This​ ​symbolic​
​initiative​ ​involves​ ​athletes​ ​wearing​ ​rainbow​​laces​​within​​their​​boots​​to​​raise​​awareness​​and​
​influence​ ​conversations​ ​regarding​ ​inclusivity​ ​for​ ​LGBT+​ ​individuals​ ​within​ ​sport​ ​(Lawley,​
​2019).​​It​​also​​includes​​a​​range​​of​​different​​advertisements,​​including​​television​​and​​screens​​at​
​football​​stadiums​​to​​increase​​its​​impact.​​Research​​from​​Hansen​​et​​al.​​(2023)​​explored​​Twitter​
​users'​ ​responses​ ​to​ ​the​ ​English​ ​Premier​ ​League's​ ​(EPL)​ ​support​ ​for​ ​the​ ​Rainbow​ ​Laces​
​campaign,​​highlighting​​the​​engagement​​metrics​​from​​four​​official​​tweets.​​They​​revealed​​that​
​there​ ​were​ ​24,997​ ​‘likes’,​ ​4,951​ ​retweets,​ ​236​ ​supportive​ ​comments​ ​compared​ ​to​ ​171​
​negative​ ​ones.​ ​They​ ​concluded​ ​that​ ​of​ ​the​ ​26​ ​million​ ​followers​ ​the​ ​EPL’s​ ​official​ ​Twitter​
​account​ ​have,​ ​this​ ​showed​ ​very​ ​little​ ​engagement.​ ​The​ ​BBC​ ​(2017)​ ​have​ ​also​ ​critiqued​ ​the​
​Rainbow​​Laces​​campaign,​​stating​​that​​it​​needs​​to​​be​​a​​sustained​​effort​​over​​a​​longer​​period​​of​
​time,​ ​rather​ ​than​​the​​short​​commitment​​of​​one​​week.​ ​Furthermore,​​research​​by​​Stonewall​
​(n.d.)​​found​​that​​56%​​of​​sport​​fans​​agree​​that​​more​​needs​​to​​be​​done,​​alongside​​the​​Rainbow​
​Laces,​ ​to​ ​create​ ​a​ ​more​ ​accepting​ ​place​ ​for​ ​LGBT+​ ​people.​ ​To​ ​promote​ ​inclusivity​ ​for​ ​the​
​LGBT+​ ​community​ ​in​ ​sport,​ ​O’Brien,​ ​Shovelton​ ​and​​Latner​​(2013)​​recognises​​that​​there​​is​​a​
​need​ ​for​ ​initiatives​ ​which​ ​address​ ​psychosocial​ ​factors,​ ​including​ ​the​ ​social​ ​factors​ ​and​
​individual​ ​thoughts​ ​and​ ​behaviours​ ​that​ ​reinforce​ ​this​ ​prejudice.​ ​Similarly,​ ​research​
​conducted​ ​by​ ​Denison​ ​and​​Kitchen​​(2015)​​found​​that​​schools,​​coaches​​and​​parents​​need​​to​
​begin​ ​discussions​ ​surrounding​ ​homophobia​ ​earlier​ ​and​ ​that​ ​there​ ​should​ ​be​ ​major​ ​public​
​education​​campaigns​​to​​improve​​acceptance​​of​​LGBT+​​people​​in​​wider​​society.​​Although​​the​
​Rainbow​ ​Laces​ ​do​ ​reinforce​ ​that​ ​athletes​ ​support​ ​LGBT+​ ​rights​ ​and​ ​brings​ ​the​ ​issue​ ​of​
​homophobia​ ​to​ ​attention,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​also​ ​recognised​ ​by​ ​scholars,​ ​including​ ​Blaise​ ​(2009)​ ​and​
​Jennett​ ​(2009)​ ​that​ ​homophobic​ ​attitudes​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​challenged​ ​and​ ​that​ ​younger​
​generations need to be educated so that overtime we develop a more accepting society.​


​In​ ​general,​ ​symbolic​ ​efforts​ ​in​ ​sports​​have​​been​​employed​​to​​address​​discrimination​​and​​to​
​increase​​awareness​​of​​political​​and​​social​​issues,​​such​​as​​racial​​bias​​and​​homophobia.​​Kilcline​
​(2017)​​raises​​the​​question​​of​​whether​​campaigns​​in​​sports​​genuinely​​promote​​social​​change​
​or​ ​if​ ​they​ ​merely​ ​trivialise​ ​significant​ ​social​ ​issues,​ ​despite​ ​their​ ​role​ ​in​ ​raising​ ​awareness.​
​Feedback​ ​from​ ​athletes​ ​has​ ​been​ ​considered,​ ​revealing​ ​that​ ​some​ ​do​ ​not​ ​view​ ​these​


                                                              ​47​
​symbolic​ ​actions​ ​as​ ​fully​ ​beneficial​ ​and​ ​have​ ​even​ ​described​ ​them​ ​as​ ​humiliating.​
​Furthermore,​ ​according​ ​to​ ​Hylton​ ​(2010),​ ​sport​ ​organisations​ ​have​ ​been​ ​accused​ ​of​ ​being​
​tokenistic​​rather​​than​​providing​​realistic​​actions​​that​​are​​sufficient​​to​​make​​progress.​​Some​​of​
​these​ ​short-term​ ​measures​ ​may​ ​not​​have​​a​​long-term​​effect,​​according​​to​​Pedersen​​(2005),​
​who​ ​claims​ ​that​ ​in​ ​order​ ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​long-term​ ​impact,​ ​initiatives​ ​must​ ​have​ ​viability​ ​and​
​commitment,​ ​which​ ​means​ ​that​ ​organisations​ ​must​ ​use​ ​funding​​and​​facilities​​in​​a​​way​​that​
​will​ ​have​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​impact.​ ​Kneeling​ ​for​​the​​BLM,​​on​​the​​other​​hand,​​has​​been​​criticised​
​for​ ​losing​ ​its​ ​message​ ​and​ ​intent,​ ​indicating​ ​that​ ​persistence​ ​might​ ​not​ ​be​ ​the​ ​solution.​ ​If​
​symbolic​ ​interventions​ ​are​ ​insufficient,​ ​other​ ​initiatives​ ​with​ ​a​ ​greater​ ​effect​ ​on​
​discrimination​ ​will​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​adopted,​ ​which​ ​may​ ​take​ ​the​ ​form​ ​of​ ​education​ ​or​
​media-based initiatives.​


​Educational anti-discrimination initiatives​


​The​ ​European​ ​Union​ ​Agency​ ​for​ ​Fundamental​ ​Rights​ ​(2010)​ ​emphasises​ ​that​ ​incidents​ ​of​
​racism,​ ​including​ ​antisemitism,​ ​are​ ​most​ ​prevalent​ ​in​​both​​professional​​and​​amateur​​men’s​
​football,​​with​​fans​​often​​being​​the​​primary​​perpetrators.​​They​​argue​​for​​increased​​investment​
​in​ ​social​ ​and​​educational​​measures​​to​​effectively​​combat​​racism​​in​​sports.​​It​​is​​important​​to​
​recognise​ ​that​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​educational​ ​approaches​ ​can​ ​be​ ​referred​ ​to​ ​by​ ​various​
​terms,​​including​​anti-racism,​​anti-bias,​​diversity,​​and​​intercultural​​education​​(Moustakas​​and​
​Kalina,​ ​2023).​ ​In​ ​response​ ​to​ ​this​ ​issue,​ ​numerous​ ​organisations​ ​have​ ​implemented​
​anti-racism​ ​educational​ ​and​ ​training​ ​workshops​ ​aimed​ ​at​ ​addressing​ ​racism​ ​and​
​discrimination​ ​(Solomos,​ ​2020).​ ​For​ ​instance,​ ​Show​ ​Racism​ ​the​ ​Red​ ​Card,​ ​the​ ​UK’s​ ​largest​
​educational​ ​charity​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​combating​ ​racism​ ​in​ ​football,​ ​offers​ ​educational​ ​workshops​
​for​​students​​aged​​eight​​to​​eighteen,​​where​​educators​​engage​​with​​young​​people​​throughout​
​the​ ​day​ ​to​ ​discuss​ ​the​ ​topic​​of​​racism.​​Additionally,​​they​​provide​​a​​one-day​​training​​session​
​and​​online​​training​​comprising​​four​​modules.​​These​​resources​​enable​​classroom​​teachers​​to​
​enhance​​their​​knowledge​​and​​equip​​them​​with​​the​​tools​​to​​challenge​​racist​​attitudes​​(Dixon,​
​Lowes​​and​​Gibbons,​​2016;​​Show​​Racism​​the​​Red​​Card,​​n.d.).​​Literature​​from​​Kingett,​​Abrams​
​and​​Purewal​​(2017)​​found​​that,​​post-initiative,​​there​​was​​an​​increase​​in​​the​​number​​of​​young​
​participants​ ​who​ ​provided​ ​‘ideal’​ ​responses​ ​to​ ​all​ ​the​ ​questions,​ ​while​ ​those​ ​answering​​all​
​questions with ‘non-ideal’ responses decreased from 16.4% to 9.2%.​


                                                              ​48​
​Similarly,​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​has​ ​developed​ ​educational​ ​initiatives​ ​that​ ​help​ ​individuals,​ ​including​
​children​ ​and​ ​college​ ​students,​ ​foster​ ​awareness​ ​of​ ​equality​ ​and​ ​inclusion​ ​in​ ​football​ ​and​
​society​ ​at​ ​large.​ ​They​ ​offer​ ​downloadable​ ​toolkits​ ​and​ ​resources​ ​on​ ​their​ ​website,​ ​making​
​them​ ​accessible​ ​for​ ​use​​at​​events​​or​​training​​programmes​​aimed​​at​​promoting​​equality​​and​
​inclusion.​​However,​​Dixon​​et​​al​.​​(2016)​​argue​​that​​short-term​​educational​​initiatives​​alone​​are​
​insufficient​ ​to​ ​create​ ​significant​​positive​​change​​in​​young​​children's​​perceptions​​of​​race​​and​
​racism,​​particularly​​when​​compared​​to​​the​​lasting​​influences​​of​​their​​parents​​and​​peers.​​This​
​highlights​​the​​need​​for​​sustained​​efforts​​and​​long-term​​strategies​​to​​effectively​​address​​these​
​issues.​

​The​ ​Ross​ ​Initiative​ ​in​ ​Sports​ ​for​ ​Equality​ ​(RISE)​ ​provides​ ​workshops​ ​that​ ​bring​ ​about​
​conversations​ ​and​ ​discussion​ ​on​ ​racism,​ ​with​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​of​ ​raising​ ​student-athlete​
​understanding​ ​of​ ​race​ ​and​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​them​ ​with​ ​the​ ​skills​ ​to​ ​be​ ​able​ ​to​ ​have​ ​positive​
​conversations​ ​surrounding​ ​the​ ​issue​ ​of​ ​racism​ ​(MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin,​​2018).​​The​​initiative​
​contains​​ten​​modules,​​supported​​with​​educational​​and​​research-related​​resources,​​which​​are​
​taught​​to​​students​​by​​their​​coaches,​​once​​a​​week​​over​​the​​course​​of​​ten​​weeks.​​Modules​​are​
​focused​ ​on​ ​a​ ​race,​ ​diversity,​ ​or​ ​identity,​ ​and​ ​aim​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​student-athletes​ ​on​ ​specific​
​issues​ ​related​ ​to​ ​the​ ​topic​ ​(Rise,​ ​n.d.).​ ​Feedback​ ​from​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​found​ ​that​ ​athletes​
​improved​​their​​attitudes​​regarding​​their​​interest​​in​​participating​​in​​diverse​​social​​and​​cultural​
​activities.​ ​Likewise,​ ​after​ ​the​​10​​weeks​​participants​​were​​more​​aware​​of​​and​​were​​happy​​to​
​engage​ ​in​ ​discussions​ ​surrounding​ ​race.​ ​In​ ​comparison​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Show​ ​Racism​ ​the​ ​Red​ ​Card​
​(n.d.)​​and​​Kick​​it​​Out​​initiatives,​​the​​RISE​​initiative​​is​​a​​10-week​​programme,​​which​​Pedersen​
​(2005)​​recognises​​would​​have​​more​​of​​a​​long-lasting​​impact,​​given​​that​​these​​modules​​will​​be​
​taught​ ​over​ ​a​ ​longer​ ​period​ ​of​ ​time.​ ​MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin​ ​(2018)​​believed​​that​​educating​
​individuals​​on​​racism​​in​​a​​sporting​​context​​provides​​a​​positive​​environment​​in​​which​​to​​have​
​these​ ​initial​ ​conversations​ ​regarding​ ​difficult​ ​issues;​ ​highlighting​ ​that,​ ​although​ ​racism​ ​is​ ​a​
​subject​ ​of​ ​widespread​ ​concern,​ ​if​ ​initial​ ​conversations​ ​can​ ​take​​place​​in​​certain​​fields,​​then​
​there​ ​is​ ​potential​ ​for​ ​gradual​ ​change.​ ​Similarly,​ ​Lea-Howarth​ ​(2006)​ ​does​ ​not​ ​believe​ ​that​
​sport​ ​should​ ​be​ ​used​ ​as​ ​a​ ​holistic​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​peace​ ​but​ ​recognises​ ​it​​could​​be​​a​
​good initiator.​




                                                             ​49​
​An​​organisation​​specifically​​trying​​to​​tackle​​antisemitism​​at​​football​​matches​​are​​Chelsea​​FC.​
​The​ ​‘Say​ ​No​ ​To​ ​Antisemitism’​ ​campaign​ ​was​​launched​​in​​2018,​​and​​is​​run​​and​​organised​​by​
​Chelsea​ ​FC​ ​themselves​ ​(Chelsea​ ​FC,​ ​2018).​ ​The​ ​initiative​ ​is​ ​funded​ ​by​ ​the​ ​club’s​ ​previous​
​owner,​ ​Roman​ ​Abramovich,​ ​who​ ​is​ ​himself​​Jewish;​​he​​wanted​​to​​tackle​​antisemitism​​whilst​
​abolishing​ ​his​ ​club’s​ ​publicised​ ​reputation​ ​for​ ​having​ ​antisemitic​ ​supporters.​ ​Additionally,​
​Chelsea​​FC​​developed​​this​​educational​​initiative​​to​​raise​​awareness​​and​​educate​​players,​​staff,​
​fans​ ​and​ ​the​ ​wider​ ​community​ ​about​ ​antisemitism.​​They​​provide​​a​​guide​​for​​safety​​officers​
​and​​stewards​​to​​educate​​them​​on​​the​​topic​​of​​antisemitism​​and​​to​​help​​them​​to​​detect​​and​
​respond​ ​to​ ​antisemitism​ ​if​ ​seen​ ​at​ ​matches.​ ​It​ ​was​ ​noted​ ​in​ ​2021,​ ​that​ ​this​ ​guide​ ​was​
​rebranded and issued to all Premier League and Football League clubs.​


​Additionally,​ ​Chelsea​ ​FC​ ​offers​ ​equality​ ​and​ ​diversity​ ​workshops​ ​in​ ​primary​ ​schools,​ ​with​ ​a​
​specific​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​Judaism​ ​and​ ​antisemitism.​ ​While​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​has​ ​yet​ ​to​ ​be​ ​formally​
​evaluated,​​Chelsea​​FC​​believes​​it​​has​​long-term​​potential​​to​​reduce​​antisemitism​​in​​football.​
​The​ ​club​ ​has​ ​partnered​ ​with​ ​the​ ​CST​ ​to​ ​gain​ ​support​ ​in​ ​developing​ ​key​ ​aspects​ ​of​ ​their​
​campaign​ ​(Poulton,​ ​2020).​ ​Research​ ​by​ ​Moustakas​ ​and​ ​Kalina​ ​(2023)​ ​suggests​ ​that​
​sport-based​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​workshops​ ​in​ ​schools​ ​have​ ​shown​ ​promise​ ​in​ ​fostering​
​individual-level​​learning​​outcomes,​​but​​they​​may​​be​​limited​​in​​addressing​​broader​​structural​
​issues.​​Therefore,​​it​​is​​important​​to​​consider​​how​​such​​initiatives​​can​​be​​expanded​​to​​create​
​more​ ​systemic​ ​change.​ ​Trenerry,​ ​Franklin​ ​and​ ​Paradies​ ​(2012)​ ​stress​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​
​collaboration​ ​when​ ​developing​ ​successful​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​programmes.​ ​By​ ​partnering​
​with​ ​organisations​ ​like​ ​the​ ​CST,​ ​a​ ​charity​ ​dedicated​ ​to​ ​protecting​ ​British​ ​Jews​ ​from​
​antisemitism,​​Chelsea​​FC​​can​​gain​​valuable​​insights​​and​​develop​​more​​effective​​strategies​​to​
​prevent​ ​antisemitism​ ​at​ ​matches.​ ​Working​ ​with​ ​external​ ​organisations​ ​and​ ​other​ ​partners​
​allows​ ​them​ ​to​ ​tap​ ​into​ ​expertise​ ​and​ ​resources​ ​that​ ​can​ ​strengthen​ ​their​ ​initiatives​ ​and​
​enhance​ ​their​ ​impact.​ ​While​ ​Chelsea​ ​FC’s​ ​workshops​ ​and​ ​similar​ ​educational​ ​programmes​
​are​ ​crucial​ ​steps​ ​towards​ ​reducing​ ​discrimination,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​address​ ​both​ ​individual​
​and​​structural​​challenges.​​Collaboration​​with​​multiple​​organisations​​and​​the​​implementation​
​of​​long-term,​​multi-faceted​​strategies​​are​​key​​to​​making​​a​​lasting​​impact​​on​​discrimination​​in​
​football.​




                                                            ​50​
​Link​ ​and​ ​Phelan​ ​(2001)​ ​states​ ​that​ ​campaigns​ ​must​ ​target​ ​individuals,​ ​communities,​
​structures​ ​and​ ​systems,​ ​who​ ​have​ ​prejudicial​ ​beliefs.​ ​This​ ​is​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​The​ ​European​
​Union​ ​Agency​ ​for​ ​Fundamental​ ​Rights​ ​(2010),​ ​who​ ​also​ ​believe​ ​that​ ​educational​ ​initiatives​
​will​​be​​more​​successful​​when​​implemented​​on​​the​​perpetrators​​of​​discriminatory​​behaviours.​
​Chelsea​ ​FC​​launched​​an​​educational​​programme​​for​​those​​supporters​​who​​were​​banned​​for​
​antisemitic​ ​behaviour​ ​to​ ​help​ ​them​ ​comprehend​ ​the​ ​consequences​ ​of​ ​their​ ​actions.​
​Individual​ ​offenders​ ​are​ ​given​ ​the​ ​opportunity​ ​to​ ​discuss​ ​the​ ​incident​ ​and​ ​the​​effect​​it​​has​
​had,​​alongside​​considering​​what​​could​​be​​done​​to​​create​​a​​more​​inclusive​​club​​(Changing​​the​
​Chants,​ ​2021a).​ ​Additionally,​ ​by​ ​completing​ ​the​ ​programme,​ ​participants​ ​can​ ​shorten​ ​the​
​duration​ ​of​ ​their​ ​punishment,​ ​whilst​​gaining​​an​​understanding​​of​​the​​repercussions​​of​​their​
​actions​ ​(Chelsea​ ​FC,​ ​2018).​ ​Link​ ​and​ ​Phelan​ ​(2001)​ ​argues​ ​that​ ​for​ ​anti-discrimination​
​initiatives​ ​to​ ​succeed,​ ​individuals​ ​must​ ​be​ ​genuinely​ ​motivated​ ​to​ ​change​ ​their​ ​beliefs​​and​
​behaviours.​


​While​​incentives​​may​​increase​​participation,​​there​​are​​doubts​​about​​whether​​supporters​​will​
​genuinely​ ​reflect​ ​on​ ​their​ ​actions​ ​or​ ​merely​ ​comply​ ​to​ ​return​ ​to​ ​matches,​ ​potentially​
​reoffending.​ ​Similarly,​ ​educational​​courses​​have​​previously​​been​​used​​as​​incentives​​to​​deter​
​repeat​ ​offenders,​ ​as​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK’s​ ​National​ ​Speed​ ​Awareness​ ​Course​ ​(Fylan,​ ​2013).​
​Research​ ​from​ ​Ipsos​ ​(2018)​ ​found​ ​that​ ​only​​5%​​of​​attendees​​reoffended​​within​​six​​months,​
​though​ ​the​ ​rate​ ​rose​ ​to​​21%​​over​​three​​years.​​These​​findings​​suggest​​that​​while​​the​​course​
​reduces​ ​short-term​ ​reoffending,​ ​its​ ​long-term​ ​impact​ ​fades​ ​as​ ​motivations​ ​to​ ​avoid​
​punishment​ ​overshadow​ ​lasting​ ​behavioural​ ​change.​ ​Additionally,​ ​Chelsea​ ​FC’s​ ​educational​
​initiative​ ​is​ ​implemented​ ​solely​ ​within​ ​the​ ​club​ ​and​ ​is​ ​not​ ​extended​ ​to​ ​others,​ ​limiting​ ​its​
​impact​ ​to​ ​Chelsea​ ​FC​ ​supporters​ ​only​ ​(Sky​ ​Sports​ ​Football,​ ​2019).​ ​Moreover,​ ​offering​ ​this​
​programme​ ​to​ ​reduce​ ​sentences​ ​may​ ​be​ ​seen​ ​as​ ​unfair​ ​to​ ​supporters​ ​of​ ​clubs​ ​without​ ​a​
​similar​ ​initiative,​ ​as​ ​they​ ​would​ ​be​​required​​to​​serve​​their​​full​​sentence.​​Expanding​​such​​an​
​initiative​​across​​all​​clubs​​would​​not​​only​​enhance​​its​​overall​​impact​​but​​also​​ensure​​fair​​access​
​for all supporters.​


​Another​​organisation​​working​​to​​eradicate​​antisemitism​​in​​European​​football​​is​​‘Changing​​the​
​Chants’.​ ​Changing​ ​the​ ​Chants​ ​is​ ​a​ ​two-year​ ​project,​ ​which​ ​has​ ​been​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​the​
​European​​Union’s​​Rights,​​Equality​​and​​Citizenship​​Programme​​(Changing​​the​​Chants,​​2021b).​


                                                             ​51​
​Their​ ​goal​ ​is​​to​​employ​​non-formal​​education​​and​​law​​enforcement​​to​​combat​​antisemitism​
​in​​European​​football,​​by​​improving​​their​​awareness​​of​​techniques​​that​​football​​teams​​can​​use​
​to​ ​educate​ ​fans​ ​about​ ​antisemitic​ ​behaviour​ ​at​ ​matches​ ​(Changing​ ​the​ ​Chants,​ ​2021b).​
​According​ ​to​ ​Changing​ ​the​ ​Chants​ ​(2021c),​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​addresses​ ​antisemitism​ ​through​
​three​ ​approaches.​ ​First,​ ​it​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​prevent​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​by​ ​encouraging​ ​individuals​​to​
​learn​ ​about​ ​Jewish​ ​history​ ​and​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​communities,​ ​fostering​ ​a​​deeper​
​understanding​ ​for​ ​the​ ​future.​ ​Second,​ ​it​ ​focuses​ ​on​ ​educating​ ​those​ ​who​ ​have​ ​already​
​engaged​​in​​misconduct,​​helping​​them​​understand​​the​​impact​​of​​their​​actions​​on​​fellow​​fans.​
​Finally,​​for​​fans​​found​​guilty​​of​​antisemitic​​behaviour​​at​​matches,​​the​​initiative​​advocates​​for​
​court-mandated​ ​educational​ ​sessions​ ​to​ ​help​ ​shift​ ​their​ ​attitudes.​ ​This​​involves​​attending​​a​
​one-day​ ​workshop​​with​​individuals​​who​​have​​a​​stadium​​ban,​​to​​educate​​them​​about​​Jewish​
​history​ ​and​ ​the​ ​impact​ ​of​ ​their​ ​comments​ ​on​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​Changing​ ​the​​Chants​
​(2021c)​​emphasises​​the​​need​​for​​diverse​​approaches,​​organisations​​and​​methods​​to​​address​
​antisemitism in football effectively.​

​In​ ​conclusion,​ ​educational​ ​initiatives​ ​have​ ​been​ ​employed​ ​to​ ​raise​ ​awareness​ ​of​
​discrimination​​in​​sport​​and​​promote​​understanding​​of​​equality​​and​​diversity.​​Macintosh​​and​
​Martin​ ​(2018)​ ​acknowledge​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​of​ ​bringing​ ​people​ ​together​ ​to​ ​address​ ​societal​
​issues​ ​while​ ​fostering​ ​socioemotional​ ​skills.​ ​However,​ ​these​ ​initiatives​ ​create​ ​opportunities​
​for​​individuals​​to​​learn​​about​​diverse​​communities​​and​​the​​harmful​​effects​​of​​discrimination.​
​Their​ ​goal​ ​is​ ​to​ ​equip​ ​participants,​ ​whether​ ​long-time​ ​supporters​ ​or​ ​young​ ​athletes,​ ​with​
​greater​​knowledge,​​fostering​​inclusivity​​and​​reducing​​discriminatory​​behaviour.​​Nevertheless,​
​scholars​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Dixon​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2016)​ ​and​ ​Pedersen​ ​(2005)​ ​have​ ​questioned​ ​the​ ​long-term​
​effectiveness​ ​and​ ​impact​ ​of​ ​these​ ​initiatives​ ​on​ ​individuals.​ ​Sayce's​ ​(2003)​ ​research​ ​on​
​disability​​discrimination​​further​​argues​​that​​education​​alone​​is​​insufficient​​for​​creating​​lasting​
​change,​ ​emphasising​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​multi-faceted,​​ongoing​​strategies.​​Sayce​​(2003)​​contends​
​that​​collaboration​​between​​various​​groups​​and​​organisations​​at​​different​​levels​​is​​essential​​to​
​identify​​and​​implement​​effective​​actions.​​Lastly,​​despite​​the​​educational​​initiatives​​discussed​
​in​ ​this​ ​chapter,​ ​Moustakas​ ​and​ ​Kalina​ ​(2023)​ ​highlight​​that​​anti-discrimination​​education​​in​
​schools remains inconsistent and inadequate, signalling the need for further improvement.​




                                                          ​52​
​Media anti-discrimination initiatives​


​The​ ​media​ ​is​ ​one​ ​of​ ​the​ ​most​ ​powerful​ ​mediums​ ​of​ ​communication​ ​in​ ​the​ ​world​
​(MacNamara,​​2005).​​Hamdy​​and​​Gomaa​​(2012)​​argue​​that​​it​​serves​​as​​a​​powerful​​vehicle​​for​
​reinforcing​ ​social​ ​movements.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​media​ ​is​ ​frequently​ ​utilised​ ​to​ ​combat​
​prejudice,​ ​whether​ ​through​ ​television,​ ​radio,​ ​or​ ​the​ ​internet​ ​(McBride,​ ​2015).​ ​In​ ​other​
​domains,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​health,​​successful​​media​​programmes​​have​​been​​utilised​​to​​influence​​and​
​promote​​healthy​​behaviours​​(Freeman​​et​​al.,​​2015).​​Sport​​media,​​with​​its​​wide​​public​​reach,​
​has​ ​the​ ​power​ ​to​ ​influence​ ​vast​ ​audiences​ ​and​ ​create​ ​iconic​ ​moments​ ​(Kilcline,​ ​2017).​
​According​​to​​Frey​​and​​Eitzen​​(1991),​​the​​media​​has​​changed​​how​​we​​perceive​​certain​​issues​
​in​​sport,​​such​​as​​gender​​and​​ethnicity.​​According​​to​​Aboud​​et​​al​.​​(2012),​​media​​can​​be​​a​​good​
​alternative​​or​​addition​​to​​portraying​​anti-discrimination​​messages.​​As​​a​​result,​​organisations​
​such​ ​as​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​and​ ​Show​ ​Racism​ ​the​ ​Red​ ​Card​ ​have​ ​used​ ​media​ ​channels​ ​to​​promote​
​their​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​campaigns​ ​and​ ​reach​ ​large​ ​audiences​ ​in​ ​order​ ​to​​improve​​cultural​
​competency and reduce discrimination.​


​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​has​ ​utilised​ ​the​ ​media​ ​to​ ​present​ ​videos​ ​and​ ​films​ ​they​ ​produced​ ​(Kick​ ​It​ ​Out,​
​2011;​ ​2018a).​ ​These​ ​are​ ​shared​ ​on​ ​the​ ​organisation’s​ ​social​ ​media​ ​platforms,​ ​such​ ​as​
​YouTube​ ​and​ ​Twitter,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​on​ ​their​ ​website,​ ​where​ ​athletes​ ​and​ ​supporters​ ​help​
​circulate​ ​them​ ​(Kick​ ​It​ ​Out,​ ​2018a).​ ​The​ ​content​​aims​​to​​highlight​​social​​issues​​in​​sport​​and​
​encourages​ ​the​ ​public​ ​to​ ​report​ ​discrimination​ ​while​ ​reducing​ ​prejudiced​ ​behaviours​ ​like​
​homophobia,​ ​racism,​ ​and​ ​transphobia.​ ​Among​ ​their​ ​productions​ ​is​ ​the​ ​‘Y​ ​word​ ​Campaign’​
​from​​2011,​​a​​two-minute​​video​​designed​​to​​address​​and​​raise​​awareness​​about​​antisemitism​
​and​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​word​ ​‘Yid’​ ​at​ ​football​ ​matches.​ ​Alongside​ ​having​ ​this​ ​online,​ ​Baddiel​
​(2021)​ ​states​ ​that​ ​the​ ​video​ ​was​ ​also​ ​shown​ ​at​ ​stadiums​ ​at​ ​the​ ​beginning​ ​of​ ​matches.​
​Although​​there​​is​​limited​​research​​exploring​​its​​impact,​​Poulton​​and​​Durell​​(2016)​​referenced​
​that​ ​the​ ​campaign​ ​had​ ​a​ ​diverse​ ​response​ ​on​ ​social​ ​media,​ ​from​ ​both​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​and​
​non-Jewish​​community.​​Although​​it​​brought​​to​​people’s​​attention​​the​​issue​​of​​antisemitism​​in​
​football,​ ​some​ ​argued​ ​that​ ​it​ ​brought​ ​more​ ​attention​ ​to​ ​Tottenham’s​​use​​of​​the​​word​​‘Yid’,​
​rather​ ​than​ ​targeting​ ​the​ ​abusers,​ ​who​ ​use​ ​the​ ​term​ ​as​ ​a​ ​form​ ​of​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse.​
​Furthermore,​ ​Baddiel​ ​(2021),​ ​who​ ​worked​ ​in​ ​the​ ​production​ ​of​ ​the​ ​short​ ​film,​ ​stated​ ​that​
​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​did​ ​not​ ​believe​ ​antisemitism​ ​to​ ​be​ ​the​ ​most​ ​important​ ​issue​ ​to​ ​tackle​ ​at​ ​that​


                                                              ​53​
​current​ ​time,​ ​with​ ​racism​ ​towards​ ​Black​ ​players​ ​and​ ​campaigns​ ​surrounding​ ​homophobia​
​being​ ​at​​the​​forefront​​of​​their​​minds.​​Kick​​It​​Out​​believed​​that​​it​​would​​take​​away​​the​​focus​
​on​ ​the​ ​“more​ ​important​ ​messages”​ ​and​ ​did​ ​not​ ​want​ ​to​ ​go​ ​ahead​ ​with​ ​it​ ​until​ ​ex-football​
​player​​Gary​​Lineker​​offered​​to​​take​​part​​(Baddiel,​​2021,​​p.​​23).​​As​​highlighted​​by​​Trenerry​​et​
​al.​ ​(2012)​ ​support​​from​​organisation​​leaders​​is​​critical​​to​​the​​effectiveness​​of​​the​​campaign.​
​This​​example​​highlights​​that​​from​​the​​offset​​it​​was​​unlikely​​that​​this​​campaign​​would​​succeed​
​given that there was little interest and support in making a meaningful campaign.​


​During​ ​the​ ​2017/2018​ ​season,​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​reported​ ​that​​antisemitism​​comprised​​10%​​of​​all​
​discrimination​ ​within​ ​football;​ ​therefore,​ ​in​ ​2018​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​launched​ ​another​ ​short​ ​film​
​which​ ​encouraged​ ​people​ ​to​ ​report​ ​incidents​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​(Curtis,​ ​2019;​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out,​
​2018b).​​Recognised​​by​​Brasted​​(2005)​​campaigns​​and​​movements​​require​​media​​attention​​to​
​spread​ ​their​ ​message​ ​and​ ​reach​ ​a​ ​larger​ ​population.​ ​However,​ ​as​ ​of​ ​October​ ​2024,​ ​the​ ​‘Y​
​word​ ​campaign’​ ​had​ ​191,000​ ​views​ ​and​ ​the​ ​video​ ​on​ ​how​ ​to​ ​report​ ​antisemitism​ ​had​​just​
​over​​6,000​​views​​(Kick​​It​​Out,​​2011,​​2018a).​​Given​​that​​the​​‘Y​​word​​campaign’​​video​​has​​been​
​online​ ​for​ ​over​ ​thirteen​ ​years,​ ​some​ ​might​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​it​ ​hasn't​ ​reached​ ​a​ ​large​ ​enough​
​audience​ ​to​ ​make​ ​a​ ​meaningful​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​with​ ​only​ ​651​
​subscribers,​​their​​videos​​are​​not​​reaching​​a​​sufficiently​​broad​​audience.​​In​​conclusion,​​while​
​Kick​​It​​Out's​​films​​highlight​​important​​societal​​issues,​​they​​may​​not​​fulfil​​their​​purpose​​unless​
​they​ ​are​ ​viewed​ ​by​ ​those​ ​who​ ​need​ ​education​ ​on​ ​the​ ​topic,​ ​including​ ​perpetrators​ ​of​
​antisemitic abuse and individuals who could report such incidents.​


​Organisations​​including​​Kick​​It​​Out​​and​​Show​​Racism​​the​​Red​​Card​​utilise​​athletes​​with​​large​
​followings​​in​​their​​campaigns​​to​​amplify​​their​​messages.​​Kniffin,​​Wansink​​and​​Shimizu​​(2015)​
​recognises​ ​that​ ​athletes​ ​are​ ​viewed​ ​by​ ​many​ ​as​ ​leaders​ ​within​ ​the​ ​sporting​ ​community.​
​Athletes​​are​​expected​​to​​act​​as​​role​​models​​and​​set​​good​​examples​​(Kennedy​​and​​Hills,​​2009);​
​therefore,​ ​they​ ​can​ ​use​ ​their​ ​platforms​ ​and​ ​voices​ ​to​ ​make​ ​positive​ ​change​ ​and​ ​to​ ​help​
​decrease​ ​discrimination​ ​(Dixon​ ​et​ ​al.,​ ​2016).​ ​MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin​ ​(2018)​ ​believe​ ​that​
​athletes​​who​​participate​​could​​have​​a​​vital​​role​​in​​combating​​discrimination,​​as​​they​​are​​able​
​to​ ​capture​ ​the​ ​attention​ ​of​ ​fans​ ​and​ ​have​ ​a​ ​greater​ ​influence​ ​amongst​ ​fans,​ ​as​ ​they​ ​are​
​regarded​​as​​role​​models​​within​​their​​communities​​and​​society​​at​​large.​​However,​​literature​​by​
​Guest​ ​and​​Cox​​(2009)​​shows​​that​​elite​​athletes​​are​​deemed​​more​​as​​iconic​​reference​​points​


                                                            ​54​
​by​ ​the​ ​public​ ​instead​ ​of​ ​active​ ​influencers,​ ​who​ ​impact​​their​​life​​choices​​and​​opinions,​​and​
​that it is friends and family members who make more of an impact upon attitudes.​


​To​ ​conclude,​ ​media-based​​initiatives​​have​​been​​used​​by​​organisations​​such​​as​​Kick​​It​​Out​​to​
​raise​ ​awareness​ ​of​ ​discrimination​ ​in​ ​sport.​ ​Clement​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2013)​ ​says​ ​that​ ​mass​ ​media​
​initiatives​ ​may​ ​reduce​ ​prejudiced​ ​attitudes​ ​and​ ​behaviours​ ​and​ ​have​ ​been​ ​used​ ​to​ ​get​
​important​ ​messages​ ​across​ ​to​ ​the​ ​public​ ​on​ ​a​ ​large​ ​scale​ ​(Freeman​ ​et​ ​al​.,​​2015).​​Although​
​sizable​ ​shares​ ​and​ ​‘viral’​ ​campaigns​ ​help​ ​to​ ​achieve​ ​this,​ ​Freeman​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2015)​ ​states​​that​
​they​ ​do​ ​not​ ​always​ ​make​ ​an​ ​impact​ ​or​ ​help​ ​to​ ​achieve​ ​the​ ​objective​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​as​
​reflected​ ​in​ ​the​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​campaign.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​Wakefield,​ ​Loken​ ​and​ ​Hornik​ ​(2010)​
​highlight​ ​that​ ​the​ ​message​ ​conveyed​ ​by​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​may​ ​be​ ​insufficient​ ​and​ ​could​ ​even​
​provoke​ ​negative​ ​reactions,​ ​potentially​ ​escalating​ ​and​ ​exacerbating​ ​discriminatory​
​behaviours.​​Celebrity​​athletes​​have​​also​​been​​used​​in​​media-based​​initiatives​​to​​help​​engage​
​with​ ​the​ ​audience;​ ​however,​ ​noted​ ​by​ ​Guest​ ​and​ ​Cox​ ​(2009)​ ​they​ ​are​ ​unlikely​ ​to​ ​make​
​significant​​changes​​upon​​attitudes​​and​​prejudices,​​and​​those​​who​​are,​​are​​usually​​long-term​
​friends and family.​


​Community integration initiatives​


​Sport​ ​has​ ​been​ ​labelled​ ​as​ ​a​ ​social​ ​connector​ ​which​ ​helps​ ​develop​ ​communities​ ​and​​bring​
​individuals​ ​from​ ​diverse​ ​cultures​​together​​(Maxwell,​​2012).​​Community​​integration​​projects​
​have​ ​used​ ​sport’s​ ​popularity​ ​and​ ​accessibility​ ​to​ ​bring​ ​communities​ ​together​ ​and​​to​​tackle​
​inequalities​ ​and​ ​discrimination​ ​(Giulianotti,​ ​2012).​ ​Academics​ ​and​ ​researchers,​ ​including​
​Giulianotti​​(2011)​​have​​gravitated​​towards​​using​​sport​​as​​potential​​avenue​​in​​bridging​​divided​
​societies,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​has​ ​been​ ​known​ ​to​ ​increase​ ​social​ ​cohesion,​ ​bridge​ ​social​ ​divides,​ ​reduce​
​prejudice​ ​and​ ​improve​ ​ethnic​ ​relationships​ ​(Edginton​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​1995;​ ​Mitchell,​​Somerville​​and​
​Hargie,​​2016).​​Those​​involved​​in​​sport​​for​​development​​and​​peace​​claim​​that​​sport​​can,​​and​
​indeed​ ​does,​ ​make​ ​a​ ​positive​​impact​​in​​regions​​affected​​by​​conflict​​(Dart,​​2019).​​Therefore,​
​sport​ ​has​ ​been​ ​used​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​bring​ ​together​ ​different​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​community​ ​in​
​countries​ ​where​ ​there​ ​are​ ​social,​ ​political​ ​and​ ​religious​ ​differences,​ ​including​ ​Northern​
​Ireland and Israel (Dart, 2019; Hassan and Telford, 2014; Leitner, Galily and Shimon, 2014).​




                                                             ​55​
​Hassan​ ​and​ ​Telford​ ​(2014)​ ​explored​ ​sporting​ ​initiatives​ ​which​ ​have​ ​been​ ​used​ ​in​ ​Northern​
​Ireland​​(henceforth,​​NI,)​​to​​investigate​​whether​​it​​promotes​​reconciliation​​between​​opposing​
​communities.​​With​​high​​levels​​of​​deprivation​​and​​isolation​​in​​parts​​of​​NI,​​where​​sectarianism​
​is​ ​persistent,​ ​sport​ ​could​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​platform​ ​in​ ​which​ ​people​ ​can​ ​develop​ ​greater​
​cohesiveness​​within​​a​​country​​whereby​​community​​division​​is​​prevalent​​(Hassan​​and​​Telford,​
​2014).​ ​Sport​ ​NI​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​building​ ​cohesion​ ​within​ ​the​ ​community​ ​by​ ​increasing​ ​sport​
​involvement​​in​​areas​​wherein​​there​​are​​groups​​who​​are​​traditionally​​marginalised​​(Sport​​NI,​
​2006).​ ​Furthermore,​ ​as​ ​noted​ ​by​ ​Hassan​ ​and​ ​Telford​​(2014),​​they​​also​​had​​other​​ambitious​
​outcomes, including healing the divided communities and improving health and well-being.​


​Sport​ ​NI​ ​has​ ​provided​ ​funding​ ​for​ ​Midnight​ ​Street​ ​Soccer,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​initially​ ​created​ ​for​
​young​ ​men​ ​residing​ ​in​​inner-city​​neighbourhoods​​(Hartmann,​​2001).​​These​​midnight​​games​
​serve​ ​as​ ​a​ ​constructive​ ​alternative​ ​for​ ​young​ ​people​ ​during​ ​high-crime​ ​hours,​ ​specifically​
​from​​10pm​​to​​2am,​​when​​antisocial​​and​​criminal​​behaviour​​tends​​to​​peak​​(Hartmann,​​2001).​
​Similar​ ​initiatives,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Midnight​ ​Basketball​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​ ​States​ ​(Hartmann,​ ​2016)​ ​and​
​Midnight​ ​Football​ ​in​ ​Sweden​ ​(Ekholm​ ​and​ ​Dahlstedt,​ ​2020),​ ​have​ ​also​​been​​established.​​In​
​NI,​​Midnight​​Street​​Soccer​​not​​only​​promotes​​a​​greater​​understanding​​of​​diversity​​within​​the​
​community​​but​​also​​provides​​opportunities​​for​​socialising​​and​​building​​relationships,​​all​​while​
​helping​ ​participants​ ​avoid​ ​disruptive​ ​behaviour​ ​(Hassan​ ​and​ ​Telford,​ ​2014).​ ​Hassan​ ​and​
​Telford​ ​(2014)​ ​highlighted​ ​that​ ​Midnight​ ​Soccer​ ​aided​ ​reconciliation​ ​and​ ​community​
​cohesion.​ ​Specifically,​ ​regardless​ ​of​ ​whether​ ​individuals​ ​were​ ​Catholic​ ​or​ ​Protestant,​
​individuals​ ​had​ ​the​ ​common​ ​goal,​ ​to​ ​play​ ​football​ ​and​ ​to​​enjoy​​themselves.​​Kilvington​​and​
​Price​ ​(2018a)​ ​contend​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​can​ ​play​ ​a​ ​vital​ ​role​ ​in​ ​fostering​ ​peace​ ​and​ ​bridging​
​communities,​ ​a​ ​concept​ ​that​​is​​echoed​​in​​the​​study​​by​​Hassan​​and​​Telford​​(2014).​​Likewise,​
​Wilson​ ​(2012a,​ ​p.​ ​5)​ ​recognises​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​has​​the​​ability​​to​​make​​some​​social​​and​​political​
​change,​ ​but​ ​only​ ​to​ ​a​ ​certain​ ​degree,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​“may​ ​not​ ​be​ ​part​ ​of​ ​any​ ​real​ ​solution​ ​to​ ​the​
​structural​ ​problems​ ​that​ ​are​ ​the​ ​underlying​ ​reasons​ ​for​ ​various​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​inequality​ ​and​
​conflict”.​ ​Most​ ​specifically,​ ​in​ ​a​ ​society​ ​which​ ​is​ ​so​ ​deeply​ ​divided​ ​Mitchell​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2016)​
​emphasised that sport does not challenge the wider issue of sectarianism.​




                                                               ​56​
​Sport​ ​has​ ​increasingly​ ​been​ ​utilised​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​promoting​ ​peace,​ ​particularly​ ​in​ ​Israel​
​(Leitner​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2014).​ ​Leitner​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2014)​ ​investigated​ ​the​ ​effects​ ​of​ ​sports​ ​programmes​
​aimed​​at​​fostering​​peace​​between​​Israelis​​and​​Palestinians.​​Their​​findings​​revealed​​a​​positive​
​shift​​in​​attitudes​​after​​a​​one-week​​programme.​​A​​related​​study​​by​​Leitner,​​Galily​​and​​Shimon​
​(2012)​ ​examined​ ​the​ ​impact​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​other​ ​recreational​ ​activities​ ​over​​the​​course​​of​​a​
​year,​ ​showing​ ​significant​ ​improvements​ ​in​ ​the​ ​attitudes​ ​of​ ​Arabs​ ​and​ ​Jews​ ​towards​ ​one​
​another.​​Initially,​​a​​pre-test​​indicated​​that​​70%​​of​​participants​​did​​not​​trust​​Israeli​​Jews​​at​​all.​
​However,​ ​a​ ​year​ ​later,​ ​a​ ​post-test​ ​showed​ ​that​​this​​figure​​had​​decreased​​to​​30%,​​indicating​
​that​ ​the​ ​peace-building​ ​programme​​positively​​influenced​​Arab​​Israelis'​​perceptions.​​Overall,​
​both studies concluded that sports could help reduce negative attitudes and promote peace.​

​Mitchell​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2020)​ ​further​ ​supported​ ​this​​notion​​by​​identifying​​five​​key​​features​​of​​sport​
​that​ ​can​ ​be​ ​leveraged​ ​in​ ​community​ ​building​ ​initiatives.​ ​Firstly,​ ​group​ ​activities​ ​can​ ​foster​
​social​ ​cohesion,​ ​helping​ ​participants​ ​connect​ ​with​ ​one​ ​another.​ ​Secondly,​ ​rule-based​ ​play​
​encourages​ ​the​ ​installation​ ​of​ ​democratic​ ​principles,​ ​teaching​ ​participants​ ​to​ ​abide​ ​by​
​agreed-upon​ ​rules.​ ​Thirdly,​ ​popular​ ​entertainment​ ​engages​ ​a​ ​large​ ​audience,​ ​providing​ ​a​
​platform​ ​for​ ​symbolic​ ​expressions​ ​of​ ​new​ ​identities.​ ​Fourthly,​ ​social​ ​interaction​ ​through​
​sports​ ​can​ ​enhance​ ​social​ ​integration,​ ​allowing​ ​individuals​ ​from​ ​different​ ​backgrounds​ ​to​
​bond.​​Finally,​​overall​​physical​​activity​​promotes​​individual​​well-being,​​which​​can​​contribute​​to​
​a​​more​​harmonious​​community.​​Despite​​these​​positive​​attributes,​​Mitchell​​et​​al.​​(2020,​​p.​​4)​
​caution​ ​that​ ​these​ ​characteristics​ ​contribute​ ​to​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​as​ ​a​ ​beneficial​ ​factor​ ​in​
​peacebuilding but emphasise that “this is far from the full peacebuilding agenda.”​

​In​ ​contrast,​ ​Dart​ ​(2019)​ ​argues​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​not​ ​an​ ​effective​ ​means​ ​of​ ​developing​ ​peace​
​between​ ​Israel​ ​and​ ​Palestine,​​asserting​​that​​“there​​is​​no​​peace”​​(p.​​1).​​Dart's​​literature​​also​
​highlights​ ​that​ ​most​ ​sports​ ​for​ ​development​ ​and​ ​peace​ ​programmes​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​Israelis​ ​and​
​Palestinian​ ​Arabs​ ​living​ ​in​ ​Israel,​ ​with​ ​few​ ​initiatives​ ​engaging​ ​Palestinians​ ​from​ ​the​ ​West​
​Bank,​​Gaza,​​or​​refugee​​camps​​in​​neighbouring​​countries.​​This​​is​​a​​limitation,​​as​​it​​neglects​​the​
​broader​ ​context​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​ ​conflict​ ​and​ ​the​ ​diverse​ ​experiences​ ​and​
​perspectives​ ​of​ ​Palestinians​ ​in​ ​these​ ​regions.​ ​Leitner​ ​et​ ​al​.​ ​(2014)​ ​also​ ​acknowledged​ ​that​
​sport​ ​is​ ​unlikely​ ​to​ ​make​ ​a​ ​meaningful​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​the​ ​broader​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​ ​conflict.​
​Overall,​ ​the​ ​notion​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​as​ ​a​ ​valuable​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​achieving​ ​peace​ ​is​ ​overly​ ​optimistic​ ​and​



                                                               ​57​
​simplistic,​ ​especially​ ​given​ ​the​ ​complexities​ ​of​ ​social​ ​relationships​ ​involved​ ​in​ ​the​
​Israeli-Palestinian conflict.​

​On​ ​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​scholars​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Walseth​ ​(2016)​ ​have​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​promoting​ ​sports​
​participation​ ​among​ ​diverse​ ​communities.​ ​In​ ​her​ ​study,​ ​Walseth​ ​(2016)​ ​examined​ ​the​
​motivations​​behind​​sports​​offerings​​by​​organisations​​within​​Muslim​​communities​​in​​Norway,​
​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​the​ ​role​ ​these​ ​organisations​ ​play​ ​in​ ​fostering​ ​social​ ​capital​ ​and​ ​integration.​ ​Her​
​research​ ​revealed​ ​that,​ ​within​ ​sporting​ ​contexts,​ ​some​​individuals​​from​​these​​communities​
​preferred​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​primarily​ ​with​ ​their​ ​own​ ​groups​ ​due​ ​to​ ​certain​ ​activities​ ​that​ ​they​
​perceived​ ​as​ ​incompatible​ ​with​ ​their​ ​values,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​drugs​ ​and​ ​mixed-gender​
​interactions.​ ​Consequently,​ ​Muslim​ ​sporting​ ​organisations​ ​provided​ ​opportunities​ ​for​
​individuals​ ​to​ ​participate​ ​in​ ​sports​ ​while​ ​adhering​ ​to​ ​their​ ​cultural​ ​and​ ​religious​ ​practices​
​(Benn, Pfister and Jawad, 2010; Jawad, Al-Sinani and Benn, 2011).​

​Overall,​ ​Walseth’s​ ​research​ ​underscored​ ​several​ ​strengths​ ​of​ ​activities​ ​tailored​ ​to​ ​specific​
​ethnic​ ​and​ ​religious​ ​groups,​ ​including​ ​the​ ​positive​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​mental​ ​health.​ ​Participants​
​reported​ ​feeling​ ​more​ ​comfortable​ ​and​ ​supported​ ​when​ ​engaging​ ​with​ ​others​ ​who​ ​share​
​similar​ ​experiences,​ ​particularly​ ​those​ ​who​ ​have​ ​faced​ ​discrimination.​ ​However,​ ​Walseth​
​(2016)​​also​​recognised​​that​​such​​initiatives​​have​​faced​​criticism​​from​​government​​bodies​​and​
​researchers​ ​for​ ​potentially​ ​reinforcing​ ​segregation​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​facilitating​ ​broader​
​integration.​

​Similarly,​ ​Maccabi​ ​GB,​ ​the​ ​Anglo-Jewish​ ​sport,​ ​health​ ​and​​wellbeing​​charity,​​offers​​sporting​
​activities​​to​​increase​​participation​​within​​the​​Jewish​​community​​(Dart,​​2021).​​Maccabi​​GB​​has​
​been​ ​running​ ​for​ ​over​ ​80​ ​years,​ ​established​ ​in​ ​response​ ​to​ ​the​ ​exclusion​ ​of​ ​Jewish​
​community​ ​members​​from​​some​​sporting​​organisations​​and​​social​​clubs​​(Douek,​​2015).​​It​​is​
​part​ ​of​ ​a​ ​global​ ​movement​ ​which​ ​functions​ ​in​ ​over​ ​70​ ​countries​ ​(Dart,​ ​2021;​ ​Maccabi​ ​GB,​
​2018).​​Maccabi​​GB​​provides​​sports​​provisions​​to​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​including​​community​
​games,​​in​​the​​hope​​of​​bringing​​together​​an​​abundance​​of​​people​​ranging​​in​​ages​​and​​abilities​
​(Maccabi​ ​GB,​ ​2018).​ ​Maccabi​ ​GB​ ​attend​ ​the​​Maccabiah​​Games,​​which​​brings​​together​​over​
​10,000​ ​Jewish​ ​athletes​ ​from​ ​85​ ​countries,​ ​to​ ​take​ ​part​ ​in​ ​what​ ​is​ ​known​ ​as​ ​‘ The​ ​Jewish​
​Olympics’.​ ​This​ ​brings​ ​people​ ​from​ ​around​ ​the​ ​world​ ​together,​ ​fostering​ ​international​
​relationships​ ​that​ ​are​ ​especially​ ​valuable​ ​for​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​as​ ​its​ ​members​ ​are​


                                                              ​58​
​dispersed​ ​globally​ ​(Kaplan,​ ​2015).​ ​Maccabi’s​ ​(2018)​ ​research​ ​shows​ ​that​ ​their​ ​work​ ​within​
​the​ ​community​ ​makes​ ​a​ ​difference​ ​to​ ​the​ ​lives​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​individuals​ ​and​ ​that​ ​those​
​individuals​ ​who​ ​engage​ ​have​ ​a​ ​higher​ ​likelihood​ ​of​ ​staying​ ​connected​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community.​ ​Maccabi’s​ ​literature,​ ​however,​ ​does​ ​not​ ​provide​ ​specifics​ ​on​ ​how​ ​their​ ​efforts​
​have​​impacted​​individual​​lives,​​making​​it​​unclear​​how​​their​​work​​leads​​to​​concrete​​personal​
​benefits.​ ​Additionally,​ ​while​ ​fostering​ ​a​ ​strong​ ​sense​ ​of​ ​belonging​ ​within​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community​ ​is​ ​highly​ ​valuable,​ ​this​ ​emphasis​​on​​internal​​unity​​may​​not​​necessarily​​promote​
​broader​​inclusion​​within​​society.​​This​​point​​is​​further​​supported​​by​​the​​research​​of​​Klein​​and​
​Kothy​ ​(2000),​ ​which​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​such​ ​groups​ ​often​ ​do​ ​not​ ​promote​ ​integration;​ ​rather,​
​they​ ​strengthen​ ​ties​ ​within​ ​their​ ​own​ ​ethnic​ ​communities,​ ​contributing​ ​to​ ​increased​
​segregation.​ ​In​ ​exploring​ ​the​ ​reasons​ ​for​ ​the​ ​existence​ ​of​ ​minority​ ​sports​ ​clubs,​ ​Walseth​
​(2016)​ ​noted​ ​a​ ​lack​ ​of​ ​research​ ​in​ ​this​ ​area,​ ​yet​​emphasised​​that​​these​​clubs​​play​​a​​crucial​
​role​ ​in​ ​fostering​ ​social​ ​belonging​ ​and​ ​creating​ ​environments​ ​where​ ​religious​ ​customs​ ​and​
​cultural​ ​practices​ ​can​ ​be​ ​honoured​ ​without​ ​hindering​ ​participation.​ ​Therefore,​ ​while​ ​these​
​groups​ ​may​ ​enhance​ ​internal​ ​cohesion,​ ​they​ ​also​ ​risk​ ​perpetuating​ ​separation​ ​from​ ​the​
​broader community.​


​Overall,​ ​initiatives​ ​have​ ​been​ ​used​ ​to​ ​attempt​ ​to​ ​increase​ ​community​ ​integration​ ​for​
​marginalised​​groups.​​They​​have​​the​​ability​​to​​bring​​together​​different​​communities,​​including​
​those​​communities​​which​​have​​been​​divided​​as​​a​​result​​of​​political​​differences.​​Nevertheless,​
​there​ ​have​ ​been​ ​debates​ ​regarding​ ​whether​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​the​ ​most​ ​appropriate​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​bridge​
​divided​ ​societies​ ​(Coalter,​ ​2008)​ ​and​ ​whether​ ​they​ ​develop​ ​peace​ ​outside​ ​of​ ​the​ ​sporting​
​field​ ​(Dart,​ ​2019).​ ​Weiss​ ​(1996)​ ​argues​ ​that​​these​​programmes​​tend​​to​​be​​overly​​optimistic​
​promises,​ ​which​ ​do​ ​not​ ​achieve​ ​the​ ​overall​ ​aim​ ​of​ ​developing​ ​a​ ​peaceful​ ​society.​ ​Some​
​scholars​​argue​​that​​there​​could​​be​​negative​​impacts​​upon​​individuals​​and​​communities​​who​
​are​ ​involved​ ​in​ ​initiatives​ ​which​ ​aim​ ​to​ ​address​ ​broader​ ​social​ ​needs.​​For​​example,​​Coalter​
​(2008)​ ​states​ ​that​ ​communities​ ​ethnic​ ​or​ ​cultural​ ​boundaries​ ​may​ ​become​ ​more​ ​apparent​
