​when​ ​engaging​ ​in​ ​sport.​ ​Additionally,​ ​Hassan​ ​and​ ​Telford​ ​(2014)​​recognise​​that​​sport​​could​
​heighten​ ​their​ ​differences​ ​and​ ​remind​ ​communities​ ​of​ ​the​ ​divisions​ ​which​ ​may​ ​already​ ​be​
​prevalent.​ ​They​ ​also​ ​state​ ​that​ ​these​​changes​​may​​only​​be​​expected​​to​​occur​​gradually​​and​
​progressively,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​Agergaard​ ​(2018)​ ​who​ ​recognised​ ​that​ ​integration​
​programmes​ ​and​ ​initiatives​ ​are​ ​processes​ ​which​ ​require​ ​time​ ​and​ ​must​ ​be​ ​continuous.​


                                                            ​59​
​Although​ ​this​ ​may​ ​be​ ​considered​ ​a​ ​criticism,​ ​if​ ​longevity​ ​is​ ​required​ ​to​ ​make​ ​a​ ​significant​
​impact upon discrimination and separated communities, then this is an acceptable reality.​


​Key insights and challenges in anti-discrimination initiatives in sport​


​To​ ​conclude,​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​often​ ​regarded​ ​as​ ​a​ ​universal​ ​language​ ​that​ ​unites​ ​communities​ ​and​
​addresses​ ​societal​ ​challenges​ ​(United​ ​Nations,​ ​2003).​ ​As​ ​outlined​ ​above,​ ​numerous​
​organisations​ ​are​ ​actively​ ​working​ ​to​ ​combat​ ​discrimination​ ​and​ ​create​ ​a​ ​more​ ​inclusive​
​sporting​ ​environment.​ ​These​ ​organisations​ ​have​ ​developed​ ​innovative​ ​anti-discrimination​
​initiatives​ ​aimed​ ​at​ ​fostering​ ​acceptance​ ​within​ ​both​ ​society​ ​and​ ​the​ ​world​ ​of​ ​sport,​
​especially​ ​for​ ​marginalised​ ​groups​ ​and​ ​individuals.​ ​For​ ​instance,​ ​Stonewall​ ​(n.d.)​ ​provides​
​rainbow​​laces​​for​​athletes​​to​​wear,​​a​​symbolic​​initiative​​that​​raises​​awareness​​of​​LGBT+​​rights,​
​while​​Kick​​It​​Out​​(2018a)​​has​​launched​​media​​campaigns​​to​​reinforce​​their​​anti-discrimination​
​messages.​ ​While​ ​these​ ​initiatives​ ​have​ ​successfully​ ​raised​ ​awareness​ ​and​ ​brought​ ​these​
​issues into the public awareness, they have also faced criticism on various fronts.​


​These​ ​efforts​ ​reflect​ ​a​ ​growing​ ​recognition​ ​of​ ​sport's​ ​capacity​ ​to​ ​drive​ ​social​ ​change​ ​and​
​address​​discrimination.​​However,​​significant​​challenges​​remain​​in​​effectively​​confronting​​both​
​individual​ ​and​ ​systemic​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination.​ ​Despite​ ​the​ ​commendable​ ​work​ ​of​ ​these​
​organisations,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​evident​ ​that​ ​these​ ​initiatives​ ​alone​ ​are​ ​insufficient​ ​to​ ​fully​ ​address​ ​the​
​broader​ ​issue​ ​of​ ​discrimination.​ ​Scholars​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Coakley​ ​(2015)​ ​and​ ​Coalter​ ​(2015)​ ​have​
​questioned​ ​the​​extent​​to​​which​​sport​​can​​genuinely​​resolve​​social​​problems,​​highlighting​​its​
​limitations in achieving lasting change.​


​Symbolic,​ ​educational,​ ​media​ ​and​ ​community-based​ ​initiatives​ ​have​ ​raised​ ​awareness​ ​of​
​societal​ ​issues​ ​in​ ​sport;​ ​nevertheless,​ ​as​ ​highlighted​ ​by​ ​Sayce​ ​(2003),​​initiatives​​need​​to​​be​
​multi-stranded​ ​and​ ​continuous.​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result,​ ​projects​ ​may​ ​require​ ​a​ ​mix​ ​of​ ​different​
​approaches​ ​and​ ​methodologies.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​this​ ​emphasises​ ​a​ ​vital​ ​recommendation​ ​to​
​initiatives​ ​and​ ​policymakers​ ​while​ ​building​ ​future​ ​initiatives,​ ​including​ ​educational,​
​media-based,​​symbolic,​​and​​community-based​​ideas.​​However,​​Kick​​It​​Out​​is​​an​​organisation​
​that​ ​has​ ​employed​ ​all​ ​three​ ​types​ ​of​ ​projects​ ​but​ ​has​ ​been​ ​criticised​ ​for​ ​not​ ​having​ ​had​
​enough​ ​impact.​ ​Arguably,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​been​ ​noted​ ​in​ ​this​ ​chapter​ ​that​ ​they​ ​do​ ​not​ ​receive​


                                                              ​60​
​significant​ ​funds​ ​from​ ​football​ ​governing​ ​bodies​ ​to​ ​influence​ ​discriminatory​ ​behaviours​
​(Kilvington​ ​and​ ​Price,​ ​2017;​ ​Penfold​​and​​Cleland,​​2022).​ ​Initiatives,​​including​​the​​Stonewall​
​(n.d.)​​rainbow​​laces​​campaign,​​have​​been​​criticised​​for​​not​​being​​a​​continued​​effort.​​Indeed,​
​Dixon​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2016)​ ​and​ ​Pedersen​ ​(2005)​ ​stress​ ​that​​initiatives​​that​​are​​created​​to​​eradicate​
​and​ ​decrease​ ​prejudice​ ​usually​ ​only​​generate​​short-term​​impact​​and​​do​​not​​have​​longevity.​
​Leitner​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2012)​ ​found​ ​that​ ​their​ ​longitudinal​ ​study​ ​had​ ​a​ ​greater,​ ​positive​ ​impact​ ​on​
​challenging​​negative​​attitudes​​towards​​conflicting​​communities,​​which​​emphasises​​that​​time​
​is​​needed​​to​​make​​a​​significant​​impact.​​To​​produce​​a​​successful​​anti-discrimination​​initiative,​
​Link​ ​and​ ​Phelan’s​ ​(2001)​​literature​​highlights​​that​​you​​must​​essentially​​challenge​​the​​power​
​that​ ​underpins​ ​discrimination​ ​and​ ​transform​ ​the​ ​beliefs​ ​of​ ​those​ ​with​ ​the​ ​power​ ​to​
​discriminate,​ ​which​ ​would​ ​require​​time.​​Nevertheless,​​Pedersen​​(2005)​​also​​recognises​​that​
​changing​ ​individuals’​ ​prejudices​ ​and​ ​opinions​ ​is​ ​easier​ ​said​ ​than​ ​done,​ ​highlighting​ ​the​
​difficulties and struggles that anti-discriminatory organisations may face.​


​Theoretical underpinning​


​Antisemitism​​in​​sport,​​particularly​​in​​football,​​remains​​a​​significant​​and​​complex​​issue,​​which​
​can​ ​manifest​ ​in​ ​various​ ​forms,​ ​from​ ​casual​ ​banter​ ​to​ ​overt​ ​hostility​ ​(Dart,​ ​2021;​ ​Poulton,​
​2020).​​However,​​when​​exploring​​key​​literature,​​it​​is​​imperative​​to​​understand​​the​​theoretical​
​frameworks​ ​that​ ​underpins​ ​the​ ​research​ ​in​ ​this​ ​area.​ ​In​ ​the​ ​realm​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​sociology,​
​theoretical​​frameworks​​are​​essential​​in​​providing​​a​​foundation​​for​​academic​​research​​(Smith,​
​2010).​ ​Social​ ​theory​ ​serves​ ​as​ ​a​ ​structure​ ​and​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​comprehending,​ ​interpreting,​ ​and​
​analysing​ ​the​ ​world​ ​around​ ​us​ ​(Smith,​ ​2010).​ ​Prior​ ​to​ ​discussing​ ​the​ ​theories​ ​employed​
​within​​this​​study,​​this​​chapter​​examines​​the​​application​​of​​various​​theories​​in​​recent​​studies​
​focusing​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​British​ ​football,​ ​highlighting​ ​the​ ​strengths​ ​and​ ​limitations​ ​of​
​these approaches.​

​Poulton​​and​​Durell​​(2016)​​applied​​the​​concept​​of​​linguistic​​reclamation,​​originally​​developed​
​by​ ​Brontsema​ ​(2004),​ ​to​ ​examine​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​in​ ​English​ ​football.​ ​This​​theory​
​explains​ ​how​​marginalised​​groups​​can​​reclaim​​derogatory​​terms​​to​​neutralise​​their​​negative​
​connotations,​​as​​seen​​with​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​fans​​adopting​​the​​term​​‘Yid’.​​Poulton’s​​(2016)​
​application​ ​of​ ​linguistic​​reclamation​​offers​​a​​valuable​​perspective​​on​​the​​complexities​​of​​fan​



                                                             ​61​
​culture​ ​in​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​antisemitism.​ ​In​ ​her​ ​later​ ​work,​ ​Poulton​ ​(2020)​ ​explored​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​English​ ​football​ ​using​ ​Kingdon’s​ ​(1984)​ ​‘multiple​ ​streams​ ​approach’​
​(henceforth,​ ​MSA),​ ​a​ ​framework​ ​that​ ​helps​ ​understand​ ​the​ ​policy​ ​process​ ​through​ ​three​
​streams:​ ​‘problems’,​ ​‘policies’,​ ​and​ ​‘politics’.​ ​By​ ​applying​ ​the​ ​MSA​ ​to​ ​examine​ ​responses​​to​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​sport,​ ​she​ ​provides​ ​a​ ​nuanced​​understanding​​of​​how​​the​​issue​​is,​​or​​is​​not,​
​addressed​​within​​football​​culture.​​While​​she​​uses​​MSA​​to​​shed​​light​​on​​the​​political​​nature​​of​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​football,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​somewhat​ ​disconnected​ ​from​ ​the​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​those​
​directly impacted by antisemitism.​

​In​ ​Poulton's​ ​(2024)​ ​most​ ​recent​ ​piece​ ​of​ ​research,​ ​she​ ​uses​ ​the​ ​notion​ ​of​ ​‘life-story​
​interviewing’​ ​to​ ​better​ ​understand​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​Anglo-Jewish​ ​football​ ​supporters​
​confronting​​antisemitism​​and​​‘banter’.​​This​​method​​centres​​on​​the​​subjective​​experiences​​of​
​individuals,​ ​revealing​ ​the​ ​complexities​ ​of​ ​their​ ​responses,​ ​including​ ​anger,​ ​acceptance​ ​and​
​rationalisation.​ ​Although​ ​this​ ​approach​ ​aligns​ ​closely​ ​with​ ​sociological​ ​methodologies,​​as​​it​
​captures​ ​the​ ​social​ ​contexts​ ​and​ ​lived​ ​realities​ ​that​ ​shape​ ​individuals'​ ​encounters​ ​with​
​antisemitism,​​the​​research​​does​​not​​actively​​engage​​with​​a​​sociological​​theory​​to​​inform​​and​
​guide the research.​

​Lunn​​(2023)​​applied​​figurational​​sociology,​​particularly​​Norbert​​Elias’s​​work,​​in​​Critical​​Issues​
​in​​Football:​​A​​Sociological​​Analysis​​of​​the​​Beautiful​​Game​,​​a​​volume​​addressing​​contemporary​
​football​ ​issues​ ​through​ ​sociological​ ​frameworks,​ ​to​ ​examine​ ​fan​ ​identity​​among​​Tottenham​
​Hotspur​ ​supporters.​ ​This​ ​work​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​two​ ​Eliasian​ ​concepts,​ ​‘the​ ​established​ ​and​ ​the​
​outsiders’​ ​(Elias​ ​and​ ​Scotson,​ ​1965),​ ​alongside​​the​​personal​​pronoun​​model​​(Elias,​​1978)​​to​
​highlight​ ​how​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​​fans​​engage​​with​​and​​express​​a​​‘Jewish​​identity,’​​focusing​
​on​ ​the​ ​controversial​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​in​ ​response​ ​to​ ​antisemitic​ ​hostility.​ ​Similarly,​
​Wilczyńska​ ​(2022)​ ​explores​ ​how​ ​Tottenham​ ​fans,​ ​despite​ ​most​ ​not​ ​being​ ​Jewish,​ ​adopt​ ​a​
​‘Jewish​​identity’​​as​​a​​form​​of​​resistance​​to​​antisemitism.​​She​​utilised​​Gans's​​(1979)​​concept​​of​
​symbolic​ ​ethnicity,​ ​which​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​later​ ​generations​ ​express​ ​their​ ​ethnic​ ​identity​
​through​ ​cultural​ ​and​ ​leisure​ ​activities,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​supporting​ ​a​ ​football​ ​team,​ ​rather​ ​than​
​through​ ​traditional​ ​institutions.​ ​However,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​note​ ​that​ ​while​ ​Gans​ ​(1979)​ ​and​
​Norbert​​Elias’s​​theories​​provide​​useful​​frameworks​​for​​understanding​​group​​identity,​​they​​are​
​not​ ​specifically​ ​tailored​ ​to​ ​address​ ​the​ ​complexities​ ​and​ ​challenges​ ​faced​ ​by​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community.​


                                                            ​62​
​Bogna​ ​Wilczyńska's​ ​broader​ ​research​ ​focuses​ ​predominantly​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​Poland.​
​Meanwhile,​ ​studies​ ​beyond​ ​the​ ​UK,​ ​like​ ​Stratton​ ​(2015)​ ​who​ ​examines​ ​the​ ​association​ ​of​
​certain​​football​​clubs​​across​​Europe​​with​​Judaism,​​linking​​this​​dynamic​​to​​broader​​themes​​of​
​national​ ​identity.​ ​He​ ​uses​ ​sociological​ ​theories​ ​related​ ​to​ ​nationalism​ ​and​ ​identity​ ​politics,​
​illustrating​ ​how​ ​antisemitism​ ​can​ ​be​ ​a​ ​means​ ​for​ ​rival​​fans​​to​​assert​​their​​own​​identities​​in​
​the​ ​face​ ​of​ ​perceived​​threats.​​Müller,​​Haut​​and​​Heim​​(2023),​​adopted​​a​​framework​​focused​
​on​ ​group​ ​identities​ ​and​ ​intergroup​ ​conflict​ ​in​ ​their​ ​exploration​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​German​
​amateur​ ​sports.​ ​This​ ​theoretical​ ​approach​ ​looks​ ​at​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​ ​identity​ ​in​ ​prolonged​
​antisemitism.​​Similar​​to​​the​​work​​being​​done​​in​​the​​UK​​with​​focus​​on​​Tottenham​​Hotspur,​​this​
​research​ ​contributes​ ​to​ ​a​ ​deeper​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​how​ ​intergroup​ ​relations​ ​can​ ​influence​
​attitudes and behaviours toward the Jewish community in sport.​


​Literature​​from​​Seijbel,​​van​​Sterkenburg​​and​​Oonk​​(2022)​​has​​used​​the​​social​​media​​platform​
​Twitter​​to​​explore​​antisemitic​​rhetoric​​among​​Dutch​​football​​supporters​,​​with​​another​​piece​
​having​​a​​greater​​focus​​on​​the​​impact​​on​​online​​abuse​​during​​the​​Covid-19​​pandemic​​(Seijbel,​
​van​ ​Sterkenburg​ ​and​ ​Spaaij,​ ​2023).​ ​The​ ​theory​ ​used​ ​in​ ​both​ ​pieces​ ​is​ ​Goffman's​
​dramaturgical​​theory​​of​​human​​interaction​​and​​behaviour,​​which​​has​​been​​applied​​previously​
​to​​online​​hate​​speech​​by​​Kilvington​​and​​Price​​(2018b)​​and​​Kilvington​​(2021).​​When​​applying​​it​
​to​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​of​ ​antisemitic​ ​rhetoric,​ ​both​ ​papers​ ​argue​​that​​while​​Twitter​​is​​an​​overtly​
​front-stage​ ​space,​ ​the​ ​online​ ​element​ ​of​ ​social​ ​media​ ​can​ ​make​ ​it​ ​feel​ ​like​ ​a​ ​back-stage​
​environment where people are more prone to express prejudice and engage in hate speech.​


​It​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​note​ ​that​ ​some​ ​researchers​ ​exploring​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​have​ ​not​
​explicitly​ ​used​ ​any​ ​social​​theory​​to​​guide​​their​​research.​​For​​example,​​Dart​​and​​Long​​(2021)​
​investigate​ ​the​ ​nature​ ​and​ ​extent​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​community​ ​sporting​ ​environments​ ​in​
​Britain​ ​but​ ​do​ ​not​ ​use​ ​a​​specific​​theoretical​​framework​​to​​guide​​its​​discussion​​and​​analysis.​
​Instead,​ ​it​ ​draws​ ​on​ ​existing​ ​literature​ ​related​ ​to​ ​Jews​ ​and​ ​sport​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​broader​
​discussions​ ​on​​antisemitism.​​Similarly,​​another​​piece​​of​​literature​​from​​Dart​​(2021)​​explores​
​how​​sport​​shapes​​the​​Jewish​​identity​​of​​British​​Jews​​without​​the​​use​​of​​any​​theory.​​This​​can​
​indicate​ ​that​ ​this​ ​topic​ ​can​ ​be​ ​explored​ ​through​ ​conceptual​ ​discussions​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​using​
​certain​ ​theoretical​ ​frameworks.​ ​While​ ​this​ ​literature-informed​ ​approach​ ​provides​ ​valuable​




                                                           ​63​
​insights,​ ​it​ ​arguably​ ​limits​ ​the​ ​opportunity​ ​for​ ​theoretical​ ​engagement​ ​and​ ​may​ ​miss​ ​the​
​nuanced conceptual dynamics of antisemitism in sporting contexts.​


​After​​reviewing​​the​​literature​​on​​antisemitism​​in​​football​​within​​the​​field​​of​​sport​​sociology,​​it​
​becomes​ ​clear​ ​that​ ​some​ ​researchers​ ​have​ ​conducted​ ​their​ ​studies​ ​without​ ​incorporating​
​any​ ​theoretical​ ​framework,​ ​while​ ​others​ ​have​ ​used​ ​theories​ ​that​ ​focus​ ​more​ ​broadly​ ​on​
​general​ ​social​ ​dynamics​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​on​ ​the​ ​specific​ ​nuances​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​identity​ ​or​
​antisemitism.​ ​The​ ​use​ ​of​​theory​​in​​sport​​sociological​​research​​has​​been​​discussed​​by​​Thiel,​
​Seiberth​ ​and​ ​Mayer​ ​(2018),​ ​who​ ​emphasise​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​theory​ ​in​ ​research,​
​particularly​ ​in​ ​the​ ​social​ ​sciences.​ ​They​ ​conclude​ ​that​ ​empirical​ ​studies​ ​should​ ​be​
​underpinned​ ​by​ ​a​ ​coherent​ ​theoretical​ ​framework​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​meaningful​ ​explanations​ ​for​
​findings.​


​Therefore,​ ​when​ ​exploring​ ​discrimination​ ​in​ ​sport,​ ​particularly​ ​antisemitism,​ ​critical​ ​race​
​theory​ ​(henceforth,​ ​CRT)​ ​and​ ​HebCrit​ ​will​ ​be​ ​utilised​ ​in​​this​​thesis​​as​​frameworks​​to​​better​
​understand​ ​and​ ​examine​ ​the​ ​inequalities​ ​experienced​ ​by​ ​marginalised​ ​communities,​ ​with​
​particular​​focus​​on​​the​​Jewish​​community.​​With​​that​​in​​mind,​​this​​section​​will​​explore​​these​
​two​ ​theories,​ ​providing​ ​a​ ​comprehensive​ ​analysis​ ​of​​how​​antisemitism​​manifests​​in​​today's​
​society,​ ​the​ ​factors​ ​contributing​ ​to​ ​this​ ​discrimination,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​the​
​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​Firstly,​ ​this​ ​section​ ​begins​ ​by​ ​exploring​ ​the​ ​term​​‘race’,​​leading​​into​​the​
​theory of CRT.​


​Race and critical race theory​


​Du​ ​Bois​​(2015)​​recognised​​that​​race​​is​​one​​of​​the​​most​​significant​​organisational​​features​​of​
​society,​ ​functioning​ ​as​ ​a​ ​framework​ ​that​ ​categorises​ ​individuals​ ​based​ ​on​ ​observable​
​characteristics.​ ​This​ ​perspective​ ​highlights​ ​how​ ​race​​has​​historically​​shaped​​social​​dynamics​
​and​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​exert​ ​influence​ ​in​ ​contemporary​ ​society​ ​(Meer,​ ​2014).​ ​Smith​ ​and​​Hattery​
​(2015)​​further​​assert​​that​​race​​impacts​​various​​aspects​​of​​an​​individual’s​​life,​​including​​access​
​to​​healthcare,​​education​​and​​employment​​opportunities.​​However,​​the​​debate​​over​​whether​
​race​ ​is​ ​a​ ​biological​ ​or​ ​social​ ​construct​ ​remains​ ​contentious,​ ​leading​ ​to​ ​significant​ ​divisions​
​among scholars (Andreasen, 2000; Armstrong and Ng, 2005; Morning, 2014).​


                                                            ​64​
​In​ ​the​ ​late​ ​nineteenth​ ​century,​ ​some​​anthropologists​​argued​​that​​race​​is​​a​​purely​​biological​
​phenomenon,​ ​asserting​ ​that​ ​humans​​could​​be​​categorised​​into​​distinct​​biological​​races​​that​
​significantly​ ​influence​ ​behaviour​ ​and​ ​identity​ ​(Neuberger,​ ​2019).​ ​Emirbayer​ ​and​ ​Desmond​
​(2009)​ ​explore​ ​this​ ​debate​ ​through​ ​the​ ​concepts​ ​of​ ​phenotype​ ​and​ ​ancestry.​ ​Phenotype​
​refers​ ​to​ ​observable​ ​physical​ ​traits​ ​such​ ​as​ ​height,​ ​hair​ ​texture,​ ​eye​ ​colour,​ ​and​ ​skin​ ​tone,​
​while​ ​ancestry​​encompasses​​an​​individual's​​family​​lineage,​​reflecting​​the​​racial​​backgrounds​
​of​ ​one’s​ ​parents​ ​and​ ​their​ ​ancestors​ ​(Kaplan,​ ​2003).​ ​Both​ ​phenotype​​and​​ancestry​​support​
​the​ ​argument​ ​that​ ​race​ ​is​ ​inherently​ ​biological.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​genetic​ ​research​ ​has​
​consistently​​shown​​that​​there​​are​​no​​significant​​biological​​differences​​between​​these​​‘races’​
​(Bevan, 2004).​


​Conversely,​ ​contemporary​ ​sociologists,​ ​including​ ​Greenberg​ ​(1998),​ ​Nye​ ​(2018)​ ​and​
​Ladson-Billings​ ​(2018),​ ​contend​ ​that​ ​race​ ​is​ ​not​ ​a​ ​biological​ ​construct​ ​but​ ​rather​ ​a​ ​socially​
​constructed​​concept​​(Ritzer​​and​​Stepnisky,​​2022).​​The​​National​​Research​​Council​​(2004,​​p.​​2)​
​describes​​race​​as​​a​​“social​​construct​​based​​on​​observed​​or​​ascribed​​characteristics​​that​​have​
​acquired​ ​socially​ ​significant​ ​meaning.”​ ​This​ ​perspective​ ​highlights​ ​how​ ​society​ ​creates​
​categories​​based​​on​​specific​​characteristics,​​providing​​them​​with​​meaning​​and,​​consequently,​
​defining​ ​races​ ​(Meer,​ ​2014).​ ​This​ ​notion​ ​that​ ​race​ ​is​ ​a​ ​social​ ​construct​​is​​a​​central​​tenet​​of​
​CRT,​ ​which​ ​will​ ​be​ ​explored​ ​in​ ​the​ ​following​ ​section​ ​of​ ​this​ ​chapter.​ ​CRT​ ​examines​ ​the​
​intersection​ ​of​ ​race,​ ​law,​ ​and​ ​power,​ ​and​ ​this​ ​section​ ​will​ ​discuss​ ​its​ ​key​ ​tenets​ ​and​
​application​ ​for​ ​understanding​ ​racial​ ​inequalities​ ​in​ ​society.​ ​Additionally,​ ​it​ ​will​ ​bring​ ​to​
​attention​ ​existing​ ​literature​ ​that​ ​has​ ​utilised​ ​CRT​ ​within​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​sociology,​
​highlighting​ ​how​ ​this​ ​framework​ ​has​ ​been​​applied​​to​​analyse​​issues​​such​​as​​discrimination,​
​representation, and access to opportunities in sports.​


​One​​of​​the​​most​​significant​​events​​of​​the​​1950s​​was​​the​​civil​​rights​​movement,​​a​​decade-long​
​struggle​ ​during​ ​which​ ​African-Americans​ ​fought​ ​for​ ​equal​ ​rights​ ​(Jones,​ ​2002).​ ​The​
​movement​​aimed​​to​​challenge​​legal​​inequalities,​​resulting​​in​​landmark​​legislation​​such​​as​​the​
​Civil​​Rights​​Act​​(1964),​​the​​Voting​​Rights​​Act​​(1965),​​and​​the​​Fair​​Housing​​Act​​(1968).​​Despite​
​these​ ​advancements,​ ​African-Americans​ ​continued​ ​to​ ​face​ ​social​ ​disadvantages​ ​even​ ​after​
​the​ ​civil​ ​rights​ ​movement​ ​officially​ ​concluded​ ​in​ ​1968​​(Jones,​​2002).​​As​​the​​movement​​lost​


                                                              ​65​
​momentum,​​concerns​​grew​​regarding​​the​​persistent​​prevalence​​of​​racial​​discrimination​​in​​the​
​United States throughout the 1970s (Brown and Jackson, 2013).​

​In​ ​response​ ​to​ ​this​ ​ongoing​ ​inequality,​ ​a​ ​group​ ​of​ ​lawyers,​ ​activists,​ ​and​ ​legal​ ​scholars,​
​including​ ​Derrick​ ​Bell,​ ​Allan​ ​Freeman,​ ​and​ ​Richard​ ​Delgado,​ ​developed​ ​CRT​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​
​Stefancic,​ ​2001).​ ​Defined​ ​by​ ​Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic​ ​(2001,​ ​p.​ ​3)​ ​as​ ​a​ ​“collection​​of​​activists​
​and​ ​scholars​ ​interested​ ​in​ ​studying​ ​and​ ​transforming​ ​the​ ​relationship​ ​among​ ​race,​ ​racism,​
​and​ ​power,”​ ​CRT​ ​seeks​ ​to​ ​critically​​analyse​​the​​law​​and​​its​​intersection​​with​​race,​​aiming​​to​
​challenge​ ​systemic​ ​racial​ ​discrimination​ ​and​ ​inequalities​ ​(Ladson-Billings​ ​and​ ​Tate,​ ​2006).​
​Taylor​ ​(2006)​ ​notes​ ​that​ ​critical​ ​race​ ​theorists​ ​broadened​ ​the​ ​definition​ ​of​ ​racism​ ​to​
​encompass​ ​the​ ​hierarchical​ ​and​ ​structural​ ​norms​ ​that​ ​sustain​ ​oppressive​ ​relationships​ ​and​
​inequalities​ ​in​ ​status,​ ​wealth,​ ​and​ ​education,​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​merely​ ​focusing​ ​on​ ​individual​
​actions.​ ​By​ ​examining​ ​both​ ​implicit​ ​and​ ​explicit​ ​impacts​ ​of​ ​race​ ​and​ ​racism​ ​on​ ​social​
​structures​ ​and​ ​practices​ ​(Yasso,​ ​2005),​ ​CRT​ ​provides​ ​a​ ​framework​ ​for​ ​articulating​ ​the​
​historical​​and​​contemporary​​challenges​​for​​Black​​Americans,​​while​​effectively​​acknowledging​
​their​ ​perceptions​ ​of​ ​the​ ​law​ ​and​ ​society​ ​(Brown​ ​and​ ​Jackson,​ ​2013;​ ​DeCuir​ ​and​ ​Dixson,​
​2004).​

​CRT​​emerged​​from​​the​​foundation​​of​​Critical​​Legal​​Studies​​(henceforth,​​CLS),​​which​​aimed​​to​
​scrutinise​ ​the​ ​law's​ ​effects​ ​on​ ​individuals​ ​and​ ​groups​ ​within​ ​various​ ​cultural​ ​and​ ​social​
​contexts​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001;​ ​Ladson-Billings​ ​and​ ​Tate,​ ​2006).​ ​While​ ​CLS​ ​offered​
​valuable​ ​insights​ ​into​ ​the​ ​incomprehensibility​ ​and​ ​disjointedness​ ​of​ ​legal​ ​decisions,​ ​often​
​favouring​​those​​who​​created​​the​​laws,​​it​​largely​​overlooked​​the​​specific​​inequalities​​faced​​by​
​racial​ ​and​ ​ethnic​ ​minorities​ ​(Brown​ ​and​ ​Jackson,​ ​2013).​ ​Originating​ ​in​ ​the​​field​​of​​law,​​CRT​
​critiques​​how​​the​​social​​construction​​of​​race​​and​​institutionalised​​racism​​create​​systems​​that​
​unfairly​​disadvantage​​racial​​and​​ethnic​​minorities,​​while​​also​​proposing​​alternative​​criticisms​
​and​ ​interventions​ ​(Hylton,​ ​2010).​ ​Overall,​ ​CRT​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​framework​​for​​addressing​
​legal issues related to race (Caldwell and Crenshaw, 1996; Jones, 2002).​

​Since​ ​its​ ​creation,​ ​CRT​ ​has​ ​rapidly​ ​expanded​ ​beyond​ ​legal​ ​studies.​ ​Although​ ​interest​ ​from​
​scholars​ ​in​​other​​disciplines​​began​​to​​emerge​​in​​the​​late​​1990s​​(Jones,​​2002),​​CRT​​has​​since​
​diversified​​into​​various​​fields,​​including​​education​​(Ladson-Billings,​​1998;​​Ladson-Billings​​and​
​Tate,​ ​2006),​ ​social​ ​sciences​ ​(Yosso​ ​and​ ​Solórzano,​ ​2005),​ ​and​ ​healthcare​ ​(López,​ ​2003).​


                                                             ​66​
​Furthermore,​​CRT​​has​​been​​instrumental​​in​​exploring​​how​​race​​intersects​​with​​other​​forms​​of​
​discrimination,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​gender​ ​and​ ​social​ ​class,​ ​a​ ​concept​ ​known​ ​as​ ​intersectionality​
​(Crenshaw,​ ​1993).​ ​Despite​ ​this​ ​diversification,​ ​most​ ​scholars​ ​employing​ ​a​ ​CRT​ ​framework​
​continue​ ​to​ ​centre​ ​their​ ​work​ ​around​ ​race,​ ​aiming​ ​to​ ​challenge​ ​racial​ ​prejudice​ ​and​
​discrimination within their respective fields and society at large (Fletcher and Hylton, 2019).​

​Tenets of CRT​


​Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic​ ​(2001,​ ​p.​ ​16)​ ​identified​ ​five​ ​fundamental​ ​concepts​ ​of​ ​CRT;​ ​the​
​understanding​​of​​these​​tenets​​is​​crucial​​for​​critical​​race​​theorists,​​advocates,​​and​​others​​who​
​are working to eliminate racial injustice.​


    ​1)​ ​Racism is “ordinary, not aberrational.”​


​This​ ​tenet​ ​reinforces​ ​that​ ​racism​ ​is​ ​a​ ​deeply​ ​embedded​ ​and​ ​normalised​ ​feature​ ​of​​society.​
​This​​normalisation​​makes​​it​​appear​​natural​​and​​often​​invisible​​within​​the​​political,​​legal,​​and​
​educational​ ​systems​ ​(Manglitz,​ ​Guy​ ​and​ ​Hunn,​ ​2006).​ ​White​ ​superiority​ ​similarly​ ​remains​
​unnoticed​ ​due​ ​to​​its​​ingrained​​presence​​in​​these​​structures​​(Delgado,​​1995).​​As​​critical​​race​
​theorists​ ​maintain,​ ​racism​ ​is​ ​so​ ​deeply​ ​embedded​ ​in​ ​our​ ​social​ ​order​ ​that​ ​it​ ​often​ ​goes​
​unquestioned​​and​​it​​is​​not​​always​​openly​​acknowledged​​or​​displayed​​(Delgado​​and​​Stefancic,​
​2001;​ ​Gillborn,​ ​2005).​ ​According​ ​to​ ​Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic​ ​(2001),​ ​racism​ ​is​ ​a​ ​common,​
​everyday​ ​experience​ ​for​ ​most​ ​people​ ​of​ ​colour,​ ​and​ ​its​ ​impacts​ ​are​ ​felt​ ​across​ ​various​
​spheres​ ​of​ ​life,​ ​including​ ​education,​ ​employment,​ ​housing,​​and​​healthcare​​(Santiago-Rivera​
​et al.​, 2016).​

​This​ ​pervasive​ ​and​ ​often​ ​invisible​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​racism​​directly​​challenges​​the​​notion​​of​​'colour​
​blindness.'​ ​While​ ​advocates​ ​of​ '​color​ ​blindness'​ ​claim​ ​that​ ​ignoring​ ​race​ ​and​ ​treating​
​everyone​​equally​​will​​create​​a​​non-racist​​society​​(Möschel,​​2011),​​critical​​race​​theorists​​argue​
​that​ ​such​ ​an​ ​approach​ ​only​ ​serves​ ​to​ ​conceal​ ​racial​ ​inequalities.​ ​By​ ​ignoring​ ​race,​ '​color​
​blindness'​ ​masks​ ​the​ ​ongoing​ ​discrimination​ ​that​ ​exists​ ​in​ ​society​ ​and​ ​prevents​ ​individuals​
​from​​being​​held​​accountable​​for​​racist​​actions​​(Bonilla-Silva,​​2006;​​DeCuir​​and​​Dixson,​​2004).​
​In​ ​doing​ ​so,​​it​​allows​​systemic​​racism​​to​​persist​​unchallenged​​within​​institutions​​(Bergerson,​
​2003; Delgado and Stefancic, 2001).​


                                                           ​67​
    ​2)​ ​The concept of interest convergence or material determinism.​

​Bell​ ​(1980)​ ​and​ ​Crenshaw​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(1995)​ ​discuss​ ​that​ ​race​ ​is​ ​a​ ​social​ ​construct,​ ​shaped​ ​by​
​human​ ​interactions,​ ​and​ ​that​ ​racism​ ​serves​ ​to​ ​benefit​ ​those​​in​​positions​​of​​power,​​namely,​
​White​​elites​​and​​the​​working-class​​caucasians.​​Coined​​by​​Bell​​in​​1980,​​the​​concept​​of​​interest​
​convergence​​claims​​that​​White​​elites​​hold​​the​​power​​to​​make​​decisions,​​and​​laws​​that​​grant​
​rights​ ​to​ ​racial​ ​and​ ​ethnic​ ​minorities​ ​are​ ​typically​ ​enacted​ ​only​ ​when​ ​they​ ​align​ ​with​ ​the​
​interests​ ​of​ ​those​ ​in​ ​power,​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​because​ ​they​ ​are​ ​morally​​just​​(Bell,​​1980;​​Hartlep,​
​2009;​​Museus​​and​​Iftikar,​​2013).​​As​​a​​result,​​Black​​people​​may​​gain​​civil​​rights,​​but​​only​​when​
​their​ ​goals​ ​coincide​ ​with​ ​those​ ​of​ ​White​ ​elites​​(Bell,​​1980).​​Critical​​race​​theorists​​recognise​
​that​ ​for​ ​marginalised​ ​and​ ​racially​ ​oppressed​ ​groups​ ​to​ ​make​ ​progress,​ ​their​ ​interests​​must​
​align with those of the dominant group.​

​Laws​ ​and​ ​legal​ ​systems​ ​have​ ​historically​ ​been​ ​structured​ ​to​ ​protect​ ​White​ ​privilege​ ​and​
​maintain​ ​the​ ​dominance​ ​of​ '​White​ ​supremacy'​ ​(Harris,​ ​1993).​ ​A​ ​related​ ​concept,​ ​material​
​determinism,​ ​holds​ ​that​ ​progress​ ​in​ ​addressing​ ​racial​ ​inequalities​ ​is​ ​more​ ​likely​​when​​such​
​progress​​benefits​​the​​economic​​or​​material​​interests​​of​​the​​dominant​​group​​(Graham,​​2011).​
​Both​​interest​​convergence​​and​​material​​determinism​​reinforce​​the​​idea​​of​​White​​supremacy,​
​where​ ​advantages​​are​​given​​to​​those​​who​​are​​White​​while​​others​​are​​disadvantaged​​due​​to​
​their​ ​racial​ ​identity​ ​(Hylton,​ ​2008).​​According​​to​​Mills​​(1997),​​White​​supremacy​​operates​​as​
​an​ ​often-unacknowledged​ ​global​ ​political​ ​system​ ​that​ ​has​ ​shaped​ ​modern​ ​society.​
​Understanding​ ​White​ ​supremacy​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​confronting​ ​racial​​inequality​​and​​explaining​
​race-based oppression (Gillborn, 2005; Harris, 1995).​

    ​3)​ ​Race is a social construct.​


         ​“[Race]​ ​is​ ​a​ ​verb…​ ​we​ ​are​ ​‘raced’​ ​through​ ​a​ ​constellation​ ​of​ ​practices​ ​that​
         ​construct and control racial subjectivities.” (Thomas, 1993, p. 1806)​

​This​ ​quote​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​race​ ​is​ ​not​ ​a​ ​fixed​ ​or​ ​objective​ ​category,​ ​but​ ​rather​ ​a​ ​socially​
​constructed​ ​classification​ ​system​ ​shaped​ ​by​ ​societal​ ​norms​ ​and​ ​interactions​ ​(Abrams​ ​and​
​Moio,​ ​2009).​ ​Numerous​ ​scholars,​ ​including​ ​Thomas​ ​(1993),​​Greenberg​​(1998),​​Meer​​(2014)​
​and​​Goulbourne​​(2001),​​affirm​​that​​race​​is​​fundamentally​​a​​social​​construct.​​This​​concept​​is​​a​



                                                              ​68​
​fundamental​ ​tenet​ ​of​ ​CRT,​ ​which​ ​proposes​ ​that​ ​race​ ​is​ ​created​ ​through​ ​social​ ​thought​
​(Delgado​​and​​Stefancic,​​2001)​​and​​that​​individuals​​are​​classified​​and​​stratified​​based​​on​​their​
​physical​​appearance.​​This​​classification​​system​​serves​​as​​a​​mechanism​​for​​oppression,​​where​
​attributes​ ​such​ ​as​ ​skin​ ​tone,​ ​hair​ ​texture,​ ​and​ ​eye​ ​colour​ ​become​ ​markers​ ​for​ ​racial​
​categorisation (Emirbayer and Desmond, 2009).​

​As​​racial​​groupings​​have​​evolved​​over​​time,​​race​​cannot​​be​​regarded​​as​​an​​objective​​fact​​or​​a​
​static​​variable.​​Instead,​​it​​should​​be​​understood​​as​​a​​social​​construct,​​an​​ideology​​expressed​
​through​ ​specific​ ​power​ ​dynamics​ ​(Omi,​ ​2001).​ ​Ultimately,​ ​race​ ​has​ ​been​ ​developed​ ​and​
​utilised​​as​​a​​means​​of​​social​​control​​(Coates,​​2003).​​Coakley​​and​​Pike​​(2014)​​elaborate​​on​​this​
​notion​ ​by​ ​discussing​ ​racial​ ​ideology,​ ​which​ ​encompasses​ ​societal​ ​beliefs​ ​about​ ​how​ ​to​
​categorise​ ​individuals​ ​into​ ​biologically​ ​defined​ ​groups.​​These​​ideologies​​ascribe​​significance​
​to​ ​physical​ ​characteristics​ ​and​ ​assess​ ​individuals​ ​according​ ​to​ ​racial​ ​classifications,​ ​further​
​supporting the idea that race is a socially constructed phenomenon.​

    ​4)​ ​The concept of storytelling and counter-storytelling.​

​Kozol​​(1991)​​took​​the​​view​​that​​inequalities​​within​​society​​stem​​from​​a​​racialised​​society​​that​
​tends​ ​to​ ​hinder​ ​and​ ​suppress​ ​discussions​ ​about​ ​race​ ​and​ ​racism.​ ​Given​ ​that​ ​racism​ ​is​
​frequently​​unnoticed,​​it​​is​​crucial​​to​​educate​​on​​the​​ongoing​​inequalities​​and​​the​​realities​​of​
​racial​ ​discrimination​ ​(Ladson-Billings,​ ​2013).​ ​Critical​ ​race​ ​theorists​ ​view​ ​storytelling​ ​as​ ​an​
​essential​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​highlighting​ ​inequality​ ​and​ ​everyday​ ​racism.​ ​Storytelling​ ​can​ ​educate,​
​motivate,​ ​document​ ​history,​ ​and​ ​entertain​ ​(Collins​ ​and​ ​Cooper,​ ​1997);​​however,​​it​​serves​​a​
​specific​ ​purpose​ ​in​​this​​context:​​it​​is​​a​​“methodological​​tool​​for​​giving​​voice​​to​​marginalised​
​persons and their communities” (Aguirre, 2000, p. 321).​

​Storytelling​ ​provides​ ​rich,​ ​qualitative​ ​data​ ​which​ ​is​ ​articulated​ ​by​​members​​of​​the​​minority​
​groups​ ​who​​have​​been​​racially​​discriminated​​against​​and​​previously​​silenced,​​allowing​​them​
​to​​communicate​​and​​share​​their​​lived​​experiences​​through​​their​​own​​words​​(Delgado,​​1989;​
​Solorzano​​and​​Yasso,​​2002).​​This​​methodology​​enables​​those​​who​​do​​not​​understand​​or​​are​
​not​ ​affected​ ​by​ ​racial​​inequality​​to​​investigate​​and​​comprehend​​the​​injustice​​that​​racial​​and​
​ethnic​ ​minorities​ ​face​ ​(Taylor,​ ​2006).​ ​Therefore,​ ​individuals​ ​are​ ​encouraged​ ​to​ ​share​ ​their​




                                                           ​69​
​prejudice​ ​and​ ​discrimination​ ​experiences​ ​because​ ​it​ ​is​​a​​powerful​​way​​to​​expose,​​confront,​
​and change racial superiority (Tate, 1995).​

         ​“Stories,​​parables,​​chronicles,​​and​​narratives​​are​​powerful​​means​​for​​destroying​
         ​mindset” (Delgado, 1995, p. 2413)​

​Counter-storytelling​ ​is​ ​a​ ​concept​ ​which​ ​legitimises​ ​racial​ ​oppressed​ ​groups'​ ​experiences​​by​
​telling​​stories​​that​​refute​​the​​dominant​​perception​​of​​truth,​​allowing​​people​​to​​see​​what​​has​
​always​​been​​there​​but​​from​​a​​different​​viewpoint​​(Bergerson,​​2003;​​DeCuir​​and​​Dixson,​​2004;​
​Taylor,​ ​2006).​ ​Both​ ​story-telling​ ​and​ ​counter-storytelling​ ​have​ ​been​ ​used​ ​in​ ​the​ ​U.S​
​educational​ ​system​ ​as​ ​a​ ​methodology​ ​which​ ​has​ ​explored​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​students​ ​of​
​colour​​(Solorzano​​and​​Yasso,​​2002).​​Research​​from​​DeCuir​​and​​Dixson​​(2004,​​p.27)​​found​​that​
​those​ ​students​ ​were​ ​“uncelebrated”​ ​at​ ​their​ ​school​ ​which​ ​stated​ ​that​ ​they​ ​“celebrate”​
​diversity.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​their​ ​stories​ ​reinforced​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that​ ​racism​ ​persists​ ​in​ ​the​ ​life​ ​of​
​African-American​ ​students​ ​and​ ​that​ ​racism​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​be​ ​hidden​ ​within​ ​normality.​
​Counter-stories​ ​can​ ​be​ ​used​ ​to​ ​help​ ​people​ ​unlearn​ ​beliefs​ ​that​ ​they​​previously​​held​​to​​be​
​true;​​without​​them​​the​​truth​​would​​never​​be​​declared​​to​​the​​public​​(Hartlep,​​2009).​​Delgado​
​(1989)​ ​also​ ​emphasises​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​acknowledging​ ​that​ ​counter-storytelling​ ​helps​
​oppressed​ ​groups​ ​in​ ​developing​ ​solidarity​ ​and​ ​mutual​ ​understanding.​ ​It​ ​brings​ ​together​
​communities​ ​who​ ​have​ ​shared​ ​similar​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​communal​ ​understandings,​
​allowing​​individuals​​to​​sympathise​​with​​and​​support​​one​​another​​(Solorzano​​and​​Yasso,​​2002;​
​Taylor,​ ​1998).​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​to​ ​be​ ​effective,​ ​narratives​ ​and​ ​stories​​must​​be​​or​​appear​​to​​be​
​noncoercive,​ ​inviting​ ​the​ ​reader​ ​to​ ​suspend​ ​judgement,​ ​allowing​ ​them​ ​to​ ​then​ ​determine​
​what reality they want to accept (Delgado, 1995).​

    ​5)​ ​The concept of intersectionality.​


​Crenshaw​​(1989)​​developed​​the​​notion​​of​​intersectionality,​​a​​concept​​which​​emphasises​​the​
​multidimensionality​ ​of​ ​minority​​individuals'​​lived​​experiences.​​Delgado​​and​​Stefancic​​(2001,​
​p.​ ​51)​ ​have​ ​defined​ ​intersectionality​ ​as​​“the​​examination​​of​​race,​​sex,​​class,​​national​​origin,​
​and​ ​sexual​ ​orientation​ ​and​ ​how​ ​their​ ​combinations​ ​play​ ​out​ ​in​ ​various​ ​settings”.​
​Intersectionality​ ​calls​ ​attention​ ​to​​the​​law's​​inadequacy​​in​​addressing​​discrimination​​against​
​people​​who​​fall​​into​​two​​or​​more​​minority​​categories,​​such​​as​​Black​​women​​(Ladson-Billings​


                                                             ​70​
​and​​Tate,​​2006).​​As​​a​​result,​​it​​is​​critical​​to​​consider​​how​​an​​individual's​​identity​​markers,​​such​
​as​ ​race,​ ​gender,​ ​class,​ ​nationality,​ ​sexual​ ​orientation,​​disability,​​religious​​and​​cultural​​views,​
​interact​​to​​create​​various​​types​​of​​discrimination​​(Modiri,​​2012).​​In​​addition,​​intersectionality​
​addresses​​how​​an​​individual​​sees​​themselves,​​how​​they​​view​​reality​​and​​how​​others​​relate​​to​
​themselves​​(Thomas​​et​​al.​,​​2018).​​Intersectionality​​fosters​​an​​understanding​​of​​how​​different​
​aspects​​of​​a​​person's​​identity​​interact​​to​​produce​​various​​forms​​of​​discrimination​​or​​privilege​
​(Gillborn,​ ​2015).​ ​Subsequently,​ ​intersectionality​ ​brings​ ​to​​our​​attention​​how​​individuals​​can​
​witness​ ​and​ ​receive​ ​racism​ ​differently​ ​to​ ​another​ ​individual​ ​based​ ​upon​ ​their​ ​additional​
​identity​ ​markers.​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​men​ ​and​ ​women​ ​may​ ​experience​ ​racism​ ​differently​ ​to​ ​one​
​another.​ ​Therefore,​ ​to​ ​address​ ​feminist​ ​hierarchy,​ ​hegemony,​ ​and​ ​exclusivity,​ ​feminist​ ​and​
​anti-racism​ ​scholars​ ​including​ ​Harris​ ​and​ ​Leonardo​ ​(2018),​ ​have​ ​turned​ ​to​ ​the​ ​concept​ ​of​
​intersectionality​ ​using​ ​it​ ​as​ ​a​ ​primary​ ​analytical​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​the​ ​interconnectedness​ ​of​
​gender​ ​and​ ​race​​(Nash,​​2008).​​To​​conclude,​​intersectionality​​reinforces​​that​​race​​should​​not​
​be​ ​explored​ ​independently,​ ​without​ ​considering​ ​class,​ ​sexuality,​ ​gender​ ​and​ ​other​ ​identity​
​markers as well (Hiraldo, 2010).​


​Critiques of CRT​


​While​​CRT​​has​​been​​widely​​used​​by​​scholars​​to​​investigate​​race​​in​​their​​chosen​​field​​and​​has​
​proven​ ​to​ ​be​ ​a​ ​powerful​ ​theoretical​ ​and​ ​analytical​ ​tool,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​also​ ​sparked​ ​debate​​among​
​others.​ ​In​ ​particular,​ ​certain​ ​tenets​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​have​ ​been​ ​critiqued.​ ​Specifically,​ ​the​
​methodological​ ​emphasis​ ​on​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​narratives​ ​have​ ​been​ ​critiqued,​ ​as​ ​Ladson-Billings​
​and​ ​Tate​ ​(2006)​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​the​ ​notion​ ​of​ ​storytelling​​and​​counter-storytelling​​has​​been​
​scrutinised​ ​for​ ​being​ ​both​ ​subjective​ ​and​ ​‘unscientific’.​ ​Given​ ​that​ ​the​​story​​is​​told​​through​
​the​ ​lens​ ​of​ ​one​ ​person's​ ​experience,​ ​there​ ​could​ ​be​ ​multiple​ ​perspectives​ ​making,​ ​it​
​subjective.​ ​Likewise,​ ​qualitative​ ​methods​ ​such​ ​as​ ​interviews​ ​encourage​​individuals​​to​​share​
​their​ ​lived​ ​experiences,​ ​and​ ​as​ ​stated​ ​by​ ​Hennink,​ ​Hutter​ ​and​ ​Bailey​ ​(2020),​ ​narratives​ ​of​
​people's​ ​lives​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​source​ ​of​ ​in-depth,​ ​rich​ ​data​ ​which​ ​is​ ​used​​in​​qualitative​​research.​
​These​ ​methods​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​have​ ​and​ ​continue​ ​to​ ​be​ ​popular​ ​tools​ ​used​ ​within​
​academic​ ​research.​ ​Although​ ​story-telling​​and​​counter-storytelling​​can​​be​​subjective,​​within​
​qualitative​​research​​and​​academia​​we​​value​​individuals'​​opinions​​and​​experiences;​​therefore,​
​individual​ ​stories​ ​of​ ​racism​ ​are​ ​just​ ​as​ ​important​ ​to​ ​help​ ​make​ ​social​ ​change.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​also​


                                                             ​71​
​important​ ​to​ ​consider​ ​that​ ​story-telling​ ​can​ ​become​ ​complicated​ ​when​ ​people​ ​tell​ ​other​
​people's​ ​stories​ ​that​ ​were​ ​not​ ​part​ ​of​ ​their​ ​own​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​how​ ​they​ ​could​ ​be​
​misinterpreted (Schiff, Noy and Cohler 2012).​


​Although​ ​research​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​White​ ​individuals​ ​can​ ​play​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​role​​in​​anti-racism​
​efforts,​​despite​​being​​outsiders​​to​​the​​direct​​experience​​of​​racial​​discrimination​​(Lin,​​Kennette​
​and​​Van​​Havermaet,​​2023),​​the​​concept​​of​​interest​​convergence​​has​​been​​criticised,​​as​​claims​
​have​​been​​made​​that​​if​​an​​individual​​who​​is​​considered​​‘racially​​privileged’​​wishes​​to​​actively​
​work​ ​against​ ​racism,​ ​the​ ​concept​ ​of​ ​interest​ ​convergence​ ​will​ ​suggest​ ​that​ ​they​ ​are​ ​only​
​working​ ​to​ ​diminish​ ​racism​ ​to​ ​receive​ ​praise,​ ​escape​ ​scrutiny,​ ​or​ ​to​​avoid​​confronting​​their​
​own​​racist​​behaviours.​​However,​​according​​to​​Bergerson​​(2003),​​White​​critical​​race​​theorists​
​can​​theorise​​about​​race​​and​​use​​it​​to​​educate​​people​​about​​these​​concerns​​in​​order​​to​​bring​
​about​​change,​​even​​though​​they​​may​​not​​interact​​with​​CRT​​to​​the​​same​​extent​​as​​those​​who​
​encounter racial injustice.​

​Darder​​and​​Torres​​(2003)​​have​​stated​​that​​class​​has​​been​​discussed​​too​​superficially,​​and​​that​
​there​ ​is​ ​a​​lack​​of​​consideration​​regarding​​intersectionality​​between​​class​​and​​race,​​which​​to​
​them​​is​​a​​failure​​of​​CRT.​​However,​​Hylton​​(2008)​​states​​that​​this​​criticism​​can​​be​​justified,​​to​
​some​ ​extent,​ ​as​ ​there​ ​is​ ​no​ ​theoretical​ ​framework​ ​which​ ​has​​been​​able​​to​​tackle​​all​​of​​the​
​crucial​ ​issues​ ​within​ ​society.​ ​Similarly,​ ​critics​ ​argued​ ​that​ ​CRT​ ​does​ ​not​ ​take​ ​into​
​consideration​ ​an​ ​individual's​ ​class​​and​​gender,​​and​​focuses​​primarily​​on​​an​​individual's​​race​
​(Hiraldo,​​2010).​​However,​​since​​the​​notion​​of​​intersectionality​​was​​developed​​in​​1989,​​it​​has​
​been​​utilised​​to​​explore​​the​​interconnectedness​​of​​race​​and​​other​​identity​​markers​​including​
​class​ ​and​ ​gender.​ ​Nevertheless,​​intersectionality​​was​​criticised​​by​​Butler​​(1990)​​for​​implying​
​that​​all​​forms​​of​​discrimination​​are​​parallel,​​which​​means​​that​​CRT​​and​​intersectionality​​fails​
​to identify what is unique and individual type of oppression.​

​While​ ​the​ ​theory​ ​emerged​ ​and​ ​has​ ​centred​ ​most​ ​specifically​ ​on​ ​the​ ​United​ ​States,​ ​many​
​attempts​ ​have​ ​been​ ​made​ ​to​ ​use​ ​CRT​ ​in​ ​scholarly​ ​literature​ ​focusing​ ​on​ ​race​ ​in​ ​Europe​
​(Moffitt,​ ​Juang​ ​and​ ​Syed,​ ​2019),​ ​Australia​ ​(Vass,​ ​2015),​ ​and​ ​Africa​ ​(Modiri,​ ​2012).​ ​Certain​
​tenets​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​are​ ​not​ ​as​ ​applicable​ ​in​ ​other​ ​parts​ ​of​ ​the​ ​world​ ​as​ ​they​ ​are​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​
​States​​and​​CRT​​has​​subsequently​​been​​criticised​​for​​its​​usage​​in​​other​​cultures.​​This​​is​​not​​to​
​suggest​​that​​racial​​prejudice​​is​​not​​a​​problem​​in​​other​​cultures,​​but​​that​​the​​nature​​of​​racism​


                                                                ​72​
​and​ ​racial​ ​discrimination​ ​varies​ ​between​ ​countries​ ​(Erel,​ ​2007).​ ​Research​ ​suggests​ ​that​
​racism​ ​manifests​ ​differently​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​ ​States​ ​and​ ​the​ ​United​ ​Kingdom,​ ​with​ ​varying​
​impacts​ ​on​​health​​and​​social​​outcomes.​​Research​​from​​Muennig​​and​​Murphy​​(2011)​​looked​
​into​​health​​care​​disparities,​​and​​found​​that​​racism​​tends​​to​​be​​more​​overt​​and​​has​​a​​stronger​
​negative​ ​effect​ ​between​ ​Blacks​ ​and​ ​Whites​ ​in​ ​the​ ​US;​ ​whereas​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​health​ ​care​
​outcomes​​are​​considered​​better​​for​​Blacks​​(Muennig​​and​​Murphy,​​2011).​​Consequently,​​CRT​
​might​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​adapted​ ​based​ ​on​ ​the​ ​country​ ​a​ ​scholar​ ​is​ ​studying.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​
​highlight​​that,​​for​​this​​research,​​applying​​CRT​​in​​the​​UK​​does​​not​​necessitate​​adhering​​to​​the​
​exact same methods as used in the United States (Burdsey, 2011).​


​Questions​ ​have​ ​been​​raised​​regarding​​racial​​issues​​along​​a​​‘Black-White’​​binary.​​Racism​​was​
​once​ ​described​ ​by​ ​Marable​ ​(1992,​ ​p.​ ​5)​ ​as​​“a​​system​​of​​ignorance,​​exploitation,​​and​​power​
​used​​to​​oppress​​African-Americans,​​Latinos,​​Asians,​​Pacific​​Americans,​​American​​Indians,​​and​
​other​ ​people​ ​on​ ​the​ ​basis​ ​of​ ​ethnicity,​ ​culture,​ ​mannerisms,​ ​and​ ​color.”​ ​This​ ​definition​ ​is​
​crucial​ ​because​ ​discussions​ ​about​ ​race​ ​and​ ​prejudice​ ​have​ ​evolved​ ​from​ ​a​ ​Black-White​
​debate​ ​to​ ​involve​ ​various​ ​appearances,​ ​perspectives,​ ​and​ ​experiences.​ ​However,​ ​CRT​ ​has​
​been​​critiqued​​for​​not​​addressing​​other​​races​​that​​are​​neither​​'Black'​​nor​​'White',​​highlighting​
​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​a​ ​more​ ​nuanced​ ​understanding​ ​of​​diverse​​racial​​groups​​beyond​​the​​Black​​and​
​White​​binary​​(Kim​​and​​Ng,​​2019).​​Nonetheless,​​researchers​​have​​used​​CRT​​to​​develop​​critical​
​frameworks​ ​to​ ​address​ ​other​ ​racial​ ​and​ ​ethnic​ ​groups.​ ​For​ ​example,​​LatCrit​​(Valdes,​​1998),​
​TribalCrit​ ​(Brayboy,​ ​2001)​ ​and​ ​AsianCRT​ ​are​ ​theories​​that​​emerged​​from​​CRT​​(Chang,​​1993;​
​1998).​ ​These​ ​theories​ ​were​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​respond​​to​​the​​needs​​of​​Latinos,​​American​​Indians​
​and​ ​Asian​ ​Americans,​ ​while​ ​broadly​ ​maintaining​ ​CRT's​ ​fundamental​ ​principles​ ​(Brayboy,​
​2005).​​Similarly,​​Rubin​​(2020)​​claims​​that​​CRT​​fails​​to​​properly​​discuss​​the​​Jewish​​community,​
​and​​therefore,​​this​​study​​offers​​an​​exciting​​opportunity​​to​​advance​​knowledge​​of​​the​​Jewish​
​population​ ​through​ ​HebCrit​​(Rubin,​​2020),​​a​​framework​​that​​arose​​from​​CRT​​to​​address​​the​
​Jewish population's needs.​


​HebCrit​


​While​ ​CRT​ ​is​ ​a​ ​valuable​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​discussing​ ​‘race’​ ​related​ ​problems,​ ​Rubin​ ​(2020,​ ​p.​ ​501)​
​claims​​that​​it​​"does​​not​​go​​far​​enough​​in​​identifying​​and​​addressing​​the​​specific​​needs​​of​​the​


                                                             ​73​
​Jewish​ ​peoples".​ ​Furthermore,​ ​when​ ​discussing​ ​CRT​ ​in​ ​relation​ ​to​ ​Judaism,​ ​according​ ​to​
​Creed​​(2020),​​it​​may​​become​​problematic,​​placing​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community​​at​​risk.​
​This​​is​​due​​to​​their​​assumed​​‘Whiteness’,​​which​​has​​benefits​​according​​to​​CRT;​​however,​​they​
​are​​often​​subjected​​to​​discrimination​​and​​oppression,​​which​​is​​difficult​​to​​comprehend​​given​
​that​ ​CRT​ ​recognises​ ​those​ ​who​ ​are​​considered​​‘White'​​belong​​to​​the​​dominant​​community.​
​Schlosser​​(2006)​​recognised​​that​​the​​possibility​​that​​Jewish​​problems​​have​​been​​overlooked​
​in​ ​the​ ​past​ ​as​ ​being​ ​Jewish​ ​is​ ​considered​ ​an​ ​invisible​ ​minority​ ​status.​ ​Rubin​ ​(2020,​​p.​​499)​
​recognises​​that​​Jews​​are​​“often​​overlooked​​and​​ignored​​in​​multicultural,​​diversity,​​and​​ethnic​
​studies”​​although​​“Jews​​continue​​to​​face​​specific​​concerns​​and​​obstacles​​in​​both​​the​​United​
​States​​and​​around​​the​​world.”​​Judaken​​(2018)​​states​​that​​antisemitism​​is​​still​​under-theorised​
​and​ ​calls​ ​for​ ​the​ ​creation​ ​of​ ​a​ ​new​ ​theoretical​ ​framework​ ​to​ ​investigate​ ​antisemitism.​
​Therefore,​ ​in​ ​2020,​​Rubin​​(2020)​​introduced​​the​​concept​​of​​'HebCrit,'​​which​​he​​defines​​as​​a​
​theoretical​ ​framework​ ​that​ ​can​​be​​used​​to​​address​​the​​challenges​​that​​many​​Jewish​​people​
​face​ ​in​ ​terms​ ​of​ ​racism​ ​and​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Furthermore,​​he​​contends​​that​​HebCrit​​gives​​the​
​Jewish​ ​community​ ​a​ ​voice​ ​in​ ​critical​ ​racial​ ​studies​ ​and​ ​acknowledges​ ​Jewish​ ​people's​
​complex role on the racial spectrum.​


​As​ ​acknowledged​ ​previously,​ ​while​ ​antisemitism​ ​shares​ ​commonalities​ ​with​ ​other​​forms​​of​
​racism,​​it​​also​​manifests​​in​​unique​​ways,​​often​​through​​particular​​stereotypes​​and​​persistent​
​conspiracy​​narratives,​​necessitating​​frameworks​​like​​HebCrit​​that​​build​​on​​but​​move​​beyond​
​traditional​​CRT​​approaches.​​It​​is​​important​​to​​note​​that​​the​​word​​HebCrit​​is​​derived​​from​​the​
​outdated​​racial​​slur​​directed​​at​​Jews,​​‘hebe’.​ ​Similarly,​​to​​the​​use​​of​​the​​term​​‘Yid’,​​it​​has​​been​
​reclaimed​ ​as​​a​​point​​of​​critical​​strength,​​according​​to​​Rubin​​(2020).​​This​​chapter​​will​​outline​
​the​ ​concept​ ​of​ ​HebCrit,​ ​which​ ​has​ ​been​ ​used​ ​as​ ​a​ ​method​ ​for​ ​analysing​ ​inequalities​
​experienced​ ​by​ ​American​ ​Jews.​ ​When​ ​referring​ ​to​ ​British​ ​Jews,​ ​this​ ​research​ ​focuses​ ​on​
​those​​who​​are​​of​​Eastern,​​Central,​​or​​Western​​European​​ancestry,​​or​​Ashkenazim,​​the​​ethnic​
​group​​that​​makes​​up​​about​​95%​​of​​British​​Jews​​(Burton​​et​​al.​,​​2009).​​Furthermore,​​this​​thesis​
​will be the first to explore the applicability of the HebCrit framework with a focus on the UK.​




                                                             ​74​
​Tenets of HebCrit​


​Similar to CRT, Rubin (2020, p. 502) developed five key tenets of HebCrit:​

    ​1)​ ​Jews continue to be discriminated against and persecuted.​

​For​ ​centuries,​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​has​ ​been​ ​subjected​ ​to​ ​bigotry​ ​and​ ​unjust​ ​judgement​
​(Goldberg​ ​and​ ​Durkheim,​ ​2008).​ ​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​its​ ​long-standing​ ​history,​ ​Rubin​ ​(2020)​
​acknowledges​​that​​antisemitism​​is​​on​​the​​rise​​in​​the​​United​​States​​and​​Europe.​​In​​the​​United​
​States,​ ​Jew’s​ ​account​ ​for​ ​56.9%​ ​of​ ​religious​ ​hate-crime,​ ​making​ ​them​ ​the​ ​largest​ ​group​ ​of​
​religious​ ​reported​ ​hate-crime​ ​victims​ ​(Federal​ ​Bureau​​of​​Investigation,​​2019).​​Antisemitism,​
​according​​to​​Rubin​​(2020),​​is​​a​​global​​problem​​that​​has​​impacted​​many​​Jewish​​communities​
​across​ ​Europe​ ​too.​ ​89%​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​population​ ​within​ ​the​ ​EU​ ​believes​ ​that​​antisemitism​
​has​ ​risen​ ​in​ ​their​ ​country​ ​in​ ​the​ ​last​ ​five​ ​years​ ​(European​ ​Union​ ​Agency​ ​for​ ​Fundamental​
​Rights,​ ​2018).​ ​Statistics​ ​from​ ​the​ ​CST​ ​(2020)​ ​support​ ​this​ ​statement​ ​as​ ​incidents​ ​of​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​rose​ ​by​ ​7%​ ​from​ ​the​ ​previous​ ​year,​ ​making​ ​it​ ​the​ ​highest​ ​annual​
​number​ ​the​ ​CST​ ​has​ ​ever​ ​registered.​ ​Subsequently,​ ​antisemitism​​in​​the​​United​​Kingdom,​​in​
​particular,​ ​remains​ ​a​ ​source​ ​of​ ​concern​ ​(Boyd​ ​and​ ​Staetsky,​ ​2015;​ ​May,​ ​2017;​ ​Sherwood,​
​2019).​​According​​to​​National​​Hate​​Crime​​figures,​​Jewish​​people​​in​​the​​UK​​are​​the​​group​​most​
​likely to be victims of religiously motivated hate crimes per capita (Home Office, 2020).​

​The​ ​Anti-Defamation​ ​League​​(2020)​​claim​​that​​the​​cause​​of​​rising​​global​​antisemitism​​is,​​far​
​right​​nationalism,​​extreme​​left​​antisemitism,​​sometimes​​disguised​​as​​anti-Israel​​rhetoric,​​and​
​Islamist​​radicalism.​​Several​​authors,​​including​​MacDonald-Dennis​​(2006)​​and​​Judaken​​(2018),​
​have​​argued​​that​​Jewish​​inequality​​is​​widely​​ignored​​in​​both​​culture​​and​​academic​​literature,​
​which Rubin (2020, p. 504) agrees with, then saying:​

       ​“CRT​ ​does​ ​not​ ​adequately​ ​address​ ​Jewish​ ​persecution​ ​in​ ​both​ ​U.S​ ​society​ ​and​
       ​around​​the​​world​​and​​how​​it​​affects​​the​​individual.​​Therefore,​​there​​is​​a​​need​​for​
       ​HebCrit and bringing Jewish animus to the forefront of critical race research.”​




                                                           ​75​
    ​2)​ ​Jews are a racialised group.​

​Adorno​ ​and​ ​Horkheimer​ ​(2000,​ ​p.​ ​270)​ ​state​ ​that​​some​​theorists​​argue​​that​​“Jews​​have​​no​
​national​​or​​racial​​characteristics​​and​​simply​​form​​a​​group​​through​​their​​religious​​opinions​​and​
​tradition”.​​According​​to​​Rubin​​(2020,​​p.​​504)​​the​​“apparent​​reason​​for​​the​​lack​​of​​application​
​of​ ​CRT​ ​for​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​is​ ​the​ ​question​ ​of​ ​race”.​ ​Zauzamer​ ​(2019)​ ​rightfully​ ​notes​ ​that​
​Judaism​ ​is​ ​a​ ​religion.​ ​However,​​not​​all​​who​​identify​​as​​Jewish​​are​​religious,​​as​​could​​be​​said​
​for​​many​​religions.​​Judaism​​can​​be​​passed​​through​​ancestry,​​which​​can​​grant​​individuals​​with​
​genetic​​characteristics​​(Zauzamer,​​2019).​​Therefore,​​Greenberg​​(2015)​​explains​​how​​Jews​​are​
​continually​ ​navigating​ ​between​ ​faith​ ​and​ ​nationality,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​race​ ​and​ ​colour,​ ​and​ ​how​
​Jews have never felt at ease within these divisions.​

​There​ ​have​ ​been​ ​ongoing​ ​controversies​ ​since​ ​the​ ​18th​ ​century​ ​about​ ​whether​ ​Jews​ ​are​ ​a​
​racial,​ ​social,​ ​ethnic,​ ​or​ ​cultural​​community​​(Chervyakov,​​Gitelman​​and​​Shapiro,​​1997;​​Hart,​
​2005).​ ​Emirbayer​ ​and​ ​Desmond​ ​(2009)​ ​emphasised​ ​that​ ​although​ ​ethnicity​ ​and​ ​race,​
​alongside​​nationality,​​are​​closely​​connected,​​race​​and​​ethnicity​​are​​in​​fact​​dissimilar.​​Harrison​
​and​ ​Belcher​ ​(2006)​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​the​ ​concept​ ​of​ ​‘race’​ ​is​ ​based​ ​upon​ ​superficial,​ ​observable​
​physical​ ​differences,​ ​including​ ​skin​ ​colour​ ​and​ ​hair​ ​textures.​ ​On​ ​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​Coakley​
​(2015)​ ​recognises​ ​ethnicity​ ​as​ ​a​ ​term​​which​​brings​​attention​​to​​the​​cultural​​differences​​and​
​shared​ ​lifestyles.​ ​Emirbayer​ ​and​ ​Desmond​ ​(2009)​ ​state​ ​that​ ​this​ ​may​ ​include​ ​cultures,​
​nationalities,​ ​and​ ​religions.​ ​Subsequently,​ ​race​ ​and​ ​religion​ ​are​ ​frequently​ ​regarded​ ​as​
​distinct​​entities.​​Zauzamer​​(2019)​​mentions​​that​​the​​ongoing​​discussion​​as​​to​​what​​Judaism​​is​
​has become so complex, that even fellow Jews do not agree on what it is.​

​According​​to​​Kaplan​​(2003)​​and​​Jacobson​​(2000),​​Jews​​were​​considered​​a​​separate​​race​​with​
​a​ ​distinct​ ​physiognomy​ ​during​ ​the​ ​nineteenth​ ​and​ ​early​ ​twentieth​ ​centuries.​ ​In​ ​addition,​
​Rubin​ ​(2020,​ ​p.​ ​504)​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​“in​ ​recent​ ​years,​ ​there​ ​has​ ​been​ ​much​ ​debate​ ​as​ ​to​
​whether​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​biological​ ​component​ ​to​ ​being​​Jewish”.​​According​​to​​Kahn​​(2013),​​some​
​scientists​​may​​highlight​​concrete​​evidence​​that​​supports​​a​​biological​​basis​​for​​Jewishness,​​but​
​others,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Patai​ ​and​ ​Patai​ ​(1989),​ ​disagree,​ ​whose​ ​study​ ​looked​​at​​both​​psychological​
​and​​biological​​causes,​​and​​they​​argued​​that​​Jews​​were​​not​​a​​race.​​Nevertheless,​​Rubin​​(2020,​
​p.​ ​505)​ ​emphasises​ ​that​ ​“this​​debate​​will​​continue​​as​​genetic​​testing​​methods​​advance​​and​
​expand over time”.​


                                                            ​76​
​Greenberg​ ​(2015)​ ​and​ ​Ladson-Billings​ ​(2018),​ ​on​ ​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​are​ ​among​ ​a​ ​group​ ​of​
​writers​ ​who​ ​claim​ ​race​ ​is​ ​socially​ ​constructed.​ ​An​ ​individual's​ ​observable​ ​or​ ​assigned​
​characteristics​ ​gives​​them​​a​​socially​​significant​​meaning,​​which​​categorises​​them​​into​​a​​race​
​(National​ ​Research​ ​Council,​ ​2004).​ ​Defining​ ​race​ ​by​ ​visible​ ​traits​ ​creates​ ​challenges​​for​​the​
​Jewish​​community,​​as​​Baddiel​​(2021)​​points​​out,​​because​​they​​may​​not​​always​​have​​distinct,​
​recognisable​ ​features​ ​that​ ​make​ ​them​ ​visibly​ ​identifiable.​ ​Since​ ​racism​ ​is​ ​often​ ​linked​ ​to​
​physical​​traits,​​Giliadi​​(2020,​​p.​​2)​​states​​that​​Jews​​have​​been​​excluded​​from​​the​​category​​of​
​being​ ​oppressed,​ ​despite​ ​historical​ ​and​ ​ongoing​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​oppression,​ ​as​ ​they​ ​“don't​
​have​​the​​‘look’,​​don’t​​have​​the​​‘sound’,​​don't​​have​​the​​‘behaviour​​of​​the​​oppressed’”.​​This​​is​
​due​​to​​societal​​stereotypes​​about​​how​​such​​groups​​should​​look,​​sound,​​or​​act.​​For​​instance,​
​Jewish​ ​individuals,​ ​particularly​ ​those​ ​of​ ​European​ ​descent,​ ​may​ ​lack​ ​the​ ​physical​ ​markers​
​often​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​marginalised​ ​groups,​ ​do​ ​not​ ​exhibit​ ​distinct​ ​linguistic​​traits,​​and​​may​
​not​ ​fit​ ​behavioural​ ​stereotypes​ ​of​ ​economic​ ​marginalisation​ ​in​ ​line​ ​with​ ​antisemitic​​beliefs​
​that Jews are economically advantaged.​

​Furthermore,​​Rubin​​(2020,​​p.​​205)​​claims​​that​​“Jews​​are​​not​​considered​​to​​be​​a​​distinct​​race,​
​but​​rather,​​lumped​​into​​the​​category​​of​​being​​White”​​as​​a​​result​​of​​being​​‘raced’​​by​​observing​
​an​​individual's​​characteristics.​​Kaplan​​(2003)​​states​​that,​​although​​Jews​​are​​not​​considered​​a​
​race​ ​in​ ​terms​ ​of​ ​biology,​​phenotype,​​or​​genetics,​​they​​are​​viewed​​as​​such​​in​​terms​​of​​social​
​background;​ ​a​ ​race​ ​with​ ​a​ ​common​ ​history,​ ​descent,​ ​and​ ​appearance,​ ​which​ ​forms​ ​an​
​essential​ ​part​ ​of​ ​their​ ​image​ ​and​ ​identity.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​Jews,​ ​like​ ​other​ ​people​ ​that​ ​are​
​generally​​referred​​to​​as​​a​​‘race’,​​may​​be​​recognised​​by​​both​​others​​and​​oneself.​ ​Rubin​​(2020,​
​p.​ ​505)​ ​concludes​ ​“that​ ​Jews​ ​are​ ​a​ ​race​ ​and​ ​need​ ​to​​be​​studied​​as​​such​​in​​CRT”,​​as​​it​​does​
​create,​ ​however,​ ​a​ ​difficult​ ​and​ ​divisive​ ​phenomenon,​ ​with​ ​disagreements​ ​about​ ​whether​
​antisemitism​ ​can​ ​entail​ ​both​ ​bigotry​ ​and​ ​religious​ ​prejudice,​ ​and​ ​whether​ ​it​ ​should​ ​be​
​considered a distinct form of racism (Back and Solomos, 2000; Meer, 2014).​

    ​3)​ ​Jews, and their perception as White, creates invisibility and tension.​

​The​ ​intersection​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​and​ ​White​ ​identities​ ​is​ ​a​ ​complex​ ​issue​ ​that​ ​has​ ​received​
​significant​ ​scholarly​ ​attention​ ​(Blumenfeld,​ ​2006;​ ​Goldstein,​ ​2006;​ ​Rubin,​ ​2019;​ ​Tanner,​
​2020).​​Baddiel​​(2021)​​suggests​​that​​Jews​​may​​be​​less​​easily​​identifiable​​unless​​visibly​​marked​
​by​ ​religious​ ​symbols,​ ​contributing​ ​to​ ​a​ ​perception​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​as​ ​White​ ​and,​ ​thus,​


                                                             ​77​
​rendering​​them​​relatively​​invisible.​​Because​​CRT​​largely​​focuses​​on​​Black​​and​​White​​groups,​​it​
​often​ ​fails​ ​to​ ​fully​ ​encompass​ ​other​ ​communities,​ ​including​ ​Jewish​ ​people,​ ​who​ ​may​ ​not​
​identify​ ​strictly​ ​within​ ​this​ ​binary​ ​framework​ ​(Lozano,​ ​2017;​ ​Rubin,​ ​2020).​ ​Rubin​ ​(2020,​ ​p.​
​506)​ ​states​ ​that​ ​the​ ​Black/White​ ​binary​ ​is​ ​“problematic​ ​for​ ​many​​Jewish​​people​​since​​they​
​fall​ ​within​ ​this​ ​nebulous​ ​‘space​ ​between’”​ ​which​ ​creates​ ​tension.​ ​Biale,​ ​Galchinsky​ ​and​
​Heschel​ ​(1998,​ ​p.​ ​5)​ ​describe​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​as​ ​holding​ ​a​ ​unique​ ​insider/outsider​ ​status,​
​positioned​ ​"somewhere​ ​between​ ​the​ ​dominant​ ​role​ ​of​ ​the​ ​White​ ​majority​ ​and​ ​the​
​marginalised​ ​status​ ​of​ ​people​ ​of​ ​color​ ​[sic]."​ ​Similarly,​ ​Bush​ ​(2021)​ ​states​ ​that​ ​within​ ​the​
​Jewish​​community​​there​​is​​a​​lively​​debate​​regarding​​whether​​any​​British​​Jews​​are​​‘White’.​​As​
​previously​ ​mentioned,​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​is​ ​diverse​ ​in​ ​terms​ ​of​ ​ethnic​ ​and​ ​racial​
​backgrounds;​​however,​​in​​2001,​​97%​​of​​British​​Jews​​classified​​themselves​​as​​White​​(Office​​for​
​National Statistics, 2001).​


       ​“ The​ ​Jew​ ​can​ ​be​ ​unknown​ ​in​ ​his​ ​Jewishness.​ ​He​ ​is​ ​not​ ​wholly​ ​what​ ​he​ ​is.​​One​
       ​hopes,​ ​one​ ​waits.​ ​His​ ​actions,​ ​his​ ​behaviour​ ​are​ ​the​ ​final​ ​determinant.​ ​He​ ​is​ ​a​
       ​white​ ​man,​ ​and,​ ​apart​ ​from​ ​some​ ​rather​ ​debatable​ ​characteristics​ ​he​ ​can​
       ​sometimes go unnoticed…” (Fanon, 1993. p. 115)​


​Fanon’s​ ​statement​ ​(1993,​ ​p.​ ​115)​ ​points​ ​out​ ​the​ ​ambiguity​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​identity​ ​within​ ​rigid​
​racial​ ​categories.​ ​By​ ​saying​ ​that​ ​“the​ ​Jew​ ​can​ ​be​ ​unknown​ ​in​ ​his​ ​Jewishness”​​and​​may​​“go​
​unnoticed,”​ ​Fanon​ ​highlights​ ​how​ ​Jewish​ ​identity​ ​often​ ​doesn’t​ ​fit​ ​neatly​ ​into​​typical​​racial​
​labels.​ ​This​ ​conditional​ ​visibility​ ​reveals​ ​a​ ​unique​ ​vulnerability,​ ​as​ ​Jewish​ ​identity​ ​depends​
​largely​ ​on​ ​how​ ​others​ ​perceive​ ​it.​ ​Since​ ​most​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​identify​ ​as​ ​White,​
​“Jews​​are​​considered​​to​​be​​White;​​thus,​​they​​are​​able​​to​​benefit​​from​​White​​privilege,”​​writes​
​Rubin​ ​(2020,​ ​p.​ ​500).​ ​The​ ​previous​ ​quote​ ​from​ ​Fanon​ ​(1993)​ ​reinforces​ ​this​ ​idea.​ ​If​ ​an​
​individual​​is​​recognised​​as​​White​​by​​their​​peers​​based​​on​​first​​physical​​encounters,​​they​​have​
​the 'benefit' of being identified with and being a part of the majority (Crenshaw​​et al.,​​1995).​


​However,​​as​​Baddiel​​(2021,​​p.​​31)​​points​​out,​​“Jews​​don't​​really​​suffer​​from​​being​​thought​​of​
​as​​separate​​as​​long​​as​​people​​don't​​realise,​​they're​​Jews.”​​This​​quote​​emphasises​​that​​Jewish​
​people​ ​do​ ​not​ ​face​ ​racial​ ​discrimination​ ​until​ ​they​ ​are​ ​known​ ​as​ ​Jewish,​ ​reinforcing​ ​the​
​notion​​that​​Jews​​are​​viewed​​as​​White,​​leading​​to​​invisibility​​and​​apprehension.​​Rubin​​(2020)​


                                                             ​78​
​supports​​this​​by​​highlighting​​the​​Jews​​are​​both​​victims​​of​​and​​members​​of​​a​​privileged​​class.​
​It​ ​also​ ​demonstrates​​how​​they​​were​​also​​not​​completely​​welcomed​​by​​White​​society​​or​​the​
​majority.​​As​​a​​result,​​when​​Jewish​​hate​​and​​bigotry​​emerge,​​the​​community​​is​​not​​recognised​
​or​​covered​​for​​other​​needs​​and​​concerns,​​as​​they​​are​​led​​to​​believe​​that​​their​​skin​​colour​​has​
​benefited​ ​them​ ​(Creed,​ ​2020).​ ​This​ ​is​ ​problematic​ ​for​ ​HebCrit​ ​as​ ​through​ ​the​ ​lens​ ​of​ ​a​
​traditional​ ​critical​ ​race​ ​theorist,​ ​would​ ​contend​ ​that​ ​those​ ​who​ ​are​ ​seen​ ​as​ ​White,​ ​gain​
​access​​to​​many​​privileges.​ ​Rubin​​(2020,​​p.​​507)​​concludes​​that​​“race​​for​​the​​Jewish​​peoples​
​has​​never​​been​​solidified;​​they​​were​​once​​considered​​to​​be​​a​​separate​​race​​and​​now​​they​​are​
​seen as being part of the dominant White culture.”​

    ​4)​ ​Jews’ political and economic power is hyperbolic.​

​CRT​ ​emphasises​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​of​ ​power​ ​and​ ​respecting​ ​those​ ​who​ ​wield​ ​it​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020).​
​Understanding​ ​the​ ​relationship​ ​between​ ​race​ ​and​ ​power​ ​is​ ​critical​ ​for​ ​social​ ​progress​
​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001).​ ​Despite​​Jews​​being​​discriminated​​against​​and​​mistreated​​for​
​decades,​ ​“Jews​ ​are​ ​now​ ​believed​ ​to​ ​have​ ​an​ ​inordinate​ ​amount​ ​of​ ​power​ ​and​ ​control​ ​in​
​political​​and​​economic​​realms.”​​(Rubin,​​2020,​​p.​​508).​​This​​is​​still​​a​​common,​​but​​false,​​Jewish​
​stereotype​​and​​conspiracy​​theory​​(Kofta,​​Soral​​and​​Bilewicz,​​2020;​​Rubin,​​2020).​​According​​to​
​Anti-Defamation​​League​​(2020)​​data​​from​​2015,​​35%​​of​​people​​worldwide​​believe​​Jews​​have​
​too​​much​​power​​in​​the​​business​​world.​​Similarly,​​34%​​agree​​that​​Jews​​wield​​too​​much​​power​
​in​ ​global​​financial​​markets.​​In​​the​​United​​Kingdom,​​20%​​of​​people​​agree​​that​​Jews​​have​​too​
​much​ ​power​ ​in​ ​both​ ​business​ ​and​​international​​financial​​markets​​(Anti-Defamation​​League,​
​2020).​

​Baddiel​ ​(2021)​ ​tackles​ ​this​ ​issue​ ​by​ ​citing​ ​data​ ​from​ ​the​ ​New​ ​World​ ​Wealth​ ​(2015),​ ​which​
​indicates​ ​that​ ​just​ ​1.7%​ ​of​ ​the​ ​world's​ ​13.1​ ​million​ ​millionaires​​are​​Jewish,​​as​​compared​​to​
​other​ ​religions,​ ​56.2%​ ​identified​ ​as​ ​Christian,​ ​6.5%​ ​as​ ​Muslim,​​and​​3.9%​​as​​Hindu​​(Baddiel,​
​2021).​​Despite​​that​​this​​small​​percentage​​contradicts​​the​​stereotype​​that​​all​​Jews​​are​​wealthy​
​and​ ​influential,​ ​it​ ​should​ ​be​ ​noted​ ​that​​Jews​​account​​for​​just​​0.5%​​of​​the​​global​​population​
​(Board​​of​​Deputies,​​2020),​​and​​as​​a​​result,​​Jews​​are​​demographically​​overrepresented​​among​
​the​ ​wealthiest.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​Biale​ ​(1986)​ ​and​ ​Rubin​ ​(2020)​ ​challenge​​whether​​wealth​​and​
​power​ ​are​​synonymous​​in​​society,​​because​​as​​Rubin​​(2020,​​p.​​208)​​quotes,​​“if​​Jews​​were​​so​
​powerful, they would have had the ability to prevent the Holocaust from ever occurring”.​


                                                           ​79​
    ​5)​ ​Jewish personal stories have value.​

​In​ ​cultures​ ​where​ ​prejudice​ ​is​ ​common,​ ​Solórzano​ ​and​ ​Bernal​ ​(2001)​ ​emphasised​ ​the​
​importance​​of​​storytelling.​​Rubin​​(2020,​​p.​​509)​​states​​that​​“in​​order​​for​​critical​​race​​theorists​
​to​ ​better​ ​understand​ ​the​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​people,​ ​there​ ​must​ ​be​ ​a​ ​greater​
​embrace​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​counter-stories”.​ ​This​ ​has​ ​been​ ​reflected​ ​in​ ​research​ ​conducted​ ​by​ ​Ellis​
​and​ ​Patti​ ​(2014)​ ​and​ ​Schiff​​et​​al​.​​(2012)​​who​​recognised​​the​​value​​of​​storytelling​​within​​the​
​Jewish​ ​community​ ​and​ ​the​ ​important​ ​contribution​ ​it​ ​gives​ ​to​ ​others'​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​life​
​narratives​​and​​lived​​experiences​​of​​the​​Holocaust.​​These​​experiences​​teach​​people​​about​​the​
​persecution​​the​​Jewish​​community​​experienced​​during​​this​​time​​by​​retelling​​these​​narratives​
​(Saxena,​ ​2019).​ ​Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​International​ ​Holocaust​ ​Remembrance​ ​Alliance​ ​(n.d.)​
​highlight​ ​many​ ​key​ ​benefits​ ​of​ ​storytelling,​ ​and​ ​state​ ​that​ ​stories​ ​from​ ​Holocaust​​survivors​
​provide​ ​a​ ​face​ ​to​ ​history,​ ​which​ ​encourages​ ​students​ ​to​ ​learn​ ​and​ ​develop​ ​an​ ​effective​
​understanding​​of​​history​​from​​an​​personal​​perspective.​​In​​addition,​​it​​teaches​​young​​people​
​the​​impact​​and​​ramifications​​that​​extreme​​persecution​​and​​discrimination​​can​​have.​​Because​
​of​ ​its​ ​effectiveness,​ ​personal​ ​stories​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Holocaust​ ​have​ ​become​ ​frequently​ ​used​​within​
​European​ ​and​ ​the​ ​United​ ​States​ ​to​ ​combat​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​​to​​educate​​individuals​​on​​the​
​lived experiences of the Jewish community (Moisan, Andor and Strickler, 2012; Simon, 2003).​

​In​​relation​​to​​anti-racist​​action​​and​​advocacy,​​Delgado​​(1989)​​and​​Lawson​​(1995)​​identify​​four​
​main​ ​principles​ ​of​ ​storytelling​ ​and​ ​counter-storytelling.​ ​To​ ​begin​ ​with,​ ​Delgado​ ​(1989)​ ​and​
​Lawson​ ​(1995)​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​stories​ ​can​ ​promote​ ​community​ ​among​ ​those​ ​who​ ​are​ ​socially​
​marginalised​​by​​putting​​familiar​​faces​​to​​theory​​and​​practice.​​Second,​​by​​providing​​a​​context​
​for​ ​understanding​ ​they​ ​can​ ​challenge​ ​the​ ​dominant​ ​thoughts​ ​in​ ​society.​ ​Thirdly,​ ​they​ ​will​
​provide​​new​​insights​​into​​the​​lives​​of​​those​​marginalised​​in​​society,​​showing​​that​​they​​are​​not​
​alone.​ ​Finally,​ ​storytelling​ ​educates​ ​others​ ​by​ ​combining​ ​elements​ ​from​ ​both​ ​the​​narrative​
​and​ ​fact,​ ​resulting​ ​in​ ​a​ ​richer​​meaning​​than​​either​​the​​narrative​​or​​reality​​alone.​​Therefore,​
​telling​ ​these​ ​stories​ ​have​ ​value​ ​because​ ​it​ ​reinforces​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community's​ ​lived​
​experiences.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​stories​ ​of​ ​racial​ ​privilege​ ​will​ ​be​ ​exposed,​ ​analysed,​ ​and​
​challenged​ ​by​ ​storytelling​ ​(Solórzano​ ​and​ ​Yosso,​ ​2002).​ ​However,​ ​Rubin​ ​(2020,​ ​p.​ ​509)​
​expresses that:​




                                                           ​80​
       ​“...there​​are​​few,​​if​​any,​​research​​studies​​that​​analyse​​the​​stories​​(or​​narratives)​​of​
       ​Jews​ ​in​ ​the​​twenty-first​​century,​​especially​​as​​it​​relates​​to​​issues​​of​​antisemitism​
       ​and internalised antisemitism.”​

​To​ ​conclude,​ ​HebCrit​ ​is​ ​made​ ​up​ ​of​ ​five​ ​main​ ​tenets.​ ​To​ ​begin​ ​with,​ ​it​ ​acknowledges​ ​that​
​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​continue​ ​to​ ​face​ ​discrimination.​ ​Second,​ ​it​ ​emphasises​
​that​​they​​are​​a​​racially​​segregated​​community.​​Thirdly,​​it​​explored​​the​​perceived​​idea​​that​​all​
​Jews​ ​are​ ​White​ ​and​ ​the​ ​impact​ ​it​ ​has.​ ​Fourthly,​ ​it​ ​states​ ​that​ ​the​ ​power​ ​that​ ​Jews​ ​are​
​perceived​​to​​have​​is​​deliberately​​exaggerated.​​Finally,​​it​​emphasises​​the​​significance​​of​​Jewish​
​story-telling​ ​and​ ​counter-storytelling​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020).​ ​These​ ​main​ ​themes​ ​may​ ​be​ ​useful​ ​in​
​gaining​​a​​better​​understanding​​of​​Judaism​​and​​the​​Jewish​​community.​​In​​addition,​​HebCrit,​​as​
​a​ ​whole,​ ​could​ ​become​ ​a​ ​valuable​ ​tool​ ​and​ ​framework​ ​for​ ​exploring​ ​and​ ​discussing​
​antisemitism.​

​Applications of HebCrit​

​As​ ​of​ ​November​ ​2024,​ ​Rubin’s​ ​(2020)​ ​theory​ ​of​ ​HebCrit​ ​had​ ​eleven​ ​citations​ ​in​ ​Google​
​Scholar.​ ​It​ ​was​ ​cited​ ​in​ ​eight​ ​pieces​ ​of​ ​peer​ ​reviewed​ ​literature,​ ​two​ ​doctoral​​theses​​and​​a​
​masters’​ ​dissertation.​ ​Muller​ ​(2024)​ ​employed​ ​HebCrit​ ​in​ ​conjunction​ ​with​ ​CRT​ ​to​ ​explore​
​college​​students'​​perceptions​​of​​racism​​and​​antisemitism​​within​​an​​educational​​context.​​The​
​study​​involved​​twelve​​students​​participating​​in​​a​​semester-long​​course​​that​​utilised​​the​​lives​
​of​ ​Anne​ ​Frank​ ​and​ ​Emmett​ ​Till​ ​to​ ​derive​ ​pedagogical​ ​strategies​ ​for​ ​combating​ ​racism​ ​and​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​the​ ​classroom.​ ​By​ ​applying​ ​HebCrit,​ ​Muller​ ​(2024)​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​Jewish​
​experiences,​ ​addressing​ ​issues​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​the​ ​complex​ ​positioning​ ​of​​Jews​​within​
​the​​racial​​spectrum,​​which​​facilitated​​a​​clearer​​understanding​​of​​the​​challenges​​faced​​by​​the​
​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​This​ ​theme​ ​of​ ​educational​ ​context​ ​and​ ​the​ ​portrayal​ ​of​ ​Jewish​
​experiences​ ​continues​ ​in​ ​Eargle's​ ​(2024)​ ​critique​ ​of​ ​how​ ​the​ ​Holocaust​ ​is​ ​represented​ ​in​
​social​​studies​​standards​​in​​South​​Carolina.​​Using​​Rubin’s​​(2020)​​theory,​​Eargle​​asserts​​that​​the​
​Holocaust​ ​education​ ​standards​ ​contribute​ ​to​ ​the​ ​marginalisation​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​experiences,​
​advocating​ ​for​ ​changes​ ​that​ ​recognise​ ​and​ ​address​ ​these​ ​issues​ ​through​ ​Jewish​
​counternarratives, although their exploration and application of the theory remain minimal.​




                                                             ​81​
​Selznick​​and​​Greenes​​(2024)​​also​​investigated​​challenges​​faced​​by​​Jewish​​students​​on​​college​
​campuses,​ ​employing​ ​HebCrit​ ​to​ ​outline​ ​these​ ​difficulties.​ ​While​​they​​list​​the​​five​​tenets​​of​
​HebCrit,​ ​they​ ​do​ ​not​ ​consistently​ ​apply​ ​it​ ​as​ ​a​ ​theoretical​ ​framework.​ ​They​ ​emphasise​​the​
​complexity​​of​​engaging​​with​​these​​principles​​for​​both​​Jewish​​and​​non-Jewish​​students,​​staff,​
​and​ ​faculty,​ ​acknowledging​ ​that​ ​fully​ ​integrating​ ​HebCrit​ ​poses​ ​challenges​ ​despite​ ​its​
​inherent​ ​value.​ ​This​ ​nuanced​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​identity​ ​in​ ​educational​ ​settings​ ​is​
​echoed​ ​in​ ​Selznick​ ​et​ ​al.'s​ ​(2024)​ ​longitudinal​ ​study,​ ​which​ ​explores​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​
​college​ ​students'​ ​appreciative​ ​attitudes​ ​towards​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​population.​ ​Although​ ​they​
​reference​​the​​framework,​​they​​do​​not​​directly​​engage​​with​​HebCrit,​​they​​suggest​​its​​potential​
​for​ ​future​ ​application​ ​in​ ​engaging​ ​with​ ​Jews​ ​and​ ​Judaism.​ ​The​ ​integration​ ​of​ ​spiritual​
​perspectives​ ​within​ ​educational​ ​frameworks​ ​is​ ​further​ ​explored​ ​by​ ​Malone​ ​and​ ​Lachaud​
​(2022),​ ​who​ ​developed​ ​an​ ​emerging​ ​theory​ ​titled​ ​FaithCrit,​ ​which​ ​complements​ ​CRT​ ​in​
​addressing​ ​issues​ ​of​ ​injustice,​ ​prejudice,​ ​and​ ​oppression.​ ​They​ ​reference​ ​Rubin’s​ ​work​
​primarily​ ​in​ ​their​ ​future​ ​recommendations,​ ​advocating​​for​​models​​rooted​​in​​CRT​​within​​the​
​field​ ​of​ ​faith​ ​and​ ​religion.​ ​Similarly,​ ​Silverman​ ​(2024)​ ​discusses​ ​the​ ​implications​ ​of​​modern​
​antisemitism​ ​on​ ​Jewish-American​ ​youth​ ​athletes​ ​in​ ​central​ ​Ohio,​ ​citing​ ​Rubin’s​ ​theory​ ​as​​a​
​valuable framework for addressing the rising incidents of antisemitism in the US.​

​Beyond​ ​the​ ​American​ ​context,​ ​Cohen​ ​(2024)​ ​investigates​ ​resistance​ ​to​ ​multicultural​
​education​ ​among​ ​Israeli​ ​Jewish​ ​undergraduate​ ​students​​in​​a​​multiculturalism​​course.​​While​
​employing​​Critical​​Whiteness​​Studies,​​Cohen​​references​​Rubin’s​​theory​​to​​argue​​that​​“Jews​​in​
​Israel​ ​gain​ ​advantages​ ​not​ ​only​ ​through​ ​their​ ​alignment​ ​with​ ​the​ ​nation’s​ ​identity​ ​but​​also​
​from​​their​​status​​as​​a​​privileged​​racial​​category”​​(p.​​4).​​This​​perspective,​​though​​not​​explicitly​
​linked​​to​​HebCrit,​​may​​be​​rooted​​in​​Rubin’s​​assertion​​that​​Jews’​​perceived​​Whiteness​​creates​
​invisibility​ ​and​ ​tension.​ ​Notably,​ ​this​ ​research​ ​was​ ​conducted​ ​in​ ​Israel,​ ​raising​ ​questions​
​about​​the​​applicability​​of​​HebCrit​​in​​different​​national​​contexts​​and​​how​​cultural​​and​​political​
​differences may affect its understanding and implementation.​

​Horsved​ ​(2022)​ ​similarly​ ​examines​ ​contemporary​ ​threats​ ​posed​ ​by​​white​​supremacy​​to​​the​
​Jewish​​community​​in​​the​​U.S.​​Using​​Rubin’s​​theory,​​they​​focus​​on​​the​​perception​​of​​Jews​​as​
​White,​ ​which​ ​they​ ​argue​ ​creates​ ​both​ ​invisibility​ ​and​ ​tension.​ ​However,​ ​this​ ​narrow​ ​focus​
​limits​​their​​analysis​​by​​not​​engaging​​with​​the​​complexities​​outlined​​by​​Rubin​​in​​the​​remaining​
​tenets.​ ​Horsved​ ​concludes​ ​that​ ​Jewish​​experiences,​​informed​​by​​Rubin’s​​HebCrit,​​should​​be​


                                                           ​82​
​integrated​​into​​the​​CRT​​framework​​to​​better​​address​​the​​unique​​needs​​and​​challenges​​of​​the​
​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​Lastly,​ ​Dover's​ ​(2020)​ ​doctoral​ ​dissertation​ ​conducted​ ​in​ ​Mexico​
​acknowledges​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​limitation:​ ​the​ ​frequent​ ​neglect​ ​of​ ​Jews​ ​and​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​
​multicultural​ ​discussions,​ ​which​ ​he​ ​explicitly​ ​recognises​ ​by​ ​citing​ ​Rubin’s​ ​theory.​ ​This​
​oversight​ ​underscores​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​a​ ​more​ ​inclusive​ ​approach​ ​that​ ​incorporates​ ​Jewish​
​perspectives into broader discourses on multiculturalism and social justice.​

​Having​ ​discussed​ ​the​ ​eleven​ ​pieces​​of​​literature,​​it​​is​​important​​to​​note​​that​​aside​​from​​the​
​work​​of​​Muller​​(2024),​​very​​little​​research​​utilises​​HebCrit​​as​​a​​primary​​theoretical​​framework​
​for​ ​in-depth​ ​analysis​ ​or​ ​application.​ ​Instead,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​often​ ​mentioned​ ​only​ ​in​ ​future​
​recommendations​ ​or​ ​as​ ​a​ ​secondary​ ​consideration.​ ​Although​ ​Horsved’s​ ​(2022)​ ​dissertation​
​claims​ ​to​​apply​​HebCrit​​to​​analyse​​the​​threats​​posed​​by​​White​​supremacy,​​it​​only​​addresses​
​one​ ​key​ ​tenet​ ​of​ ​the​ ​theory.​​Furthermore,​​of​​the​​eleven​​pieces​​of​​literature​​reviewed,​​nine​
​were​ ​conducted​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​ ​States,​ ​while​ ​one​ ​was​ ​conducted​ ​in​ ​Mexico​ ​and​ ​another​ ​in​
​Israel.​ ​With​ ​this​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​there​ ​has​ ​been​ ​no​ ​research​ ​within​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport,​ ​or​ ​football​
​specifically,​ ​that​ ​has​ ​used​ ​the​ ​theory.​ ​This​ ​thesis,​ ​on​ ​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​represents​ ​the​ ​first​
​piece​​of​​scholarly​​literature​​to​​use​​HebCrit​​to​​investigate​​the​​Jewish​​community​​in​​the​​United​
​Kingdom.​


​Because​ ​of​ ​its​ ​uniqueness​ ​and​ ​modernity,​ ​it​ ​can​​be​​difficult​​to​​consider​​HebCrit's​​strengths​
​and​ ​weaknesses.​ ​However,​ ​HebCrit​ ​makes​ ​no​ ​reference​ ​to​ ​intersectionality,​ ​one​ ​of​ ​the​
​central​ ​tenets​ ​of​ ​CRT.​ ​Intersectionality​ ​could​ ​be​ ​used​ ​to​ ​investigate​ ​how​ ​being​ ​Jewish​
​interacts​​with​​other​​types​​of​​discrimination​​such​​as​​ethnicity​​and​​gender.​​According​​to​​recent​
​literature​​from​​The​​Board​​of​​Jewish​​Deputies,​​those​​who​​identify​​as​​Black,​​of​​Color,​​Sephardi,​
​Mizrahi,​ ​and/or​ ​Yemenite​ ​Jews​ ​have​ ​expressed​ ​feelings​ ​of​ ​segregation​ ​and​ ​unequal​
​treatment​ ​within​ ​the​​Jewish​​community,​​which​​includes​​synagogue​​attendance​​and​​Bar/Bat​
​Mitzvahs​​(Bush,​​2021).​​Individuals​​with​​two​​or​​more​​minority​​identity​​markers​​(for​​example,​
​being​​Jewish​​and​​Black)​​can​​be​​viewed​​differently​​within​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​according​​to​
​the​ ​report.​ ​Bush’s​ ​(2021)​ ​makes​ ​recommendations​ ​for​ ​making​​Jewish​​life​​more​​inclusive​​to​
​many​ ​people​ ​who​ ​may​ ​have​ ​felt​ ​marginalised​ ​and​ ​excluded.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​been​
​suggested​ ​that​ ​‘Ashkenormativity’,​ ​the​ ​belief​ ​that​ ​all​ ​Jews​ ​are​ ​Ashkenazi,​ ​be​ ​discussed​​and​




                                                               ​83​
​considered​ ​(Bush,​ ​2021).​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​proposed​ ​that​ ​discussing​ ​intersectionality​ ​while​
​studying the Jewish culture would strengthen the theory of HebCrit.​


​CRT and HebCrit in sport​


​Despite​​our​​perception​​of​​sports​​as​​a​​level​​playing​​field,​​it​​is​​a​​racially​​contested​​domain​​and​
​there​​continues​​to​​be​​complex​​issues​​of​​racism​​within​​sport​​(Coakley​​and​​Pike,​​2014;​​Hylton,​
​2005).​ ​Sport​ ​is​ ​a​ ​global​ ​success​ ​and​ ​is​ ​watched,​ ​played,​ ​and​ ​enjoyed​ ​by​ ​many​ ​people,​
​therefore,​ ​it​ ​can​ ​highlight​ ​racial​ ​disparities​ ​in​ ​society​ ​more​ ​than​ ​other​ ​fields​ ​(Hartmann,​
​2000).​​In​​addition,​​Hartmann​​(2000)​​emphasises​​how​​sport​​has​​reinforced​​discrimination​​and​
​inequalities​​which​​are​​seen​​within​​society,​​which​​includes​​racism​​and​​antisemitism.​​A​​variety​
​of​ ​literature,​ ​from​ ​scholars​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Carrington​ ​and​ ​McDonald​ ​(2002),​ ​Harris​ ​(1994)​ ​and​
​Washington​​and​​Karen​​(2001),​​has​​investigated​​race​​in​​the​​field​​of​​sport,​​demonstrating​​that​
​racism has been prevalent throughout sport.​


​Hylton​ ​(2010,​ ​p.​ ​335)​ ​believes​ ​that​ ​CRT​ ​is​ ​an​ ​“important​ ​theoretical​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​anti-racists​ ​in​
​sport”,​​as​​it​​is​​essential​​for​​exposing​​and​​challenging​​racism​​and​​white​​privilege​​within​​sport.​
​In​ ​addition,​ ​CRT​ ​can​ ​provide​ ​knowledge​ ​and​ ​alternative​ ​vocabulary,​ ​which​ ​can​ ​be​ ​used​ ​to​
​understand​ ​research​ ​surrounding​ ​race​ ​and​ ​racism​ ​(Hylton,​ ​2008).​ ​Professor​ ​Kevin​ ​Hylton’s​
​work​ ​focuses​ ​on​ ​equality​ ​and​ ​diversity​ ​in​ ​sport,​ ​with​ ​a​ ​greater​ ​focus​ ​on​ '​race',​ ​racism​ ​and​
​racialisation.​​Hylton​​has​​provided​​the​​“most​​substantive​​theoretical​​contributions​​to​​the​​use​
​of​ ​CRT​ ​in​ ​studying​ ​sport”,​ ​which​ ​has​ ​contributed​ ​to​ ​our​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​race​ ​and​ ​racism​
​within​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​(Burdsey,​ ​2011​ ​p.​ ​42).​ ​Hylton​ ​(2010,​ ​p.​ ​336)​ ​has​ ​used​ ​CRT​ ​to​
​“challenge​​orthodoxies,​​narrow​​‘race’​​thinking​​and​​under-theorised​​approaches​​in​​sport”.​​In​
​addition,​ ​Hylton’s​ ​(2018)​ ​belief​ ​is​ ​that​ ​the​ ​theory​ ​can​ ​contribute​ ​to​ ​abolishing​ ​racialised​
​norms and ideologies which have been created and sustained within sport.​


​Hylton​ ​(2015)​ ​recognises​ ​how​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​people​ ​are​ ​organised​ ​and​ ​categorised​ ​into​ ​groups,​
​based​​upon​​their​​race.​​Hylton​​(2008)​​emphasises​​that​​there​​is​​a​​common​​misconception​​that​
​an​ ​individual's​ ​success​ ​within​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​dictated​ ​by​ ​their​ ​genes​ ​and​ ​some​ ​of​ ​their​ ​cultural​
​background.​​Likewise,​​Hall​​(2002)​​recognises​​that​​White​​athletes​​continue​​to​​be​​described​​as​
​hardworking​ ​in​ ​comparison,​ ​and​ ​that​ ​subsequently,​ ​their​​achievements​​are​​therefore​​more​


                                                              ​84​
​impressive​​and​​worth​​more​​esteem;​​this​​racist​​orthodoxy​​continues​​to​​exist​​within​​sport.​​By​
​stating​​that​​an​​athlete’s​​success​​results​​from​​either​​their​​genes​​or​​upbringing,​​discredits​​the​
​athletes​ ​hard​ ​work​​and​​success.​​In​​addition,​​Younge​​(2000)​​reinforces​​that​​these​​views​​lead​
​to​ ​the​ ​misunderstanding​ ​that​ ​those​ ​Black​ ​athletes​ ​who​ ​are​ ​naturally​ ​talented​ ​at​ ​sport​ ​are​
​subsequently​ ​less​ ​equipped​ ​intellectually.​ ​These​ ​racialised​ ​ideologies,​ ​concepts​ ​and​
​stereotypes​​remain​​prevalent​​and​​unchallenged​​within​​sport​​(Hylton,​​2008).​​This​​can​​be​​seen​
​within​ ​sports​ ​such​​as​​American​​football,​​where​​there​​is​​an​​over-representation​​in​​particular​
​positions.​​Specifically,​​White​​athletes​​are​​considered​​generally​​intellectually​​superior​​and​​are​
​placed​ ​in​ ​positions​ ​whereby​ ​intelligence​ ​is​ ​valued.​ ​On​ ​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​Black​ ​athletes​ ​are​
​considered​ ​to​ ​be​ ​dominant​ ​in​ ​more​ ​physical​ ​positions.​ ​This​ ​is​ ​known​ ​as​ ​‘racial​ ​stacking’​
​(Rosenblatt, 1967).​


​In​ ​addition,​ ​Hylton​ ​(1995)​ ​has​ ​used​ ​CRT​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​the​ ​lived​ ​experience​ ​of​ ​those​ ​athletes,​
​whose​ ​stories​ ​are​ ​underrepresented,​ ​putting​​race​​to​​the​​centre​​of​​any​​focus.​​This​​coincides​
​with​​one​​of​​the​​key​​tenets​​of​​CRT,​​story-telling​​and​​counter-storytelling.​​Hylton​​(1995;​​2003)​
​recognised​ ​that​ ​the​ ​voices​ ​of​ ​the​ ​racialised​ ​population,​ ​including​ ​Black​ ​athletes,​ ​Black​
​spectators,​ ​and​ ​Black​ ​referees,​ ​were​ ​hardly​ ​heard​ ​inside​ ​sport​ ​(Hylton,​ ​2008).​ ​CRT​
​encourages​ ​‘others,'​ ​who​ ​are​ ​often​ ​left​ ​out​ ​of​ ​dominant​ ​viewpoints,​ ​to​ ​tell​ ​their​ ​stories,​
​allowing​ ​their​ ​backgrounds​ ​and​ ​identities​ ​to​ ​be​ ​reflected​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​(Hylton,​ ​2008).​ ​Hylton’s​
​(2018)​​research​​explored​​the​​personal​​stories​​of​​Black​​football​​coaches,​​their​​personal​​stories​
