​highlighted​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​betrayal,​ ​White​ ​privilege,​ ​violence,​ ​and​ ​other​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​racism.​
​These​​perspectives​​and​​personal​​experiences​​aid​​society​​in​​gaining​​a​​better​​understanding​​of​
​the​​systemic​​problems​​affecting​​sport's​​organisation.​​Similarly,​​counter-narrative​​assists​​us​​in​
​focusing​ ​on​ ​White​ ​privilege,​ ​racism,​ ​and​ ​equality,​ ​which​ ​are​ ​all​ ​issues​ ​that​ ​conventional​
​theorists tend to overlook within sport (Hylton, 2008).​


​In​​accordance​​with​​the​​first​​tenet​​of​​CRT,​​racism​​remains​​an​​ordinary​​factor​​which​​shapes​​the​
​experiences​​of​​many​​Black​​athletes​​(Love,​​Deeb​​and​​Waller,​​2019).​​Although​​racism​​may​​not​
​be​​recognised​​by​​some​​in​​sport,​​racism​​in​​organisational​​structures,​​policies​​and​​practices​​can​
​result​ ​in​ ​racial​ ​minorities​ ​being​ ​treated​ ​unjustly,​ ​sometimes​ ​without​ ​intention.​ ​Therefore,​
​CRT​ ​has​ ​been​ ​used​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​to​ ​investigate​ ​policies​ ​and​ ​practices,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​to​ ​challenge​
​institutional​ ​structures​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​that​ ​have​ ​discriminated​ ​against​ ​people​ ​based​​on​​their​​race​


                                                             ​85​
​(Burdsey,​​2011;​​Hylton,​​2005).​​Most​​specifically,​​CRT​​has​​been​​used​​to​​analyse,​​sport​​policies​
​and​​practices​​which​​are​​deemed​​as​​multicultural​​or​​have​​colour-blind​​viewpoints,​​to​​shift​​the​
​thought to ensure it is race-centred (Hylton, 2008).​


​Overall,​ ​Hylton’s​ ​(2010)​ ​work​ ​exploring​ ​anti-racism​ ​organisations,​ ​concludes​ ​that​ ​if​ ​a​ ​CRT​
​framework​ ​were​ ​to​ ​be​ ​used​ ​by​ ​academics,​ ​campaigners​ ​and​ ​organisations,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​the​
​potential​​to​​challenge​​mainstream​​agendas.​​CRT​​therefore​​rejects​​and​​challenges​​widely​​held​
​beliefs,​ ​and​ ​scholars​ ​and​ ​critical​ ​race​ ​theorists​ ​use​ ​CRT​ ​and​ ​its​ ​tenets​ ​to​ ​explain​ ​the​
​fundamental​ ​formations​ ​of​ ​racial​ ​power​ ​and​ ​challenge​ ​commonly​ ​held​ ​thoughts​ ​in​ ​sport​
​(Hylton,​​2008).​​In​​addition​​to​​Hylton,​​other​​scholars​​including​​Burdsey​​(2011)​​and​​Love,​​Deeb​
​and Waller (2019) have used CRT to explore racism within sport.​


​Burdsey​​(2011)​​uses​​sport​​as​​an​​indicator​​and​​key​​example​​to​​support​​the​​notion​​that​​racism​
​is​​not​​unusual​​or​​abnormal,​​the​​first​​tenet​​of​​CRT.​​Whilst​​he​​recognises​​that​​overt​​and​​explicit​
​forms​ ​of​ ​racism​ ​are​ ​being​ ​eradicated,​ ​Burdsey​ ​(2011)​​emphasises​​how​​racial​​minorities​​are​
​still​​discriminated​​against​​on​​an​​individual,​​structural​​and​​institutional​​level.​​Burdsey’s​​(2011)​
​literature​ ​has​ ​explored​ ​the​ ​exclusion​ ​of​ ​British​ ​Asians​ ​within​ ​the​ ​Premier​ ​League.​ ​Racial​
​formations​ ​refer​ ​to​ ​the​ ​“reinforcement​ ​of​ ​Whiteness​ ​in​ ​mainstream,​ ​grassroots​ ​football​​as​
​well​ ​as​ ​the​ ​professional​ ​game”​ ​(Hylton,​​2010,​​p.​​343).​​Burdsey​​(2011;​​2019)​​highlights​​how​
​racial​ ​formations​ ​are​ ​evident​ ​at​ ​the​ ​highest​ ​level​ ​for​ ​football,​ ​which​ ​impacts​​British​​Asians​
​from​​gaining​​high​​authority​​roles,​​which​​subsequently,​​prevents​​them​​from​​challenging​​both​
​racial​ ​and​ ​cultural​ ​stereotypes.​ ​In​​addition,​​Rankin-Wright​​and​​Hylton​​(2020)​​have​​explored​
​managerial​​and​​coaching​​positions​​within​​sport​​focusing​​upon​​Black-women,​​whilst​​using​​the​
​notion​ ​of​ ​intersectionality.​​Their​​literature​​discusses​​how​​the​​experience​​of​​Black-women​​in​
​coaching​ ​roles​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​addressed​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​the​ ​oppression​ ​Black,​ ​female,​​coaches​
​experience within the sporting field (Rankin-Wright and Hylton, 2020).​

​The​ ​concept​ ​of​ ​interest​ ​convergence​ ​is​ ​explored​ ​by​ ​Love,​ ​Deeb​ ​and​ ​Waller​ ​(2019).​ ​They​
​explain​ ​how​ ​anti-racism​ ​responses​​and​​efforts​​to​​aid​​racialised​​minority​​communities​​are​​in​
​place​​only​​because​​they​​are​​concerned​​that​​their​​standing​​in​​the​​world​​will​​diminish​​or​​that​
​bids​ ​for​ ​mega-events​ ​may​ ​be​ ​harmed.​ ​Likewise,​ ​that​ ​sponsorships​ ​could​ ​be​ ​negatively​
​affected​​and​​that​​public​​sector​​funds​​may​​become​​more​​difficult​​to​​access.​​Finally,​​they​​are​​in​



                                                            ​86​
​position​​to​​demonstrate​​that​​sport​​is​​inclusive.​​This​​is​​closely​​linked​​to​​the​​Rooney​​Rule​​which​
​has​ ​been​ ​put​​in​​place​​to​​ensure​​that​​within​​the​​NFL​​that​​at​​least​​one​​member​​of​​the​​Black,​
​Asian,​​and​​Minority​​Ethnic​​community​​is​​interviewed​​for​​a​​head​​coach​​or​​senior​​role.​​Collins​
​(2007)​ ​states​ ​how​ ​the​ ​Rooney​ ​Rule​ ​has​ ​been​ ​viewed​ ​and​ ​considered​ ​as​ ​tokenistic.​ ​In​
​addition,​​Kilvington​​(2019,​​p.​​23)​​explored​​the​​Rooney​​Rule​​in​​the​​context​​of​​English​​football​
​and​ ​discussed​ ​whether​ ​it​ ​would​ ​be​​merely​​a​​tokenistic​​gesture,​​which​​is​​being​​done​​just​​to​
​‘tick​​a​​box’.​​These​​critiques​​suggest​​a​​broader​​concern​​about​​the​​effectiveness​​of​​policies​​that​
​are​ ​intended​ ​to​ ​enhance​ ​representation.​ ​While​ ​such​ ​measures​ ​may​ ​initially​ ​appear​
​beneficial,​ ​they​ ​risk​ ​becoming​ ​superficial​ ​solutions​ ​that​ ​do​ ​not​ ​address​ ​the​ ​underlying​
​systemic issues.​

​Leonard​ ​(2004)​ ​considers​ ​sport​ ​to​ ​be​ ​one​ ​of​ ​the​ ​most​ ​powerful​​discursive​​spaces​​in​​which​
​colour-blindness​ ​is​ ​in​ ​place​ ​and​ ​that​ ​supposedly,​ ​sport​ ​does​ ​not​​see​​colour​​and​​that​​talent​
​alone​ ​decides​ ​how​ ​successful​ ​an​ ​individual​ ​is.​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​valuing​ ​individuals​ ​on​
​success​ ​and​​talent,​​it​​becomes​​hard​​to​​show​​people​​that​​racial​​minorities​​are​​systematically​
​excluded​ ​from​ ​opportunities​ ​to​ ​succeed,​ ​by​ ​individual,​ ​structural​ ​and​ ​institutional​ ​racism;​
​likewise,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​presumed​ ​that​ ​the​ ​success​ ​of​ ​a​ ​team​ ​or​ ​individual​ ​will​ ​outweigh​ ​racism​
​(Bergerson,​ ​2003).​ ​This​ ​is​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​Love,​ ​Deeb​ ​and​ ​Waller​ ​(2019)​ ​who​ ​state​ ​that​ ​the​
​success​​and​​accolades​​of​​Black​​athletes​​in​​high-profile​​sports​​are​​used​​to​​claim​​that​​sport​​no​
​longer has a racism issue.​

​Overall,​ ​as​ ​Burdsey​ ​(2011)​ ​states​ ​CRT​ ​is​ ​important​ ​within​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​UK​ ​sport​ ​and​
​furthermore,​ ​believes​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​could​ ​become​ ​a​ ​key​ ​field​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​apply​ ​the​​theory​​to​
​analyse​​race​​and​​racism.​ ​However,​​for​​the​​purpose​​of​​this​​project,​​when​​exploring​​the​​British​
​Jewish​ ​community​ ​HebCrit​ ​will​ ​be​ ​used​ ​as​ ​a​ ​theoretical​ ​tool​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​analyse​
​discrimination​​and​​experiences​​of​​segregation.​​At​​present​​there​​is​​no​​previous​​research​​that​
​has​ ​used​​HebCrit​​to​​investigate​​antisemitism​​in​​sports,​​especially​​British​​football.​​Therefore,​
​this​ ​study​ ​will​ ​examine​ ​the​ ​utility​ ​of​ ​HebCrit​ ​by​ ​looking​ ​at​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​in​ ​British​
​football.​ ​Given​ ​its​ ​uniqueness,​ ​this​ ​thesis​ ​would​ ​be​ ​the​ ​first​ ​to​ ​extend​ ​HebCrit​ ​as​​a​​critical​
​framework​ ​to​ ​the​ ​British​ ​community,​ ​thus​ ​discussing​ ​the​ ​current​ ​and​ ​pressing​ ​problem​ ​of​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​football.​​By​​employing​​HebCrit,​​this​​research​​offers​​a​​critical​​perspective​​for​
​understanding​ ​the​ ​intricacies​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​British​ ​football,​ ​making​ ​an​ ​original​
​contribution​ ​to​ ​the​ ​body​ ​of​ ​knowledge.​ ​Additionally,​ ​the​ ​findings​ ​of​ ​this​​study​​will​​provide​


                                                              ​87​
​valuable​ ​insights​ ​that​ ​can​ ​guide​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​focused​ ​on​
​recognising​​and​​challenging​​antisemitism.​​Recognising​​and​​challenging​​antisemitism​​is​​crucial​
​not​ ​only​​within​​the​​realm​​of​​academic​​research​​but​​also​​in​​practical​​applications;​​therefore,​
​the​ ​next​ ​chapter​ ​will​ ​explore​ ​the​ ​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​model​ ​as​ ​a​ ​vital​ ​framework​ ​for​
​empowering​ ​individuals​ ​to​ ​actively​ ​confront​ ​and​ ​address​ ​antisemitic​ ​behaviour​ ​in​ ​British​
​football and society more broadly.​

​Bystander intervention model​


​In​ ​1964,​ ​the​ ​rape​ ​and​ ​murder​ ​of​ ​Kitty​ ​Genovese​ ​occurred​ ​while​ ​38​ ​witnesses​ ​looked​ ​on​
​without​ ​intervening,​ ​prompting​ ​Darley​ ​and​​Latané​​(1968)​​to​​investigate​​the​​reasons​​behind​
​this​ ​inaction,​ ​ultimately​ ​leading​ ​to​ ​the​ ​creation​ ​of​ ​the​ ​‘bystander​ ​intervention​ ​model’​
​(henceforth,​ ​BIM).​ ​A​ ​bystander​ ​is​ ​a​​person​​who​​is​​present​​at​​an​​event​​or​​incident​​but​​does​
​not​ ​actively​ ​take​ ​part​ ​(Powell,​ ​2011).​​Individuals​​in​​society​​have​​witnessed​​and​​will​​witness​
​events​ ​around​ ​them;​ ​they​ ​can​ ​either​ ​take​ ​action​​or​​watch​​the​​events​​unfold​​(Public​​Health​
​England, 2020).​


​Hawkins,​​Pepler​​and​​Craig​​(2001)​​investigated​​bystander​​behaviour​​in​​the​​context​​of​​bullying​
​in​​primary​​schools;​​they​​discovered​​that​​just​​19%​​of​​onlookers​​will​​intervene​​and​​take​​action.​
​Cantor​​et​​al.​​(2015),​​on​​the​​other​​hand,​​studied​​bystander​​behaviour​​in​​university​​students​​in​
​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​sexual​ ​violence​ ​and​ ​harassment​ ​and​ ​discovered​ ​that​ ​49.2%​ ​of​ ​those​ ​who​
​witnessed​​an​​incident​​of​​sexual​​violence​​or​​harassment​​took​​some​​form​​of​​action,​​either​​by​
​seeking​​help​​or​​intervening​​directly.​​These​​findings​​from​​Hawkins​​et​​al.​​(2001)​​and​​Cantor​​et​
​al.​​(2015)​​can​​highlight​​that​​individuals​​are​​reluctant​​to​​intervene​​and​​help​​victims;​​however,​
​these​ ​statistics​ ​also​ ​highlight​ ​that​ ​there​ ​are​ ​a​ ​multitude​ ​of​ ​factors​ ​which​ ​could​ ​impact​ ​an​
​individual’s​ ​decision​ ​to​ ​intervene,​​which​​will​​be​​discussed​​later​​in​​this​​chapter.​​The​​purpose​
​of​​this​​chapter​​is​​to​​explore​​the​​BIM​​and​​how​​it​​has​​been​​employed​​in​​academic​​research,​​as​
​well​ ​as​ ​a​ ​practical​ ​tool,​ ​for​ ​making​ ​society​ ​a​ ​safer​ ​and​ ​more​ ​positive​ ​place.​ ​Furthermore,​
​potential​ ​barriers​ ​and​ ​considerations​ ​for​ ​following​ ​the​ ​BIM​ ​will​ ​be​ ​discussed,​ ​alongside​
​critiques of the models’ limitations.​




                                                             ​88​
​The​ ​BIM​ ​may​ ​be​ ​taught​ ​and​ ​utilised​ ​to​ ​empower​ ​people​ ​to​ ​become​ ​‘assertive​ ​bystanders’​
​rather​​than​​‘passive​​bystanders’​​(Public​​Health​​England,​​2020).​​Individuals​​who​​will​​challenge​
​the​​abuser​​while​​also​​comforting​​the​​victim​​are​​known​​as​​‘assertive​​bystanders’​​(Salmivalli​​et​
​al.​,​​1996).​​Bystanders​​who​​become assertive​​send​​a​​significant​​message​​to​​both​​the​​attacker​
​and​​present bystanders​​about​​the unacceptability​​of​​the​​problematic​​situation​​and​​the​​social​
​acceptability​ ​of​ ​addressing​ ​it​ ​(Fenton​ ​and​ ​Mott,​ ​2017).​ ​In​ ​1970,​ ​Latané​ ​and​ ​Darley​ ​(1970)​
​presented​ ​a​ ​five-step​ ​psychological​ ​process​ ​model,​ ​in​ ​which​ ​a​​bystander​​should​​follow​​five​
​steps,​ ​as​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​Figure​ ​1.​ ​By​ ​learning​ ​and​ ​using​ ​this​ ​five-step​ ​model,​ ​individuals​ ​will​
​hopefully​​learn​​to​​recognise​​potentially​​harmful​​and​​socially​​negative​​circumstances,​​making​
​changes​​and​​safely​​intervening,​​and​​challenging​​the​​potentially​​harmful​​scenario​​(Latané​​and​
​Darley, 1970).​




​Figure 1.​​The five-step ‘bystander intervention model’​​(Latané and Darley, 1970).​

​The​ ​BIM​ ​is​ ​a​ ​practical​ ​strategy​​that​​allows​​individuals​​to​​investigate​​ways​​to​​combat​​violent​
​and​ ​negative​ ​behaviours​ ​(Cissner,​ ​2009).​ ​The​ ​BIM​ ​has​ ​been​ ​used​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​tackle​ ​and​
​prevent​​numerous​​issues​​in​​society,​​which​​may​​include​​sexual​​assault​​(Moynihan​​et​​al.​,​​2011)​
​and​ ​bullying​ ​(Aboud​ ​and​ ​Joong,​ ​2008).​ ​The​ ​methodology​ ​of​ ​the​ ​bystander​ ​intervention​
​model​​has​​also​​been​​a​​foundation​​for​​campaigns​​such​​as​​‘See​​it.​​Say​​it.​​Sorted.’​​which​​is​​used​
​on​ ​public​ ​transport,​ ​asking​ ​all​ ​passengers​ ​to​ ​be​ ​vigilant​ ​and​ ​to​ ​report​ ​anything​ ​suspicious​
​(British​ ​Transport​ ​Police,​ ​2021).​ ​Similarly,​ ​the​ ​Breaking​ ​the​ ​Silence​ ​(2021)​ ​campaign​



                                                            ​89​
​encourages​​people​​to​​‘Step​​Up.​​Step​​In.​​Be​​Safe.'​​in​​order​​to​​combat​​harassment​​and​​sexual​
​assault’.​

​The​​BIM​​has​​primarily​​been​​employed​​in​​educational​​settings,​​particularly​​university​​settings​
​(Burn,​ ​2009;​ ​Labhardt​ ​et​ ​al​.,​ ​2017),​ ​with​ ​Corboz,​ ​Flood​ ​and​ ​Dyson​ ​(2016)​ ​citing​ ​a​ ​rapid​
​growth​​in​​the​​deployment​​of​​bystander​​programmes​​in​​recent​​years.​​It​​has​​been​​utilised​​as​​a​
​form​ ​of​ ​student​ ​training​ ​to​ ​prevent​ ​rape​ ​and​ ​violence​ ​against​ ​women,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​alcohol​
​abuse​​and​​harassment.​​Research​​from​​Moynihan​​et​​al​.​​(2011)​​and​​Cissner​​(2009)​​has​​shown​
​the​​effectiveness​​of​​the​​BIM,​​having​​an​​increased​​likelihood​​to​​help​​after​​completing​​specific​
​intervention​​programmes​​including​​‘Bringing​​in​​the​​Bystander’​​(Culture​​of​​Respect,​​2021)​​and​
​‘Mentors​​in​​Violence​​Prevention’​​(MVP​​Strategies,​​2021).​​Burns​​et​​al​.​​(2019)​​addressed​​how​
​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​programmes​ ​have​ ​successfully​ ​decreased​ ​participants'​ ​false​ ​beliefs​
​about​​rape​​and​​abuse,​​such​​as​​‘victim-blaming’,​​while​​also​​increasing​​their​​understanding​​of​
​sexual​​violence​​and​​rape,​​such​​as​​recognising​​and​​identifying​​when​​someone​​is​​at​​danger.​​For​
​example,​​Banyard,​​Moynihan​​and​​Plante​​(2007)​​found​​that​​two​​months​​after​​taking​​part​​in​​a​
​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​programme,​ ​individuals​ ​showed​ ​enhancements​ ​in​ ​their​ ​knowledge,​
​attitudes​ ​and​ ​behaviours;​ ​however,​ ​the​ ​control​ ​group​ ​showed​ ​no​ ​improvements,​ ​which​
​reinforces the importance of the bystander intervention.​


​Literature​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​assertive​ ​bystanders​ ​are​ ​particularly​ ​helpful​ ​in​ ​instances​ ​of​ ​group​
​bullying,​ ​on​ ​which​ ​there​ ​has​ ​been​ ​significant​ ​research​ ​(Aboud​ ​and​ ​Joong,​ ​2008;​ ​Polanin,​
​Espelage​ ​and​ ​Pigott,​ ​2012;​ ​Salmivalli,​ ​Voeten​​and​​Poskiparta,​​2011).​​Nickerson​​et​​al​.​​(2014)​
​states​ ​that​ ​bystander​​intervention​​programmes​​can​​be​​successfully​​utilised​​to​​aid​​witnesses​
​to​ ​stop​ ​or​ ​lessen​ ​the​ ​bullying. ​ ​Research​ ​that​ ​focuses​ ​upon​ ​bullying​ ​in​ ​schools​ ​has​ ​taught​
​children​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​bystander​ ​behaviour​ ​in​ ​particular​ ​scenarios​ ​and​ ​settings,​
​including​​high​​school​​and​​primary​​school​​bullying​​(Polanin​​et​​al.​,​​2012).​​Polanin​​et​​al.​​(2012)​
​conducted​ ​a​​meta-analysis​​examining​​12​​school-based​​bullying​​prevention​​programmes​​and​
​their​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​behaviour.​ ​Results​ ​found​ ​that​ ​participants​ ​who​
​underwent​ ​an​ ​intervention​ ​demonstrated​ ​stronger​ ​intervention​ ​behaviours​ ​and​
​subsequently​​were​​more​​likely​​to​​take​​action​​in​​bullying​​situations.​​Research​​has​​found​​that​
​when​ ​a​ ​bystander​ ​intervenes​ ​it​ ​has​ ​had​​a​​positive​​impact​​upon​​levels​​of​​bullying;​​however,​
​Jenkins​ ​and​ ​Nickerson​ ​(2017)​ ​point​ ​out​ ​that​ ​in​ ​order​ ​for​ ​students​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​in​ ​incident​​of​


                                                             ​90​
​bullying,​​they​​must​​understand​​the​​impact​​bullying​​can​​have,​​and​​that​​individuals​​should​​be​
​told​ ​different​ ​ways​ ​they​​can​​help.​​In​​educational​​settings,​​Salmivalli​​et​​al.​​(2011)​​found​​that​
​the​ ​notion​ ​of​ ​bystanders​ ​reporting​ ​the​ ​bullies​ ​to​ ​adults​ ​significantly​​reduced​​the​​incidence​
​rates.​


​This​ ​study​ ​focuses​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​British​ ​football,​ ​which,​ ​as​ ​previously​ ​said,​ ​has​
​sparked debates over​​where​​antisemitism​​belongs​​in​​race​​and​​ethnicity​​studies.​​However,​​for​
​the​ ​purposes​ ​of​ ​this​ ​chapter,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​beneficial​ ​to​ ​review​ ​literature​ ​on​ ​racial​ ​and​ ​ethnic​
​name-calling,​​and​​studies​​in​​sport​​which​​have​​either​​used​​a​​BIM​​or​​have​​observed​​bystander​
​behaviour.​ ​The​ ​BIM​ ​has​ ​been​ ​used​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​discriminatory​ ​behaviour,​ ​with​ ​focus​ ​on​
​weight-based​ ​discriminatory​ ​teasing​ ​(Paluck,​ ​2011)​ ​and​ ​racial​ ​discrimination​ ​(Aboud​ ​and​
​Joong,​ ​2008;​ ​Mulvery​​et​​al.,​​2016).​​Aboud​​and​​Joong​​(2008)​​explored​​bystander​​behaviours​
​to​​examine​​racial​​and​​ethnic​​name-calling.​​They​​found​​that​​when​​examining​​name-calling​​in​
​schools,​​being​​an​​assertive​​bystander​​can​​be​​effective​​for​​making​​change,​​as​​these​​individuals​
​have​ ​the​ ​potential​ ​to​ ​change​ ​individuals’​ ​attitudes​ ​regarding​ ​tolerance​ ​and​ ​acceptance​
​(Aboud​ ​and​ ​Joong,​ ​2008).​ ​For​ ​an​ ​individual​ ​to​ ​become​ ​an​ ​assertive​ ​bystander​ ​when​
​witnessing​ ​race-based​ ​humour,​ ​they​ ​need​ ​to​ ​recognise​ ​the​ ​harm​ ​the​ ​comments​ ​can​​cause​
​and then willingly challenge the group (Mulvery​​et​​al.,​​2016).​


​Research​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​programmes​ ​can​ ​be​ ​effective​ ​in​ ​addressing​
​racism​​within​​educational​​environments.​​For​​example,​​the​​'Speak​​Out​​Against​​Racism'​​(SOAR)​
​programme,​ ​introduced​ ​in​ ​Australian​ ​primary​ ​schools,​ ​led​ ​to​ ​notable​ ​improvements​ ​in​
​students’​ ​prosocial​ ​skills,​ ​teachers’​ ​perceptions​ ​of​ ​inter-racial​ ​climate,​ ​and​ ​students'​
​commitment​ ​to​ ​anti-racist​ ​values​ ​(Priest​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2021).​ ​Bystander​ ​anti-racism,​ ​defined​ ​as​
​actions​​taken​​by​​individuals​​in​​response​​to​​racist​​incidents,​​has​​shown​​promising​​benefits​​for​
​targets,​ ​bystanders,​ ​and​ ​perpetrators​ ​alike​ ​(Nelson​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2011).​ ​The​ ​literature​ ​shows​ ​that​
​bystander​​anti-racism​​can​​have​​productive​​effects​​for​​targets,​​bystanders,​​and​​perpetrators.​​It​
​can​ ​help​ ​stop​ ​the​ ​perpetration​ ​of​ ​racism,​ ​reduce​ ​its​ ​escalation,​ ​prevent​ ​harms​ ​and​
​strengthen​​social​​norms​​against​​racism.​​In​​medical​​education,​​anti-racism​​bystander​​training​
​has​ ​been​ ​proposed​ ​to​ ​address​ ​inequities​ ​in​ ​care​ ​and​ ​health​ ​disparities,​ ​with​ ​evidence​
​indicating​ ​greater​ ​confidence​ ​and​ ​efficacy​ ​among​ ​participants​ ​in​ ​responding​ ​to​ ​racist​
​incidents​ ​(Ragheb,​ ​Vinson​ ​and​ ​Roberson,​ ​2024).​ ​Collectively,​ ​these​ ​findings​ ​emphasise​ ​the​


                                                            ​91​
​potential​ ​of​ ​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​programmes​ ​to​ ​foster​ ​anti-racism​ ​across​ ​diverse​
​educational settings.​


​There​ ​is​ ​a​ ​limited​ ​number​ ​of​ ​studies​ ​on​ ​the​ ​BIM​ ​used​ ​within​ ​physical​ ​exercise​ ​and​ ​sport;​
​research​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​this​ ​intervention​ ​mainly​ ​explores​ ​athletes’​ ​ability​ ​and​
​willingness​​to​​prevent​​unwanted​​sexual​​behaviour​​within​​college​​sports​​(Kroshus,​​Paskus​​and​
​Bell,​ ​2018;​ ​McMahon,​ ​2015).​ ​There​ ​is​ ​also​ ​limited​ ​research​ ​using​ ​the​ ​BIM​ ​when​ ​exploring​
​sport​ ​fandom.​ ​Recent​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​Kovalenko​ ​and​ ​Fenton​​(2024)​​has​​explored​​bystander​
​intervention​​in​​sports​​contexts,​​particularly​​focusing​​on​​football.​​The​​research​​indicates​​that​
​bystander​ ​programmes​ ​can​ ​be​ ​effective​ ​in​ ​improving​ ​attitudes​ ​and​ ​behaviours​ ​related​ ​to​
​violence​ ​prevention​ ​among​ ​football​ ​club​ ​members.​ ​However,​ ​Block​ ​and​ ​Lesneskie​ ​(2018)​
​address​ ​the barriers​ ​that​ ​prevent​ ​a​​fan​​from​​acting​​as​​an​​assertive​​bystander​​during​​violent​
​situations​ ​at​ ​sporting​ ​events​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​ ​States.​ ​This​ ​includes​ ​the​ ​fear​ ​of​ ​harming​
​themselves​​or​​others​​if​​they​​intervene,​​as​​well​​as​​the​​belief​​that​​the​​stewards​​are​​responsible​
​for handling the issues.​


​BIM - Practical considerations​


​It​ ​has​ ​been​ ​argued​ ​that​ ​learning​ ​and​ ​applying​ ​this​ ​five-step​ ​process​ ​can​ ​help​ ​individuals​
​create​ ​a​​more​​positive​​and​​safer​​environment​​(Banyard​​et​​al​.,​​2007).​​Research​​has​​explored​
​various​​factors​​influencing​​a​​person's​​likelihood​​of​​becoming​​an​​assertive​​bystander​​through​
​the​ ​five-step​ ​intervention​ ​model.​ ​Key​ ​factors​ ​include​ ​psychological​ ​barriers​ ​(Latané​ ​and​
​Darley,​ ​1970),​ ​age​ ​(Mulvey​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2016),​ ​gender​ ​(Cappadocia​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2012),​ ​personal​ ​traits​
​(Abbott​ ​and​ ​Cameron,​ ​2014),​ ​education,​ ​training,​ ​and​ ​environmental​ ​context​ ​(Harris​ ​and​
​Robinson, 1973; Latané and Darley, 1968).​

​Latané​ ​and​ ​Darley​ ​(1970)​ ​outlined​ ​three​ ​primary​ ​psychological​ ​barriers​ ​that​ ​can​ ​impede​
​bystander​ ​intervention.​ ​The​ ​first​ ​barrier,​ ​‘diffusion​ ​of​ ​responsibility’,​ ​arises​ ​when​ ​there​ ​are​
​multiple​ ​bystanders,​ ​leading​ ​each​ ​individual​ ​to​ ​feel​ ​less​ ​personal​ ​responsibility.​ ​This​
​phenomenon,​ ​known​ ​as​ ​the​ ​‘bystander​ ​effect’,​ ​occurs​ ​because​ ​the​ ​presence​ ​of​ ​other​
​witnesses​ ​creates​ ​an​ ​assumption​ ​that​ ​someone​ ​else​ ​will​ ​act,​ ​often​ ​resulting​ ​in​ ​collective​
​inaction​ ​(Darley​ ​and​ ​Latané,​ ​1968;​ ​Latané​ ​and​ ​Nida,​ ​1981).​ ​The​ ​second​​barrier,​​‘evaluation​



                                                             ​92​
​apprehension’,​ ​refers​​to​​the​​fear​​of​​public​​judgement.​​People​​may​​hesitate​​to​​intervene​​out​
​of​ ​concern​ ​that​ ​their​ ​actions​ ​could​ ​be​ ​scrutinised​ ​or​ ​judged​ ​inadequate​ ​by​ ​others.​ ​For​
​instance,​​potential​​bystanders​​might​​worry​​about​​making​​a​​mistake,​​appearing​​incompetent,​
​or​ ​even​ ​facing​ ​legal​ ​consequences​ ​if​ ​their​ ​intervention​ ​is​ ​deemed​ ​inappropriate​ ​or​ ​unsafe​
​(Emeghara,​ ​2020).​ ​The​ ​third​ ​barrier,​ ​‘pluralistic​ ​ignorance’,​ ​is​ ​when​ ​individuals​ ​base​ ​their​
​response​ ​on​ ​the​ ​perceived​ ​reactions​ ​of​ ​others​ ​around​ ​them.​ ​If​ ​no​ ​one​ ​else​ ​appears​
​concerned,​ ​a​ ​bystander​ ​might​ ​assume​ ​that​ ​the​ ​situation​ ​is​ ​not​ ​an​ ​emergency,​​leading​​to​​a​
​lack​ ​of​ ​response.​ ​This​ ​tendency​ ​to​ ​conform​ ​to​ ​the​ ​behaviour​ ​of​ ​others​ ​can​ ​discourage​
​intervention,​​as​​bystanders​​may​​mistakenly​​interpret​​the​​situation​​as​​non-urgent​​(Emeghara,​
​2020).​

​Together,​ ​these​ ​barriers​ ​reveal​ ​the​ ​complex​ ​social​ ​and​ ​psychological​ ​dynamics​ ​that​ ​can​
​prevent​​people​​from​​stepping​​in​​during​​critical​​situations.​​This​​barrier​​is​​particularly​​relevant​
​in​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​​sports​​fandom,​​as​​supporters​​are​​often​​influenced​​by​​the​​prevailing​​group​
​norms​​within​​the​​sports​​arena.​​Individuals​​may​​feel​​pressure​​to​​join​​in​​antisemitic​​chanting​​or​
​remain​​passive​​rather​​than​​intervene.​​As​​a​​result,​​these​​three​​psychological​​barriers​​make​​it​
​less likely for individuals to take action in such settings (Latané and Darley, 1970).​

​Similarly,​ ​Abrams​ ​and​ ​Rutlands​ ​(2008)​ ​found​ ​when​ ​exploring​ ​bullying​ ​in​ ​schools​ ​that​
​individuals​ ​may​ ​not​ ​want​ ​to​ ​intervene​ ​as​ ​they​ ​are​ ​worried​ ​that​ ​they​ ​could​ ​be​ ​rejected​ ​by​
​their​ ​peers​ ​and​ ​that​ ​it​ ​could​ ​have​ ​a​ ​potential​ ​social​ ​cost,​ ​resulting​ ​in​ ​social​ ​exclusion.​ ​In​
​addition,​​Thornberg​​et​​al.​​(2012)​​found​​that​​before​​intervening​​in​​bullying​​situations,​​children​
​aged​ ​9-15​ ​would​ ​socially​ ​evaluate​ ​the​ ​situation​ ​by​ ​either​ ​considering​ ​where​ ​they​ ​and​ ​the​
​bully​​were​​positioned​​in​​the​​social​​rank,​​or​​by​​reflecting​​upon​​the​​impact​​it​​could​​have​​upon​
​their​ ​friendships.​ ​Mendoza,​ ​Lane​ ​and​ ​Amodio​ ​(2014)​​suggest​​that​​it​​depends​​on​​how​​likely​
​acting​ ​would​ ​affect​ ​an​ ​individual's​ ​level​ ​of​ ​social​ ​exclusion.​ ​If​ ​intervening​ ​would​​result​​in​​a​
​substantial risk of social exclusion, the person is less inclined to do so.​

​Abbott​ ​and​ ​Cameron​ ​(2014)​ ​suggest​ ​that​ ​personal​ ​traits​ ​strongly​ ​influence​ ​a​ ​person’s​
​likelihood​ ​of​ ​intervening,​ ​noting​ ​that​ ​assertive​ ​bystanders​ ​are​ ​typically​ ​empathetic​ ​and​
​culturally​ ​aware.​ ​Individuals​ ​with​ ​more​ ​frequent​ ​intergroup​ ​contact​ ​are​ ​also​ ​more​​likely​​to​
​respond​ ​in​ ​situations​ ​like​ ​name-calling​ ​(Abbott​ ​and​ ​Cameron,​ ​2014).​ ​However,​ ​research​
​indicates​​that​​in​​severe​​emergencies,​​people​​are​​more​​inclined​​to​​help.​​For​​instance,​​Latané​


                                                               ​93​
​and​​Darley​​(1968),​​along​​with​​Fischer​​et​​al​.​​(2011),​​found​​that​​the​​likelihood​​of​​intervention​
​increases​​in​​scenarios​​involving​​visible​​injury,​​asthma​​attacks,​​or​​physical​​illness,​​likely​​due​​to​
​heightened​ ​arousal​ ​(Fischer​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2011).​ ​Those​ ​who​ ​refrained​ ​from​ ​acting​ ​often​ ​felt​ ​that​
​someone​​with​​more​​expertise​​was​​needed,​​and​​they​​were​​more​​likely​​to​​contact​​emergency​
​services rather than provide direct assistance (Latané and Darley, 1968).​

​Research​ ​has​ ​also​ ​shown​ ​that​ ​a​ ​person's​ ​gender​ ​can​​significantly​​impact​​their​​likelihood​​of​
​intervening​​in​​various​​situations.​​Card​​et​​al.​​(2008)​​found​​that​​females​​tend​​to​​be​​more​​likely​
​to​​help​​in​​covert​​forms​​of​​bullying,​​while​​males​​are​​more​​inclined​​to​​engage​​in​​overt​​bullying​
​behaviours,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​physical​ ​confrontations.​ ​Additionally,​ ​Faul,​ ​Aikman​ ​and​ ​Sasser​ ​(2016)​
​noted​​that​​men​​are​​more​​often​​the​​recipients​​of​​direct​​assistance,​​whereas​​women​​are​​more​
​likely​ ​to​ ​have​ ​bystanders​ ​call​ ​emergency​ ​services.​ ​Overall,​ ​the​ ​literature​ ​emphasises​ ​that​
​several​ ​critical​ ​factors,​ ​including​ ​gender,​ ​environment,​ ​age,​ ​and​ ​psychological​ ​influences,​
​must be considered when analysing bystander behaviour.​


​Despite​​the​​extensive​​body​​of​​literature​​discussed​​above​​which​​has​​drawn​​upon​​the​​BIM,​​the​
​model​ ​is​ ​not​ ​without​ ​its​ ​critiques.​ ​Research​ ​which​ ​has​ ​used​ ​a​ ​BIM​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​a​ ​greater​
​understanding​​of​​helping​​behaviours​​and​​bystander​​effect has​​been​​criticised​​by​​Faul,​​Aikman​
​and​ ​Sasser​ ​(2016)​ ​due​ ​to​ ​the​ ​methodology​ ​involved,​ ​since​ ​they​ ​arise​ ​from​ ​artificial​​means​
​which​ ​may​ ​not​ ​truly​​reflect​​the​​real​​world,​​thus​​reducing​​the​​validity​​of​​the​​study. Likewise,​
​some​​research​​heavily​​relied​​on​​self-reporting​​of​​reading​​written​​instances​​(Faul,​​Aikman​​and​
​Sasser,​​2016).​​Amar,​​Sutherland​​and​​Kesler​​(2012)​​also​​recognise​​that​​issues​​may​​arise​​due​​to​
​self-reporting​ ​given​ ​that​ ​participants​ ​may​ ​exaggerate​ ​their​ ​answers​ ​or​ ​give​ ​answers​ ​which​
​may​ ​be​ ​considered​ ​more​ ​socially​ ​acceptable​ ​(Salters-Pedneault,​ ​2020);​ ​in​ ​this​ ​instance​
​individuals​ ​may​ ​claim​ ​they​ ​would​ ​intervene​ ​when​ ​in​ ​reality​ ​they​ ​might​ ​not.​ ​Levine​ ​et​ ​al.​
​(2002)​ ​stated​ ​that​ ​while​ ​Latané​ ​and​ ​Darley​ ​(1968)​ ​did​ ​well​ ​to​ ​emphasise​ ​the​ ​need​ ​of​
​bystanders​​intervening,​​it​​was​​not​​adequate​​because​​they​​did​​not​​translate​​their​​findings​​into​
​practical​​strategies.​​Nonetheless,​​it​​is​​possible​​to​​argue​​that​​since​​2002,​​certain​​organisations​
​have​​used​​Latané​​and​​Darley’s​​(1968)​​findings​​and​​model​​as​​a​​foundation​​to​​adopt​​practical​
​strategies,​ ​including​ ​‘Bringing​ ​in​ ​the​ ​Bystander’​ ​and​ ​‘See​ ​it.​ ​Say​ ​it.​ ​Sorted’.​ ​Public​ ​Health​
​England​ ​(2016)​ ​claims​ ​that​ ​for​ ​bystander​ ​interventions​ ​to​ ​be​ ​successful​ ​they​ ​must​ ​be​
​comprehensive,​ ​underpinned​ ​by​ ​a​ ​theory,​ ​and​ ​be​ ​delivered​ ​by​ ​an​ ​individual​ ​who​ ​is​ ​well​


                                                             ​94​
​trained​ ​in​ ​the​ ​area​ ​of​ ​discussion.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​they​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​delivered​ ​at​ ​an​​appropriate​
​time​ ​and​ ​be​​of​​significant​​length​​and​​duration.​​They​​found​​that​​short,​​one-off​​interventions​
​had limited capacity to change individuals’ behaviours.​


​To​​summarise,​​a​​variety​​of​​scholars​​have​​used​​the​​work​​of​​Latané​​and​​Darley​​(1968;​​1970)​​on​
​the​​bystander​​effect​​and​​the​​BIM​​to​​investigate​​behaviours​​as​​well​​as​​implementing training​
​to​ ​observe​ ​how​ ​the​ ​model​ ​impacts​ ​in​ ​certain​ ​situations.​ ​As​ ​previously​ ​stated,​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​
​shortage​​of literature​​researching​​the BIM​​in​​the​​context​​of​​both​​racism​​and​​sport.​​Therefore,​
​this​​research​​will​​become​​the​​first​​piece​​of​​literature​​which​​will​​employ​​the​​BIM​​in​​a​​practical​
​manner​​to​​help​​individuals​​recognise​​and​​respond​​to​​harmful​​antisemitic​​attitudes,​​language,​
​and​ ​behaviours​ ​in​ ​a​ ​footballing​ ​context​ ​and​ ​broader​ ​society.​ ​Furthermore, it​ ​is​ ​essential to​
​identify​​the​​barriers​​that​​may​​impede​​people​​from​​becoming​​assertive​​bystanders​​at​​football​
​games,​ ​and​ ​to​ ​devise​ ​techniques​ ​to​ ​overcome​ ​these​ ​barriers​ ​so​ ​that​ ​people​ ​feel​ ​secure​​in​
​their​ ​abilities. Alongside​ ​the​ ​potential​ ​barriers,​ ​the​ ​limitations​ ​of​ ​the​ ​model​ ​have​ ​been​
​discussed​​and​​will​​be​​taken​​into​​consideration​​when​​applying​​the​​model​​to​​the​​development​
​of the initiative.​


​Chapter summary​

​This​​review​​of​​literature​​has​​provided​​an​​in-depth​​exploration​​of​​antisemitism,​​highlighting​​its​
​historical​​and​​contemporary​​manifestations​​across​​different​​contexts,​​with​​a​​particular​​focus​
​on​ ​its​ ​prevalence​ ​within​ ​sporting​ ​contexts.​ ​This​ ​review​ ​revealed​ ​several​ ​critical​ ​factors​
​influencing​​antisemitism,​​such​​as​​the​​visibility​​of​​Jewish​​identity​​(Rubin,​​2020),​​the​​impact​​of​
​geopolitical​ ​events​ ​(CST,​ ​2024),​ ​and​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​ ​sport,​ ​specifically​ ​football,​ ​in​ ​amplifying​
​prejudice​​(Curtis,​​2019).​​Specific​​attention​​is​​given​​to​​antisemitism​​in​​European​​football,​​with​
​case​​studies​​from​​countries​​including​​the​​Netherlands,​​Germany,​​and​​the​​UK​​(Stratton,​​2015).​
​These​ ​discussions​ ​reveal​ ​how​ ​stereotypes​ ​and​ ​negative​ ​behaviours​ ​persist​ ​in​ ​fan​ ​culture,​
​often​ ​directed​ ​at​ ​clubs​ ​like​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur,​ ​which​ ​are​ ​perceived​ ​to​ ​have​ ​Jewish​ ​ties​
​(Kershaw,​​2019;​​Lunn,​​2023;​​Poulton​​and​​Durell,​​2016).​​Existing​​sporting,​​anti-discrimination​
​initiatives​ ​were​ ​also​ ​examined,​ ​highlighting​ ​sport's​ ​potential​ ​both​ ​as​ ​a​ ​space​ ​for​ ​prejudice​
​(Anderson​​and​​White,​​2017;​​Kilvington​​and​​Price,​​2018a;​​Wood,​​2013)​​and​​as​​a​​platform​​for​




                                                             ​95​
​promoting​ ​tolerance​ ​(Kidd,​ ​2008;​ ​Marivoet,​ ​2014),​ ​whilst​ ​assessing​ ​current​ ​challenges​ ​and​
​limitations in combating antisemitism effectively.​

​Theoretical​​perspectives,​​including​​CRT​​(Delgado​​and​​Stefancic,​​2001),​​HebCrit​​(Rubin,​​2020),​
​and​ ​the​ ​BIM​ ​(Latané​ ​and​ ​Darley,​ ​1968)​ ​have​​been​​discussed​​in​​preparation​​for​​shaping​​the​
​development​ ​of​ ​an​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiative,​ ​and​ ​for​ ​furthering​ ​an​ ​understanding​ ​of​
​antisemitism​​as​​a​​socially​​embedded​​and​​complex​​form​​of​​discrimination.​​These​​frameworks​
​reinforce​ ​the​ ​structural​ ​inequalities​ ​and​ ​challenges​ ​faced​ ​by,​ ​most​ ​specifically,​ ​Jewish​
​individuals,​ ​whilst​ ​emphasising​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​education​ ​in​​shifting​​social​​norms​​within​
​sports​​and​​society.​​Together,​​these​​theories​​provide​​a​​foundation​​for​​asking​​critical​​questions​
​about​ ​how​ ​antisemitism​ ​is​ ​experienced​ ​through​ ​sport​ ​in​ ​society.​ ​This​ ​allows​ ​for​ ​a​ ​deeper​
​exploration​ ​of​ ​the​ ​ways​ ​structural​ ​inequalities​ ​are​ ​challenged​ ​within​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​sport,​
​highlighting​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​ ​education​ ​in​ ​shifting​ ​these​​norms.​​Following​​on​​from​​this​​literature​
​review,​ ​the​ ​methodology​ ​chapter​​addresses​​the​​research​​approach,​​design,​​and​​procedures​
​taken​​to​​develop​​an​​educational​​initiative​​aimed​​to​​combat​​antisemitism​​through​​the​​use​​of​
​sports, especially football.​




                                                           ​96​
​Chapter 3 - Methodology​


​Introduction​


​The​ ​previous​ ​chapter​ ​offered​ ​an​ ​overview​ ​of​ ​current​ ​literature​ ​pertinent​​to​​addressing​​the​
​proposed​ ​research​ ​questions.​ ​Additionally,​ ​it​ ​introduced​ ​key​ ​theories​ ​that​ ​will​ ​serve​ ​as​
​foundational​ ​frameworks​ ​throughout​ ​this​ ​project.​ ​This​ ​current​ ​chapter​ ​will​ ​introduce​ ​and​
​discuss​ ​the​ ​methodology​ ​for​ ​this​ ​research​ ​project,​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​gather​ ​in-depth​ ​qualitative​
​data​ ​that​ ​could​​be​​used​​to​​develop​​an​​evidence-based​​and​​co-created​​educational​​initiative​
​focused​ ​on​ ​eradicating​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​British​ ​Football,​ ​with​ ​input​​from​​anti-discrimination​
​experts​ ​and​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​In​ ​comparable​ ​studies,​ ​Poulton​ ​and​ ​Durell​ ​(2016)​
​analysed​ ​fan​ ​discourse​ ​on​ ​two​ ​unofficial​ ​Tottenham​ ​fan​ ​message​ ​boards,​ ​while​ ​Poulton​
​(2020)​ ​gathered​ ​qualitative​ ​data​ ​through​ ​a​ ​critical​ ​review​ ​of​ ​campaign​ ​initiatives​ ​and​
​interviews​ ​with​ ​key​ ​stakeholders​ ​involved​ ​in​ ​combating​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​sports​ ​and​​society.​
​Like​​Poulton’s​​(2020)​​study,​​this​​project​​also​​started​​with​​interviews​​with​​experts​​in​​sport​​and​
​discrimination.​ ​However,​ ​Zohrabi​ ​(2013)​​states​​that​​by​​collecting​​information​​from​​a​​variety​
​of​ ​sources​ ​and​​techniques,​​there​​is​​greater​​data​​to​​support​​the​​findings​​and​​strengthen​​the​
​validity​​of​​the​​project;​​therefore,​​as​​outlined​​below,​​this​​research​​project​​was​​a​​multi-method​
​study which utilised interviews, focus groups, and questionnaires as data collection tools.​

​This​ ​chapter​ ​begins​ ​by​ ​introducing​ ​the​ ​philosophical​ ​perspectives​ ​underpinning​ ​the​ ​thesis,​
​which​​serves​​as​​the​​foundation​​for​​the​​methodological​​approach. Finally,​​it​​discusses​​ethical​
​considerations,​ ​all​ ​of​ ​which​​apply​​across​​the​​entire​​project,​​encompassing​​the​​three​​phases​
​of data collection.​

​Paradigm and philosophical position​

​One​​key​​aim​​of​​any​​given​​research​​is​​to​​advance​​knowledge​​in​​the​​chosen​​field​​(Collis,​​Hussey​
​and​ ​Hussey,​ ​2003;​ ​Jones​ ​and​ ​Gratton,​ ​2015).​ ​However,​ ​Punch​ ​(2009)​ ​notes​ ​that​ ​the​
​philosophical​ ​assumptions​ ​underlying​ ​a​ ​researcher’s​​work​​are​​often​​implicit.​​Understanding​
​these​ ​philosophical​ ​foundations​ ​is​ ​crucial,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​helps​ ​academics​ ​become​ ​aware​ ​of​ ​the​ ​key​
​decisions​ ​made​ ​during​ ​the​​research​​process​​and​​the​​influence​​of​​these​​assumptions​​on​​the​
​interpretation​ ​of​ ​findings​ ​(Bracken,​ ​2010).​ ​The​ ​phrases​ ​‘paradigms’​ ​and​ ​‘philosophical​


                                                           ​97​
​positions’​​are​​often​​used​​within​​academic​​research​​to​​identify​​and​​explore​​the​​shared​​beliefs​
​and​ ​agreements​ ​among​ ​various​ ​scientific​ ​groups​ ​regarding​ ​how​ ​research​​should​​be​​carried​
​out​ ​(Punch,​ ​2009).​ ​The​​term​​paradigm​​was​​defined​​by​​Guba​​(1990,​​p.​​17)​​as​​“a​​basic​​set​​of​
​beliefs​ ​that​ ​guide​ ​action”.​ ​A​ ​researcher's​ ​paradigm​ ​encompasses​ ​the​ ​following:​ ​ontology,​
​epistemology,​ ​and​ ​research​ ​methodology​ ​(Denzin​ ​and​ ​Lincoln,​ ​2005).​ ​With​ ​that​ ​in​ ​mind,​
​when​ ​conducting​ ​research,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​and​ ​have​ ​awareness​ ​of​ ​the​
​researcher’s​ ​ontological,​ ​epistemological,​ ​and​ ​methodological​ ​positions​ ​(Ahmed,​ ​2008;​
​Seliger, 1989).​


​Ontology​​helps​​us​​to​​understand​​what​​entities​​exist​​in​​the​​world,​​and​​the​​reality​​and​​nature​
​of​ ​those​ ​entities​ ​(Bryman​ ​and​ ​Bell,​ ​2011).​ ​It​ ​helps​ ​us​ ​to​ ​address​ ​what​ ​is​ ​reality​ ​alongside​
​developing​​an​​understanding​​of​​what​​is​​real​​(Scotland,​​2012).​​The​​ontological​​position​​that​​is​
​‘realism’​ ​attempts​ ​to​ ​uncover​ ​the​ ​truth,​ ​by​ ​revealing​ ​scientific​ ​facts​ ​through​ ​experiment​
​(Cohen,​ ​Manion​ ​and​ ​Morrison,​ ​2007).​ ​On​ ​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​‘relativism’​ ​is​ ​based​ ​upon​ ​how​
​people​ ​perceive​ ​reality,​ ​and​ ​that​ ​facts​ ​depend​ ​on​ ​the​ ​viewpoint​ ​of​ ​the​ ​observer​ ​(Coll​ ​and​
​Chapman,​​2000).​​Those​​who​​adopt​​a​​realist​​philosophy​​believe​​that​​there​​is​​one​​single​​truth,​
​rather​ ​than​ ​there​ ​being​ ​multiple​​truths,​​which​​a​​relativist​​would​​believe​​(Guba​​and​​Lincoln,​
​1994).​ ​Ontology​ ​and​ ​epistemology​ ​are​ ​closely​ ​related,​ ​as​ ​both​ ​concern​ ​fundamental​
​questions​ ​about​ ​the​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​reality​ ​and​ ​knowledge.​​While​​ontology​​helps​​us​​define​​what​
​entities​ ​and​ ​truths​ ​exist​ ​in​ ​the​ ​world,​ ​epistemology​ ​explores​ ​how​ ​we​ ​come​ ​to​ ​know​ ​and​
​understand these truths (Bryman and Bell, 2011; Crotty, 2003).​


​Epistemology​​regards​​the​​study​​of​​knowledge​​and​​is​​“a​​way​​of​​understanding​​and​​explaining​
​how​ ​we​ ​know​ ​what​ ​we​ ​know”​ ​(Crotty,​ ​2003,​ ​p.​ ​3).​ ​Understanding​ ​a​ ​researcher's​
​epistemological​​stance​​is​​essential​​because​​it​​allows​​academics​​to​​see​​how​​it​​influenced​​the​
​researcher's​​knowledge​​acquisition​​and​​findings​​(Bracken,​​2010).​​There​​are​​several​​different​
​forms​ ​of​ ​epistemological​ ​perspectives,​ ​and​ ​both​ ​objectivity​ ​and​ ​subjectivity​ ​are​ ​frequently​
​addressed​ ​in​ ​this​ ​dichotomy​ ​(Bryman,​ ​2012).​ ​Objectivism​ ​is​ ​an​ ​epistemological​ ​position​
​usually​ ​adopted​ ​by​ ​those​ ​researching​​natural​​sciences,​​aiming​​to​​use​​objective​​facts​​to​​find​
​the​ ​one​ ​truth​ ​(Diesing,​ ​1966).​ ​In​ ​contrast​ ​to​ ​an​ ​objectivist,​ ​a​ ​subjectivist​ ​researcher​ ​views​
​reality​ ​as​ ​shaped​ ​by​ ​individuals'​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​acknowledges​ ​their​ ​own​ ​role​ ​in​
​interpreting​ ​that​ ​reality​ ​(Bryman​ ​and​ ​Bell,​ ​2011).​ ​Subjectivists​ ​typically​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​the​ ​social​


                                                              ​98​
​sciences,​ ​exploring​ ​human​ ​behaviour,​ ​experiences,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​individual​​meanings​​that​​shape​
​concepts​ ​around​ ​them​ ​(Gratton​ ​and​ ​Jones,​ ​2015).​ ​Subjective​ ​research​ ​often​ ​draws​ ​from​
​interpretations​ ​of​ ​personal​ ​experiences,​ ​often​ ​gathered​ ​through​ ​unstructured​ ​or​
​semi-structured​ ​interviews​ ​(Bahari,​ ​2010).​ ​This​ ​approach​ ​is​ ​closely​ ​aligned​ ​with​
​interpretivism,​​which​​aims​​to​​gain​​subjective​​knowledge​​to​​understand​​why​​and​​how​​events​
​occur​​by​​interpreting​​reality​​through​​individual​​experiences,​​interpretations,​​and​​motivations​
​(Jones​ ​and​ ​Gratton,​ ​2015).​ ​Unlike​ ​the​ ​positivist​ ​belief​ ​that​ ​social​ ​phenomena​ ​can​ ​be​
​examined​ ​with​ ​the​ ​same​ ​methods​ ​used​ ​in​ ​the​ ​natural​ ​sciences,​ ​interpretivism​ ​views​ ​the​
​social​ ​world,​ ​comprising​ ​individuals,​ ​communities,​ ​and​ ​institutions,​ ​as​ ​best​ ​understood​
​through​ ​techniques​ ​suited​ ​to​ ​its​ ​unique​ ​complexities​ ​(Potrac,​ ​Jones​ ​and​ ​Nelson,​ ​2014).​
​Rather​ ​than​ ​seeking​ ​quantitative​ ​answers,​ ​interpretivism​ ​aims​​to​​uncover​​explanations​​and​
​insights that deepen our understanding of the social world (Hennink​​et al.​, 2020).​


​There​ ​are​ ​three​ ​fundamental​ ​philosophical​ ​positions,​ ​shaped​ ​by​ ​both​ ​ontology​ ​and​
​epistemology:​​positivism,​​constructivism,​​and​​critical​​realism​​(Alters,​​1997).​​The​​philosophical​
​position​ ​that​ ​is​ ​positivism​ ​takes​ ​a​ ​realist​ ​and​ ​objective​​stance,​​by​​assuming​​that​​we​​should​
​produce​ ​knowledge​ ​in​ ​an​ ​objective​ ​way​ ​(Burton,​ ​Brundrett​ ​and​​Jones,​​2014).​​On​​the​​other​
​hand,​ ​a​ ​constructive​ ​approach​ ​takes​ ​a​ ​relativist​ ​and​ ​subjective​ ​stance.​ ​In​ ​social​ ​sciences,​
​constructivism​ ​can​ ​influence​ ​the​ ​studies​ ​by​ ​focusing​ ​on​ ​the​ ​experiences​​of​​people​​and​​the​
​discourses​ ​that​ ​exist.​ ​Due​ ​to​ ​the​​nature​​of​​this​​research,​​a​​relativist​​ontological​​perspective​
​was​​adopted.​​In​​addition,​​to​​develop​​understanding​​and​​knowledge,​​this​​study​​gathered​​data​
​which​ ​was​ ​not​ ​quantifiable,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​individuals’​ ​feelings,​ ​thoughts,​ ​and​ ​experiences;​
​therefore,​​a​​subjectivist,​​interpretivist​​approach​​was​​adopted.​​Subsequently,​​a​​constructivist​
​philosophical position was maintained throughout the research process.​


​When​ ​conducting​ ​research,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​evaluate​ ​the​ ​research's​ ​quality​ ​and​ ​due​ ​to​ ​the​
​subjective,​ ​interpretivist​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​the​​research​​question,​​the​​next​​section​​aims​​to​​highlight​
​important​ ​indicators​ ​that​ ​should​ ​be​ ​taken​ ​into​ ​account​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​high-quality,​ ​qualitative​
​research.​​The​​terms​​validity,​​reliability,​​trustworthiness,​​and​​reflexivity​​are​​amongst​​some​​of​
​the key markers that will be discussed.​




                                                            ​99​
​Validity, reliability and trustworthiness​


​Typically,​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​credibility​ ​and​ ​rigour​ ​within​ ​academic​ ​research,​ ​the​ ​terms​ ​validity​ ​and​
​reliability​ ​are​ ​discussed.​ ​The​ ​term​ ​validity​ ​has​ ​been​ ​defined​ ​by​ ​Smith​ ​(2022,​ ​p.520)​ ​as​ ​“a​
​concept​​concerned​​with​​the​​integrity​​of​​the​​conclusions​​generated​​from​​research”.​​The​​word​
​reliability​ ​is​ ​broadly​ ​defined​ ​as​ ​“the​ ​dependability,​ ​consistency,​ ​and/​ ​or​ ​repeatability​ ​of​ ​a​
​project’s​​data​​collection,​​interpretation,​​and/or​​analysis”​​(Miller,​​2008,​​p.​​745).​​Essentially,​​it​
​is​ ​the​ ​ability​ ​to​ ​obtain​ ​the​ ​same​ ​results​ ​if​ ​the​ ​study​ ​were​ ​to​ ​be​ ​repeated.​ ​Both​ ​terms​ ​are​
​often​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​quantitative​ ​research,​ ​and​ ​therefor,e​ ​there​ ​has​ ​been​ ​substantial​
​discussion among academics about their applicability to qualitative research (Bryman, 2012).​
​Due​ ​to​ ​the​ ​subjective​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​qualitative​ ​research,​ ​questions​ ​around​ ​validity​ ​often​ ​stem​
​from​ ​the​ ​frequent​ ​critique​ ​that​ ​qualitative​ ​research​ ​is​ ​‘unscientific’​ ​and​ ​based​ ​upon​
​subjective​​opinions​​(Gray,​​2022).​​Subsequently,​​qualitative​​researchers​​may​​instead​​reflect​​on​
​the​ ​‘trustworthiness’​ ​of​ ​a​ ​project​ ​and​ ​‘reflexivity’​ ​(Korstjens​ ​and​ ​Moser,​ ​2018;​ ​Lincoln​ ​and​
​Guba,​ ​1985).​ ​An​ ​interpretivist​ ​approach​ ​is​ ​widely​ ​used​ ​in​ ​qualitative​ ​research,​ ​which​
​frequently​​allows​​the​​researcher​​to​​add​​their​​own​​subjective​​perspective​​based​​on​​their​​own​
​beliefs​ ​and​ ​experiences,​ ​thus​ ​affecting​ ​the​ ​trustworthiness​ ​of​ ​the​ ​research.​ ​Therefore,​
​individuals​ ​are​ ​urged​ ​to​ ​evaluate​ ​their​ ​role​ ​in​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process​ ​when​ ​conducting​
​qualitative​​research​​(Gray,​​2022)​​by​​using​​the​​concept​​of​​reflexivity​​to​​critically​​reflect​​on​​how​
​their​ ​perspectives​ ​and​ ​experiences​​influence​​the​​research.​​In​​the​​latter​​part​​of​​this​​chapter,​
​the​ ​researcher​ ​reflects​ ​on​ ​their​ ​role​ ​in​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process,​ ​in​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​having​ ​regular​
​reflective​​discussions​​with​​their​​supervisory​​team.​​This​​corresponds​​with​​the​​work​​of​​Lincoln​
​and​ ​Guba​ ​(1985),​ ​who​​highlight​​various​​techniques​​for​​ensuring​​trustworthiness,​​which​​will​
​be discussed later in this chapter.​


​The​ ​term​ ​validity​ ​does​ ​not​ ​often​ ​align​ ​with​ ​projects​ ​of​ ​a​ ​qualitative​ ​nature​ ​and​ ​the​
​constructivist​ ​position​ ​adopted​ ​by​ ​the​ ​researcher;​ ​therefore,​ ​the​ ​term​ ​validity​ ​is​ ​often​
​substituted​​with​​the​​idea​​of​​‘trustworthiness’,​​introduced​​by​​Lincoln​​and​​Guba​​(1985).​​Due​​to​
​the​ ​qualitative​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​this​ ​research​ ​project,​ ​the​ ​concept​ ​of​ ​‘trustworthiness’​ ​has​
​subsequently​​been​​taken​​into​​consideration​​to​​ensure​​high-quality​​research.​​Trustworthiness​
​has​ ​been​ ​referred​ ​to​ ​by​ ​Cypress​ ​(2017,​ ​p253)​ ​as​ ​“quality,​ ​authenticity,​ ​and​ ​truthfulness​ ​of​
​findings​ ​of​ ​qualitative​ ​research”​ ​a​ ​concept​ ​that​ ​has​ ​since​ ​been​ ​used​ ​by​ ​qualitative​


                                                               ​100​
​researchers​ ​to​ ​assess​ ​the​ ​quality​ ​of​ ​their​ ​work.​ ​To​ ​ensure​ ​trustworthiness​ ​in​ ​qualitative​
​research,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​must​ ​meet​ ​the​ ​criteria​ ​established​ ​by​ ​Lincoln​ ​and​ ​Guba​ ​(1985),​
​which​​include​​'credibility',​​'dependability',​​'confirmability'​​and​​'transferability'.​​These​​criteria​
​will be discussed in more detail below.​

​‘Credibility’​ ​refers​ ​to​ ​the​ ​researcher’s​ ​ability​ ​to​ ​evaluate​ ​the​ ​study​ ​design​ ​and​ ​procedures​
​used​ ​to​ ​reach​ ​conclusions​ ​(Gray,​ ​2022).​ ​Researchers​ ​must​ ​ask,​ ​“how​ ​congruent​ ​are​ ​the​
​findings​ ​with​ ​reality?”​ ​(Stahl​ ​and​ ​King,​ ​2020,​ ​p.26).​ ​It’s​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​ensure​​that​​the​​results​
​authentically​ ​represent​ ​the​ ​participants’​ ​experiences​ ​(Cypress,​ ​2017).​ ​In​ ​contrast,​
​‘dependability’​ ​emphasises​ ​the​ ​consistency​ ​and​ ​repeatability​ ​of​ ​results​ ​(Polit​ ​and​ ​Beck,​
​2020),​​indicating​​that​​research​​should​​be​​logical,​​traceable,​​and​​well-documented​​(Tobin​​and​
​Begley,​​2004).​​Auditing​​can​​demonstrate​​dependability;​​auditing​​involves​​examining​​both​​the​
​process​​and​​the​​product​​(Lincoln​​and​​Guba,​​1985),​​with​​an​​auditor​​verifying​​that​​the​​data​​is​
​accurately​ ​represented.​ ​In​ ​this​ ​study,​ ​the​ ​research​ ​team,​ ​including​ ​the​ ​primary​ ​researcher​
​and​ ​supervisory​ ​team,​ ​performed​ ​this​ ​role​ ​through​ ​regular​ ​discussions​ ​and​ ​reflective​
​conversations.​

​‘Confirmability’​ ​ensures​ ​that​ ​the​​study’s​​conclusions​​are​​shaped​​by​​participants​​rather​​than​
​researcher​​bias​​or​​interest​​(Connelly,​​2016).​​Hadi​​and​​José​​(2016)​​emphasise​​the​​importance​
​of​ ​reflexivity,​ ​where​ ​researchers​ ​reflect​ ​on​ ​their​ ​biases​ ​and​​assumptions.​​The​​researcher​​in​
​this​ ​study​ ​engaged​ ​in​ ​reflexivity​ ​by​ ​considering​ ​how​ ​personal​ ​views​ ​might​ ​influence​ ​data​
​interpretation,​​as​​seen​​in​​the​​next​​chapter.​​Finally,​​‘transferability’​​refers​​to​​how​​the​​findings​
​might​ ​be​ ​applied​ ​in​ ​other​ ​contexts​ ​(Connelly,​ ​2016).​ ​To​ ​aid​ ​transferability,​ ​researchers​ ​are​
​encouraged​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​thick​ ​descriptions,​ ​which​ ​offer​ ​a​ ​detailed​ ​account​ ​of​ ​the​ ​research​
​process.​​The​​researcher’s​​thick​​descriptions​​were​​shared​​with​​the​​supervisory​​team​​to​​ensure​
​their​​suitability​​for​​transferability,​​allowing​​future​​researchers​​to​​assess​​the​​relevance​​of​​the​
​findings to different settings (Nowell​​et al.​, 2017).​

​‘ Triangulation’​ ​is​ ​one​ ​such​ ​technique​ ​which​ ​helps​ ​to​ ​achieve​ ​trustworthiness,​ ​ensuring​
​credibility​ ​and​ ​confirmability​ ​by​ ​combining​ ​different​ ​research​ ​methods​ ​and​​data​​(Atkinson,​
​2012,​ ​p.217).​ ​Four​​types​​of​​triangulations​​are​​commonly​​used:​​‘data’,​​‘investigator’,​​‘theory’​
​and​ ​‘methodological’.​ ​In​ ​this​ ​study,​ ​data​ ​triangulation​ ​involved​ ​multiple​ ​data​ ​collection​
​phases​ ​across​ ​different​ ​times​ ​and​ ​participants,​ ​providing​ ​a​ ​richer,​ ​more​ ​diverse​ ​dataset.​


                                                             ​101​
​Investigator​ ​triangulation​ ​occurred​​as​​the​​supervisory​​team​​assisted​​with​​data​​handling​​and​
​engaged​ ​in​ ​reflective​ ​discussions.​ ​Theory​ ​triangulation​ ​was​ ​achieved​ ​by​ ​applying​ ​multiple​
​theoretical​​perspectives,​​namely​​HebCrit,​​CRT,​​and​​BIM.​​Finally,​​methodological​​triangulation​
​was​ ​evident​ ​through​ ​the​​use​​of​​interviews,​​focus​​groups,​​and​​questionnaires​​to​​explore​​the​
​same research question.​

​Reflexivity​


​The​ ​term​ ​reflexivity​ ​has​ ​been​ ​defined​ ​by​ ​Hennink​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2020,​ ​p.​ ​330)​ ​as​ ​“the​ ​practice​ ​of​
​acknowledging​ ​the​ ​potential​ ​influence​ ​of​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​or​ ​the​ ​research​ ​setting​ ​on​ ​data​
​generation​ ​and​ ​interpretation”.​ ​Suddaby​ ​(2006,​ ​p.​ ​640)​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​
​reflexivity,​ ​stating​ ​that​ ​researchers​ ​“must​ ​engage​ ​in​ ​ongoing​ ​self-reflection​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​
​they​ ​take​ ​personal​ ​biases,​ ​world-views,​ ​and​ ​assumptions​ ​into​ ​account​ ​while​ ​collecting,​
​interpreting,​ ​and​ ​analysing​ ​data”.​ ​Dupruis​ ​(1999)​ ​focuses​ ​on​ ​‘personal​ ​reflexivity’,​ ​which​ ​is​
​the​ ​process​ ​through​ ​which​ ​a​ ​researcher​ ​considers​ ​how​ ​their​ ​values,​ ​attitudes,​ ​beliefs,​ ​and​
​goals​ ​have​ ​shaped​ ​the​ ​research.​ ​In​ ​interpretivist​ ​research,​ ​it​ ​is​​essential​​to​​reflect​​on​​one's​
​positionality,​ ​as​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​plays​ ​a​ ​key​ ​role​ ​in​ ​interpreting​ ​data​ ​and​ ​observations,​
​potentially​ ​influencing​ ​the​ ​resulting​ ​interpretations​ ​(Thomas,​ ​2017).​ ​Therefore,​ ​personal​
​reflexivity​ ​was​ ​utilised​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​minimise​ ​potential​ ​research​ ​bias​ ​within​ ​this​ ​study;​ ​the​
​next​ ​section​ ​engages​ ​with​ ​and​ ​reflects​ ​upon​ ​the​​researcher’s​​religious​​upbringing,​​sporting​
​background and other factors that may impact the research process.​


​I​​was​​raised​​by​​a​​Jewish​​mother​​and​​a​​Christian​​father,​​and​​while​​neither​​of​​them​​persuaded​
​me​​to​​follow​​a​​particular​​religion,​​they​​shared​​the​​values​​that​​were​​most​​important​​to​​them.​
​Additionally,​ ​we​ ​would​ ​share​ ​Jewish​ ​and​ ​Christian​ ​holy​ ​festivals​ ​as​ ​a​ ​family.​ ​They​ ​believed​
​that​​when​​I​​grew​​older,​​I​​would​​decide​​for​​myself​​which​​religion​​to​​follow.​​Even​​though​​I​​am​
​not​​religious​​today,​​I​​still​​enjoy​​learning​​about​​‘my​​religions’​​and​​my​​family's​​religious​​history.​
​I​ ​recently​ ​discovered,​ ​in​ ​November​ ​2022,​ ​that​ ​I​ ​am​ ​43.6%​ ​Ashkenazi​ ​Jewish​ ​through​ ​a​
​DNA-estimate​ ​test​ ​in​ ​an​ ​effort​ ​to​ ​learn​ ​more​ ​about​ ​my​ ​heritage​ ​and​ ​that​ ​of​ ​my​ ​family.​ ​As​
​previously​​mentioned,​​even​​though​​I​​would​​describe​​myself​​as​​neither​​religiously​​Jewish​​nor​
​Christian,​ ​this​ ​outcome​ ​has​ ​naturally​ ​given​ ​me​ ​a​ ​stronger​ ​sense​ ​of​ ​connection​ ​to​​Judaism.​




                                                              ​102​
​With​ ​this​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​reflect​ ​upon​ ​how​ ​my​ ​religious​ ​identity,​ ​views​ ​and​
​background may have influenced this research.​


​While​​I​​do​​not​​consider​​myself​​religious,​​I​​may​​have​​biases​​toward​​the​​Jewish​​faith​​as​​a​​result​
​of​​my​​heritage,​​family​​history,​​and​​upbringing​​in​​the​​Jewish​​community.​​Subsequently,​​I​​feel​
​that​​my​​connection​​to​​the​​Jewish​​faith​​has​​given​​me​​a​​strong​​desire​​to​​make​​society​​a​​safer​
​and​ ​more​​accepting​​place​​for​​the​​Jewish​​community.​​To​​make​​sure​​that​​my​​personal​​beliefs​
​did​ ​not​ ​influence​ ​the​ ​process,​ ​guidance​ ​to​ ​encourage​ ​dialogue​ ​and​ ​idea​ ​exchanges​​among​
​other​​researchers​​were​​followed​​(Gray,​​2022).​​As​​the​​primary​​researcher,​​I​​interacted​​with​​a​
​group​​of​​supervisors​​who​​made​​sure​​that​​my​​personal​​ideas​​and​​ideals​​did​​not​​get​​in​​the​​way​
​of​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​Dupuis​​(1999)​​recognised​​the​​importance​​of​​reporting​
​the​​researcher's​​values​​and​​beliefs,​​to​​ensure​​that​​they​​are​​made​​explicit​​to​​the​​reader,​​which​
​can be seen in the previous paragraph.​


​Although​ ​I​ ​am​ ​not​​an​​avid​​football​​fan,​​my​​interest​​in​​the​​subject​​derives​​from​​my​​religious​
​background,​ ​my​ ​extended​ ​(Jewish)​ ​family's​ ​experiences​ ​at​ ​football​ ​games,​ ​and​ ​my​
​commitment​ ​to​ ​bringing​ ​positive​​change​​to​​marginalised​​communities.​​Not​​being​​a​​football​
​fan​​comes​​with​​its​​advantages​​and​​disadvantages.​​On​​the​​one​​hand,​​I​​have​​no​​interest​​in​​the​
​performance​​of​​any​​club,​​particularly​​those​​listed​​in​​this​​article,​​and​​so​​my​​interest​​is​​purely​
​motivated​ ​by​ ​my​ ​interest​ ​in​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​and​ ​my​ ​personal​ ​religious​ ​background.​ ​On​
​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​because​ ​I​ ​am​ ​not​ ​a football​​fan,​​some​​would​​claim​​that​​I​​am​​less​​aware​​of​
​the​​fan​​culture​​that​​exists​​among​​football​​fans,​​particularly​​among​​those​​who​​are​​believed​​to​
​be​​supporters​​of​​a​​‘Jewish​​Club'​​or​​who​​belong​​to​​a​​club​​that​​is​​perceived​​to​​be​​‘antisemitic'.​
​To​​overcome​​some​​of​​these​​challenges,​​in​​my​​prior​​study,​​I​​was​​able​​to​​get​​an​​understanding​
​of​ ​what​ ​it​ ​means​ ​to​ ​be​ ​a​ ​football​ ​fan,​ ​especially​ ​one​ ​who​ ​supports​ ​a​ ​well-known​ ​‘Jewish​
​club,'​​Tottenham​​Hotspur.​​This​​was​​achieved​​through​​gaining​​in​​depth,​​qualitative​​data​​from​
​a large sample (n=596) of Tottenham supporters (Lunn, 2023).​


​Brett​ ​and​ ​Wheeler​ ​(2022,​ ​p.12)​ ​state​ ​that​ ​“it’s​ ​not​ ​enough​ ​to​ ​just​ ​state​​your​​identity”​​and​
​recommend​​engaging​​with​​reflective​​discussions​​throughout​​the​​research​​process.​​This​​helps​
​to​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​greater​ ​engagement​ ​and​ ​reflection,​ ​by​ ​giving​ ​thoughts​ ​to​ ​and​ ​reporting​ ​on​
​moments​ ​of​ ​doubt​ ​and​ ​tough​ ​decisions.​ ​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​Lincoln​ ​and​ ​Guba​ ​(1986),​​Brett​​and​


                                                            ​103​
​Wheeler​ ​(2021)​ ​agree​ ​that​ ​the​ ​reflective​ ​process​ ​can​ ​help​​to​​recognise​​and​​strengthen​​the​
​validity​ ​and​ ​trustworthiness​ ​of​ ​the​ ​study.​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​since​ ​questionnaires,​ ​focus​ ​groups​
​and​ ​interviews​ ​are​ ​facilitated​ ​by​ ​researchers,​ ​the​ ​data​ ​acquired​ ​during​ ​qualitative​ ​studies​
​may​​be​​influenced​​by​​underlying​​beliefs,​​therefore,​​as​​stated​​by​​Haynes​​(2012),​​reflexivity​​is​
​an​ ​important​ ​consideration​​in​​qualitative​​research.​​For​​that​​reason,​​the​​researcher​​engaged​
​in​​persistent​​reflexive​​discussions​​with​​their​​supervisory​​team​​throughout​​the​​duration​​of​​the​
​study​ ​to​ ​gain​ ​insight​ ​into​ ​how​ ​their​ ​own​ ​personal​ ​beliefs​ ​and​ ​experiences​ ​impacted​ ​their​
​involvement in the research design process.​


​Methodological position​


​A​ ​methodological​ ​position​ ​helps​ ​individuals​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​what​ ​is​ ​being​ ​done​ ​to​​generate​
​the​ ​knowledge​ ​(Slevitch,​ ​2011).​ ​Given​ ​this,​ ​the​ ​methodology​ ​selected​ ​depends​ ​on​ ​the​
​research​ ​aims,​ ​objectives​ ​and​ ​questions​ ​(Crabtree​​and​​Miller,​​1999).​​A​​deductive​​approach,​
​sometimes​ ​referred​ ​to​ ​as​ ​‘top-down’​ ​approach,​ ​is​ ​utilised​ ​when​ ​attempts​ ​are​ ​made​ ​to​
​validate​ ​theory.​ ​Initially,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​will​​begin​​with​​a​​theory​​suited​​to​​the​​topic​​at​​hand​
​and​ ​then​ ​narrow​ ​it​ ​down​ ​to​ ​a​ ​hypothesis,​ ​making​ ​it​ ​an​ ​approach​ ​which​ ​requires​ ​a​
​theory-driven​ ​hypothesis​ ​(Trochim​ ​and​ ​Donnelly,​ ​2001).​ ​Then​ ​data​ ​is​ ​collected​ ​to​ ​develop​
​research​ ​findings,​ ​which​ ​leads​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​to​ ​either​ ​confirm​ ​or​ ​reject​ ​the​ ​hypothesis​
​(Nelson,​ ​Potrac​ ​and​ ​Groom,​ ​2014).​ ​On​ ​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​an​ ​inductive​​approach,​​also​​known​
​informally​ ​as​ ​a​ ​‘bottom-up’​ ​approach,​ ​is​ ​usually​ ​adopted​ ​when​ ​developing​ ​either​ ​theory,​
​models​​or​​explanations​​from​​data​​which​​has​​been​​collected​​and​​analysed​​(Jones​​and​​Gratton,​
​2015).​ ​This​ ​method​ ​starts​ ​with​ ​observations,​​which​​produce​​patterns​​that​​are​​then​​used​​to​
​build​ ​a​ ​hypothesis.​ ​This​ ​will​ ​lead​ ​to​ ​the​ ​creation​ ​of​ ​either​ ​a​ ​theory​ ​or​ ​a​​set​​of​​conclusions​
​(Trochim​ ​and​ ​Donnelly,​ ​2001).​ ​This​ ​is​ ​a​ ​popular​ ​technique​ ​among​ ​academics​ ​who​ ​take​ ​an​
​interpretivist, epistemological stance (Hennink​​et​​al​., 2020).​


​For​ ​this​ ​research,​ ​an​ ​inductive​ ​approach​ ​was​ ​adopted​ ​when​ ​developing​ ​the​ ​educational​
​initiative.​ ​However,​ ​this​ ​research​ ​also​ ​followed​ ​abductive​ ​reasoning;​ ​an​ ​abductive​
​methodology​​has​​been​​defined​​by​​Denzin​​(1978,​​p.​​177)​​as​​“a​​combination​​of​​deductive​​and​
​inductive​ ​thinking,​ ​whereby​ ​theory​ ​and​ ​practice​ ​inform​ ​one​ ​another.”​ ​Abductive​ ​research​
​requires​​switching​​constantly,​​back​​and​​forth,​​between​​data​​collection,​​experience​​reflection​


                                                               ​104​
​and​​the​​theoretical​​concepts​​(Nelson​​and​​Cushion,​​2006).​​Denzin​​(1978)​​states​​that​​the​​data​
​does​ ​not​ ​stand​ ​alone;​ ​rather,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​understood​ ​through​ ​theory,​ ​implying​ ​that​ ​theory​ ​and​
​practice​ ​are​ ​mutually​ ​informative.​ ​This​ ​study​ ​used​ ​two​ ​theories,​ ​CRT​ ​and​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​
​2020)​ ​to​ ​offer​ ​a​ ​degree​ ​of​ ​interpretation​ ​to​ ​the​ ​data​ ​by​ ​combining​ ​an​ ​inductive​ ​thematic​
​analysis​​with​​a​​deductive​​abstraction​​of​​these​​topics.​​A​​deductive​​method​​was​​used​​to​​give​​a​
​more​ ​thorough​ ​and​ ​theoretical​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​creating​ ​and​ ​building​ ​themes by​ ​utilising​
​principles​​developed​​from​​these​​theories.​​When​​creating​​an​​initiative​​to​​reduce​​antisemitism​
​in​ ​football,​ ​however,​ ​inductive​ ​reasoning​ ​was​ ​utilised​ ​to​ ​create​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​initiative​​or​
​model.​


​Ethical considerations​


​After​​discussing​​the​​philosophical​​approach​​to​​the​​methodology​​of​​this​​study,​​attention​​now​
​turns​​to​​the​​ethical​​considerations.​​Smajdor​​et​​al.​​(2009)​​state​​that​​when​​researching​​human​
​participants,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​a​ ​fundamental​ ​part​ ​of​ ​the​​process​​to​​get​​ethical​​clearance​​from​​an​​ethics​
​research​ ​committee.​ ​Gelling​ ​(2016,​ ​p.40)​ ​emphasises​ ​that​ ​its​ ​purpose​ ​is​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​“that​
​research​ ​participants​ ​can​ ​be​ ​confident​ ​that​​possible​​risks​​have​​been​​considered,​​minimised​
​and​​deemed​​acceptable”.​​An​​ethics​​application​​highlights​​to​​the​​committee​​the​​possible​​risks​
​that​​participants​​may​​face​​because​​of​​taking​​part​​in​​the​​project​​(Watson​​and​​Gelling,​​2012).​
​Due​ ​to​ ​the​ ​multi-phase​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​the​ ​project,​ ​three​ ​ethical​ ​clearance​ ​applications​ ​were​
​submitted​ ​to​ ​the​​Oxford​​Brookes​​University​​Research​​Ethics​​Committee​​(henceforth,​​UREC),​
​which​ ​approved​ ​each​ ​phase.​ ​The​ ​first​ ​application​ ​(approval​ ​number:​ ​201435)​ ​covered​ ​the​
​initial​​phase,​​which​​involved​​interviews​​(Appendix​​A).​​The​​second​​phase,​​approved​​through​​a​
​subsequent​ ​application​ ​(approval​ ​number:​ ​221627),​ ​involved​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​(Appendix​ ​B).​
​Lastly,​​a​​third​​application​​to​​extend​​Phase​​2,​​for​​a​​final​​round​​of​​data​​collection​​was​​approved​
​(approval​​number:​​221627)​​for​​the​​use​​of​​questionnaires​​for​​the​​final​​book​​review​​(Appendix​
​C).​ ​Each​ ​phase​ ​will​ ​discuss​ ​its​ ​specific​ ​ethical​ ​considerations​ ​in​ ​detail​ ​in​ ​its​ ​corresponding​
​methods chapter.​




                                                             ​105​
​Chapter summary​


​This​ ​chapter​ ​has​ ​outlined​ ​the​ ​philosophical​​underpinnings,​​methodological​​framework,​​and​
​ethical​​considerations​​guiding​​this​​research​​project.​​By​​adopting​​a​​constructivist​​philosophical​
​position​ ​with​ ​a​ ​relativist​ ​ontology​ ​(Guba​ ​and​ ​Lincoln,​ ​1994)​ ​and​ ​an​ ​interpretivist​
​epistemology​​(Bryman​​and​​Bell,​​2011;​​Crotty,​​2003),​​the​​study​​ensures​​a​​focus​​on​​subjective,​
​qualitative​​data​​reflective​​of​​individual​​experiences​​and​​societal​​dynamics.​​The​​triangulation​
​of​​methods​​(Atkinson,​​2012),​​alongside​​reflexive​​practices​​(Hennink​​et​​al.,​​2020),​​contributes​
​to​​the​​trustworthiness​​of​​the​​research​​findings,​​ensuring​​their​​credibility,​​dependability,​​and​
​applicability​ ​across​ ​contexts​ ​(Lincoln​ ​and​ ​Guba,​ ​1985).​ ​The​ ​methodological​ ​and​ ​ethical​
​framework​​outlined​​in​​this​​chapter​​applies​​to​​the​​entirety​​of​​the​​research​​process,​​serving​​as​
​a​​foundation​​for​​all​​phases​​of​​data​​collection​​and​​analysis.​​This​​approach,​​which​​draws​​upon​
​abductive​​reasoning​​to​​bridge​​theory​​and​​practice​​(Denzin,​​1978;​​Nelson​​and​​Cushion,​​2006),​
​aligns​​with​​the​​project's​​aim​​to​​produce​​insights​​that​​support​​the​​co-creation​​of​​educational​
​initiatives aimed at reducing antisemitism in British football.​

​As​​the​​research​​progresses,​​the​​focus​​now​​shifts​​to​​the​​specific​​methods​​employed​​in​​Phase​
​1,​ ​interviews​ ​with​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts.​ ​This​ ​next​ ​chapter​ ​will​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​detailed​
​account​ ​of​ ​the​ ​procedures,​ ​participants​ ​and​ ​analysis​ ​used​ ​to​ ​extract​ ​insights​ ​from​ ​these​
​crucial stakeholders.​




                                                         ​106​
​Chapter 4- Phase 1 Methods - Expert interviews​


​Introduction​


​Having​ ​outlined​ ​the​ ​philosophical​ ​perspectives,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​the​ ​principles​ ​of​ ​validity,​
​trustworthiness,​​and​​overarching​​ethical​​considerations​​guiding​​this​​thesis,​​this​​chapter​​now​
​shifts to the specific methodological considerations for Phase 1: expert interviews.​


​This​ ​chapter​ ​begins​ ​by​ ​addressing​ ​the​ ​ethical​ ​considerations​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​conducting​
​expert​ ​interviews,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​the​ ​research​ ​is​ ​conducted​ ​with​ ​integrity​ ​and​ ​respect​ ​for​
​participants.​ ​It​ ​then​ ​details​ ​the​ ​participant​ ​sampling​ ​strategy,​ ​explaining​ ​how​ ​experts​​were​
​identified​ ​and​ ​selected​ ​for​ ​their​ ​relevant​ ​knowledge​ ​and​ ​experience.​ ​Following​ ​this,​ ​the​
​methods​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​are​ ​outlined,​ ​describing​ ​the​ ​procedures​​used​​to​​gather​​focused​
​and​​meaningful​​data.​​Finally,​​the​​approach​​to​​data​​analysis​​is​​discussed,​​illustrating​​how​​the​
​data was systematically examined to ensure credibility and relevance to the research aims.​


​Ethical considerations​


​DiCicco‐Bloom​ ​and​​Crabtree​​(2006)​​discuss​​that​​when​​completing​​face-to-face​​interviews​​or​
​focus​​groups,​​there​​are​​four​​key​​ethical​​considerations.​​Firstly,​​it​​is​​critical​​for​​the​​researcher​
​to​ ​reduce​ ​the​ ​risk​ ​of​ ​potential​​harm​​(Langdridge​​and​​Hagger-Johnson,​​2009).​​Anything​​that​
​may​ ​cause​ ​harm,​ ​including​ ​psychological​ ​harm​​from​​sensitive​​discussions,​​was​​noted​​in​​the​
​ethics​ ​application.​ ​Antisemitism​ ​is​ ​considered​ ​a​ ​sensitive​ ​topic​ ​and,​ ​therefore,​ ​should​ ​be​
​discussed​ ​with​ ​care.​ ​If​ ​participants​ ​felt​ ​uncomfortable​ ​or​ ​distressed​ ​because​ ​of​ ​the​
​discussion,​ ​they​ ​would​ ​be​ ​directed​​to​​contact​​information​​for​​relevant​​charities​​and​​mental​
​health organisations provided in the information sheet, which could offer support.​


​Secondly,​ ​researchers​ ​must​ ​protect​ ​the​ ​interviewee’s​​identity​​(DiCicco‐Bloom​​and​​Crabtree,​
​2006).​ ​Both​ ​confidentiality​ ​and​ ​anonymity​ ​are​ ​considered​ ​“the​ ​most​ ​important​ ​ethical​
​considerations​ ​in​ ​social​ ​science​ ​research”​ ​(Langdridge​ ​and​ ​Hagger-Johnson,​ ​2009,​ ​p502).​​It​
​was​ ​particularly​ ​important​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​participants​ ​remained​ ​anonymous​ ​when​ ​dealing​
​with​​anti-discrimination​​experts,​​ensuring​​that​​neither​​the​​participant​​nor​​their​​organisation​


                                                         ​107​
​could​ ​be​ ​identified​ ​from​ ​the​ ​data​ ​sets.​ ​Therefore,​ ​for​ ​the​ ​purpose​ ​of​ ​this​ ​research,​
​participants have been given a pseudonym to ensure that their identity remains anonymous.​


​Thirdly,​​interviewees​​should​​be​​informed​​about​​the​​nature​​of​​the​​study,​​and​​lastly, reduce​​the​
​risk​​of​​mistreating​​participants​​(DiCicco‐Bloom​​and​​Crabtree,​​2006).​​To​​do​​so,​​the​​researcher​
​ensured​ ​that​ ​all​ ​participants​ ​received​ ​an​ ​information​ ​sheet​ ​(Appendix​ ​D),​ ​which​​contained​
​details​ ​of​ ​the​ ​study​ ​and​ ​provided​ ​an​ ​opportunity​ ​to​​ask​​any​​additional​​questions​​they​​may​
​have.​​The​​information​​sheet​​allowed​​the​​participants​​to​​make​​an​​informed​​decision​​regarding​
​whether​ ​to​ ​participate​ ​in​ ​that​ ​specific​ ​research​ ​project​ ​(Gelling,​ ​2016).​ ​Furthermore,​
​participants​ ​were​ ​informed​​in​​the​​information​​sheet,​​GDPR​​privacy​​notice​​(Appendix​​E)​​and​
​consent​ ​form​ ​(Appendix​ ​F)​ ​that​ ​they​ ​had​ ​the​ ​right​ ​to​ ​withdraw​ ​from​ ​the​ ​data​ ​collection​
​process​​at​​any​​time.​​This​​right​​was​​also​​reaffirmed​​to​​them​​during​​the​​interview,​​to​​limit​​the​
​possibility​ ​of​ ​mistreatment.​ ​Participants​ ​were​ ​also​ ​informed​ ​that​ ​they​ ​could​ ​skip​ ​any​
​questions they felt uncomfortable answering.​


​Anti-discrimination expert interviews​


​With​ ​the​ ​ethical​ ​considerations​ ​outlined,​ ​the​​discussion​​now​​shifts​​to​​the​​first​​phase​​of​​the​
​data​​collection​​process,​​interviews​​with​​anti-discrimination​​experts.​​Interviews​​are​​utilised​​as​
​a​ ​data​ ​collecting​ ​technique​ ​to​ ​acquire​ ​in-depth,​ ​rich,​ ​qualitative​ ​data​ ​(DiCicco‐Bloom​ ​and​
​Crabtree,​ ​2006;​ ​Sutton​ ​and​ ​Austin,​ ​2015).​ ​In​ ​an​ ​interpretivist​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​gathering​
​qualitative,​ ​in-depth​ ​data​ ​on​ ​people’s​ ​thoughts​ ​and​ ​opinions,​ ​interviews​ ​are​ ​a​​widely​​used​
​and​​valuable​​method​​of​​data​​collection​​(Jones​​and​​Gratton,​​2015).​​Furthermore,​​as​​Cleland,​
​Dixon​ ​and​ ​Kilvington​ ​(2019)​ ​and​ ​Culver,​ ​Gilbert​ ​and​ ​Trudel​​(2003)​​point​​out,​​interviews​​are​
​the​ ​most​ ​common​ ​data​ ​collecting​ ​method​ ​used​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​studies​ ​to​​gather​​qualitative​​data.​
​Arguably,​ ​an​​interview​​is​​the​​most​​appropriate​​tool​​to​​employ​​for​​investigating​​and​​learning​
​about people's ideas, attitudes and perceptions (Denscombe, 2014).​


​Furthermore,​ ​Michie,​ ​van​ ​Stralen​ ​and​ ​West​ ​(2011)​ ​emphasise​ ​the​ ​value​ ​of​ ​examining​ ​past​
​programmes​​aimed​​at​​promoting​​behavioural​​change,​​whether​​successful​​or​​not.​​Therefore,​
​this​ ​research​ ​involved​ ​interviews​ ​with​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​to​ ​draw​ ​insights​
​from​​previous​​initiatives.​​These​​interviews​​provided​​valuable​​knowledge​​on​​creating​​effective​


                                                          ​108​
​initiatives,​ ​along​ ​with​ ​insights​ ​into​ ​personal​ ​experiences,​ ​relevant​ ​methodologies,​ ​and​
​potential challenges.​


​Participants​


​Researchers​ ​guided​ ​by​ ​an​ ​interpretivist​ ​paradigm​​may​​seek​​to​​gain​​a​​deeper​​understanding​
​on​ ​the​ ​topic​ ​at​ ​hand​ ​by​ ​interviewing​ ​those​ ​who​ ​have​ ​experienced​ ​the​ ​phenomenon​
​first-hand,​ ​gaining​ ​a​ ​deeper​ ​understanding​​of​​human​​behaviours​​(Hennink​​et​​al.,​​2020).​​For​
​that​ ​reason,​ ​a​ ​purposeful​ ​sampling​ ​technique​ ​was​ ​used​ ​to​ ​recruit​ ​participants,​ ​which​ ​has​
​been​ ​defined​ ​as​ ​“identifying​ ​and​ ​selecting​ ​individuals​ ​or​ ​groups​ ​of​ ​individuals​ ​that​ ​are​
​especially​​knowledgeable​​about​​or​​experienced​​with​​a​​phenomenon​​of​​interest”​​(Palinkas​​et​
​al.,​ ​2015,​ ​p.​ ​534).​ ​This​ ​sampling​ ​approach​ ​can​ ​be​ ​advantageous​ ​for​ ​obtaining​ ​data​ ​from​
​specialised groups,​​but​​it​​also​​means​​that​​the​​findings​​are​​not​​generalisable​​to​​the​​rest​​of​​the​
​population because it concentrates on a specific target group (Dudovskiy, 2021).​


​Within​​this​​phase​​of​​the​​research,​​a​​total​​number​​of​​fourteen​​participants​​were​​recruited​​for​
​interviews.​​The​​participants​​in​​this​​study​​were​​recognised​​as​​anti-discrimination​​experts.​​Von​
​Soest​ ​(2023,​ ​p.​ ​278)​ ​states​ ​that​ ​“experts​ ​have​ ​specific​ ​knowledge​ ​about​ ​an​ ​issue,​
​development,​​or​​event”.​​Therefore,​​for​​this​​research,​​an​​anti-discrimination​​expert​​is​​defined​
​as​ ​someone​ ​with​ ​substantial​ ​knowledge,​ ​expertise​ ​and​ ​proven​ ​experience​ ​in​ ​developing,​
​designing​ ​or​ ​actively​ ​contributing​ ​to​ ​anti-discriminatory​ ​initiatives.​ ​More​ ​specifically,​ ​these​
​participants​ ​possess​ ​specialised​ ​knowledge​ ​and​ ​highly​ ​developed​ ​skills​ ​in​ ​areas​ ​such​ ​as​
​sports,​​antisemitism​​and​​Jewish​​studies,​​making​​them​​uniquely​​qualified​​to​​provide​​valuable​
​insights.​ ​Fu​​and​​Simmons​​(2021)​​emphasise​​that​​a​​significant​​benefit​​of​​expert​​interviews​​is​
​the​ ​ability​ ​to​ ​gather​ ​detailed​ ​insights​ ​into​ ​micro-level​ ​processes​ ​and​ ​real-world​
​decision-making​​practices.​​Therefore,​​participants​​were​​contacted​​via​​email​​to​​request​​their​
​permission​ ​to​ ​participate,​ ​along​​with​​being​​provided​​with​​the​​participant​​information​​sheet​
​(Appendix​ ​D).​ ​Those​ ​who​ ​chose​ ​to​ ​participate​ ​agreed​ ​on​ ​the​ ​condition​ ​of​ ​anonymity,​
​guaranteeing​ ​that​ ​all​ ​of​ ​the​ ​information​ ​they​ ​provided​ ​would​ ​be​ ​kept​ ​private​ ​and​
​confidential.​




                                                         ​109​
​Six​ ​participants​ ​were​ ​recruited​ ​using​ ​a​ ​snowball​ ​sampling​ ​technique,​ ​in​ ​which​ ​initial​
​participants​ ​identified​ ​other​ ​individuals​ ​of​ ​research​ ​interest​ ​for​ ​recruitment​ ​(Biernacki​ ​and​
​Waldorf,​ ​1981).​ ​This​ ​approach​ ​involves​ ​gaining​ ​participants​ ​through​ ​referrals​ ​from​ ​initial​
​contacts,​ ​who​ ​recommend​ ​others​ ​with​​the​​specific​​characteristics​​and​​relevant​​experiences​
​required​ ​for​ ​the​ ​study​ ​(Handcock​ ​and​ ​Gile,​ ​2011).​ ​This​ ​can​ ​be​ ​beneficial​ ​when​ ​trying​ ​to​
​recruit​​difficult-to-reach​​individuals,​​since​​others​​may​​be​​able​​to​​identify​​them;​​nevertheless,​
​this​ ​may​ ​indicate​ ​a​ ​lack​ ​of​ ​variety​ ​in​ ​the​ ​sample​ ​(Hennink​ ​et​ ​al​.,​ ​2020).​​These​​participants​
​were​ ​introduced​ ​to​ ​the​ ​research​ ​team​ ​via​ ​a​ ​gatekeeper​ ​with​ ​whom​ ​they​ ​had​ ​an​ ​initial​
​connection.​


​Out​ ​of​ ​the​ ​fourteen​ ​participants,​ ​the​​majority​​identified​​as​​male​​(n=11),​​and​​the​​remaining​
​(n=3)​ ​identified​ ​as​ ​female.​ ​Four​ ​out​ ​of​ ​the​ ​fourteen​ ​participants​ ​were​ ​at​ ​a​ ​top​​managerial​
​level,​ ​being​ ​either​ ​a​ ​Co-CEO​ ​(n=1),​ ​Chairman​ ​(n=1)​ ​or​ ​Director​ ​(n=2).​ ​Five​ ​of​ ​the​ ​experts​
​worked​ ​within​ ​Equality,​ ​Diversity​ ​and​​Inclusion​​(henceforth,​​EDI)​​and​​were​​either​​managers​
​(n=2),​​consultants​​(n=2)​​or​​policymakers​​(n=1).​​The​​remaining​​participants​​worked​​within​​the​
​process​ ​of​ ​designing​ ​initiatives​ ​within​ ​sport,​ ​education,​ ​and​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​(n=5),​ ​and​
​their​​job​​titles​​included​​development​​officer​​(n=1),​​project​​manager​​(n=2),​​education​​officer​
​(n=1) or assistant (n=1).​


​Together,​​this​​group​​offered​​a​​well-rounded​​range​​of​​viewpoints​​critical​​to​​understanding​​and​
​addressing​ ​the​ ​complexities​ ​within​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​efforts​ ​across​ ​multiple​ ​sectors.​
​However,​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​​limitation​​in​​the​​depth​​of​​expertise​​some​​individuals​​might​​bring​​to​​the​
​feedback​​regarding​​the​​development​​of​​initiatives.​​While​​the​​study​​includes​​a​​range​​of​​roles,​
​such​ ​as​ ​Co-CEOs,​ ​Chairmen,​ ​and​ ​Directors,​ ​who​ ​likely​ ​bring​ ​strategic​ ​and​ ​high-level​
​perspectives,​ ​other​ ​participants​ ​occupy​ ​more​ ​operational​ ​positions,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​assistants​ ​or​
​officers.​ ​These​ ​roles​ ​might​ ​lack​ ​the​ ​authority,​ ​experience,​ ​or​ ​strategic​ ​insight​ ​necessary​ ​to​
​drive​ ​or​ ​conceptualise​ ​initiatives​ ​independently.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​the​ ​diversity​ ​of​ ​roles​ ​allows​
​for​ ​insights​ ​from​ ​both​ ​the​ ​ground-level​ ​implementation,​ ​offered​ ​by​ ​assistants​ ​and​ ​officers,​
​and​ ​the​ ​high-level​ ​decision-making​​processes​​shared​​by​​top​​managers​​and​​directors.​​This​​is​
​supported​ ​by​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​Von​ ​Soest​ ​(2023),​ ​who​ ​recommends​ ​selecting​ ​experts​ ​whose​
​role​ ​is​ ​to​ ​make​ ​decisions,​ ​alongside​ ​those​ ​experts​ ​who​ ​analyse​ ​and​ ​apply​ ​the​ ​decisions​​to​
​ensure that a variety of perspectives and expertise are considered.​


                                                             ​110​
​Procedure​


​The​ ​recruitment​ ​process​ ​began​ ​on​ ​July​ ​1st​ ​2021,​ ​when​ ​participants​ ​were​ ​given​ ​an​
​information​​sheet​​(Appendix​​D)​​regarding​​the​​study,​​a​​GDPR​​privacy​​notice​​(Appendix​​E)​​and​
​were​ ​asked​ ​if​ ​they​ ​wished​ ​to​ ​participate.​ ​Those​ ​who​ ​agreed​ ​to​ ​an​ ​interview​ ​were​ ​given​ ​a​
​consent​​form​​to​​sign​​(Appendix​​F),​​which​​recorded​​that​​participants​​had​​given​​their​​informed​
​consent,​ ​agreeing​ ​to​ ​take​ ​part​ ​in​ ​the​​research​​project​​(Gelling,​​2016).​​They​​will​​understand​
​that​​by​​participating,​​they​​will​​be​​having​​an​​open​​meeting​​with​​the​​intention​​to​​provide​​data​
​that​ ​will​ ​be​ ​used​ ​for​ ​research​ ​purposes​ ​only​ ​(Denscombe,​ ​2014).​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​the​ ​consent​
​form​​also​​stated​​that​​participants​​had​​read​​and​​understood​​the​​information​​sheet,​​that​​they​
​were​​willing​​to​​be​​audio​​and​​video​​recorded​​for​​transcription​​purposes,​​and​​that​​they​​would​
​accept​ ​anonymised​ ​quotes​ ​throughout​ ​the​ ​writing​ ​process.​ ​Most​ ​importantly,​ ​the​ ​consent​
​form​ ​highlighted​ ​to​ ​participants​ ​that​ ​their​ ​involvement​ ​was​ ​voluntary​ ​and​ ​that​ ​they​ ​could​
​withdraw​ ​from​ ​the​ ​interview​ ​process​ ​at​ ​any​ ​given​ ​time.​​Prior​​to​​the​​interview,​​participants​
​were​​requested​​to​​countersign​​the​​document​​and​​send​​it​​back​​to​​the​​researcher.​​Interviews​
​began a week later, on the 8th of July 2021 and finished on the 8th September 2021.​

​For​ ​the​ ​purposes​ ​of​ ​this​ ​study,​ ​interviews​ ​were​ ​conducted​ ​through​ ​an​ ​online​ ​video​
​conferencing​​software.​​Face-to-face​​interviews​​would​​have​​been​​preferred;​​however,​​due​​to​
​the​ ​coronavirus​ ​pandemic,​ ​interviews​ ​were​ ​conducted​ ​online​ ​to​ ​comply​ ​with​ ​government​
​guidelines,​​and​​for​​the​​convenience​​and​​comfort​​of​​both​​the​​researcher​​and​​the​​participants.​
​Although​​face-to-face​​interviews​​have​​the​​advantage​​of​​enabling​​the​​interviewer​​to​​interpret​
​the​​interviewee's​​nonverbal​​and​​informal​​communication,​​including​​body​​language​​and​​facial​
​expressions​ ​(Jones​ ​and​​Gratton,​​2015),​​using​​technological​​mediums,​​including​​online​​video​
​calls​ ​and​ ​telephone​ ​interviews​ ​has​ ​become​​increasingly​​popular​​(Janghorban,​​Roudsari​​and​
​Taghipour,​ ​2014;​ ​Novick,​ ​2008).​ ​Benefits​ ​of​ ​conducting​ ​online​ ​interviews​ ​include​ ​the​
​potential​ ​for​ ​participants​ ​to​ ​feel​ ​more​ ​relaxed​ ​and​ ​the​ ​reduction​ ​in​ ​pressure​ ​to​ ​disclose​
​private​​information.​​Furthermore,​​online​​interviews​​tend​​to​​be​​less​​time-consuming​​for​​both​
​interviewer and interviewee, and, overall, they are more cost-effective (Cleland​​et al.​, 2019).​




                                                           ​111​
​The​ ​interviews​ ​were​ ​of​ ​a​ ​semi-structured​ ​nature;​ ​semi-structured​ ​interviews​​can​​positively​
​influence​ ​the​ ​occurrence​ ​of​ ​unforeseen​ ​data​ ​as​ ​they​ ​allow​ ​for​ ​probing​ ​and​ ​further​
​questioning​ ​(Gray,​ ​2022).​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​an​ ​interview​ ​guide​ ​(Appendix​ ​G)​ ​was​ ​utilised​ ​as​
​recommended​ ​by​ ​Maykut​ ​and​ ​Morehouse​ ​(1994).​ ​The​ ​guide​ ​served​ ​as​ ​a​ ​prompt​ ​which​
​reminded​ ​the​ ​interviewer​ ​of​ ​key​ ​concepts,​ ​topics,​ ​and​ ​questions​ ​to​ ​cover​ ​(Hennink​ ​et​ ​al​.,​
​2020).​​The​​interview​​consisted​​of​​14​​questions​​which​​Creswell​​(2007,​​p.163)​​advised​​should​
​be​ ​“open​ ​ended,​ ​general​ ​and​ ​focussed​ ​on​ ​understanding​ ​the​ ​central​ ​phenomenon​ ​of​ ​the​
​study”.​ ​Most​ ​of​ ​the​ ​questions​ ​were​ ​derived​ ​from​ ​the​ ​research​ ​aim​ ​and​ ​question​ ​to​ ​gain​
​information​ ​regarding​ ​expert’s​ ​experiences​ ​in​ ​working​ ​on​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​programmes​
​and​ ​initiatives.​ ​Interviews​ ​lasted​ ​between​ ​25-68​ ​minutes​ ​and​ ​were​ ​audio​ ​recorded​ ​for​
​transcription​ ​purposes.​ ​Once​ ​all​ ​the​ ​interviews​ ​were​ ​complete,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​began​
​transcribing​ ​the​ ​data,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​later​ ​analysed​ ​using​ ​thematic​ ​analysis.​ ​An​ ​example​ ​of​ ​a​
​transcribed​​data​​set​​can​​be​​seen​​in​​Appendix​​H,​​illustrating​​the​​process​​of​​coding​​and​​theme​
​development.​


​Thematic analysis (TA)​


​Aligning​​with​​an​​interpretivist​​view,​​this​​research​​project​​used​​thematic​​analysis​​(henceforth,​
​TA)​ ​to​ ​analyse​ ​the​ ​interview​ ​data,​ ​which​ ​Guest,​ ​MacQueen​ ​and​ ​Namey​ ​(2012)​ ​state​ ​it​ ​is​​a​
​popular​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​analysing​ ​text​​resulting​​from​​interviews.​​Formally​​introduced​​by​​Braun​​and​
​Clarke​ ​(2006,​ ​p.​ ​4),​ ​they​ ​state​ ​that​ ​“thematic​ ​analysis​ ​should​ ​be​ ​seen​ ​as​ ​a​ ​foundational​
​method​​for​​qualitative​​analysis”.​​TA​​entails​​identifying​​and​​exploring​​patterns,​​often​​known​​as​
​themes,​ ​within​ ​the​ ​data​ ​sets​ ​(Braun​ ​and​ ​Clarke,​ ​2006).​ ​It​ ​is​​a​​six-step​​approach,​​as​​seen​​in​
​Figure​ ​2,​ ​that​ ​starts​ ​with​​the​​qualitative​​data​​and​​looks​​for​​similarities​​and​​contrasts​​before​
​focusing​​on​​the​​link​​between​​the​​different​​parts​​of​​the​​data​​set​​(Braun​​and​​Clarke,​​2006).​​TA​
​seeks​ ​to​ ​come​ ​up​ ​with​ ​descriptive​ ​and/or​ ​explanatory​ ​findings​ ​based​ ​on​ ​the​ ​concept​ ​of​
​‘themes’ (Gale​​et al.​, 2013).​

​It​ ​was​ ​important​ ​for​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​to​ ​consider​ ​how​ ​the​ ​process​ ​aligned​ ​with​ ​abductive​
​reasoning​ ​which​ ​was​ ​adopted​ ​throughout​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process.​ ​As​ ​mentioned​ ​previously,​
​abductive​​reasoning​​has​​been​​defined​​as​​“a​​combination​​of​​deductive​​and​​inductive​​thinking,​
