​whereby​ ​theory​ ​and​ ​practice​ ​inform​ ​one​ ​another”​ ​(Denzin,​ ​1978,​ ​p.​ ​177).​ ​Tavory​ ​and​


                                                            ​112​
​Timmermans​ ​(2014)​ ​state​ ​that​ ​the​ ​process​ ​of​ ​abductive​ ​analysis​ ​involves​ ​going​ ​back​ ​and​
​forth​​between​​the​​research​​evidence​​and​​considerations​​of​​theory.​​With​​that​​in​​mind,​​during​
​this​​research,​​the​​researcher​​ensured​​to​​follow​​abductive​​reasoning​​by​​exploring​​pre-existing​
​theories​ ​mentioned​ ​within​ ​the​ ​literature​ ​review.​ ​This​ ​included​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020),​ ​CRT​
​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001)​ ​and​ ​the​ ​BIM​ ​(Latané​ ​and​ ​Darley,​ ​1970).​ ​In​ ​particular,​ ​the​
​researcher​ ​examined​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​interview​ ​data​ ​while​ ​taking​ ​into​ ​account​ ​their​ ​prior​
​knowledge​ ​gained​ ​by​ ​studying​ ​the​ ​theories​ ​and​ ​their​ ​main​ ​tenets​ ​when​ ​approaching​ ​step​
​three​ ​of​ ​TA,​ ​searching​ ​for​ ​themes.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​whilst​ ​reviewing​ ​the​ ​themes,​ ​abductive​
​reasoning​ ​occurred,​ ​as​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​refined​ ​and​ ​deconstructed​ ​the​ ​themes​ ​into​ ​smaller​
​components, some of which aligned with the tenets of HebCrit and CRT.​




​Figure 2.​​Braun and Clarke (2006) propose a six-step​​process to TA.​

​Although​​Braun​​and​​Clarke​​(2006)​​highlight​​the​​following​​stages,​​literature​​from​​Nowell​​and​
​Norris​​(2017,​​p.​​4)​​stated​​that​​“it​​is​​actually​​an​​iterative​​and​​reflective​​process​​that​​develops​
​over​​time​​and​​involves​​a​​constant​​moving​​back​​and​​forward​​between​​phases.”​​The​​reason​​for​
​this​ ​is​ ​to​​ensure​​trustworthiness​​within​​the​​qualitative​​data.​​However,​​when​​conducting​​TA,​
​the​ ​process​ ​often​ ​begins​ ​with​ ​familiarising​ ​yourself​ ​with​ ​the​ ​data,​ ​which​ ​requires​ ​the​



                                                         ​113​
​development​ ​of​ ​a​ ​systematic​ ​method​ ​for​ ​organising,​ ​sorting​ ​and​ ​storing​ ​data​ ​(Gale​ ​et​ ​al.​,​
​2013).​ ​Secondly,​ ​coding​ ​takes​ ​place,​ ​which​ ​includes​ ​creating​ ​a​ ​phrase​ ​or​ ​label​ ​to​ ​describe​
​how​​the​​data​​has​​been​​interpreted.​​Codes​​have​​been​​defined​​as​​“a​​descriptive​​or​​conceptual​
​label​ ​that​ ​is​ ​assigned​ ​to​ ​excerpts​ ​of​​raw​​data​​in​​a​​process​​called​​coding”​​(Gale​​et​​al​.,​​2013,​
​p.2).​​When​​generating​​themes​​within​​inductive​​research,​​they​​should​​be​​developed​​via​​open​
​coding​​(Williams​​and​​Moser,​​2019).​​Essentially,​​this​​is​​a​​process​​of​​breaking​​down​​the​​data​​to​
​develop​ ​temporary​ ​categories.​ ​Themes​ ​occur​ ​when​ ​“careful​ ​reading​ ​and​ ​re-reading​ ​of​ ​the​
​data”​ ​has​ ​happened​ ​(Rice​ ​and​ ​Ezzy,​ ​1999,​ ​p.​ ​258).​ ​When​ ​themes​ ​were​ ​fully​ ​established,​
​suitable​ ​names​ ​were​ ​given​ ​and​ ​a​ ​definition​ ​of​ ​each​ ​theme​ ​was​ ​provided.​ ​Finally,​ ​themes​
​were​​then​​utilised​​for​​the​​write-up​​process​​of​​this​​thesis.​​Five​​themes​​constructed​​from​​the​
​interview​ ​data​ ​were​ ​named​ ​and​ ​defined​ ​in​ ​Table​ ​2.​ ​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​its​​name​​and​​definition,​
​each theme was composed of numerous subthemes, which are also recorded in Table 2.​

                                                     ​115​
​Chapter 5 - Phase 1- Results and discussion​

​Introduction​


​As​ ​discussed​ ​in​ ​the​ ​previous​ ​chapter,​ ​upon​ ​completing​ ​the​ ​analysis​ ​of​ ​the​ ​interviews​ ​with​
​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​ ​five​ ​themes​ ​were​ ​identified​ ​and​ ​constructed;​ ​these​ ​themes​
​included​ ​a​ ​number​ ​of​ ​sub-themes,​ ​which​ ​can​ ​be​ ​viewed​ ​in​ ​Table​ ​2.​ ​This​ ​chapter​ ​will​ ​be​
​broken​ ​into​ ​five​ ​sections,​ ​with​ ​each​ ​section​ ​delving​ ​further​ ​into​ ​each​ ​of​ ​its​ ​sub-themes,​
​followed​ ​by​ ​a​ ​summary​ ​of​ ​how​ ​these​ ​themes​ ​will​ ​affect​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​progress.​
​Furthermore,​​the​​preceding​​chapter​​(Chapter​​6)​​will​​include​​a​​discussion​​on​​how​​the​​Phase​​1​
​interview data was integrated and implemented into the proposed initiative.​


​Theme 1 - Essential aspects of an initiative​


​This​ ​chapter​ ​begins​ ​by​ ​discussing​ ​the​ ​first​ ​theme​ ​of​ ​‘​essential​ ​aspects​​of​​an​​initiative​’​.​​The​
​qualitative​​data,​​which​​was​​constructed​​from​​the​​expert​​interview​​data,​​highlighted​​the​​most​
​crucial​ ​elements​ ​behind​ ​previous​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives.​ ​As​ ​discussed​ ​within​ ​the​
​literature​ ​review​ ​chapter,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​evident​ ​that​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives​ ​within​ ​sport​ ​have​
​been​ ​recognised​ ​as​ ​a​ ​useful​ ​tool​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​address​ ​discrimination​ ​(Magrath​ ​and​ ​Stott,​
​2019).​​It​​was​​acknowledged,​​although,​​that​​these​​attempts​​had​​limitations.​​Therefore,​​it​​was​
​critical​ ​to​​reflect​​upon​​the​​successes​​and​​failures​​of​​previous​​projects​​in​​order​​to​​make​​sure​
​that​ ​these​ ​were​ ​taken​ ​into​ ​account​ ​when​ ​creating​ ​this​ ​one.​ ​Therefore,​ ​the​ ​most​ ​crucial​
​points​ ​have​ ​been​ ​categorised​ ​into​ ​four​ ​sub-themes​ ​entitled​ ​‘​educational​ ​impact​’,​​‘​resource​
​implementation​’, ‘​audience demographics​’ and ‘​conversation​​stimulation​’.​


​Educational impact​


​Education​ ​has​ ​been​ ​thought​ ​of​ ​as​ ​a​ ​key​ ​factor​ ​when​ ​challenging​ ​and​ ​changing​​individuals’​
​anti-discriminatory​ ​viewpoints​ ​(European​ ​Union​ ​Agency​ ​for​ ​Fundamental​ ​Rights,​ ​2010).​
​Previous​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin​ ​(2018)​ ​and​ ​Solomos​ ​(2020)​ ​highlights​ ​how​
​educational​ ​initiatives​ ​can​ ​have​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​impact​ ​on​​challenging​​discriminatory​​attitudes​
​and​ ​beliefs.​ ​The​ ​contributions​ ​from​ ​the​ ​interviewees​ ​support​ ​this,​ ​with​ ​Nate​ ​(Head​ ​of​


                                                             ​116​
​Education)​ ​stating​ ​that​ ​“there​ ​are​ ​lots​ ​of​ ​people​ ​who​ ​won't​ ​understand​ ​why​ ​that​ ​is​
​unacceptable​ ​and​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​of​ ​what​ ​is​ ​antisemitism,​ ​we​ ​need​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​that​ ​to​ ​start​
​addressing​ ​the​ ​issues”.​ ​This​ ​remark​ ​emphasises​ ​that​ ​without​ ​education​ ​and​ ​knowledge,​
​people​​are​​unable​​to​​grasp​​what​​is​​acceptable,​​emphasising​​the​​necessity​​of​​education​​in​​line​
​with the comments of most participants:​


       ​People​ ​who​ ​usually​ ​have​ ​the​ ​most​ ​racist​ ​views​ ​are​ ​probably​ ​educated​ ​by​ ​the​
       ​Daily Mail. (Keagan - EDI Manager)​



​Similarly,​​Keagan's​​comment​​suggests​​that​​a​​lack​​of​​education​​may​​increase​​the​​likelihood​​of​
​individuals​ ​holding​ ​discriminatory​ ​viewpoints.​ ​While​ ​Keagan's​ ​statement​ ​reflects​ ​his​
​perspective,​ ​it​ ​risks​ ​stigmatising​ ​individuals​ ​based​ ​on​ ​media​ ​preferences,​ ​hindering​
​constructive​​discussions​​on​​discrimination.​​It​​also​​oversimplifies​​the​​complex​​roots​​of​​racism,​
​shaped​ ​by​ ​societal,​ ​cultural,​ ​and​ ​psychological​ ​factors.​ ​However,​ ​his​ ​point​ ​underscores​ ​the​
​significant​ ​influence​ ​of​ ​the​ ​media​ ​in​ ​shaping​ ​public​ ​attitudes​ ​towards​ ​race​ ​and​
​discrimination,​ ​which​ ​can​ ​hinder​ ​someone's​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​these​ ​issues​ ​by​ ​reinforcing​
​stereotypes​​and​​promoting​​biased​​narratives.​​Despite​​not​​focusing​​on​​sport​​specifically,​​Ben,​
​Kelly​ ​and​ ​Paradies​ ​(2020)​ ​investigate​ ​the​ ​successful​ ​strategies​ ​for​ ​combating​ ​prejudice​​and​
​racial/ethnic​ ​discrimination.​ ​They​ ​discuss​ ​education-based​​initiatives​​and​​media​​campaigns,​
​which​ ​suggest​ ​that​ ​they​ ​can​ ​often​ ​reduce​ ​racism.​ ​However,​ ​they​ ​call​ ​for​ ​further​
​comprehensive​​analysis,​​rather​​than​​exploring​​the​​effects​​of​​pre-​​and​​post-​​intervention.​​For​
​example,​​interviewees​​working​​in​​the​​field​​of​​EDI​​stated​​the​​importance​​of​​their​​role​​and​​the​
​implementation​​of​​policies​​in​​the​​workplace,​​in​​which​​they​​“bring​​in​​guidance​​and​​education​
​around that​​(the topic)​” (Emily - EDI manager). To​​this end, one interviewee noted that:​



       ​Changing​​people's​​mindset​​is​​100%​​education,​​but​​we​​need​​to​​ask​​ourselves​​what​
       ​is​​education​​because​​education​​can​​be​​anything​​from​​some​​information​​that​​you​
       ​put​ ​into​ ​a​ ​match​ ​day​ ​programme​ ​all​ ​the​ ​way​ ​through​ ​to​ ​going​ ​into​ ​primary​
       ​schools. (Keagan - EDI Manager)​




                                                         ​117​
​The​​point​​above​​emphasises​​the​​value​​of​​education​​while​​also​​reinforcing​​that​​education​​may​
​be​​obtained​​in​​a​​variety​​of​​ways,​​raising​​the​​question​​of​​which​​will​​be​​the​​most​​effective​​way​
​to​ ​implement​ ​education.​ ​According​ ​to​ ​Dixon​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2016),​ ​short-term​ ​educational​
​interventions​ ​are​ ​insufficient​ ​to​ ​dramatically​ ​improve​​young​​children's​​views​​regarding​​race​
​and​ ​racism.​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result,​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​need​ ​for​ ​a​ ​longer-term​ ​educational​ ​programme,​ ​which​
​might be accomplished by utilising a resource that can be sustained over time.​


​Resource implementation​


​It​ ​became​ ​evident​ ​throughout​ ​the​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​process​ ​that​ ​Matthew,​ ​Jake,​ ​Craig​ ​and​
​Keagan​​all​​believed​​the​​success​​of​​an​​initiative​​comes​​directly​​from​​a​​resource​​or​​a​​“tangible​
​tool”.​ ​This​ ​resonated​ ​with​ ​several​ ​sources​ ​which​ ​similarly​ ​highlighted​ ​that​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​
​symbolic,​ ​practical​ ​initiatives,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​the​ ​‘Rainbow​ ​Laces’​ ​campaign​ ​and​ ​‘No​ ​Room​ ​for​
​Racism’​ ​t-shirts​ ​provide​ ​success​ ​in​ ​raising​ ​awareness​ ​of​ ​the​ ​current​ ​issues​ ​faced​​in​​society,​
​and​ ​sport​ ​specifically,​ ​which​ ​subsequently​ ​can​ ​lead​​to​​education​​(Carrington,​​2010;​​Lawley,​
​2019).​ ​Through​ ​the​ ​implementation​ ​of​ ​symbolic​ ​and​ ​practical​ ​initiatives,​ ​conversations​
​surrounding discrimination can be easily encouraged:​


       ​If​​you're​​going​​to​​deliver​​(an​​initiative)​,​​do​​it​​around​​a​​resource…it​​depends,​​how​
       ​much​ ​time​ ​you're​ ​going​ ​to​ ​get...it​ ​will​ ​be​ ​much​ ​easier​ ​to​ ​do​ ​that​ ​around​ ​a​
       ​resource. (Matthew - Development Officer)​


​Nevertheless,​ ​upon​ ​closer​ ​examination,​ ​past​ ​research​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​practical,​ ​symbolic​
​initiatives​​do​​not​​go​​far​​enough​​and​​can​​also​​lack​​rigour​​(Kershaw,​​2020).​​For​​example,​​whilst​
​Emily’s​​(EDI​​Manager)​​organisation​​use​​symbolic​​initiatives​​to​​raise​​awareness​​of​​the​​current​
​issues LGBT+ athletes face, she acknowledged this challenge by commenting that:​


       ​I​ ​think​​the​​best​​way​​to​​portray​​it​​is,​​like​​it's​​(the​​initiative)​​the​​icing​​but,​​like​​you​
       ​kind​ ​of​ ​need​ ​the​ ​cake​ ​underneath​ ​there.​ ​So,​ ​my​ ​job​ ​is​​to​​give​​people​​the​​cake,​
       ​but it's not good enough to just celebrate and we're almost gone beyond that.​




                                                             ​118​
​In​​agreement​​with​​Emily​​is​​Amy​​(EDI​​Manager),​​who​​argues​​that​​“​(initiatives)​​have​​got​​to​​be​
​backed​​up​​by​​something​​far​​more​​substantial”.​​Doing​​so​​is​​Matthew​​(Education​​Development​
​Officer),​ ​who​ ​utilised​ ​a​ ​resource​ ​to​ ​tackle​ ​discriminatory​ ​behaviours​ ​and​ ​discusses​ ​the​
​importance of the resource they use when working with young learners:​


       ​…if​​you've​​got​​kids​​who​​are​​maybe​​more​​difficult​​to​​engage​​with​​but​​if​​you've​​got​
       ​a​ ​good​ ​book​ ​and​ ​a​ ​good​ ​resource​ ​it's​ ​much​ ​easier​ ​to​ ​bring​ ​the​ ​kids​ ​in​ ​then​
       ​because they wanted to talk about it.​


​The​​interview​​data,​​from​​Emily,​​Amy​​and​​Matthew,​​alongside​​the​​literature​​review​​on​​current​
​sports​ ​based​ ​anti-discriminatory​ ​initiatives,​ ​have​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​a​ ​physical​ ​and​
​tangible​ ​resource​ ​to​ ​be​ ​used​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​individuals.​ ​Both​ ​reinforced​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that​ ​once​ ​an​
​individual​ ​has​ ​engaged​ ​with​ ​the​​resource​​there​​is​​then​​a​​greater​​opportunity​​for​​discussion​
​and learning to take place.​


​Audience demographics​


​The​ ​contributions​ ​from​ ​the​ ​interviewees​ ​to​ ​this​ ​point​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​necessity​ ​of​​using​​a​
​resource​ ​as​ ​a​ ​practical​ ​tool​​for​​educating​​people.​​However,​​it​​is​​critical​​to​​evaluate​​who​​the​
​resource​ ​should​ ​be​ ​developed​ ​for.​ ​Therefore,​ ​the​ ​next​ ​important​ ​factor​ ​to​ ​consider​ ​is​
​captured​​in​​the​​‘​audience​​demographics​’​​sub-theme​.​​Keagan​​highlighted​​that​​we​​must​​“treat​
​people​ ​as​ ​individuals”​ ​and​ ​that​ ​“we​ ​shouldn't​ ​jump​ ​to​ ​the​ ​conclusion​ ​that​ ​each​ ​group…​ ​a​
​certain​ ​group​ ​is​ ​like​​that”,​​referring​​to​​certain​​discriminatory​​behaviour​​and​​attitudes​​based​
​upon​​their​​demographics,​​including​​age,​​gender,​​ethnicity​​or​​other​​protected​​characteristics.​
​This​​point,​​further​​critiques​​Keagan’s​​previous​​comment​​regarding,​​racist​​individuals​​get​​their​
​understanding​ ​from​ ​certain​ ​news​ ​outlets.​ ​However,​ ​the​ ​interviewees​ ​suggested​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​
​easier​ ​to​ ​challenge​ ​and​ ​change​ ​racist,​ ​transphobic,​ ​xenophobic,​ ​and​ ​homophobic​​attitudes​
​when working with young people:​


       ​It’s​​the​​future…​​we​​invest​​in​​young​​people​​and​​we​​help​​them​​find​​their​​voices​​on​
       ​these things. (Daniel - Director)​




                                                            ​119​
​Jennett​​(2009)​​argues​​that​​it​​is​​easier​​to​​challenge​​young​​individuals'​​opinions​​and​​attitudes,​
​than​​at​​an​​older​​age,​​as​​it​​allows​​them​​to​​talk​​openly​​about​​discrimination​​without​​as​​many​
​preconceived​ ​viewpoints.​ ​Therefore,​ ​the​ ​contribution​ ​made​ ​by​ ​Daniel​ ​supports​ ​previous​
​academic​​research.​​In​​addition,​​this​​strategy​​was​​supported​​by​​a​​range​​of​​experts,​​specifically​
​Matthew​ ​(Education​ ​Development​ ​Officer),​ ​who​ ​found​ ​when​ ​implementing​ ​their​ ​strategy​
​that​ ​the​ ​ages​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​implement​ ​initiatives​ ​on​ ​and​ ​have​ ​greater​ ​impact​ ​upon​ ​is​ ​10-11​
​years:​


       ​…because​ ​they're​ ​old​ ​enough​ ​to​ ​have​ ​an​ ​understanding,​ ​and​ ​in​ ​Glasgow​ ​and​
       ​West​ ​Scotland,​ ​they'll​ ​easily​ ​have​ ​been​ ​exposed​ ​regularly​ ​to​ ​those​ ​types​ ​of​
       ​attitudes,​ ​but​ ​hopefully​ ​young​ ​enough​ ​to​ ​have​ ​an​​open​​mind.​​Also,​​Primary​​7…​
       ​there​ ​are​ ​other​ ​role​ ​models​ ​in​ ​their​​school…​​so​​from​​Primary​​1,​​all​​the​​way​​up,​
       ​they​ ​always​ ​look​ ​up​ ​to​ ​Primary​ ​7s​ ​and​ ​their​ ​behaviour​ ​will​ ​be​ ​mirrored.​ ​We're​
       ​also​ ​preparing​ ​them​ ​for​ ​that​ ​transition​ ​to​ ​secondary​ ​school​ ​when​ ​they​ ​will​ ​be​
       ​able​ ​to​ ​meet​ ​new​ ​people​ ​with​ ​different​ ​backgrounds,​ ​different​ ​diversity,​ ​and​
       ​obviously​​they'll​​come​​with​​their​​values​​and​​attitudes​​and​​oppose​​their​​attitudes​
       ​on others.​


​This​​comment​​supports​​the​​arguments​​of​​Blaise​​(2009)​​and​​Jennett​​(2009)​​who​​contend​​we​
​must​ ​educate​ ​individuals​ ​when​ ​they​ ​are​ ​younger​ ​so​ ​that​ ​over​ ​time​ ​society​ ​creates​​a​​more​
​accepting​ ​and​ ​inclusive​ ​generation,​ ​creating​ ​a​ ​more​ ​accepting​ ​society.​ ​Likewise,​ ​Naveen​
​(Head​​of​​Education)​​stated​​how​​“it​​is​​essential​​to​​work​​with​​young​​people,​​so​​that​​we​​can​​try​
​now​​and​​build​​a​​better​​generation​​for​​the​​future”.​​Similarly,​​Darren​​(Initiative​​Advisor)​​-​​who​
​worked​ ​on​ ​two​ ​separate​ ​projects,​ ​which​ ​focused​ ​specifically​ ​on​ ​antisemitism,​ ​one​ ​with​ ​an​
​older​ ​generation​ ​and​ ​another​ ​with​ ​a​ ​younger​ ​generation​ ​-​ ​found​ ​that​ ​it​ ​was​ ​“easier​ ​to​
​influence” individuals aged thirteen and fourteen:​


       ​I​ ​was​ ​part​ ​of​ ​research​ ​exploring​ ​antisemitic​ ​incidents​​in​​secondary​​education​​in​
       ​2013…​ ​There​ ​were​ ​many​ ​incidents​ ​visible​ ​in​ ​the​ ​year​ ​that​ ​we​​did​​the​​research.​
       ​The​ ​way​ ​young​ ​people​ ​outed​ ​themselves​ ​in​ ​antisemitic​ ​ways​ ​wasn't​ ​that​
       ​shocking,​ ​but​ ​one​ ​context​ ​was​ ​very​ ​surprising​ ​to​ ​us,​ ​and​ ​that​ ​was​ ​that​ ​the​
       ​teachers…​​more​​than​​half…​​reported​​an​​antisemitic​​incident…​​report​​that​​it​​came​


                                                            ​120​
       ​out​ ​of​ ​football​ ​context,​ ​and​ ​that​ ​was​ ​surprising​ ​because​ ​we​ ​didn't​ ​talk​ ​about​
       ​stadiums and matches within the classroom.​


​On​ ​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​Link​ ​and​ ​Phelan​ ​(2001)​ ​emphasises​ ​that​ ​campaigns​ ​should​ ​focus​ ​on​
​individuals,​​communities,​​structures,​​and​​systems​​harbouring​​prejudiced​​beliefs.​​Therefore,​​it​
​is​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​prioritise​ ​educating​ ​those​ ​who​ ​hold​ ​antisemitic​ ​attitudes​ ​and​ ​beliefs.​ ​As​
​previously​ ​mentioned,​ ​some​ ​football​ ​clubs​ ​have​ ​already​ ​implemented​ ​educational​
​workshops​ ​for​ ​fans​ ​found​ ​engaging​ ​in​ ​antisemitic​ ​behaviour.​ ​Attending​ ​these​ ​workshops​
​allows​​individuals​​who​​have​​been​​banned​​from​​games​​to​​have​​their​​suspension​​shortened​​as​
​an​ ​incentive.​ ​However,​ ​Craig​ ​(EDI​ ​Consultant)​ ​observed​ ​that​ ​“ultimately,​ ​all​ ​of​ ​them​ ​want​
​their​ ​suspension​​reduced​​because​​they​​want​​to​​come​​back​​to​​the​​club.”​​This​​raises​​ongoing​
​questions​​about​​the​​sincerity​​of​​participants'​​engagement​​with​​these​​courses,​​whether​​they​
​are​​genuinely​​seeking​​to​​learn​​and​​educate​​themselves​​or​​simply​​aiming​​to​​reduce​​their​​ban.​
​If​​attendees​​view​​the​​workshops​​as​​a​​meaningless​​'box-ticking'​​exercise,​​the​​initiative​​may​​fail​
​to​ ​effectively​ ​reduce​ ​antisemitic​ ​behaviour.​ ​Matthew,​ ​on​ ​the​ ​other​ ​hand,​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​with​
​"early​ ​intervention​ ​you​ ​get​ ​much​ ​more​ ​buy-in…​ ​you​ ​will​ ​have​ ​much​ ​more​ ​enthusiasm",​
​emphasising​​that​​anti-discrimination​​initiatives​​receive​​greater​​curiosity​​and​​genuine​​interest​
​at a younger age, rather than those fans already harbouring antisemitic attitudes.​


​A​​challenge​​that​​could​​be​​faced​​here​​is​​that,​​in​​the​​short-term,​​this​​educational​​initiative​​may​
​not​ ​be​ ​sufficient​ ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​substantial​ ​positive​ ​effect​ ​upon​ ​young​ ​children’s​ ​views,​ ​in​
​comparison​​to​​the​​long-term​​influences​​of​​their​​parents,​​who​​may​​already​​withhold​​negative​
​opinions​ ​(Dixon​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2016).​ ​Matthew​ ​recognised​ ​this​ ​as​ ​a​ ​key​ ​limitation​ ​of​ ​his​ ​initiative;​
​however,​​he​​discussed​​the​​importance​​of​​allowing​​parents​​“to​​ask​​questions​​or​​express​​their​
​concerns…​ ​and​ ​that​ ​a​ ​level​ ​of​ ​dialogue​ ​was​​the​​healthy​​way​​around​​it”.​​Although​​Matthew​
​was​​the​​only​​interviewee​​who​​discussed​​the​​importance​​of​​parental​​involvement,​​both​​prior​
​research​ ​and​ ​Matthew’s​ ​feedback​ ​both​ ​reinforce​ ​that​ ​working​ ​with​ ​parents,​ ​and​ ​allowing​
​them to also be involved in the process is crucial.​




                                                              ​121​
​Conversation stimulation​


​It​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​that​ ​any​ ​initiative​ ​stimulates​ ​conversation​ ​surrounding​ ​discrimination,​
​particularly​ ​focusing​​on​​the​​specific​​form​​of​​discrimination​​being​​addressed​​(MacIntosh​​and​
​Martin,​​2018).​​Keagan​​recognised,​​when​​working​​in​​an​​EDI​​setting,​​that​​the​​more​​something​
​is​ ​spoken​ ​about,​ ​the​ ​easier​ ​it​ ​becomes​ ​to​ ​change​ ​the​ ​perception​ ​in​ ​the​ ​general​ ​public.​ ​In​
​agreement,​​Matthew​​has​​been​​working​​on​​his​​educational​​initiative​​for​​almost​​20​​years​​and​
​shared​​how​​he​​measures​​its​​progress.​​His​​criterion​​for​​success​​was​​that​​individuals​​were​​able​
​to​​freely​​discuss​​prejudice​​as​​a​​result​​of​​it,​​as​​well​​as​​recognise​​and​​actively​​challenge​​it.​​This​
​is​ ​important​ ​information​ ​because​ ​he​ ​feels​ ​that​ ​as​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​being​ ​educated,​ ​people​​have​
​grown​​more​​aware​​of​​contemporary​​issues​​and​​are​​better​​equipped​​to​​discuss​​them.​​He​​also​
​reinforced​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​critical​ ​not​ ​to​ ​push​ ​personal​ ​opinions​ ​on​ ​others,​ ​and​ ​to​ ​"always​ ​ask​
​questions,​ ​not​ ​tell".​ ​By​ ​doing​ ​so,​ ​pupils​ ​are​ ​able​ ​to​ ​build​ ​their​ ​own​ ​thoughts​ ​while​ ​also​
​stimulating them around what they are learning, and so, dialogues will lead to knowledge.​


​When​ ​working​ ​in​ ​the​ ​EDI​ ​field,​ ​Jake​ ​recognised​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​have​ ​“proper​
​conversations​​around​​cultural​​stuff​​and​​values”.​​Emily​​too,​​works​​in​​the​​field​​of​​EDI​​and​​states​
​that​ ​implementations​ ​of​ ​policies​ ​within​ ​the​ ​workplace​ ​“allow​ ​people​ ​to​ ​start​ ​to​ ​have​ ​the​
​conversations​ ​about​ ​LGBT+​ ​identities.”​ ​Similarly,​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​of​​Amy’s​​(EDI​​Manager)​​campaign​
​was to:​


       ​…create​ ​a​ ​conversation​ ​around​ ​LGBT+​ ​inclusion​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​in​ ​modern​ ​society…​ ​[it​
       ​gives]​ ​the​ ​time​ ​and​ ​space​ ​to​ ​say​ ​“okay,​ ​I​ ​haven’t​ ​thought​ ​about​ ​LGBT+​ ​inclusion​
       ​before”... and in the sense help people raise their own understanding and awareness.​


​Overall,​ ​Jake,​ ​Emily,​ ​and​ ​Amy,​ ​who​ ​strive​ ​to​ ​promote​ ​equality,​ ​diversity,​ ​and​ ​inclusion​ ​in​
​sport,​ ​seek​​to​​encourage​​conversations​​and​​open​​dialogue​​within​​the​​area​​of​​sport​​in​​order​
​to​ ​make​ ​it​ ​as​ ​inclusive​ ​as​ ​possible,​ ​therefore​ ​highlighting​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​stimulating​
​conversations​ ​around​ ​topics​ ​relating​ ​to​ ​discrimination.​ ​This​ ​supports​ ​prior​ ​research​ ​by​
​MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin​ ​(2018)​ ​who​ ​examined​ ​anti-racist​ ​initiatives​ ​and​ ​highlighted​ ​the​
​importance​​of​​educating​​individuals​​in​​a​​sporting​​context.​​Although​​it​​should​​not​​be​​used​​as​​a​
​holistic​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​tackling​ ​problems,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​racism​ ​(Lea-Howart,​ ​2006),​ ​MacIntosh​ ​and​


                                                             ​122​
​Martin​ ​(2018)​ ​concluded​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​provides​ ​an​ ​environment​ ​in​​which​​to​​have​​these​​initial​
​and open conversations regarding current societal issues.​


​Theme 2 - The environment​


​The​​second​​theme​​is​​titled​​‘​the​​environment​’​.​​This​​theme​​highlights​​the​​idea​​that​​the​​setting​
​in​ ​which​ ​an​ ​initiative​ ​is​ ​conducted​ ​is​ ​critical​ ​to​ ​its​ ​effectiveness​ ​since​ ​it​ ​may​ ​influence​
​participants'​​engagement​​and​​enthusiasm​​of​​the​​initiative.​​Organisations​​such​​as​​Chelsea​​FC,​
​Anne​​Frank​​Trust​​and​​The​​Holocaust​​Educational​​Trust​​currently​​deliver​​educational​​initiatives​
​in​ ​various​ ​different​ ​environments,​ ​including​ ​community​ ​groups,​ ​workplaces​ ​and​ ​schools.​
​With​ ​this​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​there​ ​are​ ​three​ ​sub-themes​ ​relating​ ​to​ ​this​ ​overarching​ ​theme​ ​of​ '​the​
​environment'​ ​of​ ​an​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiative;​ ​they​ ​are:​ ​‘safe​ ​spaces’​,​ ​‘informal​
​environments​’​,​​and ‘​trusted leaders'.​


​Safe spaces​


​The​ ​interviewees​ ​stressed​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​addressing​ ​and​ ​discussing​ ​misconceptions,​
​asserting​ ​that​ ​creating​ ​a​ ​“safe​​and​​non-judgmental​​environment”​​is​​crucial​​when​​educating​
​people​ ​about​​discrimination.​​This​​approach​​fosters​​open​​conversations,​​enabling​​individuals​
​to​​challenge​​and​​reflect​​on​​their​​beliefs.​​Emily​​commented​​that​​her​​work​​in​​the​​field​​of​​EDI​​is​
​important​​because​​it​​helps​​“to​​bring​​people​​to​​have​​the​​conversation​​in​​a​​safe​​space”.​​Keagan​
​supported​ ​this​ ​point​ ​by​ ​recognising​ ​that​ ​the​ ​environment​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​for​ ​engaging​
​participants and ensuring they get the most out of the initiative:​


       ​…you​​need​​to​​create​​a​​safe​​space,​​where​​it's​​specifically​​about​​EDI​​that​​can​​bring​
       ​people together to talk about things that they normally wouldn't.​


​Experts​ ​used​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘safe​ ​space’​ ​which​ ​prompted​ ​discussion​ ​around​ ​what​ ​constituted​ ​a​
'​safe​​space'.​​Schools,​​community​​groups,​​places​​of​​religion,​​and​​job​​placements​​were​​among​
​the​ ​spaces​ ​explored​ ​with​ ​experts.​ ​Daniel​ ​(Director)​ ​acknowledges​ ​that​ ​the​ ​form​ ​of​
​discrimination​ ​he​ ​works​ ​to​ ​combat​ ​is​ ​not​ ​only​ ​a​ ​societal​​issue​​but​​also​​prevalent​​in​​sports,​
​workplaces, and communities. As a result, he offers workshops in these settings:​


                                                            ​123​
         ​But​ ​is​ ​it​ ​only​ ​an​ ​issue​ ​in​ ​society?​ ​Well,​ ​no,​ ​we​ ​would​ ​argue​ ​it​ ​isn’t,​ ​and​ ​at​
         ​(organisation​ ​name)​ ​we​ ​work​ ​to​ ​tackle​ ​stuff​ ​in​ ​sport,​ ​we​ ​also​ ​do​ ​things​ ​in​
         ​workplaces and things in communities, we do things in school.​


​Additionally,​ ​Daniel​ ​recounted​ ​an​ ​instance​ ​where​ ​he​ ​attended​ ​a​ ​workplace​ ​to​ ​conduct​ ​an​
​educational workshop; however, it did not go as planned:​


         ​We​ ​went​ ​there​ ​to​ ​do​ ​a​ ​bit​ ​of​ ​work​ ​and​ ​I​ ​went​ ​into​ ​the​ ​room,​ ​we​ ​go​ ​to​ ​the​
         ​people's​ ​depo,​ ​so​ ​in​ ​this​ ​case​ ​I’m​ ​going​ ​to​ ​work​ ​in​ ​a​ ​refuge​ ​portakabin​ ​with​
         ​10-15​ ​big​ ​guys,​ ​all​ ​tattoos​ ​and​ ​many​ ​quite​ ​clear​ ​their​ ​background,​ ​their​
         ​allegiances,​​everyone​​with​​arms​​folded​​and​​nobody​​said​​a​​word…​​I​​couldn't​​get​
         ​any​ ​kind​ ​of​ ​rapport,​ ​they​ ​expressed​ ​they​ ​didn't​ ​want​ ​to​ ​talk​ ​basically,​ ​just​
         ​stonewalled.​


​Nevertheless,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​interesting​ ​to​ ​see​ ​that​ ​nearly​ ​four​ ​years​ ​later,​​Daniel​​was​​invited​​back​
​and they took a different approach:​


         ​We​ ​took​ ​a​ ​different​ ​turn,​ ​and​ ​we​ ​worked​ ​with​ ​everyone.​ ​The​ ​director​ ​was​
         ​involved​​in​​it.​​So,​​it​​was​​a​​mixture​​of​​people,​​and​​people​​got​​to​​talk​​about​​their​
         ​views​ ​and​ ​attitudes.​ ​And​ ​so,​​we​​did​​this​​programme​​for​​three​​or​​four​​months,​
         ​and​​then​​we​​kept​​in​​touch​​with​​the​​guy,​​and​​he​​said,​​you​​know,​​there​​had​​been​
         ​a huge change in the workplace attitudes.​


​After​ ​modifying​ ​the​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​be​ ​more​ ​accommodating​ ​of​ ​the​ ​expressed​ ​views​ ​and​
​attitudes,​​it​​became​​clear​​that​​the​​workshop​​had​​a​​bigger​​impact.​​Similarly,​​by​​incorporating​
​the​​director,​​they​​avoided​​singling​​out​​people​​with​​perceived​​bad​​attitudes​​and​​perspectives,​
​which may have led to them feeling judged.​


​When​​discussing​​sensitive​​topics​​amongst​​young​​children,​​Naveen​​believes​​that​​his​​initiative​
​took​ ​place​ ​in​ ​a​ ​safe​ ​space,​ ​a​ ​school,​ ​where​ ​they​ ​can​ ​express​ ​themselves​ ​and​ ​challenge​
​misconceptions.​ ​To​ ​create​ ​a​ ​safe​ ​space,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​also​ ​important​ ​to​ ​Craig​ ​that​ ​individuals​


                                                               ​124​
​perceived​ ​this​ ​to​ ​be​ ​somewhere​ ​they​ ​felt​ ​unjudged​ ​for​ ​their​ ​actions,​ ​and​ ​said​ ​that​ ​those​
​individuals​​who​​have​​come​​to​​education​​workshops​​as​​a​​result​​of​​their​​antisemitic​​behaviour​
​were​ ​not​ ​accused​ ​of​ ​being​​antisemitic,​​“...but,​​instead,​​what​​they​​took​​part​​in​​or​​put​​up​​on​
​social​ ​media​ ​had​ ​antisemitic​ ​content​ ​in​​it.”​​This,​​therefore,​​made​​individuals​​feel​​unjudged,​
​contributing to a more positive and supportive environment.​


​On​​the​​other​​hand,​​when​​discussing​​the​​notion​​of​​a​​safe​​environment,​​literature​​by​​Leonardo​
​and​​Porter​​(2010)​​ask​​‘safety​​for​​whom?’,​​in​​addition​​to​​acknowledging​​that​​when​​addressing​
​race​​amongst​​individuals​​in​​a​​safe​​setting​​simply​​encourages​​a​​“safe​​space​​where​​Whites​​can​
​avoid​ ​publicly​ ​looking​ ​racist”​ ​(p.​ ​139).​ ​Similarly,​ ​they​ ​investigated​ ​how​ ​it​ ​can​ ​become​
​especially​ ​difficult​ ​and​ ​uncomfortable​​for​​those​​who​​benefit​​from​​that​​privilege,​​concluding​
​that​ ​those​ ​individuals​ ​should​ ​take​ ​ownership​ ​of​​feeling​​uncomfortable​​in​​discussions​​about​
​discrimination,​​as​​it​​encourages​​them​​to​​act​​on​​their​​viewpoints​​and​​feelings.​​As​​a​​result,​​it​​is​
​critical​ ​to​ ​consider​ ​that,​ ​while​ ​individuals​ ​may​ ​feel​ ​uncomfortable​ ​because​ ​of​ ​their​
​potentially​ ​prejudiced​ ​viewpoints,​ ​they​ ​should​ ​come​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​their​​wrongdoings,​​not​
​by​​being​​overtly​​judged,​​but​​by​​experiencing​​discomfort​​in​​a​​setting​​where​​they​​feel​​safe​​and​
​supported in doing so.​


​Informal environment​


​In​​addition​​to​​the​​environment​​of​​the​​initiative​​being​​'safe',​​it​​was​​argued​​that​​it​​was​​essential​
​that​​the​​environment​​was​​also​​'informal'.​​The​​agreement​​from​​the​​expert​​interviews​​was​​that​
​the​​environment​​in​​which​​the​​individuals​​participate​​in​​the​​initiative​​is​​“an​​informal​​place​​to​
​express​ ​and​ ​challenge​ ​misconceptions”​ ​(Naveen).​ ​For​ ​those​​individuals​​who​​participated​​in​
​initiatives​ ​as​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​their​ ​previous​ ​discriminatory​ ​actions,​ ​an​ ​informal​ ​environment​
​helped​ ​in​ ​making​ ​individuals​ ​feel​ ​less​ ​stigmatised​ ​for​ ​their​ ​behaviour;​ ​subsequently,​
​individuals​ ​were​ ​also​ ​more​ ​inclined​ ​to​ ​open​ ​up​ ​and​ ​communicate​ ​their​​worries​​due​​to​​the​
​informality.​


​Matthew​​also​​stressed​​the​​need​​to​​ensure​​that​​it​​was​​presented​​casually,​​adding​​that​​this​​is​​a​
​fundamental benefit of their initiative:​




                                                           ​125​
       ​…we​ ​have​ ​the​ ​advantage​ ​that​ ​we​​deliver​​in​​an​​informal​​manner​​but​​in​​a​​formal​
       ​setting…​ ​I​ ​am​ ​(​name​)​ ​I’m​ ​not​ ​Mr​ ​(​last-name)​,​​you​​know.​​I​​mean…​​then​​I’ll​​have​
       ​jeans​ ​on​ ​and​ ​teachers​ ​definitely​ ​don’t​ ​have​ ​jeans​ ​on…​ ​you​ ​know,​ ​that​ ​sort​ ​of​
       ​thing. Or I’ll wear my full-on football kit.​


​This​ ​implied​ ​that​ ​by​ ​delivering​ ​their​ ​sessions​ ​in​ ​a​ ​less​ ​formal​ ​manner,​ ​children​ ​would​ ​feel​
​more comfortable having open conversations.​


​Trusted leaders​


​Trusted​ ​adults​ ​have​ ​an​ ​important​ ​role​ ​to​ ​play​ ​in​ ​many​ ​people's​ ​lives,​ ​especially​ ​young​
​individuals​​(Meltzer,​​Muir​​and​​Craig,​​2016).​​When​​developing​​an​​initiative,​​it​​is​​important​​to​
​consider​​who​​will​​be​​delivering​​the​​content​​and​​to​​take​​into​​account​​the​​traits​​an​​educator​​or​
​instructor​​should​​have.​​Amy​​(EDI​​Manager)​​argued​​that,​​when​​working​​with​​the​​community,​
​trusted individuals are needed in order to help people make change:​


       ​Fundamentally,​ ​a​ ​lot​ ​of​ ​this​ ​comes​ ​down​ ​to​ ​trusted​ ​relationships.​ ​You​ ​need​ ​to​
       ​build​ ​that​ ​relationship​ ​with​ ​somebody​ ​to​ ​trust…​​it's​​also​​about​​people​​who​​can​
       ​influence​ ​on​ ​a​ ​very​ ​small,​ ​micro-level​ ​to​ ​influence​ ​the​ ​change​​that's​​needed​​to​
       ​get people more active.​


​It​​was​​argued​​that​​individuals'​​behaviours​​were​​influenced​​by​​the​​individual​​who​​was​​leading​
​the initiative, as they trusted the individual.​


         ​The​​phrase​​[trusted​​leaders]​​was​​used​​a​​lot​​with​​community​​leaders​​but​​that​​it​
         ​was​ ​a​ ​phrase​ ​that​ ​covered​ ​everything​ ​from​ ​formal​ ​appointments​ ​to​ ​informal​
         ​appointments…​​I​​worked​​with​​Muslim​​sports​​foundation​​on​​a​​number​​of​​things,​
         ​and​ ​they​ ​were​ ​going​ ​into​ ​the​ ​Madrasas,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​the​​Islamic​​schools,​​and​​the​
         ​Imam​ ​was​ ​able​ ​to​ ​add​ ​sport​ ​physical​ ​activity​ ​to​ ​the​ ​end​ ​of​ ​the​ ​madrasa​
         ​session…​ ​then​ ​the​ ​mums​ ​who​ ​would​ ​come​ ​to​ ​pick​ ​the​ ​kids​ ​up​ ​started​ ​saying​
         ​well​​we're​​waiting​​for​​our​​kids,​​what​​can​​you​​do​​for​​us,​​can​​you​​run​​a​​session​​for​
         ​us. (Amy)​


                                                            ​126​
​This​ ​quote​ ​from​ ​Amy​ ​(EDI​ ​Manager)​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Imam​ ​as​ ​a​ ​trusted​
​leader,​ ​enabling​ ​him​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​both​ ​the​ ​children​ ​and,​ ​subsequently,​ ​the​ ​mothers​ ​in​ ​sport​
​due​ ​to​ ​his​ ​influential​ ​role​ ​within​ ​the​ ​community.​ ​As​ ​discussed​ ​previously,​ ​Matthew​
​(Educational​​Development​​Officer),​​found​​that​​he​​felt​​trusted​​by​​the​​students​​he​​worked​​with​
​and​​found​​that​​it​​helped​​to​​keep​​them​​engaged.​​Furthermore,​​persons​​who​​have​​previously​
​been​ ​marginalised​ ​as​ ​a​ ​consequence​ ​of​ ​their​ ​protected​ ​characteristics​ ​have​ ​been​ ​seen​ ​as​
​trustworthy​​leaders,​​with​​experts​​including​​Craig,​​Darren,​​Warren,​​and​​James​​recognising​​the​
​need​ ​to​ ​include​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​marginalised​ ​population​ ​in​ ​the​ ​initiative.​ ​Individuals​
​engaging​ ​in​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​were​ ​able​ ​to​ ​question​ ​their​ ​beliefs​ ​by​ ​incorporating​ ​and​ ​sharing​
​first-hand accounts, according to experts.​


​Various​ ​initiatives​ ​discussed​ ​with​ ​the​ ​experts,​ ​including​ ​Darren,​ ​James,​​Emily​​and​​Matthew​
​were​​delivered​​by​​teachers​​in​​educational​​establishments,​​either​​primary​​or​​secondary.​​None​
​of​​the​​experts​​specifically​​mentioned​​teachers​​being​​considered​​trusted​​individuals;​​however,​
​it​​should​​be​​noted​​that​​previous​​research​​from​​Meltzer,​​Muir​​and​​Craig​​(2016)​​found​​teachers​
​to​ ​be​ ​considered​ ​this.​ ​Teachers​ ​with​ ​a​ ​more​ ​formal​ ​role​ ​than​ ​community​ ​leaders​ ​and​
​volunteers​ ​can​ ​be​ ​regarded​ ​as​ ​role​ ​models​ ​and​ ​have​ ​a​ ​big​ ​influence​ ​on​ ​pupils,​ ​and​ ​their​
​perspectives​ ​and​ ​teachings​ ​can​​have​​a​​significant​​impact​​on​​the​​attitudes​​of​​young​​children​
​and adults (Lumpkin, 2008).​


​Theme 3 - Sport as a conversational tool​


​The​ ​earlier​ ​literature​ ​review​ ​explored​ ​sport​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​social​ ​change,​ ​emphasising​ ​its​
​potential​ ​to​ ​drive​ ​positive​ ​outcomes​ ​while​​also​​recognising​​that​​it​​can​​contribute​​to​​certain​
​challenges​​and​​issues.​​Giulianotti​​(2011)​​highlights​​that​​sport,​​whether​​at​​grassroots​​level​​or​
​global​​events,​​plays​​a​​critical​​role​​in​​the​​formation​​of​​peaceful,​​harmonious​​environments,​​as​
​well​​as​​being​​a​​tool​​that​​may​​foster​​harmony​​and​​connect​​societies.​​Nevertheless,​​Anderson​
​and​ ​White​ ​(2017)​ ​draw​ ​attention​ ​to​ ​many​ ​issues​ ​that​ ​are​ ​evident​ ​in​​sport,​​such​​as​​sexism,​
​homophobia​ ​and​ ​violence.​ ​These​ ​arguments​ ​were​ ​reinforced​ ​in​ ​the​ ​interviews​ ​with​
​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​ ​with​ ​four​ ​sub-themes​ ​developed​ ​in​ ​this​ ​regard:​ ​‘​sport​ ​as​ ​a​




                                                           ​127​
​positive​ ​or​ ​negative​ ​tool​’​,​ ​‘addressing​ ​social​ ​issues​ ​through​ ​sport​’,​ ​and​ ​‘​sport​ ​and​
​partnerships​’​.​


​Sport as a positive or negative tool​


​Previous​​literature​​from​​scholars,​​including​​Giulianotti​​(2011)​​and​​Kidd​​(2008),​​reinforced​​the​
​idea​ ​the​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​becoming​ ​increasingly​ ​recognised​ ​as​ ​a​ ​powerful​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​tackling​
​discrimination​ ​and​ ​making​ ​society​ ​a​ ​more​ ​inclusive​ ​place.​ ​This​ ​was​ ​echoed​ ​by​ ​Craig,​ ​who​
​argued:​


       ​…football​ ​has​ ​a​ ​real​ ​opportunity​ ​not​ ​just​ ​to​ ​address​ ​discriminatory​ ​behaviour​
       ​within​​the​​game,​​but​​you​​know,​​like…​​(organisation​​name)​​has​​recognised​​it,​​used​
       ​their platform, and the power has an impact on wider society.​


​This​ ​perspective​ ​recognises​ ​that​ ​sport,​ ​and​ ​notably​ ​football,​ ​serves​ ​as​ ​a​​powerful​​platform​
​that​​may​​be​​utilised​​for​​positive​​impact​​-​​a​​sentiment​​reiterated​​by​​many​​of​​the​​interviewees,​
​such as Daniel:​


       ​Football​ ​has​​the​​three​​P’s:​​‘passion’,​​‘pantomime’​​and​​‘poison’…​​People​​are​​very​
       ​passionate,​ ​you'll​ ​probably​ ​have​ ​seen.​ ​If​ ​you​ ​look​ ​at​ ​England…​ ​you've​​seen​​the​
       ​passion​​behind​​that…​​you​​get​​the​​pantomime​​element​​where​​people​​will​​say​​that​
       ​people​ ​will​ ​go​ ​to​ ​football​ ​matches,​ ​and​ ​perhaps​ ​not​ ​behave​ ​in​​a​​way​​that​​they​
       ​don't​ ​outside​ ​of​ ​football…​ ​and​ ​then​ ​get​ ​poison​ ​-​ ​you​ ​get​ ​the​ ​stuff​ ​that​ ​really​
       ​people will go and hurl abuse at people.​


​Daniel’s​ ​statement​ ​supports​ ​the​ ​work​ ​of​ ​Anderson​ ​and​ ​White​ ​(2017),​ ​who​ ​have​ ​drawn​
​attention​ ​to​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​not​ ​necessarily​ ​beneficial​ ​for​ ​social​ ​change,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​can​
​exacerbate​ ​problematic​ ​issues​ ​in​ ​sport.​ ​Specifically,​ ​Daniel​ ​pointed​ ​out​ ​how​ ​sport​ ​can​ ​be​
​poisonous​​when​​it​​comes​​to​​abuse​​at​​football​​matches.​​Likewise,​​this​​quote​​below​​from​​Craig​
​(EDI​ ​Consultant),​ ​supports​ ​the​ ​view​ ​that​ ​although​ ​sport,​ ​specifically​ ​football,​ ​has​ ​many​
​benefits, it also has its limitations:​




                                                             ​128​
       ​Football​​is​​a​​global​​game,​​and​​it​​has​​a​​global​​platform,​​and​​that​​is​​a​​double-edged​
       ​sword​ ​because​ ​you​ ​know​ ​it,​ ​it​ ​can​ ​bring​ ​people​ ​together​ ​really​ ​well​ ​and,​
       ​obviously, as we know it can be hugely divisive.​


​This​ ​dichotomy​ ​was​ ​reflected​ ​in​ ​the​ ​2020​ ​UEFA​ ​European​ ​Championships​ ​Final,​ ​whereby​
​football​ ​united​ ​the​ ​nation​ ​and​ ​brought​ ​much​ ​happiness​ ​to​ ​many​ ​after​ ​a​ ​year​ ​of​ ​isolation;​
​nevertheless,​​when​​England​​reached​​the​​finals,​​and​​ultimately​​lost​​of​​Italy​​on​​penalties,​​fans​
​began​ ​to​ ​racially​ ​abuse​ ​those​​footballers​​such​​as​​Marcus​​Rashford,​​Bukayo​​Saka,​​and​​Jadon​
​Sancho​​who​​failed​​to​​score​​their​​penalty​​(Evans​​et​​al​.,​​2021).​​This​​problem​​was​​highlighted​​by​
​Jake (EDI Consultant):​


       ​…football​ ​is​ ​the​ ​nation's​ ​game,​ ​and​ ​it's​ ​so​ ​big.​ ​And​ ​we​ ​saw​ ​in​ ​the​ ​space​ ​of​ ​30​
       ​seconds,​ ​with​ ​a​ ​few​ ​guys​ ​missing​ ​some​ ​spot​ ​kicks,​ ​how​ ​all​ ​of​ ​that​ ​can​ ​change.​
       ​There​ ​was​ ​such​ ​brilliant​ ​momentum​ ​around​​that.​​Because​​of​​the​​way​​the​​game​
       ​ended it all just goes out the window.​


​Jake​ ​expands​ ​on​ ​the​ ​notion​​that​​sport​​may​​be​​problematic,​​recognising​​that​​a​​fundamental​
​issue in terms of equality and diversity within sport begins with corporate buy-in:​


       ​…within​​the​​sport​​sector,​​it’s​​just​​not​​representative​​of​​the​​population​​at​​all.​​We​
       ​just​ ​don’t​ ​have​ ​the​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​around​ ​the​ ​table…​ ​especially​ ​so​ ​at​
       ​leadership​​level,​​still​​being​​run​​by​​White,​​middle​​class,​​straight,​​men...​​struggling​
       ​to​ ​see​ ​past​ ​maybe​ ​their​ ​own​ ​privilege​ ​or​ ​maybe​ ​their​ ​own​ ​kind​ ​of​ ​lived​
       ​experiences,​ ​thinking​ ​they​ ​are​ ​doing​ ​a​ ​good​ ​job​ ​when​ ​actually​ ​they​ ​could​ ​take​
       ​more of an expansive viewpoint.​


​Furthermore,​ ​Amy​ ​believes​ ​that​ ​"sport​ ​is​ ​led​ ​by​ ​people​ ​who​ ​are​ ​super​ ​passionate​ ​about​
​sport,"​​which​​may​​lead​​to​​problems​​in​​the​​areas​​of​​EDI​​since​​those​​who​​are​​passionate​​about​
​the​​game​​do​​not​​want​​to​​see​​change​​and​​struggle​​to​​understand​​the​​flaws​​within​​their​​sport.​
​She​​found​​that​​bringing​​in​​individuals​​from​​outside​​of​​sport​​had​​a​​powerful​​effect​​since​​they​
​could​ ​see​ ​what​ ​needed​ ​to​ ​be​ ​done​ ​and​ ​were​ ​not​ ​opposed​ ​to​ ​making​ ​the​ ​necessary​
​adjustments.​​For​​example,​​Amy​​argued​​that​​although​​"true​​cricket​​people​​got​​a​​little​​worried​


                                                               ​129​
​about​ ​the​ ​number​ ​of​ ​non-cricketers​ ​coming​ ​into​ ​the​ ​business,"​ ​she​ ​added​ ​that​ ​it​ ​was​
​"actually​ ​those​ ​attitudes​ ​and​ ​behaviours​​that​​fundamentally​​change​​things​​as​​well."​​On​​the​
​whole,​ ​both​ ​Jake​ ​and​ ​Amy​ ​have​​highlighted​​the​​need​​for​​corporations​​to​​be​​more​​inclusive​
​and​ ​have​ ​greater​ ​diversity;​ ​nonetheless,​ ​the​ ​general​ ​consensus​ ​was​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​has​ ​“a​
​wonderful​ ​opportunity​ ​to​ ​make​ ​the​ ​game​ ​better​ ​and​ ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​wider​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​society”​
​(Craig - EDI Consultant).​


​Addressing social issues through sport​


​Although​​sport​​can​​be​​problematic​​and​​provides​​a​​platform​​in​​which​​individuals​​can​​express​
​their​ ​discriminatory​ ​views,​ ​Craig​ ​reiterated​​that​​sport​​can​​provide​​a​​large​​platform​​in​​which​
​to​ ​bring​ ​about​ ​conversations,​ ​arguing​ ​that​ ​“we​ ​use​ ​the​ ​badge​​of​​(club​​name)​​to​​talk​​about​
​the diversity and inclusion”. On this note, Emily (EDI Manager) agreed:​


       ​…sport​ ​brings​ ​conversations​ ​about​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​to​ ​people​ ​who​ ​never​
       ​would have been exposed to them ever before.​


​As​ ​a​ ​result,​ ​we​ ​can​ ​acknowledge​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​offers​ ​an​ ​opportunity​ ​to​ ​highlight​​social​​issues​
​and​​bring​​them​​to​​the​​forefront​​of​​public​​awareness​​for​​meaningful​​discussion.​​The​​following​
​point​ ​from​ ​Craig​​highlights​​the​​profound​​influence​​of​​football​​on​​society,​​suggesting​​that​​its​
​impact​ ​extends​ ​beyond​ ​being​ ​merely​ ​a​ ​mirror​​of​​societal​​values​​and​​behaviours.​​Instead,​​it​
​positions​​football​​as​​a​​driving​​force​​that​​shapes​​societal​​norms,​​attitudes,​​and​​interactions.​​By​
​emphasising​ ​the​​vast​​participation​​and​​viewership,​​Craig​​recognises​​football’s​​central​​role​​in​
​society and its potential to influence and address broader societal issues.​


       ​14.1​ ​million​ ​people​ ​play​ ​football​ ​in​ ​England,​ ​on​ ​a​ ​regular​ ​basis​ ​and​ ​you’ve​ ​got​
       ​hundreds​ ​of​ ​thousands​ ​of​ ​fans​ ​going​ ​to​ ​games​ ​week​ ​in,​ ​week​ ​out,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​
       ​watching​​it​​on​​TV.​​We​​often​​say​​that​​football​​is​​a​​reflection​​of​​society,​​but​​actually​
       ​I think that society is a reflection of football. (Craig)​


​As​ ​noted​ ​in​ ​the​ ​previous​ ​theme,​​a​​number​​of​​interviewees​​emphasised​​the​​need​​for​​a​​safe​
​space​ ​in​ ​which​ ​people​ ​are​ ​able​ ​to​ ​have​ ​discussions​ ​regarding​ ​discrimination.​ ​Emily​


                                                            ​130​
​recognised​ ​that​ ​“sport​ ​has​ ​become​ ​the​ ​safe​ ​space​​and​​maybe​​the​​space​​where​​we​​can​​get​
​the​ ​messages​ ​out”.​ ​Darren​ ​(Initiative​ ​Advisor)​ ​concurs,​ ​believing​ ​that​ ​sport,​ ​specifically​
​football, has the potential to “act as an amplifier”.​


​Furthermore,​ ​MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin​ ​(2018)​ ​discovered​ ​that​ ​via​ ​sports-based​ ​initiatives,​
​young​ ​people​ ​gained​ ​the​ ​skills​ ​necessary​ ​to​ ​engage​​in​​positive​​conversations​​about​​racism.​
​They​ ​concluded​ ​that​ ​learning​ ​via​ ​sports​ ​gives​ ​a​ ​favourable​ ​setting​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​have​ ​these​
​early​​dialogues​​about​​tough​​subjects,​​emphasising​​that,​​while​​racism​​is​​a​​general​​concern,​​if​
​initial​ ​conversations​ ​can​ ​take​ ​place​ ​in​ ​particular​ ​disciplines,​ ​progressive​ ​change​ ​is​​possible.​
​This​ ​sentiment​ ​was​ ​echoed​​by​​a​​number​​of​​the​​interviewees;​​for​​example,​​Keagan​​believed​
​that:​


          ​…I​ ​guess​ ​the​ ​general​ ​principle​ ​is​ ​if…​ ​whatever​ ​the​ ​issue​ ​is,​ ​if​ ​you​ ​bring​ ​people​
          ​together​ ​-​ ​and​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​a​ ​good​ ​way​ ​to​ ​have​ ​conversations​ ​and​ ​really​ ​engage​
          ​through football - then you can probably overcome most, most issues.​


​In​​today’s​​society,​​it​​is​​widely​​recognised​​that​​athletes​​can​​utilise​​their​​platforms​​to​​promote​
​social​ ​change​ ​(Dixon​ ​et​ ​al.,​ ​2016).​ ​Amy,​ ​who​ ​incorporates​ ​symbolic​ ​initiatives​ ​within​ ​her​
​organisation,​ ​highlighted​ ​that​ ​when​ ​athletes​ ​use​ ​their​ ​platforms​ ​to​ ​discuss​ ​and​ ​educate​
​others​​about​​the​​history​​of​​discrimination,​​the​​initiative​​is​​more​​effective.​​She​​explained​​that​
​this​ ​approach​ ​not​ ​only​ ​stimulates​ ​conversation​ ​but​ ​also​ ​“increases​ ​awareness​ ​in​ ​wider​
​society​​by​​actively​​and​​positively​​supporting​​people​​who​​have​​historically​​felt​​marginalised”.​
​Therefore,​ ​sporting​ ​organisations,​ ​events,​ ​competitions,​ ​and​ ​athletes,​ ​when​ ​utilised​
​effectively, are key stakeholders with the potential to drive social change.​


​Sport and partnerships​


​The​ ​sporting​ ​industry​ ​is​ ​experiencing​ ​continuous​ ​growth,​ ​with​ ​its​ ​value​​estimated​​to​​reach​
​over​​$440​​billion​​in​​2020​​and​​projected​​to​​exceed​​$506​​billion​​in​​2024.​​This​​expanding​​sector​
​encompasses​ ​a​ ​wide​ ​array​ ​of​​organisations,​​services,​​and​​resources​​(The​​Business​​Research​
​Company,​ ​2021;​ ​2024).​ ​Previous​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​Trenerry​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2012)​ ​emphasised​ ​the​
​importance​ ​of​ ​working​ ​alongside​ ​other​ ​organisations​ ​and​ ​working​ ​collaboratively,​ ​when​


                                                                 ​131​
​developing​ ​a​ ​successful​ ​initiative.​ ​By​ ​working​ ​within​ ​the​​sporting​​domain,​​partnerships​​can​
​be​ ​developed​ ​with​ ​organisations​ ​who​ ​have​ ​the​ ​ability​ ​to​ ​make​ ​change.​ ​It​ ​was​ ​evident​
​throughout​ ​the​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​process​​that​ ​interviewees​​had​​developed​​partnerships​​with​
​other​ ​individuals,​ ​organisations,​ ​businesses​ ​or​ ​charities,​ ​which​​played​​a​​crucial​​role​​in​​their​
​success.​ ​Amy​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​her​​initiative​​was​​developed​​outside​​of​​sport​​and​​brought​​into​
​the​ ​sector.​ ​The​ ​ability​ ​of​ ​stakeholders​ ​and​ ​organisations​​within​​the​​sports​​field​​to​​generate​
​funds​ ​and​ ​raise​ ​awareness​ ​among​ ​fans​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​her​ ​work​ ​and​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​success.​
​Moreover,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​not​ ​only​ ​the​ ​money​ ​generated​ ​by​ ​other​ ​organisations​ ​within​ ​sport​ ​that​ ​is​
​beneficial,​​but​​also​​the​​wealth​​of​​knowledge​​provided​​by​​external​​partners,​​which​​is​​essential​
​for its success.​


​Theme 4 - First-hand experiences​


​The​ ​fourth​ ​theme​ ​is​ ​entitled​ ​‘​first-hand​ ​experiences​’;​ ​the​ ​general​ ​consensus​ ​from​ ​the​
​interviewees​ ​stressed​ ​that​ ​hearing​ ​first-hand​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​stories​ ​are​ ​critical​ ​to​ ​any​
​anti-discrimination​ ​initiative's​​effectiveness.​​By​​integrating​​and​​connecting​​with​​members​​of​
​groups​ ​who​ ​have​ ​faced​ ​hostility​ ​and​ ​abuse,​ ​individuals​ ​can​ ​build​ ​relationships​ ​and​ ​gain​ ​a​
​deeper​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​their​ ​culture​ ​and​ ​experiences.​ ​In​ ​this​ ​regard,​ ​the​ ​sub-themes​​are​
​labelled​ ​as​ ​‘​importance​ ​of​ ​storytelling​’​,​ ​‘interacting​ ​with​ ​and​ ​integrating​ ​the​ ​marginalised​
​community’​​and ‘​relatability​’​.​


​Importance of storytelling​


​In​​societies​​where​​prejudice​​and​​exclusion​​are​​frequent,​​both​​CRT​​and​​HebCrit​​(Rubin,​​2020)​
​emphasise​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​ ​storytelling.​ ​In​ ​particular,​ ​Rubin's​ ​(2020)​ ​fifth​ ​tenet,​ ​named​ ​‘Jewish​
​personal​ ​stories​ ​have​ ​value’,​ ​discusses​ ​how​ ​stories​ ​help​ ​us​ ​better​ ​comprehend​ ​Jewish​
​people's​ ​life​ ​narratives​ ​and​ ​lived​ ​experiences.​ ​By​ ​repeating​ ​these​ ​stories,​ ​people​ ​can​​learn​
​about​ ​the​ ​oppression​ ​that​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​has​ ​faced​ ​and​ ​become​ ​better​ ​educated​
​through​ ​this.​ ​Warren,​ ​whose​ ​organisation​ ​is​ ​dedicated​ ​to​​combating​​antisemitism,​​stated​​a​
​key strength is the interaction between supporters and Jewish individuals:​




                                                           ​132​
       ​…meeting​​Jewish​​people​​living​​in​​the​​city​​and​​supporting​​the​​same​​club​​as​​them…​
       ​who​ ​tell​ ​them​​what​​it​​actually​​means​​when​​they​​hear​​in​​the​​stadium​​thousands​
       ​of​​people​​singing​​“Jews​​to​​the​​gas,​​Jews​​to​​the​​gas”​​while​​remembering​​their​​own​
       ​family dying in the concentration camps.​


​This​ ​quote​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​telling​ ​stories​ ​to​ ​help​ ​individuals​ ​gain​ ​a​ ​better​
​understanding​ ​of​ ​how​ ​their​ ​comments​ ​can​ ​impact​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​By​ ​sharing​
​personal​ ​stories,​ ​Jewish​ ​individuals​ ​help​ ​others​ ​understand​ ​the​ ​real-life​ ​consequences​ ​of​
​such​ ​hate,​ ​fostering​ ​empathy​​and​​connection.​​Additionally,​​it​​emphasises​​how​​marginalised​
​communities​ ​continue​ ​to​ ​face​ ​hostility​ ​even​ ​in​ ​spaces​ ​meant​ ​for​ ​unity,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​sports​
​stadiums,​ ​reinforcing​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​broader​ ​societal​ ​change.​ ​By​ ​sharing​ ​personal​ ​stories,​
​individuals​ ​can​ ​form​ ​a​ ​stronger​ ​connection​ ​to​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​gain​ ​a​ ​deeper​
​understanding of the challenges faced by marginalised communities:​


       ​The​​most​​important​​thing​​is​​that​​it​​absolutely​​needs​​to​​be​​informed,​​every​​single​
       ​time,​​by​​Jewish​​people​​and​​experts​​on​​the​​Jewish​​community​​and​​antisemitism…​
       ​it’s​ ​just​ ​really​ ​important​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​informed​​by​​those​​people​​with​​personal​​lived​
       ​experiences. (Warren - EDI Consultant)​


​This​ ​quote​ ​from​ ​Warren,​ ​emphasises​ ​the​ ​significance​ ​of​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​the​ ​voices​ ​of​ ​those​
​who​ ​are​ ​directly​ ​affected​ ​by​ ​the​ ​issue​ ​are​ ​central​ ​to​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​ensuring​ ​authenticity,​
​relevance,​ ​and​ ​sensitivity​ ​in​ ​its​ ​approach.​ ​By​ ​prioritising​ ​these​ ​voices,​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​can​ ​be​
​more​ ​effective​ ​in​ ​addressing​ ​the​ ​complexities​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​its​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​the​
​community.​ ​Warren's​ ​organisation​ ​is​ ​not​ ​the​ ​only​ ​initiative​ ​that​ ​uses​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​to​
​educate individuals and combat discrimination:​


       ​We​ ​were​ ​very,​ ​very​ ​lucky​ ​to​ ​have​​an​​83-year-old​​lady​​at​​that​​time​​being​​part​​of​
       ​our​ ​team.​ ​She​ ​has​ ​a​ ​Jewish​ ​background,​ ​Jewish​ ​family​ ​history…​ ​also​ ​history​ ​of​
       ​people​ ​being​ ​murdered​ ​during​ ​the​ ​Shoah​ ​[the​ ​Holocaust​ ​in​ ​Hebrew]...​​she​​was​
       ​really​​able​​to​​confront​​those​​guys​​with​​the​​pain​​she​​feels​​when​​she​​hears​​things​
       ​like that. (Darren - Initiative Advisor)​




                                                             ​133​
​Alongside Warren and Darren, Craig also used first-hand stories to educate the public:​


         ​…one​​of​​the​​most​​important​​elements​​for​​me​​of​​education​​is​​about…​​individuals​
         ​hearing​ ​first-hand​ ​from​ ​people​ ​who​ ​are​ ​affected​ ​by​ ​antisemitism.​ ​There​ ​is​
         ​nothing​ ​that​ ​I​ ​say​ ​in​ ​an​​education​​session​​that​​has​​as​​much​​impact​​as​​hearing​
         ​from​ ​somebody​ ​who​ ​has​ ​either​ ​been​ ​directly​ ​affected​ ​by​ ​antisemitism​
         ​themselves​​or​​has,​​you​​know,​​relatives,​​grandparents,​​parents​​who​​experienced​
         ​the​​atrocities​​of​​the​​Holocaust,​​for​​example.​​Because​​you​​can't​​argue​​with​​that.​
         ​(Craig)​


​Both​​Darren​​and​​Craig​​have​​emphasised​​that​​hearing​​personal​​stories​​can​​be​​more​​impactful​
​in​ ​educating​ ​people,​ ​as​ ​those​ ​directly​ ​affected​ ​are​ ​able​ ​to​ ​share​ ​their​ ​own​ ​experiences.​
​According​​to​​Catherine,​​the​​role​​of​​individuals​​in​​the​​EDI​​sector​​is​​"to​​amplify​​their​​personal​
​voices​​to​​connect​​with​​the​​audience"​​through​​first-hand​​accounts.​​In​​conclusion,​​the​​experts​
​agreed​​that​​when​​people​​hear​​the​​stories​​of​​marginalised​​communities,​​they​​are​​more​​likely​
​to engage, leading to a deeper understanding and more effective education.​


​Interacting with and integrating the marginalised community​


​Research​ ​by​ ​Hassan​ ​and​ ​Telford​ ​(2014)​ ​and​ ​Leitner​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2014)​ ​found​ ​that​ ​integrating​
​marginalised​ ​or​ ​differing​ ​communities​ ​together​ ​reduced​ ​anti-discriminatory​ ​attitudes.​
​Keagan​ ​retold​ ​the​​story​​of​​when​​a​​fan's​​racist​​attitudes​​and​​viewpoints​​changed​​once​​being​
​integrated with the community, he previously made racist comments towards:​


       ​…so​ ​after​​he​​made​​racist​​gestures,​​he​​then​​worked​​on​​a​​weekly​​basis​​with​​Black​
       ​and​​Asian​​coaches​​and​​actually​​became​​one​​of​​the​​most​​active​​people​​within​​that​
       ​group...​ ​So,​ ​there​ ​are​ ​interventions,​ ​when…​​you​​know,​​just​​really​​just​​through,​​I​
       ​think, where you use sport to bring people together.​


​Keagan​​further​​explains​​that​​individuals​​who​​have​​not​​engaged​​with​​specific​​groups​​are​​likely​
​unaware​ ​of​ ​cultural​ ​differences​ ​and​ ​may​ ​hold​ ​"unpleasant​ ​views".​ ​By​ ​integrating​ ​these​
​communities,​ ​people​ ​can​ ​learn​ ​about​ ​the​ ​misconceptions​ ​and​ ​beliefs​ ​society​ ​has​ ​instilled​


                                                          ​134​
​over​ ​time.​ ​Similarly,​ ​Craig​ ​argued​ ​that​ ​fostering​ ​community​ ​integration​ ​helps​ ​in​ ​building​
​meaningful connections:​


       ​The​ ​women's​ ​squad​ ​went​ ​out​ ​to​ ​Israel​ ​and​ ​(​club​ ​name)​ ​Women​​played​​against​
       ​the​ ​Israeli​ ​women's​ ​national​ ​team,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​a​ ​great​ ​sort​ ​of…​ ​you​ ​know,​ ​way​​of​
       ​building​ ​relationships​ ​and​ ​building​ ​bridges,​ ​and​ ​starting​ ​to​ ​understand​​some​​of​
       ​the cultural issues.​


​Craig​ ​discovered​ ​that​ ​through​ ​combining​ ​groups,​ ​people​ ​had​ ​a​ ​better​ ​grasp​ ​of​​the​​cultural​
​distinctions​ ​between​ ​them.​ ​His​ ​job​ ​also​ ​included​ ​assisting​ ​offenders​ ​who​ ​had​ ​made​
​antisemitic​ ​remarks​ ​during​ ​sports​ ​events.​ ​Offenders​ ​had​ ​the​ ​chance​ ​to​ ​meet​ ​with​ ​Jewish​
​individuals​ ​during​ ​these​ ​educational​ ​workshops.​ ​One​​poignant​​example​​was​​when​​a​​Jewish​
​participant​ ​explained​ ​that​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​was​ ​one​ ​that​ ​their​ ​grandparents​ ​had​ ​heard​​while​
​being​​lined​​up​​to​​be​​sent​​to​​the​​gas​​chambers​​during​​the​​Holocaust.​​This​​personal​​testimony​
​highlighted​ ​the​ ​deep​ ​emotional​ ​and​ ​historical​ ​weight​ ​of​ ​such​ ​language,​ ​helping​ ​offenders​
​realise​​the​​real-world​​consequences​​of​​their​​actions​​and​​the​​lasting​​trauma​​that​​such​​words​
​continue​ ​to​ ​inflict​ ​on​ ​Jewish​​communities.​​Through​​these​​interactions,​​Craig​​found​​that​​the​
​offenders​ ​gained​ ​a​ ​more​​empathetic​​understanding​​of​​the​​impact​​of​​their​​behaviour,​​which​
​was​ ​crucial​ ​in​ ​changing​ ​their​ ​attitudes​ ​and​ ​preventing​​further​​discrimination.​​His​​work​​also​
​involved​ ​“bringing​ ​holocaust​ ​survivors​ ​to​ ​meet​ ​with​ ​players,​ ​fans​ ​and​ ​staff…so​ ​they​ ​can​
​understand​ ​more​ ​about​ ​historical​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​how​ ​it​ ​aligns​ ​with​ ​modern​ ​day​
​antisemitism.”​​Craig​​noted​​that​​when​​offenders​​were​​integrated​​and​​had​​the​​opportunity​​to​
​meet​ ​individuals​ ​from​ ​marginalised​ ​communities​ ​and​ ​hear​ ​their​ ​firsthand​ ​accounts,​ ​they​
​began​​to​​change​​their​​perspectives.​​This​​emphasised​​the​​value​​of​​both​​first-hand​​storytelling,​
​as​ ​noted​ ​in​ ​Rubin’s​ ​(2020)​​theory​​of​​HebCrit,​​and​​integrating​​marginalised​​communities.​​By​
​including​ ​individuals​ ​from​ ​the​ ​marginalised​ ​community​ ​into​ ​an​ ​initiative,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​possible​ ​to​
​provide​ ​a​ ​face​ ​to​ ​history,​ ​which​ ​encourages​ ​individuals​ ​to​ ​learn​ ​and​ ​develop​ ​an​ ​effective​
​understanding of history (The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, n.d.).​




                                                            ​135​
​Relatability​


​In​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport,​​it​​is​​recognised​​that​​athletes​​can​​be​​role​​models​​for​​young​​individuals,​
​inspiring​​and​​motivating​​them​​to​​participate​​in​​sport​​(Adriaanse​​and​​Crosswhite,​​2008;​​Payne​
​et​​al.,​​2003).​​What​​research​​has​​also​​shown​​is​​for​​those​​marginalised​​individuals​​having​​a​​role​
​model​​who​​is​​relatable​​to​​themselves​​increases​​their​​involvement​​within​​sport​​(Vescio,​​Wilde​
​and​ ​Crosswhite,​ ​2005).​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​when​ ​exploring​ ​it​ ​in​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​education​ ​and​
​identity,​ ​research​ ​from​ ​Keane,​ ​Heinz​ ​and​ ​Lynch​ ​(2020)​ ​reinforce​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​having​
​something​​to​​relate​​to.​​Their​​research​​found​​that​​children​​from​​lower​​socio-economic​​groups​
​expressed​ ​a​ ​desire​ ​for​ ​teachers​ ​they​ ​could​ ​relate​ ​to.​ ​To​ ​educate​ ​young​ ​children,​ ​Matthew​
​uses​​a​​book​​which​​was​​“written​​by​​a​​local​​author​​and​​she​​based​​it​​on​​prejudices​​that​​her​​son​
​had​​survived…​​it​​was​​written​​exactly​​based​​on​​kids”.​​This​​meant​​that​​not​​only​​was​​it​​informed​
​by​​the​​community,​​but​​was​​also​​relatable​​to​​other​​students​​reading​​the​​book.​​In​​addition,​​by​
​using​ ​sport​ ​as​ ​the​ ​subject​ ​matter​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​anti-discriminatory​ ​behaviours,​ ​the​
​stories​ ​can​ ​become​ ​more​ ​relatable​ ​to​ ​those​ ​who​ ​are​ ​interested​ ​in​ ​and​ ​passionate​ ​about​
​sport,​ ​most​ ​specifically​ ​football.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​he​ ​also​ ​stated​ ​that​ ​“kids​ ​can​ ​identify​ ​with​ ​it​
​because​ ​it's​ ​something​ ​that​ ​they’ve​ ​been​ ​exposed​ ​to”.​ ​Amy​ ​similarly​ ​highlighted​ ​the​
​importance of making initiatives relatable:​


       ​…it​ ​makes​​a​​huge​​difference​​there…​​when​​somebody​​feels​​marginalised​​and​​not​
       ​accepted,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​also​ ​small​ ​gestures​ ​that​ ​work…​ ​LGBT+​​people​​will​​have​​seen​​and​
       ​feel​​appreciated.​​Sometimes​​a​​small​​gesture​​done​​in​​the​​right​​way​​can​​have​​a​​big​
       ​impact​ ​directly​ ​for​ ​the​ ​group​ ​that​ ​feels​ ​marginalised…​ ​It's​ ​about​ ​actively​ ​and​
       ​positively supporting people who have historically felt marginalised.​


​Not​ ​only​ ​will​ ​making​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​relatable​ ​assist​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​and​ ​entice​ ​people​ ​into​ ​the​
​resource​ ​-​ ​it​ ​will​ ​also​ ​make​ ​them​ ​feel​ ​more​ ​accepted​ ​and​ ​appreciated.​ ​As​ ​Amy​ ​highlights,​
​when​ ​the​ ​material​ ​resonates​ ​with​ ​individuals,​ ​they​ ​feel​ ​valued​ ​and​ ​seen,​ ​which​ ​can​
​significantly​ ​enhance​ ​their​ ​learning​ ​experience.​ ​Those​ ​who​ ​are​ ​members​​of​​a​​marginalised​
​group​ ​will​ ​then​ ​recognise​ ​and​ ​believe​ ​that​ ​organisations​ ​are​ ​working​ ​to​ ​improve​ ​their​
​awareness and knowledge of their community.​




                                                              ​136​
​This​ ​theme​ ​is​ ​closely​ ​linked​ ​to​ ​the​ ​previously​ ​mentioned​ ​sub-theme​ ​of​ ​‘trusted​ ​leader,’​ ​as​
​highlighted​ ​by​ ​Amy.​ ​She​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​the​ ​Imam​ ​played​ ​a​ ​crucial​ ​role​ ​in​ ​encouraging​ ​young​
​Muslim​ ​children​ ​to​ ​become​ ​more​ ​involved​ ​in​ ​sport.​​It​​could​​be​​argued​​that​​the​​Imam,​​as​​a​
​relatable​ ​figure​ ​to​ ​these​ ​children,​ ​was​ ​key​ ​in​ ​fostering​ ​their​ ​interest​ ​and​ ​participation​ ​in​
​sport.​ ​His​ ​position​ ​within​ ​the​ ​community​ ​and​ ​his​ ​ability​ ​to​ ​connect​ ​with​ ​the​​children​​on​​a​
​personal​​level​​likely​​made​​them​​feel​​more​​comfortable​​and​​motivated​​to​​engage​​in​​activities​
​they might not have otherwise considered.​


​Theme 5 - Structuring subject content​


​The​ ​final​ ​theme​ ​centres​ ​on​ ​the​ ​interviewees'​ ​argument​ ​that​ ​clearly​ ​defining​ ​the​ ​subject​
​matter​​is​​essential​​for​​effectively​​educating​​people.​​This​​section​​will​​therefore​​detail​​the​​key​
​structural​ ​elements​ ​that​ ​experts​ ​believe​ ​should​ ​be​ ​included​ ​in​ ​the​ ​project.​ ​This​ ​theme​ ​is​
​divided​ ​into​ ​three​ ​sub-themes,​ ​namely​ ​‘​broad-to-narrow​ ​structure​’,​ ​‘​educating​ ​about​
​Judaism and antisemitism​’,​​and​​‘​bystander intervention​’​.​


​Broad-to-narrow structure​


​During​ ​the​ ​interview​ ​process,​ ​it​ ​became​ ​clear​ ​that​ ​when​ ​creating​ ​an​​educational​​initiative,​
​the​​central​​subject​​matter​​-​​which​​in​​this​​case​​would​​be​​antisemitism​​-​​should​​not​​be​​the​​only​
​form​ ​of​ ​discrimination​ ​discussed,​ ​and​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​critical​ ​to​ ​discuss​​discrimination​​as​​a​​whole​
​before​ ​focusing​ ​on​ ​the​ ​specific​ ​issue​ ​at​ ​hand.​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​Naveen’s​ ​(Head​ ​of​ ​Education)​
​initiative​ ​begins​​by​​having​​a​​broad​​conversation​​about​​discrimination,​​in​​order​​to​​“train​​and​
​learn​​all​​forms​​of​​discrimination”;​​it​​is​​then​​narrowed​​down​​to​​his​​central​​focus.​​Like​​Naveen,​
​Darren's​​(Initiative​​Advisor)​​initiative​​also​​has​​a​​narrow​​focus,​​which​​he​​states​​is​​the​​greatest​
​strength​​of​​their​​initiative.​​He​​explains​​that​​the​​project’s​​concentrated​​approach​​to​​a​​specific​
​form​ ​of​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​in​ ​European​ ​football​ ​allows​ ​for​ ​a​ ​more​ ​targeted​ ​and​ ​effective​
​strategy. As he puts it:​


       ​…it​ ​is​ ​a​ ​very​ ​narrow​ ​look​ ​at​ ​a​ ​specific​ ​form​ ​of​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​in​ ​European​
       ​football,​​which​​I​​would​​argue,​​is​​one​​of​​the​​strengths…​​simultaneously,​​one​​of​​the​
       ​limitations​ ​of​ ​the​ ​project,​ ​although​ ​I’m​ ​sort​ ​of​ ​convinced​ ​that​ ​the​ ​narrowness​


                                                            ​137​
       ​provides​​more​​strength​​than​​limitations,​​because​​it​​lets​​you​​work​​for​​more…​​sort​
       ​of, focused and to the point then.​

​While​​Darren​​acknowledges​​that​​the​​narrow​​focus​​could​​be​​seen​​as​​a​​limitation,​​he​​strongly​
​believes​ ​that​ ​it​ ​brings​ ​greater​ ​strength​ ​to​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​allowing​ ​for​ ​a​ ​more​ ​focused​ ​and​
​precise​ ​approach.​ ​This​ ​emphasis​ ​on​ ​specificity​ ​ensures​ ​that​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​can​ ​tackle​ ​the​
​problem​​at​​hand​​more​​effectively.​​However,​​this​​narrow​​focus​​also​​presents​​the​​challenge​​of​
​potentially​ ​overlooking​ ​broader​ ​issues​ ​of​ ​discrimination.​ ​Therefore,​ ​in​ ​line​ ​with​ ​Naveen’s​
​comment​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​for​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​to​ ​begin​ ​with​ ​a​ ​broader​ ​discussion​ ​that​
​encompasses​​various​​forms​​of​​discrimination,​​providing​​context​​and​​a​​broader​​understanding​
​of​ ​the​ ​issue.​ ​From​​there,​​the​​initiative​​can​​narrow​​its​​focus​​to​​the​​specific​​topic​​at​​hand.​​By​
​doing​​so,​​it​​creates​​a​​framework​​that​​not​​only​​addresses​​the​​immediate​​issue​​but​​also​​helps​
​individuals understand how it fits within the wider context of society.​

​Matthew​ ​made​ ​a​ ​similar​ ​point​ ​when​ ​addressing​ ​other​ ​forms​ ​of​​discrimination,​​stating​​that​
​it's​​necessary​​to​​"talk​​about​​them​​but​​in​​relation​​to​​other​​people...​​so​​we​​don't​​single​​them​
​out​ ​as​ ​a​ ​special​ ​case".​ ​Matthew's​ ​perspective​ ​emphasises​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​discussing​
​discrimination​ ​within​ ​a​ ​broader​ ​context,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​no​ ​group​ ​is​ ​seen​ ​as​ ​uniquely​
​victimised​​or​​isolated.​​While​​it​​is​​crucial​​to​​address​​prejudice​​in​​relation​​to​​other​​marginalised​
​populations,​ ​an​ ​initiative​ ​must​ ​also​ ​clearly​ ​highlight​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​topic​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​people​ ​fully​
​understand​​the​​specific​​issues​​at​​hand.​​Balancing​​a​​broader​​context​​with​​a​​clear​​focus​​allows​
​for​ ​a​ ​deeper,​ ​more​ ​inclusive​ ​approach,​ ​addressing​ ​the​ ​key​ ​issue​ ​while​ ​acknowledging​ ​the​
​interconnected nature of various forms of discrimination.​


​As​ ​discussed​ ​in​ ​the​ ​literature​ ​review,​ ​MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin​ ​(2018)​ ​explore​ ​an​​educational​
​initiative​ ​RISE,​ ​who​ ​provide​ ​workshops​ ​which​ ​explore​ ​and​ ​educate​ ​individuals​ ​on​ ​racism.​
​Over​ ​the​ ​course​ ​of​ ​ten​ ​weeks​ ​students​ ​completed​ ​ten​ ​modules.​ ​The​ ​first​ ​initial​ ​topic​ ​was​
​titled​ ​“understanding​ ​our​ ​identities”,​ ​and​ ​then​ ​it​ ​continued​ ​to​ ​gradually​ ​bring​ ​about​
​conversations​ ​and​ ​discussion​ ​on​​inclusion​​and​​equality,​​and​​then​​racism​​through​​a​​range​​of​
​modules.​ ​Overall,​ ​both​ ​literature​ ​and​ ​data​ ​from​ ​the​ ​interviews​ ​found​ ​that​ ​it​​is​​essential​​to​
​not​​only​​discuss​​the​​topic​​at​​hand,​​but​​to​​frame​​the​​key​​topic​​around​​a​​broader​​conversation​
​on discrimination.​



                                                            ​138​
​Educating about Judaism and antisemitism​


​According​​to​​Beller​​(2015),​​the​​word​​antisemitism​​is​​still​​widely​​misunderstood.​​Nate​​agrees​
​with​ ​Beller​ ​(2015)​ ​in​ ​that​ ​certain​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​general​ ​public​ ​are​ ​unable​ ​to​ ​recognise​
​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​have​ ​a​ ​limited​ ​grasp​ ​of​ ​it,​ ​arguing​ ​that​ ​“I​ ​think​ ​it​ ​comes​ ​back​ ​to​ ​a​ ​fairly​
​basic​​thing:​​people​​don’t​​understand​​what​​antisemitism​​is”.​​The​​interviews​​with​​participants​
​from​ ​Jewish​ ​charities​ ​and​ ​organisations​ ​identified​ ​key​ ​areas​ ​they​ ​considered​ ​essential​ ​for​
​educating​ ​others​ ​about​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Several​ ​of​ ​these​ ​areas​ ​align​ ​with​ ​Rubin's​ ​(2020)​ ​five​
​main​ ​tenets,​ ​which​ ​are​ ​regarded​ ​as​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​most​ ​important​ ​issues​ ​to​ ​address​ ​when​
​teaching about antisemitism.​


​Authors​ ​including​ ​Neuberger​ ​(2019)​ ​have​ ​highlighted​ ​key​ ​misconceptions​​about​​the​​Jewish​
​community,​​a​​phenomenon​​that​​also​​emerged​​in​​the​​interviews,​​especially​​with​​antisemitism​
​specialists.​ ​These​ ​interviews​ ​revealed​ ​that​ ​many​ ​misconceptions​ ​persist​ ​about​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community.​ ​According​ ​to​ ​Naveen,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​for​ ​people​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​both​ ​historical​
​prejudices​ ​and​ ​their​ ​continued​ ​relevance​ ​in​ ​today's​ ​culture.​ ​Nate​ ​agrees,​ ​stressing​ ​the​
​importance​​of​​educating​​people​​on​​what​​defines​​antisemitism​​and​​the​​potential​​harm​​it​​can​
​cause:​


       ​This​ ​idea​ ​that​ ​the​ ​Jews​ ​control​ ​the​ ​media,​ ​the​ ​Jews​ ​all​ ​overrepresented​ ​and​​in​
       ​politics​ ​and​ ​business,​ ​etc…​ ​all​ ​of​ ​that…​ ​there​ ​are​ ​lots​ ​of​ ​people​ ​who​ ​won't​
       ​understand​ ​why​ ​that​ ​is​ ​unacceptable.​ ​And​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​of​​‘what​​is​​antisemitism?’...​
       ​we need to educate that to start addressing the issues.​



​One​ ​of​ ​the​ ​most​ ​common​​preconceptions​​directed​​against​​the​​Jewish​​community​​is​​that​​of​
​power​​and​​wealth.​​According​​to​​Neuberger​​(2019),​​this​​is​​because​​Jews​​are​​depicted​​as​​being​
​overly​​strong,​​overly​​wealthy,​​or​​as​​part​​of​​capitalism's​​oppressor​​class.​​Furthermore,​​one​​of​
​Rubin's​ ​fundamental​ ​tenets​ ​(2020)​ ​was​ ​that​ ​Jewish​ ​political​ ​and​ ​economic​ ​strength​ ​is​
​overstated,​ ​emphasising​ ​the​ ​need​ ​of​ ​teaching​ ​this​ ​stereotype.​ ​Supporting​ ​Rubins​ ​(2020)​
​tenet​ ​and​ ​Nate's​ ​comment,​ ​was​ ​Naveen,​ ​who​ ​when​ ​conducting​ ​educational​ ​campaigns​
​believes​ ​it​ ​is​ ​critical​ ​to​ ​combat​ ​stereotypes​ ​and​ ​prejudices​ ​that​ ​people​ ​currently​ ​have,​



                                                                ​139​
​particularly the belief that Jews possess political and economic power.​

​Another​ ​of​ ​Rubin's​ ​(2020)​ ​five​ ​main​ ​tenets​ ​is​ ​that​ ​Jews​ ​continue​ ​to​ ​be​ ​oppressed​ ​and​
​discriminated​ ​against.​ ​Rubin​ ​(2020)​ ​recognises​ ​that​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​widespread​ ​belief​ ​that​ ​the​
​Jewish​ ​community​ ​is​ ​no​ ​longer​ ​persecuted;​ ​Catherine​ ​brought​ ​this​ ​to​ ​attention​ ​when​ ​she​
​discussed​ ​how​ ​antisemitism​ ​is​ ​seen​ ​as​ ​more​ ​of​ ​an​ ​underlying​ ​issue​ ​than​ ​other​ ​forms​ ​of​
​discrimination,​ ​resulting​ ​in​ ​the​ ​general​ ​public​ ​believing​ ​antisemitism​ ​is​ ​no​ ​longer​
​problematic.​ ​She​ ​also​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​need​ ​of​ ​individuals​ ​in​ ​society​ ​to​ ​understand​​unique​
​cultural​​variations.​​In​​particular,​​there​​are​​problems​​and​​issues​​within​​the​​Jewish​​community,​
​such​​as​​the​​perception​​that​​all​​Jews​​are​​White,​​which​​leads​​to​​invisibility​​and​​conflict​​(Rubin,​
​2020), which Catherine saw as having an influence.​


​Furthermore,​​there​​is​​a​​lot​​of​​debate​​concerning​​the​​usage​​of​​the​​term​​‘Yid’​​in​​the​​context​​of​
​sport,​ ​especially​ ​football​ ​(Poulton​ ​and​ ​Durell,​ ​2016).​ ​The​ ​term​ '​Yid'​ ​originated​ ​as​ ​a​
​non-derogatory​​word,​​meaning​​'Jew',​​originally​​used​​as​​a​​term​​of​​endearment.​​When​​used​​by​
​non-Jews,​ ​and​ ​said​ ​in​ ​English,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​usually​ ​considered​ ​a​ ​derogatory​ ​epithet​ ​used​ ​by​
​antisemites​​(Cloake​​and​​Fisher,​​2016;​​Poulton,​​2013).​​Catherine​​believes​​it​​is​​critical​​to​​teach​
​the​​term​​Yid​​and​​its​​applications,​​as​​well​​as​​to​​link​​and​​compare​​it​​to​​other​​race​​hate​​terms​​in​
​order​​to​​offer​​context.​​Matthews'​​educational​​project​​made​​it​​a​​point​​to​​inform​​pupils​​about​
​the​​use​​of​​race-hating​​language​​in​​the​​context​​of​​sectarianism.​​However,​​parents​​who​​did​​not​
​want​ ​their​ ​children​ ​to​ ​be​ ​exposed​​to​​this​​language​​found​​this​​to​​be​​an​​issue.​​Matthew​​was​
​able​ ​to​ ​resolve​ ​this​ ​issue​ ​by​ ​having​ ​open​ ​dialogues​ ​with​ ​the​ ​parents,​ ​emphasising​ ​the​
​importance of teaching this to young children.​


​Craig's​ ​job​ ​includes​ ​raising​ ​awareness​ ​in​ ​order​ ​to​ ​"understand​ ​what​ ​antisemitic​ ​behaviour​
​looks​ ​like...​ ​y​ ​word,​ ​gas​ ​chamber​ ​hissing​ ​sounds,​ ​and​​you​​know,​​Nazi​​salutes."​​When​​asked​
​about​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’,​ ​he​ ​replied​ ​that​ ​after​ ​being​ ​informed​ ​on​ ​its​ ​usage​ ​and​
​significance,​ ​individuals​ ​who​ ​attended​​educational​​programmes​​realised​​that​​"it's​​not​​just​​a​
​bit​ ​of​ ​banter."​ ​This​ ​is​ ​a​ ​positive​ ​observation​ ​in​ ​the​ ​sense​ ​that​ ​individuals​ ​who​ ​are​ ​more​
​knowledgeable​ ​about​ ​its​ ​use​ ​recognise​ ​the​ ​huge​ ​impact​ ​it​ ​may​ ​have​ ​on​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community,​ ​and​ ​as​ ​a​ ​result,​ ​it​ ​will​ ​help​ ​to​ ​limit​ ​its​ ​use​ ​during​ ​football​ ​games.​ ​However,​​In​
​2014,​ ​39%​ ​of​ ​non-Jewish​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​supporters​ ​and​ ​29%​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​Tottenham​



                                                              ​140​
​Hotspur​​fans​​said​​they​​use​​the​​term​​Yid​​as​​it​​was​​a​​part​​of​​their​​team's​​"history​​and​​identity".​
​Furthermore,​​Poulton's​​(2016)​​study​​revealed​​that​​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​fans​​use​​the​​name​​as​
​a​​term​​of​​pride​​and​​fondness​​to​​repel​​antisemitic​​criticism​​(Poulton,​​2016).​​This​​is​​supported​
​by​​Keagan​​who​​believes​​that​​“if​​people​​had​​a​​collective​​understanding​​of​​the​​word,​​it​​would​
​encourage people not to use it”.​


​This​ ​sub-theme​ ​has​ ​recognised​ ​the​ ​key​ ​topics​ ​that​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​addressed​ ​when​ ​teaching​
​about​ ​antisemitism.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​contributions​ ​from​ ​the​ ​interviewees​ ​have​
​supported​ ​Rubin’s​ ​(2020)​ ​theory​ ​known​ ​as​ ​HebCrit.​ ​These​ ​principles,​ ​in​ ​combination​ ​with​
​personal​ ​accounts​ ​of​ ​prejudice,​ ​would​ ​be​ ​critical​ ​in​ ​educating​ ​others​ ​about​​discrimination,​
​particularly antisemitism.​


​Bystander intervention​


​Bystander​ ​intervention​ ​is​ ​a​ ​useful​ ​technique​ ​that​ ​teaches​ ​people​ ​how​ ​to​​avoid​​violent​​and​
​unwanted​ ​behaviours​ ​(Cissner,​ ​2009).​ ​Furthermore,​ ​it​ ​enables​ ​people​ ​to​​become​​'assertive​
​bystanders'​ ​rather​ ​than​ '​passive​ ​bystanders'​ ​(Public​ ​Health​ ​England,​ ​2020).​ ​Assertive​
​onlookers​​are​​people​​who​​will​​confront​​the​​abuser​​while​​simultaneously​​soothing​​the​​victim​
​(Salmivalli​ ​et​ ​al​.,​ ​1996).​ ​Data​ ​from​ ​the​ ​interview​ ​transcripts​ ​stated​ ​that​ ​"It​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​to​
​teach​​the​​skills​​and​​tools​​to​​become​​upstanders​​and​​how​​to​​respond,"​​Naveen​​said.​​He​​also​
​emphasised​ ​the​ ​necessity​ ​of​ ​empowering​ ​young​ ​people​ ​in​ ​how​ ​to​ ​confront​ ​discriminatory​
​behaviour,​ ​with​ ​a​ ​particular​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​how​ ​to​ ​report​ ​it,​ ​by​ ​showcasing​ ​charities​ ​and​
​organisations​ ​that​ ​aim​​to​​find,​​punish,​​or​​educate​​individuals​​who​​use​​discriminatory​​words​
​or​ ​acts.​ ​Prior​ ​research​​by​​Cantor​​et​​al​.​​(2015)​​found​​that​​just​​19%​​of​​bystanders​​in​​a​​school​
​setting​​will​​intervene​​and​​take​​action.​​Nonetheless,​​Polanin​​et​​al.​​(2012)​​conducted​​a​​study​​of​
​12​ ​groups​​that​​participated​​in​​a​​bullying​​prevention​​programme​​to​​investigate​​the​​influence​
​on​ ​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​behaviour.​ ​It​ ​was​ ​discovered​ ​that​ ​the​​control​​groups,​​those​​who​
​underwent​ ​an​ ​intervention,​ ​exhibited​ ​more​ ​intervention​ ​behaviour​ ​and​ ​were​ ​thus​ ​more​
​inclined​ ​to​ ​act​ ​in​ ​bullying​ ​situations.​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result,​ ​both​ ​existing​ ​research​ ​and​ ​data​ ​from​​the​
​interviews​ ​have​ ​underlined​ ​the​ ​need​ ​of​ ​teachers​​and​​adults​​teaching​​young​​people​​how​​to​
​intervene or take action in the face of prejudice in an effective and safe manner.​
​In​​a​​sporting​​context,​​fans​​who​​attended​​educational​​sessions​​organised​​by​​Craig​​to​​increase​


                                                              ​141​
​their awareness of antisemitic behaviour were told to:​


       ​…think​​about​​how​​they​​may​​challenge​​their​​mates​​if​​they​​start​​to​​engage​​in​​that​
       ​(antisemitic)​ ​behaviour​ ​as​ ​well,​ ​and​ ​everyone​ ​has​ ​a​ ​role​ ​to​ ​play​ ​in​ ​creating​ ​an​
       ​inclusive game.​


​Craig​ ​emphasises​ ​the​ ​need​ ​of​ ​teaching​ ​people​ ​how​ ​to​ ​intervene​ ​when​ ​they​ ​encounter​
​antisemitic​ ​behaviour.​ ​This​ ​comment​ ​demonstrates​​an​​awareness​​of​​why​​it​​is​​so​​important,​
​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​the​ ​notion​ ​that​ ​if​ ​everyone​ ​is​ ​educated​ ​to​​be​​an​​active​​bystander,​​the​​game​​will​
​become​ ​more​ ​inclusive​ ​and​ ​inviting.​ ​However,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​note​ ​that​ ​this​ ​focus​ ​on​
​individual​ ​responsibility​ ​may​ ​oversimplify​ ​the​ ​complexity​ ​of​​tackling​​antisemitism​​in​​sports.​
​Simply​ ​encouraging​ ​fans​ ​to​ ​challenge​ ​their​ ​peers​ ​may​ ​not​ ​address​ ​deeper​ ​systemic​ ​issues,​
​such as entrenched cultural attitudes.​


​Applying insights to the development of an educational resource​


​This​​final​​subsection​​will​​explore​​how​​the​​themes​​identified​​throughout​​this​​chapter​​directly​
​influenced​ ​the​ ​design​ ​and​ ​development​ ​of​ ​the​ ​educational​ ​resource​ ​aimed​ ​at​ ​addressing​
​antisemitism​​in​​sports.​​When​​summarising​​his​​arguments,​​Craig​​emphasised​​his​​belief​​that​​a​
​successful​​sporting​​initiative​​includes​​a​​“direct​​educational​​training​​toolkit​​that​​you’ve​​got​​at​
​your​ ​disposal;​ ​to​ ​help​ ​you​ ​understand​ ​the​​issues,​​think​​about​​how​​it​​is​​relevant​​to​​you​​and​
​then​​put​​things​​in​​place​​to​​address​​it”.​​In​​other​​words,​​the​​initiative​​should​​equip​​people​​with​
​the​​knowledge,​​personal​​insight,​​and​​tools​​they​​need​​to​​effectively​​respond​​to​​and​​challenge​
​discrimination.​​With​​that​​in​​mind,​​the​​purpose​​of​​the​​current​​project​​is​​to​​provide:​​a​​resource​
​that​​can​​be​​made​​available​​to​​help​​people​​understand​​antisemitism,​​one​​that​​is​​relevant​​to​​a​
​specific​ ​audience,​ ​and​ ​one​ ​that​ ​can​ ​eventually​ ​help​ ​individuals​ ​learn​ ​about​ ​antisemitism,​
​alongside​ ​other​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination.​ ​As​ ​a​​result,​​the​​following​​section​​summarises​​how​
​each​ ​theme​ ​has​ ​shaped​ ​the​ ​design​ ​of​ ​the​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiative​ ​discussed​ ​in​ ​the​
​subsequent chapters of this thesis.​




                                                            ​142​
​Essential aspects of an initiative​


​With​​a​​rapid​​increase​​in​​antisemitic​​abuse​​seen​​in​​society​​(CST,​​2019;​​European​​Union​​Agency​
​for​ ​Fundamental​ ​Rights,​ ​2018),​ ​there​ ​is​​a​​need​​to​​educate​​young​​individuals​​to​​ensure​​that​
​the​ ​next​ ​generation​ ​hold​ ​less​ ​discriminatory​ ​views​ ​and​ ​are​ ​able​ ​to​​challenge​​antisemitism,​
​when​ ​needed.​ ​This​ ​supports​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin​ ​(2018)​ ​and​ ​Solomos​
​(2020)​ ​who​ ​previously​ ​explored​ ​educational​ ​initiatives​ ​on​ ​discrimination.​ ​Analysis​ ​of​ ​the​
​interviews​ ​highlighted​ ​that​ ​resources​ ​found​ ​that​ ​resources​ ​are​ ​essential​ ​when​ ​educating​
​individuals.​ ​Resources​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​means​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​draw​ ​people​ ​into​ ​the​ ​topic​ ​at​ ​hand​​as​
​highlighted​ ​by​​Lawley​​(2019)​​who​​explored​​the​​impact​​of​​Rainbow​​Laces.​​Therefore,​​for​​the​
​purpose​ ​of​ ​this​ ​research​​project​​a​​book​​(Appendix​​I)​​was​​created​​and​​was​​used​​as​​a​​way​​of​
​engaging​​individuals.​​In​​addition​​to​​the​​book's​​narrative,​​discussion​​points​​were​​provided​​so​
​that​ ​for​ ​each​ ​chapter​​individuals​​can​​reflect​​upon​​what​​they​​have​​read​​to​​stimulate​​greater​
​engagement,​​which​​previous​​symbolic​​based​​initiatives​​have​​been​​critiqued​​for​​(Bennett​​and​
​Jonsson,​​2017;​​Pedersen​​2005).​​A​​book​​was​​selected,​​as​​the​​data​​set​​reinforced​​that​​it​​should​
​be​​targeted​​at​​10-11​​year​​olds,​​as​​changing​​and​​challenging​​attitudes​​at​​a​​young​​age​​proves​
​easier​​than​​those​​who​​have​​had​​time​​to​​already​​develop​​their​​opinions​​and​​views.​​This​​is​​in​
​line​​with​​comments​​from​​Matthew,​​and​​also​​research​​from​​Jennett​​(2009).​​It​​was​​envisaged​
​that​ ​the​ ​planned​ ​initiative​ ​would​ ​have​ ​a​ ​positive​ ​impact​ ​upon​ ​young​ ​readers,​ ​which​ ​will​
​stimulate​ ​conversations​ ​around​ ​discrimination,​ ​most​ ​specifically​ ​antisemitism​ ​which​ ​will​
​subsequently help to educate them.​


​The environment​


​The​ ​discussion​ ​surrounding​ ​the​ ​second​ ​theme​ ​of​ '​the​ ​environment'​ ​emphasised​ ​the​
​importance​ ​of​ ​creating​ ​a​ ​safe​ ​space​ ​for​ ​individuals​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​in​ ​open​ ​conversations.​
​However,​​as​​Leonardo​​and​​Porter​​(2010)​​noted,​​it​​was​​crucial​​to​​consider​​who​​the​​safe​​space​
​was​ ​intended​ ​for​ ​during​ ​the​ ​development​ ​process.​ ​The​ ​research​ ​indicated​ ​that​ ​fostering​
​these​ ​open​ ​dialogues​ ​requires​ ​both​ ​a​ ​trusted​ ​individual​ ​and​ ​a​ ​comfortable,​ ​informal​
​environment.​​The​​need​​for​​a​​safe​​space,​​combined​​with​​considerations​​of​​age​​demographics,​
