​highlighted​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​delivering​ ​these​ ​initiatives​ ​within​ ​a​ ​school​ ​setting,​ ​which​ ​is​
​generally​ ​seen​ ​as​ ​a​ ​safe​ ​environment​ ​for​ ​most​ ​children.​ ​Teachers​ ​would​ ​serve​ ​as​ ​trusted​


                                                           ​143​
​facilitators,​ ​responsible​ ​for​ ​presenting​ ​the​ ​issue​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​within​ ​mainstream​
​classrooms.​​These​​teachers​​would​​have​​access​​to​​all​​relevant​​resources,​​including​​books​​and​
​any further educational materials, to support their efforts.​


​Sport as a conversational tool​


​Sport,​ ​as​ ​mentioned​ ​previously,​ ​is​ ​a​ ​platform​ ​for​ ​achieving​ ​social​​change​​that​​may​​be​​both​
​beneficial​ ​and​ ​harmful​ ​(Anderson​ ​and​ ​White,​ ​2017;​ ​Giulianotti,​ ​2011;​ ​Kidd,​ ​2008).​ ​In​ ​this​
​initiative,​ ​sport​ ​wasn’t​ ​implemented​ ​through​ ​means​ ​of​ ​physical​ ​activity,​ ​like​ ​Leitner​ ​et​ ​al.​
​(2014)​ ​who​ ​used​ ​sports​ ​programmes​ ​to​ ​aid​ ​peace​ ​between​ ​Israel​ ​and​ ​Palestine.​ ​However,​
​instead​ ​it​ ​was​ ​used​ ​to​ ​discuss​ ​discrimination​ ​more​ ​broadly​ ​through​ ​a​ ​story.​ ​Previous​
​initiatives​ ​including​​the​​RISE​​initiative​​have​​used​​sport​​as​​a​​tool​​to​​engage​​individuals​​in​​the​
​discussion​ ​of​ ​racism​ ​(MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin,​​2018).​​This​​was​​also​​reinforced​​by​​the​​experts​
​whereby​ ​the​ ​majority​ ​of​ ​interviewees​ ​utilise​ ​sport​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​individuals​ ​in​
​conversations​​around​​discrimination.​​Football​​is​​a​​global​​activity​​which​​is​​enjoyed​​by​​millions​
​of​​people,​​and​​has​​the​​ability​​to​​capture​​the​​attention​​of​​individuals​​worldwide,​​from​​various​
​generations​ ​(Hartmann,​ ​2000).​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result,​ ​when​ ​building​ ​this​ ​resource,​ ​one​ ​of​ ​the​ ​most​
​important​​characteristics​​will​​be​​that​​sport,​​primarily​​football,​​will​​be​​used​​as​​the​​focus​​point​
​to attract students' attention.​


​Additionally,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​support​ ​from​ ​organisations​ ​within​ ​the​ ​sporting​ ​field​ ​is​
​beneficial​​as​​they​​have​​the​​platform​​and​​money​​to​​broadcast​​the​​initiative​​on​​a​​larger​​scale.​
​This​ ​is​ ​evident​ ​within​ ​current​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives,​ ​whereby​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​have​
​received​ ​£3​ ​million​ ​pounds​ ​from​ ​Sky​ ​Sports​ ​to​ ​advance​ ​their​ ​current​ ​anti-discrimination​
​initiative​​(Sky​​Sports,​​2021).​​Therefore,​​it​​would​​be​​beneficial​​to​​seek​​support​​from​​additional​
​organisations​​within​​the​​fields​​of​​sport​​and​​antisemitism​​as​​the​​project​​progresses​​or​​as​​the​
​initiative​ ​develops.​ ​Naveen​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​“starting​ ​from​ ​the​ ​ground,​ ​and​
​then​​working​​in​​partnership,”​​suggesting​​that​​it​​would​​be​​possible​​to​​launch​​this​​project​​on​​a​
​smaller scale as part of this research and then expand it through collaborative efforts.​




                                                           ​144​
​First-hand experiences​


​Delgado​​(1995,​​p.​​2413)​​states​​that​​“stories,​​parables,​​chronicles,​​and​​narratives​​are​​powerful​
​means​ ​for​ ​destroying​ ​mindset”.​ ​Therefore,​ ​it​ ​is​​critical​​that​​storytelling​​was​​included​​in​​this​
​educational​​initiative​​because​​mixing​​aspects​​from​​both​​the​​narrative​​and​​the​​facts​​produces​
​a​​deeper​​meaning​​than​​either​​the​​narrative​​or​​the​​facts​​alone.​​Furthermore,​​key​​principles​​of​
​CRT​​and​​HebCrit​​were​​explored​​in​​this​​research,​​both​​of​​which​​emphasise​​the​​importance​​of​
​storytelling.​ ​The​ ​fourth​ ​tenet​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​necessity​ ​of​ ​narrative​ ​and​
​counter-storytelling​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001).​ ​Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​fifth​ ​tenet​ ​of​ ​HebCrit​
​(Rubin,​ ​2020)​ ​is​ ​that​ ​Jewish​ ​personal​ ​tales​ ​have​ ​importance.​ ​With​ ​the​ ​majority​ ​of​ ​experts​
​supporting​​these​​points​​and​​stating​​that​​firsthand​​experiences​​and​​stories​​are​​believed​​to​​be​
​the​ ​most​ ​influential,​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​has​ ​been​ ​informed​ ​by​ ​the​ ​marginalised​ ​community​ ​by​
​including​ ​the​ ​stories​ ​of​ ​various​ ​individuals​ ​impacted​ ​by​ ​discrimination,​ ​most​ ​notably​
​antisemitism.​​Likewise,​​it​​is​​important​​that​​first-hand​​experiences​​and​​current​​issues​​that​​are​
​relatable​ ​to​ ​young​ ​people​ ​were​ ​portrayed​ ​within​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​so​ ​that​ ​students​​could​​identify​
​with,​​and​​be​​more​​engaged​​with​​the​​resource.​​Hoffman​​(2010)​​explores​​how​​Caldecott​​Book​
​award​ ​winning​ ​books​ ​are​ ​particularly​ ​relatable​ ​to​ ​the​ ​audience​ ​of​ ​children,​​reinforcing​​the​
​importance of making it relatable.​


​Experts​ ​also​ ​revealed​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​integrating​ ​the​ ​marginalised​ ​group;​ ​as​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​
​this,​ ​there​ ​is​ ​hope​ ​that,​ ​in​ ​the​ ​future,​ ​Jewish​ ​individuals​ ​may​ ​be​ ​able​ ​to​ ​contribute​ ​to​
​delivering​ ​parts​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book.​ ​This​ ​will​ ​provide​ ​students​ ​with​ ​the​ ​opportunity,​ ​first,​ ​to​​hear​
​stories​ ​from​ ​someone​ ​who​ ​may​ ​have​ ​experienced​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​narratives​ ​in​ ​the​ ​book​
​firsthand,​​and​​second,​​to​​engage​​with​​a​​member​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​which,​​for​​some​
​students,​​may​​be​​a​​new​​experience.​​This​​is​​consistent​​with​​previous​​research​​by​​Edginton​​et​
​al.​​(1995)​​and​​Mitchell​​et​​al.​​(2016),​​who​​stated​​that​​there​​is​​a​​potential​​avenue​​for​​bridging​
​divided​ ​societies,​ ​and​ ​sport​ ​has​ ​been​ ​known​ ​to​ ​reduce​ ​prejudice​ ​and​ ​improve​ ​ethnic​
​relationships by integrating different communities and individuals.​




                                                             ​145​
​Structuring subject content​


​Subject​​content​​is​​essential​​to​​consider​​when​​developing​​an​​initiative.​​It​​was​​crucial​​that​​the​
​book​ ​not​ ​only​ ​helped​ ​children​ ​understand​ ​all​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination​ ​but​ ​also​ ​prioritised​
​education​ ​on​ ​antisemitism,​ ​given​ ​the​ ​current​ ​lack​ ​of​ ​readily​ ​available​ ​resources​ ​for​ ​young​
​people​ ​on​ ​this​ ​topic.​ ​To​ ​ensure​ ​this,​ ​the​ ​book​ ​deliberately​ ​includes​ ​references​ ​to​ ​other​
​marginalised​​groups,​​such​​as​​people​​of​​different​​religions,​​races,​​the​​LGBT+​​community,​​and​
​those​ ​with​ ​disabilities.​ ​When​ ​focusing​ ​most​ ​specifically​ ​on​ ​antisemitism,​ ​the​ ​contributions​
​found five key considerations when educating young people on antisemitism:​


    ​1.​ ​Challenging historical and harmful stereotypes.​
    ​2.​ ​Demonstrating that antisemitism is often not a direct form of discrimination.​
    ​3.​ ​Identifying​​race​​hate​​words​​associated​​with​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​in​​relation​​to​​the​
         ​sporting context.​
    ​4.​ ​Understanding the cultural differences between communities.​
    ​5.​ ​The identification of the Jewish community.​


​As​ ​a​ ​result,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​critical​ ​to​ ​include​ ​these​ ​elements​ ​in​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​to​ ​guarantee​ ​that​
​children​ ​and​ ​young​ ​people​ ​were​ ​educated​ ​on​ ​the​ ​essential​ ​topics​ ​addressed​ ​with​ ​the​
​experts.​​However,​​as​​previously​​noted,​​the​​resource​​should​​be​​shaped​​by​​the​​experiences​​of​
​the​​marginalised​​group,​​in​​this​​case,​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​and​​as​​such,​​additional​​concerns​
​raised​​by​​Jewish​​participants​​will​​be​​highlighted​​in​​future​​rounds​​of​​data​​collection​​(Phase​​3​
​and​ ​4).​ ​Finally,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​emphasised​ ​that​ ​young​ ​individuals​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​educated​ ​on​ ​the​
​importance​ ​of​ ​being​ ​an​​active​​bystander.​​As​​a​​result,​​the​​initiative​​will​​ensure​​that​​students​
​are​ ​taught​ ​the​ ​significance​ ​of​ ​this​ ​role,​ ​encouraging​​them​​to​​become​​'assertive​​bystanders'​
​rather​ ​than​ '​passive​ ​bystanders'​ ​(Public​ ​Health​ ​England,​ ​2020).​ ​The​ ​book​ ​highlights​ ​key​
​aspects​ ​of​ ​the​ ​BIM​ ​through​ ​its​ ​sporting​ ​context,​ ​making​ ​these​ ​concepts​ ​accessible​ ​to​ ​the​
​reader.​ ​Additionally,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​that​ ​children​ ​are​ ​made​ ​aware​ ​of​ ​local​ ​and​ ​national​
​organisations​​and​​charities​​they​​can​​contact​​if​​they​​feel​​the​​need​​to​​report​​any​​discriminatory​
​behaviour.​




                                                            ​146​
​Chapter summary​


​In​ ​conclusion,​ ​the​​anti-discrimination​​expert​​interviews​​have​​provided​​valuable​​insights​​into​
​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​anti-discriminatory​ ​initiatives,​ ​reinforcing​ ​the​ ​opportunity​ ​to​​develop​​an​
​educational​​resource​​that​​enhances​​individuals'​​understanding​​of​​antisemitism.​​The​​findings​
​and​ ​their​ ​practical​ ​applications​ ​aim​ ​to​ ​contribute​ ​significantly​ ​to​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport,​
​particularly​​in​​light​​of​​current​​and​​recent​​developments​​that​​show​​antisemitic​​behaviour​​and​
​language​ ​remain​ ​prevalent,​ ​especially​ ​in​ ​football​ ​across​ ​Europe​ ​and,​ ​more​ ​specifically,​ ​in​
​Britain​ ​(Curtis,​ ​2019;​ ​Poulton,​ ​2016;​ ​Stratton,​ ​2015).​ ​While​ ​several​ ​efforts​​are​​underway​​to​
​combat​ ​antisemitism​ ​more​ ​broadly,​ ​including​ ​the​ ​work​ ​of​ ​numerous​ ​Jewish​ ​charities​ ​and​
​organisations,​​there​​is​​a​​notable​​lack​​of​​focus​​within​​the​​sporting​​arena.​​Although​​Chelsea​​FC​
​has​​been​​running​​the​​‘Say​​No​​to​​Antisemitism’​​campaign​​since​​2019​​(Chelsea​​FC,​​2018),​​little​
​is​ ​known​ ​about​ ​its​ ​effectiveness,​​and​​it​​remains​​unclear​​which​​aspects​​of​​the​​campaign​​are​
​making a tangible impact on reducing antisemitism in sport.​


​Overall,​ ​the​ ​contributions​ ​from​ ​the​ ​interviewees​ ​demonstrate​ ​that​ ​implementing​
​anti-discrimination​​initiatives​​in​​sport​​has​​a​​purpose​​and​​may​​be​​beneficial​​to​​social​​change.​
​The​​research​​shows​​that​​this​​may​​be​​accomplished​​in​​specific​​settings​​when​​trusted​​leaders​
​can​ ​use​ ​a​ ​resource​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​individuals​ ​while​ ​also​​igniting​​discussion​​about​​the​​topic.​​To​
​have​​a​​bigger​​impact,​​the​​topic​​matter​​should​​be​​reinforced​​by​​the​​marginalised​​community.​
​In​ ​summary,​ ​the​ ​overarching​ ​goal​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​developed​ ​throughout​ ​this​ ​thesis​ ​aligns​
​with​​Craig's​​perspective,​​who​​stated​​that​​social​​change​​through​​anti-discrimination​​initiatives​
​is:​


        ​…very,​ ​very​ ​challenging,​ ​but​ ​I​ ​think​ ​we've​​got​​a​​wonderful​​opportunity​​to​​make​
        ​the​ ​game​ ​better​ ​and​ ​to​​have​​a​​wider​​impact​​on​​society,​​particularly​​on​​an​​issue​
        ​such as antisemitism.​




                                                          ​147​
​Chapter 6 - Phase 2 - Creation of Educational Resource​

​Introduction​


​As​​a​​result​​of​​the​​Phase​​1​​findings,​​the​​aim​​of​​Phase​​2​​was​​to​​create​​an​​educational​​book​​for​
​use​ ​in​ ​schools,​ ​aimed​ ​at​​teaching​​children​​aged​​10-11​​years​​about​​antisemitism,​​with​​sport​
​serving​​as​​the​​central​​narrative​​theme.​​To​​develop​​the​​book,​​elements​​of​​‘creative​​nonfiction’​
​(henceforth,​​CNF)​​were​​drawn​​upon​​to​​guide​​the​​researcher.​​CNF​​has​​been​​defined​​by​​Smith,​
​McGannon​​and​​Williams​​(2015,​​p.1)​​as​​“a​​type​​of​​creative​​analytic​​practice​​that​​tells​​a​​story​
​which​ ​is​ ​grounded​ ​in​ ​research​ ​data​ ​and​ ​draws​ ​on​ ​literary​ ​conventions”.​ ​Through​ ​CNF,​ ​an​
​author​ ​can​ ​demonstrate​ ​that​ ​stories​ ​are​ ​founded​ ​on​ ​data​ ​that​ ​has​ ​been​ ​gathered​ ​and​
​organised​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​being​ ​entirely​ ​made​ ​up​ ​or​ ​imagined​​(Smith​​et​​al​.,​​2015).​​As​​a​​result,​
​while​ ​the​ ​stories​ ​are​ ​fictional,​ ​they​ ​are​ ​also​ ​factual​ ​as​ ​they​​are​​grounded​​by​​people's​​lived​
​experiences​​and​​real​​events,​​but​​then​​reconstructed​​by​​the​​author​​(Cheney,​​2001;​​Kotišová,​
​2019).​

​CNF​ ​has​ ​grown​ ​in​ ​popularity​ ​within​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​exercise,​ ​as​ ​Smith​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2015)​
​points​​out​​that​​many​​researchers​​have​​expressed​​their​​qualitative​​findings​​through​​CNF.​​For​
​instance,​ ​Smith's​​(2013)​​and​​Smith​​et​​al.​​(2013)​​have​​conducted​​a​​variety​​of​​studies​​looking​
​at​ ​people's​ ​experiences​ ​with​ ​spinal​ ​cord​ ​injuries​ ​and​ ​participation​ ​in​ ​sports​ ​and​ ​physical​
​exercise;​ ​CNF​ ​has​ ​been​ ​used​ ​within​ ​their​ ​studies​ ​to​ ​communicate​ ​the​ ​complexities​ ​of​
​implementing​ ​and​ ​sustaining​ ​psychical​ ​activity​ ​after​ ​a​ ​spinal​ ​cord​ ​injury.​ ​Additionally,​
​McGannon​​and​​Cameron's​​(2013)​​study​​examines​​the​​experiences​​of​​female​​exercisers​​with​
​body​ ​anxiety.​ ​Another​ ​study​ ​by​ ​Blodgett​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2017)​ ​used​ ​CNF​ ​to​ ​gain​ ​a​ ​better​
​understanding​​of​​intersecting​​identities​​within​​elite​​female​​boxers.​​Cheney​​(2001,​​p1)​​states​
​that​ ​“creative​ ​nonfiction​ ​doesn’t​ ​just​ ​report​ ​facts,​ ​it​ ​delivers​ ​facts​ ​in​ ​ways​ ​that​ ​move​ ​the​
​reader toward a deeper understanding of a topic”.​

​With​ ​that​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​of​ ​the​ ​educational​​book​​was​​to​​deliver​​concepts​​from​​both​​the​
​interview​ ​data​ ​and​ ​theories​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​story​ ​that​ ​guides​ ​the​ ​reader​ ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​better​
​knowledge​ ​of​ ​discrimination,​ ​specifically,​ ​antisemitism,​ ​and​ ​how​ ​to​ ​effectively​ ​address​ ​it.​
​Although​ ​the​ ​story​ ​was​ ​not​ ​solely​ ​created​ ​by​ ​participants'​ ​experiences,​ ​it​​was​​informed​​by​




                                                              ​148​
​real-world​ ​stories​ ​and​ ​experiences​ ​that​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​was​ ​made​ ​aware​ ​of​ ​through​ ​the​
​interview process, in addition to stories seen in the news and the media.​

​Principles and best practice in CNF​

​According​ ​to​ ​Gutkind​ ​(1996),​ ​CNF​ ​is​ ​based​ ​on​ ​5​ ​key​ ​tenets​ ​known​ ​as​ ​‘​the​ ​5​ ​Rs​’;​ ​these​​are​
​‘Real-life​ ​immersion’,​ ​‘Reflection’,​ ​‘Research’,​ ​‘Reading’,​ ​and​ ​‘‘Riting’​ ​[sic].​ ​The​ ​first​ ​tenet​
​involves​ ​immersing​ ​oneself​ ​in​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​others.​ ​Gutkind​ ​(1996)​ ​states​ ​that​ ​some​
​researchers​ ​may​ ​find​ ​themselves​ ​exploring​ ​their​ ​own​ ​experiences,​ ​but​​it​​is​​key​​to​​immerse​
​themselves​ ​in​ ​the​ ​lived​ ​events​ ​of​ ​the​ ​participants​ ​to​ ​gain​ ​a​ ​better​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​their​
​world.​​‘Reflection’​​is​​the​​stage​​whereby​​the​​researcher​​makes​​sense​​of​​the​​stories,​​but​​uses​
​their​ ​abilities​ ​to​ ​retell​ ​individuals'​ ​experiences.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​this​ ​is​ ​the​ ​stage​ ​where​ ​the​
​writer's​​creativity​​is​​more​​crucial​​(Schinke​​et​​al.​,​​2016;​​Smith​​et​​al.​,​​2015).​​‘Research’​​entails​
​familiarising​ ​yourself​ ​with​ ​the​ ​topic.​ ​For​ ​the​ ​purpose​ ​of​ ​this​ ​research,​ ​the​ ​author​ ​and​
​researcher​​undertook​​a​​literature​​review​​and​​therefore​​became​​more​​knowledgeable​​on​​the​
​topic​​(Thomas,​​2017).​​In​​addition,​​interviews​​were​​conducted​​beforehand​​with​​experts,​​who​
​had​ ​a​ ​wealth​ ​of​ ​knowledge​ ​of​ ​the​ ​subject​ ​matter.​ ​Additionally,​ ​this​ ​research​ ​involves​
​collecting​​data​​at​​later​​stages,​​which​​will​​continuously​​inform​​the​​story​​through​​ongoing​​data​
​gathering.​ ​‘Reading’​ ​is​ ​something​ ​that​ ​will​ ​naturally​ ​occur​ ​during​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process,​
​specifically,​ ​this​ ​will​​occur​​when​​reviewing​​the​​literature​​within​​the​​field.​​However,​​it​​is​​also​
​important​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​literature​ ​with​ ​similar​ ​characteristics,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​writing​ ​style,​ ​plot,​ ​and​
​appropriateness,​ ​to​ ​the​ ​work​ ​the​ ​author​ ​is​ ​creating.​ ​For​ ​this​ ​research,​ ​the​ ​researcher​
​examined​​a​​variety​​of​​books​​aimed​​at​​children​​aged​​10-11​​years,​​including​​works​​by​​authors​
​like​ ​Jacqueline​ ​Wilson,​ ​Roald​ ​Dahl,​ ​and​ ​Jeff​ ​Kinney,​ ​whose​ ​books​ ​are​ ​commonly​ ​read​ ​by​
​children​ ​in​ ​this​ ​age​ ​group.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​engaged​ ​with​ ​educational​ ​activity​
​books​​commonly​​used​​in​​teaching​​settings​​for​​children​​aged​​10-11.​​The​​final​​‘r’​​is​​for​​‘‘riting’​
​(writing).​ ​This​ ​is​ ​the​ ​point​ ​at​ ​which​​the​​author​​is​​able​​to​​finalise​​the​​process​​by​​completing​
​the written part of it.​

​Throughout​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​​the​​current​​initiative,​​the​​steps​​outlined​​by​​Gutkind​​(1996)​
​were​​followed.​​Furthermore,​​it​​should​​also​​be​​considered​​that​​a​​range​​of​​recommendations​
​from​ ​Smith​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2015)​ ​were​ ​helpful​ ​during​ ​the​ ​process.​ ​They​ ​offer​ ​a​ ​variety​ ​of​ ​crucial​
​guidelines​ ​for​ ​the​ ​process​ ​in​ ​their​ ​chapter​ ​on​ ​CNF,​ ​some​ ​of​ ​which​ ​complement​ ​those​ ​of​


                                                                ​149​
​Gutkind​ ​(1996).​ ​Although​ ​Smith​ ​and​ ​colleagues​ ​(2015)​ ​emphasise​ ​14​ ​recommendations,​ ​a​
​selection​​of​​these​​were​​taken​​into​​account​​and​​embedded​​within​​the​​production​​of​​the​​book.​
​For​ ​example,​ ​Smith​​et​​al.​​(2015)​​start​​by​​discussing​​ontology​​and​​epistemology,​​highlighting​
​how​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​needs​ ​to​ ​be​ ​aware​ ​of​ ​how​ ​their​ ​own​ ​ontology​ ​and​ ​epistemology​ ​may​
​have​​had​​an​​impact​​on​​the​​way​​the​​project​​was​​developed​​as​​a​​whole.​​Given​​the​​potential​​for​
​the​​aforementioned​​personal​​influences​​and​​experiences​​in​​terms​​of​​their​​effect​​on​​the​​story,​
​the​​production​​of​​the​​book​​was​​undertaken​​with​​reflection​​in​​mind.​​Smith​​et​​al.​​(2015)​​also​
​recognise​​that​​when​​creating​​a​​story,​​it​​is​​crucial​​to​​select​​and​​develop​​characters​​accordingly.​
​Based​ ​upon​ ​the​ ​results​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​interviews,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​making​ ​the​ ​initiative​
​relatable​​was​​key.​​This​​aligns​​with​​Entwistle's​​(2018)​​literature,​​which​​explains​​how​​and​​why​
​student​ ​learning​ ​approaches​ ​have​ ​been​ ​thoughtfully​ ​and​ ​meaningfully​ ​developed.​ ​By​
​ensuring​ ​the​ ​book​ ​was​ ​crafted​ ​to​ ​resonate​ ​with​ ​readers,​ ​it​ ​became​ ​both​ ​meaningful​ ​and​
​authentic​ ​to​ ​their​ ​learning​ ​experience.​ ​Therefore,​ ​when​ ​selecting​ ​and​ ​developing​ ​the​
​characters,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​important​ ​to​ ​make​ ​them​ ​relatable​ ​to​ ​the​ ​target​ ​audience,​ ​children​​aged​
​10-11​ ​years.​ ​The​ ​author​ ​made​ ​sure​ ​to​ ​make​ ​the​​characters​​more​​relatable​​to​​the​​intended​
​audience​​by​​taking​​into​​account​​the​​following​​factors​​as​​she​​was​​developing​​the​​educational​
​initiative.​​For​​instance,​​the​​main​​characters​​in​​the​​story​​are​​the​​same​​age​​as​​those​​reading​​it​
​and​ ​are​ ​going​ ​through​ ​the​ ​same​ ​life​ ​transition​ ​as​ ​children​ ​ending​ ​up​ ​Year​ ​6​ ​and​ ​starting​
​secondary school.​

​Strengths and limitations of CNF​

​It​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​consider​ ​the​ ​strengths​ ​and​ ​limitations​ ​of​ ​using​ ​CNF​ ​as​​a​​tool​​in​​which​​to​
​present​​information.​​Its​​key​​strength​​is​​that​​CNF​​enables​​a​​researcher​​to​​organise​​data​​into​​a​
​meaningful​ ​discourse​ ​(Kotišová,​ ​2019).​ ​The​ ​stories​ ​produced​ ​by​ ​CNF,​ ​particularly​ ​in​ ​the​
​subject​ ​of​ ​sociology,​ ​can​ ​aid​ ​us​ ​in​ ​comprehending​ ​why​ ​other​ ​cultures​​or​​groups​​may​​differ​
​from​ ​our​ ​own,​ ​through​​their​​capacity​​to​​illustrate​​individuals’​​stories​​and​​lived​​experiences,​
​which​ ​has​ ​proven​ ​very​ ​helpful​ ​for​ ​the​ ​goals​ ​of​ ​this​ ​antisemitism​​initiative​​(Kotišová,​​2019).​
​Similarly,​ ​Clayton​ ​(2010)​ ​makes​ ​the​ ​point​ ​that​ ​reading​ ​CNF​​enables​​the​​reader​​to​​viscerally​
​enter​ ​the​ ​world​ ​of​ ​the​ ​participants.​ ​It​ ​allows​ ​the​ ​reader​ ​to​ ​gain​ ​insights​​into​​another​​lived​
​experience​​and​​reflect​​upon​​the​​character's​​experiences.​​With​​this​​in​​mind,​​when​​developing​
​the​​book,​​it​​was​​important​​to​​make​​the​​story​​relatable​​to​​the​​target​​audience.​​This​​was​​also​
​highlighted​ ​during​ ​the​ ​interview​ ​process,​ ​as​ ​experts​ ​recognised​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​


                                                             ​150​
​relatability.​ ​Smith​​et​​al.​​(2013)​​recognise​​CNF’s​​main​​advantage​​of​​being​​able​​to​​appeal​​to​​a​
​variety​ ​of​ ​audiences​ ​rather​​than​​solely​​academics.​​This​​is​​due​​to​​the​​language​​and​​emotion​
​portrayed​ ​throughout​ ​CNF,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​often​ ​avoids​ ​terminology​ ​that​ ​when​ ​used​ ​in​ ​academic​
​readings,​ ​can​ ​be​ ​challenging.​ ​The​ ​works​ ​of​ ​Rogers​ ​(2015),​ ​who​ ​used​ ​individual​ ​stories​ ​to​
​discuss​ ​motherhood,​ ​and​ ​Haegele​ ​and​ ​Maher​ ​(2021),​ ​who​ ​were​ ​able​ ​to​ ​portray​ ​the​
​experiences​ ​of​ ​autistic​ ​students​ ​in​ ​PE,​ ​are​ ​examples​ ​of​ ​how​ ​CNF​ ​has​ ​been​ ​used​ ​to​
​communicate​ ​to​ ​a​ ​broader​ ​audience.​ ​Since​ ​the​ ​suggested​ ​initiative​ ​is​ ​targeted​ ​towards​
​children,​ ​who​ ​may​ ​then​ ​deepen​​their​​comprehension​​of​​the​​subject​​of​​antisemitism,​​this​​is​
​one of its main strengths.​

​On​​the​​other​​hand,​​a​​key​​limitation​​that​​should​​be​​acknowledged​​is​​that​​writing​​good​​CNF​​is​
​difficult​​(Smith​​et​​al.​,​​2015).​​Good​​CNF​​can​​take​​a​​long​​time​​to​​create,​​so​​the​​author​​needs​​to​
​be​​very​​committed​​to​​the​​project​​(Root,​​2008).​​It​​should​​be​​acknowledged​​that​​the​​author​​of​
​this​​story​​is​​a​​novice​​writer​​whose​​capacity​​to​​effectively​​communicate​​the​​message​​may​​be​
​constrained.​​As​​a​​result​​of​​the​​researcher​​being​​a​​novice​​writer,​​it​​can​​also​​be​​challenging​​to​
​ensure​​that​​the​​core​​message​​is​​entertaining​​(Root,​​2008).​​For​​the​​purpose​​of​​this​​research,​​it​
​is​ ​key​ ​that​​the​​core​​teachings​​of​​antisemitism​​be​​incorporated​​into​​a​​narrative​​that​​children​
​will​ ​find​ ​interesting​ ​and​ ​entertaining​ ​in​ ​order​ ​for​ ​the​ ​research's​ ​main​ ​messages​ ​to​ ​be​
​understood​ ​by​ ​the​ ​intended​ ​audience.​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​this,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​followed​ ​up​ ​the​
​writing​ ​process​ ​with​​focus​​groups​​in​​order​​to​​gain​​feedback​​on​​whether​​the​​story​​had​​been​
​written effectively and whether it would be enjoyable for young children.​

​It​ ​should​ ​also​ ​be​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​there​ ​are​ ​challenges​ ​inherent​ ​in​ ​the​ ​philosophical​ ​position​
​highlighted​​by​​the​​researcher​​in​​earlier​​sections​​of​​the​​methodology​​chapter.​​Specifically,​​as​
​the​ ​researcher​ ​selected​ ​which​ ​parts​ ​of​ ​the​ ​data​ ​set​ ​to​ ​incorporate​ ​into​ ​the​ ​narrative,​ ​this​
​process​ ​is​ ​not​ ​solely​ ​objective.​ ​While​ ​this​ ​subjectivity​ ​may​ ​be​​seen​​as​​a​​potential​​bias,​​it​​is​
​deemed​ ​as​ ​a​ ​necessary​ ​aspect​ ​of​ ​co-constructing​ ​the​ ​narrative.​ ​The​ ​researcher​ ​played​ ​an​
​active​​role​​in​​shaping​​the​​story,​​drawing​​from​​the​​data​​to​​capture​​the​​meaning​​conveyed​​by​
​participants.​ ​This​ ​means​ ​the​ ​narratives​ ​presented​ ​are​ ​a​​collaborative​​creation​​between​​the​
​researcher​ ​and​ ​the​ ​participants.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​recognise​ ​that​ ​the​
​researcher’s​ ​interpretation​ ​and​ ​presentation​​of​​these​​stories​​can​​influence​​which​​narratives​
​are​ ​emphasised​ ​and​ ​how​ ​they​ ​are​ ​framed.​ ​In​ ​this​​sense,​​the​​researcher​​contributed​​to​​the​



                                                             ​151​
​creation​ ​of​ ​a​ ​narrative​ ​that​ ​may​ ​not​ ​otherwise​ ​be​ ​told,​ ​but​ ​which​ ​reflects​ ​the​ ​meanings​
​derived from the interview data.​

​In​​addition,​​within​​the​​novel​​there​​are​​stories​​being​​told​​that​​are​​not​​solely​​derived​​from​​the​
​data​​sets,​​but​​are​​also​​influenced​​by​​stories​​seen​​within​​the​​media,​​and​​those​​shaped​​by​​the​
​researcher’s​ ​own​ ​religious​ ​identity​ ​and​ ​experiences.​ ​These​ ​external​ ​sources​ ​of​ ​narrative​
​creation​​present​​potential​​challenges​​around​​the​​authenticity​​of​​the​​story,​​as​​they​​introduce​
​elements​ ​that​ ​may​ ​not​​be​​directly​​linked​​to​​the​​participants’​​voices.​​However,​​it​​is​​essential​
​to​ ​recognise​ ​that​ ​the​ ​researcher’s​ ​identity​ ​and​ ​personal​ ​experiences​ ​are​ ​also​ ​a​ ​part​​of​​the​
​co-construction​ ​of​ ​the​ ​narrative.​ ​The​ ​researcher​ ​is​ ​not​ ​just​ ​a​ ​passive​ ​receiver​ ​of​ ​the​
​participants' stories, but an active contributor to shaping the overall narrative.​

​To​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​the​ ​stories​​remain​​authentic​​and​​reflective​​of​​the​​individuals​​involved,​​focus​
​groups​​have​​been​​utilised​​at​​a​​later​​stage​​of​​this​​research.​​These​​groups​​allowed​​participants​
​to​ ​engage​ ​directly​ ​with​ ​the​ ​narrative,​ ​providing​ ​feedback​ ​and​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​the​ ​stories​
​remain​ ​true​ ​to​ ​their​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​perspectives.​ ​This​ ​collaborative​ ​process,​ ​while​
​influenced​ ​by​ ​external​ ​media​ ​and​ ​the​ ​researcher’s​ ​personal​ ​insights,​ ​ensures​​that​​the​​final​
​narrative reflects the lived realities of the participants.​

​Integration and implementation of Phase 1 interview data​

​In​ ​considering​ ​the​ ​co-creation​ ​aspect​ ​of​ ​this​ ​semi-structured​ ​approach,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​
​recognise​​how​​the​​researcher’s​​background​​and​​expertise​​influence​​both​​the​​development​​of​
​questions​​and​​the​​process​​of​​meaning-making​​throughout​​the​​project.​​As​​mentioned​​earlier,​
​CNF​ ​is​ ​rooted​ ​in​ ​real​ ​events​ ​and​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​(Cheney,​ ​2001),​ ​and​ ​the​ ​interview​ ​data​
​analysed​​through​​thematic​​analysis​​in​​Phase​​1​​played​​a​​crucial​​role​​in​​shaping​​the​​narrative.​
​The​ ​semi-structured​ ​interviews​ ​allowed​ ​for​​a​​flexible​​yet​​guided​​exploration​​of​​key​​themes,​
​enabling​​participants​​to​​share​​their​​insights​​while​​also​​allowing​​the​​researcher’s​​questions​​to​
​be​​shaped​​by​​personal​​background​​and​​contextual​​understanding.​​This​​interplay​​between​​the​
​researcher’s​ ​own​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​the​ ​participants'​ ​narratives​ ​was​ ​pivotal​ ​in​ ​driving​ ​the​
​questioning​ ​process​ ​and​ ​grounding​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​educational​ ​objectives.​ ​Subsequently,​ ​the​
​interview​ ​data​ ​which​​was​​analysed​​through​​the​​use​​of​​TA​​in​​Phase​​1,​​was​​utilised​​to​​inform​
​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book.​ ​The​ ​previous​ ​chapter,​ ​which​ ​covered​ ​the​ ​results​ ​and​



                                                           ​152​
​discussion​ ​of​ ​Phase​ ​1,​ ​identified​ ​key​ ​themes​ ​that​ ​were​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​implement​ ​during​ ​the​
​creation​ ​of​ ​this​ ​initiative;​ ​the​ ​forthcoming​ ​discussion​ ​thus​ ​explains​ ​this​ ​implementation​
​process.​

​First,​ ​it​ ​was​​acknowledged​​that​​an​​initiative​​should​​have​​a​​‘broad-to-narrow’​​structure.​​This​
​means​ ​first​ ​examining​ ​the​ ​problem​ ​of​ ​discrimination​ ​as​ ​a​ ​whole,​ ​before​ ​progressively​
​examining​​the​​kind​​of​​prejudice​​that​​is​​most​​important​​for​​the​​initiative.​​In​​this​​example,​​the​
​book's​​first​​chapter​​explores​​discrimination​​in​​general​​and​​then​​talks​​about​​a​​‘broad’​​range​​of​
​distinct​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination​ ​-​ ​for​ ​example,​ ​racism,​ ​homophobia,​ ​and​ ​ableism.​ ​For​
​instance,​​in​​the​​story,​​when​​the​​players​​kneel,​​it​​sparks​​a​​discussion​​(pg.​​9)​​about​​racism​​and​
​the​​significance​​of​​the​​gesture,​​which​​is​​widely​​associated​​with​​the​​Black​​Lives​​Matter​​(BLM)​
​movement​ ​and​ ​its​ ​symbolic​ ​use​ ​in​ ​protesting​ ​racial​ ​injustice​ ​(Walker,​ ​Taylor​ ​and​ ​Chansky,​
​2021).​ ​The​ ​story​ ​then​ ​starts​ ​to​ ​primarily​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​Chapter​ ​4​ ​following​ ​the​
​broader​ ​discussion​ ​on​ ​discrimination.​ ​These​ ​chapters​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​are​ ​what​ ​led​ ​to​ ​the​
'​narrow'​​structure​​recommended​​by​​experts,​​as​​they​​focus​​specifically​​on​​the​​key​​discussion​
​of​ ​antisemitism​​within​​the​​broader​​context​​of​​discrimination.​​Similar​​approaches​​have​​been​
​seen​​in​​previous​​initiatives,​​such​​as​​the​​educational​​initiative​​RISE,​​which​​provides​​workshops​
​that​ ​explore​ ​and​ ​educate​ ​individuals​ ​on​ ​racism​ ​(MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin,​ ​2018).​ ​Over​ ​the​
​course​ ​of​ ​ten​ ​weeks,​​students​​completed​​ten​​modules,​​whereby​​the​​conversation​​gradually​
​built​ ​from​ ​inclusion​ ​and​ ​equality​ ​more​ ​broadly,​ ​and​ ​then​ ​specifically​ ​to​ ​racism​ ​through​ ​a​
​range of modules (MacIntosh and Martin, 2018).​

​In​ ​addition,​ ​those​ ​experts​ ​working​ ​specifically​ ​in​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​addressed​ ​what​
​they​ ​perceived​ ​as​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​errors​ ​in​ ​people's​ ​understanding​​of​​Judaism​​and​​the​​Jewish​
​community.​ ​This​ ​included​ ​challenging​ ​historical​ ​and​ ​harmful​ ​stereotypes​ ​and​ ​the​
​identification​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​​community.​​With​​that​​in​​mind,​​it​​was​​crucial​​to​​embed​​some​​of​
​the​​key​​teachings​​of​​Judaism​​throughout​​the​​story;​​therefore,​​to​​learn​​more​​about​​the​​Jewish​
​community,​ ​the​ ​students​ ​in​ ​the​ ​book​ ​visit​ ​a​ ​synagogue​ ​in​​Chapter​​8​​(pg.​​41).​​It​​was​​hoped​
​that​ ​those​ ​children​ ​taking​ ​part​ ​in​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​should​ ​gain​ ​a​ ​greater​ ​knowledge​ ​of​ ​what​
​Judaism​ ​is​ ​as​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​this​ ​chapter.​ ​Antisemitic​​remarks​​also​​refer​​to​​significant​​historical​
​teaching​​moments​​within​​Chapters​​5,​​6,​​and​​9,​​such​​as​​Hitler​​(pg.​​32)​​and​​Auschwitz​​(pg.​​31),​
​which​​will​​help​​to​​increase​​students'​​understanding​​of​​the​​previous​​discrimination​​the​​Jewish​
​community​ ​has​ ​faced​ ​and​ ​will​ ​help​ ​in​ ​challenging​ ​any​ ​stereotypes​ ​children​ ​may​ ​have​


                                                            ​153​
​regarding​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​The​ ​interview​ ​data​ ​also​ ​revealed​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​
​identifying​​race​​hate​​words​​associated​​with​​the​​Jewish​​community​​in​​relation​​to​​the​​sporting​
​context.​​Therefore,​​the​​narrative​​throughout​​the​​story​​focuses​​on​​an​​individual​​who​​attends​
​matches​​and​​becomes​​confused​​by​​a​​new​​term​​he​​is​​hearing,​​‘Yid.’​​This​​confusion​​highlights​
​the​ ​complexities​ ​surrounding​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​such​ ​terms​ ​in​ ​sports,​ ​and​ ​also​ ​discusses​ ​the​
​importance of understanding the harmful effects of using such terms.​

​The​ ​interview​ ​data​ ​revealed​ ​that​ ​teachers​ ​and​ ​leaders​ ​with​ ​prior​ ​experience​ ​using​
​education-based​ ​initiatives​ ​consistently​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​resources​ ​that​
​encourage​ ​active​ ​discussions.​ ​These​ ​participants​ ​highlighted​ ​that​ ​such​ ​resources​ ​not​ ​only​
​make​​initiatives​​more​​accessible​​and​​user-friendly​​but​​also​​significantly​​enhance​​their​​pupils’​
​engagement​ ​and​ ​learning​ ​outcomes.​ ​In​ ​response​ ​to​ ​this,​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​content​ ​has​ ​been​
​designed​​to​​integrate​​structured​​questions​​and​​discussion​​points​​within​​each​​chapter.​​These​
​have​ ​been​ ​carefully​ ​embedded​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​they​ ​align​ ​with​ ​the​ ​core​ ​themes​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​
​providing​ ​educators​ ​with​ ​questions​ ​which​ ​could​ ​facilitate​ ​meaningful​ ​classroom​ ​dialogues.​
​Furthermore,​​this​​will​​increase​​the​​educational​​impact​​of​​the​​book​​by​​providing​​points​​which​
​will​ ​encourage​ ​collaborative​ ​learning,​ ​critical​ ​thinking,​ ​and​ ​a​ ​deeper​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​the​
​subject​​matter.​​These​​discussion​​points​​have​​been​​placed​​at​​the​​end​​of​​each​​chapter,​​creating​
​a​ ​clear​ ​and​ ​user-friendly​ ​format.​ ​This​ ​layout​ ​not​ ​only​ ​allows​ ​for​ ​a​ ​logical​ ​progression​
​throughout​ ​each​ ​chapter​ ​but​ ​also​ ​provides​ ​flexibility​ ​for​ ​teachers​ ​to​ ​adapt​ ​the​ ​material​ ​to​
​suit their pupils’ needs.​

​Integration and implementation HebCrit, CRT and BIM​

​Ellis​​(2004)​​highlights​​a​​key​​strength​​of​​CNF​​which​​is​​that,​​due​​to​​the​​theoretical​​nature​​of​​a​
​story,​ ​CNF​ ​allows​ ​an​ ​author​ ​to​ ​successfully​ ​communicate​ ​theory​ ​through​ ​their​ ​accounts.​
​Therefore,​ ​in​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​interview​ ​data,​​the​​story​​that​​was​​created​​drew​​on​​a​
​variety​​of​​theories​​that​​were​​covered​​in​​the​​literature​​review​​chapter​​of​​this​​thesis.​​Through​
​abductive​ ​reasoning,​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020),​ ​CRT​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001),​ ​and​ ​BIM​
​(Latané​​and​​Darley,​​1970)​​were​​theories​​which​​were​​integrated​​within​​the​​initiative.​​Although​
​CRT​ ​was​ ​developed​ ​as​ ​an​ ​avenue​ ​to​ ​articulate​ ​the​ ​historical​ ​and​ ​current​ ​fears​ ​of​ ​Black​
​Americans​​(Brown​​and​​Jackson,​​2013;​​DeCuir​​and​​Dixson,​​2004),​​its​​application​​to​​this​​project​
​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​is​ ​still​ ​relevant.​ ​With​ ​HebCrit,​ ​a​ ​subfield​ ​within​ ​CRT,​ ​arguing​ ​that​ ​Jewish​


                                                           ​154​
​people​ ​should​ ​be​ ​viewed​ ​as​ ​a​ '​race'​ ​and​ ​that​ ​their​ ​treatment​ ​shows​ ​they​ ​are​ ​a​ ​racialised​
​group, the following CRT tenets were incorporated into the development of the book:​

​1)​     ​The concept of storytelling and counter-storytelling.​

​Using​ ​CNF​ ​allows​ ​for​​a​​writer​​to​​retell​​the​​stories​​of​​the​​marginalised​​community​​(Kotišová,​
​2019).​ ​A​ ​key​ ​tenet​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​is​ ​that​​there​​is​​an​​importance​​to​​telling​​these​​stories​​as​​it​​allows​
​individuals​ ​to​ ​communicate​ ​and​ ​share​ ​their​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​through​ ​their​ ​own​ ​words​
​(Delgado,​ ​1989;​ ​Solorzano​ ​and​ ​Yasso,​ ​2002).​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​Ladson-Billings​ ​(2013)​ ​reinforces​
​that​ ​racism​ ​is​ ​not​ ​often​​publicly​​acknowledged,​​stating​​the​​importance​​of​​informing​​people​
​about​ ​the​ ​inequalities​ ​that​ ​exist,​ ​whilst​ ​emphasising​ ​that​ ​racial​ ​discrimination​ ​is​ ​ongoing.​
​Through​ ​CNF,​ ​the​ ​book​ ​was​ ​able​ ​to​ ​retell​ ​the​ ​stories​ ​of​ ​marginalised​ ​communities,​ ​mainly​
​stories of antisemitism, more specifically.​

​2)​     ​Racism is “ordinary, not aberrational”.​


​Secondly,​​through​​CNF,​​it​​is​​evident​​that​​racism​​is​​an​​ingrained​​feature​​of​​our​​society,​​looking​
​natural​ ​to​ ​people​ ​who​ ​are​ ​part​ ​of​ ​the​ ​culture,​ ​and​ ​unrecognisable​ ​within​ ​structures​
​(Manglitz,​​Guy​​and​​Hunn,​​2006;​​Santiago-Rivera​​et​​al.​,​​2016).​​It​​is​​with​​this​​tenet​​in​​mind​​that​
​the​ ​book​​aims​​to​​teach​​individuals​​within​​the​​first​​chapter,​​most​​prominently,​​about​​racism.​
​In​ ​addition,​ ​within​ ​the​ ​book​ ​it​ ​helps​ ​to​ ​recognise​ ​that​ ​racism​ ​exists​ ​throughout​ ​society,​
​making​ ​reference​ ​to​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​education​ ​specifically,​ ​which​ ​some​ ​children​ ​might​ ​not​ ​be​
​aware​ ​of.​ ​Although​ ​notions​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​were​ ​embedded​ ​through​ ​the​​development​​of​​the​​story,​
​there​ ​was​​greater​​focus​​on​​the​​implementation​​of​​the​​five​​tenets​​of​​HebCrit​​due​​to​​it​​being​
​more​​specific​​to​​the​​discussion​​of​​antisemitism​​(Rubin,​​2020).​​Therefore,​​during​​the​​creation​
​of the book, the five key tenets of HebCrit were carefully embedded through the story.​


​3)​     ​Jews continue to be discriminated against and persecuted.​


​According​ ​to​ ​Rubin's​ ​(2020)​ ​theorisation​ ​of​ ​HebCrit,​ ​Jews​ ​continue​ ​to​ ​be​ ​discriminated​
​against​ ​and​ ​persecuted.​ ​Antisemitism​ ​is​ ​occasionally​ ​displayed​ ​in​ ​the​ ​narrative,​ ​both​ ​in​
​educational​ ​settings​ ​(p.46)​ ​and​ ​in​ ​football-related​ ​contexts​ ​(p.22​ ​and​ ​34).​ ​With​ ​a​ ​range​ ​of​
​scholars​ ​-​ ​including​ ​MacDonald-Dennis​ ​(2006),​ ​Judaken​ ​(2018),​ ​and​ ​Rubin​ ​(2020)​ ​-​


                                                            ​155​
​contending​ ​that​ ​Jewish​ ​inequality​ ​is​ ​largely​ ​disregarded​ ​in​ ​society​ ​and​ ​our​ ​culture,​ ​this​
​chapter​ ​enabled​ ​the​​children​​to​​recognise​​that​​Jewish​​people​​are​​discriminated​​against​​and​
​that​ ​antisemitism​ ​does​ ​exist.​ ​Noting​​that​​antisemitism​​remains​​prevalent​​in​​today's​​society,​
​Goldberg​ ​and​ ​Durkheim​ ​(2008)​ ​reinforce​ ​how​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​have​ ​been​
​discriminated​​against​​and​​subjected​​to​​bigotry​​for​​centuries.​​Thus,​​alongside​​the​​story​​that​​is​
​told​ ​to​ ​pupils​ ​which​ ​focuses​ ​on​ ​the​​present,​​the​​initiative's​​teachings​​and​​discussion​​points​
​also​​provided​​historical​​context​​(p.​​32)​​and​​supporting​​resources​​to​​educate​​students​​on​​this​
​subject.​

​4)​     ​Jews, and their perception as White, creates invisibility and tension.​

​As​​mentioned​​in​​the​​review​​of​​literature,​​97%​​of​​British​​Jews​​in​​the​​UK​​classified​​themselves​
​as​ ​White​ ​(Office​ ​for​ ​National​ ​Statistics,​ ​2001),​ ​which​​has​​created​​a​​perception​​that​​all​​Jews​
​are​ ​White.​ ​Additionally,​ ​Jews​ ​are​ ​often​ ​perceived​ ​as​ ​difficult​ ​to​ ​identify​ ​unless​ ​they​ ​are​
​wearing​ ​a​ ​religious​ ​identifier,​ ​which​​can​​make​​their​​presence​​less​​visible​​in​​certain​​contexts​
​(Baddiel,​ ​2021).​ ​In​ ​Chapter​ ​5​ ​of​ ​the​ ​novel,​ ​the​ ​main​ ​character​ ​discovers​ ​that​ ​his​ ​friend​
​Marcus​ ​is​​Jewish,​​saying​​“How​​would​​I​​know?​​You​​don’t​​look​​Jewish”​​(p.28).​​This​​discussion​
​point​​has​​been​​crafted​​into​​the​​story​​to​​emphasise​​the​​notion​​that​​not​​all​​Jewish​​people​​have​
​the​​same,​​traditional​​image​​that​​is​​typically​​associated​​with​​Hasidic,​​Orthodox​​Jews​​(Baddiel,​
​2021;​ ​Rubin,​​2020),​​and,​​although​​97%​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community​​have​​regarded​​themselves​
​as​​White,​​the​​community​​can​​be​​diverse​​in​​terms​​of​​ethnic​​and​​racial​​backgrounds​​(Office​​for​
​National Statistics, 2001).​

​5)​     ​Jews’ political and economic power is hyperbolic.​

​The​​tenet​​that​​Jews’​​political​​and​​economic​​power​​is​​hyperbolic​​is​​addressed​​within​​Chapter​
​6,​​whereby​​the​​main​​character​​attends​​a​​football​​match​​and​​hears​​a​​range​​of​​discriminatory​
​phrases​​(p.​​34).​​These​​phrases​​support​​Rubin’s​​(2020)​​and​​Kofta​​et​​al​’s​​(2020)​​comments​​that​
​Jews​ ​are​ ​currently​ ​thought​ ​to​ ​control​ ​excessive​ ​amounts​ ​of​ ​political​ ​and​ ​economic​ ​power.​
​One​​phrase​​refers​​to​​the​​hyperbolic​​economic​​power​​that​​the​​Jewish​​community​​is​​perceived​
​to​ ​be​ ​“Greedy​ ​money-grabbing​ ​Yids”.​​The​​quote​​used​​within​​the​​story​​has​​been​​taken​​from​
​real​ ​abuse​ ​that​ ​Tottenham’s​ ​Jewish​​chairman,​​Daniel​​Levy,​​has​​received​​from​​opposing​​fans​
​(Ferrer,​​2013).​​In​​addition,​​34%​​hold​​views​​that​​Jews​​wield​​too​​much​​power​​in​​global​​financial​



                                                           ​156​
​markets​ ​(Anti-Defamation​ ​League,​ ​2020),​ ​which​ ​is​ ​still​ ​a​ ​common​ ​stereotype​ ​about​ ​the​
​Jewish​ ​community​ ​(Kofta​ ​et​ ​al.,​ ​2020;​ ​Rubin,​ ​2020).​ ​Therefore,​ ​within​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​the​
​teacher​ ​is​ ​guided​ ​to​ ​lead​ ​a​ ​discussion,​ ​and​ ​then​ ​inform​ ​children​ ​why​ ​such​ ​phrases​ ​are​
​antisemitic, and how references to economic and political power can be offensive.​

​6)​     ​Jewish personal stories have value.​

​When​ ​developing​ ​the​ ​first​ ​draft​ ​of​ ​the​​book,​​it​​was​​essential​​to​​utilise​​the​​stories​​of​​Jewish​
​individuals.​ ​Like​ ​the​ ​key​ ​tenet​ ​of​ ​CRT,​ ​sharing​ ​the​ ​stories​ ​of​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​faced​ ​by​ ​the​
​Jewish​ ​community​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​in​ ​the​ ​hope​ ​of​ ​reducing​ ​antisemitic​ ​attitudes​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020).​
​Solórzano​ ​and​ ​Bernal​ ​(2001)​ ​emphasise​ ​that​ ​in​ ​cultures​ ​where​ ​prejudice​ ​is​ ​common,​
​storytelling​ ​has​ ​great​ ​significance.​ ​Additionally,​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​campaigns​ ​like​ ​Chelsea​
​FC's​ ​‘Say​ ​No​ ​To​​Antisemitism’​​campaign,​​which​​used​​the​​experiences​​of​​Holocaust​​survivors​
​to​​educate​​others,​​have​​demonstrated​​the​​value​​of​​re-telling​​stories.​​The​​value​​of​​storytelling​
​within​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​and​​its​​significant​​contribution​​to​​others'​​understanding​​of​​life​
​narratives​ ​and​ ​the​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Holocaust,​​has​​been​​highlighted​​by​​Patti​​(2014)​
​and​​Schiff​​et​​al.​​(2012),​​among​​others.​​Therefore,​​the​​stories​​within​​the​​book​​are​​built​​upon​
​some​​personal​​stories​​of​​those​​experts​​from​​the​​Jewish​​charities​​and​​organisations​​(Phase​​1),​
​and​​those​​stories​​which​​are​​seen​​more​​predominantly​​within​​the​​media​​(Curtis,​​2019;​​Ferrer,​
​2013).​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​the​ ​chants​ ​and​ ​phrases​ ​which​ ​are​ ​aimed​ ​towards​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​
​that​​are​​seen​​in​​papers​​and​​online​​are​​included​​on​​p.​​34​​(Clavane,​​2012;​​Poulton​​and​​Durell,​
​2016).​ ​Furthermore,​ ​as​ ​mentioned​ ​previously,​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​the​ ​stories​ ​remain​ ​authentic​
​and​ ​reflective​ ​of​ ​the​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​have​ ​been​
​utilised​​at​​a​​later​​stage​​of​​this​​research​​(Phase​​3).​​Through​​these​​focus​​groups,​​individuals​​can​
​either​ ​confirm​ ​that​ ​the​ ​stories​ ​accurately​ ​reflect​ ​their​​lives​​or​​provide​​additional​​narratives​
​that could be embedded into the story.​

​7)​     ​Jews are a racialised group.​

​Finally,​ ​Jews​ ​are​ ​a​ ​racialised​ ​group.​ ​As​ ​mentioned​ ​previously,​​although​​it​​is​​rightfully​​noted​
​that​ ​Judaism​ ​is​ ​a​ ​religion​ ​(Zauzamer,​ ​2019),​ ​there​ ​is​ ​also​ ​continued​ ​debate​ ​as​ ​to​ ​whether​
​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​biological​ ​component​ ​to​ ​being​ ​Jewish​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020).​ ​Therefore,​ ​Rubin​ ​(2020)​
​argues​​that​​Jews​​are​​a​​racialised​​group​​and​​subsequently​​should​​be​​studied​​in​​racial​​studies.​



                                                             ​157​
​However,​​this​​is​​a​​tenet​​that​​has​​not​​been​​deeply​​embedded​​into​​the​​story,​​as​​the​​researcher​
​felt​ ​that​ ​this​ ​notion​ ​may​ ​be​ ​too​ ​complex​ ​to​ ​embed​ ​for​ ​children​ ​aged​ ​10-11.​​Nevertheless,​
​discussions​ ​of​ ​race​ ​and​ ​racism​ ​(p.​ ​9),​ ​alongside​ ​religion​ ​and​​religious​​discrimination​​(p.​​32)​
​take​ ​place​ ​within​ ​the​ ​story,​ ​and​ ​conversations​ ​on​ ​this​ ​topic​ ​can​ ​be​ ​brought​ ​to​ ​attention​
​through​​the​​discussion​​points​​which​​are​​provided​​to​​the​​instructor​​who​​would​​then​​be​​able​
​to explore this with the children further.​

​Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​interview​ ​data​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​teaching​ ​the​ ​younger​
​generation​ ​the​ ​skills​ ​to​ ​become​ ​assertive​ ​bystanders.​ ​The​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​creating​​assertive​
​bystanders​ ​has​ ​been​ ​articulated​ ​in​ ​the​ ​earlier​ ​stage​ ​of​ ​this​ ​thesis​ ​in​ ​the​ ​literature​ ​review​
​section.​​By​​using​​BIM,​​people​​can​​learn​​and​​be​​empowered​​to​​become​​‘assertive​​bystanders’​
​rather​ ​than​ ​‘passive​​bystanders’​​(Public​​Health​​England,​​2020;​​Salmivalli​​et​​al.​,​​1996).​​It​​is​​a​
​practical​​strategy​​that​​allows​​individuals​​to​​investigate,​​appropriately,​​ways​​to​​combat​​violent​
​and​ ​negative​ ​behaviours​ ​(Cissner,​ ​2009).​ ​An​ ​assertive​ ​bystander​ ​is​ ​one​ ​who​ ​sends​ ​a​
​significant​​message​​about​​the unacceptability​​of​​the​​problematic​​situation​​(Fenton​​and​​Mott,​
​2017).​

​Within​​the​​book,​​the​​main​​character​​witnesses​​both​​discrimination​​and​​bullying.​​At​​first​​the​
​character​ ​is​ ​not​ ​certain​ ​whether​​they​​should​​intervene;​​but​​then,​​with​​the​​teachings​​of​​the​
​importance​ ​of​ ​being​ ​an​ ​active​ ​bystander,​ ​he​ ​then​ ​is​ ​able​ ​to​ ​intervene​ ​(pg.​ ​34).​ ​Previous​
​research​ ​by​ ​Polanin​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2012)​ ​examined​​the​​importance​​of​​using​​the​​BIM​​in​​educational​
​settings,​ ​similar​ ​to​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​ ​the​ ​environment​ ​in​ ​which​ ​this​ ​initiative​ ​will​ ​be​
​implemented.​ ​Their​ ​findings​ ​indicated​ ​that​ ​students​ ​who​ ​participated​ ​in​ ​the​ ​intervention​
​training​ ​were​ ​more​ ​likely​ ​to​ ​take​ ​action​ ​in​ ​bullying​ ​situations.​ ​Alike​ ​Polanin​​et​​al.​​(2012),​​a​
​variety​ ​of​ ​academic​ ​literature​ ​has​ ​investigated​ ​how​ ​it​​can​​be​​used​​to​​prevent,​​minimise,​​or​
​lessen​ ​bullying​ ​(Jenkins​ ​and​ ​Nickerson,​ ​2017,​​2019;​​Nickerson​​et​​al.,​​2014).​​As​​a​​result,​​this​
​demonstrated​​the​​benefits​​of​​applying​​the​​model​​to​​the​​content​​of​​the​​book.​​Therefore,​​the​
​stories​ ​and​ ​teachings​ ​within​ ​these​ ​chapters​ ​will​ ​help​ ​to​ ​inform​ ​the​ ​readers​ ​around​ ​the​
​importance​ ​of​ ​being​ ​an​ ​active​ ​bystander.​​Within​​the​​final​​chapter,​​children​​will​​be​​assigned​
​the​ ​task​ ​of​ ​finishing​ ​off​ ​the​ ​story​ ​(pg.​ ​47).​ ​It​ ​is​ ​anticipated​ ​and​ ​hoped​ ​that,​ ​with​ ​effective​
​instruction,​​the​​kids​​will​​remember​​the​​lessons​​of​​the​​BIM​​and​​make​​reference​​to​​it​​in​​their​
​final chapter.​



                                                                ​158​
​Chapter summary​

​In​​conclusion,​​CNF​​has​​been​​utilised​​in​​this​​research​​to​​develop​​the​​first​​draft​​(Appendix​​I)​​of​
​an​ ​educational​ ​resource​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​teach​​children​​about​​antisemitism​​through​​the​​lens​​of​
​sport.​​Research​​found​​that​​CNF​​has​​been​​used​​as​​a​​tool​​in​​sport​​research,​​offering​​a​​nuanced​
​approach​ ​to​ ​storytelling​ ​that​ ​engages​ ​readers​ ​but​ ​also​ ​fosters​ ​a​ ​deeper​ ​understanding​ ​of​
​complex​​issues​​within​​the​​field​​(Smith,​​2013;​​Smith​​et​​al​.,​​2013).​​This​​chapter​​explored​​how​
​CNF​​was​​employed​​to​​develop​​an​​educational​​initiative​​for​​children​​aged​​10-11,​​using​​a​​sport​
​as​ ​a​ ​medium​ ​to​ ​promote​ ​engagement​ ​and​ ​discussion.​ ​The​ ​narratives​ ​were​ ​guided​ ​by​
​interview​ ​data,​ ​providing​ ​authentic​ ​guidance​ ​when​ ​developing​ ​the​ ​stories,​ ​while​ ​also​
​integrating​ ​relevant​ ​theories​ ​such​ ​as​ ​CRT​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001),​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​
​2020)​ ​and​ ​BIM​ ​(Latané​ ​and​ ​Darley,​ ​1970).​ ​These​ ​theoretical​ ​frameworks​ ​were​ ​crucial​ ​in​
​shaping​ ​the​ ​narratives,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​they​ ​reflected​ ​real-world​ ​issues.​ ​This​ ​approach​ ​has​
​enabled​ ​the​​integration​​of​​real-world​​experiences​​and​​theoretical​​frameworks,​​ensuring​​the​
​content is both engaging and educational, while also addressing a critical social issue.​

​The​​next​​chapter​​focuses​​on​​the​​methods​​employed​​in​​the​​third​​phase​​of​​the​​research,​​which​
​involved​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​with​ ​participants​ ​from​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​This​ ​allowed​ ​the​
​researcher​​to​​evaluate​​whether​​the​​stories​​resonated​​with​​their​​lived​​experiences.​​This​​step​
​was​ ​crucial​ ​in​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​employing​ ​CNF​ ​allowed​​the​​narratives​​to​​be​​both​​relevant​​and​
​impactful​​for​​the​​intended​​audience,​​while​​also​​accurately​​reflecting​​the​​lived​​experiences​​of​
​the community.​




                                                         ​159​
​Chapter 7 - Phase 3 methods - Focus group interviews​


​Introduction​


​The​ ​focus​ ​of​ ​discussion​ ​will​ ​now​ ​move​ ​onto​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​of​ ​the​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​process​ ​which​
​involved​​the​​completion​​of​​focus​​groups.​​For​​the​​purpose​​of​​this​​research,​​focus​​groups​​were​
​employed​​to​​gain​​feedback​​on​​the​​draft​​book​​for​​the​​initiative​​(Appendix​​I).​​Focus​​groups​​are​
​a​​common​​tool​​for​​gathering​​qualitative​​data,​​and​​they​​are​​especially​​popular​​in​​sociological​
​research​ ​(Braun​ ​and​ ​Clarke,​ ​2013;​ ​Brett​ ​and​ ​Wheeler,​​2021;​​Morgan,​​1996a).​​The​​term​​has​
​been​ ​defined​ ​by​ ​Acocella​ ​and​ ​Cataldia​ ​(2020,​ ​p.​ ​4)​ ​as​ ​“a​ ​non-standard​ ​technique​ ​for​
​information​​gathering​​based​​on​​an​​apparently​​informal​​discussion​​among​​a​​group​​of​​people​
​selected​ ​on​ ​the​ ​basis​ ​of​ ​specific​ ​characteristics,​ ​outlined​ ​for​ ​the​ ​cognitive​ ​purposes​ ​of​ ​the​
​research”.​ ​By​ ​voicing​ ​their​ ​thoughts​ ​or​ ​hearing​ ​others’​ ​opinions,​ ​participants​ ​can​ ​gain​ ​a​
​better​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​both​ ​their​ ​own​ ​perspectives​ ​and​ ​those​ ​of​ ​others.​ ​Reflecting​ ​and​
​evaluating​ ​opinions​ ​during​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​allows​ ​participants​ ​to​ ​articulate​ ​their​ ​thoughts​
​(Teufel-Shone and Williams, 2010).​


​Gray​​(2022)​​discusses​​the​​importance​​of​​feedback​​gained​​through​​focus​​groups​​for​​schemes​
​which​ ​could​ ​be​ ​used​​to​​promote​​a​​positive​​message​​or​​prototypes​​of​​products.​​In​​addition,​
​Acocella​ ​and​ ​Cataldi​ ​(2020)​ ​assert​ ​that​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​are​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​study​ ​social​
​representations,​ ​which​ ​aligns​ ​with​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​of​ ​this​ ​project​ ​to​​explore​​these​​representations​
​through​ ​the​​use​​of​​feedback.​​This​​feedback​​is​​a​​critical​​component​​in​​developing​​a​​product,​
​programme,​ ​or​​initiative,​​as​​it​​enables​​the​​researcher​​to​​gain​​valuable​​insights​​into​​people's​
​beliefs​ ​and​ ​perceptions​ ​of​ ​the​ ​concept​ ​(Gray,​ ​2022).​ ​Additionally,​ ​this​​format​​also​​provides​
​researchers​ ​with​ ​a​ ​better​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​the​ ​differences​ ​and​ ​similarities​ ​among​ ​certain​
​populations (Zacharakis​​et al.​, 2011).​


​Alongside​ ​the​ ​work​​of​​Gray​​(2022),​​experts​​from​​the​​Phase​​1​​interviews​​also​​acknowledged​
​that​​feedback​​was​​a​​crucial​​instrument​​for​​assessing​​the​​effectiveness​​of​​an​​initiative,​​as​​well​
​as​​learning​​the​​strengths​​and​​limitations​​of​​the​​project.​​For​​example,​​MacIntosh​​and​​Martin​
​(2018)​​who​​utilised​​the​​RISE​​initiative,​​found​​through​​feedback​​that,​​although​​students​​found​
​that​ ​the​ ​topic​ ​and​ ​resources​ ​were​ ​not​ ​as​ ​informative​ ​and​ ​engaging​ ​as​ ​they​ ​could​​be,​​they​


                                                            ​160​
​concluded​ ​that​ ​with​ ​certain​ ​amendments,​ ​the​ ​RISE​ ​initiative​ ​could​ ​have​ ​potential.​ ​This​
​highlights​ ​how​ ​feedback​​when​​developing​​anti-discrimination​​initiatives​​is​​essential​​to​​learn​
​what​ ​amendments​ ​are​ ​needed​ ​to​ ​give​ ​the​ ​project​ ​more​ ​potential.​ ​For​ ​the​ ​purpose​ ​of​​this​
​research, focus groups were used to trial the educational initiative which was developed.​


​Focus​​groups​​are​​useful​​in​​encouraging​​individuals​​to​​participate​​in​​a​​discussion,​​commenting​
​on​ ​the​ ​study​ ​topic​ ​by​ ​reflecting​ ​on​ ​their​ ​own​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​points​ ​of​ ​view​ ​(Powell​ ​and​
​Single,​ ​1996).​ ​Focus​ ​groups​ ​have​ ​also​ ​been​ ​referred​ ​to​ ​as​ ​group​ ​interviews,​ ​as​ ​they​ ​are​
​effectively​ ​interviews​ ​which​ ​involve​ ​more​ ​participants​ ​(Kamberelis​ ​and​ ​Dimitriadis,​ ​2013).​
​They​ ​often​ ​involve​ ​a​ ​group​ ​of​ ​people​ ​containing​ ​between​ ​four​ ​to​ ​eight​ ​participants​ ​(Gray,​
​2022;​ ​Jones​ ​and​ ​Gratton,​ ​2015).​ ​Like​ ​interviews,​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​is​ ​guided​ ​and​ ​interactive​
​(Powell​ ​and​ ​Single,​ ​1996).​ ​Focus​ ​groups​ ​have​ ​the​ ​advantage​ ​of​ ​gaining​ ​a​ ​large​ ​volume​ ​of​
​in-depth​ ​qualitative​ ​data,​ ​alongside​ ​exploring​ ​a​ ​range​ ​of​ ​topics​ ​which​ ​generate​ ​a​ ​range​ ​of​
​different​ ​viewpoints​ ​(Hennick,​ ​Hutter​ ​and​ ​Bailey,​ ​2020;​ ​Smith,​ ​2010).​ ​Due​ ​to​ ​the​​nature​​of​
​the​ ​focus​ ​group,​ ​large​ ​quantities​ ​of​ ​data​ ​can​ ​be​ ​collected​ ​over​ ​a​ ​shorter​ ​period​ ​of​ ​time​
​(Langdridge and Hagger-Johnson, 2009).​


​Focus​​groups​​have​​been​​used​​by​​a​​variety​​of​​academics​​in​​the​​field​​of​​sport,​​including​​Slater​
​and​ ​Tiggemann​ ​(2010),​​who​​held​​six​​focus​​groups​​with​​girls​​between​​the​​ages​​of​​13​​and​​15​
​years​​to​​better​​understand​​the​​reasons​​behind​​the​​decline​​in​​girls'​​participation​​in​​sports​​and​
​physical​ ​activity​ ​and​ ​to​ ​compare​ ​it​ ​to​ ​boys'​ ​involvement​ ​in​ ​these​ ​activities.​ ​Likewise,​​focus​
​groups​ ​were​ ​used​ ​by​ ​Ireland​ ​and​ ​Watkins​ ​(2010)​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​attitudes​ ​of​ ​football​ ​fans​
​regarding​ ​diet​ ​and​ ​the​​food​​options​​served​​at​​football​​stadiums.​​They​​stated​​how​​the​​focus​
​groups​ ​provided​ ​greater​ ​discussion​ ​and​ ​increased​ ​level​ ​of​​interaction​​within​​the​​debate​​on​
​attitudes​ ​towards​ ​food​ ​and​ ​healthy​ ​lifestyles.​ ​More​ ​specifically​ ​within​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport​
​sociology,​ ​Phipps​ ​(2019)​ ​conducted​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​with​ ​LGBT+​ ​people​ ​and​ ​LGBT+​ ​officers​ ​at​
​universities​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​barriers​​to​​participation​​within​​university​​sport​​for​​trans​​people.​​The​
​data​ ​from​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​found​ ​that​ ​further​ ​action​ ​is​ ​required​ ​within​​university​​sport​​to​
​make​​sure​​that​​it​​is​​inclusive​​to​​all.​​Likewise,​​Van​​Sterkenburg​​and​​Peeters​​(2019)​​conducted​
​five​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​to​ ​learn​ ​more​ ​about​ ​how​ ​Dutch​ ​viewers​ ​perceive​ ​race​ ​and​ ​ethnicity​ ​in​
​televised​​football.​​Focus​​groups​​were​​carefully​​chosen​​for​​their​​study​​because​​they​​offered​​a​
​good representation of the context in which football fans often watch and discuss games.​


                                                            ​161​
​Literature​ ​on​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​highlight​ ​that​ ​these​ ​groups​ ​are​ ​an​ ​effective​ ​method​ ​within​
​qualitative​​research,​​as​​they​​enable​​the​​collection​​of​​individual​​viewpoints​​on​​a​​specific​​issue,​
​particularly​ ​by​ ​fostering​ ​increased​ ​interaction​ ​between​ ​participants​ ​and​ ​encouraging​ ​more​
​in-depth​ ​discussion.​ ​Another​ ​core​ ​strength​ ​of​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​is​ ​their​​ability​​to​​offer​​a​​setting​
​where​​participants​​may​​discover​​they​​are​​not​​alone​​when​​tackling​​certain​​delicate​​challenges​
​(Goldman,​ ​1962).​ ​In​ ​this​ ​study,​ ​which​ ​addresses​ ​discrimination,​ ​this​ ​is​ ​a​ ​key​ ​strength,​​as​​it​
​helps​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​participants​​do​​not​​feel​​isolated​​in​​their​​experiences,​​fostering​​a​​sense​​of​
​shared understanding and support.​


​Although​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​can​ ​be​ ​a​ ​beneficial​ ​tool​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​gather​ ​large​ ​quantities​ ​of​ ​data​
​there​​are​​concerns​​that​​participants​​with​​dominant​​personalities​​will​​lead​​the​​discussion​​and​
​persuade​​others​​in​​the​​group​​to​​agree​​with​​their​​point​​of​​view​​(Bloor,​​2001).​​Subsequently,​​it​
​is​​important​​to​​be​​mindful​​of​​the​​group​​dynamics​​within​​the​​groups.​​In​​addition,​​focus​​groups​
​can​ ​prove​ ​difficult​ ​when​ ​recording​ ​and​ ​transcribing​ ​the​ ​data​​set.​​As​​a​​result,​​it​​is​​critical​​to​
​have​ ​a​ ​facilitator​ ​who​ ​is​ ​experienced​ ​and​ ​capable​ ​of​ ​managing​ ​the​ ​groups​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​
​everyone​​is​​involved​​but,​​also,​​a​​facilitator​​who​​can​​ensure​​that​​participants​​are​​not​​speaking​
​over one another (Langdridge and Hagger-Johnson, 2009).​

​Strategies​ ​for​ ​handling​ ​and​ ​managing​ ​these​ ​potential​ ​limitations​ ​were​ ​taken​ ​into​
​consideration​​by​​ensuring​​that​​the​​focus​​groups​​were​​led​​by​​the​​researcher,​​who​​acted​​as​​a​
​skilled​ ​facilitator.​ ​The​ ​researcher​ ​possesses​ ​experience​ ​in​ ​managing​ ​group​ ​dynamics​
​effectively,​ ​encouraging​ ​equal​ ​participation​ ​from​ ​all​ ​members,​ ​and​ ​preventing​ ​any​ ​one​
​individual​ ​from​ ​dominating​ ​the​ ​discussion.​ ​This​ ​dual​ ​role​ ​allowed​ ​for​ ​both​ ​effective​
​facilitation​ ​and​ ​a​ ​deeper​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​the​ ​data​ ​being​ ​collected.​ ​To​ ​address​ ​the​
​challenges​ ​of​ ​recording​ ​and​ ​transcribing​ ​the​ ​data,​ ​multiple​ ​recording​ ​devices​​were​​used​​to​
​ensure​​accuracy​​and​​minimise​​the​​risk​​of​​missed​​information.​​Additionally,​​participants​​were​
​reminded​ ​of​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​respectful​ ​dialogue,​ ​allowing​ ​for​ ​a​ ​balanced​ ​exchange​ ​of​
​ideas.​​By​​implementing​​these​​strategies,​​the​​research​​aimed​​to​​create​​an​​environment​​where​
​all​​participants​​felt​​comfortable​​sharing​​their​​perspectives,​​while​​also​​ensuring​​that​​the​​data​
​collected was detailed, reliable, and comprehensive.​




                                                             ​162​
​Phase 3 - Ethical considerations​

​An​ ​additional​ ​application​ ​for​ ​ethical​ ​clearance​ ​was​ ​submitted​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Oxford​ ​Brookes​ ​UREC​
​prior​ ​to​ ​participant​ ​recruitment.​​In​​addition​​to​​the​​earlier​​ethical​​considerations​​mentioned​
​in​​Chapter​​4,​​such​​as​​the​​need​​to​​protect​​the​​participants​​identity​​and​​informing​​participants​
​about​ ​the​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​the​ ​study​ ​(DiCicco-Bloom​ ​and​ ​Crabtree,​ ​2006;​ ​Langdridge​ ​and​
​Hagger-Johnson,​​2009),​​there​​were​​some​​additional​​ethical​​considerations​​that​​needed​​to​​be​
​taken​​into​​account​​due​​to​​the​​nature​​of​​the​​focus​​groups.​​Firstly,​​as​​Gray​​(2022)​​and​​Hennink​
​(2013)​​noted,​​it​​can​​be​​challenging​​to​​maintain​​anonymity​​when​​conducting​​focus​​groups.​​As​
​a​ ​result,​ ​confidentiality​ ​can​ ​only​ ​be​ ​guaranteed​ ​within​ ​limited​ ​parameters​ ​that​ ​would​ ​be​
​made​ ​clear​ ​in​ ​the​ ​consent​ ​form​ ​(Smith,​ ​1995).​ ​It​ ​was​ ​crucial​ ​that​ ​only​ ​first​ ​names​ ​were​
​utilised​ ​during​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​and​ ​that​ ​no​ ​other​ ​directly​ ​identifiable​ ​information,​​such​​as​
​the​​name​​of​​the​​organisation​​or​​school​​that​​they​​represent,​​was​​used​​(Acocella​​and​​Cataldia,​
​2020;​ ​Carey​ ​and​ ​Asbury,​ ​2016).​ ​Similarly,​ ​it​ ​can​ ​be​ ​challenging​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​what​ ​is​ ​said​
​within​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​does​ ​not​ ​go​ ​beyond​ ​the​ ​group,​ ​which​​can​​create​​ethical​​challenges​
​(Morgan​​et​​al.​,​​1998).​​To​​try​​and​​prevent​​this,​​participants​​agreed​​to​​maintain​​the​​anonymity​
​of the data shared by all participants and researchers throughout the focus group session.​


​Participants​


​Like​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​interviews,​ ​participants​ ​were​ ​recruited​ ​using​ ​a​ ​purposeful​ ​sampling​
​technique​​to​​recruit​​those​​participants​​with​​relevant​​experiences​​and​​knowledge.​​As​​seen​​in​
​Table​ ​3,​ ​participants​​were​​split​​into​​3​​categories.​​These​​categories​​were​​titled,​​‘members​​of​
​the Jewish community’, ‘school educators’ and ‘anti-discrimination experts’.​

 ​Focus group/​         ​Definition​                                                                 ​Number of​

​Table​ ​3.​ ​Table​ ​including​ ​definitions​ ​and​ ​sample​ ​of​ ​the​ ​participants​ ​recruited​ ​for​ ​data​
​collection.​

​As​ ​highlighted​ ​by​ ​Powell​ ​and​ ​Single​ ​(1996)​ ​it​ ​is​ ​critical​ ​that​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​participants​ ​share​
​essential​ ​characteristics​ ​or​ ​traits​ ​that​ ​are​ ​relevant​ ​to​ ​the​ ​study.​ ​In​ ​this​ ​research,​ ​it​ ​was​
​essential​ ​to​ ​learn​ ​about​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​the​ ​three​ ​groups:​ ​educators,​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community,​​and​​anti-discrimination​​experts.​​The​​feedback​​from​​these​​groups​​were​​crucial​​as​
​it​ ​was​ ​important​​to​​understand​​educators'​​opinions​​on​​the​​potential​​impact​​the​​book​​could​
​have,​​alongside​​understanding​​whether​​the​​stories​​are​​reflective​​of​​the​​experiences​​of​​Jewish​
​community.​ ​The​ ​feedback​ ​from​ ​experts​ ​also​​has​​significance,​​as​​these​​individuals​​are​​those​
​who have knowledge of developing such initiatives.​

​Members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community​​were​​essential​​participants​​for​​the​​focus​​groups,​​as​​prior​
​findings​​from​​the​​expert​​interviews​​indicated​​that​​any​​initiative​​needed​​to​​be​​guided​​by​​the​
​perspectives​ ​and​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​the​ ​marginalised​ ​community.​ ​Therefore,​ ​their​ ​input​ ​was​
​crucial​ ​in​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​was​ ​both​ ​relevant​ ​and​ ​reflected​ ​the​ ​true​ ​needs​ ​and​
​concerns​​of​​the​​community.​​This​​also​​resonates​​with​​the​​arguments​​of​​CRT​​and​​HebCrit,​​with​
​both​ ​theories​ ​containing​ ​tenets​ ​which​ ​highlight​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​storytelling​ ​and​
​articulating​ ​the​ ​stories​ ​of​ ​the​ ​marginalised​ ​community.​ ​CRT​ ​reinforces​ ​that​ ​the​ ​notion​ ​of​
​storytelling​ ​enables​ ​individuals​ ​who​​have​​been​​racially​​discriminated​​against​​and​​previously​
​silenced​ ​to​ ​communicate​ ​their​ ​lived​ ​experience​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001).​ ​Similarly,​



                                                             ​164​
​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020)​ ​finds​ ​value​ ​in​ ​storytelling​ ​as​ ​it​ ​improves​ ​the​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​life​
​narratives,​ ​particularly​ ​those​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​this,​ ​by​ ​articulating​
​their​ ​stories,​ ​individuals​ ​from​ ​these​ ​communities​ ​provide​ ​rich,​ ​qualitative​ ​data​ ​which​ ​will​
​then​​be​​used​​through​​CNF.​​This​​approach​​allows​​for​​the​​authentic​​voices​​and​​experiences​​of​
​the​​community​​to​​be​​captured​​in​​a​​way​​that​​is​​compelling​​to​​the​​reader,​​ensuring​​that​​their​
​narratives​​are​​reflected​​in​​the​​story.​​Therefore,​​through​​abductive​​reasoning​​it​​was​​crucial​​to​
​take​ ​into​ ​account​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​communities​ ​opinions,​ ​as​ ​this​ ​will​ ​guarantee​ ​that​​the​​project​
​reflects the community.​

​Focus​ ​groups​ ​with​ ​school​​educators​​were​​also​​conducted​​for​​the​​purpose​​of​​this​​study.​​The​
​participants​​in​​these​​groups​​were​​either​​teachers​​or​​teaching​​assistants​​(TAs),​​as​​the​​initiative​
​was​ ​designed​ ​with​ ​the​ ​intention​ ​that​ ​both​ ​teachers​​and​​TAs​​would​​play​​a​​role​​in​​delivering​
​the​​programme.​​These​​educators​​were​​integral​​to​​understanding​​how​​the​​initiative​​could​​be​
​implemented​ ​in​ ​a​ ​school​ ​setting.​ ​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​their​ ​role​ ​in​ ​delivering​ ​the​ ​programme,​
​teachers​ ​and​ ​TAs​ ​add​ ​significant​ ​value​ ​to​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​by​ ​providing​ ​insights​ ​into​ ​the​
​practical​ ​aspects​ ​of​ ​implementing​ ​educational​ ​initiatives.​ ​Their​ ​experience​ ​in​ ​managing​
​diverse​ ​classroom​ ​environments​ ​allows​ ​them​ ​to​ ​offer​ ​valuable​ ​perspectives​ ​on​ ​how​ ​to​
​engage​ ​students​ ​effectively​ ​with​ ​sensitive​ ​topics,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​discrimination.​
​The​ ​final​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​consisted​ ​of​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts​ ​who​ ​had​ ​previously​
​participated​ ​in​ ​the​ ​interviews.​ ​These​ ​participants​ ​were​ ​particularly​ ​skilled​ ​in​ ​creating​
​initiatives​ ​within​ ​sport​ ​to​ ​combat​ ​discrimination,​ ​and​ ​their​ ​insights​ ​were​ ​crucial​​in​​shaping​
​the effectiveness of the proposed programme.​

​Initially,​​participants​​who​​were​​either​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community​​or​​educators​​were​
​recruited​ ​via​ ​social​ ​media,​ ​including​ ​Facebook,​ ​LinkedIn​ ​and​ ​Twitter.​ ​On​ ​the​ ​3rd​ ​February​
​2023,​ ​adverts​ ​were​ ​also​ ​placed​ ​on​ ​social​ ​media​ ​to​ ​gain​​participants​​(Appendix​​J).​​With​​the​
​increased​​use​​of​​social​​media​​platforms,​​researchers​​explored​​ways​​to​​utilise​​social​​media​​as​
​a​​promising​​method​​for​​identifying​​and​​recruiting​​potential​​participants​​for​​research​​projects​
​(Gearhart,​​2015).​​Four​​participants​​were​​recruited​​via​​social​​media;​​however,​​due​​to​​a​​lack​​of​
​interest,​ ​institutions,​ ​synagogues,​ ​and​ ​schools​ ​were​ ​contacted​ ​to​ ​take​ ​part​ ​in​ ​the​ ​research​
​through​ ​their​ ​institutional​ ​email​ ​addresses.​ ​Educators​ ​noted​ ​that,​ ​at​ ​the​ ​time​ ​of​ ​data​




                                                           ​165​
​collection,​​staff​​members​​faced​​limited​​time​​and​​increased​​pressures​​due​​to​​the​​shortage​​of​
​teaching staff and were therefore unable to participate.​

​Nevertheless,​ ​as​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​Table​ ​3,​ ​twelve​ ​primary​ ​school​ ​teachers​ ​were​ ​recruited​ ​and​ ​nine​
​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community​​were​​recruited.​​Additionally,​​four​​of​​the​​14​​experts​​who​
​took​​part​​in​​the​​initial​​interview​​in​​2021​​were​​involved​​in​​this​​round​​of​​data​​collection.​​Only​
​28%​​of​​participants​​were​​retained​​to​​take​​part,​​since​​the​​original​​experts​​had​​either​​changed​
​roles​ ​or​ ​organisation​​and​​were​​no​​longer​​contactable,​​had​​initially​​declined​​to​​be​​contacted​
​for​ ​a​ ​follow-up​ ​interview,​ ​or​ ​were​ ​short​ ​on​ ​time.​ ​Overall,​​25​​participants​​were​​recruited​​to​
​take​ ​part​ ​in​ ​providing​ ​feedback​ ​on​ ​the​ ​draft​ ​initiative​ ​(Table​ ​3).​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​Appendix​ ​K​
​contains​​vignettes​​for​​this​​round​​of​​data​​collection,​​which​​contain​​brief​​descriptions​​of​​each​
​participant​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​context​ ​on​ ​their​ ​roles.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​it​ ​should​ ​be​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​some​
​participants​ ​fell​ ​into​ ​more​ ​than​ ​one​ ​category​ ​(i.e.​ ​educator,​ ​Jewish,​​expert);​​therefore,​​this​
​has​​been​​highlighted​​within​​the​​vignettes​​to​​provide​​a​​clearer​​understanding​​of​​their​​diverse​
​roles and perspectives within the study.​

​Krueger​ ​and​ ​Casey​ ​(2002)​ ​suggest​ ​that​ ​typically​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​normally​ ​have​ ​five​ ​to​ ​eight​
​participants,​​and​​the​​work​​of​​Thomas,​​Frankland​​and​​Bloor​​(2000)​​suggests​​that​​focus​​groups​
​can​ ​range​ ​from​ ​numbers​ ​as​ ​small​ ​as​ ​three​ ​to​ ​fourteen.​ ​With​ ​that​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​the​ ​number​ ​of​
​participants​​in​​each​​group​​has​​been​​shown​​in​​Table​​4.​​Literature​​from​​Kieffer​​et​​al.​​(2005)​​and​
​Krueger​ ​(2014)​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​smaller​​groups​​are​​often​​more​​productive,​​as​​they​​provide​​more​
​time​ ​and​ ​opportunity​ ​for​ ​each​ ​participant​ ​to​ ​discuss​ ​their​ ​thoughts​ ​and​ ​opinions.​
​Additionally,​ ​smaller​ ​groups​ ​allow​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​to​ ​easily​ ​manage​ ​the​ ​active​ ​discussions​
​(Morgan, 1996b).​

​It​ ​should​ ​be​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​some​ ​participants​ ​chose​ ​not​ ​to​ ​participate​ ​in​ ​a​ ​focus​ ​group,​ ​but​
​individual​ ​interviews,​ ​owing​ ​to​ ​time​ ​constraints,​ ​a​ ​desire​ ​to​ ​remain​ ​anonymous​ ​and​ ​keep​
​their​​feedback​​confidential,​​or​​simply​​because​​it​​was​​their​​personal​​decision.​​The​​majority​​of​
​participants​ ​who​ ​did​ ​not​ ​take​ ​part​​in​​a​​focus​​group​​were​​the​​experts​​as​​it​​was​​not​​deemed​
​suitable,​ ​due​ ​to​ ​their​ ​similar​ ​lines​ ​of​ ​work.​ ​As​ ​a​​result,​​the​​researcher​​primarily​​used​​focus​
​groups​ ​to​ ​get​ ​feedback,​ ​but​ ​also​ ​conducted​ ​individual​ ​and​ ​paired​ ​interviews​ ​and,​ ​in​ ​one​
​instance,​ ​received​ ​responses​ ​via​ ​email.​ ​Limitations​ ​for​ ​having​ ​individual​ ​interviews​ ​and​




                                                            ​166​
​smaller​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​have​ ​been​ ​considered,​ ​given​ ​that​ ​Thomas​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2000)​ ​states​ ​that​
​smaller focus groups can equate to limited discussion.​

                                                         ​167​
​Procedure​


​Before​ ​beginning​ ​any​ ​data​ ​collection,​​participants​​were​​provided​​with​​an​​information​​sheet​
​(Appendix​ ​L)​ ​and​ ​a​ ​GDPR​ ​privacy​ ​notice​ ​(Appendix​ ​M).​ ​Those​ ​who​ ​expressed​ ​interest​ ​in​
​participating​​were​​then​​asked​​to​​sign​​a​​consent​​form​​(Appendix​​N).​​Once​​all​​participants​​had​
​consented​ ​to​ ​participate,​ ​they​ ​were​ ​then​ ​given​ ​the​ ​proposed​ ​initiative,​ ​‘Joe’s​ ​Footballing​
​Journey’,​ ​via​ ​email,​ ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​read​ ​through​ ​before​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​group.​ ​Once​ ​participants​ ​had​
​read through the initiative, a focus group or interview date was arranged with participants.​

​The​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​stage​ ​began​ ​with​ ​the​ ​first​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​on​ ​the​ ​4th​ ​May​ ​2023,​ ​and​
​concluded​ ​on​ ​15th​ ​September​ ​2023.​ ​Focus​ ​groups​ ​were​ ​conducted​ ​both​ ​online​ ​and​ ​in​
​person,​​ensuring​​a​​secure​​location​​for​​both​​researchers​​and​​participants.​​Kitzinger​​(1994)​​and​
​Langdridge​​and​​Hagger-Johnson​​(2009)​​highlight​​the​​importance​​of​​employing​​activities​​and​
​techniques​ ​before​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​questions​ ​to​ ​establish​ ​rapport​​among​​participants.​​Rapport,​
​as​ ​defined​ ​by​ ​Hennink,​ ​Hutter​​and​​Bailey​​(2020,​​p.​​330),​​is​​“a​​relationship​​of​​trust​​between​
​an​​interviewer​​and​​interviewee​​that​​creates​​a​​comfortable​​environment​​for​​an​​interviewee​​to​
​share​ ​their​ ​experiences​ ​openly”.​ ​While​ ​this​ ​definition​ ​underscores​ ​the​ ​value​ ​of​
​rapport-building​​in​​interviews,​​it​​is​​equally​​important​​for​​focus​​group​​participants​​to​​establish​
​rapport​ ​with​ ​one​ ​another.​ ​Carey​ ​(1995)​ ​further​​suggests​​that​​identifying​​similarities​​among​
​participants​ ​can​ ​strengthen​ ​rapport​ ​and​ ​foster​ ​group​ ​trust,​ ​making​ ​it​ ​a​ ​crucial​ ​step​ ​in​ ​the​
​data​ ​gathering​ ​process.​ ​To​ ​facilitate​​this,​​the​​focus​​groups​​were​​organised​​with​​attention​​to​
​shared​ ​characteristics,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​religion​ ​and​ ​career,​ ​to​ ​help​ ​build​ ​rapport​ ​and​ ​create​ ​a​
​comfortable, trusting environment for discussion.​

​Once​​rapport​​was​​established,​​feedback​​on​​the​​initiative​​was​​sought​​through​​the​​process​​of​​a​
​focus​​group.​​This​​data​​was​​collected​​by​​asking​​participants​​questions​​(Appendix​​O)​​regarding​
​their​ ​opinions​​on​​the​​initiative.​​Hennink​​et​​al.​​(2020)​​advises​​using​​a​​discussion​​guide​​when​
​conducting​ ​focus​ ​groups;​ ​this​ ​is​ ​similar​ ​to​ ​an​ ​interview​ ​guide​​containing​​key​​questions​​and​
​topics​ ​to​ ​discuss.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​it​​is​​essential​​that​​questions​​are​​carefully​​designed;​​a​​‘funnel’​
​approach​​was​​recommended​​by​​Morgan​​(1996b).​​This​​entails​​using​​introductory​​questions​​to​
​gain​ ​a​​basic​​understanding​​and​​then​​narrowing​​down​​to​​the​​core,​​key​​questions.​​Therefore,​
​within​​these​​focus​​group​​participants​​were​​asked​​a​​range​​of​​questions​​(Appendix​​O).​​First,​​a​



                                                            ​168​
​list​​of​​general​​questions​​was​​provided,​​which​​were​​open​​to​​all​​participants,​​regardless​​of​​the​
​focus​​group​​they​​were​​in.​​Following​​this,​​a​​set​​of​​tailored​​questions​​were​​created​​to​​address​
​the​ ​specific​ ​requirements​ ​of​ ​the​ ​participants​ ​in​ ​each​ ​chosen​ ​group.​ ​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​these​
​pre-written​ ​questions,​ ​the​ ​semi-structured​​nature​​of​​the​​focus​​group​​allowed​​for​​additional​
​questions​​to​​be​​asked​​based​​on​​the​​initial​​responses​​provided​​by​​the​​participants.​​The​​focus​
​groups​​lasted​​between​​51​​and​​74​​minutes,​​while​​the​​individual​​interviews​​ranged​​from​​37​​to​
​58 minutes.​

​Thematic analysis​


​Once​​the​​focus​​groups​​were​​complete,​​the​​data​​sets​​were​​transcribed​​and​​analysed.​​The​​data​
​was​ ​then​ ​analysed​ ​using​ ​TA​ ​to​ ​identify​ ​areas​ ​for​ ​improvement​ ​and​ ​key​ ​strengths​ ​of​ ​the​
​proposed​ ​initiatives.​ ​TA​ ​was​ ​employed​ ​to​ ​examine​ ​the​ ​qualitative​ ​information​ ​that​ ​was​
​produced​ ​as​​a​​result​​of​​the​​focus​​groups.​​The​​process​​of​​TA​​has​​been​​outlined​​previously​​in​
​Chapter​ ​4​ ​(see​ ​p.111);​​and​​as​​was​​previously​​said,​​TA​​is​​a​​useful​​method​​for​​analysing​​large​
​data​ ​sets​ ​(Guest,​ ​MacQueen​ ​and​ ​Namey,​ ​2012).​ ​Specifically,​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​Hecker​ ​and​
​Kalpokas​ ​(2024)​ ​states​ ​that​ ​TA​ ​is​ ​a​ ​valuable​ ​approach​ ​in​​qualitative​​research,​​especially​​for​
​analysing​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​data.​ ​It​ ​allows​ ​researchers​ ​to​ ​identify,​​examine,​​and​​report​​recurring​
​patterns​ ​in​ ​the​ ​data,​ ​offering​ ​meaningful​​interpretations​​of​​the​​diverse​​perspectives​​shared​
​by​ ​participants.​ ​Therefore,​ ​using​ ​this​ ​type​ ​of​ ​analysis​​to​​examine​​the​​focus​​group​​data​​sets​
​was​ ​appropriate.​ ​While​ ​analysing​ ​the​ ​data,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​adhered​ ​to​ ​the​ ​six​ ​key​ ​steps​
​outlined​​by​​Braun​​and​​Clarke​​(2006)​​as​​seen​​in​​Figure​​1.​​The​​first​​step​​was​​to​​become​​familiar​
​with​​the​​data.​​Next,​​the​​researcher​​generated​​initial​​codes,​​followed​​by​​searching​​for​​themes​
​within​ ​the​​data.​​After​​identifying​​these​​potential​​themes,​​the​​researcher​​reviewed​​them​​for​
​coherence​ ​and​ ​relevance.​ ​The​ ​themes​ ​were​ ​then​ ​defined​ ​in​ ​more​ ​detail​ ​to​ ​clarify​ ​their​
​meaning.​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​this​ ​process,​ ​six​ ​themes​ ​were​ ​developed,​ ​which​ ​are​ ​presented​ ​in​
​Table 5. Finally, the researcher wrote up the findings based on the analysed data (Chapter 8).​

                                                      ​170​
​Chapter 8 - Phase 3 - Results and discussion​

​Introduction​


​As​ ​mentioned​​in​​the​​previous​​chapter,​​six​​themes​​were​​identified​​and​​constructed​​after​​the​
​focus​​groups​​and​​interviews​​with​​anti-discrimination​​experts,​​educators,​​and​​members​​of​​the​
​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​These​​themes,​​along​​with​​several​​sub-themes,​​are​​presented​​in​​Table​​5.​
​Consequently,​ ​this​ ​chapter​ ​is​ ​structured​ ​into​ ​six​ ​sections,​ ​each​ ​focusing​ ​on​ ​one​ ​of​ ​these​
​themes​ ​in​ ​greater​​detail,​​and​​concluding​​with​​a​​summary​​of​​how​​each​​theme​​will​​influence​
​the​ ​initiative's​ ​development.​ ​Before​ ​delving​ ​into​ ​the​ ​key​ ​findings​ ​of​ ​the​ ​third​ ​phase,​ ​it​ ​is​
​important​ ​to​ ​highlight​ ​that​ ​throughout​ ​this​ ​chapter,​ ​references​ ​are​ ​made​ ​to​ ​previous​
​literature​ ​on​ ​other​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination,​ ​educational​ ​resources​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​combat​
​various​ ​prejudices,​ ​and​ ​personal​ ​narratives​ ​from​ ​other​ ​marginalised​ ​groups.​ ​Although​ ​the​
​experiences​ ​may​​differ,​​these​​sources​​remain​​valuable​​to​​this​​research,​​as​​they​​often​​reflect​
​shared​ ​underlying​ ​themes​ ​of​ ​oppression.​ ​Recognising​ ​these​ ​commonalities​ ​provides​ ​a​
​broader​ ​perspective​ ​on​​the​​challenges​​faced​​by​​marginalised​​groups​​and​​the​​strategies​​that​
​can be used to address them.​


​Theme 1 - Recommended additions​


​Gray​​(2022)​​discusses​​the​​value​​in​​gaining​​feedback​​through​​focus​​groups​​for​​the​​promotion​
​of​ ​a​ ​prototype​ ​or​ ​product,​ ​and​ ​subsequently,​ ​the​ ​first​ ​theme​ ​was​ ​titled​ ​‘recommended​
​additions’​,​​a​​theme​​that​​highlighted​​recommendations​​made​​by​​participants​​which​​should​​be​
​considered​ ​when​ ​amending​ ​the​ ​draft​ ​book.​ ​In​ ​this​ ​research,​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​and​ ​interviews​
​were​​used​​to​​gain​​feedback​​on​​the​​draft​​copy​​of​​the​​children's​​book,​​due​​to​​their​​popularity​
​in​​sociological​​research​​(Braun​​and​​Clarke,​​2013;​​Brett​​and​​Wheeler,​​2021)​​and​​the​​ability​​to​
​allow​ ​participants​ ​to​ ​share​ ​their​ ​knowledge​ ​and​ ​experiences.​ ​Specifically,​ ​the​ ​focus​​groups​
​allowed​ ​for​ ​a​ ​group​ ​of​ ​people​ ​to​ ​be​ ​selected​ ​on​ ​the​ ​basis​ ​of​ ​their​ ​specific​ ​characteristics​
​(Acocella​ ​and​ ​Cataldia,​ ​2020),​ ​these​ ​being,​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​ ​educators,​ ​and​
​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​Focus​ ​groups​ ​gave​ ​opportunity​ ​for​ ​suggestions​ ​to​ ​be​
​made​ ​and​ ​subsequently​ ​adopted​​as​​amendments.​​Within​​this​​theme,​​both​​additions​​to​​the​
​storyline​ ​(Table​ ​6),​ ​and​ ​pedagogical​ ​additions​ ​(Table​ ​7)​ ​were​ ​recommended​ ​by​ ​the​


                                                             ​171​
​participants.​ ​Therefore,​ ​the​ ​sub-themes​ ​were​ ​titled​ ​‘additional​ ​storylines’​​and​​‘pedagogical​
​additions’.​
