​A​ ​selection​ ​of​ ​these​ ​recommendations​ ​were​ ​implemented,​ ​when​ ​the​ ​book​ ​was​ ​revised;​
​nevertheless,​ ​as​ ​Keagan​ ​made​ ​his​ ​recommendation​ ​-​ ​“you​ ​know,​ ​you​ ​could​ ​talk​ ​about​ ​the​
​synagogue​​having​​a​​football​​team…”​​-​​he​​also​​emphasised​​the​​significance​​of​​being​​selective​
​and​​avoiding​​“contriving​​something​​for​​the​​sake​​of​​trying​​to​​shoehorn​​it​​in”.​​Therefore,​​it​​was​
​essential​ ​to​ ​assess​ ​the​ ​number​ ​of​ ​changes​ ​made​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​they​ ​were​ ​suitable​ ​for​ ​the​
​storyline​​and​​context,​​rather​​than​​accepting​​all​​of​​them​​without​​question.​​Similarly,​​in​​Table​​7​
​practical​​additions​​were​​discussed,​​and​​offered​​by​​participants;​​these​​too​​were​​selected​​with​
​careful​​consideration.​​The​​table​​above​​shows​​which​​storyline​​recommendations​​were​​added;​
​those​ ​with​ ​a​ ​page​​number,​​indicate​​that​​they​​were​​implemented​​into​​the​​amended​​version​
​of the book (Appendix P). However, the following amendments have been expanded upon:​


    ​1)​ ​A female role model​


​As​ ​discussed​ ​in​ ​the​ ​later​ ​part​ ​of​ ​this​ ​chapter,​​in​​Theme​​4,​​titled​​‘football​​as​​an​​educational​
​tool’​,​ ​women’s​ ​football​ ​is​ ​gaining​ ​considerable​ ​popularity​ ​(Griffin​ ​et​ ​al.,​ ​2020​;​ ​Williams,​
​2003).​​Nevertheless,​​the​​importance​​of​​female​​role​​models,​​particularly​​in​​football,​​has​​been​
​recognised​ ​by​ ​players,​ ​academics​ ​(Allison,​ ​Culvin​ ​and​ ​Pope,​ ​2024;​ ​Dunn,​ ​2018)​ ​and​
​participants​ ​from​ ​this​ ​research,​ ​which​ ​heightened​ ​the​ ​need​ ​to​ ​create​ ​a​ ​female​ ​role​ ​model​
​within​ ​the​ ​book.​​In​​doing​​so,​​there​​is​​hope​​that​​young​​children,​​particularly​​young​​girls,​​are​
​inspired​​and​​will​​develop​​the​​confidence​​to​​participate​​and​​continue​​taking​​part​​in​​sport.​​For​
​the​ ​purpose​ ​of​ ​teaching​ ​young​ ​children​ ​about​ ​antisemitism,​ ​a​ ​female​ ​role​​model​​may​​also​
​encourage​ ​young​ ​children​ ​to​ ​continue​ ​reading​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​ ​increase​ ​their​ ​level​ ​of​
​engagement.​ ​In​​addition,​​academic​​research​​has​​shown​​how​​football​​has​​been​​perceived​​to​
​be​ ​a​ ​male-dominated​ ​sport​ ​(Clark​ ​and​ ​Paechter,​ ​2007;​ ​Jakubowska,​ ​Antonowicz​ ​and​



                                                            ​174​
​Kossakowski,​​2020).​​However,​​as​​Keagan​​discusses,​​the​​power​​of​​having​​a​​female​​role​​model​
​in​ ​the​ ​story​ ​not​ ​only​ ​inspires​ ​young​ ​girls​ ​and​ ​boys​ ​to​ ​participate​ ​in​ ​sport,​​but​​helps​​young​
​children​​to​​think​​differently​​about​​the​​stereotypes​​that​​are​​associated​​with​​football,​​such​​as​​it​
​being​ ​a​ ​sport​ ​for​ ​boys​ ​and​ ​men​ ​only.​ ​Literature​ ​from​ ​Ronkainen,​ ​Ryba​ ​and​​Selänne​​(2019)​
​found​ ​that​ ​young​ ​men​ ​often​ ​chose​ ​well-known​ ​athletes​ ​as​ ​their​ ​role​ ​models,​ ​while​ ​young​
​women​​were​​more​​reflective,​​and​​selected​​role​​models​​based​​on​​biographical​​similarities,​​for​
​example,​​a​​mother​​or​​grandmother.​​Therefore,​​by​​having​​a​​female​​role​​model​​in​​the​​story,​​it​
​not​​only​​challenges​​gender​​stereotypes​​but​​also​​encourages​​young​​girls​​to​​see​​themselves​​as​
​capable​ ​athletes​ ​in​ ​a​ ​space​ ​traditionally​ ​dominated​ ​by​ ​men.​ ​The​ ​integration​ ​of​ ​the​​female​
​role​​model​​can​​be​​seen​​on​​p.​​4​​of​​the​​amended​​book,​​whereby​​Joe​​opens​​up​​his​​programme​
​and​ ​reads​ ​about​ ​the​ ​upcoming​ ​games,​​which​​includes​​Bradstock​​Rovers​​Women​​Team​​who​
​are​​top​​of​​the​​League.​​In​​addition,​​alongside​​Khan​​(Zara’s​​role​​model),​​there​​is​​also​​mention​
​of Zara’s female role model later on, on p. 12.​


         ​2)​​Subtle integration of other forms of discrimination.​


​In​ ​the​ ​first​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​(expert​ ​interviews),​ ​a​ ​sub-theme​ ​that​​was​​constructed​
​was​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​should​ ​have​ ​a​ ​‘broad-to-narrow’​ ​structure.​ ​Given​ ​this,​ ​the​
​draft​ ​book​ ​starts​ ​with​ ​discussions​ ​around​ ​discrimination​ ​more​ ​broadly,​ ​then​ ​focuses​ ​on​
​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​Judaism.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​some​ ​participants​ ​acknowledged​ ​that​​there​​could​
​be​ ​an​ ​increase​ ​in​ ​possible​ ​discussions​ ​around​ ​other​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination,​ ​specifically​
​Islamophobia.​​Although​​teachings​​of​​all​​form’s​​discrimination​​are​​highly​​important,​​the​​aims​
​and​ ​intentions​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​are​ ​that​ ​students​ ​learn​ ​more​ ​about​ ​Judaism​ ​and​ ​antisemitism,​
​therefore​​it​​was​​deemed​​that​​the​​draft​​version​​allows​​for​​significant​​discussions​​to​​take​​place​
​and​ ​additional​ ​stories​ ​are​ ​not​ ​required.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​Keagan’s​ ​recommendation​ ​was​
​creative​​and​​was​​one​​that​​would​​be​​realistic​​to​​the​​story;​​therefore,​​it​​was​​decided​​to​​subtly​
​embed​​a​​part​​where,​​after​​the​​initial​​incident​​takes​​place,​​in​​Chapter​​5​​Zara​​talks​​to​​Noah,​​as​
​a​​friend,​​who​​has​​also​​faced​​discrimination​​in​​the​​past​​for​​being​​Muslim​​(p.​​27).​​She​​mentions​
​to​​Noah​​that​​she​​told​​a​​teacher​​what​​happened,​​because​​all​​schools​​will​​have​​rules​​against​​all​
​types​ ​of​ ​discrimination.​ ​This​ ​not​ ​only​ ​integrates​ ​other​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination,​ ​but​ ​also​
​teaches​ ​children​ ​the​ ​value​ ​in​ ​talking​ ​to​ ​someone,​ ​preferably​ ​an​ ​adult,​ ​about​ ​bullying​ ​and​
​discrimination, which aligns with the teachings of the BIM.​


                                                             ​175​
​Pedagogical additions​


         ​When​​I​​think​​about​​a​​resource,​​I​​think​​of​​all​​the​​ways​​that​​are​​more​​likely​​to​​get​
         ​it​​delivered.​​How​​can​​I​​make​​it​​such​​that​​it​​is​​much,​​much​​simpler​​for​​someone​
         ​to​ ​say,​ ​"we​ ​can​ ​pick​ ​this​ ​up,​ ​and​ ​I​ ​can​ ​deliver​ ​this?​ ​Matthew​ ​(Development​
         ​Officer)​


​Matthew’s​ ​comment​ ​above​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​need​ ​to​ ​adapt​ ​a​ ​resource​ ​to​ ​increase​ ​the​
​likelihood​ ​that​ ​staff​ ​members​ ​will​​feel​​confident​​enough​​to​​teach​​it.​​Therefore,​​pedagogical​
​additions​​have​​been​​provided,​​to​​ensure​​that​​it​​would​​practically​​work​​within​​schools.​​During​
​the​ ​focus​ ​groups,​ ​members​ ​of​ ​staff​ ​were​ ​asked​ ​if​ ​the​ ​resources​ ​provided​ ​(book​ ​and​
​discussion​ ​points)​ ​were​ ​sufficient,​ ​to​ ​which​ ​Carly​ ​responded​​with​​“maybe​​have​​at​​the​​back​
​further​ ​suggestions…​ ​just​ ​so​ ​there's​ ​just​ ​some​ ​other​ ​ideas​ ​that​ ​they​ ​can​ ​do​ ​just​​to​​extend​
​learning”.​ ​This​ ​idea​ ​was​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​other​ ​members​ ​of​ ​staff​ ​who​ ​liked​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​of​ ​some​
​“extra​ ​activities”,​ ​as​ ​these​ ​additional​ ​tasks​ ​would​ ​give​ ​greater​ ​impact.​ ​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​this,​
​Keagan recommended:​


       ​…have​​a​​sliding​​scale.​​Really​​easy​​for​​the​​schools​​that​​want​​to​​do​​something,​​but​
       ​haven't​​got​​the​​time​​or​​are​​a​​bit​​lazy,​​and​​then​​to​​the​​schools​​that​​really​​want​​to​
       ​go for it, you’ve got the works… and maybe put in some contacts.​


​With​​that​​in​​mind,​​a​​resource​​pack​​was​​created​​for​​teachers​​(Appendix​​Q),​​which​​includes​​a​
​list of activities the schools can do to extend their learning about Judaism; this includes:​

​Table​ ​7.​ ​Pedagogical​ ​recommendations​ ​and​ ​suggested​ ​additions​ ​to​ ​enhance​ ​the​​initiative's​
​effectiveness.​

​In​ ​the​ ​same​ ​way​ ​that​ ​the​ ​story​​line​​changes​​were​​carefully​​considered,​​it​​was​​important​​to​
​select​ ​the​ ​pedagogical​ ​suggestions​ ​thoughtfully,​ ​avoiding​ ​overwhelming​ ​the​ ​users​ ​of​ ​the​
​educational​​resource​​with​​too​​many​​options.​​The​​need​​for​​a​​glossary​​of​​key​​terms​​was​​made​
​clear​ ​from​​the​​offset,​​with​​members​​of​​staff​​highlighting​​that​​there​​were​​specific​​terms​​and​
​language​ ​within​ ​the​ ​book​ ​that​ ​even​ ​they,​ ​as​ ​adults,​ ​were​ ​not​​aware​​of.​​Likewise,​​Matthew​



                                                         ​179​
​went​ ​on​​to​​discuss​​the​​importance​​of​​a​​glossary,​​stating​​that​​“if​​you've​​done​​that​​as​​part​​of​
​the resource, it enhances the resource”. In his role, he elaborated that he:​

       ​…commissioned​ ​one​ ​of​ ​the​ ​boys​ ​who​ ​works​ ​for​ ​me​ ​to​ ​do​ ​a​ ​glossary​ ​of​ ​terms​
       ​around​ ​sectarianism.​ ​For​ ​the​ ​last​ ​10​ ​years,​ ​the​ ​most​ ​downloaded​ ​document​​of​
       ​the​ ​Organisation​ ​Name​ ​website​ ​on​ ​the​ ​government​ ​webpage​ ​has​ ​been​ ​that​
       ​glossary.​

​This​ ​comment​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​significance​ ​of​ ​a​ ​glossary,​ ​noting​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​when​
​educating people about specific types of discrimination.​

​Alongside,​ ​the​ ​addition​ ​of​ ​imagery​ ​and​ ​a​ ​glossary,​ ​the​ ​following​ ​practical​ ​activities​ ​were​
​advised,​ ​using​ ​a​ ​sliding​ ​scale​ ​which​ ​allows​ ​educators​ ​using​ ​the​ ​resources​ ​decide​ ​whether​
​they​ ​wish​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​in​ ​further​ ​activities​ ​or​ ​not.​ ​Some​ ​of​ ​these​​pedagogical​​additions​​have​
​been​​discussed​​in​​greater​​depth;​​however,​​others​​have​​been​​provided​​as​​learning​​enrichment​
​tasks​​for​​staff​​and​​students​​to​​connect​​with​​the​​wider​​community​​and​​discourses.​​This​​can​​be​
​seen in the resource pack (Appendix Q):​

    ​1)​ ​Class based tasks and provide links to additional resources and webpages:​


​Pedagogical​ ​additions​ ​might​ ​include​ ​class-based​ ​tasks,​ ​which​ ​may​​involve​​a​​research​​based​
​task​ ​exploring​ ​what​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​or​ ​social​ ​inclusion​ ​initiative​ ​their​ ​own​ ​teams​ ​are​
​involved​ ​in.​ ​Likewise,​ ​Matthew​​recommended​​an​​activity,​​known​​as​​the​​circle​​of​​influences,​
​which he explains further:​

         ​And​​then​​what​​you​​can​​do​​is​​you​​can​​go​​and​​look​​at​​the​​character​​in​​the​​book.​
         ​And​ ​your​ ​main​ ​character​ ​you​ ​could​ ​talk​ ​about​ ​so​ ​here's​ ​a​ ​list​ ​of​ ​his​ ​main​
         ​influences.​​So,​​it's​​got​​his​​grandad,​​his​​mom,​​his​​pal,​​the​​boy​​Noah​​that​​he​​has​
         ​just​ ​met,​ ​this​​school,​​changing​​school​​and​​getting​​them​​to​​arrange​​it​​to​​what​
         ​circle they think has influenced him the most.​

​Likewise,​ ​class​ ​based​ ​activities​ ​could​ ​include​ ​accessing​ ​additional​ ​resources​ ​and​ ​webpages​
​(such​ ​as​ ​BBC​ ​Bitesize)​ ​to​ ​allow​ ​children​ ​to​ ​increase​ ​their​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​religious​
​backgrounds,​​whereby​​teachers​​could​​set​​research-based​​tasks​​for​​in-class​​and​​independent​


                                                            ​180​
​learning.​​Therefore,​​additional​​web​​pages​​have​​been​​provided​​as​​suggestions​​for​​members​​of​
​staff.​

     ​2)​ ​Promotion of interfaith activities​

​Alongside​ ​class-based​ ​activities,​ ​teachers​ ​could​ ​develop​ ​religious​ ​and​ ​inter-faith​
​understanding​ ​through​ ​hosting​ ​intra-school​ ​collaborations​ ​and​ ​external​ ​activities.​
​Intra-school​ ​activities​ ​might​ ​involve​ ​bringing​ ​together​ ​other​ ​schools​ ​with​ ​different​
​demographics​​to​​develop​​relationships,​​similar​​to​​a​​project​​that​​Keagan​​did​​as​​part​​of​​his​​role​
​as EDI Manager:​

           ​We​​had​​the​​Faith​​in​​Football​​projects​​at​​Wembley,​​where​​we​​brought​​Catholic,​
           ​Jewish,​​and​​Muslim​​schools​​together​​one​​day​​a​​week​​for​​about​​2​​months.​​So,​​all​
           ​the​ ​kids​ ​which​ ​I​ ​think​​were​​about​​this​​age,​​they​​all​​did​​activities​​for​​half​​a​​day​
           ​together​ ​and​ ​it​ ​was​ ​really​ ​interesting​ ​because​ ​I​ ​just​ ​did​ ​stuff​ ​about​ ​Wembley​
           ​and​ ​about​ ​football​ ​and​ ​then​ ​they​ ​sort​ ​of​ ​by​ ​the​ ​end​ ​realised​ ​“Oh,​ ​look!​ ​You​
           ​know​​you​​pray,​​and​​we​​pray,​​and​​it's​​quite​​similar,​​and​​look,​​our​​lunches​​aren’t​
           ​that different”, and by the end of it some of the schools twinned up.​

​Research​ ​from​ ​Chrysanthopoulos​ ​(2010)​ ​and​ ​Hemming​ ​(2011)​​highlights​​the​​importance​​of​
​developing​ ​religious​ ​and​ ​multicultural​ ​values​ ​in​ ​schools​ ​to​ ​foster​ ​tolerance,​ ​respect,​ ​and​
​understanding​ ​among​ ​diverse​ ​student​ ​populations.​ ​Additionally,​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​Wilson​
​(2012b)​​explored​​the​​‘the​​Dialogue​​Society’,​​a​​charitable​​organisation​​dedicated​​to​​promoting​
​social​ ​cohesion​ ​by​ ​fostering​ ​dialogue​ ​between​ ​communities​ ​across​ ​religious​ ​and​ ​cultural​
​divides.​ ​They​ ​found​ ​that​ ​it​ ​serves​ ​as​ ​a​ ​platform​ ​for​ ​individuals​ ​to​ ​share​ ​narratives​ ​and​
​perspectives,​ ​uncover​ ​shared​ ​values,​ ​and​ ​embrace​ ​their​ ​differences​ ​with​ ​mutual​
​understanding.​ ​Therefore,​ ​the​ ​recommendation​ ​to​ ​host​ ​a​ ​‘Religion’​ ​or​ ​‘Culture​ ​Day’​​would​
​allow​​schools​​to​​learn​​more​​about​​the​​diverse​​backgrounds​​of​​their​​students.​​This​​could​​help​
​children​ ​feel​ ​more​ ​comfortable​ ​with​ ​their​ ​own​ ​religion​ ​while​ ​encouraging​ ​the​ ​school​ ​to​
​create​​an​​environment​​where​​students​​can​​appreciate​​and​​learn​​about​​each​​other's​​cultures​
​(Hemming,​ ​2011).​ ​Furthermore,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​been​ ​suggested​ ​that​ ​schools​ ​celebrate​ ​religious​
​holidays​ ​alongside​ ​their​ ​students,​ ​with​ ​ideas​ ​such​ ​as​ ​incorporating​ ​foods​ ​related​ ​to​ ​those​
​occasions​ ​as​ ​a​ ​way​ ​to​ ​foster​ ​understanding​ ​and​ ​inclusivity.​ ​By​ ​using​ ​these​ ​resources​ ​to​



                                                              ​181​
​provide​ ​a​ ​space​ ​for​ ​shared​ ​experiences,​ ​children​ ​can​ ​relate​ ​to​ ​one​ ​another​ ​on​ ​a​ ​more​
​personal​ ​level.​ ​This​ ​will​ ​be​ ​further​ ​expanded​ ​upon​ ​in​ ​the​ ​sub-theme​ ​titled​ ​‘importance​ ​of​
​relatability.’​

​Schools​ ​might​ ​also​ ​have​ ​a​ ​greater​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​their​​use​​of​​resources​​by​​taking​​students​​to​​a​
​synagogue​ ​or​ ​Jewish​ ​museum,​​which​​would​​help​​them​​better​​comprehend​​the​​religion​​and​
​their​​beliefs.​​If​​children​​were​​to​​attend​​the​​synagogue,​​it​​would​​also​​help​​to​​put​​some​​of​​the​
​lessons​ ​they​ ​would​ ​have​ ​learned​ ​in​ ​the​ ​eighth​ ​chapter​ ​into​ ​practice.​ ​Schools​ ​have​ ​been​
​encouraged​​to​​consider​​getting​​in​​touch​​with​​organisations​​that​​present​​talks​​and​​assemblies,​
​such​​as​​the​​CST,​​The​​Anne​​Frank​​Trust​​and​​Jewish​​Museum​​London.​​These​​organisations​​will​
​have​ ​specialised​ ​training​ ​and​ ​expertise​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​religion,​ ​subsequently​ ​their​​skills​​and​
​knowledge​ ​could​ ​improve​ ​the​ ​effectiveness​ ​of​ ​the​ ​resource.​ ​Likewise,​ ​it​ ​would​ ​give​ ​the​
​children opportunities to ask questions they may have.​


​To​ ​conclude,​ ​having​ ​gathered​ ​data​ ​from​ ​a​ ​range​ ​of​ ​educators,​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​
​and​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​a​ ​variety​ ​of​ ​amendments​​were​​advised.​​These​​fell​
​into​ ​two​ ​categories;​ ​one​ ​being​ ​related​ ​to​ ​the​ ​storyline​ ​within​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​ ​the​ ​other​ ​on​
​pedagogical​​approaches.​​The​​amendments​​highlighted​​in​​this​​theme​​focused​​on​​adjustments​
​to​ ​the​ ​storyline,​ ​along​ ​with​ ​pedagogical​ ​additions​ ​that,​ ​overall,​ ​were​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​enhance​
​the​​impact​​of​​educating​​young​​children​​about​​the​​topic​​of​​antisemitism.​​These​​amendments​
​can​​be​​seen​​in​​the​​amended​​copy​​of​​the​​book​​(Appendix​​P),​​and​​the​​resource​​pack​​for​​staff​
​(Appendix Q).​


​Theme 2 - Importance of relatability​


​This​ ​second​ ​theme​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​value​ ​of​ ​personal​ ​stories,​ ​providing​ ​an​ ​opportunity​ ​for​
​children​ ​to​ ​connect​ ​more​ ​deeply​ ​with​ ​the​ ​resource.​ ​Numerous​ ​sources,​ ​including​ ​Capuzza​
​(2020),​ ​Watson,​ ​Latter​ ​and​ ​Bellew​ ​(2015)​ ​and​ ​Van​ ​Horn​ ​(2015),​​reinforce​​the​​strength​​that​
​children's​ ​books​ ​can​ ​have,​ ​allowing​ ​them​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​who​ ​they​ ​are,​ ​and​​consider​​how​​they​
​can​ ​relate​ ​to​ ​others,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​a​ ​key​ ​theme​ ​which​ ​emerged​ ​through​ ​this​ ​stage​ ​of​ ​data​
​collection.​ ​This​ ​theme​ ​emphasises​ ​that​ ​personalising​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​for​ ​the​ ​reader​ ​helps​
​children​​engage​​with​​it​​more​​effectively,​​while​​fostering​​a​​stronger​​sense​​of​​self​​and​​empathy​


                                                            ​182​
​for​ ​others.​ ​It​ ​was​ ​first​ ​highlighted​ ​during​ ​the​ ​initial​ ​round​ ​of​ ​expert​ ​interviews​ ​in​ ​Phase​ ​1,​
​where​​the​​importance​​of​​relatability​​was​​stressed.​​As​​a​​result,​​it​​became​​a​​crucial​​element​​in​
​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​the​ ​draft​ ​book.​ ​The​ ​theme​ ​is​ ​further​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​sub-themes​ ​titled​
​‘reflective​ ​of​ ​lived​ ​experiences,’​ ​‘the​ ​characters,’​ ​and​ ​‘transferability,’​ ​all​ ​of​ ​which​ ​reinforce​
​the value of making the resource relatable and impactful.​


​Reflective of the lived experiences​


​When​​speaking​​to​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​it​​was​​crucial​​to​​determine​​whether​​the​​story​​was​
​representative​ ​of​ ​their​ ​experiences.​ ​This​ ​was​​crucial​​to​​ensure​​the​​authenticity​​of​​the​​story​
​and​ ​to​ ​support​ ​one​ ​of​ ​Rubin's​ ​(2020)​ ​key​ ​principles,​ ​which​ ​asserts​ ​that​ ​Jewish​ ​personal​
​experiences​ ​hold​ ​significance.​ ​This​ ​emphasises​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​relatability​ ​in​ ​raising​
​awareness​ ​about​ ​Judaism​ ​and​ ​combating​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Giving​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​a​ ​voice​ ​in​
​particular​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​in​ ​the​ ​effort​ ​to​ ​reduce​ ​antisemitic​​attitudes​​(Rubin,​​2020).​​The​​value​​of​
​presenting​ ​the​ ​stories​ ​of​ ​people​ ​of​ ​colour​ ​is​ ​also​ ​reinforced​ ​by​ ​a​ ​key​ ​tenet​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​since​​it​
​enables​ ​people​ ​to​ ​express​ ​and​ ​share​ ​their​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​in​ ​their​ ​own​ ​terms​ ​(Delgado,​
​1989; Solorzano and Yasso, 2002). Bethan (Educator) said:​


       ​I​​think​​Chapter​​5​​is​​the​​most​​influential,​​when​​Joe’s​​friend​​gets​​upset​​with​​him​​for​
       ​using​ ​‘Yiddo’​ ​and​ ​for​ ​saying​ ​I​​didn’t​​know​​you​​were​​Jewish.​​It’s​​a​​good​​teaching​
       ​moment for how influential the language we use can be.​


​In​ ​Chapter​ ​5,​ ​the​ ​moment​ ​Joe​ ​finds​ ​out​ ​Noah​​is​​Jewish​​(p.​​26)​​and​​says​​“I’m​​Sorry,​​Noah,​​I​
​didn’t​ ​know.​ ​How​ ​would​ ​I​ ​know?​ ​You​ ​don’t​ ​look​ ​Jewish”​ ​was​ ​a​ ​key​ ​moment​ ​that​ ​was​
​reflected during data collection; Brian (Jewish) draws upon the line:​


          ​Noah​ ​took​ ​offence​ ​when​ ​there​​was​​no​​offence​​meant,​​but​​that​​is​​so​​often​​the​
          ​case.​ ​“Oh,​ ​you​ ​don't​ ​look​ ​Jewish”​ ​like​ ​that​ ​is​ ​some​ ​sort​ ​of​​compliment?​​They​
          ​mean​ ​it​ ​as​ ​a​ ​compliment,​ ​and​ ​it's​ ​so​ ​un-complementary,​ ​and​​it's​​so​​lacking​​in​
          ​understanding. What does a Jewish person look like?​


​In addition, for Iris (Jewish), she felt this line was reflective of her own experiences:​


                                                               ​183​
       ​the​​little​​sort​​of​​quips​​of,​​‘oh,​​you​​don't​​look​​Jewish’​​all​​that​​sort​​of​​thing.​​That’s​
       ​something I have faced.​


​The​​phrase​​from​​Brian,​​“but​​that​​is​​so​​often​​the​​case”,​​reinforces​​that​​this​​section​​is​​reflective​
​of​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​given​ ​that​ ​Brian,​ ​and​ ​Iris,​ ​experienced​ ​this​ ​more​
​frequently​ ​than​ ​outsiders​ ​might​ ​consider.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​Brian​ ​also​​explores​​the​​idea​​that​​not​
​looking,​ ​what​ ​may​ ​be​ ​perceived​ ​to​ ​be,​ ​stereotypically​ ​Jewish,​ ​is​ ​often​ ​said​ ​in​ ​a​
​complimentary​ ​tone.​ ​This​ ​part​ ​of​ ​the​ ​story​ ​was​ ​intentionally​ ​constructed​ ​through​ ​the​
​embedment​​of​​a​​key​​tenet​​of​​HebCrit,​​which​​is​​the​​notion​​that​​Whiteness​​creates​​invisibility​
​(Rubin,​ ​2020).​ ​With​ ​97%​ ​of​ ​British​ ​Jews​ ​in​ ​the​​UK​​classifying​​themselves​​as​​White,​​there​​is​
​often​ ​a​ ​perception​ ​that​ ​they​ ​are​ ​not​ ​minorities​ ​and​ ​subsequently​ ​harder​ ​to​ ​identify.​
​However,​ ​this​ ​creates​ ​tension,​ ​as​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​the​ ​draft​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​and​ ​can​ ​sometimes​ ​be​
​challenging​ ​for​ ​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​as​​discussed​​by​​Leah.​​Leah​​reflects​​on​​a​
​personal​​experience​​when​​a​​university​​student​​told​​her,​​'I​​didn’t​​know​​what​​to​​do​​about​​you.​
​You’re​ ​White,​ ​but​ ​you're​ ​not​ ​one​ ​of​ ​us,​ ​you’re​ ​a​ ​Jew.'"​ ​This​ ​distasteful​ ​comment​ ​supports​
​Rubin’s​​(2020)​​argument​​about​​the​​invisibility​​of​​Jewishness,​​and​​it​​was​​crucial​​to​​reflect​​this​
​in​​the​​story.​​Dart​​(2021)​​also​​noted​​that​​Jews​​have​​historically​​been​​viewed​​as​​‘others,’​​with​
​antisemites​​perceiving​​them​​as​​non-White.​​Baddiel's​​(2021,​​p.31)​​comment​​further​​supports​
​this​ ​by​​pointing​​out​​that​​“Jews​​don't​​really​​suffer​​from​​being​​thought​​of​​as​​separate​​as​​long​
​as​ ​people​ ​don't​ ​realise,​ ​they're​ ​Jews”.​ ​This​ ​part​ ​of​ ​the​ ​draft​ ​book​ ​also​ ​created​ ​much​
​discussion​ ​with​ ​educators​ ​at​ ​SH​ ​School.​ ​Carly​ ​said​ ​“the​ ​fact​ ​that​ ​he's​ ​saying​ ​that​​he​​didn't​
​know​​you​​were​​Jewish,​​that​​shouldn’t​​have​​come​​into​​it​​anyway.​​You​​shouldn’t​​be​​saying​​it​​in​
​the​ ​first​ ​place,​ ​whether​ ​the​ ​person​ ​is​​Jewish​​or​​not.”​​Within​​this​​conversation,​​both​​Rachel​
​and​ ​Jasmine​ ​(Educators)​ ​also​ ​spoke​ ​about​ ​this​ ​line​ ​as​ ​they​ ​felt​ ​it​ ​had​ ​significant​ ​power,​
​specifically​ ​as​ ​they​ ​felt​ ​it​ ​was​ ​reflective​ ​of​ ​what​ ​some​ ​of​​the​​children​​they​​teach​​can​​often​
​experience, whether they are in Joe or Noah’s position.​


​As​​mentioned​​previously,​​it​​is​​essential​​that​​the​​book​​was​​reflective​​of​​the​​experiences​​of​​the​
​Jewish community, which was made evident through HebCrit (Rubin, 2020).​




                                                             ​184​
       ​I​ ​do​ ​have​ ​that​ ​memory​ ​of​ ​being​ ​told​ ​to​ ​go​ ​back​ ​to​ ​where​ ​you​ ​came​ ​from​ ​at​
       ​primary​ ​school​ ​and​ ​did​ ​not​ ​really​ ​understand​ ​what​ ​that​ ​meant.​ ​I​ ​talked​ ​to​ ​my​
       ​parents​​and​​obviously​​got​​an​​answer…​​I​​think​​it's​​still​​unfortunately​​possible​​that​
       ​that will happen in the primary school, in playgrounds. (Iris- Jewish)​


​Iris​ ​commented​ ​upon​ ​her​ ​experiences​ ​in​ ​primary​ ​school,​ ​nevertheless,​ ​Patrick​ ​(Jewish)​
​reflected​ ​and​ ​said​ ​that​ ​“antisemitism​ ​existed​ ​a​ ​bit​ ​for​ ​me​ ​at​ ​school”,​ ​suggesting​ ​a​ ​less​
​pronounced​ ​experience​ ​compared​ ​to​ ​Iris.​ ​In​ ​contrast,​ ​some​ ​Jewish​ ​participants​​stated​​that​
​their​ ​experiences​ ​were​ ​different,​ ​as​ ​they​ ​had​ ​never​ ​encountered​ ​antisemitism​​during​​their​
​childhood.​ ​They​ ​attended​ ​schools​ ​with​ ​like-minded​ ​peers,​ ​having​ ​grown​ ​up​ ​in​
​neighbourhoods​​where​​the​​majority​​of​​residents​​were​​Jewish.​​This​​was​​supported​​by​​Nancy’s​
​(Jewish,​ ​Educator)​ ​comment,​ ​“I​ ​would​ ​say​ ​if​ ​I​ ​asked​ ​the​ ​kids​ ​at​ ​my​ ​school,​ ​they​ ​probably​
​wouldn't​​know​​what​​antisemitism​​was​​let​​alone​​they​​have​​experienced​​it”.​​However,​​similarly​
​to​ ​Iris​ ​and​ ​Patrick,​ ​the​ ​children​ ​that​ ​Nancy​ ​is​ ​referring​ ​to​ ​attend​ ​a​ ​Jewish​ ​school​ ​and​ ​are​
​therefore​​unlikely​​to​​witness​​antisemitism​​in​​school.​​Furthermore,​​this​​raises​​the​​question​​of​
​whether,​ ​if​ ​children​ ​struggle​​to​​recognise​​or​​understand​​what​​antisemitism​​is,​​it​​necessarily​
​means they are not experiencing it.​


​Nevertheless,​​Nancy,​​Patrick,​​and​​Iris​​continued​​to​​reflect​​on​​how​​these​​experiences​​shaped​
​their​ ​children's​ ​upbringing,​ ​drawing​ ​connections​ ​to​ ​both​ ​recent​ ​events​ ​and​ ​their​ ​own​
​experiences​​as​​adults.​​Leah​​(Jewish,​​Educator)​​said​​that​​as​​she​​got​​older,​​she​​was​​faced​​with​
​significant antisemitic abuse:​


       ​Unfortunately,​​I​​then​​went​​on​​to​​work​​for​​UJS​​(The​​Union​​of​​Jewish​​Students).​​So,​
       ​you​​can​​imagine​​what​​I​​was​​subjected​​to​​when​​I​​worked​​for​​the​​UJS…​​I​​don't​​think​
       ​it will end here for Noah, it is quite true to life, unfortunately.​


​Leah's​​remark​​supports​​the​​idea​​that​​the​​story​​is​​representative​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community​​by​
​predicting​​that​​Noah​​will​​sadly​​continue​​to​​encounter​​antisemitism​​as​​he​​ages.​​Although​​both​
​Iris​​and​​Leah​​draw​​upon​​antisemitic​​incidents,​​which​​highlighted​​that​​the​​story​​is​​reflective​​of​
​some​​of​​the​​experiences​​Jewish​​individuals​​may​​face,​​Nancy​​(Jewish,​​Educator)​​also​​discusses​
​how​​the​​story​​is​​reflected​​through​​situational​​elements​​of​​the​​book​​including​​“that​​Noah​​had​


                                                              ​185​
​come​​to​​secondary​​school​​on​​his​​own,​​which​​I​​think​​is​​quite​​a​​common​​experience​​for​​Jewish​
​kids who have been to a Jewish Primary School schools”.​


​Using​ ​Latino​ ​CRT​ ​(LatCrit)​ ​as​ ​a​ ​framework,​ ​Solórzano​ ​and​ ​Bernal​ ​(2001)​ ​emphasise​ ​that​ ​in​
​cultures​ ​where​ ​prejudice​ ​is​ ​common,​ ​storytelling​ ​has​ ​great​ ​significance.​ ​They​ ​explore​ ​the​
​many​ ​benefits​ ​of​ ​storytelling,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​how​ ​it​ ​fosters​ ​community​ ​by​ ​demonstrating​ ​that​
​people​ ​are​ ​not​ ​alone​ ​in​ ​their​ ​experiences,​ ​how​ ​it​​gives​​people​​a​​context​​for​​understanding​
​and​ ​transforming​ ​pre-existing​ ​beliefs,​ ​and​ ​how​ ​it​ ​challenges​ ​people's​ ​apparent​ ​views.​ ​As​
​these​​personal​​narratives​​frequently​​validate​​the​​experiences​​of​​a​​minority​​community,​​both​
​the​ ​HebCrit​ ​and​ ​CRT​ ​theories​ ​emphasise​ ​the​ ​significance​ ​of​ ​storytelling​ ​and​ ​sharing​ ​with​
​experiences​​in​​either​​being​​Jewish​​or​​a​​person​​of​​colour​​(Delgado​​and​​Stefancic,​​2001;​​Rubin,​
​2020).​​Therefore,​​it​​was​​essential​​that​​the​​experiences​​of​​the​​children​​in​​the​​book​​were​​not​
​only​ ​reflective​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​but​ ​also​ ​of​ ​other​ ​marginalised​ ​communities,​
​including​​both​​the​​Muslim​​characters​​Khan​​and​​Zara.​​Likewise,​​when​​storytelling​​is​​used​​as​​a​
​teaching​ ​and​ ​learning​ ​approach,​ ​it​ ​allows​ ​children​ ​to​ ​share​ ​their​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​diversity​
​(Koening and Zorn, 2002). Chris (Jewish) discussed how the book:​


       ​introduced​ ​the​ ​Muslim​ ​player​ ​and​ ​the​ ​fact​​that​​he​​couldn't​​go​​through​​a​​whole​
       ​match​ ​because​ ​of​ ​Ramadan​ ​and​ ​I​​think​​that​​was​​great.​​You've​​introduced​​other​
       ​aspects of society.​


​In​ ​addition,​ ​there​ ​was​ ​reference​ ​to​ ​some​ ​structural​ ​challenges​ ​that​ ​football​ ​fans​ ​with​
​disabilities​​may​​face​​when​​going​​to​​football​​matches.​​Both​​Carly​​and​​Jasmine​​(Educators),​​felt​
​that​ ​it​ ​was​ ​brought​ ​into​ ​the​ ​story​ ​well​ ​to​ ​the​ ​extent​ ​that​ ​it​ ​was​ ​subtly​ ​embedded​ ​but​
​provided​ ​enough​ ​detail​ ​for​ ​discussion.​ ​These​ ​experiences​ ​were​ ​not​ ​reflective​ ​of​ ​a​ ​specific​
​individual​​lived​​experience,​​but​​were​​created​​using​​media-based​​experiences​​and​​data​​from​
​surveys​​conducted​​by​​other​​organisations,​​such​​as​​Level​​Playing​​Field,​​who​​work​​to​​improve​
​the match-day experience for all disabled sports fans.​




                                                           ​186​
​The characters​


       ​Books​ ​provide​ ​windows​ ​by​ ​which​ ​children​ ​can​ ​look​ ​outside​ ​of​ ​their​ ​own​
       ​experiences and live vicariously through others… (Prater and Dyches, 2008, p.13)​


​As​​emphasised​​by​​Prater​​and​​Dyches​​(2008),​​this​​sub-theme​​supports​​the​​importance​​of​​the​
​characters​ ​in​ ​the​ ​story​ ​and​ ​their​ ​creation​ ​in​ ​order​ ​to​ ​make​ ​them​ ​relatable​ ​to​ ​potential​
​children,​ ​allowing​ ​them​ ​to​ ​compare​ ​their​ ​own​ ​experiences​ ​with​ ​those​ ​of​ ​the​ ​characters​​in​
​the​ ​book​ ​and​ ​identifying​ ​similarities​ ​and​ ​differences.​ ​Keane​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2020)​ ​voices​ ​the​
​importance​ ​of​​children​​having​​something​​or​​someone​​to​​relate​​to.​​Specifically,​​in​​a​​sporting​
​context,​​it​​is​​recognised​​that​​athletes​​can​​be​​role​​models​​for​​young​​individuals,​​inspiring​​and​
​motivating​​them​​to​​participate​​in​​sport​​(Adriaanse​​and​​Crosswhite,​​2008;​​Payne​​et​​al.,​​2003).​
​Keagan​ ​recognises​ ​a​ ​key​ ​strength​ ​of​ ​the​​book​​being​​the​​characters,​​stating​​“I​​guess​​anyone​
​else​ ​reading​ ​it​ ​might​ ​identify​ ​with​​them,​​but​​also​​give​​them​​that​​quality​​of​​understanding”.​
​Numerous​ ​participants​ ​shared​ ​the​ ​view​ ​that​ ​the​ ​children​ ​were​ ​able​ ​to​ ​relate​ ​to​ ​the​
​characters,​ ​particularly​ ​Patrick​ ​who​ ​said,​ ​“I​ ​liked​ ​how​ ​the​ ​children​​can​​put​​themselves​​into​
​the​ ​characters'​ ​shoes”.​ ​Another​ ​participant​ ​who​ ​made​ ​a​ ​similar​ ​remark​ ​was​ ​Hannah,​
​commenting​​“I​​liked​​the​​way​​it​​was​​quite​​personal​​and​​it​​related​​to​​people​​that​​perhaps​​you​
​could​ ​relate​ ​to​ ​yourselves​ ​the​ ​family​ ​and​ ​the​ ​characters”.​ ​Alongside​ ​being​ ​able​ ​to​ ​see​
​themselves​​in​​the​​characters,​​Carly​​expressed​​that​​the​​characters​​increase​​engagement​​in​​the​
​story,​​stating​​“the​​football​​part…​​it's​​not​​a​​dominant​​part​​of​​the​​story.​​It's​​the​​characters,​​and​
​their​ ​backgrounds,​ ​which​ ​is​​more,​​I​​would​​say,​​overarching​​rather​​than​​just​​football”.​​When​
​developing​ ​the​ ​draft​ ​copy​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​intended​ ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​football​ ​as​ ​it​
​provided​ ​the​ ​context​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​discuss​ ​discrimination​ ​and​ ​possibly​ ​help​ ​to​ ​engage​
​particular​​audiences;​​nevertheless,​​although​​it​​is​​evident​​from​​the​​data​​sets​​that​​football​​was​
​not​ ​the​ ​dominant​ ​part,​ ​it​ ​played​ ​a​ ​role​ ​which​ ​has​ ​been​ ​explored​ ​in​ ​greater​ ​detail​ ​in​ ​the​
​fourth​​theme,​​‘football​​as​​an​​educational​​tool’​.​​Rachel​​also​​agreed​​with​​this,​​and​​found​​that​
​the​ ​key​ ​part​ ​of​ ​the​ ​story​ ​was​​based​​upon​​the​​characters​​and​​their​​backgrounds.​​“I​​thought​
​this​​went​​beyond​​the​​kids​​who​​are​​just​​footballers…​​because​​you​​have​​different​​characters…​
​so you have Zara who is Muslim, and Noah who is Jewish”.​




                                                              ​187​
​For​ ​children​ ​from​ ​marginalised​ ​communities,​ ​having​ ​a​ ​role​​model​​who​​is​​relatable​​to​​them​
​increases​ ​their​ ​likelihood​ ​of​ ​engagement​ ​(Vescio,​ ​Wilde,​ ​and​ ​Crosswhite,​ ​2005).​​Therefore,​
​the​ ​representation​ ​of​ ​marginalised​ ​communities​ ​has​ ​significant​ ​importance​ ​and​ ​was​
​subsequently​ ​embedded​ ​into​ ​the​ ​book.​ ​Literature​ ​from​ ​Kapuzza​ ​(2020)​ ​explored​​children's​
​books​​featuring​​transgender​​characters.​​They​​concluded​​that​​children’s​​literature​​plays​​a​​vital​
​role​​in​​identity​​development,​​recognising​​how​​they​​can​​help​​children​​identify​​with​​others​​and​
​their​ ​feelings.​ ​Tom​ ​(Educator),​ ​supported​ ​this​ ​research​ ​by​ ​touching​ ​on​ ​the​ ​feelings​ ​of​ ​the​
​characters:​


       ​there's​ ​a​ ​good​ ​variety​ ​of​ ​characters,​ ​and​ ​it's​ ​nice,​ ​the​ ​way​ ​they​ ​relate​ ​to​ ​each​
       ​other​ ​as​ ​well.​ ​There's​ ​a​ ​lot​ ​of​ ​things​ ​which​ ​we​ ​would​ ​explore​ ​regarding​ ​their​
       ​personalities, emotions and backgrounds.​


​Therefore,​​as​​reinforced​​by​​Carly​​and​​Rachel​​(Educators),​​having​​increased​​visibility​​of​​these​
​characters​ ​helps​ ​children​ ​to​ ​relate​ ​to​ ​them​ ​throughout,​ ​and​ ​subsequently​ ​feel​ ​more​
​connected​ ​and​ ​valued,​ ​especially​ ​for​ ​those​ ​belonging​ ​to​ ​a​ ​minority​ ​group,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​the​
​characters​​of​​Noah​​and​​Zara.​​Having​​Zara​​as​​one​​of​​the​​main​​characters,​​as​​a​​girl​​and​​also​​a​
​Muslim​​means​​that​​young​​females,​​and​​Muslim​​children​​reading​​the​​book​​are​​able​​to​​reflect​
​on​​her​​experiences​​and​​relate​​to​​her.​​In​​the​​fourth​​theme,​​‘football​​as​​an​​educational​​tool’​,​​a​
​sub-theme explores the role of gender further.​


​However,​​Zara’s​​and​​Khan’s​​religion​​also​​plays​​a​​critical​​role​​in​​representation;​​Leah​​states​​“I​
​think​ ​the​ ​fact​ ​that​ ​you've​ ​got​ ​a​ ​Muslim​ ​child​ ​in​ ​it​ ​as​ ​well,​ ​I​ ​think,​ ​is​ ​really​ ​important”.​
​Likewise, Noah’s character plays a role for Jewish readers, including Leah (Jewish, Educator):​


       ​I​​think​​the​​fact​​that​​you've​​got​​the​​diversity​​of​​the​​group​​of​​kids​​that​​make​​friends​
       ​in​ ​the​ ​secondary​ ​school,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​fact​ ​that​ ​the​​child​​who​​came​​from​​the​​Jewish​
       ​school is… ‘the only Jew in the village’, I think is quite poignant.​


​By​​having​​these​​diverse​​characters,​​which​​children​​can​​relate​​to,​​it​​allows​​them​​to​​reflect​​and​
​consider if they have faced similar situations, which Lauren discussed:​




                                                               ​188​
       ​The​ ​thoughts​ ​and​ ​the​ ​feelings​ ​that​ ​would​ ​come​ ​into​ ​the​ ​story​ ​I​ ​liked​ ​as​ ​well,​
       ​certain​ ​points​ ​that​ ​were​ ​really​ ​good,​​because​​it​​really​​made​​the​​children​​reflect​
       ​on themselves. Do they feel the same as that child or not?​


​The​​final​​chapter​​which​​allows​​children​​to​​develop​​and​​create​​their​​own​​ending​​to​​the​​book​
​was​​popular​​with​​teachers,​​experts,​​and​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​as​​it​​would​​give​
​the​​children​​a​​feeling​​of​​agency,​​allowing​​them​​to​​reflect​​on​​what​​they​​would​​do​​next.​​In​​this​
​vein,​​Jasmine​​commented​​“I​​think​​that's​​such​​a​​lovely​​idea​​that​​they​​decide​​how​​it​​ends​​and​
​they​ ​can​ ​think​ ​“Oh,​ ​if​ ​I​ ​was​ ​in​ ​that​ ​situation,​ ​what​ ​would​ ​I​ ​do?”.​ ​Supporting​ ​Jasmine's​
​comments was Nate, who reinforced the importance of the final chapter:​


       ​I​ ​thought​ ​the​ ​chance​ ​for​ ​interaction​ ​and​ ​reflection​ ​was​ ​good,​ ​especially​ ​at​ ​the​
       ​end​​where​​the​​young​​people​​can​​produce​​their​​own​​ending​​using​​the​​information​
       ​learnt throughout.​


​However,​​it​​is​​important​​to​​acknowledge​​that​​due​​to​​the​​nature​​of​​the​​story,​​it​​was​​difficult​​to​
​fully​ ​represent​ ​every​ ​marginalised​ ​community​ ​through​ ​the​ ​characters.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​the​
​story​ ​includes​ ​some​ ​discussion​ ​of​ ​sexuality,​ ​race,​​and​​disability,​​which​​teachers​​can​​explore​
​further​​if​​they​​wish.​​Additionally,​​the​​provided​​discussion​​points​​can​​help​​teachers​​reflect​​on​
​the​ ​diverse​ ​cultures,​ ​religions,​ ​and​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​other​ ​children.​ ​Finally,​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​
​recommended​​tasks​​in​​the​​resource​​pack​​encourage​​schools​​to​​organise​​interfaith​​or​​cultural​
​days, allowing children to celebrate their backgrounds and heritage.​


​Transferability and relatability​


​During​ ​the​ ​interview,​ ​Keagan​ ​(EDI​ ​Manager)​ ​mentioned​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​“making​ ​the​
​experiences​​as​​transferable​​as​​possible”,​​therefore​​being​​able​​to​​replicate​​this​​story​​in​​other​
​contexts​ ​or​ ​settings.​ ​As​ ​part​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​interviews,​ ​a​​key​​theme​​was​​the​​interaction​​of​
​marginalised​ ​communities.​ ​Discussions​ ​with​ ​experts​ ​stated​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​including​
​individuals​ ​from​ ​the​ ​marginalised​ ​community​ ​into​ ​an​ ​initiative,​ ​with​ ​supporting​ ​research​
​which​ ​found​ ​that​ ​integrating​ ​marginalised​ ​or​ ​differing​ ​communities​ ​together​ ​reduced​
​anti-discriminatory​ ​attitudes​ ​(Hassan​ ​and​ ​Telford,​ ​2014;​ ​Leitner​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2014).​ ​Two-thirds​​of​


                                                            ​189​
​Jewish​ ​people​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​live​ ​in​​Greater​​London​​and​​the​​neighbouring​​counties,​​despite​​the​
​fact​ ​that​ ​they​ ​are​ ​distributed​ ​throughout​ ​the​ ​country​ ​(Boyd​​and​​Staetsky,​​2014).​​Given​​the​
​relatively​ ​low​ ​representation​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​within​ ​the​ ​larger​ ​UK​ ​population,​ ​roughly​
​300,000,​​and​​a​​centralised​​population​​centre​​within​​London,​​the​​opportunity​​for​​the​​general​
​public​​to​​interact​​with​​someone​​of​​the​​Jewish​​faith​​is​​notably​​low.​​With​​that​​in​​mind,​​it​​was​
​integral​​that​​students,​​who​​possibly​​may​​not​​know​​a​​Jewish​​person,​​can​​transfer​​themselves​
​into the story and gain a better understanding of what Judaism is.​


​Chris​ ​highlighted​ ​this​ ​as​ ​one​ ​of​ ​the​ ​key​ ​strengths​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​stating​ ​“I​ ​thought​ ​it​ ​was​ ​a​
​really​ ​good​ ​read​ ​from​ ​the​ ​perspective​ ​of​ ​children​ ​and​ ​young​ ​adults​ ​that​ ​have​ ​had​ ​no​
​interaction​ ​at​ ​all​ ​with​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community”.​ ​The​ ​International​ ​Holocaust​ ​Remembrance​
​Alliance​​(n.d.)​​highlighted​​that​​by​​including​​individuals​​from​​the​​marginalised​​community​​into​
​an​ ​initiative,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​possible​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​face​ ​to​ ​history,​ ​which​ ​encourages​​students​​to​​learn​
​and develop an effective understanding of history. Chris continues to say that:​


       ​I​ ​think​ ​a​ ​problem​ ​for​ ​the​​kids,​​if​​you​​live​​in​​an​​area​​in​​the​​UK,​​where​​there's​​no​
       ​interaction​​with​​Jewish​​people.​​You're​​gonna​​have​​little​​understanding​​unless​​it's​
       ​brought into the classroom.​


​Nancy also made a similar point, arguing that most children:​


       ​…don't​ ​know​ ​anyone​ ​Jewish,​ ​like,​​you​​can't​​walk​​down​​the​​street​​and,​​or​​watch​
       ​television​ ​now​ ​not​ ​see​ ​someone​ ​that​ ​is​ ​Black​ ​or​ ​Asian​ ​but​ ​you​ ​can't​ ​tell​ ​that​
       ​someone is Jewish…they can see a Jewish kid is just like any other kid.​


​This​​strengthens​​the​​need​​for​​such​​resources​​as​​it​​will​​give​​children​​the​​opportunity​​to​​learn​
​more​ ​about​ ​Jewish​ ​people,​ ​alongside​ ​being​ ​able​ ​to​ ​transfer​ ​themselves​ ​into​ ​the​ ​story.​ ​In​
​addition,​ ​as​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​first​ ​theme,​ ​‘recommended​ ​additions’,​ ​Keagan​ ​mentions​ ​the​ ​value​ ​of​
​being able to share and transfer individual experiences:​


       ​We​ ​had​ ​the​ ​Faith​ ​in​ ​Football​ ​projects​ ​at​ ​Wembley,​ ​where​ ​we​​brought​​Catholic,​
       ​Jewish​ ​and​​Muslim​​schools​​together​​one​​day​​a​​week​​for​​about​​2​​months.​​So,​​all​


                                                               ​190​
          ​the​ ​kids​ ​which​ ​I​ ​think​ ​were​ ​about​ ​this​ ​age,​ ​they​ ​all​ ​did​ ​activities​ ​for​ ​half​​a​​day​
          ​together​​and​​it​​was​​really​​interesting​​because​​I​​just​​did​​stuff​​about​​Wembley​​and​
          ​about​​football​​and​​then​​they​​sort​​of​​by​​the​​end​​realised​​“Oh,​​look!​​You​​know​​you​
          ​pray,​ ​and​ ​we​ ​pray,​ ​and​ ​it's​ ​quite​ ​similar,​ ​and​ ​look,​ ​our​ ​lunches​ ​aren’t​ ​that​
          ​different”, and by the end of it some of the schools twinned up.​


​By​ ​having​ ​schools​ ​host​ ​inter-faith​ ​days,​ ​it​ ​allows​​for​​children​​from​​different​​backgrounds​​to​
​come​ ​together.​ ​Keagan​ ​builds​ ​upon​ ​his​​experiences​​below,​​stating​​that​​by​​bringing​​children​
​together​​from​​different​​backgrounds​​and​​communities,​​they​​develop​​a​​cultural​​awareness​​of​
​one​ ​another.​ ​Likewise,​ ​in​ ​Theme​ ​1,​ ​there​ ​were​ ​also​ ​discussions​ ​of​ ​other​ ​ways​ ​to​ ​integrate​
​marginalised​ ​communities​ ​together​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​their​ ​cultures​ ​and​ ​religions.​ ​Nancy​ ​(Jewish,​
​Educator)​ ​reinforces​ ​that​ ​alongside​ ​additional​ ​cultural​ ​days​​and​​by​​reading​​the​​book,​​it​​will​
​also:​


          ​allow​​children​​to​​realise​​that​​Jewish​​people​​are​​just​​the​​same​​as​​everybody​​else.​
          ​You​ ​might​ ​not​​know​​they​​are​​Jewish​​but​​you​​know,​​he​​likes​​football,​​he​​went​​to​
          ​primary school, he's at school and that antisemitism is a thing that is real.​


​In​ ​conclusion,​ ​the​ ​responses​ ​from​ ​participants​ ​highlighted​ ​that​ ​the​ ​resource's​ ​relatable​
​elements​​were​​a​​major​​strength.​​These​​included​​the​​characters​​and​​the​​storylines​​that​​were​
​representative​ ​of​ ​the​ ​difficulties​ ​that​ ​minority​ ​individuals​ ​would​ ​have​ ​encountered.​
​Participants​ ​were​ ​able​​to​​connect​​their​​own​​personal​​experiences​​and​​later​​empathise​​with​
​the​​characters​​due​​to​​the​​relatable​​nature​​of​​the​​characters​​and​​storylines.​​Here,​​time​​should​
​be​​taken​​to​​recognise​​that,​​whilst​​prior​​research​​discussed​​in​​this​​theme​​examined​​the​​role​​of​
​literature​ ​in​ ​helping​ ​children​ ​explore​ ​diverse​ ​personal​ ​experiences​ ​such​ ​as​ ​gender​ ​identity​
​(Capuzza,​ ​2020),​ ​adoption​ ​(Watson,​ ​Latter​ ​and​ ​Bellew,​ ​2015),​ ​and​ ​LGBT+​ ​parenting​ ​(Van​
​Horn,​​2015),​​the​​literature​​emphasises​​the​​value​​of​​children's​​novels.​​As​​a​​result,​​these​​works​
​have been utilised to explore the significance of relatability.​




                                                                   ​191​
​Theme 3 - Structure of the resource​


​This​​current​​theme​​explores​​discussion​​regarding​​the​​structure​​of​​the​​initiative.​​The​​Phase​​1​
​expert​ ​interviews​ ​revealed​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​a​ ​physical​​resource.​​Therefore,​​during​​the​​creation​
​and​​development​​of​​the​​draft​​book,​​a​​physical​​resource​​was​​produced​​to​​enhance​​education​
​experiences,​ ​highlighting​ ​that​ ​it​ ​offers​​opportunities​​for​​further​​learning​​as​​a​​child​​interacts​
​with​​it.​​Participants​​from​​all​​groups​​stated​​a​​key​​strength​​of​​the​​book​​was​​the​​way​​that​​it​​was​
​organised​​and​​delivered;​​however,​​there​​were​​also​​differing​​opinions​​on​​the​​broad-to-narrow​
​structure,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​conflicting​ ​positions​ ​on​ ​whether​ ​the​ ​book​ ​should​ ​be​ ​in​ ​an​ ​online​ ​or​
​printed​ ​format.​ ​Therefore,​ ​this​ ​theme​ ​contains​ ​four​​sub-themes,​​named​​‘discussion​​points’,​
​‘broad-to-narrow structure’, ‘the ending’, and ‘calling for a digital resource’.​


​Discussion points​


​The​​resource​​was​​designed​​as​​a​​simple​​tool​​for​​teachers​​to​​utilise​​and​​encourage​​discussion​
​around​​the​​topic​​of​​discrimination,​​namely​​antisemitism,​​with​​discussion​​points​​put​​in​​place​
​at​​the​​end​​of​​each​​chapter;​​as​​discussed​​by​​Tom,​​“it​​provides​​a​​teacher​​something​​prepared​
​to​ ​work​ ​with”.​ ​By​ ​having​ ​the​ ​book​ ​with​ ​integrated​ ​discussion​ ​points​ ​as​ ​a​ ​resource,​
​participants,​ ​including​ ​Lauren​ ​felt​ ​that​ ​“schools​ ​would​ ​just​ ​love​ ​it​ ​because​ ​it​ ​is​ ​prepared​
​work”.​ ​Bethan​ ​(Educator)​ ​also​ ​explored​ ​the​ ​impact​ ​the​ ​prepared​ ​work​ ​would​ ​have​ ​upon​
​teachers, as it would save them time:​


       ​...the​ ​discussion​ ​points​ ​would​ ​be​ ​very​ ​helpful​ ​when​ ​leading​ ​a​ ​discussion​ ​with​
       ​students.​​The​​teacher​​wouldn’t​​have​​to​​think​​about​​these​​themselves​​–​​which​​is​
       ​helpful for saving teachers time!​


​Nancy (Jewish, Educator) also made a similar comment:​


       ​The​ ​best​ ​way​ ​to​ ​teach​ ​anything​ ​is​ ​through​ ​a​ ​story…​ ​teachers​ ​love​ ​it​ ​when​
       ​someone​ ​gives​ ​them​ ​something…​ ​here​ ​is​ ​something,​ ​please​ ​go​ ​and​ ​do​ ​it…​ ​But​
       ​oh, yeah, they love it when you give them something.​




                                                            ​192​
​The​ ​prepared​ ​element​ ​of​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​therefore,​ ​came​ ​as​ ​a​ ​key​ ​strength​ ​for​ ​many​
​participants, including Chris (Jewish):​


       ​I​​thought​​it's​​very​​informative​​and​​I​​thought​​that​​if​​you​​are​​a​​teacher,​​having​​read​
       ​that​​book,​​it​​gives​​you​​plenty​​of​​examples​​on​​how​​to​​approach​​a​​class​​with​​very​
       ​good and well worded questions in the book.​


​During​ ​the​ ​initial​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection,​ ​expert​ ​participants​ ​stressed​ ​the​ ​significance​ ​of​
​developing​ ​an​ ​initiative​ ​that​ ​is​ ​relatively​ ​easy​ ​for​ ​the​ ​person​ ​either​ ​delivering​ ​or​
​understanding​ ​the​ ​content.​ ​With​ ​this​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​it​ ​was​​crucial​​to​​make​​the​​resource's​​format​
​and​ ​structure​ ​simple​ ​to​ ​follow.​ ​Diana​ ​(Teaching​​Assistant)​​noted​​that​​“it’s​​well​​laid​​out​​into​
​chapters​​and​​the​​discussion​​points.​​This​​would​​aid​​teachers​​to​​help​​children​​understand​​each​
​chapter”.​ ​Ellen​ ​also​ ​drew​ ​upon​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​points​ ​would​ ​aid​ ​educators​ ​in​
​their​ ​teachings,​ ​stating​ ​that​ ​they​ ​“were​ ​very​ ​good,​ ​and​ ​some​ ​could​​lead​​to​​a​​whole​​lesson​
​activity​ ​e.g.​ ​hot​ ​seating​ ​or​ ​a​ ​conscience​ ​alley.​ ​It​ ​could​ ​help​ ​children​ ​think​ ​of​ ​their​ ​own​
​experiences”.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​the​​structure​​and​​prepared​​elements​​of​​the​​book​​proved​​popular​
​with Matthew (Development Officer,) who mentioned:​


       ​I​​like​​the​​format.​​I​​think​​it​​really​​engages​​kids​​to​​develop,​​rather​​than​​just​​walking​
       ​around​ ​the​ ​room​ ​trying​ ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​conversation.​ ​When​ ​you​ ​engage​ ​them​ ​in​ ​a​
       ​resource​​or​​a​​reading​​or​​some​​sort​​of​​reading​​material,​​then​​that's​​the​​best​​way​
       ​to​​go​​about​​it,​​and​​then​​intersperse​​that​​with​​the​​questions,​​I​​think​​it​​is​​the​​right​
       ​way to go.​


​It​ ​was​​important​​to​​ensure​​the​​resource​​had​​the​​most​​significant​​effect​​on​​users,​​while​​also​
​making​ ​it​ ​easy​ ​for​​them​​to​​interact​​with.​​Therefore,​​to​​enhance​​its​​effectiveness,​​discussion​
​points​ ​were​ ​incorporated.​ ​Simon​ ​(Jewish)​ ​stated​ ​that​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​points​ ​serve​ ​multiple​
​purposes​ ​“not​ ​only​ ​lead​ ​to​ ​discussion,​ ​but​ ​it​ ​also​ ​reinforces​ ​what​ ​you​ ​actually​ ​said​ ​and​
​understand​ ​if​ ​the​ ​kids​ ​actually​ ​comprehend​ ​what​ ​it​ ​was​ ​about”.​ ​By​ ​incorporating​ ​these​
​discussion​ ​prompts,​ ​the​ ​intent​ ​was​ ​to​ ​encourage​ ​children​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​in​ ​meaningful​
​conversations​ ​that​ ​go​ ​beyond​ ​surface-level​ ​interaction.​ ​This​ ​will​ ​help​ ​to​ ​solidify​ ​the​ ​key​
​concepts​​presented,​​allowing​​children​​to​​reflect​​on​​and​​process​​the​​material​​more​​deeply.​​As​


                                                             ​193​
​discussed​​by​​Simon,​​the​​questions​​provide​​the​​opportunity​​for​​children​​to​​comprehend​​what​
​they​​have​​learnt,​​which​​was​​supported​​by​​Tom​​(Educator),​​“the​​questions​​are​​very​​relevant,​
​and​ ​relate​ ​very​ ​well​ ​to​ ​the​ ​piece​ ​which​ ​you've​ ​just​ ​read”.​ ​By​ ​engaging​ ​with​ ​the​ ​questions​
​alongside​​the​​reading​​of​​the​​chapter,​​it​​provides​​a​​sense​​of​​structure,​​as​​discussed​​by​​Brian:​​“I​
​do​​really​​like​​the​​idea​​of​​doing​​the​​chapter​​and​​doing​​the​​questions.​​It​​works​​very​​well”.​​The​
​discussion​ ​points​ ​were​ ​generally​ ​regarded​ ​as​ ​an​ ​effective​ ​part​ ​of​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​since​ ​they​
​offered​​pre-prepared​​content​​for​​staff​​to​​deliver​​and​​served​​as​​a​​means​​of​​determining​​how​
​well the children understood what they had comprehended.​


​However,​​where​​the​​discussion​​points​​were​​placed​​provided​​some​​element​​of​​conversation,​
​as​ ​some​ ​felt​ ​a​ ​different​ ​location​ ​would​ ​have​ ​a​ ​greater​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​the​ ​children's​ ​learning.​
​Participants​​from​​‘SH​​School’​​explored​​if​​the​​discussion​​points​​sit​​best​​at​​the​​end​​of​​a​​chapter​
​or whether they should be embedded within the chapter:​


       ​Lauren:​ ​I​ ​think​ ​you​ ​would​ ​lose​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​the​ ​story​ ​if​ ​you​ ​did​ ​[​embed​ ​questions​
       ​throughout​]​
       ​Charlotte: I like how it is.​
       ​Sophia: You could say something like ‘See section’.​
       ​Rachel: Or if it's in bold, then you know it’s a discussion point.​


​However,​ ​other​ ​teachers,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Leah​ ​(Jewish,​ ​Educator),​ ​suggested​ ​that​ ​“rather​ ​than​
​putting​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​points​ ​at​ ​the​ ​end​ ​of​ ​each​ ​chapter,​ ​it​ ​might​ ​be​ ​best​ ​to​ ​break​ ​the​
​chapter​ ​down”​ ​to​ ​better​ ​support​ ​children​ ​with​ ​lower​ ​attention​ ​spans.​ ​The​ ​placement​ ​of​
​discussion​ ​points​ ​at​ ​the​ ​end​ ​of​ ​each​ ​chapter​ ​had​ ​both​ ​advantages​ ​and​ ​drawbacks.​ ​Some​
​educators​ ​believed​ ​that​ ​integrating​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​points​ ​within​ ​the​ ​chapter​ ​could​ ​cause​
​students​ ​to​ ​lose​​focus​​on​​the​​story,​​while​​others​​thought​​it​​would​​be​​beneficial​​for​​children​
​with​​learning​​difficulties.​​The​​idea​​of​​highlighting​​key​​discussion​​points​​was​​seen​​as​​useful,​​as​
​it​ ​would​ ​allow​ ​teachers​ ​to​ ​easily​ ​return​ ​to​ ​specific​ ​questions​​when​​needed.​​Tom​​explained​
​that​ ​by​ ​bolding​ ​the​ ​relevant​ ​sections​ ​related​ ​to​ ​the​ ​questions,​ ​it​ ​would​ ​help​ ​children​
​“pinpoint​ ​easily​ ​where​ ​it​ ​is​ ​where​ ​they​ ​could​ ​find​ ​the​ ​information”.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​for​
​presentational purposes, this suggestion was not enacted.​




                                                             ​194​
​This​ ​theme,​ '​discussion​ ​points',​ ​was​ ​viewed​ ​as​ ​a​ ​valuable​ ​feature​ ​of​ ​the​ ​resource.​ ​While​
​opinions​​varied​​on​​the​​placement​​of​​these​​points,​​they​​were​​generally​​seen​​as​​a​​helpful​​tool​
​for​​teachers.​​By​​serving​​as​​learning​​cues,​​the​​provided​​pre-prepared​​content​​saves​​time​​and​
​encourages​ ​meaningful​ ​student​ ​engagement.​ ​Discussion​ ​points​ ​provided​ ​structure,​
​reinforced​ ​key​ ​concepts,​ ​and​ ​supported​ ​teachers​ ​in​ ​assessing​ ​students'​ ​comprehension,​
​making them an essential part of the resource's effectiveness.​


​Broad-to-narrow structure​


​In​​Phase​​1​​of​​data​​collection,​​interviews​​with​​the​​experts​​suggested​​that​​the​​structure​​of​​an​
​initiative​ ​is​ ​crucial,​ ​particularly​ ​when​ ​examining​ ​discrimination-related​ ​themes.​ ​Experts​
​introduced​ ​the​​idea​​of​​having​​a​​broad-to-narrow​​structure,​​supported​​by​​the​​RISE​​initiative,​
​which​ ​starts​ ​by​ ​exploring​ ​individual​ ​identities​ ​before​ ​introducing​ ​conversations​ ​and​
​discussion​ ​on​ ​inclusion​ ​and​ ​equality​ ​(MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin,​ ​2018).​​This​​was​​a​​major​​asset​
​cited by educators with regard to the book’s proposed structure:​


       ​I​ ​liked​ ​the​ ​structure,​ ​I​ ​thought​​about​​how​​you​​built​​through​​the​​story,​​and​​then​
       ​visiting​ ​the​ ​Synagogue,​ ​all​ ​of​ ​that​ ​was​ ​really​ ​clever,​ ​and​ ​everything​ ​was​
       ​sequenced very well. (Lauren - Educator)​


​The​ ​progression​ ​from​ ​broad-to-narrow,​​throughout​​the​​draft​​book,​​was​​also​​appreciated​​by​
​Chris (Jewish):​


       ​I​​thought​​you​​handled​​that​​very​​well….I​​liked​​the​​progression,​​starting​​with​​Black​
       ​Lives​ ​Matters​ ​all​ ​the​ ​way​ ​through​ ​to​ ​chapter​ ​nine​ ​with​ ​Joe's​ ​uncertainty.​ ​I​
       ​thought you dealt with it very well.​


​Beginning​ ​with​ ​different​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination​ ​and​ ​moving​ ​on​ ​to​ ​antisemitism,​ ​Chris​
​explains​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​gradual​ ​progression,​ ​highlighting​ ​key​ ​concepts​ ​that​ ​are​ ​covered​
​throughout​ ​the​ ​draft​ ​book.​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result​ ​of​ ​the​ ​broad-to-narrow​ ​structure,​ ​the​ ​writer​ ​and​
​researcher​​managed​​to​​include​​a​​variety​​of​​narratives​​that​​were​​centred​​around​​other​​forms​




                                                          ​195​
​of​ ​prejudice.​ ​This​ ​meant​ ​that​​a​​wide​​range​​of​​subjects​​were​​covered​​throughout,​​as​​Sophia​
​discusses:​


       ​I​ ​am​ ​just​ ​amazed​ ​at​ ​how​ ​much​ ​you​ ​put​ ​in​ ​and​ ​many​ ​topics​ ​you​ ​touched​ ​on….​
       ​when​ ​I​ ​initially​ ​saw​ ​it​ ​and​ ​thought,​​I​​don’t​​know​​how​​you​​are​​going​​to​​cover​​all​
       ​this​ ​in​ ​football​ ​and​ ​this​ ​is​ ​going​ ​to​ ​be​ ​quite​ ​hard​ ​and​ ​as​ ​I​ ​went​ ​through​ ​it​ ​I​
       ​became​ ​more​ ​and​ ​more​ ​invested​ ​in​ ​the​ ​characters​ ​and​ ​how​ ​it​ ​worked​ ​as​ ​the​
       ​football​ ​family,​ ​and​ ​football​ ​community​ ​and​ ​then​ ​all​ ​the​ ​aspects​ ​that​ ​could​
       ​impact​ ​upon.​ ​Really​ ​clever.​ ​(Sophia​ ​-​ ​Deputy​ ​Headteacher​ ​and​ ​Head​ ​of​ ​Early​
       ​Years)​


​Although​​the​​main​​aim​​was​​to​​educate​​on​​antisemitism,​​starting​​with​​a​​broad​​structure​​and​
​gradually​ ​focusing​ ​on​ ​this​ ​key​ ​teaching​ ​point​ ​allowed​ ​for​ ​the​​exploration​​of​​other​​forms​​of​
​discrimination​ ​as​ ​well.​ ​This​ ​approach​ ​was​ ​particularly​ ​appreciated​ ​by​ ​Iris​ ​(Jewish),​ ​who​
​valued its broader perspective.​


       ​I​​think​​it's​​obviously​​been​​very​​thoughtful​​about​​all​​the​​issues​​that​​are​​important​
       ​for​ ​children​ ​to​ ​start​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​as​ ​early​ ​as​ ​possible.​ ​So,​ ​you're​ ​covering​
       ​everything.​ ​I​ ​thought,​ ​initially,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​just​ ​going​ ​to​ ​be​ ​about​ ​antisemitism,​ ​but​
       ​actually,​ ​it's​ ​good​ ​that​ ​you're​ ​covering​ ​just​ ​gently,​ ​and​ ​bringing​ ​in​ ​all​ ​of​ ​those​
       ​issues​ ​that​ ​are​ ​important​ ​to​​young​​people​​to​​consider​​in​​terms​​of​​the​​disability,​
       ​LGBT+ issues, Black Lives Matter, racism and antisemitism.​


​However,​ ​the​ ​broad-to-narrow​ ​focus​ ​did​ ​cause​ ​confusion​ ​amongst​ ​some​ ​participants,​ ​with​
​some​ ​questioning​ ​if​ ​the​ ​book​ ​was​ ​about​ ​racism​ ​or​ ​antisemitism,​ ​including​ ​Simon,​ ​who​
​specifically​​asked:​​“I'm​​sorry,​​I​​have​​to​​go​​back​​right​​to​​the​​beginning​​here…​​is​​this​​particularly​
​antisemitism​ ​or​ ​anti-racism?”.​ ​With​​the​​draft​​book​​focusing​​on​​discrimination​​more​​broadly​
​to​ ​start,​ ​and​ ​then​ ​narrowing​ ​in​ ​on​ ​antisemitism,​ ​there​ ​was​ ​some​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​why​
​Simon​ ​may​ ​have​ ​asked​ ​this.​​With​​this​​in​​mind,​​it​​was​​essential​​to​​provide​​greater​​clarity​​on​
​the​ ​structure​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​which​ ​could​ ​be​ ​achieved​ ​through​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​an​
​additional​ ​resource​ ​pack​ ​(Appendix​ ​Q)​ ​for​ ​staff​ ​which​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​main​ ​focus​ ​points​ ​for​




                                                                ​196​
​each​ ​chapter​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​alongside​ ​which​​core​​themes​​of​​the​​Personal,​​Social,​​Health​​and​
​Economic (henceforth, PSHE) curriculum each chapter covers.​


​Likewise,​​there​​was​​more​​concern​​around​​the​​broad-to-narrow​​focus,​​as​​participants​​felt​​that​
​there​​was​​a​​vast​​quantity​​of​​topics​​for​​the​​children​​to​​discuss.​​Although​​this​​was​​seen​​as​​both​
​a​​positive​​and​​negative​​from​​participants,​​and​​for​​some​​this​​was​​considered​​a​​key​​strength​​of​
​the​ ​initiative,​ ​some​ ​felt​ ​this​ ​was​ ​possibly​ ​too​ ​much​ ​for​ ​young​ ​children​ ​to​ ​learn.​ ​This​ ​was​
​reflected​​in​​the​​comments​​from​​Iris​​(Jewish)​​who​​liked​​the​​broad​​range​​of​​topics,​​and​​forms​
​of discrimination were touched upon, stating:​


       ​…what​​I​​did​​think​​at​​first​​was​​‘Gosh​​it's​​huge!​​How​​on​​earth,​​are​​the​​kids​​going​​to​
       ​be able to absorb all this and all the questions?’​


​Likewise,​ ​Hannah​ ​(Educator)​ ​expressed​ ​that​ ​“to​ ​me,​ ​it​ ​seemed​ ​like​ ​a​ ​lot​ ​of​ ​information…I​
​think​​personally,​​there​​were​​a​​lot​​of​​issues​​covered”.​​For​​Hannah,​​she​​was​​concerned​​that​​it​
​would​ ​be​ ​too​ ​much​ ​for​ ​the​ ​children​ ​to​ ​comprehend.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​Nancy​​(Jewish,​​Educator)​
​discussed removing the chapter that focused on disability:​


       ​I​ ​guess​ ​the​ ​only​ ​bit​ ​was​ ​maybe​ ​about​ ​the​ ​disability​ ​bit,​ ​not​ ​that​ ​it's​ ​not​
       ​important,​ ​like​ ​it​ ​hugely​ ​is,​ ​but​ ​it​ ​depends​ ​on​ ​how​​long​​you​​want​​to​​work​​on​​it​
       ​and​​the​​discussion​​is​​a​​really​​important​​piece,​​because​​actually​​the​​point​​should​
       ​be​​the​​whole​​book​​is​​about​​knowing​​and​​judging​​and​​people​​that​​aren't​​the​​same​
       ​as us.​


​Although​​Nancy​​makes​​a​​valid​​point,​​when​​discussing​​the​​timescale​​for​​the​​project​​they​​then​
​felt​ ​that​ ​there​ ​was​ ​enough​ ​time​ ​provided​ ​for​ ​children​ ​to​ ​be​ ​able​ ​to​ ​discuss,​​question,​​and​
​express​ ​their​ ​understanding.​ ​This​ ​concept​ ​will​ ​be​ ​explored​ ​in​ ​greater​ ​depth​ ​later​ ​in​ ​this​
​chapter​ ​under​ ​the​ ​sub-theme​ '​discussing,​ ​questioning,​ ​and​ ​expressing,'​ ​where​ ​the​
​contribution​​of​​these​​processes​​to​​children's​​learning​​and​​comprehension​​will​​be​​examined.​
​The​​broad-to-narrow​​structure​​also​​provides​​up​​to​​9​​weeks’​​worth​​of​​content​​for​​staff,​​which​
​was​​due​​to​​previous​​literature​​exploring​​that​​a​​significant​​length​​will​​have​​greater​​impact.​​For​
​example,​ ​research​ ​from​ ​Dixon​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2016)​ ​explored​ ​the​​impact​​that​​Show​​Racism​​the​​Red​


                                                             ​197​
​Card​​has​​had,​​concluding​​that​​although​​the​​charity​​has​​been​​praised​​for​​its​​efforts​​to​​combat​
​racism,​​there​​is​​no​​long-term​​effectiveness​​due​​to​​the​​shorter​​workshops​​they​​deliver.​​This​​is​
​supported​​by​​Pedersen​​(2005)​​who​​recognised​​that​​educational​​courses​​which​​have​​content​
​taught over a longer period of time, would have more of a long-lasting impact.​


​Therefore,​ ​when​ ​developing​ ​the​ ​initiative,​​it​​was​​important​​that​​the​​book​​should​​be​​woven​
​into​ ​the​ ​curriculum​ ​over​ ​a​ ​longer​ ​duration​ ​of​ ​time.​ ​Richard​ ​mentioned​​that​​he​​particularly​
​liked​​this​​about​​the​​resource,​​saying​​“I​​like​​the​​idea​​that​​it​​is​​intended​​as​​a​​chapter​​a​​week​​or​
​chapter​​a​​day​​or​​chapter​​a​​month​​whatever​​it​​is,​​so​​that​​there's​​time​​in​​between​​to​​explore​
​the​ ​topics.”​ ​Furthermore,​ ​once​ ​Iris​ ​had​ ​acknowledged​ ​that​ ​it​​was​​intended​​to​​be​​delivered​
​over​​the​​course​​of​​9​​weeks,​​she​​felt​​it​​was​​more​​achievable.​​As​​discussed​​in​​this​​sub-theme,​
​the​ ​broad-to-narrow​ ​structure​ ​has​ ​proved​ ​helpful​ ​in​ ​teaching​ ​children​ ​the​ ​notion​ ​of​
​discrimination​ ​and​​to​​acquire​​an​​understanding​​of​​the​​numerous​​marginalised​​communities​
​that​ ​have​ ​experienced​ ​discrimination.​​Although​​this​​structure​​does​​present​​a​​wide​​range​​of​
​topics​ ​for​ ​exploration,​ ​it​​is​​advised​​that​​these​​topics​​be​​taught​​over​​a​​longer​​period​​of​​time​
​because,​ ​if​ ​they​ ​are​ ​presented​ ​in​ ​a​ ​short​ ​amount​ ​of​ ​time,​ ​it​​may​​become​​difficult​​for​​both​
​children to comprehend and teachers to instruct.​


​The ending​


​The​ ​ending​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​also​ ​acted​ ​as​ ​a​ ​discussion​ ​point​ ​for​​many​​participants,​​as​​the​​final​
​chapter​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​on​ ​p.​ ​47,​ ​invites​ ​the​ ​readers​ ​to​ ​finish​ ​the​ ​story.​ ​Tom​ ​(Educator)​
​particularly liked this element of the book:​


       ​How​​do​​you​​think​​the​​story​​will​​end?​​And​​that's​​a​​good​​leading​​question​​because​
       ​you​ ​don't​ ​give​ ​them​ ​the​ ​ending​ ​and​ ​you​ ​say:​ ​"How​ ​do​ ​you​ ​think​ ​the​ ​story​​will​
       ​end?”​


​Likewise,​ ​Leah​ ​found​ ​the​ ​ending​ ​to​ ​play​ ​an​ ​important​ ​role​ ​in​ ​the​ ​children's​ ​learning​ ​and​
​understanding;​​she​​highlights​​that​​it​​strengthens​​the​​message​​of​​the​​book,​​and​​that​​students​
​will be encouraged to think beyond the book:​




                                                            ​198​
       ​I​ ​like​ ​the​ ​fact​​that​​they​​have​​the​​question,​​how​​do​​you​​think​​the​​story​​will​​end?​
       ​Because​ ​I​​think​​it's​​really​​important​​that​​the​​children​​realise​​that​​this​​isn't​​just​​a​
       ​book​​that​​when​​you​​finish​​it,​​you​​shut​​it,​​and​​it's​​over,​​and​​you​​put​​it​​away.​​This​​is​
       ​an​​ongoing​​thing​​that​​we​​all​​need​​to​​be​​aware​​of​​and​​we​​will​​need​​to​​talk​​about,​
       ​and we need to make sure that these discussions are out in the open.​


​When​ ​deciding​ ​how​ ​to​ ​plan​ ​educational​ ​sessions,​ ​‘meaningfulness​ ​pedagogy’​ ​prioritises​
​meaningful​ ​experiences​ ​(Fletcher​ ​and​ ​Ní​ ​Chróinín,​ ​2021).​ ​It​​offers​​a​​personalised​​element,​
​which​​gives​​ownership​​to​​the​​learners​​and​​provides​​an​​individualised​​teaching​​experience​​(Ní​
​Chróinín​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2023).​ ​According​ ​to​ ​Ní​ ​Chróinín​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2023),​ ​allowing​ ​for​ ​inclusion​ ​and​
​student​​participation​​are​​two​​intrinsic​​features​​of​​the​​meaningfulness​​approach.​​As​​a​​result,​
​children​​have​​been​​encouraged​​to​​put​​themselves​​in​​the​​story​​and​​choose​​how​​it​​should​​end​
​by​​being​​given​​the​​chance​​to​​write​​the​​ending.​​Jasmine​​(Educator)​​added​​“I​​think​​that's​​such​
​a​​lovely​​idea​​that​​they​​decide​​how​​it​​ends​​and​​they​​can​​think​​“Oh,​​if​​I​​was​​in​​that​​situation,​
​what​​would​​I​​do?”.​​The​​goal​​of​​allowing​​children​​to​​finish​​the​​book​​was​​to​​encourage​​them​​to​
​articulate​ ​what​ ​they​ ​had​ ​learned,​ ​including​ ​demonstrating​ ​their​ ​ability​ ​to​ ​become​ ​active​
​bystanders, as discussed in Theme 5.​


​When​ ​designing​ ​the​ ​final​ ​chapter,​ ​the​ ​intention​ ​was​ ​to​​have​​children​​finish​​off​​the​​story​​to​
​gauge​ ​their​ ​understanding.​ ​Students​ ​will​ ​also​​be​​able​​to​​demonstrate​​other​​‘key​​teachings’,​
​such​​as​​those​​covered​​in​​Theme​​5.​​Chris​​states​​that​​it​​would​​be​​interesting​​to​​know​​“to​​what​
​effect​ ​do​ ​the​ ​kids​ ​finish​ ​that​ ​story​ ​off”​ ​as​ ​this​ ​would​ ​show​ ​how​ ​well​ ​children​ ​have​
​comprehended​ ​the​ ​narrative.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​Leah​ ​(a​ ​Jewish​ ​Educator)​ ​shares​​her​​perspective,​
​noting that:​


       ​the​ ​fact​ ​that​ ​you​ ​said​ ​“how​ ​do​ ​you​ ​think​ ​the​ ​story​ ​will​ ​end?”​ ​gives​ ​me​ ​sort​​of​
       ​hope​ ​that​ ​the​ ​children​ ​are​ ​going​ ​to​​look​​to​​a​​nice​​sort​​of​​brighter​​future​​where​
       ​they​ ​will​​call​​out​​people​​for​​being​​discriminated​​against,​​regardless​​of​​what​​that​
       ​discrimination is.​


​Leah​​remarked​​that​​allowing​​the​​children​​to​​finish​​the​​story​​instilled​​a​​sense​​of​​hope​​in​​her,​
​as​ ​she​ ​believed​ ​the​ ​younger​ ​generation​ ​would​ ​help​ ​shape​ ​a​ ​more​ ​promising​ ​future.​ ​The​


                                                              ​199​
​initiative​​was​​designed​​to​​encourage​​and​​teach​​children​​to​​be​​assertive​​bystanders.​​Research​
​by​ ​Hawkins​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2001)​ ​and​ ​Cantor​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2015)​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​people​ ​often​ ​hesitate​ ​to​
​intervene​ ​in​ ​situations​ ​of​​abuse​​or​​bullying.​​By​​helping​​children​​understand​​the​​importance​
​of​ ​being​ ​active​ ​and​ ​assertive​ ​bystanders​ ​through​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​the​ ​initiative​​aims​​to​​empower​
​them to confidently step in or report incidents if they encounter similar situations in real life.​


​Calling for a digital resource​


​During​​the​​exploration​​of​​the​​book's​​structure,​​discussions​​were​​held​​regarding​​the​​practical​
​aspects​ ​of​ ​its​ ​formatting​ ​and​ ​potential​ ​delivery​ ​methods.​ ​Among​ ​the​ ​twelve​ ​educators​
​involved,​ ​nine​ ​recommended​ ​that​ ​the​ ​book​ ​should​ ​not​ ​be​ ​a​ ​physical,​ ​tangible​ ​copy,​ ​but​
​rather​ ​an​ ​online​ ​resource​ ​that​ ​could​ ​be​ ​displayed​ ​on​ ​an​ ​electronic​ ​whiteboard.​ ​Tom​
​(Educator),​​noted​​that​​“if​​it​​is​​online,​​I​​suppose​​teachers​​could​​then​​pick​​bits​​to​​then​​put​​on​
​screen”.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​having​ ​an​ ​online​ ​resource​ ​could​ ​be​​supported​​by​​a​​physical​​copy,​​as​
​discussed by Leah:​

       ​I​​would​​probably​​have​​a​​combination,​​a​​big​​book​​on​​the​​board​​and​​then​​children​
       ​that​ ​are​ ​confident​ ​readers​ ​can​ ​follow​ ​on​ ​the​ ​board​ ​as​ ​your​ ​reading.​ ​I'm​ ​just​
       ​thinking​​of​​children​​that​​are​​maybe​​dyslexic​​or​​have​​slower​​processing​​skills​​or​​a​
       ​poorer​​working​​memory,​​having​​that​​physical​​copy​​in​​front​​of​​them​​that​​they​​can​
       ​flick​ ​to…​ ​you​ ​could​ ​have​ ​one​ ​on​​the​​whiteboard​​and​​then​​some​​physical​​copies​
       ​for​ ​those​ ​children​ ​that​ ​need​ ​it.​ ​(Leah​ ​-​ ​Member​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​Community​ ​and​
       ​Primary School Teacher)​

​Nancy​ ​(Jewish,​ ​Educator)​ ​also​ ​agreed​ ​that​ ​a​ ​digital​ ​resource​ ​would​ ​be​ ​the​ ​most​ ​suitable​
​option​​but​​suggested​​having​​both​​formats.​​She​​explained​​that​​“...online​​is​​really​​useful…​​but​​I​
​think​​there's​​something​​about​​leaving​​a​​room,​​and​​that​​a​​child​​can​​just​​go​​over,​​pick​​it​​up​​and​
​have​ ​a​ ​look​ ​at​ ​it​ ​again”.​ ​The​ ​following​ ​conversation​ ​took​ ​place​ ​in​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​at​ '​SH​
​School', where several reasons were discussed for this potential shift:​

       ​Sophia:​​I​​think​​it​​would​​be​​best​​for​​the​​teacher​​to​​just​​have​​a​​copy,​​and​​she​​would​
       ​read​ ​it​ ​and​ ​then​​choose​​the​​discussion​​points.​​You​​read​​the​​story,​​and​​then​​you​




                                                             ​200​
       ​might​ ​hone​ ​in​ ​on​ ​one​ ​particular​ ​question,​ ​because​ ​you​ ​might​ ​want​ ​to​ ​spend​
       ​longer on that want and not get around too many of the others.​

       ​Charlotte: I would read the story to them.​

       ​Lauren: Yes, I would read to them.​

       ​Interviewer: Okay, rather than they read a section each?​

       ​Charlotte: No, I would read it to them, a chapter a week and then discuss it.​

       ​Interviewer: So, there is no need for every child to have a copy?​

       ​Sophia:​​Well,​​you​​would​​just​​have​​it​​up​​on​​the​​white​​board,​​and​​then​​you​​can​​all​
       ​follow it…​

       ​Carly:​ ​Yes,​ ​because​ ​some​ ​children​ ​will​ ​find​ ​it​ ​hard​ ​to​ ​follow,​ ​listen​ ​or​ ​focus,​ ​or​
       ​they​​don’t​​learn​​the​​same,​​then​​they​​might​​have​​a​​crib​​sheet,​​but​​it​​would​​be​​on​
       ​the board so everyone can access it.​

       ​Sophia: If it’s on the board then everyone is focused on the same thing.​

       ​Charlotte:​​Then​​if​​it​​is​​on​​the​​board​​you​​can​​do​​it​​as​​guided​​reading,​​as​​every​​child​
       ​could​​read​​one​​sentence​​and​​go​​around.​​I​​think​​it​​is​​the​​teachers​​that​​should​​be​
       ​asking the questions, not them deciding.​

       ​Carly:​​What​​tends​​to​​happen​​with​​‘Read​​Write​​Inc’,​​is​​that​​the​​questions​​that​​are​
       ​in​​the​​book,​​they​​can’t​​help​​themselves​​but​​start​​flicking​​to​​where​​the​​questions​
       ​are,​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​concentrating​ ​on​ ​what​ ​they​ ​should​ ​actually​ ​be​ ​doing​ ​and​
       ​focusing​​on.​​I​​like​​the​​questions​​because​​they​​were​​clear.​​Sometimes​​they​​can​​be​
       ​quite​ ​ambiguous​ ​and​ ​you​ ​don't​ ​know​ ​what​ ​they​ ​actually​ ​mean​ ​but​ ​whereas​ ​I​
       ​think these are nice and easy to understand.​

​The​ ​conversation​ ​at​ ​SH​ ​School​ ​highlighted​ ​a​ ​strong​ ​preference​ ​for​ ​a​ ​digital​ ​resource,​ ​with​
​four​ ​out​ ​of​ ​the​ ​six​ ​teachers​ ​in​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​advocating​ ​for​ ​its​ ​electronic​ ​delivery.​
​Additionally,​ ​Carly​ ​reflected​ ​on​ ​previous​ ​educational​ ​resources,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​‘Read​ ​Write​ ​Inc,’​


                                                               ​201​
​pointing​ ​out​ ​the​ ​limitations​ ​of​ ​its​ ​practical​ ​application.​ ​This​ ​led​ ​to​​a​​reconsideration​​of​​the​
​book’s​ ​potential​ ​format,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​the​ ​guidance​ ​provided​ ​to​ ​staff​ ​when​ ​leading​ ​sessions.​
​However,​ ​the​ ​comments​​from​​Sophia​​and​​Tom​​in​​this​​sub-theme​​raised​​concerns​​about​​the​
​possible​ ​selectivity​ ​of​​teaching​​content​​by​​staff.​​It​​could​​be​​problematic​​if​​educators​​choose​
​what​​to​​teach​​based​​on​​their​​own​​understanding,​​knowledge,​​or​​biases.​​This​​selectivity​​might​
​result​ ​in​ ​key​ ​content​ ​being​ ​overlooked​ ​or​ ​misrepresented,​ ​as​ ​some​ ​adults,​ ​as​ ​discussed​ ​in​
​Theme​ ​5,​ ​may​ ​not​ ​fully​ ​grasp​​antisemitism​​and​​Judaism.​​Given​​the​​significant​​role​​teachers​
​play​ ​in​ ​children's​ ​achievement​ ​and​ ​engagement​ ​(Tellez​ ​and​ ​Waxman,​ ​2006),​ ​it​ ​is​ ​essential​
​that they avoid projecting personal assumptions onto their students.​

​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​this​ ​conversation,​ ​Matthew​ ​(Development​ ​Officer)​ ​raised​ ​that​ ​this​ ​would​
​mostly​​be​​taught​​online,​​as​​a​​result​​of​​his​​experiences​​delivering​​similar​​initiatives,​​suggesting​
​to​ ​“embed​ ​a​ ​link​ ​to​ ​find​ ​a​ ​video​ ​where​​it​​is​​actually​​creating​​that​​behaviour​​because​​it​​will​
​mostly​ ​be​ ​used​ ​online”.​ ​Therefore,​ ​the​ ​overall​ ​group​ ​consensus​ ​from​ ​both​ ​an​ ​expert​ ​and​
​educators​​was​​that​​there​​should​​be​​an​​online​​version​​for​​staff​​to​​follow​​with​​the​​children,​​but​
​physical​ ​copies​ ​for​ ​those​ ​students​ ​who​ ​may​ ​have​ ​additional​ ​needs,​ ​or​ ​would​​rather​​follow​
​along by themselves.​

​In​ ​conclusion,​ ​this​ ​theme​ ​has​ ​examined​ ​the​ ​structure​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​highlighting​ ​its​
​perceived​​strengths,​​such​​as​​enabling​​students​​to​​learn​​about​​various​​forms​​of​​discrimination​
​alongside​​antisemitism.​​It​​also​​addressed​​some​​of​​the​​complexities​​that​​arise​​from​​the​​book's​
​shift​ ​from​ ​a​ ​broad​ ​to​ ​a​ ​more​ ​focused​ ​approach.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​the​ ​final​
​chapter​ ​was​ ​discussed,​ ​emphasising​ ​how​ ​it​ ​empowers​ ​children​ ​to​ ​demonstrate​ ​their​
​understanding​ ​of​ ​being​ ​assertive​ ​bystanders.​ ​The​ ​final​ ​sub-theme​ ​revealed​ ​a​ ​shift​ ​in​
​perspective​ ​through​ ​discussions​ ​with​ ​educators,​ ​suggesting​ ​a​ ​preference​ ​for​ ​a​ ​digital​
​resource rather than the originally proposed physical format.​

​Theme 4 - Football as an educational tool​


​The​ ​fourth​ ​theme​ ​titled​ ​‘football​ ​as​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​tool’​,​​discusses​​the​​power​​and​​the​​role​
​that​ ​football​ ​plays​ ​within​ ​the​ ​story.​ ​Hansen​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2023,​ ​p.​ ​305)​ ​states​ ​that​​“sport​​has​​the​
​power​ ​to​ ​unite​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​divide​​communities”.​​In​​addition,​​literature​​from​​Kidd​​(2008)​​and​
​Merkel​​(2016)​​has​​showcased​​that​​sport​​is​​one​​of​​the​​most​​effective​​resources​​for​​promoting​


                                                              ​202​
​unity,​​tolerance,​​and​​understanding.​​It​​was​​with​​that​​in​​mind​​that​​the​​researcher​​authored​​a​
​book​​on​​discrimination​​through​​a​​story​​which​​involves​​football,​​whereby​​there​​are​​moments​
​of​ ​division​ ​and​ ​unity.​ ​On​ ​the​ ​whole,​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​was​ ​that​ ​the​ ​book​ ​uses​ ​football​ ​to​ ​provide​​a​
​platform​ ​for​ ​students​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​in​ ​wider​ ​conversations​ ​that​ ​extend​ ​beyond​ ​sport​ ​itself.​
​Within​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​groups,​ ​discussions​ ​centred​ ​around​ ​the​ '​role​ ​of​ ​football,'​ '​gender​ ​and​
​football,'​ ​and​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that​ ​the​ ​football-themed​ ​resource​ ​would​ ​have​ ​an​ ​impact​ '​even​ ​for​
​non-footballers,'​​which led to the development of​​the three sub-themes.​


​The role of football​


​With​​football​​being​​described​​by​​Roderick​​(2006)​​the​​most​​popular​​sport​​in​​the​​world,​​it​​has​
​a​ ​role​ ​in​ ​society​ ​to​ ​reflect​ ​the​ ​realities​ ​of​​broader​​social​​realities,​​and​​as​​such,​​it​​should​​be​
​used​​in​​an​​authentic​​manner​​that​​reflects​​both​​the​​positive​​and​​negative​​aspects​​of​​football's​
​role​ ​in​ ​society,​ ​as​ ​has​ ​been​ ​emphasised​ ​in​ ​previous​ ​studies​​by​​Penfold​​and​​Cleland​​(2022).​
​Paul​​discusses​​how​​football​​has​​been​​used​​in​​a​​positive​​way​​to​​educate​​children​​on​ ​a​​current​
​societal issue, specifically antisemitism:​


       ​I​ ​think​ ​it's​ ​a​ ​good​ ​way​ ​of​ ​addressing​ ​the​ ​issue​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​by​ ​looking​ ​at​
       ​something that kids are going to be interested in, namely football. (Paul - Jewish)​


​Nevertheless,​ ​although​ ​this​ ​book​ ​aimed​ ​to​ ​use​ ​football​ ​in​ ​a​ ​positive​ ​light​ ​to​ ​tackle​ ​such​
​issues,​ ​the​ ​European​ ​Union​ ​Agency​ ​for​ ​Fundamental​ ​Rights​ ​(2010)​ ​emphasised​ ​that​ ​men's​
​professional​​and​​amateur​​football​​is​​the​​sport​​in​​which​​acts​​of​​racism,​​including​​antisemitism,​
​occur​ ​most​ ​frequently​ ​and​ ​where​ ​the​ ​offenders​ ​are​ ​primarily​ ​fans.​ ​This​ ​was​ ​later​
​acknowledged​ ​by​ ​participants​ ​within​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​that​ ​football,​ ​unfortunately,​​has​​the​
​power to bring about negative, anti-discriminatory language:​


       ​It​​doesn’t​​happen​​in​​other​​sports,​​I​​go​​to​​rugby,​​and​​all​​you​​hear​​is​​“Come​​on​​you​
       ​Queens”.​ ​There​ ​is​ ​absolutely​ ​no​ ​anti-anything,​​they​​are​​only​​trying​​to​​out​​chant​
       ​each​ ​other,​ ​with​ ​their​ ​chant​ ​and​ ​the​ ​volume​ ​of​ ​the​ ​noise.​ ​(Lauren​ ​-​ ​Year​ ​6​
       ​Teacher and Head of English)​




                                                              ​203​
​The​ ​concerns​ ​that​ ​participants​ ​had​ ​was​ ​how​ ​the​ ​language​​being​​heard​​at​​football​​matches​
​can be passed onto young children, having a significant impact on them:​


       ​What​ ​do​ ​you​ ​do​ ​when​ ​they​ ​are​ ​14,​ ​they​ ​don’t​ ​need​ ​their​ ​parents​​anymore​​(​to​
       ​attend)​?​ ​I​ ​know​ ​that​ ​Club​ ​Name​ ​have​ ​their​ ​juniors’​ ​section​ ​and​ ​I​ ​wonder​ ​how​
       ​close​​are​​they​​to​​the​​action?​​And​​how​​close​​are​​they​​to​​hearing​​this?​​It​​only​​takes​
       ​one comment, one person from that group… (Rachel - Year 3 teacher)​


​The​ ​concerns​ ​raised​ ​by​ ​participants,​ ​particularly​ ​the​ ​one​ ​voiced​ ​by​ ​Rachel,​ ​highlight​ ​a​
​growing​ ​issue​ ​regarding​ ​the​ ​influence​ ​of​ ​inappropriate​ ​language​ ​and​ ​behaviour​ ​at​ ​football​
​matches​ ​on​ ​young​ ​audiences.​ ​Supporting​ ​Rachel’s​ ​point,​ ​Carly,​ ​another​ ​teacher,​ ​expressed​
​concerns​ ​about​ ​the​​influence​​of​​football​​on​​children,​​arguing​​that​​“it​​leads​​into​​it​​every​​day​
​though​ ​isn't​​it,​​so​​if​​you're​​raising​​your​​child​​to​​like​​football,​​then​​it​​will​​filter​​down”.​ ​These​
​comments​ ​reinforce​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​having​ ​football​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​in​​which​​to​​teach​​children​
​about​​discrimination​​as​​football​​has​​a​​unique​​position​​in​​society,​​which​​can​​shape​​values​​and​
​behaviours,​ ​but​ ​it​ ​also​ ​has​ ​the​ ​responsibility​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​​young​​fans​​are​​not​​exposed​​to​
​harmful​ ​influences.​ ​Educators​ ​like​ ​Rachel​ ​and​ ​Carly​ ​stress​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​creating​ ​an​
​environment​ ​where​ ​football​ ​can​ ​be​ ​used​ ​as​​a​​force​​for​​good,​​one​​that​​promotes​​inclusivity​
​and​ ​teaches​ ​children​ ​how​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​with​ ​the​ ​sport.​ ​However,​ ​Matthew​ ​(Development​
​Officer)​ ​works​ ​within​ ​schools’​ ​states​ ​that​ ​the​ ​power​ ​football​ ​has​ ​on​ ​his​ ​work​ ​can​ ​be​
​detrimental:​


       ​We​ ​do​ ​our​ ​schools’​ ​programme​ ​and​ ​the​ ​kids​ ​buy​ ​into​ ​that.​ ​We​ ​have​ ​a​ ​huge​
       ​engagement,​ ​4,800​ ​children​ ​this​ ​year,​ ​58​​schools,​​so​​the​​message​​is​​over​​there.​
       ​But​ ​if​ ​you​ ​go​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Club​ ​Name​ ​game​ ​yesterday,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​singing​ ​is​ ​just​
       ​horrendous…​​that​​stuff​​is​​still​​there,​​even​​though​​we​​teach​​them​​it​​is​​wrong.​​They​
       ​go​​to​​the​​match,​​and​​you​​know​​in​​the​​excitement,​​all​​that​​and​​their​​role​​models​
       ​and their peers are doing it. So, that's the biggest conflict.​


​Matthew’s​​quote​​highlights​​the​​significant​​conflict​​between​​the​​positive​​messages​​delivered​
​through​ ​football’s​ ​educational​ ​programmes​ ​and​ ​the​ ​harmful​ ​behaviours​ ​and​ ​language​ ​that​
​still​ ​persist​ ​within​​the​​culture​​of​​the​​sport.​​On​​one​​hand,​​the​​schools’​​programme​​he​​works​


                                                            ​204​
​on​ ​engages​ ​thousands​ ​of​ ​children,​ ​teaching​ ​them​ ​values​ ​such​ ​as​ ​respect​ ​and​ ​inclusivity.​
​However,​​on​​the​​other​​hand,​​when​​these​​children​​attend​​football​​matches,​​they​​are​​exposed​
​to​​inappropriate​​behaviour,​​such​​as​​offensive​​chants​​and​​language,​​which​​can​​undermine​​the​
​lessons they have learned.​


​These​ ​comments​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​concerns​ ​that​ ​adults​ ​have​ ​when​ ​young​ ​children​ ​attend​
​football​ ​matches,​ ​which​ ​greatly​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​importance​​of​​educating​​young​​kids​​about​
​the​ ​language​ ​and​ ​attitudes​ ​that​ ​may​ ​be​ ​observed​ ​at​ ​games.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​reinforced​
​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​faced​ ​by​ ​individuals​ ​and​ ​experts,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Matthew​ ​(Development​
​Officer),​​who​​are​​trying​​to​​address​​problems​​like​​antisemitism,​​but​​football​​may​​significantly​
​undermine​ ​the​ ​education-based​ ​work​ ​being​​done​​for​​young​​people.​​However,​​it​​is​​not​​only​
​football​​that​​creates​​these​​attitudes;​​Brian,​​who​​also​​worked​​for​​an​​organisation​​which​​aims​
​to​ ​tackle​ ​discrimination​ ​within​ ​sport,​ ​states​ ​that​​“they're​​trying​​to​​handle​​a​​problem​​which​
​isn't,​ ​solely​ ​a​ ​football​ ​problem.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​a​ ​societal​ ​issue.​ ​So,​ ​they're​​working​​in​​a​​microcosm​​of​
​society.”​ ​His​ ​comment​ ​is​ ​supported​ ​in​ ​the​ ​work​ ​of​ ​Hartmann​ ​(2000),​ ​who​ ​contends​ ​that​
​sports​ ​can​ ​perpetuate​ ​the​ ​very​ ​discrimination​ ​and​ ​inequalities​ ​prevalent​ ​in​ ​society​ ​and​
​Hylton​ ​(2018)​ ​who​ ​states​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​a​ ​microcosm​ ​of​ ​society.​ ​The​ ​issue​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​
​serves​ ​as​ ​a​ ​crucial​ ​example,​ ​existing​ ​worldwide​ ​with​ ​26%​ ​of​ ​the​ ​global​ ​population​
​acknowledging​ ​they​ ​hold​ ​antisemitic​ ​attitudes​ ​(Anti-Defamation​ ​League,​ ​2019).​ ​With​ ​a​
​quarter​​of​​the​​population​​admitting​​to​​holding​​such​​attitudes,​​it​​reinforces,​​alongside​​Brian's​
​observation,​ ​how​ ​sports​ ​organisations​ ​are​ ​grappling​ ​with​ ​challenges​ ​that​ ​mirror​ ​broader​
​societal concerns.​


​Gender and football​


​Amongst​​both​​experts​​and​​teachers,​​there​​was​​significant​​discussion​​around​​gender​​and​​the​
​impact​ ​the​ ​book​ ​might​ ​have​ ​on​ ​girls.​ ​Possibly​ ​due​ ​to​ ​the​ ​recent​ ​success​ ​of​ ​the​ ​England​
​Women’s​ ​football​ ​team,​ ​known​ ​as​​the​​Lionesses,​​at​​the​​2022​​Euros​​and​​the​​2023​​Women’s​
​World​​Cup,​​which​​has​​had​​a​​profoundly​​positive​​effect​​on​​young​​girls.​​This​​impact​​is​​reflected​
