​in​​the​​notable​​growth​​in​​girls’​​clubs,​​ticket​​sales​​for​​women's​​matches,​​media​​coverage,​​and​
​accolades​​and​​achievements​​for​​female​​footballers​​(Culvin​​and​​Bowes,​​2023;​​Williams,​​2003).​
​Leah’s comment below reinforces the importance of the Lionesses' achievements:​


                                                              ​205​
       ​I​​think​​especially​​following​​the​​Lionesses​​victory,​​I​​think​​you've​​got​​a​​real​​kind​​of​
       ​opportunity​ ​to​ ​open​ ​that​ ​up.​ ​I​ ​mean,​ ​one​ ​of​ ​my​ ​girls​ ​plays​ ​football​ ​for​ ​a​ ​local​
       ​team​ ​with​ ​a​ ​whole​ ​bunch​ ​of​​boys…​​But​​for​​her​​because​​the​​Lionesses​​won,​​the​
       ​boys​ ​don't​ ​even​ ​question​ ​the​ ​fact​ ​that​ ​she's​ ​playing​ ​football​ ​with​ ​them​ ​now.​
       ​Whereas if you've gone back 18 months…​


​Subsequently​ ​because​ ​of​ ​this​ ​“far​ ​more​ ​girls​​are​​getting​​into​​football”,​​which​​demonstrates​
​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​having​ ​female​ ​role​ ​models.​ ​Therefore,​ ​having​ ​‘Zara’​ ​as​ ​a​ ​key​ ​character​
​within​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​who​ ​is​ ​an​ ​avid​ ​football​ ​fan​ ​and​ ​player,​ ​was​ ​positively​ ​received​ ​from​ ​all​
​participants.​​Leah​​continues​​to​​say​​that​​“I​​thought​​it​​was​​a​​great​​touch​​to​​have​​a​​Muslim​​girl​
​playing​​football…​​I​​thought​​that​​was​​really​​cute”.​​Likewise,​​Brian​​also​​“really​​liked​​that​​it​​had​
​the​ ​mixed​ ​team,​ ​and​ ​that​ ​the​ ​little​ ​girl​ ​was​ ​quite​ ​a​ ​good​ ​footballer​ ​too”.​ ​The​ ​character​ ​of​
​‘Zara’​​was​​also​​well​​received​​at​​SH​​school,​​and​​because​​of​​that​​there​​were​​discussions​​about​
​why​​‘Zara’​​was​​not​​the​​main​​character​​as​​having​​a​​girl​​main​​character​​would​​have​​been​​highly​
​influential.​


       ​I​ ​definitely​ ​did​ ​actually​ ​read​ ​it​ ​twice​ ​to​ ​check,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​a​ ​girl's​ ​name.​ ​(Simon​ ​-​
       ​Jewish)​


​However,​​Simon's​​comment​​above​​reveals​​a​​lingering​​misconception​​that​​football​​is​​primarily​
​a​​sport​​for​​boys.​​Likewise,​​comments​​from​​Rachel​​(Year​​3​​Teacher)​​stating​​“but​​it​​is​​also​​nice​
​that​​you​​bought​​girls​​into​​this”​​and​​Keagan​​(EDI​​Manager)​​saying​​“obviously​​it's​​football​​and​
​now​ ​for​ ​boys​ ​and​ ​girls​ ​it​ ​appeals.​ ​You​ ​know,​ ​some​ ​girls​ ​play​ ​football​ ​as​ ​well,”​ ​further​
​emphasise​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that,​ ​despite​ ​the​ ​rapid​ ​growth​ ​of​ ​women's​ ​football,​ ​the​ ​sport​ ​is​ ​still​
​largely​ ​perceived​ ​as​ ​masculine,​ ​dominated​ ​by​ ​boys​ ​and​ ​men.​ ​While​ ​Rachel​ ​and​ ​Keagan's​
​comments​​were​​positive,​​they​​highlight​​a​​challenge​​in​​shifting​​this​​perception.​​As​​highlighted​
​in​ ​the​ ​first​ ​theme,​ ​an​ ​additional​ ​character​ ​has​ ​been​ ​added​ ​to​ ​the​ ​story,​ ​so​ ​that​ ​there​ ​is​
​mention​​of​​a​​female​​footballing​​role​​model,​​which​​will​​also​​strengthen​​throughout​​the​​story​
​that sport, specifically football can, and is, played by girls and women.​




                                                               ​206​
​While​ ​the​ ​primary​ ​focus​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​is​ ​on​ ​antisemitism,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​adopt​ ​an​
​intersectional​​approach​​that​​also​​addresses​​various​​forms​​of​​discrimination,​​allowing​​readers​
​to​ ​connect​ ​more​ ​broadly​ ​with​ ​the​ ​resource.​ ​This​ ​approach​ ​aligns​ ​with​ ​CRT,​ ​which​ ​has​
​similarly​ ​used​ ​an​ ​intersectional​ ​lens​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​how​ ​race​ ​intersects​ ​with​ ​other​ ​forms​ ​of​
​discrimination,​​such​​as​​gender​​and​​social​​class​​(Crenshaw,​​1993).​​Ultimately,​​while​​the​​goal​​is​
​to​​combat​​antisemitism​​by​​acknowledging​​other​​social​​discriminations​​like​​gender​​and​​race,​
​there is potential to also challenge children’s sexist or racist attitudes.​


​Even for the non-footballers​


​Within​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​data​ ​collection,​ ​interviews​ ​with​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​ ​a​ ​key​
​recommendation​ ​was​ ​that​ ​sport,​ ​specifically​ ​football,​ ​should​ ​be​ ​used​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​​in​​which​​to​
​engage​ ​individuals​ ​with​ ​the​ ​initiative.​ ​This​ ​supports​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​both​ ​Darnell​ ​and​
​Millington​​(2019),​​who​​reinforce​​that​​sport​​can​​be​​used​​to​​encourage​​social​​change​​for​​issues​
​that​ ​affect​ ​society​ ​on​ ​a​ ​broader​ ​scale.​ ​In​ ​particular,​ ​the​ ​review​ ​of​ ​literature​ ​observed​
​programmes​​like​​Show​​Racism​​the​​Red​​Card​​to​​lessen​​racism​​and​​Stonewall's​​Rainbow​​Laces​
​to​ ​oppose​ ​homophobia​ ​and​ ​transphobia.​ ​However,​ ​while​ ​these​ ​initiatives​ ​are​ ​widely​
​recognised,​ ​research​ ​from​ ​Magrath​​and​​Stott​​(2019)​​and​​Hansen​​et​​al.​​(2023)​​discusses​​the​
​impact​​of​​Stonewall's​​Rainbow​​Laces;​​although​​they​​promote​​educational​​conversations​​and​
​are​​frequently​​supported​​and​​well-received​​by​​fans,​​there​​are​​concerns​​about​​the​​purpose​​of​
​wearing​​them.​​Hansen​​and​​colleagues​​(2023)​​discovered​​that​​the​​Rainbow​​Laces​​campaign​​is​
​possibly​​being​​implemented​​by​​clubs​​for​​commercial​​reasons,​​as​​they​​fail​​to​​provide​​evidence​
​of​ ​them​ ​supporting​ ​the​ ​LGBT+​ ​community​ ​and​ ​movement​ ​outside​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Rainbow​ ​Laces​
​campaign.​​On​​the​​other​​hand,​​Dixon​​et​​al.​​(2016)​​explored​​the​​impact​​that​​Show​​Racism​​the​
​Red​​Card​​has​​had,​​stating​​that​​the​​charity​​has​​been​​praised​​for​​its​​efforts​​to​​combat​​racism,​
​even​ ​though​ ​the​ ​long-term​ ​impact​ ​is​ ​limited.​ ​Similar​ ​criticisms​ ​have​ ​been​ ​aimed​ ​at​ ​the​
​Stonewall​ ​Rainbow​ ​Laces​ ​campaign​​for​​having​​a​​limited​​impact​​because​​they​​are​​only​​worn​
​for one week out of the year (BBC, 2017).​


​Furthermore,​​while​​these​​initiatives​​aim​​to​​engage​​people​​through​​sport,​​they​​do​​not​​always​
​account​​for​​the​​fact​​that​​not​​everyone​​connects​​with​​or​​enjoys​​sport.​​Although​​the​​following​
​comment​ ​from​ ​Patrick,​ ​suggests​ ​a​ ​broad​ ​appeal,​ ​it​ ​reflects​ ​a​ ​somewhat​ ​naive​​assumption;​


                                                          ​207​
​while​ ​football​ ​and​ ​friendship​ ​are​ ​indeed​ ​popular​ ​among​ ​many​ ​children,​ ​this​ ​perspective​
​overlooks the fact that not all children share the same interest in sport:​


       ​It​ ​is​ ​a​ ​book​ ​about​ ​football​ ​and​ ​friendships​ ​which​ ​boys​ ​and​ ​girls​ ​love!​ ​(Patrick​​-​
       ​Jewish)​


​As​ ​stated​ ​above​ ​by​ ​Patrick,​​football​​is​​enjoyed​​by​​many​​children,​​but​​it​​must​​be​​considered​
​that​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​football​ ​are​ ​not​ ​always​ ​enjoyed​ ​by​ ​all.​​Matthew​​(Development​​Officer)​​says​
​that​​“we​​can't​​make​​the​​massive​​assumption​​that​​all​​the​​kids​​enjoy​​football”,​​which​​was​​a​​key​
​concern​​for​​the​​researcher​​that​​those​​individuals​​who​​were​​not​​interested​​in​​football​​would​
​not​​engage​​with​​the​​book.​​However,​​Rachel​​(Year​​3​​Teacher)​​commented​​that​​“even​​though​
​there​​are​​many​​who​​are​​not​​interested​​in​​football.​​I​​thought​​it​​went​​beyond​​the​​kids​​who​​are​
​just​ ​footballers”,​ ​emphasising​​that​​kids​​do​​not​​have​​to​​be​​football​​fans​​to​​enjoy​​and​​engage​
​with the book. This point was also articulated by other interviewees:​


       ​I​​mean​​I’m​​not​​a​​football​​fan.​​So,​​reading​​the​​story​​about​​football​​I​​actually​​liked​
       ​the​​way​​you​​described​​the​​football,​​how​​they're​​passing​​it​​and​​I​​was​​really​​getting​
       ​into​ ​it​ ​even​ ​though​ ​I’m​ ​not​ ​a​ ​sports​ ​fan.​ ​(Jasmine​ ​-​ ​Teacher​ ​of​ ​Languages​ ​and​
       ​Religious Studies)​


​Similarly,​ ​Jasmine,​ ​who​ ​is​ ​not​ ​a​ ​football​ ​fan,​ ​began​ ​to​ ​enjoy​ ​the​ ​features​ ​involving​ ​the​
​matches,​​suggesting​​that​​others​​who​​are​​not​​already​​fans​​of​​the​​sport​​might​​also​​develop​​an​
​interest because of this book. Sophia shared similar comments, stating that:​


       ​I​​don’t​​like​​football​​and​​when​​I​​read​​it,​​it​​was​​engaging.​​It​​was​​the​​stories​​and​​the​
       ​characters in it. The fact that it was football, just provided a nice context.​


​This​ ​comment​ ​from​ ​Sophia​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​even​ ​for​​those​​non-footballing​​fans,​​the​​football​
​has a significance and purpose in the book, which Carly also mentions:​




                                                              ​208​
       ​…the​ ​football​ ​part​ ​it's​ ​not​ ​a​ ​dominant​ ​part​ ​of​​the​​story.​​It's​​the​​characters,​​and​
       ​their​ ​backgrounds,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​more,​ ​I​ ​would​ ​say,​ ​overarching​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​just​
       ​football.​


​In​ ​summary,​ ​this​ ​theme​ ​has​ ​explored​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​football​ ​as​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​tool.​ ​It​
​acknowledges​ ​that​ ​football​ ​has​​been​​used​​to​​enhance​​the​​impact​​of​​previous​​campaigns​​to​
​address​ ​societal​ ​issues,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out’s​ ​work​ ​to​ ​tackle​ ​discrimination.​ ​Nevertheless,​
​participants​ ​reinforced​ ​that​ ​football​​matches​​specifically​​mirror​​these​​issues​​seen​​in​​society​
​by​ ​displaying​ ​higher​ ​instances​ ​of​ ​discriminatory​ ​behaviours.​ ​Discussions​ ​then​ ​explored​ ​the​
​challenges​ ​for​ ​experts​ ​aiming​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​young​​children​​about​​discrimination.​​Additionally,​
​the​ ​theme​ ​has​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​target​ ​audience,​ ​examining​ ​both​ ​gender​ ​and​ ​those​
​potentially​ ​disinterested​ ​in​ ​football.​ ​It​ ​has​ ​been​ ​pointed​ ​out​ ​that​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​impact​ ​on​
​gender-related​ ​discourses​ ​could​​be​​substantial​​due​​to​​its​​inclusion​​of​​female​​characters​​and​
​the​ ​recent​​surge​​in​​women's​​football.​​Similarly,​​it​​highlights​​how​​the​​book​​can​​be​​appealing​
​to​ ​a​ ​diverse​ ​audience,​ ​even​ ​those​ ​not​ ​particularly​ ​drawn​ ​to​ ​football,​ ​resulting​ ​from​ ​its​
​relatable storylines and characters.​


​Theme 5 - Key teachings​


​The​ ​fifth​ ​theme​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​key​ ​take​ ​home​ ​messages​ ​that​ ​children​ ​would​ ​learn​ ​after​
​completing​​the​​educational​​initiative,​​based​​on​​participants'​​perspectives​​from​​the​​interview​
​data.​​Children's​​literature​​is​​created​​with​​the​​intention​​of​​fun​​and​​enjoyment,​​as​​mentioned​
​by​ ​Yokota​ ​(2011).​ ​As​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​Theme​ ​4,​ ​‘football​ ​as​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​tool’,​ ​football​ ​was​
​incorporated​ ​in​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​design​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​children​ ​in​ ​a​ ​fun​ ​way.​ ​However,​ ​the​ ​primary​
​objective​ ​was​ ​to​ ​increase​ ​kids'​ ​comprehension​ ​of​ ​discrimination,​ ​particularly​ ​antisemitism.​
​As​ ​stated​ ​in​ ​the​ ​quote​ ​below,​ ​from​ ​Leah,​ ​teaching​​children​​from​​a​​young​​age​​is​​thought​​to​
​have significant influence upon discriminatory attitudes:​


       ​Children​ ​don't​ ​see​ ​it.​ ​It's​ ​a​ ​learned​ ​behaviour,​ ​the​ ​discrimination.​​A​​baby​​is​​not​
       ​born​ ​wanting​ ​to​ ​discriminate,​ ​and​ ​that's​ ​what​​my​​eight-year-old​​couldn't​​grasp.​
       ​Why​​would​​someone​​do​​that?​​And​​I​​think​​if​​we​​can​​get​​them​​at​​this​​age​​then​​it’s​
       ​great.​


                                                            ​209​
​The​ ​quote​ ​from​ ​Leah​ ​reinforces​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that​ ​teaching​ ​children​ ​at​ ​a​ ​young​​age​​can​​have​​a​
​significant​ ​impact​ ​on​ ​shaping​ ​their​ ​attitudes​ ​toward​ ​discrimination.​ ​Therefore,​ ​one​ ​of​ ​the​
​questions​ ​posed​ ​to​ ​participants​ ​was​ ​what​ ​they​ ​believed​ ​the​ ​key​ ​takeaways​ ​from​ ​the​ ​book​
​would​ ​be,​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​it​ ​achieved​ ​its​​intended​​objective.​​As​​a​​result,​​this​​theme​​entitled​​‘key​
​teachings’,​ ​investigates​ ​how​ ​participants​ ​interpreted​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​most​ ​important​
​lessons.​ ​This​ ​theme​ ​was​ ​created​ ​from​ ​a​ ​number​​of​​sub-themes,​​including:​​‘develop​​a​​basic​
​understanding​ ​of​ ​discrimination’,​ ​‘improving​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​Judaism​ ​and​ ​antisemitism’,​
​‘discussion, question and expression’,​​and​​‘breaking​​the cycle’.​


​Develop a basic understanding of discrimination​


​Gilmore​ ​and​ ​Howard's​ ​(2016)​ ​study​ ​on​ ​disability​ ​discrimination​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​children's​
​books​ ​can​ ​help​ ​readers​ ​accept​ ​themselves​ ​and​ ​others​ ​while​ ​challenging​ ​misconceptions,​
​preconceptions,​ ​and​ ​stereotypes.​ ​This​ ​aligns​ ​with​ ​participants'​ ​views,​ ​who​ ​believed​ ​the​
​educational​​initiative​​would​​teach​​children​​the​​basics​​of​​prejudice,​​with​​a​​particular​​focus​​on​
​antisemitism.​ ​Keagan​ ​(EDI​ ​Manager)​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​importance​​of​​helping​​children​​"get​​a​
​basic​ ​understanding​ ​that​ ​discrimination​ ​is​ ​bad,​ ​inclusion​ ​is​ ​good".​ ​Keagan’s​ ​comment​
​highlights​​discrimination​​as​​a​​broad​​issue,​​which​​Ellen​​also​​appreciates,​​noting​​"I​​liked​​that​​it​
​explores​ ​many​ ​different​ ​themes​ ​and​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination​ ​within​ ​one​ ​context".​ ​Both​
​Keagan​​and​​Ellen​​stress​​the​​value​​of​​teaching​​inclusion​​and​​combating​​discrimination,​​a​​point​
​Brian further reinforces by emphasising the positives of different cultures and backgrounds:​

       ​I'm​​hoping​​what​​they'll​​take​​away​​from​​this​​is​​an​​understanding​​and​​a​​tolerance.​
       ​And​​to​​understand​​that​​children,​​and​​your​​peers​​from​​different​​backgrounds​​are​
       ​all​​valid​​and​​they​​will​​have​​their​​things​​to​​bring​​to​​the​​table,​​and​​that​​you​​should​
       ​be​​interested​​in​​other​​people,​​not​​anti-them​​or​​not​​scared​​of​​them​​because​​they​
       ​just​​are​​the​​children…​​children​​with​​different​​backgrounds,​​and​​it​​is​​nice​​that​​they​
       ​have something to share. (Brian - Jewish)​

​Similarly,​ ​drawing​ ​upon​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​of​ ​tolerance​ ​was​ ​Iris​ ​(Jewish);​ ​she​ ​said​ ​that​ ​she​ ​hoped​
​children would learn:​



                                                           ​210​
       ​...to​​be​​tolerant​​of​​other​​people's​​different​​ideas​​and​​the​​way​​that​​they​​live​​their​
       ​lives​​and​​don’t​​have​​negative​​views​​about​​any​​religion​​really…​​it's​​tolerance,​​isn't​
       ​it?​ ​Just​ ​because​ ​it's​ ​different​​and​​you​​don't​​know​​that​​much​​about​​it,​​you​​don't​
       ​immediately say that's negative.​

​While​​tolerance​​is​​an​​important​​starting​​point,​​it​​should​​be​​noted​​that​​tolerance​​may​​not​​be​
​sufficient​ ​for​ ​fostering​ ​deep​ ​understanding​ ​and​ ​acceptance​ ​of​ ​diversity​ ​(Chinnery,​ ​2005).​
​Tolerance​​implies​​an​​unequal​​power​​dynamic,​​where​​one​​group​​has​​the​​authority​​to​​tolerate​
​or​ ​not​ ​tolerate​ ​another​ ​(Mirchandani​ ​and​ ​Tastsoglou,​ ​2000).​ ​This​ ​is​ ​reflected​ ​in​ ​the​
​perspectives​ ​of​ ​Brian​ ​and​ ​Iris,​ ​who​ ​both​ ​highlight​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​tolerance​ ​in​ ​helping​
​children​ ​understand​ ​and​ ​accept​ ​peers​ ​from​ ​diverse​ ​backgrounds.​ ​Brian​ ​emphasises​ ​that​
​children​ ​should​ ​not​ ​fear​ ​or​ ​reject​ ​others​ ​because​ ​of​ ​their​ ​differences,​ ​while​ ​Iris​ ​hopes​
​children​​will​​learn​​to​​accept​​different​​ideas​​and​​lifestyles​​without​​immediately​​labelling​​them​
​as​ ​negative.​ ​However,​ ​the​ ​challenge​ ​would​ ​remain​ ​in​ ​moving​ ​beyond​ ​mere​ ​tolerance​ ​to​
​genuinely appreciating and valuing these differences.​

​Furthermore,​ ​both​ ​Brian​ ​and​ ​Iris​ ​also​ ​explore​ ​the​ ​concept​ ​of​ ​understanding​ ​individual​
​differences,​ ​with​ ​Gilmore​ ​and​ ​Howard​ ​(2016,​ ​p.2)​ ​also​ ​discussing​​that​​“children’s​​literature​
​can​ ​potentially​ ​promote​ ​awareness​ ​of​ ​individual​ ​differences”.​ ​They​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​literature​
​serves​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​introduce​ ​young​ ​readers​​to​​perspectives​​and​​experiences​​different​​from​
​their​ ​own,​ ​fostering​ ​open-mindedness​ ​and​ ​reducing​ ​prejudices.​ ​Patrick,​ ​building​ ​on​ ​these​
​ideas,​ ​identified​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​lessons​ ​on​ ​religion​​and​​prejudice​​as​​crucial​​in​​teaching​​children​
​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​understanding​ ​other​ ​belief​ ​systems.​ ​He​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​"a​ ​basic​ ​need​ ​to​
​understand​ ​other​ ​beliefs​ ​properly​ ​and​ ​not​ ​to​ ​insult​ ​others,​ ​especially​ ​out​ ​of​ ​ignorance"​ ​is​
​vital​ ​for​ ​cultivating​ ​respect​ ​and​ ​tolerance.​ ​Chris​ ​similarly​ ​saw​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​having​ ​a​
​resource​​concentrated​​on​​his​​religion​​in​​particular,​​and​​said​​"I​​think​​there​​is​​a​​great​​need​​for​
​children to be taught from a fairly young age about the Jewish religion."​

​The​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​discussion​ ​at​ '​SH​ ​School'​ ​also​ ​draws​ ​upon​ ​a​ ​new​ ​basic​ ​understanding​ ​of​
​discrimination and how it can differentiate from children's current understanding of bullying:​

       ​Sophia: All children will know about bullying but this is different.​

       ​Carly: Yes, children think bullying is punching someone but it's not that…​


                                                           ​211​
       ​Sophia:​​It’s​​that​​lower​​level…​​not​​lower​​level​​because​​it’s​​not​​important,​​but​​that​
       ​lower level, hidden.​

       ​Rachel: It becomes almost acceptable, like the mum doing it.​

       ​Carly:​​But​​that​​is​​racism.​​The​​low-level​​abuse​​is​​bullying…​​ongoing​​low​​level​​could​
       ​I​​think,​​could​​possibly​​do​​more​​damage​​long​​term.​​Then​​you​​know​​a​​shorter​​term​
       ​of​ ​bullying,​​because​​I​​think​​it​​is​​a​​low​​level.​​It's​​that​​drip​​drip,​​and​​gradually​​you​
       ​will begin to think that because that's what you're hearing.​

       ​Jasmine:​​What​​I​​liked​​about​​it​​was,​​you​​know,​​it's​​not​​about​​the​​physical​​side,​​it's​
       ​about speech, and it’s not direct.​

​The​ ​teachers​ ​at​ ​‘SH​ ​School’​ ​reflected​ ​upon​ ​their​ ​experiences,​ ​and​ ​discussed​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​that​
​discrimination,​ ​as​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​is​ ​often​ ​misunderstood​ ​by​ ​the​ ​children,​ ​as​ ​children's​
​knowledge​​of​​bullying​​is​​often​​perceived​​to​​be​​physical.​​When​​comparing​​physical​​bullying​​to​
​verbal,​ ​Harachi,​ ​Catalano​ ​and​ ​Hawkins​ ​(1999)​ ​considered​ ​verbal​ ​bullying​​to​​have​​less​​of​​an​
​importance.​ ​However,​ ​as​ ​Carly​ ​states,​ ​the​ ​gradual,​ ​verbal​ ​discrimination​​can​​be​​considered​
​significantly​ ​worse,​ ​causing​ ​greater​ ​long-term​ ​impact.​ ​Support​ ​for​ ​this​ ​idea​ ​came​ ​from​ ​Iris​
​(Jewish),​​who​​expresses​​the​​challenges​​that​​antisemitism​​can​​often​​create​​due​​to​​the​​covert​
​nature of it:​

       ​In​ ​some​ ​ways​ ​it's​ ​more​ ​difficult​ ​to​ ​handle​ ​the​​prejudice​​against​​Jews​​compared​
       ​with​ ​other​ ​minority​ ​groups,​ ​because​ ​it​ ​can​ ​be​ ​covert.​ ​I​ ​mean,​ ​if​ ​somebody​ ​is​
       ​prejudiced​ ​against​ ​somebody​ ​disabled,​ ​it's​ ​obvious​ ​in​​the​​sense​​that,​​you​​know​
       ​that​ ​they're​ ​disabled,​ ​and​ ​it​ ​is​ ​awful…​ ​But​ ​with​ ​antisemitism,​ ​it​ ​can​ ​be​ ​very​
       ​covert.​​And​​so,​​people​​say,​​“Oh​​wow,​​no​​not​​me,​​I'm​​not​​antisemitic.​​And​​yet​​the​
       ​words are used in a way, which is sort of covert, so it's more difficult.​

​Iris​ ​draws​ ​upon​ ​the​ ​covert​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​antisemitism,​ ​arguing​ ​that​ ​at​ ​times​ ​it​ ​is​ ​not​ ​openly​
​acknowledged​ ​or​ ​displayed.​ ​In​ ​addition,​​drawing​​upon​​the​​idea​​that​​antisemitism​​is​​often​​a​
​hidden​ ​form​ ​of​ ​discrimination​ ​unlike​ ​other​ ​overt​ ​prejudice​​seen​​in​​society​​more​​often.​​She​
​uses​ ​the​​term​​covert​​to​​describe​​the​​nature​​of​​antisemitism​​which​​often​​makes​​it​​harder​​to​
​possibly​​notice,​​and​​subsequently​​then​​challenge.​​This​​supports​​the​​work​​of​​Rubin​​(2020)​​on​



                                                            ​212​
​HebCrit​ ​which​ ​acknowledges​ ​that​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​can​ ​often​ ​face​ ​challenges​ ​due​ ​to​ ​the​
​invisible​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​being​ ​Jewish​ ​as​ ​they​ ​are​ ​often​ ​perceived​ ​to​ ​have​ ​benefited​ ​from​ ​the​
​perceived​​Whiteness,​​and​​other​​stereotypical​​forms​​of​​power,​​such​​as​​economic​​and​​political​
​power.​​By​​having​​this​​conversation​​with​​Iris,​​it​​strengthens​​the​​need​​for​​this​​book,​​as​​it​​could​
​help​ ​teach​ ​children​ ​when​ ​antisemtism​ ​is​ ​prevalent​ ​and​ ​empower​ ​them​ ​to​ ​challenge​ ​it.​
​Nevertheless,​ ​it​ ​also​ ​reinforces​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​children​ ​may​ ​face​ ​when​ ​witnessing​
​antisemitism,​ ​due​ ​to​ ​it​ ​going​ ​often​ ​unrecognised.​ ​Therefore,​ ​through​ ​the​ ​teachings​ ​of​ ​this​
​book,​​staff​​also​​hoped​​that​​there​​would​​be​​increased​​awareness​​of​​discrimination​​as​​a​​form​
​of bullying, whilst learning the importance of reporting it.​

​Improving understanding of Judaism and antisemitism​


​It​​was​​also​​clear​​from​​the​​data​​collected​​and​​previous​​literature​​that​​there​​is​​frequently​​a​​lack​
​of​ ​knowledge​ ​of​ ​Judaism​ ​and​ ​antisemitism,​ ​despite​ ​the​ ​desire​ ​to​ ​teach​ ​children​ ​at​ ​a​
​fundamental​​level​​of​​understanding.​​A​​key​​strength​​highlighted​​by​​Diana​​(Teaching​​Assistant)​
​was that the resource will allow children to explore:​


       ​…an​​important​​subject​​that​​children​​should​​have​​knowledge​​of.​​The​​book​​would​
       ​inform​ ​children​ ​about​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​an​ ​informative​ ​way​ ​whilst​ ​making​ ​them​
       ​think.​


​From​ ​Diana’s​ ​comment​ ​it​ ​is​ ​evident​ ​that​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​need​ ​for​ ​greater​ ​education​ ​on​
​antisemitism. Bethan also agreed with Diana, and stated that:​


       ​I​​liked​​that​​it​​features​​themes​​not​​always​​touched​​upon​​in​​class.​​There​​isn’t​​much​
       ​of a focus on antisemitism specifically in the curriculum.​


​To​ ​support​ ​both​ ​of​ ​their​ ​comments,​ ​research​ ​from​ ​Neusner​ ​(2000;​ ​2003)​ ​has​ ​shown​ ​that​
​there​​is​​often​​confusion​​and​​a​​lack​​of​​understanding​​when​​it​​comes​​to​​the​​Jewish​​religion​​-​​a​
​position which was reflected in the arguments of Brian:​




                                                          ​213​
       ​I​​read​​this​​autobiography,​​and​​he​​said,​​when​​he​​was​​a​​child​​somebody​​asked​​him​
       ​what​ ​he​ ​wanted​ ​to​ ​be​ ​when​ ​he​ ​grew​ ​up​ ​and​ ​he​ ​said​ ​he​ ​wanted​ ​to​ ​be​ ​Jewish.​
       ​Because​ ​the​ ​only​ ​thing​ ​he​​associated​​with​​Jewish​​people​​was​​that​​they​​seemed​
       ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​lot​ ​of​ ​money​ ​and​ ​had​ ​big​ ​cars,​ ​so​​he​​thought​​that​​was​​a​​good​​job​​to​
       ​have and he didn't realise it was even a religion.​


​This​ ​quote​ ​highlights​ ​that​ ​there​ ​are​ ​often​ ​misunderstandings​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​
​including​ ​stereotypes​ ​about​ ​financial​ ​power.​ ​There​ ​are​ ​harmful,​ ​antisemitic​ ​stereotypes​
​which​ ​are​ ​often​ ​used​ ​in​ ​society​ ​and​ ​football,​ ​including​ ​that​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​have​ ​significant​
​economic​ ​and​ ​political​ ​power​ ​(Kofta​ ​et​ ​al.,​ ​2020).​​Along​​similar​​lines,​​Chris​​(Jewish)​​argued​
​that​ ​“[t]hey​ ​don’t​ ​know​ ​why​ ​they​ ​are​ ​antisemitic​ ​and​ ​that's​ ​where​ ​learning​ ​is​ ​important”.​
​Chris’​​comment​​highlights​​that​​assumptions​​are​​often​​misunderstood,​​which​​shows​​a​​lack​​of​
​understanding​ ​and​ ​which​​can​​subsequently​​lead​​to​​antisemitic​​abuse.​​Likewise,​​Iris​​(Jewish)​
​supports​​Chris’​​comment​​by​​drawing​​upon​​the​​story,​​stating​​that​​had​​the​​mother​​-​​who​​was​
​unable​ ​to​ ​teach​​Joe​​about​​the​​use​​of​​the​​term​​Yid​​-​​been​​more​​“understanding​​of​​it​​herself​
​then​ ​she​ ​would​ ​be​ ​able​ ​to​ ​talk​ ​to​ ​him,​ ​but​ ​she​ ​herself​ ​was​ ​totally​ ​ignorant​ ​about​ ​the​
​implications…​​but​​it's​​not​​overt​​in​​the​​sense​​that​​it's​​more​​ignorant,​​isn't​​it?”.​​This​​reinforces​
​that​​individuals,​​whether​​it​​be​​in​​the​​story​​or​​an​​individual's​​real​​life​​experiences​​may​​have​​a​
​lack​​of​​understanding​​about​​what​​constitutes​​antisemitic​​behaviour.​ ​Predominantly,​​research​
​by​​Boyd​​and​​Staetsky​​(2014)​​has​​found​​that​​stereotypes​​about​​Jewish​​people​​continue​​to​​be​
​misunderstood,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​also​ ​reflected​ ​in​ ​Patrick’s​ ​comments​ ​that​ ​he​​hoped​​that​​people​
​would​ ​“understand​ ​Jews​ ​are​ ​not​ ​evil​ ​and​ ​are​ ​like​ ​everyone​​else,​​albeit​​with​​different​​looks​
​like​​other​​faiths​​have”.​​In​​addition,​​this​​comment​​links​​back​​to​​the​​initial​​discussion​​in​​Theme​
​2,​ ​‘​importance​ ​of​​relatability​’,​​about​​the​​experiences​​of​​Jewish​​people,​​whereby​​there​​were​
​conversations​​about​​what​​a​​Jewish​​person​​is​​perceived​​to​​look​​like.​​Both​​of​​these​​points​​were​
​two​ ​key​ ​theoretical​ ​tenets​ ​of​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020);​ ​therefore,​ ​when​​developing​​the​​book,​
​the​​aim​​was​​to​​develop​​people's​​understanding​​around​​harmful​​stereotypes,​​about​​perceived​
​power and Whiteness as a valued characteristic.​


​Furthermore,​ ​Chris​ ​thought​ ​that​ ​the​ ​book​ ​would​ ​provide​ ​“opportunities​ ​for​ ​children​ ​and​
​parents​ ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​much​ ​better​ ​informative​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​how​ ​the​ ​hissing​ ​and​ ​the​
​chanting​​is​​hurtful”.​​In​​addition​​to​​the​​young​​children​​improving​​their​​knowledge,​​there​​was​


                                                            ​214​
​hope​ ​from​ ​participants​ ​that​ ​adults,​ ​parents,​ ​guardians​ ​and​ ​teachers,​ ​may​ ​enhance​ ​their​
​understanding of the Jewish religion:​


       ​Adults​ ​as​ ​well,​ ​you​ ​know,​ ​grown​ ​up​ ​people​ ​don't​ ​understand​ ​Judaism.​ ​Is​ ​it​ ​a​
       ​religion?​​Is​​it​​a​​race?​​Is​​it​​nationality?​​It's​​a​​whole​​misunderstanding​​in​​society,​​of​
       ​Judaism is? (Brian - Jewish)​


​Iwai​ ​(2015,​ ​p.81)​ ​says​ ​that​ ​“teachers​ ​are​ ​encouraged​ ​to​ ​model​ ​positive​ ​attitudes​ ​toward​
​diversity”.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​when​ ​gathering​ ​data,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​evident​ ​that​ ​adults,​ ​specifically​ ​the​
​teachers​ ​who​ ​may​ ​deliver​ ​the​​initiative,​​might​​also​​lack​​some​​understanding,​​as​​mentioned​
​above​ ​by​ ​Brian.​ ​This​ ​could​ ​make​ ​modelling​ ​positive​ ​attitudes​ ​difficult.​ ​This​ ​position​ ​was​
​supported​​by​​Matthew,​​who​​has​​launched​​a​​similar​​programme,​​who​​said​​"I​​wouldn’t​​assume​
​that​ ​whoever's​ ​delivering​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​would​ ​understand​ ​all​ ​of​ ​the​ ​terms​ ​and​ ​the​
​terminology​ ​themselves".​ ​Although​ ​Matthew​ ​is​ ​an​ ​expert,​ ​not​ ​a​​teacher,​​his​​comment​​was​
​supported​​by​​Charlotte,​​a​​Year​​3​​Teacher,​​who​​stated​​"I​​think​​it's​​really​​useful​​for​​the​​teachers​
​and​​it's​​educating​​us,"​​to​​which​​Jasmine​​and​​Lauren​​agreed,​​stating​​that​​they​​were​​not​​aware​
​of​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​teachings​ ​and​ ​that​ ​it​ ​would​ ​be​ ​helpful​ ​for​ ​them.​ ​Therefore,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​not​ ​only​
​essential​ ​that​ ​young​ ​children​ ​develop​ ​a​ ​better​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​cultural​ ​assumptions​ ​and​
​stereotypes, but possibly adults.​


​Discussion, question and expression​


​Kemple,​ ​Lee,​ ​and​ ​Harris​ ​(2016,​ ​p.99)​​explored​​the​​potential​​use​​of​​children's​​literature​​as​​a​
​conversation​ ​starter,​ ​describing​ ​them​ ​as​ ​“intimate​ ​and​ ​powerful​ ​tools​ ​in​ ​early​ ​childhood​
​education”.​ ​Through​​exploring​​the​​topic​​of​​race,​​they​​state​​that​​from​​a​​young​​age​​children's​
​literature​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​raise​ ​children’s​ ​awareness​ ​of​ ​other​ ​communities,​ ​to​ ​promote​
​acceptance​​of​​human​​diversity.​​Within​​both​​the​​literature​​review​​and​​Phase​​1​​results​​section​
​of​ ​this​ ​research,​ ​it​ ​became​ ​evident​ ​that​ ​this​ ​resource​ ​will​ ​be​ ​used​ ​as​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​
​promote​ ​discussion​ ​about​ ​discrimination​ ​and​ ​inequalities​​(MacIntosh​​and​​Martin,​​2018).​​In​
​Theme​​3,​​‘structure’​,​​one​​of​​the​​sub-themes​​explored​​the​​role​​of​​the​​‘​discussion​​points​’​​with​
​participants​ ​acknowledging​ ​the​ ​strengths​​of​​these​​conversation​​promoters.​​However,​​it​​was​




                                                              ​215​
​positive​ ​to​ ​find​ ​that​ ​participants​ ​particularly​ ​enjoyed​ ​that​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​on​ ​the​ ​whole,​ ​would​
​allow children to discuss, question, and express their understanding:​


       ​From​ ​a​​child's​​view,​​actually​​well,​​why​​are​​you​​saying​​that​​if​​some​​people​​find​​it​
       ​offensive?​ ​Is​ ​it​ ​okay​ ​to​ ​be​ ​offensive​ ​if​ ​you're​ ​saying​ ​that​ ​to​ ​fight​ ​back​ ​against​
       ​people​​who​​are​​offending​​you?​​(Sophia​​-​​Deputy​​Headteacher​​and​​Head​​of​​Early​
       ​Years)​


​This​ ​comment​ ​from​ ​Sophia​ ​brings​ ​to​ ​attention​ ​a​ ​key​ ​aim​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​to​ ​allow​
​children​ ​to​ ​reconsider​ ​and​ ​learn​ ​what​ ​might​ ​be​ ​offensive​ ​to​ ​marginalised​ ​communities,​
​particularly​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​Tom​ ​mentioned​ ​that​ ​“it's​ ​giving​ ​children​ ​a​
​chance​​to​​have​​inputs​​of​​their​​own​​personal​​knowledge”.​​With​​this​​in​​mind,​​children​​are​​able​
​to​ ​share​ ​their​ ​own​ ​understanding,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​particularly​ ​important​ ​when​ ​developing​ ​the​
​draft​ ​book,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​sparked​ ​discussion.​ ​This​ ​was​ ​because​ ​Keagan​ ​(EDI​ ​Manager)​
​acknowledged​​in​​his​​first​​interview​​(Phase​​1)​​that,​​the​​more​​something​​is​​spoken​​about,​​the​
​easier​ ​it​ ​becomes​ ​to​ ​change​ ​and​ ​challenge​​an​​initial​​perception,​​bringing​​about​​the​​idea​​of​
​questioning your initial understanding.​


​Although​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​simulates​ ​open​ ​conversations,​ ​it​ ​was​​also​​crucial​​to​​have​​a​​resource​
​that​ ​allowed​ ​children​ ​to​​question​​what​​they​​already​​know​​about​​discrimination,​​specifically​
​antisemitism. Diana (teaching assistant) particularly liked:​


       ​…Chapter​ ​5,​ ​because​ ​Joe​ ​says​ ​Yiddo​ ​which​ ​he’s​ ​always​ ​said​​but​​because​​of​​this​
       ​incident​ ​he​ ​then​ ​questions​ ​it,​ ​which​ ​leads​ ​him​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​how​ ​this​ ​is​ ​an​
       ​offensive​​word​​to​​the​​Jewish​​community.​​Then​​our​​students​​might​​question​​what​
       ​they say and whether it is offensive.​


​Van​ ​Horn​ ​(2015)​ ​explored​ ​LGBT+​ ​children’s​ ​literature,​ ​finding​ ​that​ ​it​ ​provides​ ​a​ ​space​ ​for​
​questioning​ ​heteronormative​ ​structures;​ ​they​ ​also​ ​found​ ​that​ ​through​ ​questioning,​ ​they​
​were​ ​able​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​greater​ ​and​ ​increase​ ​their​​involvement​​with​​the​​story.​​In​​this​​context,​
​Carly​​discusses​​how​​the​​resource​​provides​​opportunity​​to​​question​​actions​​of​​discrimination​
​and antisemitism:​


                                                              ​216​
       ​I​ ​also​ ​like​ ​when​ ​they​ ​are​ ​at​ ​the​ ​match​ ​and​ ​he​ ​starts​​to​​question​​what​​they​​are​
       ​saying.​ ​So,​ ​I​ ​thought​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​okay​ ​to​ ​start​ ​questioning,​ ​to​ ​think​ ​‘No,​ ​I’m​ ​not​
       ​happy with this, you know. Then what do I do with that?’​


​Likewise,​ ​Chris​ ​believed​ ​that​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​“encourages​ ​them​ ​to​ ​take​ ​questions,​ ​make​
​questions​​and​​ask​​questions…​​it​​provides​​seeds​​of​​thought…​​I​​just​​think​​it​​provokes​​questions​
​in​ ​children's​ ​minds”.​ ​Bethan​ ​(Educator)​ ​made​ ​a​ ​similar​ ​comment,​​suggesting​​that​​the​​book​
​will​ ​make​ ​children​ ​“consider​ ​many​ ​points​ ​of​ ​view,​ ​allowing​ ​them​ ​to​ ​question​ ​and​​consider​
​how​ ​one​ ​phrase​ ​can​ ​be​ ​interpreted​ ​differently​ ​by​ ​different​ ​people”.​ ​Leah​ ​explores​ ​an​
​example of this in her own teaching:​


       ​I​​was​​teaching​​World​​War​​Two​​with​​my​​Year​​6s​​in​​a​​different​​school​​years​​ago​​and​
       ​we​​were​​talking​​about​​Hitler.​​And​​one​​of​​the​​kids​​said​​“But​​he​​killed​​all​​the​​Jewish​
       ​people”,​​and​​one​​of​​my​​kids​​said​​“He​​clearly​​didn't​​kill​​all​​of​​them​​because​​Miss​​is​
       ​still​​here”.​​And​​so,​​it​​was​​that​​child's​​ability​​to​​actually​​think​​about​​or​​just​​take​​a​
       ​minute​​to​​say​​what​​you​​said​​is​​wrong​​because​​we've​​got​​the​​proof.​​(Leah​​-​​Jewish,​
       ​Educator)​


​Additionally,​ ​this​ ​sub-theme​ ​contains​ ​the​ ​word​ ​‘expression’,​ ​which​ ​teachers​ ​found​
​particularly​ ​appealing​ ​because​ ​it​ ​would​ ​provide​​children​​a​​chance​​to​​express​​and​​articulate​
​themselves.​​This​​emphasis​​on​​giving​​students​​the​​chance​​to​​express​​themselves​​aligns​​with​​a​
​sub-theme​ ​from​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​round,​ ​titled​ '​​safe​ ​spaces​'.​ ​This​ ​sub-theme​
​highlighted​​the​​importance​​of​​creating​​a​​safe​​environment​​where​​children​​can​​freely​​express​
​their​ ​thoughts,​ ​emotions,​ ​and​ ​ideas.​ ​Research​ ​from​ ​Chaplin​ ​and​ ​Aldao​ ​(2013)​ ​found​ ​that​
​children,​ ​particularly​ ​boys,​ ​can​ ​often​ ​find​ ​it​ ​challenging​ ​to​ ​express​ ​their​ ​emotions​ ​and​
​feelings,​​which​​Sophia​​supports​​by​​mentioning​​that​​for​​young​​boys​​it​​can​​be​​challenging​​due​
​to stereotypes associated with them being tough and strong:​


       ​Having​​those​​emotions​​raised​​in​​a​​story​​makes​​it​​acceptable​​to​​talk​​about.​​I​​think​
       ​boys​ ​especially…​ ​especially​ ​my​ ​son…​ ​when​ ​they​ ​go​ ​into​​secondary​​school,​​they​
       ​feel​ ​they've​ ​got​ ​to​​be​​all​​grown​​up,​​and​​that​​means​​not​​being​​scared,​​not​​being​


                                                               ​217​
       ​worried,​ ​not​ ​showing​ ​those​ ​emotions.​ ​So,​ ​having​ ​something​ ​in​ ​the​ ​story​ ​that​
       ​actually​ ​encourages​ ​them.​ ​(Sophia​ ​-​ ​Deputy​ ​Headteacher​ ​and​ ​Head​ ​of​ ​Early​
       ​Years)​


​Previous​​research​​by​​Elson​​and​​Nash​​(2020)​​also​​explored​​the​​role​​of​​children's​​literature​​and​
​expression,​ ​demonstrating​ ​that​ ​it​ ​can​ ​significantly​ ​influence​ ​how​ ​gender​ ​identity​ ​is​
​expressed,​ ​enabling​ ​kids​ ​to​ ​mould​ ​their​ ​conception​ ​of​ ​gender​ ​expression.​ ​By​ ​expressing​
​themselves,​ ​children​ ​are​ ​able​ ​to​​make​​connections​​with​​the​​real​​world​​and​​their​​own​​lives.​
​Lauren​ ​thought​ ​that​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​“feelings​ ​and​ ​worries,​ ​really​ ​were​ ​good.​ ​It​ ​makes​ ​it​ ​very​
​human, just giving the children the opportunity to express themselves”.​


​‘Breaking the cycle’​


​This​​sub-theme​​is​​titled​​‘breaking​​the​​cycle’​​as​​this​​was​​a​​phrase​​used​​by​​Educators​​from​​‘SH​
​School’​​in​​the​​focus​​groups.​​The​​researcher​​felt​​that​​this​​phrase​​aligned​​with​​the​​BIM,​​due​​to​
​it​​being​​a​​process​​that​​prevents​​discriminatory​​behaviours,​​and​​which​​can​​stop​​the​​cycle​​from​
​continuing.​​As​​discussed​​in​​both​​the​​literature​​review​​and​​the​​Phase​​1​​results​​and​​discussion​
​chapters,​ ​the​ ​BIM​ ​is​ ​a​ ​useful​ ​technique​ ​that​ ​teaches​ ​people​ ​how​ ​to​ ​avoid​ ​unwanted​
​behaviours​​(Cissner,​​2009).​​Furthermore,​​it​​enables​​people​​to​​become​​'assertive​​bystanders'​
​rather​ ​than​ '​passive​ ​bystanders'​ ​(Public​​Health​​England,​​2020).​​With​​this​​in​​mind,​​‘​breaking​
​the​​cycle​’​​and​​preventing​​antisemitism​​from​​recurring​​was​​noted​​by​​educators​​as​​one​​of​​the​
​book’s key teachings:​


       ​…and​​the​​mother​​was​​doing​​it,​​and​​he​​had​​to​​educate​​her​​and​​that​​was​​what​​was​
       ​really​ ​powerful.​ ​It's​ ​breaking​ ​that​ ​cycle​ ​of​ ​‘you’re​ ​doing​ ​it​ ​because​ ​that's​ ​what​
       ​everybody​ ​else​ ​is​ ​doing’,​ ​but​ ​breaking​ ​that​ ​cycle​ ​and​​saying​​‘yeah,​​no,​​this​​isn't​
       ​right’ (Lauren)​


​Highlighted​​within​​Lauren’s​​comment​​are​​some​​of​​the​​key​​teachings​​in​​the​​BIM:​​recognising​
​something​ ​is​ ​wrong,​ ​and​ ​then​ ​taking​ ​steps​ ​to​ ​change​ ​and​ ​challenge​ ​these​ ​behaviours.​
​Likewise, the phrase was used by Carly:​




                                                            ​218​
        ​He​ ​is​ ​breaking​ ​the​ ​cycle.​​It​​is​​making​​him​​think,​​‘what​​are​​we​​chanting​​and​​why​
        ​are​ ​we​ ​saying​ ​it?’...​ ​we're​ ​saying​ ​it​ ​just​ ​because​ ​it's​ ​what​ ​everyone​ ​else​ ​does…​
        ​that we follow along with the crowd. Hmm. It's like, ‘yeah, hang on, why?’​


​In​​the​​story,​​Joe​​tells​​his​​mother​​not​​to​​say​​the​​word​​‘Yid’,​​breaking​​the​​cycle.​​Ellen​​(Educator)​
​stated,​ ​“I​​felt​​the​​most​​important​​part​​was​​when​​Joe​​has​​to​​stand​​up​​to​​his​​mum”.​​The​​BIM​
​suggests​ ​that​ ​individuals​ ​have​ ​a​ ​role​ ​in​ ​preventing​ ​harm​ ​or​ ​addressing​ ​inappropriate​
​behaviour​ ​(Latané​ ​and​ ​Darley,​ ​1970),​ ​even​ ​if​ ​they​ ​are​ ​not​ ​the​​ones​​directly​​involved​​in​​the​
​situation.​​In​​this​​case,​​Joe​​is​​becoming​​an​​active​​bystander​​by​​challenging​​his​​mother’s​​use​​of​
​harmful​ ​language.​ ​Participants,​ ​including​ ​Leah,​ ​hoped​ ​that​ ​this​ ​story​ ​would​​be​​repeated​​in​
​everyday life, contending that:​


        ​…if​ ​this​ ​gives​ ​even​ ​just​ ​one​ ​child,​ ​the​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​stand​ ​up​ ​to​ ​whoever​ ​it​ ​may​ ​be…​
        ​maybe​ ​within​ ​their​ ​family​ ​or​ ​their​ ​wider​ ​community,​ ​and​ ​turn​ ​around​ ​and​ ​go,​
        ​“No”, then I think you have done a good job.​


​As​ ​Simon​ ​(Jewish)​ ​mentions,​ ​"babies​ ​aren't​ ​born​ ​racists;​ ​they​ ​get​ ​it​ ​from​ ​their​ ​parents”.​
​Although​​this​​comment​​could​​be​​considered​​a​​harmful​​presumption,​​it​​was​​a​​comment​​that​
​was made by numerous participants, including Iris (Jewish):​


        ​Children​​genuinely​​don't​​have​​any​​issues.​​That's​​only​​learnt,​​isn't​​it?​​Because​​they​
        ​come from a family that has these views that they'll just absorb, won't they?​


​Simon​​continues​​to​​say​​“and​​so​​what​​you've​​got​​to​​do​​is​​you've​​got​​to​​stop​​the​​generation."​
​With​​that​​in​​mind,​​with​​the​​teachings​​of​​this​​book​​it​​was​​also​​hoped​​that​​children​​who​​read​
​the​​story​​will​​‘​break​​the​​cycle​’​​and​​refrain​​from​​engaging​​with​​some​​of​​the​​earlier​​teachings​
​they​ ​may​ ​have​ ​received​ ​from​ ​their​ ​parents,​ ​or​ ​other​ ​figures​ ​in​ ​their​ ​lives.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​in​ ​the​ ​final​
​chapter,​ ​whereby​ ​children​ ​are​ ​instructed​ ​to​ ​finish​ ​the​ ​story,​ ​where​ ​teachers​ ​will​ ​learn​
​whether​​the​​key​​teaching​​of​​the​​BIM​​has​​been​​learnt.​​Leah​​(Jewish,​​Educator)​​mentions​​"I'd​
​like​​to​​think​​that​​he's​​educated​​enough​​of​​his​​friends​​in​​the​​book,​​that​​they​​will​​help​​educate​
​others​​in​​sort​​of​​a​​pay​​it​​forward​​kind​​of​​way,"​​which​​highlights​​her​​hopes​​that​​some​​children​
​might write about standing up against discriminatory behaviours in their final chapter.​


                                                                 ​219​
​Nevertheless,​ ​according​ ​to​ ​research​ ​by​ ​Rigby​ ​and​ ​Johnson​ ​(2006),​ ​from​ ​a​ ​sample​ ​of​ ​400​
​children,​ ​43%​ ​of​ ​students​ ​would​ ​be​ ​inclined​ ​to​ ​assist​ ​or​ ​support​​a​​victim​​of​​bullying,​​while​
​23%​​of​​students​​said​​the​​opposite.​​This​​research​​supports​​a​​comment​​made​​by​​Iris​​(Jewish),​
​whereby she felt that being an active bystander at a young age can be very challenging:​


       ​The​ ​most​ ​difficult​ ​thing,​ ​especially​ ​for​ ​a​ ​child​ ​to​ ​do​ ​is​ ​respond​ ​to​ ​something​
       ​antisemitic…​​it​​needs​​a​​lot​​of​​confidence,​​to​​be​​able​​to​​stand​​up​​and​​say​​‘this​​isn't​
       ​right’.​ ​And​ ​I​ ​think​ ​that​ ​is​ ​really,​ ​really,​ ​really​ ​difficult​ ​and​ ​even​ ​into​ ​adulthood,​
       ​some​ ​people​​just​​don't​​feel​​that​​they​​can​​tackle​​it​​because​​it's​​just​​beyond​​their​
       ​own confidence to be able to do so.​


​Although​​the​​comment​​from​​Iris​​and​​earlier​​study​​from​​Rigby​​and​​Johnson​​(2006)​​show​​that​
​children​​may​​feel​​uncomfortable​​reporting​​bullying,​​the​​goal​​of​​the​​resource​​was​​to​​motivate​
​children​​to​​act​​as​​active​​bystanders​​and​​enhance​​the​​possibility​​that​​they​​would​​report​​such​
​abuse.​​Although​​Iris​​had​​her​​reservations​​about​​children's​​abilities​​to​​challenge​​antisemitism,​
​she​ ​felt​ ​that​ ​the​ ​draft​ ​book​ ​was,​ ​“really​ ​good​ ​in​ ​order​ ​to​ ​actually​ ​give​ ​the​ ​children​
​knowledge,​​which​​is​​really​​important​​and​​very​​good,​​but​​not​​as​​strong​​in​​how​​to​​respond​​[to​
​antisemitism]”.​ ​Therefore,​ ​this​ ​highlights​​a​​challenge​​that​​teachers​​may​​face​​if​​they​​were​​to​
​implement​ ​this​ ​initiative,​ ​requiring​ ​additional​ ​resources​ ​to​​effectively​​teach​​students​​about​
​being​ ​an​ ​active​ ​bystander.​ ​Along​ ​with​ ​this​ ​challenge,​ ​other​ ​factors​ ​that​ ​may​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​
​reconsidered will be discussed in the next theme, titled ‘​challenges​’.​


​To​ ​conclude,​ ​this​ ​theme​ ​has​ ​explored​ ​the​ ​fundamental​ ​lessons​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​and​ ​what​ ​the​
​perceived​​messages​​that​​participants​​aspire​​for​​children​​to​​learn​​from​​their​​interaction​​with​
​the​ ​resource.​ ​Firstly,​​participants​​hoped​​for​​a​​development​​in​​their​​understanding,​​which​​at​
​current​ ​could​ ​be​ ​quite​ ​limited.​ ​Likewise,​ ​participants​​felt​​that​​one​​of​​the​​key​​strengths​​was​
​the​ ​opportunity​ ​for​ ​discussion​ ​and​ ​questioning,​ ​which​ ​subsequently​ ​would​ ​lead​ ​to​ ​great​
​expression​​of​​children's​​emotions​​and​​feelings.​​This​​aspect​​was​​particularly​​popular​​amongst​
​teachers​ ​who​​expressed​​that​​children​​can​​often​​find​​this​​challenging,​​yet​​the​​resource​​gives​
​them​​the​​platform​​to​​do​​so.​​Finally,​​the​​term​​‘breaking​​the​​cycle’​​was​​employed​​by​​educators​
​who​​found​​that​​the​​book​​would​​help​​to​​empower​​children​​to​​recognise​​what​​is​​offensive​​and​


                                                               ​220​
​hurtful behaviours, and actively challenge it.​


​Theme 6 - Challenges​


​This​ ​final​ ​theme​ ​has​ ​been​ ​named​ ​‘challenges’,​ ​which​ ​recognises​ ​potential​ ​barriers​ ​that​
​participants​ ​highlighted​​that​​may​​require​​some​​level​​of​​reconsideration.​​Within​​the​​Phase​​1​
​of​​data​​collection,​​experts​​discussed​​the​​challenges​​that​​come​​with​​developing​​and​​creating​
​initiatives.​ ​Within​ ​this​ ​second​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection,​ ​teachers​ ​and​ ​experts​ ​were​​keen​​to​
​provide​​challenges​​that​​may​​be​​faced.​​These​​included​​potential​​barriers​​when​​incorporating​
​the​ ​initiative​ ​into​ ​educational​ ​settings,​ ​narratives​ ​that​ ​participants​ ​believed​ ​could​ ​benefit​
​from​ ​modification,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​influence​ ​of​ ​parents​ ​on​ ​children.​ ​On​ ​the​ ​whole,​​the​​challenges​
​were​​built​​around​​bringing​​realistic​​social​​issues​​into​​education-based​​spaces.​​Therefore,​​the​
​sub-themes​ ​in​ ​this​ ​chapter​ ​are​ ​titled​ ​‘​implementation’,​ ​‘role​ ​of​ ​the​ ​parent’,​ ​‘storylines​
​triggers’​​and​​‘age suitability’.​


​Implementation​


​Due​ ​to​ ​the​ ​National​ ​Curriculum,​ ​a​ ​set​ ​of​ ​subjects​ ​and​ ​standards​ ​used​ ​by​ ​primary​ ​and​
​secondary​​schools​​to​​ensure​​that​​students​​are​​taught​​the​​same​​things,​​teachers​​in​​the​​UK​​are​
​constrained​​in​​what​​they​​can​​teach.​​The​​National​​Curriculum​​in​​the​​UK​​has​​been​​critiqued​​by​
​Tuner​ ​(2013)​​for​​its​​narrow​​focus,​​which​​focuses​​more​​on​​the​​core​​subjects,​​such​​as​​English​
​and​ ​maths,​ ​which​ ​does​ ​not​ ​allow​ ​children​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​their​ ​critical​ ​thinking​ ​skills,​ ​and​
​creativity.​ ​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​this,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​been​ ​critiqued​ ​for​ ​being​ ​too​ ​rigid,​ ​not​ ​allowing​ ​for​
​flexibility​ ​amongst​ ​teachers​ ​(Helsby​ ​and​ ​McCulloch,​ ​2002).​ ​This​ ​creates​ ​challenges​ ​for​ ​the​
​proposed​​initiative,​​with​​Keagan​​emphasising​​the​​difficulties​​the​​researcher​​would​​have​​while​
​attempting to implement and distribute this book in classrooms:​


       ​I​ ​found​ ​when​ ​we've​ ​done​ ​stuff​​I​​remember​​at​​Organisation​​Name​​with​​schools,​
       ​just​​trying​​to​​get​​anything​​into​​the​​curriculum​​was​​really​​difficult​​and​​it​​was​​like…​
       ​even​ ​those​ ​27,000​ ​schools​ ​getting​ ​a​ ​way​ ​that​ ​works.​ ​Because,​ ​you​ ​know,​ ​the​
       ​teachers​ ​are​ ​under-resourced,​ ​they’ve​ ​got​​loads​​of​​targets…​​It's​​a​​really​​difficult​
       ​pressure on the curriculum time. (Keagan - EDI Manager)​


                                                              ​221​
​Similar arguments were expressed by Leah:​


       ​The​ ​curriculum​ ​is​ ​incredibly​ ​tightly​ ​packed​ ​as​ ​it​ ​is​ ​and​ ​assuming​ ​you​ ​want​ ​this​
       ​done​​through​​the​​PSHE​​curriculum,​​which​​is​​already​​quite​​tightly​​packed.​​So,​​it's…​
       ​I​​think,​​for​​me,​​from​​a​​teaching​​perspective,​​I​​think​​part​​of​​that​​challenge​​for​​me​
       ​would​ ​be​ ​trying​ ​to​ ​fit​ ​in,​ ​and​ ​whether​ ​we​ ​could​ ​take​ ​different​ ​chapters​ ​of​ ​the​
       ​book,​ ​and​ ​try​ ​and​ ​sort​ ​of​ ​into​ ​weave​ ​them​ ​into​ ​an​ ​already​​created​​curriculum,​
       ​rather​​than​​teachers​​having​​to​​go​​back​​to​​the​​drawing​​board​​to​​create​​new​​lesson​
       ​plans.​


​Although​​it​​was​​originally​​envisaged​​that,​​in​​time,​​the​​book​​could​​be​​implemented​​in​​schools​
​across​ ​England​ ​as​​part​​of​​the​​PSHE​​or​​Religious​​Education​​(RE)​​curriculum,​​these​​comments​
​identify​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​faced​ ​by​ ​similar​ ​initiatives​​with​​comparable​​aims,​​where​​parties​​are​
​not​ ​willing​ ​or​ ​able​ ​to​ ​include​ ​it​ ​in​ ​their​ ​curriculum.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​Diana,​ ​Bethan​ ​and​ ​Ellen​
​mentioned​ ​that​ ​it​ ​would​ ​be​ ​particularly​ ​useful​ ​in​ ​PSHE.​ ​Diana​ ​said​ ​“it​ ​would​​be​​a​​valuable​
​resource​ ​in​ ​our​ ​school,​ ​and​ ​used​ ​in​ ​SCARF​ ​(PSHE)​ ​sessions​ ​over​ ​a​ ​half​ ​term”.​ ​Both​​Bethan​
​also​​agreed,​​stating​​that​​“I​​think​​it’s​​all​​very​​valuable”​​but​​also​​mentioned​​the​​idea​​of​​fitting​​it​
​into​ ​a​ ​half​ ​term​ ​“if​ ​you​ ​were​ ​aiming​ ​to​ ​do​ ​one​ ​chapter​ ​a​ ​week,​ ​I​ ​would​ ​suggest​ ​cutting​ ​it​
​down​​to​​maybe​​six​​chapters​​so​​it​​would​​fit​​nicely​​into​​a​​half​​term”.​​Therefore,​​teachers​​have​
​highlighted​ ​the​ ​value​ ​in​ ​it​ ​but​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​need​ ​for​ ​external​ ​organisations​ ​to​ ​support​ ​the​
​initiative​ ​and​ ​subsequently​ ​getting​ ​larger​ ​backing​ ​for​ ​implementation,​ ​as​ ​was​ ​noted​ ​in​ ​the​
​Phase​ ​1​ ​results​ ​and​ ​discussion​ ​and​ ​later​ ​in​ ​this​ ​area​ ​of​ ​the​ ​discussion.​ ​In​​addition,​​Keagan​
​makes​ ​references​ ​to​ ​‘Premier​ ​League​ ​Reading​ ​Stars’​ ​as​ ​a​ ​means​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​encourage​
​children​ ​to​ ​read​ ​this​ ​resource,​ ​alongside​ ​encouraging​ ​and​ ​incentivising​​schools​​to​​use​​your​
​book.​ ​Therefore,​ ​although​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​would​​be​​to​​get​​the​​resource​​into​​the​​curriculum,​​if​​it​​is​
​unsuccessful there is another opportunity to potentially disseminate the book to children.​


​In​ ​addition​ ​to​ ​the​ ​struggles​ ​of​ ​getting​ ​this​ ​into​ ​the​ ​curriculum,​ ​there​ ​are​ ​also​ ​challenges​
​around​​the​​implementation​​due​​to​​a​​possible​​lack​​of​​experience​​for​​the​​teachers.​​Chris​​states​
​that,​ ​firstly,​ ​some​ ​teachers​ ​may​ ​not​ ​feel​ ​completely​ ​comfortable​ ​in​ ​teaching​ ​the​ ​resource,​
​commenting​ ​“if​ ​you're​ ​being​​taught​​by​​someone​​that​​is​​not​​Jewish,​​they​​may​​well​​feel​​very​


                                                               ​222​
​uncomfortable​ ​about​ ​explaining​​what​​the​​history​​is​​about”.​​Specifically,​​Leah​​felt​​that​​those​
​“who​​don't​​have​​a​​faith,​​who​​haven't​​experienced​​being​​a​​minority…​​I​​think​​that​​can​​be​​quite​
​hard”.​ ​While​ ​these​ ​comments​ ​raise​ ​valid​ ​concerns,​ ​it​ ​should​ ​be​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​teachers​ ​are​
​already​ ​required​ ​to​ ​address​ ​various​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination,​ ​including​ ​racism,​ ​sexism,​ ​and​
​homophobia,​​as​​part​​of​​the​​National​​Curriculum​​(Alexander​​and​​Weekes-Bernard,​​2017).​​This​
​expectation​ ​means​ ​they​ ​must​ ​engage​ ​with​ ​sensitive​ ​topics​ ​without​ ​personal​ ​experience​​of​
​every​ ​minority​ ​group.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​teachers​ ​should​ ​be​ ​trained​ ​to​ ​handle​ ​such​ ​issues,​​and​
​there​ ​should​ ​be​ ​opportunities​ ​to​ ​support​ ​them​ ​in​ ​teaching​ ​about​ ​diversity​ ​and​ ​inclusion​
​effectively.​


​Another​ ​factor​ ​that​ ​could​​influence​​teachers’​​abilities​​to​​teach​​about​​Judaism​​was​​noted​​as​
​location,​ ​with​ ​Simon​ ​(Jewish)​ ​commenting​ ​“I​ ​think​ ​outside​​London,​​where​​it​​may​​well​​be​​a​
​harder​​discussion​​and,​​of​​course,​​the​​majority​​of​​England​​and​​the​​United​​Kingdom​​is​​outside​
​London”.​ ​This​ ​comment,​ ​although​ ​valid,​ ​might​ ​underestimate​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​ ​education​ ​in​
​fostering​​understanding,​​regardless​​of​​geographic​​location.​​While​​it​​is​​true​​that​​there​​may​​be​
​fewer​ ​Jewish​ ​communities​ ​outside​ ​of​ ​larger​ ​cities,​ ​namely​ ​London​ ​and​ ​Manchester,​ ​the​
​responsibility​​of​​educators​​is​​to​​teach​​students​​about​​diversity​​and​​inclusion​​in​​all​​forms,​​and​
​this includes expanding students’ awareness of different cultures and religions.​


​The​ ​following​ ​comment​ ​from​ ​Leah,​ ​acknowledges​ ​that​ ​these​ ​topics​ ​can​ ​raise​ ​difficult​
​questions,​​which​​teachers​​may​​not​​feel​​prepared​​to​​answer.​​However,​​with​​the​​right​​training​
​and resources, teachers can confidently address these sensitive issues:​


       ​It's​ ​like​ ​teaching​ ​sex​ ​ed:​ ​some​ ​people​ ​are​ ​very​ ​comfortable​ ​doing​​it​​and​​others​
       ​aren't.​​And​​it​​does​​open​​up​​some​​difficult​​questions,​​which​​sometimes​​maybe​​we​
       ​as​​teachers​​wouldn't​​want​​to​​answer,​​but​​also​​maybe​​parents​​would​​find​​tricky​​to​
       ​answer and come to terms with as well.​


​Leah​​utilised​​her​​teaching​​experiences​​in​​sex​​education,​​emphasising​​that​​some​​find​​it​​easier​
​to​​teach​​than​​others.​​Walker​​and​​Milton​​(2006)​​conducted​​research​​indicating​​that​​teachers​
​need​ ​to​ ​feel​ ​at​ ​ease​ ​when​​addressing​​the​​topic,​​as​​some​​teachers​​encountered​​uncertainty​
​and​ ​awkwardness​ ​while​ ​teaching​ ​it.​ ​Regarding​ ​discussions​ ​of​ ​race​ ​and​ ​culture,​​Priest​​et​​al.​


                                                           ​223​
​(2016)​ ​argue​ ​that​ ​teachers'​ ​confidence​ ​significantly​ ​influences​ ​children's​ ​participation​ ​in​
​conversations​​about​​race.​​However,​​Leah's​​comparison​​to​​teaching​​other​​subjects​​reinforces​
​that​​even​​though​​educators​​might​​struggle​​and​​feel​​uneasy​​about​​teaching​​it,​​they​​can​​do​​so​
​effectively with the right skills, experience and knowledge.​


​Role of the parent​


​Parental​ ​involvement​ ​in​ ​a​ ​child's​ ​education​ ​is​ ​often​ ​perceived​ ​positively​ ​(Zellman​ ​and​
​Waterman,​ ​1998).​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​Leah's​ ​comment​ ​regards​ ​the​ ​discomfort​ ​that​ ​might​ ​come​
​with​​this​​resource,​​by​​touching​​upon​​the​​parents,​​“it's​​a​​really​​positive​​venture,​​but​​it​​might​
​not​​succeed​​in​​every​​household”.​​At​​times,​​parents'​​own​​political​​or​​negative​​viewpoints​​can​
​hinder the success of an initiative, as Keagan states:​


          ​parents​​will​​be​​very​​opinionated,​​whether​​they've​​got​​an​​interest​​in​​antisemitism​
          ​or​​not.​​I​​find​​that​​for​​anything​​ED​​and​​I​​wise​​people​​always​​have​​an​​opinion​​and​
          ​that can be detrimental or skew the kids' opinions.​


​When​ ​exploring​ ​other​ ​social​ ​issues,​ ​parents​ ​have​ ​been​ ​observed​ ​to​ ​be​ ​reluctant​ ​to​ ​the​
​teaching​ ​of​ ​LGBT+​ ​information,​ ​with​ ​some​ ​parents​ ​objecting,​ ​according​ ​to​ ​research​ ​by​
​Gegenfurtner​ ​and​ ​Gebhard​ ​(2017).​ ​Although​ ​it​ ​is​ ​evident​ ​that​ ​some​ ​parents​ ​may​ ​have​
​objections​ ​against​ ​what​ ​is​ ​being​ ​taught​ ​to​ ​their​ ​child,​ ​Nancy​ ​(Jewish,​ ​Educator)​ ​highlights​
​that:​


          ​…if​ ​a​ ​parent​ ​is​ ​upset​ ​that​ ​we​ ​are​ ​teaching​ ​them​​[their​​child]​​the​​importance​​of​
          ​being​ ​able​ ​to​ ​speak​ ​up​ ​when​ ​you​ ​feel​ ​that​ ​you're​ ​being​ ​discriminated​ ​against,​
          ​and​ ​recognising​ ​that​ ​people​ ​can​ ​change,​ ​I​ ​think​ ​then​ ​they're​ ​probably​ ​quite​
          ​misguided.​


​As​ ​Nancy​ ​mentions,​ ​parents​ ​may​ ​object​ ​to​ ​the​ ​subject​​content​​being​​taught,​​but​​there​​are​
​also​ ​challenges​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​parents​ ​preconceived​ ​thoughts​ ​about​ ​religion,​ ​and​ ​other​
​forms of discrimination:​




                                                              ​224​
       ​I​ ​mean,​ ​even​ ​parents​ ​today,​ ​if​ ​they​ ​haven't​ ​been​ ​taught​ ​what​ ​it's​ ​like,​ ​to​ ​feel​
       ​Jewish​​or​​to​​be​​a​​Muslim,​​they’ve​​got​​no​​idea​​and​​they're​​just​​going​​to​​bring​​their​
       ​children up with the same view. (Chris - Jewish community)​


​As​​discussed​​by​​Chris,​​parents​​or​​guardians​​who​​have​​limited​​understanding​​or​​experience​​of​
​belonging​ ​to​ ​a​ ​minority​ ​group​ ​may​ ​influence​ ​their​ ​children's​ ​viewpoints.​ ​This​ ​comment​ ​is​
​supported​ ​by​ ​research​ ​from​ ​Towles-Schwen​ ​and​ ​Fazio​ ​(2001)​ ​and​ ​Odenweller​ ​and​ ​Harris​
​(2018),​​who​​discovered​​that​​children​​of​​parents​​who​​had​​higher​​levels​​of​​racial​​prejudice​​and​
​intolerance​​were​​less​​likely​​to​​engage​​positively​​with​​children​​of​​different​​races.​​Therefore,​​a​
​key​ ​concern​ ​participants​ ​had​ ​was​ ​the​ ​impact​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​might​ ​have​ ​on​ ​children​ ​whose​
​parents will continue to reinforce negative beliefs, including Iris (Jewish) who argued:​


       ​…they​ ​have​ ​this​ ​experience​ ​[​the​ ​book​],​ ​they​​go​​home,​​and​​it​​could​​well​​be​​that​
       ​the​​parents,​​unfortunately,​​will​​just​​negate​​all​​the​​things​​that​​they've​​learned…​​it​
       ​is​​covert​​antisemitism​​that​​the​​child​​would​​pick​​up​​and​​not​​even​​realise,​​and​​then​
       ​absorb it and then be part of their thinking as well?​


​Agreeing​ ​with​ ​Iris​ ​about​ ​the​ ​influence​​of​​a​​parent​​was​​Diana​​(Teaching​​Assistant),​​who​​was​
​conscious​ ​that​ ​this​ ​shouldn’t​ ​be​ ​used​ ​as​ ​homework,​ ​“I​ ​don’t​ ​think​ ​homework​ ​would​ ​be​ ​a​
​good​ ​idea​ ​as​ ​there​ ​could​ ​be​ ​parental​ ​bias​ ​there”.​ ​Ellen​ ​(Educator)​ ​also​ ​made​ ​a​ ​similar​
​comment,​ ​suggesting​ ​that​ ​“it​ ​should​ ​definitely​ ​be​ ​taught​ ​within​ ​class​ ​as​ ​it​ ​touches​ ​on​ ​too​
​many​ ​sensitive​ ​issues​ ​that​​might​​not​​be​​appropriately​​discussed​​at​​home”.​​Leah’s​​comment​
​below​​also​​illustrates​​the​​possible​​negative​​impact​​that​​parents​​could​​have​​on​​their​​children,​
​yet found this resource to be a positive way of mitigating those viewpoints:​


       ​You​ ​don't​ ​know​ ​what's​ ​going​ ​on​​at​​home.​​I​​like​​to​​believe​​by​​and​​large​​that​​the​
       ​majority​​of​​people​​are​​good​​and​​well​​meaning.​​But​​I​​also​​think​​that​​if​​you​​do​​it​​in​
       ​house,​ ​you​ ​cannot​ ​necessarily​ ​control​ ​the​ ​narrative.​ ​But​​you​​have​​the​​ability​​to​
       ​sort of nip various things in the bud should you need to. (Leah - Jewish, Educator)​




                                                             ​225​
​Subsequently,​ ​the​ ​attitudes​ ​a​ ​parent​ ​or​ ​guardian​ ​has​ ​is​ ​going​ ​to​ ​create​ ​challenges​ ​for​
​teachers​ ​alongside​ ​creating​ ​uncertainty​ ​for​ ​children,​ ​as​ ​Matthew​ ​(Development​ ​Officer)​
​states:​


       ​...confusion​ ​for​ ​young​ ​people,​ ​when​ ​you've​​got​​people​​who​​are​​influencing​​you​
       ​and​​people​​who​​are​​important​​in​​your​​life,​​but​​they're​​pretty​​much​​sending​​you​​a​
       ​negative​​message​​that​​just​​kind​​of​​happens.​​So,​​I​​think​​that​​that's​​something​​that​
       ​kids have to wrestle with every day.​


​Previously​ ​Matthew​ ​has​ ​faced​ ​this​ ​when​ ​delivering​ ​sessions​ ​within​ ​schools.​ ​He​ ​discussed​
​how​ ​he​ ​overcame​ ​this,​ ​by​ ​inviting​ ​parents​ ​into​ ​the​ ​school​ ​to​ ​address​ ​their​ ​concerns​ ​and​
​questions;​ ​therefore,​ ​initiating​ ​and​​facilitating​​conversations​​with​​parents​​would​​be​​advised​
​to​​the​​schools​​in​​the​​future,​​alongside​​providing​​a​​cover​​note​​which​​could​​be​​shared​​amongst​
​the​ ​parents.​ ​Therefore,​ ​while​ ​parental​ ​involvement​ ​can​ ​be​ ​a​ ​positive​​influence​​on​​a​​child's​
​education,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​clear​ ​that​ ​negative​ ​biases​ ​and​ ​preconceived​ ​beliefs​ ​can​ ​pose​ ​significant​
​challenges​​to​​initiatives​​aimed​​at​​teaching​​about​​discrimination​​and​​diversity.​​Going​​forward​
​it​ ​would​ ​be​ ​important​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​parents​ ​in​ ​open​ ​dialogue​ ​and​ ​providing​ ​clear​
​communication​ ​about​ ​the​ ​educational​ ​goals​ ​may​ ​help​ ​mitigate​ ​these​ ​issues​ ​and​ ​foster​ ​a​
​more supportive environment for children to learn and grow.​


​Storyline triggers​


​In​​the​​first​​theme,​​‘​amendments’​,​​participants​​highlighted​​storylines​​which​​they​​would​​add​​to​
​the​ ​narrative.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​participants​ ​were​ ​also​ ​given​ ​the​ ​opportunity​ ​to​ ​express​​which​
​parts​​of​​the​​story​​may​​not​​have​​been​​needed​​or​​could​​have​​been​​edited​​out.​​Rachel,​​a​​Year​​3​
​teacher,​ ​mentioned​ ​that​ ​“women​ ​aren’t​ ​the​ ​ones,​​they​​honestly​​are​​pretty​​quiet​​and​​don’t​
​join​ ​in​ ​with​ ​the​ ​chants”.​ ​Rachel​ ​raises​ ​this​ ​point​ ​in​ ​contrast​ ​to​ ​the​ ​portrayal​ ​in​ ​the​ ​story,​
​where​ ​it​ ​is​ ​Joe’s​ ​mother​ ​who​ ​chants​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’.​ ​To​ ​support​ ​Rachels​ ​comment,​ ​in​ ​the​
​media​ ​it​ ​is​ ​predominantly​ ​men​ ​who​ ​are​ ​seen​​to​​abuse​​fans​​and​​players​​(Cleland,​​Pope​​and​
​Williams,​​2020),​​which​​does​​bring​​about​​some​​challenges​​as​​the​​story​​may​​not​​be​​reflective​
​of​ ​individuals'​ ​everyday​ ​experiences.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​other​ ​educators,​ ​including​ ​Sophia,​
​highlighted that:​


                                                               ​226​
       ​Being​​the​​mum​​has​​more​​impact,​​because​​you​​expect​​them​​not​​to​​do​​that​​and​​to​
       ​be​​protective​​and​​caring​​of​​their​​children​​and​​even​​to​​think​​‘I​​don't​​want​​my​​child​
       ​hearing this’.​


​In​ ​order​ ​to​ ​prevent​ ​stereotyping​ ​and​ ​create​ ​a​ ​compelling​ ​story,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​and​​author​
​agreed​​it​​was​​crucial​​to​​maintain​​the​​mother​​as​​the​​parental​​figure​​who​​accompanies​​Joe​​to​
​matches.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​while​ ​it​ ​has​ ​traditionally​ ​been​ ​assumed​ ​that​ ​football​ ​fans​ ​are​
​predominantly​ ​male​ ​due​​to​​the​​sport's​​historical​​association​​with​​men,​​research​​by​​Mewett​
​and​ ​Toffoletti​ ​(2012)​ ​and​ ​Pope​ ​(2017)​ ​has​ ​explored​ ​the​ ​evolving​ ​demographics​ ​of​ ​football​
​fandom, revealing a growing number of female supporters.​


​Another consideration was discussed by Lauren:​


       ​The​ ​only​ ​particular​ ​issue​ ​for​ ​me​ ​was​ ​the​ ​hissing…​ ​which​ ​is​ ​actually​​referring​​to​
       ​the​ ​gas​ ​chambers.​ ​And​ ​I’m​ ​just​ ​wondering​​how​​a​​Form​​VI​​[​Year​​6​]​​group​​would​
       ​cope​​with​​that,​​because​​I’m​​not​​sure​​how​​much​​history​​they​​would​​have​​had…​​I​
       ​mean,​​we​​do​​teach​​the​​Second​​World​​War,​​but​​we​​don’t​​go​​into​​detail​​about​​the​
       ​gas chambers.​


​Short​​(2003,​​p.​​277)​​highlights​​the​​importance​​of​​teaching​​the​​holocaust​​at​​scholars,​​stating​
​that​​“it​​has​​long​​been​​argued​​that​​the​​Holocaust​​contains​​important​​lessons”.​​Nevertheless,​
​with​​Lauren’s​​comment​​there​​was​​discussion​​in​​the​​SH​​School​​focus​​group​​whether​​the​​book​
​would​ ​be​ ​better​ ​taught​ ​in​ ​KS3​ ​(Year​ ​7).​ ​However,​ ​five​ ​out​ ​of​ ​the​ ​six​ ​individuals​ ​thought​ ​it​
​would​ ​be​ ​best​ ​taught​ ​in​ ​a​ ​Primary​ ​setting,​ ​as​ ​planned​ ​due​ ​to​ ​the​ ​storyline​ ​of​ ​moving​​to​​a​
​secondary school. However, Leah, a Jewish, Primary school teacher also stated:​


       ​I​​think​​the​​bit​​that​​troubled​​me​​the​​most​​is​​the​​bit​​about​​the​​hissing​​and​​the​​gas​
       ​chambers.​ ​The​ ​primary​ ​history​ ​curriculum​ ​doesn't​ ​really​ ​touch​ ​on​ ​it​ ​since​ ​it's​
       ​been​​changed…​​Kids​​are​​obviously​​pretty​​aware​​of​​when​​it​​was,​​but​​less​​aware​​of​
       ​the​​perpetrators​​and​​what​​happened.​​And​​I​​think​​trying​​to​​discuss​​something​​like​
       ​the​​gas​​chambers​​with​​primary​​age​​children…​​that​​is​​absolutely​​terrifying​​to​​a​​9,​


                                                              ​227​
       ​10​ ​or​ ​11​ ​year​ ​old.​ ​And​ ​the​ ​chances​ ​are​ ​that​ ​number​ ​one​ ​would​ ​cause​ ​some​
       ​upsets​​and​​number​​two,​​it​​will​​probably​​cause​​quite​​a​​lot​​of​​parental​​involvement​
       ​in some way, shape, or form.​


​Similar​ ​to​ ​Lauren​ ​from​ ​‘SH​ ​School’,​ ​Leah​ ​thought​ ​that​ ​the​ ​initiative​​should​​be​​taught​​when​
​they are older:​


       ​I​ ​think​ ​it's​ ​absolutely​ ​fine​ ​to​ ​sort​ ​of​ ​talk​​about​​the​​fact​​that​​people​​were​​killed.​
       ​I'm​​not​​saying​​we​​should​​whitewash​​that​​part​​of​​our​​history,​​I'm​​not​​saying​​that.​
       ​So,​ ​I​ ​think​ ​it's​ ​for​ ​when​ ​they're​ ​older,​ ​and​ ​they're​ ​a​ ​little​ ​bit​​more​​mature,​​and​
       ​they understand a little bit better.​


​However,​​Richard​​(Jewish)​​highlighted​​the​​main​​issue,​​stating​​that​​“the​​Holocaust​​is​​not​​part​
​of​ ​the​​standard​​primary​​curriculum;​​it​​isn’t​​taught​​until​​secondary​​school”.​​According​​to​​the​
​Holocaust​ ​Educational​ ​Trust​ ​(n.d.),​ ​this​ ​aligns​ ​with​ ​the​ ​requirement​ ​for​ ​students​ ​to​ ​learn​
​about​​the​​Holocaust​​in​​Key​​Stage​​3,​​typically​​around​​the​​ages​​of​​13-14.​​Therefore,​​with​​this​​in​
​mind,​​the​​reference​​to​​gas​​chambers​​and​​hissing​​content​​was​​removed.​​It​​was​​recommended​
​by​ ​Paul​ ​(Jewish),​ ​that​ ​instead​ ​of​ ​referring​ ​to​ ​the​ ​holocaust​ ​and​ ​hissing​ ​at​ ​matches,​ ​that​
​phrases​ ​such​ ​as​ ​“offensive​ ​chants​ ​about​ ​Jewish​ ​people”​ ​could​ ​be​ ​used​​instead,​​as​​seen​​on​
​page​ ​20​ ​of​ ​the​ ​revised​ ​version​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book.​ ​Although​​the​​Holocaust​​is​​not​​introduced​​until​
​KS3​ ​in​ ​the​ ​National​ ​Curriculum,​ ​these​ ​changes​ ​to​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​could​ ​encourage​ ​early​
​conversations​ ​that​ ​help​ ​prepare​ ​younger​ ​children​ ​for​ ​its​ ​study​ ​later​ ​in​ ​their​ ​education.​
​Additionally,​ ​it​ ​would​ ​be​ ​beneficial​ ​for​ ​secondary​ ​school​ ​teachers,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​would​ ​provide​
​students​​with​​a​​basic​​understanding​​of​​antisemitism​​and​​Judaism.​​Based​​on​​the​​focus​​group​
​data,​​it​​would​​not​​be​​expected​​for​​teachers​​to​​cover​​the​​Holocaust​​in​​its​​entirety​​at​​this​​stage,​
​but rather to focus on the key elements necessary to understand its historical context.​


​Another​ ​issue​ ​was​ ​raised​ ​by​ ​Simon​ ​about​ ​the​ ​teachings​ ​of​​the​​use​​of​​the​​term​​‘Yid’.​​In​​the​
​media,​ ​there​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​be​ ​an​ ​ongoing​ ​debate​ ​around​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’,​ ​which​
​continues​​to​​create​​confusion.​​Literature​​from​​Poulton​​and​​Durell​​(2016)​​and​​Lunn​​(2023)​​has​
​found​ ​that​ ​there​ ​is​ ​often​ ​a​ ​split​ ​amongst​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​population​ ​about​ ​its​ ​use,​ ​and​
​subsequently​ ​it​ ​becomes​ ​challenging​ ​when​ ​understanding​ ​its​ ​usage.​ ​Similarly,​ ​within​ ​the​


                                                              ​228​
​focus​ ​groups,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​apparent​ ​that​ ​individuals​ ​had​ ​mixed​ ​feelings​ ​about​ ​how​ ​the​ ​father​
​approached​ ​the​ ​teachings​ ​of​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​word.​ ​Simon​ ​felt​ ​that​ ​the​ ​dad’s​ ​conversation​
​about​ ​it​ ​being​ ​used​ ​“threw​ ​away​ ​all​ ​the​ ​good​ ​work​ ​you've​ ​done​ ​earlier​ ​on”​ ​and​ ​that​​“the​
​father​ ​should​ ​have​ ​explained​ ​its​ ​derivation​ ​and​ ​said​ ​it's​ ​not​ ​a​​thing​​one​​uses,​​especially​​to​
​Jewish​​people,​​to​​other​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community”.​​With​​that​​in​​mind,​​it​​was​​crucial​
​to​ ​gauge​ ​a​ ​better​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​other​ ​Jewish​ ​participants'​ ​feelings​ ​on​ ​how​ ​the​ ​dad​
​approached​​the​​conversation.​​Chris​​felt​​that​​the​​“dad​​was​​very​​sensitive,​​but​​you​​know,​​in​​the​
​big​ ​wide​ ​world,​ ​not​ ​everybody​ ​is​ ​sensitive…​ ​you​ ​got​ ​around​ ​that​ ​in​ ​a​ ​good​ ​way”.​ ​Finally,​
​Patrick​ ​felt​ ​that​ ​“it​ ​was​ ​quite​ ​well​ ​dealt​ ​with​ ​but​ ​could​ ​have​ ​been​ ​expanded​ ​a​ ​little”.​
​Therefore,​​with​​this​​in​​mind,​​the​​research​​aims​​to​​reconsider​​the​​section​​and​​how​​it​​is​​written​
​and​ ​addressed,​ ​possibly​ ​through​ ​the​ ​suggestion​ ​made​ ​by​ ​Richard​ ​(Jewish),​​to​​have​​Joe​​ask​
​more questions to expand upon it:​


       ​Because​​he​​[Joe's​​Dad]​​then​​goes​​on​​to​​explain​​why​​the​​Bradstock​​fans​​started​​to​
       ​do​​that​​and​​there's​​an​​opportunity​​there​​for​​Joe​​to​​ask​​his​​dad,​​‘so​​why​​do​​people​
       ​say​​these​​things​​about​​Jews?’.​​And​​he​​could​​say,​​‘well,​​there's,​​you​​know,​​there's​
       ​a lot of things some people think’.​


​In​ ​conclusion,​ ​the​ ​‘storyline​ ​triggers’​ ​theme​ ​reveals​ ​key​ ​concerns​ ​about​ ​content​ ​related​ ​to​
​the​ ​Holocaust,​ ​the​​use​​of​​the​​term​​‘Yid’,​​and​​references​​to​​hissing,​​which​​some​​participants​
​felt​ ​were​ ​too​ ​sensitive​ ​for​ ​younger​ ​audiences.​ ​The​ ​feedback​ ​led​ ​to​ ​revisions,​ ​such​ ​as​
​removing​ ​references​ ​to​ ​gas​ ​chambers​ ​and​ ​replacing​ ​specific​ ​terminology,​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​the​
​material​ ​is​ ​age-appropriate​ ​while​ ​still​ ​addressing​ ​important​ ​issues​ ​like​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​
​discrimination.​​This​​leads​​to​​the​​next​​theme,​​‘age​​suitability​’,​​where​​the​​appropriate​​age​​for​
​teaching these sensitive topics is further explored.​


​Age suitability​


​Another​​challenge​​discussed​​by​​the​​participants​​was​​determining​​the​​appropriate​​year​​group​
​for​ ​delivering​ ​this​ ​resource​ ​if​ ​it​ ​were​ ​to​ ​be​ ​implemented​ ​in​ ​schools.​ ​Conversations​​around​
​age​​suitability​​primarily​​took​​place​​with​​participants​​who​​worked​​in​​education.​​As​​previously​
​discussed​ ​in​ ​the​ ​sub-theme,​ ​‘storyline​ ​triggers’,​ ​there​ ​was​ ​some​ ​discussion​​from​​SH​​School​


                                                            ​229​
​about​ ​the​ ​suitability​ ​of​ ​the​ ​subject​ ​content​ ​amongst​ ​young​ ​children.​ ​However,​ ​with​ ​the​
​storyline​​focusing​​also​​on​​the​​subject​​of​​transitioning​​from​​primary​​to​​secondary​​school​​there​
​was​​also​​relevance​​to​​have​​it​​aimed​​towards​​children​​aged​​10-11.​​In​​addition,​​previous​​data​
​from​​the​​Phase​​1​​interviews​​found​​that​​this​​age​​was​​crucial​​for​​challenging​​attitudes​​towards​
​discrimination.​ ​Yet​ ​Hannah​ ​(Educator),​​felt​​some​​level​​of​​confusion​​regarding​​who​​the​​story​
​was​ ​tailored​ ​for,​ ​stating​ ​“I​ ​wasn't​ ​quite​ ​sure​ ​if,​ ​if​ ​it​ ​was​ ​going​ ​to​ ​be​ ​for​ ​year​ ​five​ ​to​​six,​​or​
​seven,​​or​​eight​​or​​nine”.​​Tom​​(Educator)​​who​​worked​​alongside​​Hannah,​​also​​discussed​​how​
​each chapter would suit a certain age group:​


        ​I've​ ​found​ ​that​ ​chapters​ ​one​ ​and​ ​two,​ ​would​ ​very​ ​naturally​ ​be​ ​taught​ ​by​ ​years​
        ​five​​and​​six.​​But​​your​​chapters​​three​​and​​four​​would​​be​​most​​certainly​​secondary.​
        ​There​ ​is​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Holocaust,​ ​that​ ​would​ ​have​ ​to​ ​be​ ​for​ ​older​
        ​children…​​The​​racist​​comments​​which​​are​​made,​​that's​​all​​very​​relevant​​to​​Year​​5,​
        ​6, 7. They discuss things like that.​


​The​ ​conversation​ ​with​ ​Tom​ ​raised​ ​some​ ​challenges​ ​for​ ​the​​researcher,​​as​​the​​resource​​was​
​never​ ​designed​​to​​span​​multiple​​age​​groups.​​However,​​in​​line​​with​​earlier​​discussions​​about​
​teaching​ ​the​ ​Holocaust,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​recommended​ ​that​ ​references​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Holocaust​ ​and​ ​gas​
​chambers​ ​be​ ​removed.​ ​This​ ​adjustment​ ​would​ ​mean​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​would​ ​not​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​
​delivered​​across​​several​​year​​groups.​​Instead,​​children​​could​​build​​upon​​their​​learning​​as​​they​
​progressed​​through​​year​​groups,​​incorporating​​additional​​activities​​such​​as​​those​​pedagogical​
​suggestions proposed in Theme 1.​


​Although​​this​​does​​still​​create​​some​​challenges,​​with​​content​​being​​taught​​which​​might​​prove​
​challenging​ ​for​​younger​​children.​​Diana,​​a​​teaching​​assistant,​​mentioned​​that​​“higher​​ability​
​children​ ​would​ ​understand​ ​it​ ​most​ ​and​ ​engage​ ​well​ ​with​ ​it”,​ ​which​ ​also​ ​provides​ ​a​
​consideration​ ​of​ ​whether​ ​this​ ​is​ ​suitable​ ​for​ ​children​ ​ages​ ​10-11​​or​​whether​​it​​needs​​to​​be​
​rebranded​ ​for​ ​KS3.​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​Tom​ ​(Educator)​ ​and​ ​Iris​ ​(Jewish),​ ​felt​ ​that​ ​some​
​conversations​​would​​be​​challenging​​for​​a​​child​​age​​11​​to​​understand,​​specifically​​Iris​​(Jewish),​
​though​ ​discussions​ ​around​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​Yid,​ ​can​ ​be​ ​challenging​ ​for​ ​children​ ​to​
​comprehend:​




                                                                    ​230​
       ​So​​it's​​very​​confusing​​for​​a​​child​​to​​understand,​​for​​example,​​the​​‘Y​​word’,​​why​​it's​
       ​okay​​to​​shout​​at​​your​​football​​match,​​but​​unacceptable​​outside​​of​​it.​​I​​think​​that's​
       ​quite​ ​a​ ​difficult​ ​thing​ ​for​ ​a​ ​child​ ​to​ ​understand.​ ​It's​ ​sort​ ​of​ ​acceptable,​ ​but​ ​not​
       ​quite.​


​Also​ ​discussing​ ​the​ ​conversations​ ​around​ ​the​ ​phrase​ ​‘yid’​ ​was​ ​Tom,​ ​who​ ​said​ ​“one​ ​or​ ​two​
​questions​ ​which​ ​are​ ​a​ ​little​ ​bit​ ​controversial​ ​children​ ​probably​ ​find​ ​quite​ ​hard​ ​to​ ​actually​
​explain”. This was also agreed upon by Paul, who mentioned that:​


       ​You​​do​​need​​to​​be​​very​​simplistic​​about​​some​​things…​​the​​concept​​that​​it's​​okay,​
       ​or​​possibly​​okay,​​for​​some​​people​​to​​call​​them​​or​​to​​act​​in​​a​​way,​​which​​is​​fine​​for​
       ​them. But if somebody does it to them it isn't fine, it is quite difficult.​


​However,​ ​more​ ​broadly​ ​in​ ​society,​ ​discussions​ ​about​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​​the​​term​​‘Yid’​​have​​proven​
​confusing​​for​​a​​range​​of​​individuals,​​including​​adults,​​due​​to​​the​​nature​​of​​how​​the​​phrase​​is​
​being​​used,​​as​​seen​​in​​previous​​research​​(Poulton,​​2013;​​2016).​​Therefore,​​this​​highlights​​that​
​there​​is​​a​​need​​to​​have​​discussions​​around​​the​​use​​of​​the​​term​​‘Yid’​​in​​order​​for​​there​​to​​be​​a​
​better understanding:​


       ​I​ ​think​ ​Year​ ​Six​ ​towards​ ​the​ ​end​ ​of​ ​Year​ ​Six​ ​(SATs)​ ​with​​that​​almost​​going​​to​​be​
       ​seven​ ​is​ ​probably​ ​a​ ​good​ ​age​ ​because​ ​I​ ​am​ ​just​ ​beginning​​to​​be​​able​​to​​sort​​of​
       ​form​​those​​opinions​​and​​not,​​not​​really​​worry​​too​​much​​about​​maybe​​what​​their​
       ​peers…​ ​So​ ​I​ ​think​ ​they're​ ​emotionally​ ​mature​ ​enough​ ​to​ ​probably​ ​contemplate​
       ​some of the darker aspects. (Leah - Jewish Educator)​


​Although​​Leah​​previously​​mentioned​​some​​of​​the​​subject​​content​​being​​slightly​​daunting​​for​
​young​​children​​to​​learn,​​she​​felt​​that​​the​​end​​of​​Year​​6​​was​​a​​suitable​​age,​​which​​members​​of​
​SH​ ​School​ ​also​ ​agreed​ ​upon.​ ​However,​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​overall​ ​aligns​ ​to​​the​​correct​
​year​ ​group,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​recommended​ ​by​ ​Matthew​ ​to​ ​complete​ ​a​ ​pilot:​ ​“I​ ​would​ ​pilot​ ​it​ ​across​
​year​ ​groups​ ​and​ ​see​ ​what​ ​gets​ ​your​ ​best​ ​engagement”.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​with​ ​Matthew’s​ ​comment​ ​in​
​mind,​ ​that​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​was​ ​to​ ​trial​ ​the​ ​amended​ ​version​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​to​ ​see​ ​where​ ​the​
​greatest engagement occurs.​


                                                               ​231​
​To​​conclude,​​this​​theme​​has​​presented​​the​​researcher​​with​​several​​challenges​​that​​may​​need​
​to​ ​be​ ​taken​​into​​account​​when​​considering​​the​​longevity​​of​​the​​resource.​​They​​offer​​certain​
​problems​​that​​might​​be​​resolved,​​such​​as​​piloting​​the​​resource​​to​​decide​​the​​age​​suitability,​
​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​some​ ​issues​ ​that​ ​might​ ​not​ ​have​ ​a​ ​solution,​ ​including​ ​the​ ​removal​ ​of​ ​subject​
​content​ ​including​ ​discussions​ ​of​ ​the​ ​holocaust.​ ​The​ ​next​ ​phase​ ​of​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process​
​included​ ​making​ ​amendments​ ​to​ ​the​ ​draft​ ​copy,​ ​in​ ​which​ ​some​ ​of​ ​these​ ​comments​ ​were​
​addressed and taken into consideration.​


​Chapter summary​

​This​​chapter​​explored​​six​​key​​themes​​emerging​​from​​Phase​​3​​data,​​which​​examined​​feedback​
​from​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​ ​educators,​ ​and​ ​members​ ​of​​the​​Jewish​​community.​​These​
​themes​ ​explored​ ​both​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​and​ ​opportunities​ ​in​ ​enhancing​ ​the​ ​proposed​
​educational​ ​initiative​ ​centred​ ​around​ ​addressing​ ​antisemitism​ ​through​ ​a​​book​​designed​​for​
​10-11​ ​year​ ​olds.​ ​The​ ​findings​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​relatability,​ ​structural​
​coherence,​​the​​use​​of​​football​​as​​an​​engaging​​educational​​tool,​​and​​pedagogical​​adaptability.​
​Key​​recommendations​​included​​integrating​​diverse​​personal​​stories​​and​​characters​​to​​reflect​
​lived​ ​experiences,​ ​reinforcing​ ​the​ ​relatability​ ​of​ ​the​ ​narrative,​ ​and​ ​providing​ ​additional​
​pedagogical​ ​tools​ ​such​ ​as​ ​glossaries​ ​and​ ​cultural​ ​activities.​ ​These​​recommendations​​aim​​to​
​make​​the​​resource​​not​​only​​informative​​but​​also​​emotionally​​resonant,​​empowering​​children​
​to​​reflect​​on​​their​​identities​​and​​confront​​discrimination​​effectively.​​Additionally,​​the​​research​
​findings​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​the​ ​broad-to-narrow​ ​structure​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​beginning​ ​with​ ​general​
​discussions on discrimination before narrowing to focus on antisemitism.​

​The​ ​discussion​ ​also​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​potential​ ​of​ ​football​ ​to​ ​serve​ ​as​ ​a​ ​unifying​ ​context​ ​for​
​addressing​​societal​​issues​​while​​acknowledging​​its​​limitations​​in​​perpetuating​​existing​​biases​
​(Cleland,​ ​2015;​ ​Kidd,​ ​2008;​ ​Penfold​ ​and​ ​Cleland​ ​2022).​ ​The​ ​incorporation​ ​of​ ​diverse​
​characters,​ ​particularly​ ​female​ ​and​​Muslim​​representations,​​was​​praised​​for​​broadening​​the​
​book's​ ​appeal​ ​and​ ​challenging​ ​stereotypes.​ ​Pedagogical​ ​flexibility​ ​was​ ​discussed,​ ​with​
​proposals​ ​for​ ​digital​ ​and​ ​physical​ ​formats​ ​to​ ​accommodate​ ​various​ ​teaching​ ​contexts.​ ​The​
​narrative​ ​structure,​ ​which​ ​invited​ ​students​ ​to​ ​create​ ​their​ ​own​ ​ending,​ ​was​ ​discussed​​as​​it​
​was​ ​crafted​ ​to​ ​promote​ ​active​ ​participation,​ ​inspiring​ ​children​ ​to​ ​translate​ ​the​ ​lessons​


                                                             ​232​
​learned​ ​into​ ​real-world​ ​applications.​ ​Lastly,​ ​there​ ​were​​challenges​​associated​​with​​ensuring​
​the​ ​longevity​ ​of​ ​the​ ​resource,​ ​including​ ​age​ ​suitability​ ​and​ ​sensitive​ ​content​ ​such​ ​as​
​Holocaust​​discussions.​​Therefore,​​changes​​to​​the​​draft​​were​​made​​to​​address​​some​​of​​these​
​concerns.​​These​​amendments​​were​​made​​for​​the​​next​​round​​of​​data​​collection,​​ensuring​​that​
​the​ ​resource​ ​was​ ​more​ ​refined​ ​and​​responsive​​to​​the​​identified​​challenges.​​This,​​therefore,​
​leads​ ​into​ ​the​ ​next​ ​chapter,​ ​which​ ​outlines​ ​the​ ​methodology​ ​for​ ​Phase​ ​4​ ​of​ ​the​ ​research​
​process.​




                                                          ​233​
​Chapter 9 - Phase 4 methods - Expert book review​


​Introduction​


​The​​focus​​of​​discussion​​will​​now​​move​​onto​​the​​data​​collection​​for​​the​​book​​review​​(Phase​​4).​
​The​​proposed​​plan​​for​​the​​final​​stage​​of​​this​​project​​was​​to​​trial​​the​​initiative​​in​​May​​2024​​as​
​part​​of​​a​​pilot​​study​​within​​schools;​​however,​​the​​schools​​that​​had​​initially​​expressed​​interest​
​in​​participating​​in​​the​​trial​​indicated​​that​​they​​could​​not​​proceed​​with​​the​​project​​due​​to​​the​
​ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict.​


​Therefore,​ ​the​ ​final​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​involved​ ​conducting​ ​a​ ​‘book​ ​review’​ ​with​
​anti-discrimination​ ​experts.​ ​While​ ​the​ ​initial​ ​intention​ ​was​ ​to​ ​include​ ​individuals​ ​who​ ​had​
​participated​​in​​earlier​​phases​​of​​data​​collection​​(i.e.,​​Phase​​1​​interviews​​and/or​​Phase​​3​​focus​
​groups),​ ​this​ ​review​ ​also​ ​sought​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​new​ ​participants,​ ​particularly​ ​those​ ​with​
​specialised​​knowledge​​in​​antisemitism​​education​​and​​Jewish​​studies.​​The​​purpose​​of​​inviting​
​these​​individuals​​to​​participate​​in​​a​​book​​review​​was​​to​​gather​​valuable​​insights​​on​​the​​book's​
​publishability,​ ​practicality,​ ​implementation​ ​feasibility,​​structure​​and​​layout.​​This​​was​​distinct​
​from​ ​the​ ​earlier​ ​phases,​ ​where​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​was​ ​on​ ​discussing​ ​their​ ​own​ ​initiatives​ ​and​
​successes​ ​(Phase​ ​1),​ ​or​ ​evaluating​ ​the​ ​strengths​ ​and​ ​limitations​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initial​​draft​​of​​‘Joe’s​
​Footballing Journey’ (Phase 3).​


​Ethical considerations​


​As​ ​previously​ ​mentioned,​ ​the​ ​intention​ ​was​ ​to​ ​trial​​the​​initiative​​in​​schools,​​necessitating​​a​
​new​ ​ethics​ ​application.​ ​However,​ ​since​ ​this​ ​trial​ ​could​ ​not​ ​proceed,​ ​an​ ​amendment​ ​to​ ​the​
​Phase​ ​2​ ​ethics​ ​application​ ​was​ ​submitted​ ​and​ ​received​ ​approval​ ​(Appendix​ ​C).​ ​This​
​amendment​ ​enabled​ ​additional​ ​feedback​ ​from​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts​ ​who​ ​had​ ​been​
​consulted​ ​during​ ​Phases​ ​1​ ​and​ ​3​ ​of​ ​the​ ​project.​ ​In​ ​addition,​ ​it​ ​also​ ​allowed​ ​for​ ​new​
​‘anti-discrimination​ ​experts’​ ​to​ ​be​​recruited;​​these​​were​​individuals​​who​​had​​not​​previously​
​taken​​part​​in​​earlier​​phrases​​to​​be​​recommended​​and​​approached​​to​​participate​​in​​the​​book​
​review.​




                                                             ​234​
​As​ ​this​ ​is​ ​an​ ​extension​ ​of​ ​the​ ​previous​ ​stages​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection,​ ​the​ ​ethics​ ​application​
​highlighted​​the​​same​​risks​​which​​were​​limited,​​other​​than​​ethical​​considerations​​which​​were​
​mentioned​ ​previously​ ​in​ ​the​ ​ethics​ ​discussions​ ​(see​ ​p.​ ​107),​ ​which​ ​included​ ​psychological​
​discomfort​ ​when​ ​discussing​ ​issues​ ​such​ ​as​ ​discrimination,​ ​specifically​ ​antisemitism.​ ​To​
​address​​potential​​challenges,​​participants​​received​​a​​participant​​information​​sheet​​(Appendix​
