​R),​ ​which​ ​included​ ​the​ ​contact​ ​details​ ​for​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​and​ ​their​ ​team,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​
​information​ ​about​ ​free​ ​charities​ ​that​ ​could​ ​provide​ ​psychological​ ​support​ ​if​ ​needed.​
​Additionally,​ ​participants​ ​were​ ​informed​ ​through​ ​the​ ​participant​ ​information​ ​sheet​
​(Appendix​ ​R),​ ​the​ ​GDPR​ ​privacy​ ​notice​ ​(Appendix​ ​S),​ ​and​ ​the​ ​informed​ ​consent​ ​form​
​(Appendix​ ​T)​ ​of​ ​their​ ​right​ ​to​ ​withdraw​ ​from​ ​the​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​process​​at​​any​​time.​​They​
​were​​also​​given​​the​​option​​to​​leave​​any​​questions​​unanswered​​if​​they​​chose​​not​​to​​respond.​
​Finally,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​integral​ ​that​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​protected​ ​the​ ​interviewee’s​ ​identity​
​(DiCicco‐Bloom​​and​​Crabtree,​​2006);​​therefore,​​for​​the​​write​​up​​of​​this​​research,​​participants​
​have​ ​been​ ​given​ ​pseudonyms​ ​to​ ​protect​ ​their​ ​anonymity​ ​and​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​​all​​comments​
​remain confidential.​

​Anti-discrimination expert ‘book review’​


​The​ ​final​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​consisted​ ​of​ ​a​ ​‘book​ ​review’,​ ​which​ ​essentially​ ​was​ ​a​
​questionnaire​ ​consisting​ ​of​ ​twelve​ ​open-ended​ ​questions​ ​(Appendix​​U).​​For​​the​​purpose​​of​
​this​ ​research,​ ​the​ ​questionnaires​ ​were​ ​conducted​ ​online,​ ​as​ ​Gray​ ​(2023)​ ​discusses​ ​how​
​online​​questionnaires​​have​​become​​increasingly​​more​​popular,​​due​​to​​being​​low​​in​​cost​​and​
​ease​​in​​being​​shared.​​A​​questionnaire​​can​​either​​have​​close-ended​​or​​open-ended​​questions,​
​or​​a​​combination;​​however,​​open-ended​​questions​​are​​often​​used​​within​​qualitative​​research,​
​as​​they​​contain​​questions​​which​​allow​​respondents​​to​​address​​their​​feedback​​without​​being​
​limited​​(Allen,​​2017;​​Mwita,​​2022).​​Additionally,​​by​​allowing​​respondents​​to​​express​​feelings​
​and​​opinions​​on​​the​​particular​​question​​asked,​​it​​can​​often​​lead​​to​​a​​large​​collection​​of​​data.​
​Questionnaires​ ​offer​ ​several​ ​advantages,​ ​including​ ​the​ ​potential​ ​reduction​ ​of​ ​research​​bias​
​since​ ​no​ ​researcher​ ​is​ ​present,​ ​and​ ​they​ ​provide​ ​respondents​ ​with​ ​more​ ​time​ ​to​ ​consider​
​their​ ​feedback​​compared​​to​​methods​​like​​interviews​​or​​focus​​groups​​(Gray,​​2023;​​Jones​​and​
​Gratton,​ ​2015).​ ​Previous​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​methods​ ​involved​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​directly​ ​asking​
​questions​ ​through​ ​interviews​ ​or​ ​focus​ ​groups;​ ​therefore,​ ​this​ ​approach​ ​is​ ​particularly​



                                                           ​235​
​beneficial​ ​as​ ​it​ ​allows​ ​for​ ​greater​ ​respondent​ ​reflection​ ​and​​unbiased​​responses.​​Given​​the​
​expert​​status​​of​​the​​participants​​and​​the​​difficulty​​in​​securing​​their​​time,​​questionnaires​​were​
​utilised​ ​to​ ​allow​ ​them​ ​to​ ​respond​ ​at​ ​their​ ​convenience​ ​and​ ​to​ ​accommodate​ ​their​ ​busy​
​schedules.​


​The​​questionnaire​​provided​​valuable​​insights​​for​​this​​research,​​as​​respondents​​evaluated​​the​
​book's​ ​publishability,​ ​practicality,​ ​feasibility​ ​of​ ​implementation,​ ​structure,​ ​and​ ​layout.​
​Nevertheless,​ ​although​ ​questionnaires​ ​are​ ​widely​ ​used​ ​in​ ​research,​ ​this​ ​data​ ​collection​
​method​ ​had​ ​certain​ ​weaknesses.​ ​It​ ​did​​not​​allow​​for​​probing​​or​​following​​up​​on​​responses,​
​and​​if​​participants​​misunderstood​​any​​questions​​or​​were​​unable​​to​​answer​​them,​​they​​had​​no​
​opportunity​ ​to​ ​seek​ ​clarification​ ​(Jones​​and​​Gratton,​​2015;​​Kirk-Smith​​and​​McKenna,​​1998).​
​However,​​both​​the​​participant​​and​​the​​researcher​​had​​access​​to​​each​​other's​​contact​​details,​
​allowing​ ​them​ ​to​ ​request​ ​additional​ ​information​ ​from​ ​one​ ​another​ ​if​ ​necessary.​ ​Although​
​these​ ​challenges​ ​were​ ​taken​ ​into​ ​account,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​note​ ​that​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​
​participants​ ​had​ ​already​ ​engaged​ ​in​ ​interviews​ ​or​ ​focus​​groups.​​Therefore,​​selecting​​a​​data​
​collection​ ​method​ ​that​ ​avoided​​unnecessary​​repetition​​and​​did​​not​​appear​​to​​overuse​​their​
​time was crucial.​


​Participants​


​Participants​ ​contacted​ ​via​ ​email​ ​to​ ​take​ ​part​ ​in​ ​the​ ​book​ ​review​ ​were​ ​anti-discrimination​
​experts​ ​who​ ​had​ ​previously​ ​participated​ ​in​ ​earlier​ ​phases​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection,​ ​such​ ​as​
​interviews​​and/or​​focus​​groups.​​These​​individuals​​possessed​​specific​​knowledge​​in​​the​​fields​
​of​​education​​and​​Jewish​​studies.​​They​​were​​selected​​through​​purposeful​​sampling,​​identified​
​as"individuals​ ​or​ ​groups​ ​of​ ​individuals​ ​that​ ​are​ ​especially​ ​knowledgeable​ ​about​ ​or​
​experienced with a phenomenon of interest" (Palinkas​​et al.​, 2015, p. 534).​

​However,​ ​upon​​reaching​​out​​to​​some​​anti-discrimination​​experts​​who​​participated​​earlier​​in​
​the​ ​project,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​received​ ​responses​ ​indicating​ ​that​ ​they​ ​were​ ​either​ ​unable​ ​to​
​participate​​or​​no​​longer​​worked​​at​​their​​respective​​organisations.​​They​​provided​​suggestions​
​for​ ​alternative​ ​participants​ ​who​ ​either​ ​worked​ ​at​ ​the​ ​same​ ​organisation​ ​or​ ​external​
​companies.​ ​Consequently,​ ​snowball​ ​sampling​ ​was​ ​employed,​ ​a​ ​method​ ​where​ ​one​



                                                         ​236​
​participant​ ​refers​​the​​researcher​​to​​additional​​potential​​participants​​(Biernacki​​and​​Waldorf,​
​1981).​​In​​this​​final​​stage​​of​​the​​research,​​a​​total​​of​​six​​participants​​were​​recruited​​to​​complete​
​the book review, as detailed in Table 8 below.​

                                                          ​237​
​Procedure​


​The​​recruitment​​process​​began​​in​​May​​2024,​​whereby​​participants​​were​​emailed​​to​​request​
​their​​participation​​in​​the​​final​​part​​of​​the​​project.​​Before​​starting​​data​​collection,​​a​​participant​
​information​ ​sheet​ ​(Appendix​ ​R),​ ​GDPR​ ​privacy​ ​notice​ ​(Appendix​ ​S)​ ​and​ ​informed​ ​consent​
​form​ ​(Appendix​ ​T)​ ​were​ ​provided​ ​to​ ​participants​ ​who​ ​showed​ ​interest​ ​in​ ​the​ ​project.​
​Participants​ ​who​ ​agreed​ ​to​ ​take​ ​part​ ​returned​ ​a​ ​signed​ ​informed​ ​consent​ ​form,​ ​thereby​
​confirming​ ​that​ ​they​ ​had​ ​read​ ​the​ ​information​ ​sheet​ ​and​ ​consented​ ​to​ ​participate​ ​in​ ​the​
​research.​


​Once​​participants​​had​​returned​​their​​consent​​forms,​​they​​then​​received​​an​​amended​​copy​​of​
​the​ ​book​ ​(Appendix​ ​P)​ ​and​ ​accompanying​​resource​​pack​​(Appendix​​Q)​​to​​read.​​Participants​
​were​​told​​that​​it​​was​​expected​​that​​it​​would​​take​​no​​longer​​than​​one​​hour​​to​​read​​the​​book,​
​alongside​ ​its​ ​resource​ ​pack;​ ​however,​ ​that​ ​it​ ​could​ ​vary​ ​depending​ ​on​ ​your​ ​level​ ​of​
​engagement​​with​​the​​book.​​Finally,​​they​​were​​provided​​with​​a​​question​​sheet​​(Appendix​​U).​
​Since​ ​questionnaires​ ​can​ ​be​ ​administered​ ​online​ ​via​ ​email​ ​(Mwita,​ ​2022),​ ​this​ ​method​
​proved​ ​to​ ​be​ ​the​ ​most​ ​effective,​ ​aligning​ ​with​ ​Wright's​ ​(2005)​ ​observation​ ​that​ ​online​
​questionnaires​ ​are​ ​both​ ​time-efficient​ ​and​ ​cost-effective​ ​for​​researchers.​​The​​questionnaire​
​contained​ ​twelve​ ​open-ended​ ​questions​ ​and​ ​participants​ ​were​ ​asked​ ​to​ ​return​ ​their​
​feedback via email within 14 days of receiving it.​


​Analysis​


​After​​reviewing​​the​​data,​​themes​​and​​trends​​in​​the​​data​​set​​were​​identified​​through​​the​​use​
​of​ ​TA​ ​(Bruan​ ​and​ ​Clarke,​​2006).​​As​​discussed​​in​​previous​​chapters​​(see​​p.​​111​​for​​a​​detailed​
​explanation​ ​and​ ​rationale​ ​for​ ​this​ ​process),​ ​TA​ ​is​ ​a​ ​six-step​ ​approach​ ​that​ ​starts​ ​with​
​qualitative​ ​data​​and​​looks​​for​​similarities​​and​​contrasts​​before​​focusing​​on​​the​​link​​between​
​the​​different​​parts​​of​​the​​data​​set​​(Braun​​and​​Clarke,​​2006).​​TA​​proved​​beneficial​​for​​this​​final​
​phase​​of​​data​​collection,​​as​​it​​allowed​​for​​the​​identification​​of​​recurring​​themes​​and​​patterns​
​across​ ​participants'​ ​responses​ ​within​ ​the​ ​questionnaire,​ ​providing​ ​a​ ​rich​ ​understanding​ ​of​
​their​ ​opinions​ ​and​ ​perspectives.​ ​Through​ ​the​ ​process​ ​of​ ​TA,​ ​five​ ​themes​ ​were​ ​identified,​
​which​ ​were​ ​titled​ ​‘​developing​ ​content​ ​quality’,​ ​‘educational​ ​value’,​ ​‘usability​ ​for​​educators’,​


                                                          ​238​
​‘design​ ​and​ ​visual​ ​aesthetics’​ ​and​ ​‘distribution​ ​and​ ​accessibility’​.​ ​As​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​Table​ ​9,​ ​these​
​themes​​contained​​sub-themes​​which​​highlight​​specific​​aspects​​of​​the​​main​​themes.​​Finally,​​a​
​definition​ ​has​ ​been​ ​provided​ ​for​ ​each​ ​theme​ ​to​ ​clarify​ ​their​ ​meanings​ ​and​ ​ensure​ ​a​
​consistent understanding across the study.​

​Chapter 10 - Phase 4 - Results and discussion​


​Introduction​


​In​​line​​with​​the​​previous​​results​​and​​discussion​​chapters​​(Phases​​1​​and​​3)​,​​this​​chapter​​will​
​explore​ ​the​ ​themes​ ​which​ ​were​ ​constructed​ ​through​ ​TA.​ ​The​ ​analysis​​of​​the​​book​​review​
​with​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts​ ​led​ ​to​ ​the​ ​identification​ ​and​ ​construction​ ​of​ ​five​ ​main​
​themes,​​each​​comprising​​several​​sub-themes​​detailed​​in​​(Table​​9).​​This​​chapter​​is​​organised​
​into​ ​five​ ​sections,​ ​with​ ​each​ ​section​ ​exploring​ ​its​ ​sub-themes​ ​in​ ​depth.​ ​The​ ​chapter​
​concludes with a section outlining the future direction of the initiative.​


​Theme 1 - Developing content quality​

​The​​book​​review​​aimed​​to​​collect​​valuable​​insights​​from​​experts​​with​​experience​​in​​the​​field​
​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​Jewish​ ​education.​ ​The​ ​feedback​ ​sought​ ​focused​ ​on​ ​the​ ​book's​
​publishability,​ ​practicality,​ ​implementation​ ​feasibility,​​structure,​​and​​layout.​​Additionally,​​it​
​provided​ ​an​ ​opportunity​ ​to​ ​identify​ ​the​ ​key​ ​strengths​ ​and​ ​limitations​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​of​
​which​ ​some​ ​fall​ ​into​ ​these​ ​areas​ ​for​ ​discussion.​ ​Understanding​ ​these​ ​strengths​ ​and​
​limitations​ ​allowed​​for​​amendments​​to​​enhance​​the​​book's​​impact.​​The​​previous​​round​​of​
​data​ ​collection​ ​brought​ ​forth​ ​some​ ​‘​recommended​ ​additions’​ ​(Theme​ ​1),​ ​which​ ​proved​
​useful​​as​​they​​facilitated​​necessary​​changes.​​These​​changes​​were​​implemented​​prior​​to​​this​
​book​ ​review.​ ​Therefore,​ ​comments​ ​from​ ​the​ ​third​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​(Phase​ ​4)​​will​
​further​ ​refine​ ​and​ ​improve​ ​the​ ​book​ ​going​ ​forward.​ ​With​ ​this​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​there​ ​are​ ​two​
​sub-themes in this first theme:​​‘strengths in content​​quality’​​and ‘​areas for improvement’.​

​Strengths in content quality​


​Gray​ ​(2022)​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​obtaining​​feedback​​on​​a​​product​​or​​prototype,​
​emphasising​ ​that​​the​​feedback​​is​​crucial​​for​​its​​future​​success.​​Specifically,​​recognising​​the​
​strengths​​of​​the​​educational​​book​​and​​resource​​pack​​is​​essential​​for​​understanding​​its​​value​
​and​​potential​​impact.​​Therefore,​​participants​​were​​asked​​to​​share​​their​​thoughts​​on​​the​​key​
​strengths​​of​​the​​educational​​materials​​provided.​​Their​​feedback,​​detailed​​in​​the​​table​​below​


                                                            ​240​
​(Table​ ​10),​ ​highlights​​various​​aspects​​of​​the​​educational​​book​​and​​resource​​pack​​that​​they​
​found particularly effective.​

​Table 10.​​Quotes highlighting key strengths of the​​Educational Book and Resource Pack.​

​From​​reviewing​​Table​​10,​​it​​is​​evident​​that​​Vera,​​Aaron​​(Education​​Project​​Coordinator),​​and​
​Gia​ ​(Co-CEO​ ​and​ ​Founder)​ ​identified​ ​a​ ​key​ ​strength​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​in​ ​its​ ​exploration​ ​of​
​challenges​​that​​resonate​​with​​readers,​​particularly​​the​​transition​​from​​primary​​to​​secondary​
​school.​ ​Prater​ ​and​ ​Dyches​ ​(2008)​ ​discuss​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​children​ ​literature,​ ​as​ ​it​
​provides​ ​an​ ​opportunity​ ​for​ ​children​ ​to​ ​live​ ​vicariously​ ​through​ ​the​ ​characters.​ ​As​ ​the​
​theory​ ​of​ ​HebCrit​​emphasises​​that​​Jewish​​individuals​​continue​​to​​be​​discriminated​​against​
​(Rubin,​​2020),​​the​​primary​​goal​​of​​this​​educational​​book​​is​​to​​educate​​young​​individuals​​on​
​antisemitism​​and​​Judaism,​​a​​significant​​observation​​was​​how​​it​​also​​provided​​students​​with​
​an​​opportunity​​to​​discuss​​the​​transition​​between​​schools,​​which​​would​​resonate​​with​​Year​​6​
​students.​​Vera​​(Headteacher)​​noted​​"the​​story​​will​​resonate​​with​​many​​children​​who…​​are​
​at​ ​the​ ​end​ ​of​ ​their​ ​primary​ ​school​ ​journey"​ ​and​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​
​highlighted​ ​that​ ​a​ ​key​ ​strength​ ​is​ ​how​​it​​conveys​​"feelings​​of​​moving​​to​​a​​new​​school​​and​
​methods​​of​​connecting​​with​​people​​when​​in​​secondary​​school".​​According​​to​​Rubin's​​(2020)​
​HebCrit​ ​theory,​ ​Jewish​ ​personal​ ​stories​ ​hold​ ​significant​ ​value.​ ​Therefore,​ ​when​ ​designing​
​the​ ​book,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​incorporate​ ​narratives​​about​​antisemitism​​and​​Judaism.​​This​
​approach​​was​​combined​​with​​broader​​themes,​​such​​as​​transitioning​​to​​school,​​to​​enhance​
​relatability​ ​and​ ​foster​ ​empathy​ ​among​ ​students.​ ​This​ ​approach​ ​was​ ​explicitly​ ​explored​ ​in​
​the​ ​sub-themes​ ​‘​relatability’​ ​(Phase​ ​1)​ ​and​ ​‘importance​ ​of​ ​relatability’​ ​(Phase​ ​3).​ ​By​
​engaging​ ​students​ ​through​ ​relatable​ ​topics​ ​such​ ​as​ ​school​ ​transition,​ ​the​​book​​effectively​
​enhances its educational impact, proving to be a significant strength.​




                                                          ​242​
​During​​the​​book's​​design​​phase,​​the​​integration​​of​​discussion​​points​​was​​a​​crucial​​element​
​within​​the​​initiative,​​which​​was​​supported​​by​​Vera​​(Headteacher)​​who​​noted​​that​​“the​​story​
​and​ ​discussion​ ​points​ ​build​ ​each​ ​week”.​ ​This​ ​approach​ ​not​ ​only​ ​allowed​ ​for​ ​continuous​
​engagement​ ​but​ ​also​ ​encouraged​ ​reflective​ ​thinking​ ​among​ ​students.​ ​In​ ​Phase​ ​3,​ ​focus​
​group​ ​discussions​ ​frequently​ ​reiterated​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​these​ ​discussion​ ​points​ ​within​
​the​ ​resource's​ ​structure,​ ​leading​ ​to​ ​the​ ​emergence​ ​of​ ​the​ ​sub-theme​ ​‘​discussion​ ​points’.​
​These​ ​points​ ​served​ ​as​ ​a​ ​practical​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​teachers​ ​to​ ​facilitate​ ​discussions​ ​on​
​discrimination​ ​and​ ​antisemitism,​ ​a​ ​feature​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​ ​praised​
​by​ ​emphasising​ ​that​ ​a​ ​notable​ ​strength​ ​was​ ​the​ ​“flow​ ​of​ ​the​ ​story​ ​with​ ​discussions​​after​
​each​​chapter​​focusing​​on​​the​​key​​points​​intended”.​​The​​inclusion​​of​​these​​discussion​​points​
​aligns​​with​​literature,​​such​​as​​Van​​Horn​​(2015)​​who​​explored​​the​​importance​​of​​discussion,​
​when​ ​exploring​ ​heteronormative​ ​structures​ ​in​ ​LGBT+​ ​literature,​ ​reinforcing​ ​that​
​opportunities​​to​​‘discuss’​​plays​​a​​pivotal​​role​​in​​enhancing​​educational​​impact​​and​​retention​
​of material.​

​Gia​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​user-friendly​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​for​ ​both​ ​staff​ ​and​ ​students,​ ​by​
​stating​​“I​​think​​it​​is​​extremely​​user-friendly​​for​​staff​​and​​students”.​​This​​can​​be​​attributed​​to​
​the​ ​structured​ ​design​ ​of​ ​the​ ​story,​ ​with​ ​each​ ​chapter​ ​accompanied​ ​by​ ​discussion​ ​points.​
​This​ ​format​ ​supports​ ​easy​ ​implementation​ ​and​ ​consistent​ ​engagement,​ ​allowing​ ​for​
​seamless​ ​integration​ ​into​ ​the​ ​curriculum.​ ​The​ ​ease​ ​with​ ​which​ ​teachers​ ​can​ ​facilitate​
​discussions​ ​and​ ​the​ ​simplicity​ ​for​ ​students​ ​to​ ​follow​ ​along​ ​have​ ​made​ ​the​ ​initiative​
​particularly​ ​effective​ ​and​ ​accessible.​ ​Having​ ​a​​user-friendly​​product​​that​​is​​easy​​to​​engage​
​with​ ​for​ ​both​ ​students​ ​and​ ​staff​ ​was​ ​critical​ ​in​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​the​​initiative​​and​​has​
​been​​highlighted​​as​​a​​significant​​strength.​​Consequently,​​this​​aspect​​has​​been​​discussed​​in​
​greater​ ​depth​ ​in​ ​the​ ​later​ ​section​ ​of​ ​this​ ​chapter​​under​​the​​sub-theme​​‘​ease​​of​​use’​.​​This​
​section​ ​goes​ ​into​ ​how​​the​​straightforward​​design​​contributes​​to​​the​​overall​​success​​of​​the​
​initiative.​

​A​​key​​strength​​of​​the​​educational​​book​​was​​its​​effective​​use​​of​​football​​as​​a​​tool​​to​​address​
​important​ ​issues,​​as​​reflected​​in​​Alana’s​​(Education​​Officer)​​comment:​​"football​​is​​going​​to​
​grab​​the​​attention​​of​​many​​children​​instantly".​​This​​aligns​​with​​research​​from​​Ha​​and​​Lyras​
​(2013)​ ​and​ ​Darnell​ ​and​ ​Millington​ ​(2019)​ ​who​ ​reinforced​ ​the​ ​transformative​ ​potential​ ​of​
​sport​​to​​solve​​a​​wide​​range​​of​​societal​​problems​​and​​encourage​​social​​change,​​highlighting​


                                                            ​243​
​its​​frequent​​use​​as​​a​​tool​​to​​reduce​​discrimination.​​Additionally,​​the​​initial​​literature​​review​
​explored​ ​various​ ​initiatives​ ​that​ ​use​ ​sport​ ​to​ ​challenge​ ​anti-discriminatory​ ​attitudes,​
​including​ ​the​ ​Rainbow​ ​Laces​ ​campaign​ ​to​ ​combat​​homophobia​​(Magrath​​and​​Stott,​​2019;​
​Hansen​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2020)​ ​and​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​which​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​reduce​ ​all​ ​forms​ ​of​ ​discrimination​
​(Kilvington​​and​​Price,​​2017;​​Penfold​​and​​Cleland,​​2022).​​Furthermore,​​during​​both​​previous​
​rounds​​of​​data​​collection,​​themes​​emerged​​around​​using​​football​​and​​sport​​as​​educational​
​tools,​ ​titled​ ​‘​sport​ ​as​ ​a​​conversational​​tool’​​(Phase​​1)​​and​​‘football​​as​​an​​educational​​tool’​
​(Phase​​3)​.​​Aaron​​(Education​​Project​​Coordinator)​​emphasised​​that​​although​​the​​main​​story​
​is​ ​football-based,​​it​​effectively​​addresses​​other​​key​​aspects,​​and​​Vera​​(Headteacher)​​noted​
​that​​“the​​story​​will​​resonate​​with​​many​​children​​who​​support​​a​​football​​team/play​​football”.​
​This​​approach​​enhances​​relatability​​and​​encourages​​students​​to​​reflect​​on​​their​​experiences​
​and the story's themes.​

​When​​exploring​​the​​right​​hand​​column​​of​​Table​​10,​​the​​comments​​discuss​​the​​key​​strength​
​of​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​pack,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​designed​ ​following​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​focus​ ​groups,​ ​when​
​experts,​​staff​​and​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community​​mentioned​​the​​need​​for​​an​​additional​
​resource​ ​pack,​ ​as​ ​noted​ ​in​ ​the​ ​Phase​​3​​sub-theme​​‘​pedagogical​​additions’.​​On​​the​​whole,​
​this​ ​was​ ​very​ ​well​ ​received​ ​with​ ​comments​ ​regarding​ ​the​ ​additional​ ​key​ ​terms,​ ​links​ ​to​
​additional​ ​resources​ ​and​ ​websites.​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​Nick​ ​(Antisemitism​ ​Educator)​ ​noted​​that​
​“the​ ​resource​ ​for​ ​teachers​ ​is​ ​a​ ​comprehensive​ ​glossary​ ​and​ ​useful​ ​in​ ​and​ ​of​ ​itself”.​ ​With​
​these​​additional​​points,​​it​​acts​​as​​a​​valuable​​supporting​​document​​alongside​​the​​main​​book,​
​as​ ​highlighted​ ​by​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​ ​who​ ​said​ ​“the​ ​resource​ ​pack​ ​is​
​great as tools to use in addition to teacher knowledge and the book”.​

​However,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​also​ ​reflect​ ​critically​ ​on​ ​this​ ​feedback.​ ​There​ ​was​ ​minimal​
​discussion​​from​​participants,​​other​​than​​the​​comment​​from​​Gia,​​about​​the​​specific​​teaching​
​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​Judaism,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​primary​ ​aim.​ ​This​ ​could​ ​be​ ​due​ ​to​ ​the​
​could​​potentially​​be​​attributed​​to​​the​​wording​​of​​the​​questions.​​These​​questions​​may​​have​
​been​​designed​​to​​solicit​​feedback​​on​​pedagogical​​details​​and​​insights​​on​​how​​the​​initiative​
​could​ ​be​ ​implemented​ ​going​ ​forward,​ ​which​ ​may​ ​have​ ​directed​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​away​​from​​the​
​nuanced​ ​aspects​ ​of​ ​antisemitism.​ ​To​ ​address​ ​this,​ ​further​ ​interviews​ ​could​ ​have​ ​been​
​conducted​ ​to​ ​elicit​ ​more​ ​information,​ ​which​ ​could​ ​be​ ​an​ ​avenue​ ​for​ ​further​ ​study​ ​in​​the​
​future.​


                                                            ​244​
​While​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​relatability​ ​and​ ​structure​ ​were​ ​praised,​ ​it​​is​​essential​​to​​ensure​​that​​the​
​core​ ​message​ ​of​ ​educating​ ​children​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​remains​
​prominent​ ​and​ ​effectively​ ​conveyed.​ ​Future​ ​revisions​ ​should​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​reinforcing​ ​these​
​educational​​goals​​while​​maintaining​​the​​engaging​​and​​relatable​​nature​​of​​the​​story,​​thereby​
​enhancing​ ​the​ ​narratives​ ​developed​ ​through​ ​CRT​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001)​ ​and​
​Hebcrit’s (Rubin, 2020) key theoretical tenets.​

​Areas for improvement​


​Additionally,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​acknowledge​ ​the​ ​weaknesses​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​to​ ​improve​ ​its​
​effectiveness,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​Thompson​ ​(2020)​ ​whose​ ​work​​in​​anti-discriminatory​
​practices​ ​within​​social​​work​​highlights​​the​​need​​for​​continuous​​evaluation.​​They​​state​​that​
​continuous​ ​evaluation​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​practices​ ​remain​ ​effective​ ​and​ ​responsive​ ​to​
​various​ ​changes​​over​​time.​​These​​changes​​may​​include​​shifts​​in​​societal​​attitudes,​​updates​
​to​​legislation,​​evolving​​cultural​​dynamics,​​or​​feedback​​revealing​​gaps​​in​​current​​approaches.​
​This​​has​​been​​reflected​​within​​this​​project,​​due​​to​​the​​repeated​​cycles​​of​​data​​collection​​and​
​analysis,​​which​​shows​​commitment​​to​​ensuring​​that​​the​​voices​​of​​the​​participants​​are​​heard​
​and​ ​valued.​ ​During​ ​Phase​ ​3,​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​were​ ​crucial​ ​in​ ​offering​ ​some​ ​recommended​
​additions​​and​​highlighting​​areas​​for​​improvement,​​and​​-​​although​​these​​changes​​have​​been​
​made​ ​-​ ​there​ ​is​ ​still​ ​room​​for​​improvement,​​which​​reinforces​​the​​importance​​of​​gathering​
​continuous feedback.​

​One​ ​of​ ​the​ ​significant​ ​issues​ ​raised​ ​was​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​reformatting​ ​the​​material,​​although​
​they​​acknowledged​​that​​compatibility​​with​​their​​devices​​could​​be​​a​​factor.​​Gia​​(Co-CEO​​and​
​Founder)​​mentioned,​​"the​​material​​needs​​formatting,​​as​​there​​were​​issues​​on​​my​​computer​
​screen,"​ ​while​ ​Vera​ ​(Headteacher)​ ​noted,​ ​"the​ ​layout​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​was​ ​a​ ​bit​ ​askew​ ​in​ ​a​
​couple​​of​​places,​​but​​I​​have​​a​​Mac​​and​​it​​can​​sometimes​​do​​that,​​so​​the​​final​​version​​would​
​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​checked​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​it​ ​works​ ​in​ ​all​ ​formats".​ ​Additionally,​ ​Nick​ ​(Antisemitism​
​Educator) noted that:​




                                                            ​245​
       ​...the​ ​pagination​ ​needs​ ​attention,​ ​although​ ​I​ ​know​ ​this​ ​is​​only​​a​​draft.​​Fixes​​like​
       ​not​ ​having​ ​the​ ​last​ ​line​​of​​a​​paragraph​​bleed​​onto​​the​​next​​page​​and​​so​​on,​​but​
       ​this might be how the document gets mangled in transmission.​

​These​ ​observations​ ​highlight​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​the​ ​formatting​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​
​resource​ ​is​ ​accessible​ ​to​ ​all,​ ​and​ ​will​ ​be​ ​discussed​ ​further​ ​in​ ​the​ ​sub-theme​ ​‘​digital​
​accessibility’​.​ ​The​​second​​round​​of​​data​​collection,​​the​​Phase​​3​​focus​​groups,​​explored​​the​
​resource​​structure,​​with​​a​​sub-theme​​focusing​​on​​digital​​accessibility,​​titled​​‘​call​​for​​a​​digital​
​resource’​​(Phase​​3)​.​​Discussions​​emphasised​​the​​importance​​of​​practical​​formatting​​and​​the​
​potential​ ​mode​ ​of​ ​delivery,​ ​recommending​ ​that​ ​the​ ​book​ ​should​ ​be​ ​an​ ​online​ ​resource​
​displayed​ ​on​ ​the​ ​electronic​ ​whiteboard.​ ​This​ ​supports​ ​the​ ​work​ ​of​ ​Hennessy​​and​​London​
​(2013)​​who​​state​​explore​​how​​technology-based​​innovations​​in​​schools,​​such​​as​​interactive​
​whiteboards,​ ​can​ ​contribute​ ​to​ ​quality​ ​education​ ​for​ ​all.​ ​If​ ​implemented​ ​in​ ​schools,​ ​it​ ​is​
​crucial​ ​to​ ​have​ ​a​ ​professional​ ​with​ ​the​ ​necessary​ ​technology​ ​skills​ ​manage​ ​the​ ​final​
​documents,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​all​ ​documents​ ​and​ ​information​ ​are​ ​accessible​ ​to​ ​everyone.​
​Therefore,​​ensuring​​compatibility​​with​​all​​devices​​will​​be​​an​​ongoing​​consideration​​which​​is​
​crucial for effective implementation.​

​There​ ​was​ ​strong​ ​agreement​ ​amongst​ ​all​​participants​​that​​the​​book​​would​​benefit​​from​​a​
​professional​ ​proofreader​ ​or​ ​editor.​ ​Gia​ ​(Co-CEO​ ​and​ ​Founder)​ ​pointed​ ​out​ ​"there​ ​were​
​instances​​of​​jumping​​around​​with​​verb​​tenses​​and​​incorrect​​use​​of​​capital​​letters,"​​and​​Vera​
​(Headteacher)​ ​agreed,​ ​noting​ ​that​ ​"the​ ​tenses​ ​sometimes​ ​conflict​ ​with​ ​each​ ​other;​ ​a​
​paragraph​ ​may​ ​include​ ​both​ ​present​ ​and​ ​past​ ​tense,​ ​which​ ​can​ ​be​ ​a​ ​bit​ ​confusing".​
​Addressing​ ​these​ ​issues​ ​with​ ​the​ ​help​ ​of​ ​a​ ​professional​ ​proofreader​ ​or​ ​editor​ ​would​
​enhance​ ​the​ ​overall​ ​readability​ ​and​ ​clarity​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​making​ ​it​ ​more​ ​engaging​ ​for​ ​its​
​intended​​audience.​​This​​comment​​was​​supported​​by​​Nick​​(Private​​and​​public​​Antisemitism​
​Educator)​​who​​felt​​the​​"the​​text​​is​​too​​dense​​and​​written​​completely​​without​​flair​​or​​style​​-​
​the​ ​narrative​ ​verges​ ​on​ ​the​​boring”​​reinforced​​the​​importance​​of​​having​​the​​story​​written​
​by​​a​​specific​​children's​​author,​​as​​elaborated​​upon​​by​​Nick​​(Private​​and​​public​​Antisemitism​
​Educator) below:​

       ​It​ ​will​ ​be​ ​a​​useful​​starting​​point​​for​​any​​professional​​writer​​with​​the​​appropriate​
       ​expertise​ ​commissioned​ ​to​ ​write​ ​the​ ​story…​ ​writing​ ​for​ ​children​ ​is​ ​a​ ​specialist​


                                                            ​246​
       ​skill…​​finding​​a​​professional​​children’s​​story​​writer​​who​​can​​work​​to​​your​​learning​
       ​outcomes.​

​Alana​​(Education​​Officer)​​also​​agreed​​that​​a​​professional​​children's​​writer​​would​​benefit​​the​
​initiative:​

       ​It​​needs​​some​​editing​​in​​terms​​of​​grammar​​and​​to​​make​​it​​flow​​better​​(an​​editor​
       ​will​ ​know​ ​how​ ​to​ ​tweak​ ​sentences​ ​to​ ​make​ ​it​ ​sound​ ​like​ ​it's​ ​written​ ​by​ ​a​
       ​professional children’s writer.​

​By​​altering​​the​​presentation​​of​​the​​text​​and​​narrative,​​it​​was​​argued​​that​​the​​story​​will​​flow​
​more​ ​smoothly,​ ​effectively​ ​conveying​ ​the​ ​overall​ ​message​ ​and​ ​objectives​ ​of​ ​the​ ​text.​
​Nevertheless,​​it​​is​​crucial​​that​​the​​story​​is​​amended​​with​​caution​​as​​Rubin​​(2020)​​states​​that​
​Jewish​ ​personal​ ​stories​ ​have​ ​value,​ ​given​ ​that​ ​the​ ​narrative​ ​has​ ​been​ ​developed​​through​
​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​creative​ ​nonfiction​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​the​ ​story​ ​is​ ​grounded​ ​in​ ​the​ ​research​ ​data​
​(Smith​ ​et​ ​al.,​ ​2015).​ ​Creative​ ​non-fiction​ ​was​ ​used​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​that​ ​story​ ​illustrates​
​individuals'​​stories​​and​​is​​reflective​​of​​their​​lived​​experiences​​(Smith​​et​​al.​,​​2015).​​This​​was​
​crucial​​as​​the​​sub-theme​​‘importance​​of​​storytelling’​​(Phase​​1)​​discussed​​the​​importance​​of​
​having​ ​the​ ​narrative​ ​informed​ ​by​ ​the​ ​community;​ ​therefore,​ ​amending​ ​the​ ​story​ ​in​​great​
​depth could possibly reduce its value and effectiveness.​

​Lastly,​ ​concerns​ ​were​ ​raised​ ​about​ ​certain​ ​aspects​ ​of​ ​the​ ​story's​ ​content,​ ​which​ ​were​
​identified​ ​as​ ​potential​ ​issues.​ ​Specifically,​ ​these​ ​concerns​ ​centred​ ​around​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​
​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​within​ ​the​ ​story​ ​and​ ​its​ ​appropriateness​ ​in​ ​the​ ​current​ ​social​ ​climate.​ ​Sarah​
​(Antisemitism Educator) expressed her reservations, stating:​

       ​I​​have​​huge​​concerns​​about​​telling​​children​​who​​have​​no​​knowledge​​of​​the​​term​
       '​Yid'​ ​a​ ​story​ ​such​ ​as​ ​the​ ​one​ ​you​ ​have​ ​written...​ ​I​ ​am​ ​very​ ​concerned​ ​in​ ​the​
       ​current climate.​

​Both​ ​of​ ​the​ ​points​ ​raised​ ​by​ ​Sarah,​ ​regarding​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​word​ ​‘Yid’​ ​and​ ​the​ ​current​
​gio-political​ ​climate,​ ​along​ ​with​ ​similar​ ​feedback,​ ​will​ ​be​ ​explored​ ​in​​greater​​depth​​under​
​the​ ​sub-theme​ ​‘appropriateness​ ​for​​the​​target​​audience.’​​A​​further​​weakness​​and​​area​​for​
​improvement​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​the​ ​story's​​content​​was​​from​​Sarah​​(Antisemitism​​Educator)​



                                                             ​247​
​that​ ​“it​ ​covers​ ​rather​ ​a​ ​lot​ ​of​ ​different​ ​but​ ​important​ ​issues…​ ​I​ ​think​ ​too​ ​many.”​ ​Sarah’s​
​comment​​raises​​a​​valid​​concern​​about​​the​​scope​​of​​the​​story,​​suggesting​​that​​attempting​​to​
​address​ ​multiple​ ​complex​ ​issues​ ​within​ ​a​ ​single​ ​resource​ ​might​ ​dilute​ ​its​ ​focus​ ​on​
​antisemitism.​ ​This​ ​was​ ​echoed​ ​in​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​groups,​ ​where​ ​some​ ​participants​ ​questioned​
​whether​ ​the​ ​book’s​ ​broad​ ​range​ ​of​ ​topics​ ​could​ ​be​ ​effectively​ ​covered.​ ​A​​narrower​​focus​
​might​ ​allow​ ​for​ ​deeper​ ​engagement​ ​with​ ​key​ ​teachings,​ ​namely​ ​antisemitism,​ ​without​
​overwhelming​ ​students​ ​or​ ​teachers.​ ​However,​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​
​offered​​a​​contrasting​​perspective,​​advocating​​for​​broadening​​the​​initiative​​to​​include​​other​
​forms of discrimination. He suggested that:​

       ​Reference/support​​to​​other​​groups​​discriminated​​against​​would​​be​​good.​​I​​know​
       ​this​ ​pack​ ​is​ ​specifically​ ​looking​ ​at​ ​antisemitism;​ ​however,​ ​it​​is​​also​​important​​to​
       ​recognise​ ​discrimination​ ​against​ ​other​ ​communities​ ​as​ ​something​ ​we​ ​can​​think​
       ​about and recognise.​

​This​ ​viewpoint​ ​aligns​ ​with​ ​discussions​ ​in​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​under​ ​the​
​‘broad-to-narrow​​structure’​​sub-theme,​​which​​highlighted​​the​​potential​​benefits​​of​​creating​
​a​ ​more​ ​inclusive​ ​educational​ ​resource.​ ​A​ ​balanced​ ​approach,​ ​which​ ​is​ ​already​ ​being​
​implemented,​ ​involves​ ​maintaining​ ​a​ ​primary​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​while​ ​gradually​
​incorporating​​references​​to​​other​​forms​​of​​discrimination.​​This​​method​​provides​​both​​depth​
​in addressing antisemitism and inclusivity by acknowledging broader issues of prejudice.​

​Summary​


​Through​ ​comprehensive​ ​analysis​ ​under​ ​the​ ​theme​ ​of​ ​‘developing​ ​content​ ​quality,’​ ​the​
​gathered​ ​feedback​ ​offered​ ​valuable​ ​insights​ ​into​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​strengths​ ​and​ ​areas​ ​for​
​improvement.​​Participants​​highlighted​​the​​book's​​comprehensive​​content​​on​​antisemitism,​
​practical​ ​activities​ ​that​ ​encourage​ ​student​ ​engagement,​ ​and​ ​clear​ ​organisation​ ​that​
​facilitates​​teacher​​implementation.​​The​​inclusion​​of​​relatable​​themes,​​such​​as​​the​​transition​
​from​ ​primary​ ​to​ ​secondary​ ​school,​ ​was​ ​also​ ​recognised​ ​as​​a​​significant​​strength,​​allowing​
​students​​to​​connect​​with​​the​​material​​personally.​​Additionally,​​the​​integration​​of​​discussion​
​points​ ​throughout​ ​the​ ​chapters​ ​was​ ​praised​ ​for​ ​encouraging​ ​reflective​ ​thinking​ ​and​
​meaningful conversations about discrimination.​


                                                              ​248​
​However,​​critical​​areas​​for​​improvement​​were​​identified.​​Formatting​​issues​​were​​frequently​
​mentioned,​ ​with​ ​participants​ ​noting​ ​that​ ​the​ ​material​​may​​not​​display​​consistently​​across​
​various​​devices.​​There​​was​​a​​strong​​consensus​​on​​the​​need​​for​​professional​​proofreading​​to​
​enhance​​clarity​​and​​readability.​​Some​​expressed​​concerns​​about​​the​​scope​​of​​the​​content,​
​suggesting​ ​that​ ​addressing​ ​multiple​ ​complex​ ​issues​ ​within​ ​a​ ​single​ ​resource​ ​might​ ​dilute​
​the​​focus​​on​​antisemitism.​​Addressing​​these​​issues​​will​​ultimately​​strengthen​​its​​impact​​as​
​an educational resource aimed at reducing antisemitism.​

​Theme 2 - Educational value​


​The​ ​purpose​ ​of​ ​creating​ ​this​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​was​ ​to​ ​enhance​ ​individuals'​
​understanding​​of​​antisemitism,​​particularly​​through​​the​​vehicle​​of​​sport.​​Feedback​​from​​the​
​initial​ ​expert​​interviews​​(Phase​​1)​​reinforced​​that​​formal​​and​​supported​​education​​is​​often​
​the​​most​​effective​​way​​to​​address​​societal​​issues,​​such​​as​​antisemitism,​​forming​​the​​Phase​​1​
​sub-theme​ ​‘educational​ ​impact’​.​ ​Literature​ ​supports​ ​this,​ ​emphasising​ ​that​ ​formal​
​education​​is​​a​​crucial​​factor​​in​​challenging​​and​​changing​​discriminatory​​viewpoints​​(Crozier,​
​2012; Hughes, 2016).​

​Given​ ​this,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​how​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​ ​resource​ ​pack​ ​could​ ​deliver​
​‘educational​ ​value’​,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​it​ ​increases​ ​children's​ ​awareness​ ​of​ ​Judaism​ ​and​ ​the​
​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​This​ ​theme​ ​of​ ​‘educational​ ​value’​ ​includes​ ​3​ ​sub-themes​ ​entitled​
​‘​relevance​ ​to​ ​the​ ​curriculum’,​ ​‘learning​ ​outcomes​ ​clarity’,​ ​and​ ​‘appropriateness​ ​for​ ​target​
​audience’.​

​Relevance to curriculum​


​Literature​ ​from​ ​MacIntosh​ ​and​ ​Martin​ ​(2018)​ ​and​ ​Solomos​ ​(2020)​ ​reinforces​ ​that​
​educational​ ​initiatives​ ​can​ ​significantly​ ​impact​ ​challenging​ ​discriminatory​ ​attitudes​ ​and​
​beliefs.​ ​Supporting​ ​this​ ​literature​ ​were​ ​experts​ ​who​ ​participated​ ​in​ ​the​ ​first​ ​and​ ​second​
​rounds​​of​​data​​collection,​​discussing​​the​​value​​of​​embedding​​anti-discrimination​​initiatives,​
​specifically​ ​within​ ​the​ ​Personal,​ ​Social,​ ​Health​ ​and​ ​Economic​ ​(PSHE)​​element​​of​​England’s​
​National​ ​Curriculum.​ ​Additionally,​ ​Waugh​ ​and​ ​Waugh​ ​(2022)​ ​highlight​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​
​incorporating​ ​children's​ ​literature​ ​into​ ​the​ ​PSHE​ ​curriculum​ ​to​ ​enhance​ ​discussion.​ ​PSHE​


                                                          ​249​
​provides​​a​​platform​​for​​addressing​​sensitive​​topics​​such​​as​​antisemitism​​and​​discrimination,​
​encouraging​ ​students​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​empathy,​ ​understanding,​​and​​respect​​for​​others​​(Waugh​
​and Waugh, 2022; Willis, Clague and Coldwell, 2013).​


​This​ ​consensus​ ​was​ ​reinforced​ ​during​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​4​ ​book​ ​review,​ ​whereby​ ​participant​
​feedback​​indicated​​that​​the​​educational​​resource​​could​​fit​​well​​into​​the​​PSHE​​curriculum,​​as​
​intended. Vera (Headteacher) emphasised:​

       ​PSHE​ ​is​ ​an​ ​important​ ​and​ ​valued​​subject​​in​​primary​​schools​​and​​one​​that​​I​​very​
       ​much​ ​enjoy​ ​teaching.​ ​The​ ​educational​ ​resource​ ​you​ ​have​ ​produced​ ​has​ ​many​
       ​positive attributes.​

​She​​further​​noted​​that​​it​​"has​​clear​​links​​to​​the​​PSHE​​National​​Curriculum,​​which​​is​​great​​for​
​planning."​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​ ​agreed,​ ​highlighting​ ​that​ ​the​ ​resource​
​"clearly​ ​sets​ ​out​ ​the​ ​core​ ​PSHE​ ​themes,"​ ​reinforcing​ ​a​ ​key​ ​strength​ ​of​​the​​resource​​pack.​
​This​ ​feedback​ ​reinforces​ ​the​ ​relevance​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​ ​its​ ​resources​ ​to​ ​the​ ​curriculum,​
​reaffirming​​their​​suitability​​for​​the​​target​​students,​​in​​addition​​to​​reinforcing​​that​​there​​is​​a​
​lack of resources in this area (Pearce, Foster and Pettigrew, 2020).​

​However,​ ​participants​ ​who​ ​took​ ​part​ ​in​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​also​ ​highlighted​ ​some​ ​potential​
​challenges​ ​with​ ​embedding​ ​this​ ​initiative​ ​into​ ​the​ ​curriculum,​ ​as​ ​noted​ ​within​ ​the​
​sub-theme​​of​​‘flexibility​​in​​implementation’​​outlined​​in​​Phase​​3​​of​​the​​data​​collection.​​Leah​
​pointed​ ​out​ ​that​ ​the​ ​curriculum,​ ​especially​ ​PSHE,​ ​is​ ​quite​ ​densely​ ​packed.​ ​This​ ​comment​
​was echoed during the book review, where Vera (Headteacher) noted:​

       ​Lots​ ​of​ ​primary​ ​schools​ ​will​ ​have​ ​already​ ​bought​ ​into​ ​a​ ​PSHE​ ​scheme​ ​that​ ​will​
       ​take​ ​them​ ​from​ ​Early​​Years​​through​​to​​the​​end​​of​​KS2,​​so​​this​​would​​have​​to​​be​
       ​slotted into an already tight curriculum.​

​This​ ​feedback​ ​reinforces​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​challenge,​ ​integrating​ ​the​ ​book​ ​into​ ​schools​ ​would​
​require​ ​careful​ ​planning​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​it​ ​fits​ ​within​ ​the​ ​current​ ​curriculum​ ​structure.​ ​The​
​densely​ ​packed​ ​nature​ ​of​ ​the​ ​PSHE​ ​curriculum​ ​means​ ​that​ ​schools​ ​often​ ​have​ ​limited​
​flexibility​ ​to​ ​introduce​ ​new​​materials​​(Hilton,​​2009;​​Waugh​​and​​Waugh,​​2022).​​The​​nature​
​of​​the​​curriculum​​poses​​a​​potential​​barrier;​​therefore,​​there​​is​​a​​broader​​issue​​in​​supporting​


                                                           ​250​
​any​​cultural​​change​​initiatives​​through​​such​​resources​​in​​the​​future.​​Given​​that​​this​​concern​
​had​ ​been​ ​raised​ ​previously​ ​during​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​groups,​ ​participants​ ​in​ ​this​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​
​collection​​were​​asked​​for​​recommendations​​on​​how​​to​​distribute​​the​​resource​​into​​schools.​
​Experts​ ​made​ ​some​ ​suggestions​ ​which​ ​have​ ​been​ ​discussed​​in​​a​​later​​sub-theme​​entitled​
​‘​marketing and dissemination’​.​

​Learning outcomes clarity​


​When​ ​developing​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​an​ ​expert​​during​​the​​Phase​​1​​interviews,​​Nate​​mentioned​
​the​​importance​​of​​aligning​​the​​aims​​of​​the​​initiative​​to​​the​​curriculum.​​With​​this​​in​​mind,​​a​
​resource​​pack​​was​​developed​​highlighting​​where​​the​​PSHE​​curriculum​​has​​been​​addressed​
​within​ ​the​ ​book.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​although​ ​it​ ​was​ ​evident​ ​from​ ​the​ ​comments​ ​raised​​in​​the​
​previous​​theme​​that​​participants​​felt​​the​​educational​​resource​​could​​fit​​well​​into​​the​​PSHE​
​curriculum,​ ​there​ ​were​ ​some​ ​concerns​ ​from​ ​participants​ ​that​ ​the​ ​learning​ ​outcomes​
​required greater clarity. Nick (Antisemitism Educator) commented that:​


       ​The​ ​learning​ ​outcomes​ ​are​ ​unclear​ ​for​ ​me,​ ​buried​ ​as​ ​they​ ​were​ ​in​ ​opening​
       ​remarks​ ​in​ ​the​ ​Teacher’s​ ​Resource​​Pack.​​Perhaps​​make​​these​​more​​prominent…​
       ​By​ ​the​ ​end​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​children​ ​will​ ​be​ ​able​ ​to…​ ​Recognise…​ ​Define…​
       ​Discuss…​

​This​​comment​​highlights​​the​​need​​to​​clarify​​the​​educational​​purpose​​and​​learning​​outcomes​
​of​​the​​initiative.​​Learning​​outcomes​​are​​used​​in​​an​​education​​setting​​within​​lessons​​to​​guide​
​students'​ ​understanding​​and​​measure​​their​​progress​​(Adam,​​2006;​​Prøitz,​​2010).​​With​​this​
​in​ ​mind,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​for​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​the​ ​learning​ ​outcomes​ ​are​
​addressed​ ​in​ ​a​ ​clearer​ ​manner.​ ​Nick's​ ​suggestion​ ​to​ ​make​ ​them​ ​more​ ​prominent​ ​by​
​including​ ​terms​ ​such​ ​as​ ​‘recognise’,​​‘define’,​​and​​‘discuss’​​is​​highly​​relevant,​​and​​when​​the​
​book​​is​​taken​​to​​external​​publishers​​following​​the​​PhD,​​this​​amendment​​will​​be​​made.​​This​
​aligns​ ​well​ ​with​ ​Bloom's​ ​taxonomy​ ​(1956)​ ​which​ ​continues​ ​to​ ​be​ ​used​ ​throughout​
​education​ ​as​ ​a​ ​framework​ ​for​ ​categorising​ ​educational​ ​objectives.​ ​However,​ ​the​
​development​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​also​ ​revealed​ ​challenges​ ​in​ ​balancing​ ​the​​clarity​​of​​learning​
​outcomes​​with​​the​​commitment​​to​​the​​authentic​​voices​​central​​to​​frameworks​​like​​CRT​​and​
​HebCrit.​ ​Therefore,​​by​​integrating​​clearer​​objectives​​this​​will​​ensure​​that​​students​​and​​staff​


                                                          ​251​
​are​ ​aware​ ​of​ ​what​ ​they​ ​are​ ​expected​ ​to​ ​learn​ ​and​ ​achieve​ ​by​ ​the​ ​end​ ​of​ ​each​ ​chapter.​
​Furthermore,​​it​​will​​provide​​staff​​with​​a​​structured​​approach​​to​​assess​​student​​progress​​and​
​tailor their teaching methods accordingly (Prøitz, 2010).​

​Sarah​ ​also​ ​raised​ ​concerns​ ​regarding​ ​the​ ​aims​ ​and​ ​objectives​ ​of​ ​the​​initiative,​​specifically​
​questioning​​whether​​the​​book​​would​​successfully​​achieve​​its​​intended​​goals.​​She​​expressed​
​doubt that the book would meet its educational objectives, stating:​

       ​I​ ​am​ ​scared​ ​the​ ​raison​ ​d'être​ ​won't​ ​be​ ​achieved,​​which​​I​​think​​is​​sad​​as​​a​​lot​​of​
       ​thought and planning has gone into the story, the planning, and the resources.​

​However,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​​consider​​her​​additional​​remark:​​"I​​also​​feel​​that​​in​​the​​current​
​climate,​​maybe​​it​​is​​not​​the​​right​​time​​for​​a​​story​​such​​as​​this".​​This​​comment​​suggests​​that​
​she​​felt​​the​​timing​​was​​inappropriate,​​with​​an​​emphasis​​on​​the​​phrase​​"current​​climate."​​It​
​can​ ​be​ ​inferred​ ​that​ ​she​ ​may​ ​be​ ​referring​ ​to​ ​the​ ​ongoing​ ​conflict​ ​between​ ​Israel​ ​and​
​Palestine,​ ​which​ ​has​ ​contributed​ ​to​​a​​rise​​in​​antisemitism​​in​​the​​UK​​(Freedman​​and​​Hirsh,​
​2024;​​Seymour,​​2024).​​As​​mentioned​​in​​the​​methodology​​chapter,​​schools​​that​​had​​initially​
​shown​ ​interest​ ​in​ ​the​ ​project​ ​later​ ​withdrew,​ ​citing​ ​the​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​ ​conflict​ ​as​ ​the​
​reason​ ​for​ ​their​ ​hesitation.​ ​Sarah’s​ ​comment,​ ​therefore,​ ​reinforces​ ​this​ ​concern​ ​that​ ​the​
​initiative may face challenges due to the sensitive political environment.​

​Nevertheless,​​the​​foundational​​principles​​of​​this​​thesis​​remain​​deeply​​committed​​to​​a​​belief​
​that,​​at​​a​​time​​when​​antisemitism​​is​​on​​the​​rise,​​there​​is​​an​​urgent​​need​​for​​more​​education​
​on​​the​​discrimination​​faced​​by​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​rather​​than​​avoiding​​the​​subject.​​This​
​mirrors​​the​​societal​​response​​during​​the​​resurgence​​of​​the​​BLM​​movement​​and​​the​​murder​
​of​​George​​Floyd,​​which​​reignited​​calls​​for​​anti-racist​​education​​in​​schools​​(Asare,​​2022).​​This​
​movement​ ​spurred​ ​an​ ​increased​ ​demand​ ​for​ ​diverse​ ​and​ ​inclusive​ ​teachings,​ ​particularly​
​for​ ​younger​ ​students​ ​(Agarwal​ ​and​ ​Sen,​ ​2021).​ ​In​ ​response,​ ​teachers​ ​and​ ​organisations​
​developed​ ​pedagogical​ ​tools​ ​to​ ​address​ ​racism​ ​within​ ​the​ ​classrooms​ ​(Furrey,​ ​2023).​
​Therefore,​ ​this​ ​supports​ ​the​ ​idea​ ​of​ ​actively​ ​confronting​ ​prejudice​ ​through​ ​education,​
​fostering​​an​​environment​​that​​promotes​​understanding,​​empathy,​​and​​social​​responsibility,​
​particularly​ ​during​ ​times​ ​of​ ​heightened​ ​social​ ​and​ ​cultural​ ​tension,​ ​when​​such​​efforts​​are​
​needed​ ​the​ ​most.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​it​ ​may​ ​also​ ​be​ ​worth​ ​considering​ ​whether,​ ​in​ ​light​ ​of​



                                                             ​252​
​Sarah’s​ ​feedback,​ ​it​ ​would​ ​be​ ​worth​ ​considering​ ​the​ ​timing​ ​of​ ​the​ ​project,​ ​alongside​ ​the​
​importance​​of​​having​​a​​professional​​writer​​and​​editor​​to​​amend​​the​​storyline​​to​​ensure​​that​
​it addresses links between the current climate and antisemitism within the UK.​

​Appropriateness for target audience​


​It​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​consider​ ​the​ ​appropriateness​ ​of​ ​the​ ​story​ ​for​ ​the​ ​intended​ ​audience,​ ​to​
​ensure​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​both​ ​engaging​ ​and​ ​developmentally​ ​suitable,​ ​capturing​ ​their​ ​attention​
​while​ ​also​ ​being​ ​accessible,​ ​relatable,​ ​and​ ​challenging​ ​enough​ ​to​ ​promote​ ​meaningful​
​learning​ ​experiences.​ ​Feedback​ ​from​ ​participants​ ​was​ ​categorised​ ​into​ ​two​ ​areas:​ ​a)​ ​the​
​appropriateness​ ​of​ ​vocabulary,​ ​and​ ​b)​ ​the​ ​suitability​ ​of​ ​the​ ​content.​ ​Although​ ​previous​
​focus​ ​groups​ ​in​ ​Phase​ ​3,​ ​which​ ​included​ ​primary​ ​school​ ​educators,​ ​generally​ ​agreed​​that​
​the book was suitable for 10-11 year olds, Vera (Headteacher) raised a concern:​

       ​It​​certainly​​is​​fine​​for​​all​​of​​KS2,​​but​​I​​think​​there​​could​​be​​more​​variety​​in​​terms​​of​
       ​storytelling​ ​vocabulary​ ​and​ ​techniques.​ ​It​ ​feels​​quite​​young,​​and​​I​​know​​that​​10​
       ​and 11-year-olds could access and enjoy a more sophisticated story.​

​Vera’s​ ​feedback​ ​highlights​​the​​need​​for​​a​​balance​​between​​simplicity​​and​​sophistication​​in​
​the​ ​storytelling​ ​style,​ ​supporting​ ​her​ ​earlier​ ​suggestion​ ​to​ ​enhance​ ​engagement.​ ​By​
​incorporating​ ​a​ ​richer​ ​vocabulary,​ ​the​ ​story​ ​could​ ​potentially​ ​better​ ​captivate​ ​older​
​students,​ ​thus​ ​increasing​ ​both​ ​engagement​ ​and​ ​educational​ ​value.​ ​Alana​ ​(Education​
​Officer)​​echoed​​this​​sentiment​​when​​asked​​if​​the​​language​​in​​the​​educational​​resource​​was​
​appropriate​ ​for​ ​the​ ​target​ ​audience.​ ​Her​ ​response​ ​-​ ​"Yes,​ ​but​ ​it​ ​may​ ​seem​ ​simplistic​ ​to​
​some"​​-​​reinforces​​Vera’s​​point​​that​​the​​story​​may​​not​​be​​challenging​​enough​​for​​all​​readers.​
​This​​resonates​​with​​one​​oft-cited​​challenge​​with​​CNF​​which​​is​​that​​crafting​​high-quality​​CNF​
​can​​be​​challenging​​(Smith​​et​​al.​,​​2015),​​especially​​for​​novice​​writers​​who​​may​​find​​it​​difficult​
​to​​make​​the​​core​​message​​engaging​​(Root,​​2008).​​Additionally,​​it​​is​​essential​​to​​maintain​​a​
​balance​ ​between​ ​keeping​ ​readers​ ​engaged​ ​and​ ​conveying​ ​the​ ​necessary​ ​educational​
​messages.​ ​Both​ ​pieces​ ​of​ ​feedback​ ​suggest​ ​that​ ​while​ ​the​ ​current​ ​version​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​is​
​accessible,​ ​improvements​ ​could​ ​be​ ​made​ ​to​ ​better​ ​target​ ​the​ ​upper​ ​age​ ​range​ ​of​ ​KS2​
​students.​ ​Alternative​ ​narrative​ ​approaches,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​exploring​ ​themes​ ​and​ ​contexts​ ​that​
​resonate​​with​​KS2​​readers'​​interests,​​could​​be​​considered​​for​​future​​works.​​Furthermore,​​as​


                                                             ​253​
​suggested​ ​previously,​ ​this​ ​could​ ​be​ ​achieved​ ​through​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​a​ ​professional​ ​children's​
​writer.​

​Conversely,​ ​other​ ​participants,​ ​including​ ​Gia​ ​(Co-CEO​ ​and​ ​Founder),​ ​Sarah​ ​(Antisemitism​
​Educator),​​and​​Aaron​​(Education​​Project​​Coordinator),​​found​​the​​book​​suitable​​for​​children​
​aged​​10-11​​years.​​Aaron​​appreciated​​that​​it​​was​​"kept​​simple​​and​​has​​definitions​​if​​needed”,​
​while​ ​Sarah​ ​(Antisemitism​ ​Educator)​ ​felt​ ​it​ ​was​ ​appropriate​ ​as​ ​it​ ​was​ ​“short​ ​and​
​manageable”.​ ​This​ ​contrasts​ ​with​ ​Vera's​ ​perspective.​ ​To​ ​some​ ​extent,​ ​simplicity​ ​is​ ​a​
​strength,​ ​as​​it​​ensures​​accessibility​​for​​all​​students,​​regardless​​of​​reading​​ability.​​Simplified​
​language​ ​and​ ​clear​ ​definitions​ ​help​ ​prevent​ ​confusion.​ ​Maintaining​ ​clarity​ ​and​ ​ease​ ​of​
​understanding​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​for​ ​this​ ​initiative,​ ​especially​ ​when​ ​the​ ​goal​ ​is​ ​to​ ​communicate​
​complex​ ​ideas​ ​and​ ​sensitive​ ​topics​ ​in​ ​a​ ​way​ ​that​ ​resonates​ ​with​ ​young​ ​readers​ ​without​
​overwhelming them.​

​When​ ​asked​ ​about​ ​the​ ​appropriateness​ ​of​ ​the​ ​language​ ​used,​ ​Gia​ ​(Co-CEO​​and​​Founder)​
​commented:​

            ​In​​the​​main,​​yes.​​For​​example,​​the​​adjective​​'distasteful'​​may​​not​​be​​understood​
            ​by​​this​​age​​group.​​I​​think​​the​​verb​​'chant'​​needs​​more​​explanation​​about​​how​​it​
            ​can be used in a threatening way, to differentiate it from 'sing’.​

​Gia’s​ ​feedback​ ​indicates​ ​that​ ​while​ ​the​ ​overall​ ​language​ ​is​ ​suitable,​ ​certain​ ​words​ ​and​
​concepts​​may​​need​​additional​​clarification​​to​​ensure​​student​​comprehension.​​The​​resource​
​was​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​deepen​ ​students'​ ​learning​ ​and​ ​comprehension​ ​on​ ​a​ ​topic​ ​that​ ​lacks​
​sufficient​ ​educational​ ​focus.​ ​Therefore,​ ​Gia’s​ ​comment​ ​reinforces​ ​the​​goal​​of​​encouraging​
​students​​to​​engage​​with​​complex​​ideas​​while​​providing​​the​​necessary​​support​​to​​help​​them​
​grasp​​key​​terms.​​This​​can​​be​​addressed​​by​​expanding​​the​​glossary​​within​​the​​resource​​pack​
​to​ ​explain​ ​terms,​ ​especially​ ​within​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​sport.​ ​Together,​ ​the​ ​comments​ ​reveal​
​differing​ ​opinions​ ​on​ ​the​ ​language​ ​used​ ​in​ ​the​ ​educational​ ​resource.​​While​​the​​book​​was​
​generally​ ​considered​ ​appropriate​​for​​its​​target​​audience,​​incorporating​​more​​sophisticated​
​storytelling​​elements​​and​​offering​​further​​explanations​​for​​complex​​terms​​could​​enhance​​its​
​effectiveness.​




                                                           ​254​
​In​ ​addition​​to​​discussing​​vocabulary,​​the​​conversation​​around​​the​​story’s​​suitability​​for​​the​
​target​ ​audience​ ​also​ ​addressed​ ​the​ ​relevance​ ​of​ ​its​ ​content.​ ​Nick​ ​(Private​ ​and​ ​public​
​Antisemitism​ ​Educator)​​raised​​concerns​​about​​the​​subject​​matter,​​remarking​​"I​​do​​wonder​
​though​ ​how​ ​much​ ​the​ ​casual​ ​use​ ​of​ ​antisemitic​ ​language​ ​is​ ​prevalent."​ ​His​ ​comment​
​suggests​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​careful​ ​refining​ ​of​ ​the​ ​storyline,​ ​suggesting​ ​that​ ​the​ ​story's​ ​focus​
​could​​be​​reconsidered.​​However,​​during​​Phase​​3​​focus​​groups​​with​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​
​community,​ ​a​ ​key​ ​question​ ​posed​ ​was​ ​whether​ ​the​ ​story​ ​accurately​ ​reflected​ ​their​ ​life​
​experiences.​​None​​of​​the​​participants​​echoed​​Nick’s​​concerns​​or​​found​​the​​story​​unrealistic.​
​As​​detailed​​in​​the​​Phase​​3,​​results​​and​​discussion​​chapter​​(see​​p.​​171),​​under​​the​​sub-theme​
​titled​​‘reflective​​of​​lived​​experiences’,​​participants​​generally​​felt​​the​​story​​was​​representative​
​of​​real-life​​situations.​​Leah’s​​comment,​​for​​instance,​​highlights​​this,​​"I​​don't​​think​​it​​will​​end​
​here​ ​for​ ​Noah,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​quite​ ​true​ ​to​ ​life,​ ​unfortunately,"​ ​suggesting​ ​that​ ​casual​ ​antisemitic​
​language may indeed be as prevalent as portrayed in the story.​

​Additionally,​​Sarah​​(Antisemitism​​Educator)​​expressed​​concerns​​about​​introducing​​the​​term​
​‘Yid’ to children, stating:​

       ​I​​have​​huge​​concerns​​about​​telling​​children​​who​​have​​no​​knowledge​​of​​the​​term​
       '​Yid'​ ​a​ ​story​ ​such​ ​as​ ​the​ ​one​ ​you​ ​have​ ​written...​ ​I​ ​am​ ​very​ ​concerned​ ​in​ ​the​
       ​current​​climate,​​in​​particular,​​that​​children​​will​​pick​​on​​others,​​particularly​​Jewish​
       ​pupils, and it will have the opposite effect than intended.​

​Sarah’s​ ​concern​ ​reflects​ ​potential​ ​misinterpretation​ ​of​ ​sensitive​ ​content,​ ​particularly​ ​the​
​term​ ​‘Yid.’​ ​Understandably,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​the​ ​message​ ​does​ ​not​ ​become​
​misinterpreted​ ​and​ ​result​ ​in​ ​unintended​ ​negative​ ​outcomes.​ ​Navigating​ ​these​ ​differing​
​viewpoints​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​conveying​ ​the​​educational​​message​​without​​causing​​harm.​​On​​the​
​other​ ​hand,​​avoiding​​the​​term​​entirely​​may​​leave​​children​​without​​an​​understanding​​of​​its​
​meaning​ ​and​ ​implications,​ ​potentially​​leading​​to​​confusion​​or​​misuse​​later​​on,​​particularly​
​as​ ​the​ ​term’s​ ​prevalence​ ​in​ ​contexts​ ​like​ ​professional​ ​football​ ​means​ ​they​ ​are​ ​likely​ ​to​
​encounter​ ​it​ ​elsewhere.​​This​​presents​​a​​challenge​​for​​the​​researcher,​​who​​must​​weigh​​the​
​risk​​of​​children​​misusing​​the​​term​​against​​the​​potential​​for​​future​​misunderstandings​​if​​it​​is​
​not addressed.​




                                                             ​255​
​This​​concern​​was​​echoed​​by​​Simon,​​a​​member​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​who​​participated​
​in​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​and​ ​expressed​ ​similar​ ​reservations​ ​about​ ​teaching​ ​the​ ​term​
​‘Yid’,​​as​​noted​​in​​the​​Phase​​3​​sub-theme​​‘​storyline​​triggers.’​​With​​two​​individuals​​raising​​this​
​issue,​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​level​ ​of​ ​uncertainty​ ​surrounding​ ​the​ ​term's​ ​inclusion.​ ​Although​ ​these​
​concerns​​represent​​the​​minority,​​only​​two​​participants​​across​​two​​phases​​of​​data​​collection,​
​it​​is​​important​​not​​to​​dismiss​​them.​​Sarah’s​​comment​​also​​alludes​​to​​the​​current​​geopolitical​
​climate,​​which​​has​​heightened​​antisemitism​​in​​the​​UK.​​She​​mentioned​​this​​in​​the​​previous​
​sub-theme,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Israel​ ​and​ ​Palestine​ ​conflict​ ​has​ ​continued​ ​to​ ​raise​
​challenges​ ​for​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​alongside​ ​this​ ​project.​ ​Therefore,​ ​the​ ​future​ ​of​​the​
​initiative​ ​is​ ​unknown​ ​and​ ​may​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​adapted​ ​to​ ​address​ ​these​ ​challenges​ ​going​
​forward,​​with​​consideration​​regarding​​the​​ethics​​of​​introducing​​a​​sensitive​​topic​​to​​children​
​without​​carefully​​managing​​the​​potential​​for​​unintended​​negative​​consequences.​​This​​again​
​reinforces​​the​​importance​​of​​careful​​content​​editing​​to​​ensure​​that​​the​​material​​is​​sensitive​
​to both the educational goals and the current political climate.​

​Summary​

​To​ ​conclude,​ ​this​ ​theme​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​educational​ ​value​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​in​ ​addressing​
​antisemitism​ ​through​ ​engaging​ ​and​ ​relevant​ ​content.​ ​Key​ ​literature​ ​emphasises​ ​the​
​significance​​of​​using​​education​​to​​challenge​​discriminatory​​attitudes​​(Crozier,​​2012;​​Hughes,​
​2016),​​reinforcing​​its​​role​​in​​reducing​​antisemitism.​​This​​theme​​examines​​the​​importance​​of​
​aligning​ ​with​ ​the​ ​PSHE​ ​curriculum.​ ​Despite​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​posed​ ​by​ ​the​ ​already​ ​packed​
​curriculum​ ​(Hilton,​ ​2009),​ ​participant​ ​feedback​ ​suggested​ ​that​ ​the​ ​educational​ ​resource​
​could​​be​​effectively​​integrated​​into​​PSHE.​​Nevertheless,​​participants​​highlighted​​the​​need​​to​
​provide​​greater​​clarity​​on​​what​​the​​learning​​outcomes​​are​​to​​guide​​both​​staff​​and​​students​
​(Adam, 2006; Prøitz, 2010).​

​The​ ​final​ ​sub-theme​ ​examined​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​appropriateness​ ​for​ ​the​ ​chosen​ ​target​
​audience.​ ​Feedback​ ​suggested​ ​that,​ ​with​​certain​​adjustments,​​such​​as​​incorporating​​more​
​advanced​ ​language,​ ​the​ ​initiative​​aligns​​well​​with​​the​​intended​​age​​group.​​However,​​there​
​were​ ​concerns​ ​about​​the​​story's​​suitability,​​particularly​​regarding​​the​​use​​of​​the​​term​​'Yid'​
​and​ ​whether​ ​teaching​ ​this​ ​content​ ​is​ ​appropriate​ ​in​ ​today’s​ ​socio-political​ ​climate.​ ​With​
​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​concerns​ ​highlighted​ ​within​ ​this​ ​theme,​ ​it​ ​does​ ​leave​ ​some​ ​level​ ​of​


                                                          ​256​
​apprehensiveness​​regarding​​if​​this​​initiative​​could​​address​​antisemitism​​through​​the​​use​​of​
​sport​ ​or​ ​merely​ ​raises​ ​awareness​ ​without​ ​producing​ ​meaningful​ ​change.​ ​Additionally,​
​although​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​accepts​ ​these​ ​comments​ ​and​ ​recognises​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​around​
​discussing​ ​the​ ​term,​ ​this​ ​book​ ​has​ ​been​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​address​ ​the​ ​use​​of​​explicit​​language​
​and​ ​the​ ​need​ ​to​ ​call​ ​it​ ​out​ ​through​ ​the​ ​teachings​ ​of​ ​the​ ​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​model​
​(Latané​​and​​Darley,​​1970).​​Nevertheless,​​this​​comment​​may​​provide​​further​​reconsideration​
​regarding​​the​​age​​appropriateness​​of​​this​​initiative​​and​​whether​​it​​should​​be​​tailored​​to​​the​
​older age group if there are concerns about its impact upon young children.​



​Theme 3 - Usability for educators​


​The​ ​intention​ ​behind​ ​conducting​ ​the​ ​book​ ​review​ ​was​ ​to​ ​gain​​a​​deeper​​understanding​​of​
​experts'​​opinions​​on​​the​​proposed​​children's​​book​​and​​accompanying​​resource​​pack,​​which​
​are​ ​designed​ ​for​ ​students​ ​to​ ​read​ ​and​ ​for​ ​teachers​ ​to​ ​facilitate.​ ​With​ ​this​​in​​mind,​​it​​was​
​imperative​ ​to​ ​gather​ ​insights​ ​regarding​ ​the​ ​design​ ​and​​usability​​of​​these​​products,​​as​​this​
​would​ ​provide​ ​valuable​ ​feedback​ ​for​ ​refining​ ​and​ ​improving​ ​them.​ ​Specifically,​
​understanding​ ​the​ ​experts'​ ​perspectives​ ​on​ ​these​ ​aspects​ ​would​ ​help​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​the​
​materials​ ​are​ ​not​ ​only​ ​engaging​ ​and​ ​educational​ ​for​ ​students​ ​but​ ​also​ ​practical​ ​and​
​user-friendly​​for​​teachers.​​Therefore,​​this​​theme​​‘usability​​for​​educators’​​explores​​these​​two​
​notions through two sub-themes entitled ‘​ease of use’​​and​​‘design effectiveness’.​


​Ease of use​


​Since​ ​the​ ​goal​ ​is​ ​to​ ​implement​ ​this​ ​initiative​ ​in​ ​schools,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​evaluate​ ​the​
​user-friendliness​ ​of​ ​both​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​pack.​ ​This​ ​would​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​the​
​content​​could​​be​​delivered​​smoothly​​and​​was​​accessible​​to​​everyone.​​When​​asked​​whether​
​the​​children's​​book​​and​​resource​​pack​​were​​user-friendly,​​participants​​responded​​positively.​
​Gia​ ​(Co-CEO​ ​and​ ​Founder)​ ​remarked​ ​"I​ ​think​ ​it​ ​is​ ​extremely​ ​user-friendly​ ​for​ ​staff​ ​and​
​students".​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​ ​agreed,​ ​stating:​ ​"Yes,​ ​kept​ ​nice​ ​and​
​simple.​ ​If​ ​it​ ​is​ ​just​ ​being​ ​read,​ ​then​ ​it​ ​is​ ​simple​ ​for​ ​a​ ​teacher​ ​to​ ​deliver."​​Although​​Aaron​
​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​ ​felt​ ​that​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​was​ ​simple​​to​​use,​​he​​also​​raised​​a​



                                                                ​257​
​point​​that​​while​​the​​material​​is​​straightforward​​for​​reading,​​it​​might​​become​​challenging​​if​
​teachers​ ​are​ ​expected​ ​to​ ​go​ ​beyond​ ​simply​ ​reading​ ​it.​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​if​ ​teachers​ ​need​ ​to​
​facilitate​ ​interactive​ ​activities​ ​or​ ​lead​ ​complex​ ​discussions,​ ​the​ ​simplicity​ ​of​ ​the​ ​resource​
​might not be sufficient.​

​Therefore,​ ​participants​ ​offered​ ​suggestions​ ​to​ ​enhance​ ​the​ ​usability​ ​and​ ​effectiveness​ ​of​
​the​ ​resources.​ ​Vera,​ ​for​ ​example,​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​incorporating​ ​more​ ​interactive​ ​tasks​ ​and​
​activities would make the sessions more dynamic and impactful:​

       ​The​ ​PSHE​ ​resources​ ​that​ ​work​ ​best​ ​for​ ​teachers​ ​are​ ​ones​ ​that​ ​have​ ​a​ ​different​
       ​activity​ ​to​ ​accompany​ ​each​ ​lesson.​ ​All​ ​the​ ​lessons​ ​here​​are​​discussion-based.​​It​
       ​would​ ​be​ ​valuable​ ​to​ ​have​ ​ideas​ ​for​ ​follow-on​ ​activities​ ​for​ ​each​ ​chapter,​ ​e.g.,​
       ​making a poster to kick start discussions.​

​This​ ​recommendation​ ​is​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​research​​from​​Davies,​​Newton​​and​​Newton​​(2018),​
​which​ ​emphasises​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​hands-on​ ​and​ ​child-led​ ​activities​ ​in​ ​fostering​
​engagement.​ ​Currently,​ ​the​ ​educational​ ​resource​ ​includes​ ​two​ ​activity​ ​opportunities:​​a)​​a​
​role-play​​exercise,​​and​​b)​​a​​chapter-ending​​task​​that​​allows​​students​​to​​complete​​the​​story.​
​However,​​as​​Vera​​(Headteacher)​​pointed​​out,​​expanding​​the​​range​​of​​activities​​could​​further​
​enhance​ ​student​ ​involvement.​ ​Sarah​ ​(Antisemitism​ ​Educator)​ ​also​ ​suggested​ ​that​
​adjustments could be made to the story to make it:​

       ​...more​​exciting​​and​​engaging…more​​variety​​in​​both​​the​​story​​and​​the​​discussion​
       ​and tasks. They could use roleplay, hot seating, role on the wall, etc.​

​These​ ​suggestions​ ​reinforce​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​diverse​ ​teaching​ ​methods​ ​to​ ​cater​ ​to​
​different​ ​learning​ ​preferences​ ​and​ ​keep​ ​students​ ​engaged​ ​(Miller,​ ​2001).​ ​Vera​
​(Headteacher)​ ​also​ ​suggested​ ​the​ ​addition​ ​of​ ​comprehensive​ ​lesson​ ​plans​ ​with​
​accompanying​ ​resources,​ ​which​ ​could​ ​increase​ ​the​ ​initiative’s​ ​ease​ ​of​ ​use​ ​for​ ​educators.​
​Similarly,​​a​​comment​​from​​Nick,​​suggested​​that​​additional​​resources​​would​​develop​​greater​
​and more meaningful discussions:​

       ​...any​ ​resources​ ​that​ ​support​ ​teachers​ ​in​ ​the​ ​thorny​ ​task​ ​of​ ​having​ ​meaningful​
       ​discussions with young people on difficult topics is very much to be welcomed.​



                                                            ​258​
​The​​feedback​​from​​these​​participants​​suggests​​that​​while​​the​​book​​is​​easy​​to​​use​​for​​basic​
​reading,​ ​additional​ ​support​ ​or​ ​guidance​ ​might​ ​be​ ​necessary​ ​for​ ​more​ ​active​ ​teaching​
​methods.​ ​Incorporating​ ​these​ ​techniques,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​role​ ​playing,​ ​would​ ​not​ ​only​ ​make​ ​the​
​educational​ ​resource​ ​more​ ​interactive​ ​but​ ​also​ ​more​ ​effective​ ​in​ ​conveying​ ​its​ ​message​
​(Piscitelli,​ ​2020).​ ​The​ ​resource​ ​was​ ​designed​ ​to​ ​accommodate​ ​students​ ​with​ ​diverse​
​learning​ ​needs​ ​from​ ​the​ ​outset,​ ​ensuring​ ​it​ ​is​ ​accessible​ ​to​ ​all.​ ​Additional​ ​tasks​ ​and​
​challenges​​could​​be​​incorporated​​to​​stretch​​students​​with​​higher​​abilities,​​fostering​​further​
​engagement​ ​and​ ​deeper​ ​learning.​ ​Although​ ​time​ ​and​ ​resource​ ​constraints​ ​have​ ​limited​
​these​​possibilities,​​such​​additions​​could​​be​​implemented​​with​​the​​assistance​​of​​educational​
​consultants or stakeholders in future iterations of the program.​

​As​​a​​result​​of​​the​​Phase​​3​​focus​​groups,​​the​​subtheme​​‘pedagogical​​additions’​​emphasised​
​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​supplementary​ ​resources​ ​to​ ​assist​ ​staff​ ​in​ ​effectively​
​implementing​ ​the​ ​initiative.​ ​Vera​ ​(Headteacher)​ ​commented​ ​on​ ​these​ ​resources,​ ​with​
​specific​​reference​​to​​the​​additional​​vocabulary​​and​​glossary,​​stating​​that​​"the​​accompanying​
​vocabulary/glossary​​is​​well​​thought​​out,​​making​​it​​easy​​to​​use".​​Similarly,​​when​​asked​​about​
​the​​organisation​​of​​the​​resource​​pack,​​Aaron​​(Education​​Project​​Coordinator)​​felt​​that​​it​​was​
​organised​ ​"very​ ​well,​ ​clear,​ ​concise"​ ​and​ ​Nick​ ​(Antisemitism​ ​Educator)​ ​stated​ ​that​ ​“the​
​resource​​for​​teachers​​is​​a​​comprehensive​​glossary​​and​​useful​​in​​and​​of​​itself”.​​Ensuring​​that​
​the​ ​additional​ ​resource​ ​pack​ ​is​ ​comprehensible​ ​and​ ​succinct​ ​is​ ​critical​ ​for​ ​the​
​implementation​ ​of​ ​this​ ​resource,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​ensures​ ​that​ ​it​ ​will​ ​be​ ​delivered​ ​in​ ​line​ ​with​ ​the​
​researcher's intentions.​

​Teacher confidence and training​


​Building​​on​​the​​discussion​​of​​usability​​for​​educators,​​Gia​​(Co-CEO​​and​​Founder)​​noted​​"I​​am​
​sure​​most​​teachers​​would​​find​​it​​a​​usable​​resource​​as​​it​​introduces​​a​​difficult​​and​​sensitive​
​topic​​through​​the​​prism​​of​​loving​​sport."​​While​​she​​praised​​the​​use​​of​​sport​​as​​an​​effective​
​lens​​to​​facilitate​​discussions​​on​​sensitive​​issues,​​her​​remark​​that​​most​​teachers​​would​​find​​it​
​usable​ ​implies​ ​that​ ​some​ ​educators​ ​may​ ​still​​struggle​​with​​the​​resource.​​As​​highlighted​​in​
​the​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​sub-theme,​ ​‘challenges’,​ ​there​ ​may​ ​be​ ​specific​ ​obstacles​ ​to​ ​implementation,​
​particularly​​due​​to​​a​​potential​​lack​​of​​experience​​among​​teachers.​​This​​concern​​is​​especially​
​pertinent​​for​​non-Jewish​​staff​​members,​​who​​may​​feel​​uncomfortable​​or​​underprepared​​to​


                                                             ​259​
​teach​ ​such​ ​topics​ ​(see​ ​p.​ ​222).​ ​This​ ​challenge​ ​is​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​literature,​ ​as​ ​Priest​ ​et​ ​al.​
​(2016)​ ​explain​ ​that​ ​teachers'​ ​confidence​ ​in​ ​addressing​ ​sensitive​ ​topics,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​race​ ​and​
​culture,​ ​directly​ ​impacts​ ​children's​ ​engagement​ ​in​ ​these​ ​conversations.​ ​Therefore,​ ​Gia's​
​insights,​ ​along​ ​with​ ​the​ ​data​​from​​Phase​​3,​​emphasise​​the​​need​​to​​explore​​strategies​​that​
​make the resource more accessible and user-friendly for all educators.​

​To​ ​address​ ​these​ ​challenges,​ ​providing​ ​additional​ ​training​ ​or​​creating​​adaptable​​materials​
​that​ ​can​ ​be​ ​easily​ ​modified​ ​to​ ​suit​ ​different​ ​teaching​ ​styles​ ​could​ ​be​ ​crucial.​ ​Aaron​
​(Education​​Project​​Coordinator)​​also​​echoed​​this​​sentiment,​​stating​​"I​​do​​think​​it​​would​​be​
​beneficial​​for​​teachers​​to​​have​​some​​education​​on​​the​​topics​​(if​​they​​are​​not​​fully​​aware)​​so​
​that​ ​they​ ​are​ ​best​ ​equipped​ ​to​ ​teach​ ​this​ ​kind​ ​of​ ​thing."​ ​Aaron's​ ​(Education​ ​Project​
​Coordinator)​ ​comment​ ​reinforces​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​enhanced​ ​teacher​ ​education,​ ​which​​could​
​ensure​ ​that​ ​all​ ​teachers,​ ​regardless​ ​of​ ​their​ ​experience​ ​or​ ​comfort​​level,​​feel​​confident​​in​
​using​​the​​resource​​effectively.​​It​​is​​important​​to​​note,​​however,​​that​​literature​​from​​Vaught​
​and​ ​Castagno​ ​(2020)​ ​found​ ​that​ ​after​ ​education​ ​training,​ ​teachers'​ ​awareness​ ​of​ ​issues​
​related​ ​to​ ​race​ ​or​ ​culture​ ​did​ ​not​​lead​​to​​increased​​empathy​​or​​understanding.​​Instead,​​it​
​caused​ ​the​ ​teachers​ ​to​ ​reinterpret​ ​or​ ​reshape​ ​the​ ​meaning​ ​of​ ​the​ ​issues​ ​in​ ​a​ ​way​ ​that​
​reinforced​ ​pre-existing,​ ​culturally​ ​ingrained,​ ​and​ ​racist​ ​ideas.​ ​Therefore,​ ​rather​ ​than​
​breaking​ ​down​ ​harmful​ ​frameworks,​ ​their​ ​awareness​ ​unintentionally​ ​supported​ ​and​
​perpetuated​ ​them.​ ​Although​ ​this​ ​research​ ​was​ ​conducted​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​ ​States,​ ​where​
​attitudes​ ​towards​ ​race​ ​differ,​ ​shaped​ ​by​ ​distinct​ ​historical,​ ​social,​ ​and​ ​political​ ​contexts,​
​both​ ​nations​ ​deal​ ​with​ ​issues​ ​of​ ​racism.​ ​Although​ ​the​ ​way​ ​these​ ​issues​ ​manifest​​and​​are​
​addressed​ ​can​ ​vary​ ​significantly,​ ​this​ ​research​ ​has​ ​shown​ ​that​ ​education​ ​training​​for​​staff​
​must​ ​be​ ​carefully​ ​designed​ ​and​ ​contextualised​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​it​​not​​only​​raises​​awareness​​but​
​also fosters genuine understanding and empathy, alongside challenging existing biases.​

​Alana​​(Education​​Officer)​​felt​​that​​the​​book​​was​​user-friendly​​but​​expressed​​concerns​​about​
​the​​teacher's​​role:​​“I​​think​​it​​should​​be​​used​​with​​teacher​​input​​only…​​we​​hope​​all​​teachers​
​are​​not​​racists​​or​​antisemites,​​but​​unfortunately,​​many​​are”.​​Given​​that​​teachers​​play​​a​​vital​
​role​​in​​antiracist​​education​​(Boyd​​and​​Arnold,​​2000;​​Carr​​and​​Klassen,​​1996;​​Lynagh,​​Gilligan​
​and​ ​Handley,​ ​2010),​ ​it​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​for​ ​staff​ ​to​ ​be​ ​educated​ ​to​ ​critically​ ​engage​ ​with​ ​the​
​material​​while​​also​​feeling​​comfortable​​and​​confident​​in​​delivering​​the​​subject​​content.​​This​
​concern​​was​​previously​​raised​​with​​Matthew,​​during​​the​​sub-theme​​‘​trusted​​leaders’​​in​​the​


                                                              ​260​
​initial​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​interviews,​ ​emphasising​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​having​ ​dependable​ ​individuals​
​lead​​the​​initiative​​and​​facilitate​​open​​conversations.​​Literature​​from​​Siddiqui​​(2024)​​stresses​
​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​teachers​ ​understanding​ ​their​ ​own​ ​prejudices,​ ​biases,​ ​and​ ​stereotypes​
​when​ ​facilitating​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​workshops​ ​or​​projects.​​Siddiqui​​(2024)​​discusses​​how​
​time​ ​and​ ​honesty​ ​are​ ​required​ ​from​ ​teachers​ ​to​ ​address​ ​their​​own​​prejudices,​​which​​can​
​impact​ ​how​ ​they​ ​choose​ ​to​ ​deliver​ ​similar​ ​resources.​ ​Subsequently,​​it​​is​​crucial​​to​​ensure​
​that​ ​the​ ​teachers​​delivering​​the​​content​​are​​trusted​​with​​this​​topic​​and​​feel​​confident​​and​
​well-prepared​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​with​ ​all​ ​aspects​ ​of​ ​the​ ​material.​ ​If​ ​possible,​ ​it​ ​would​ ​include​
​providing​ ​training​ ​and​ ​support​ ​to​ ​help​ ​them​ ​navigate​ ​sensitive​ ​topics,​ ​such​ ​as​
​discrimination​​and​​antisemitism​​and​​foster​​inclusive​​discussions.​​By​​doing​​so,​​the​​resource​
​can be implemented effectively, achieving its intended educational outcomes.​

​Nevertheless,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​been​ ​highlighted​ ​in​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​Kitchen​ ​and​ ​Bellini​ ​(2012)​ ​and​
​Greytak,​ ​Kosciw​ ​and​ ​Boesen​ ​(2013)​ ​in​ ​their​ ​research​ ​on​ ​LGBT+​ ​education​ ​that​ ​many​
​educators​​may​​lack​​the​​necessary​​training​​and​​support​​to​​effectively​​address​​these​​sensitive​
​issues.​ ​More​ ​specifically,​ ​Vernikoff​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(2022)​ ​found​ ​that​ ​while​ ​most​ ​educators​ ​believe​
​antisemitism​​is​​problematic,​​it​​is​​frequently​​overlooked​​due​​to​​ambiguities​​in​​defining​​Jews​
​and​ ​perceptions​ ​of​ ​its​ ​lack​ ​of​ ​urgency.​ ​Therefore,​ ​this​ ​can​ ​hinder​ ​teachers’​ ​ability​ ​to​
​facilitate​ ​meaningful​ ​discussions​ ​and​ ​promote​ ​an​ ​inclusive​ ​classroom​ ​environment.​ ​The​
​earlier​ ​remarks​ ​from​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​ ​and​ ​Gia,​ ​along​ ​with​ ​insights​
​from​ ​focus​ ​group​ ​participants,​ ​suggest​ ​that​ ​staff​ ​may​ ​need​ ​additional​ ​training​ ​and​
​knowledge​ ​to​ ​confidently​ ​address​ ​sensitive​ ​topics,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​antisemitism​ ​(Lynagh,​ ​Gilligan​
​and​​Handley,​​2010).​​However,​​a​​critical​​examination​​of​​this​​perspective​​reveals​​that​​merely​
​increasing​​training​​is​​insufficient,​​especially​​for​​those​​who​​already​​hold​​negative​​viewpoints​
​or​ ​attitudes​ ​toward​ ​these​ ​subjects.​ ​Such​​prejudices​​can​​undermine​​their​​ability​​to​​engage​
​thoughtfully​ ​with​ ​the​​material.​​There​​are​​significant​​concerns​​about​​the​​education​​of​​staff​
​members​ ​who​ ​not​ ​only​ ​lack​ ​a​ ​fundamental​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​but​ ​may​ ​also​
​harbour​​biases​​that​​influence​​their​​teaching​​practices.​​Without​​addressing​​these​​underlying​
​attitudes,​ ​training​ ​may​ ​not​ ​translate​ ​into​ ​effective​ ​practice,​ ​potentially​ ​leading​ ​to​
​misunderstandings or inadequate responses to sensitive subjects in the classroom.​




                                                           ​261​
​Flexibility in implementation​


​As​​discussed​​in​​the​​previous​​sub-theme,​​staff​​may​​possess​​varying​​levels​​of​​understanding,​
​which​ ​can​ ​significantly​ ​influence​ ​their​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​both​ ​teaching​ ​and​ ​implementing​ ​this​
​resource.​ ​This​ ​variation​ ​in​ ​knowledge​ ​and​ ​expertise​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​the​ ​resource​
​accommodates​ ​a​ ​degree​ ​of​ ​flexibility,​ ​allowing​ ​teachers​ ​to​ ​adapt​ ​the​ ​content​ ​to​ ​their​
​individual​ ​teaching​ ​styles​ ​and​​proficiency​​levels.​​In​​their​​research,​​Lebbakhar,​​Hoskins​​and​
​Chappell​ ​(2022)​ ​critiqued​ ​the​ ​PSHE​ ​curriculum​ ​for​ ​its​ ​rigidity,​ ​which​ ​restricted​ ​teachers’​
​ability​ ​to​ ​adapt​ ​the​ ​content​ ​to​ ​suit​ ​diverse​ ​classroom​ ​contexts.​ ​Therefore,​ ​while​
​implementing​ ​this​ ​initiative,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​for​ ​staff​ ​to​ ​closely​ ​adhere​ ​to​ ​the​​resource​​as​​the​
​curriculum​​outlines​​to​​ensure​​consistency.​​However,​​the​​flexibility​​that​​the​​resource​​allows​
​also​ ​presents​ ​potential​ ​challenges​ ​in​ ​maintaining​ ​uniformity​ ​and​ ​effectiveness​ ​across​
​different teaching contexts.​

​One​​implemented​​strategy​​that​​supports​​staff​​in​​navigating​​this​​flexibility​​is​​the​​provision​​of​
​structured​ ​discussion​ ​points,​ ​which​ ​has​ ​been​ ​a​ ​notable​ ​strength​ ​of​ ​this​ ​initiative.​ ​These​
​discussion​ ​points​ ​serve​ ​as​ ​a​ ​guide​ ​to​ ​foster​ ​dialogue,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​key​ ​teachings​ ​are​
​addressed.​​Despite​​this​​structured​​support,​​some​​staff​​raised​​concerns​​about​​the​​selection​
​and​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​points​ ​during​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​(see​ ​p.​ ​195).​ ​They​
​expressed​ ​that​ ​the​ ​flexibility​ ​to​ ​choose​ ​which​ ​points​ ​to​ ​address​ ​may​ ​lead​ ​to​​inconsistent​
​coverage​ ​of​ ​important​ ​topics.​ ​In​ ​the​ ​final​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection,​ ​Alana​ ​(Education​
​Officer),​ ​reflecting​​on​​the​​resource’s​​strengths,​​remarked,​​“for​​teachers​​it​​is​​great​​that​​you​
​include​ ​some​ ​potential​ ​discussion​ ​points.”​ ​While​ ​Alana​ ​(Education​ ​Officer)​ ​praised​ ​the​
​inclusion​ ​of​ ​these​ ​points,​ ​her​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​word​ ​‘potential’​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​staff​ ​might​ ​not​
​engage​ ​with​ ​all​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​prompts,​ ​instead​ ​selectively​ ​focusing​ ​on​ ​those​ ​they​ ​deem​
​most relevant or comfortable discussing.​

​This selectivity was also raised by Aaron (Education Project Coordinator), who observed:​

       ​When​ ​facilitating​ ​it,​ ​some​ ​teachers​ ​will​ ​highlight​ ​different​ ​areas​ ​as​ ​more​
       ​important​ ​than​ ​others.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​trusting​ ​the​ ​teachers​ ​to​ ​take​ ​away​ ​the​ ​key​ ​points,​
       ​which is helped by the discussion points at the end of each chapter.​




                                                              ​262​
​Aaron’s​​(Education​​Project​​Coordinator)​​comment​​reinforces​​the​​value​​of​​discussion​​points​
​in​ ​keeping​ ​teachers​​aligned​​with​​the​​resource’s​​objectives,​​yet​​it​​also​​highlights​​the​​risk​​of​
​inconsistency.​ ​The​​possibility​​that​​teachers​​may​​prioritise​​certain​​aspects​​of​​the​​story​​over​
​others​ ​poses​​a​​challenge,​​especially​​if​​it​​results​​in​​diminished​​emphasis​​on​​sensitive​​topics​
​such​ ​as​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​Judaism.​ ​While​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​trust​ ​teachers'​ ​professional​
​judgement,​​selective​​engagement​​with​​the​​resource​​could​​undermine​​the​​initiative's​​goal​​of​
​fostering comprehensive and inclusive discussions on these critical issues.​

​Summary​


​In​​conclusion,​​the​​expert​​feedback​​on​​the​​children's​​book​​and​​accompanying​​resource​​pack​
​has​ ​provided​ ​valuable​ ​insights​ ​into​ ​the​ ​usability.​​The​​positive​​responses​​regarding​​ease​​of​
​use​ ​and​ ​the​ ​narrative-based​​approach​​highlight​​the​​strengths​​of​​the​​materials​​in​​engaging​
​both​​students​​and​​teachers.​​However,​​the​​feedback​​also​​reinforces​​the​​need​​for​​additional​
​support,​​such​​as​​interactive​​activities​​and​​lesson​​plans​​(Piscitelli,​​2020).​​Furthermore,​​there​
​is​​a​​greater​​need​​for​​education​​amongst​​staff​​members,​​as​​experts​​felt​​that​​some​​members​
​of​ ​staff​​might​​struggle​​with​​teaching​​the​​subject​​(Priest​​et​​al.​,​​2016;​​Vaught​​and​​Castagno,​
​2020).​ ​This​ ​could​ ​also​ ​mean​ ​that​ ​staff​ ​teach​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​inconsistently,​ ​meaning​ ​there​
​might​ ​be​ ​some​ ​flexibility​ ​in​ ​implementation​.​ ​Addressing​​these​​areas​​in​​the​​future​​will​​be​
​crucial​ ​for​ ​enhancing​ ​the​ ​effectiveness​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​it​ ​helps​ ​to​ ​develop​
​meaningful learning and discussions on discrimination and antisemitism, specifically.​


​Theme 4 - Design and visual aesthetics​

​This​​theme​​delves​​into​​critical​​aspects​​that​​were​​previously​​touched​​upon​​in​​the​​sub-theme​
​‘areas​ ​for​ ​improvement,’​ ​regarding​ ​the​ ​design​ ​and​ ​visual​ ​aesthetics,​ ​identifying​ ​key​
​enhancements​​that,​​if​​effectively​​implemented,​​could​​significantly​​elevate​​the​​engagement​
​of​ ​Year​ ​6​ ​students.​ ​However,​ ​these​ ​two​ ​sub-themes​ ​have​ ​significant​ ​importance​ ​as​ ​by​
​focusing​ ​on​ ​the​ ​design​ ​and​ ​visual​ ​elements,​ ​this​ ​section​ ​explores​ ​how​ ​thoughtful​ ​and​
​intentional​​improvements​​can​​make​​a​​considerable​​difference​​in​​how​​students​​interact​​and​
​engage​​with​​the​​material.​​The​​theme​​is​​divided​​into​​two​​sub-themes:​​‘design​​effectiveness’​
​and​ ​‘visual​ ​engagement’,​ ​both​ ​of​ ​which​ ​highlight​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​an​ ​engaging​ ​and​
​well-structured resource in driving educational outcomes.​


                                                             ​263​
​Design effectiveness​


​This​ ​sub-theme,​ ​titled​ ​‘design​ ​effectiveness’,​ ​delves​ ​into​ ​the​ ​feedback​​provided​​about​​the​
​design​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​ ​its​ ​accompanying​ ​resources,​ ​examining​ ​how​ ​these​ ​elements​
​contribute​ ​to​ ​the​ ​initiative’s​ ​educational​ ​objectives.​ ​One​ ​participant,​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​
​Project​ ​Coordinator),​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​key​ ​aspects​ ​of​ ​the​ ​design​ ​that​ ​aid​ ​in​ ​conveying​
​important messages to students:​

       ​I​​think​​the​​format​​and​​additional​​resources​​complement​​the​​intended​​message​​of​
       ​the​ ​text,​ ​providing​ ​young​ ​people​ ​with​ ​information​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​
       ​discrimination​ ​as​ ​a​ ​whole,​ ​utilising​ ​possible​ ​real-life​ ​experiences​ ​that​ ​young​
       ​people​ ​hear​ ​about​ ​but​ ​may​ ​not​ ​fully​ ​understand​ ​on​ ​a​ ​day-to-day​ ​basis.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​a​
       ​well-thought-out​ ​text​ ​and​ ​provides​ ​additional​ ​support​ ​for​ ​teachers​ ​who​ ​will​ ​be​
       ​delivering it.​

​Aaron’s​​(Education​​Project​​Coordinator)​​reflection​​emphasises​​the​​thoughtful​​consideration​
​given​ ​to​ ​the​ ​text,​ ​format,​ ​and​ ​additional​ ​resources.​ ​He​​also​​underlines​​the​​importance​​of​
​incorporating​ ​real-life​ ​experiences​ ​to​ ​help​ ​students​ ​grasp​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​associated​ ​with​
​discrimination.​ ​This​ ​approach​ ​aligns​ ​with​ ​educational​ ​theories​ ​such​ ​as​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​
​2020)​ ​and​ ​CRT​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001),​ ​both​ ​of​ ​which​ ​highlight​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​
​storytelling​ ​in​ ​teaching​ ​about​ ​inequality.​ ​During​ ​the​​Phase​​3​​focus​​groups,​​the​​sub-theme​
​‘reflective​ ​of​ ​lived​ ​experiences’​ ​underscored​ ​the​ ​significance​ ​of​ ​making​ ​the​ ​story​ ​and​
​resources​ ​reflect​ ​the​ ​real-world​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​marginalised​ ​communities,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​
​students could connect with the material on a deeper level.​

​Before​ ​the​ ​initial​ ​data​ ​collection,​ ​a​ ​thorough​ ​review​ ​of​ ​literature​ ​on​ ​anti-discrimination​
​initiatives​ ​was​ ​conducted,​ ​including​ ​Chelsea​ ​FC's​ ​‘Say​ ​No​ ​To​ ​Antisemitism’​ ​campaign​ ​and​
​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​(Kilvington​ ​and​ ​Price,​ ​2017;​ ​Penfold​ ​and​ ​Cleland,​ ​2022).​ ​This​ ​exploration​ ​of​
​current​​programmes​​provided​​a​​foundation​​for​​developing​​an​​initiative​​specifically​​focused​
​on​ ​football​ ​and​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Although​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​was​ ​aware​ ​of​ ​existing​ ​efforts,​ ​the​
​Phase​ ​1​ ​expert​ ​interviews​ ​and​ ​subsequent​ ​data​ ​analysis​ ​revealed​ ​that​ ​a​ ​narrative-based​
​approach​​would​​be​​the​​most​​effective​​method​​for​​this​​initiative,​​reinforcing​​the​​educational​


                                                            ​264​
​potential​​of​​storytelling.​​Much​​like​​the​​work​​being​​done​​by​​Sense​​over​​Sectarianism​​(n.d.),​
​using​​storytelling​​to​​educate​​young​​children​​about​​sectarianism​​is​​an​​effective​​way​​to​​foster​
​understanding, tolerance, and empathy from an early age.​

​As​​the​​initiative​​progressed,​​the​​feedback​​gathered​​during​​Phase​​3​​confirmed​​the​​success​​of​
