​this​ ​narrative-driven​ ​design.​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​ ​observed​ ​that​ ​the​
​discussion​​prompts​​at​​the​​end​​of​​each​​chapter​​"keep​​students​​engaged​​and​​thinking​​about​
​the​ ​overall​ ​intention,"​ ​allowing​ ​for​ ​deeper​ ​reflection​ ​and​ ​interaction.​ ​Vera​ ​(Headteacher)​
​echoed​ ​this​ ​sentiment,​ ​praising​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​storytelling​ ​as​ ​a​ ​powerful​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​introduce​
​sensitive​ ​issues​ ​like​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​a​ ​way​ ​that​ ​is​ ​relatable​ ​to​ ​young​ ​students.​ ​This​​aligns​
​with​ ​literature​ ​by​ ​Kapuzza​ ​(2020),​ ​who​ ​found​ ​that​ ​framing​ ​educational​ ​content​ ​within​ ​a​
​story​ ​enhances​ ​students'​​ability​​to​​connect​​with​​and​​internalise​​the​​material.​​Additionally,​
​Gia​ ​(Co-CEO​ ​and​ ​Founder)​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​clarity​ ​and​ ​structure​ ​provided​ ​by​ ​the​
​chapter-based​ ​format,​ ​which​ ​organises​ ​the​ ​content​ ​into​ ​digestible​ ​and​ ​focused​ ​sections,​
​further contributing to student engagement.​

​Nevertheless,​ ​Nick​ ​(Antisemitism​ ​Educator)​ ​observed​ ​that​ ​the​ ​book​ ​itself​​“feels​​more​​like​
​an​​instruction​​manual​​than​​a​​story”​​but​​suggested​​that​​“with​​the​​appropriate​​refining,​​I​​can​
​see​​this​​as​​a​​welcome​​resource​​for​​teachers​​struggling​​to​​deal​​with​​complicated​​and​​difficult​
​topics”.​ ​While​ ​this​ ​feedback​ ​begins​ ​critically,​ ​pointing​ ​out​ ​that​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​lacks​ ​the​
​engagement​ ​typical​​of​​a​​story,​​it​​is​​noteworthy​​that​​Nick​​still​​recognises​​its​​potential​​value​
​for​​teachers,​​particularly​​those​​grappling​​with​​challenging​​subjects.​​However,​​it​​is​​essential​
​to​ ​critically​ ​assess​ ​this​​piece​​of​​feedback,​​as​​although​​Nick's​​comment​​about​​the​​resource​
​reading​ ​more​ ​like​ ​an​ ​instruction​​manual​​could​​provide​​valuable​​insights​​for​​improving​​the​
​product,​ ​it​ ​represents​ ​the​ ​opinion​ ​of​ ​a​ ​single​ ​participant​ ​across​ ​both​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​focus​
​groups​ ​and​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​4​ ​book​ ​review.​ ​Relying​ ​heavily​ ​on​ ​one​ ​individual's​ ​opinion​ ​may​
​overlook​​broader​​user​​experiences,​​so​​further​​input​​is​​needed​​to​​determine​​whether​​this​​is​
​a recurring issue or an isolated concern.​

​Overall,​ ​the​ ​feedback​ ​emphasised​​the​​effectiveness​​of​​the​​current​​narrative-based​​design,​
​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​the​ ​value​ ​of​ ​the​ ​discussion​ ​points.​ ​Building​ ​on​ ​this​ ​feedback,​ ​this​ ​research​
​highlights​ ​how​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​CNF​ ​has​ ​facilitated​ ​the​ ​sharing​ ​and​ ​development​ ​of​ ​personal​
​narratives​ ​in​ ​creating​ ​this​ ​book,​ ​aligning​ ​with​ ​the​ ​core​ ​principles​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​


                                                             ​265​
​Stefancic,​​2001)​​and​​HebCrit​​(Rubin,​​2020).​​While​​the​​existing​​format​​has​​been​​successful​​in​
​promoting​ ​engagement​ ​and​ ​reflection,​ ​a​ ​minority​ ​expressed​ ​that​ ​the​ ​narrative​ ​felt​ ​more​
​like​​a​​manual​​than​​a​​storybook.​​These​​insights​​will​​be​​considered​​in​​future​​iterations​​of​​the​
​book​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​it​ ​remains​ ​accessible,​ ​engaging,​ ​and​ ​relevant​ ​for​ ​both​ ​students​ ​and​
​educators.​

​Visual engagement​

​Visual​ ​aids​ ​and​ ​imagery​ ​are​ ​critical​ ​in​ ​maintaining​ ​student​ ​engagement,​ ​especially​ ​when​
​presenting​ ​complex​ ​or​ ​sensitive​ ​topics​ ​to​ ​younger​ ​audiences​ ​(Cardillo,​ ​2017).​ ​Effective​
​visual​ ​elements​ ​can​ ​enhance​ ​comprehension,​ ​spark​ ​interest,​ ​and​ ​make​ ​the​ ​learning​
​experience​ ​more​ ​memorable​ ​(Dolati​ ​and​ ​Richards,​ ​2012).​ ​One​ ​strength​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​as​
​noted​ ​by​ ​Gia,​​was​​the​​quality​​of​​the​​illustrations,​​as​​she​​enthusiastically​​commented,​​"the​
​illustrations​ ​are​ ​great."​ ​Her​ ​positive​ ​feedback​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​well-crafted​
​visuals in complementing the narrative.​


​However,​ ​other​ ​participants​ ​pointed​ ​out​ ​room​ ​for​ ​improvement​ ​in​ ​this​ ​area.​ ​Both​ ​Aaron​
​(Education​​Project​​Coordinator)​​and​​Vera​​(Headteacher)​​raised​​concerns​​about​​the​​quantity​
​of​ ​images.​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator)​ ​emphasised​ ​that​ ​incorporating​ ​more​
​visuals​ ​would​ ​"ensure​ ​this​ ​is​ ​accessible​ ​for​ ​all​ ​Year​ ​6​ ​students,"​ ​suggesting​​that​​a​​greater​
​number​ ​of​​illustrations​​could​​cater​​to​​different​​learners'​​needs​​and​​increase​​the​​material's​
​overall​ ​appeal.​ ​Visual​ ​content,​ ​particularly​ ​in​ ​books​ ​designed​ ​for​ ​young​ ​audiences,​ ​can​
​serve​​as​​a​​crucial​​aid​​for​​students​​who​​may​​struggle​​with​​text-heavy​​materials​​(Brill,​​2011).​
​Vera​ ​(Headteacher)​ ​echoed​ ​this​ ​sentiment,​ ​pointing​ ​out​ ​that​ ​in​ ​many​ ​classroom​​settings,​
​stories​ ​like​ ​this​ ​are​ ​typically​ ​delivered​ ​via​ ​PowerPoint​ ​presentations.​ ​She​ ​added,​ ​"More​
​illustrations​ ​would​ ​be​ ​good​ ​too,​​as​​most​​stories​​like​​this​​are​​shared​​through​​a​​PowerPoint​
​and​​teachers/children​​do​​not​​like​​lots​​of​​text​​up​​on​​the​​screen".​​Vera’s​​comment​​highlights​
​the​ ​fact​​that​​many​​educators​​prefer​​visual​​content​​over​​text-heavy​​slides​​to​​keep​​students​
​engaged​ ​and​ ​prevent​ ​cognitive​ ​overload.​ ​More​ ​illustrations​ ​could​ ​help​ ​ensure​ ​that​ ​key​
​concepts​​are​​effectively​​communicated,​​especially​​in​​digital​​presentations​​where​​images​​are​
​often​​more​​impactful​​than​​dense​​blocks​​of​​text.​​Furthermore,​​Nick​​(Antisemitism​​Educator)​
​commented​ ​on​ ​the​ ​professionalism​ ​of​ ​the​ ​images​ ​suggesting​ ​that​ ​“the​ ​illustrations​ ​are​
​inappropriately​ ​young”​ ​highlighting​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​“finding​ ​an​ ​illustrator​ ​or​ ​graphic​


                                                            ​266​
​artist​​who​​can​​produce​​images​​that​​bring​​the​​narrative​​to​​life,”​​while​​acknowledging​​that​​“I​
​realise that all this might have funding implications.”​

​This​ ​comment​ ​from​ ​Nick​ ​discusses​ ​the​ ​financial​ ​challenges​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​faced​ ​and​ ​the​
​impact​​these​​had​​on​​achieving​​the​​project's​​full​​potential.​​During​​the​​Phase​​3​​focus​​groups,​
​educators​​and​​experts​​discussed​​the​​absence​​of​​images​​in​​the​​book,​​emphasising​​the​​need​
​for​ ​greater​ ​imagery​ ​to​ ​complement​ ​the​ ​text​ ​and​ ​further​ ​student​ ​engagement.​
​Consequently,​ ​revisions​ ​to​ ​the​ ​book​ ​included​ ​the​ ​incorporation​ ​of​​images.​​Due​​to​​limited​
​access​​and​​funding​​for​​a​​professional​​illustrator,​​the​​researcher​​utilised​​Artificial​​Intelligence​
​(AI)​​to​​create​​images​​for​​the​​book.​​Nevertheless,​​using​​AI​​presented​​numerous​​challenges.​
​Firstly,​ ​when​ ​using​ ​specific​ ​terms​ ​to​ ​generate​ ​images​ ​such​ ​as​​‘children’​​and​​‘football’,​​the​
​majority​ ​of​ ​generated​ ​images​ ​consisted​ ​of​ ​individuals​ ​who​ ​were​ ​white,​ ​without​ ​visible​
​disabilities​​and​​male​​presenting​​due​​to​​biases​​and​​stereotypes​​ingrained​​in​​the​​AI​​data​​sets.​
​Similarly,​ ​when​ ​typing​ ​in​ ​words​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​Judaism,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​‘synagogue’,​ ​the​
​characters​ ​were​ ​presented​ ​as​ ​Orthodox​ ​Jewish​​individuals.​​As​​mentioned​​in​​the​​literature​
​review​​and​​theory​​of​​HebCrit​​(2020),​​Judaism​​encompasses​​a​​diverse​​range​​of​​appearances,​
​and​​therefore,​​assuming​​that​​all​​Jewish​​people​​look​​like​​Orthodox​​Jews​​is​​a​​stereotype​​that​
​has​​been​​integrated​​into​​the​​AI​​data​​sets.​​Although​​it​​may​​be​​argued​​that,​​a​​key​​challenge​
​with​​AI​​is​​its​​reliance​​on​​well-crafted​​prompts,​​requiring​​users​​to​​develop​​the​​skill​​to​​create​
​these​ ​effectively​ ​for​ ​optimal​ ​outcomes,​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​Kong​ ​(2022)​ ​explores​ ​AI​ ​fairness​
​regarding​​women​​of​​colour,​​questioning​​why​​algorithm​​datasets​​contain​​only​​a​​few​​images​
​of​ ​Black​ ​women​ ​while​ ​reinforcing​ ​that​ ​these​ ​datasets​ ​include​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​number​ ​of​
​images​ ​of​ ​white​ ​men.​ ​Therefore,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​recognise​ ​that​ ​future​ ​education​
​designers​​may​​encounter​​challenges​​when​​using​​AI​​for​​similar​​initiatives,​​particularly​​those​
​aimed​ ​at​ ​promoting​ ​greater​ ​equality,​ ​diversity,​ ​and​ ​inclusion.​ ​The​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​both​
​Naudts​ ​(2024)​ ​and​ ​Kong​ ​(2022)​ ​supports​ ​that​ ​AI​ ​algorithms​ ​often​ ​reinforce​ ​existing​
​structures of oppression and domination.​

​Drawing​ ​on​ ​comments​ ​from​ ​Aaron​ ​(Education​ ​Project​ ​Coordinator),​ ​Vera,​ ​and​ ​Nick,​ ​it​ ​is​
​unsurprising​ ​that​ ​participants​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​more​ ​images​ ​under​ ​the​​'Areas​​for​
​Improvement'​ ​sub-theme​ ​to​ ​boost​ ​children's​ ​engagement.​ ​These​ ​comments​ ​echo​ ​earlier​
​discussions,​ ​emphasising​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​incorporating​ ​images​​throughout​​the​​story​​to​
​maintain​ ​high​ ​levels​ ​of​ ​engagement​ ​among​ ​young​ ​readers.​ ​This​ ​feedback​ ​supports​


                                                           ​267​
​literature​ ​which​ ​reinforces​ ​the​ ​crucial​ ​role​ ​visual​ ​aids​ ​and​ ​imagery​ ​play​ ​in​ ​capturing​ ​and​
​sustaining students' attention (Cardillo, 2017; Dolati and Richards, 2012).​

​Summary​

​Theme​ ​4​ ​focuses​ ​on​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​‘design​ ​and​ ​visual​ ​aesthetics’​ ​in​ ​enhancing​ ​the​
​engagement​ ​of​ ​Year​ ​6​ ​students​ ​with​ ​the​ ​proposed​ ​educational​ ​materials.​ ​The​ ​theme​ ​is​
​divided​ ​into​ ​two​ ​sub-themes:​ ​‘design​ ​effectiveness’​ ​and​ ​‘visual​ ​engagement’.​ ​‘Design​
​effectiveness’​ ​explores​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​ ​thoughtful​ ​design​ ​in​ ​conveying​ ​key​ ​messages​ ​about​
​antisemitism​​and​​discrimination.​​Participants​​praised​​the​​use​​of​​real-life​​experiences​​and​​a​
​narrative-based​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​facilitate​ ​student​ ​understanding​ ​and​ ​reflection.​ ​‘visual​
​engagement’​ ​explores​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​ ​illustrations​ ​in​ ​maintaining​ ​student​ ​interest.​ ​While​
​participants​ ​appreciated​ ​the​ ​quality​ ​of​ ​the​ ​existing​ ​images,​ ​there​ ​was​ ​consensus​ ​on​ ​the​
​need​​for​​more​​visuals​​to​​cater​​to​​different​​learners'​​needs​​and​​enhance​​overall​​accessibility.​
​The​ ​challenges​ ​of​ ​using​ ​AI-generated​ ​images​ ​were​ ​also​ ​discussed,​ ​particularly​ ​regarding​
​biases​ ​in​ ​representation.​ ​It​ ​was​ ​concluded​ ​that​ ​addressing​ ​these​ ​concerns​ ​is​ ​key​ ​to​
​improving​ ​the​ ​book’s​ ​visual​ ​appeal​ ​and​ ​ensuring​ ​it​ ​promotes​ ​diversity​ ​and​ ​inclusion​
​effectively.​


​Theme 5 - Distribution and accessibility​

​This​ ​final​ ​theme​ ​will​ ​explore​ ​strategies​ ​to​​improve​​the​​‘dissemination​​and​​accessibility’​​of​
​the​ ​resource,​ ​particularly​ ​if​​the​​goal​​is​​to​​have​​it​​widely​​implemented​​in​​schools.​​Ensuring​
​that​​the​​initiative​​reaches​​a​​broader​​audience​​is​​crucial​​for​​maximising​​its​​impact,​​especially​
​in​ ​addressing​ ​issues​ ​like​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​discrimination.​ ​After​ ​analysing​ ​the​ ​data,​ ​this​
​theme​ ​contains​ ​only​ ​two​ ​sub-themes,​ ​‘digital​ ​accessibility’​ ​and​ ​‘marketing​ ​for​
​dissemination’.​


​Digital accessibility​

​Closely​​aligned​​with​​the​​previous​​sub-theme​​of​​‘​visual​​engagement’​,​​one​​of​​the​​significant​
​issues​​raised​​was​​the​​need​​for​​reformatting​​the​​material​​to​​make​​it​​more​​accessible​​for​​both​
​students​ ​and​ ​staff.​ ​Reformatting​ ​the​ ​material​ ​would​ ​also​ ​make​ ​it​ ​easier​ ​to​ ​navigate​ ​and​
​understand,​​as​​well​​as​​more​​visually​​appealing.​​Participants​​noted​​that​​formatting​​problems​


                                                            ​268​
​made​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​more​ ​challenging​ ​to​ ​use,​ ​which​ ​could,​ ​in​ ​turn,​ ​complicate​ ​teachers'​
​efforts​​to​​facilitate​​its​​use.​​Three​​participants​​noted​​this,​​although​​they​​acknowledged​​that​
​compatibility​ ​with​ ​their​ ​devices​ ​could​ ​be​ ​a​ ​factor.​ ​Gia​ ​(Co-CEO​ ​and​ ​Founder)​ ​mentioned,​
​"the​ ​material​ ​needs​ ​formatting,​​as​​there​​were​​issues​​on​​my​​computer​​screen,"​​while​​Vera​
​(Headteacher) noted:​


       ​The​ ​layout​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​was​ ​a​ ​bit​ ​askew​ ​in​​a​​couple​​of​​places,​​but​​I​​have​​a​​Mac​
       ​and​ ​it​ ​can​ ​sometimes​​do​​that,​​so​​the​​final​​version​​would​​need​​to​​be​​checked​​to​
       ​ensure it works in all formats.​


​Additionally, Nick (Antisemitism Educator) noted that:​


       ​The​​pagination​​needs​​attention,​​although​​I​​know​​this​​is​​only​​a​​draft.​​Fixes​​like​​not​
       ​having​ ​the​ ​last​​line​​of​​a​​paragraph​​bleed​​onto​​the​​next​​page​​and​​so​​on,​​but​​this​
       ​might be how the document gets mangled in transmission.​


​These​ ​observations​ ​highlight​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​the​ ​formatting​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​
​resource​​is​​accessible​​to​​all.​​Although​​it​​was​​acknowledged​​that​​this​​formatting​​provided​​an​
​issue​ ​for​ ​participants​ ​with​ ​certain​ ​devices,​ ​this​ ​feedback​ ​reinforces​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​
​ensuring​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​is​ ​accessible​ ​to​ ​everyone.​ ​Moving​ ​forward,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​address​
​these​ ​formatting​ ​problems​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​is​ ​user-friendly​ ​for​ ​both​ ​staff​ ​and​
​students.​ ​Ensuring​ ​digital​ ​accessibility,​ ​refining​ ​the​ ​content​ ​with​ ​professional​ ​editing,​
​increasing​ ​imagery,​ ​and​​adapting​​teaching​​methods​​could​​all​​be​​steps​​towards​​creating​​an​
​initiative that can be engaging and accessible for its target audience.​

​Additionally,​ ​Alana​ ​(Education​ ​Officer)​ ​commented​ ​that​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​would​ ​be​ ​more​
​effective​​if​​“it​​could​​be​​printed​​out​​easily​​but​​to​​make​​it​​more​​accessible​​could​​you​​have​​a​
​weblink​ ​to​ ​it​ ​so​ ​pupils​ ​could​ ​download​ ​it​ ​at​ ​a​ ​click?”.​ ​Within​ ​the​ ​second​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​
​collection,​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​explored​ ​the​ ​resource​ ​structure,​ ​with​ ​a​ ​sub-theme​ ​focusing​ ​on​
​digital​​accessibility,​​titled​​‘​call​​for​​a​​digital​​resource’​​(Phase​​3)​.​​Discussions​​emphasised​​the​
​importance​​of​​practical​​formatting​​and​​the​​potential​​mode​​of​​delivery,​​recommending​​that​
​the​ ​book​ ​should​ ​be​ ​an​ ​online​ ​resource​ ​displayed​ ​on​ ​the​ ​electronic​ ​whiteboard.​ ​If​



                                                             ​269​
​implemented​ ​in​ ​schools,​ ​it​ ​is​​crucial​​to​​have​​a​​professional​​with​​the​​necessary​​technology​
​skills​ ​manage​ ​the​ ​final​ ​documents,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​all​ ​documents​ ​and​ ​information​ ​are​
​accessible​​to​​everyone.​​Therefore,​​ensuring​​compatibility​​with​​all​​devices​​will​​be​​an​​ongoing​
​consideration, crucial for effective implementation.​

​Marketing for dissemination​

​This​ ​sub-theme​ ​explores​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​how​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​could​ ​be​ ​disseminated,​
​looking​ ​into​ ​ways​ ​that​ ​certain​ ​platforms​ ​could​ ​leverage​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​to​ ​reach​ ​a​ ​wider​
​audience​ ​and​ ​maximise​ ​its​ ​impact.​ ​As​ ​part​ ​of​ ​the​ ​‘book​ ​review’​ ​participants​​were​​asked​
​what​ ​some​ ​of​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​might​ ​be​ ​when​ ​trying​ ​to​ ​implement​ ​and/or​ ​publish​ ​this​
​resource​ ​and​ ​for​ ​any​ ​advice​ ​on​ ​the​​process.​​With​​this​​in​​mind,​​Gia​​(Co-CEO​​and​​Founder)​
​suggested,​​"consult​​with​​RS​​[Religious​​Studies],​​Citizenship​​teachers​​as​​well​​as​​Diversity​​and​
​Inclusion​ ​advisors​ ​in​ ​some​ ​local​ ​authorities".​ ​As​ ​part​ ​of​ ​the​ ​previous​ ​focus​ ​groups,​
​participants​ ​consisted​ ​of​ ​EDI​ ​advisors,​ ​alongside​ ​teachers,​ ​and​ ​although​ ​this​ ​approach​
​helped​​to​​amend​​the​​current​​book,​​engaging​​with​​a​​broader​​range​​and​​greater​​quantity​​of​
​stakeholders​​would​​be​​beneficial​​as​​they​​could​​also​​provide​​insights​​into​​how​​the​​resource​
​can​​be​​adapted​​to​​meet​​the​​specific​​needs​​of​​different​​schools.​​This​​remark​​echoes​​earlier​
​observations​ ​from​ ​the​ ​first​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​in​ ​Phase​ ​1,​ ​specifically​ ​under​ ​the​
​sub-theme​ ​‘sport​ ​and​ ​partnership.’​ ​It​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​significance​ ​of​ ​collaborating​ ​with​
​other​​organisations​​and​​working​​together​​to​​develop​​a​​successful​​initiative​​(Trenerry​​et​​al.​,​
​2012).​​Although​​the​​goal​​is​​to​​integrate​​the​​work​​into​​the​​PSHE​​curriculum,​​consulting​​with​
​other​ ​stakeholders​ ​could​ ​provide​ ​alternative​ ​placements​ ​for​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​outside​ ​of​ ​the​
​school​ ​environment.​ ​Given​ ​the​ ​challenges,​ ​it​ ​might​ ​be​ ​positioned​​in​​programmes​​such​​as​
​‘Premier​​League​​Reading​​Stars’,​​as​​suggested​​by​​Keagan​​in​​the​​expert​​interviews​​under​​the​
​sub-theme of ‘implementation’ in Phase 1.​

​Additionally,​​Alana's​​(Education​​Officer)​​suggestion​​of​​“getting​​the​​word​​spread​​to​​teachers​
​about​​it.​​Maybe​​try​​the​​Association​​of​​Citizenship​​Teachers,​​and​​via​​PSHE​​teachers​​Facebook​
​groups​ ​etc.”​ ​would​​leverage​​the​​project,​​by​​creating​​a​​network​​of​​advocates​​who​​can​​help​
​disseminate​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​among​ ​educators.​ ​Such​ ​engagement​ ​might​ ​not​ ​only​ ​enhance​
​visibility​ ​but​ ​also​ ​encourage​ ​buy-in​ ​from​ ​teachers​ ​who​ ​can​ ​support​ ​its​ ​implementation​
​within​ ​their​ ​classrooms.​ ​Ultimately,​ ​the​ ​support​ ​of​ ​external​ ​organisations​ ​and​ ​key​


                                                          ​270​
​stakeholders​ ​is​ ​vital​ ​for​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​successful​ ​implementation​ ​(Trenerry​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2012).​
​This​​necessity​​was​​consistently​​echoed​​in​​previous​​rounds​​of​​data​​collection;​​therefore,​​it​​is​
​encouraging​ ​to​ ​note​ ​Nick’s​ ​final​ ​remarks:​ ​"I​ ​would​ ​support​ ​this​ ​initiative's​ ​aims​ ​and​
​intentions,"​ ​along​ ​with​ ​Alana’s​ ​(Education​ ​Officer)​ ​comment,​ ​"this​ ​is​ ​a​ ​great​ ​project​ ​and​
​hopefully​​will​​make​​a​​real​​difference​​when​​it​​is​​up​​and​​running".​​These​​endorsements​​from​
​experts​ ​in​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​serve​ ​to​ ​reinforce​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​credibility​ ​and​ ​the​
​belief that it can affect meaningful change once in place.​

​Summary​

​This​​final​​theme​​explored​​strategies​​for​​improving​​the​​‘distribution​​and​​accessibility’​​of​​the​
​educational​ ​resource​ ​and​ ​was​ ​divided​ ​into​ ​two​ ​sub-themes.​ ​The​ ​first​ ​sub-theme,​ ​‘Digital​
​accessibility’​​focused​​on​​the​​need​​to​​reformat​​the​​resource​​for​​easier​​use​​by​​students​​and​
​staff.​ ​Participants​ ​pointed​ ​out​ ​issues​ ​with​ ​formatting​ ​across​​different​​devices,​​highlighting​
​the​​importance​​of​​ensuring​​compatibility​​and​​user-friendliness.​​Recommendations​​included​
​creating​ ​a​ ​more​ ​accessible​ ​digital​ ​version,​ ​potentially​ ​downloadable​ ​via​ ​a​ ​weblink,​ ​and​
​ensuring​ ​that​ ​the​ ​material​ ​could​ ​be​ ​presented​ ​on​ ​electronic​ ​whiteboards.​ ​The​ ​final​
​sub-them,​ ​‘marketing​ ​for​ ​dissemination’​,​ ​then​ ​discussed​ ​strategies​ ​to​ ​increase​ ​the​
​initiative's​ ​reach,​ ​emphasising​ ​collaboration​ ​with​ ​a​ ​broader​ ​range​ ​of​ ​stakeholders.​
​Suggestions​ ​for​ ​dissemination​ ​included​ ​leveraging​ ​teacher​ ​networks​ ​and​ ​platforms​ ​and​
​engaging with external organisations to form partnerships.​

​Chapter summary​

​In​ ​conclusion,​ ​this​ ​final​ ​round​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​has​ ​been​ ​valuable​ ​in​ ​providing​​a​​deeper​
​understanding​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​potential​ ​for​ ​publishability,​ ​practicality,​ ​implementation​
​feasibility,​ ​structure,​ ​and​ ​layout.​ ​Although​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​was​ ​generally​ ​well​ ​received,​ ​and​
​many​ ​strengths​ ​were​ ​presented,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​note​ ​that​​this​​round​​of​​data​​collection​
​revealed​ ​increased​ ​negative​ ​feedback​ ​from​ ​stakeholders,​ ​namely​ ​Nick​ ​(Private​ ​and​​public​
​Antisemitism​​Educator)​​and​​Sarah,​​regarding​​the​​professionalism​​of​​the​​product,​​reinforcing​
​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​a​ ​professional​ ​writer,​ ​editor,​ ​or​ ​illustrator.​ ​Additionally,​ ​Sarah​ ​(Antisemitism​
​Educator)​ ​concerns​ ​were​ ​raised​ ​about​ ​the​ ​appropriateness​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​for​ ​children,​




                                                             ​271​
​particularly​ ​in​ ​light​ ​of​ ​the​ ​current​ ​political​ ​climate​ ​and​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid,’​ ​which​
​carries a risk of misinterpretation and could significantly affect the initiative’s impact.​

​With​ ​this​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​plans​ ​for​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​will​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​refining​ ​the​ ​content​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​it​
​aligns​ ​with​ ​both​ ​educational​ ​objectives​ ​and​ ​the​ ​sensitivities​ ​of​ ​the​ ​target​ ​audience.​
​Securing​ ​funding​ ​will​ ​be​ ​pivotal​ ​to​ ​supporting​ ​these​ ​improvements,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​ensuring​
​high-quality​ ​production.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​engagement​ ​with​ ​diverse​ ​stakeholders,​ ​including​
​those​ ​in​ ​sports,​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​work,​ ​and​ ​Jewish​ ​education,​ ​combined​ ​with​
​dissemination​ ​efforts​​across​​various​​platforms,​​will​​be​​critical​​to​​maximising​​the​​initiative's​
​impact​​and​​ensuring​​its​​sustainability​​within​​educational​​contexts.​​This​​chapter​​finalises​​the​
​discussion​​of​​the​​original​​empirical​​data​​collected​​throughout​​the​​process​​of​​this​​thesis.​​The​
​next,​ ​and​ ​final,​ ​chapter​ ​will​ ​build​ ​upon​ ​this​ ​by​ ​synthesising​ ​the​ ​findings​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​a​
​comprehensive reflection on the overall process and its broader implications.​




                                                               ​272​
​Chapter 11 - Conclusion​


​Introduction​


​Given​ ​the​ ​project's​ ​relatively​​underexplored​​research​​area,​​this​​concluding​​chapter​​seeks​​to​
​provide​​a​​thorough​​critical​​analysis​​of​​the​​research​​journey,​​offering​​a​​reflective​​evaluation​​of​
​the​ ​project​ ​as​ ​a​ ​whole.​ ​Firstly,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​will​ ​reflect​ ​on​ ​key​ ​aspects​​of​​the​​theoretical​
​and​​methodological​​approaches​​underpinning​​the​​development​​of​​this​​project,​​while​​offering​
​a​​critical​​analysis​​of​​the​​journey​​undertaken​​in​​the​​delivery​​of​​the​​project.​​The​​latter​​part​​of​
​this​ ​chapter​ ​seeks​ ​to​ ​conclude​ ​the​ ​thesis​ ​with​ ​a​ ​comprehensive​ ​summary​ ​of​ ​the​ ​research​
​implications​​before​​transitioning​​into​​an​​evaluation​​of​​whether​​the​​aim​​and​​objectives​​of​​this​
​thesis​​were​​achieved.​​Subsequently,​​an​​exploration​​of​​the​​original​​contributions​​this​​research​
​makes​​to​​the​​field​​will​​be​​discussed,​​before​​outlining​​potential​​directions​​for​​future​​research​
​stemming​ ​from​ ​this​ ​project.​ ​Finally,​ ​the​ ​chapter​ ​concludes​ ​with​ ​a​ ​short​​personal​​reflection​
​from the researcher.​


​The​ ​project​ ​aimed​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​a​ ​successful​ ​educational​ ​initiative​​to​​address​​antisemitism​​in​
​British​ ​football,​ ​given​ ​its​ ​aforementioned​ ​prevalence​ ​and​ ​impact​​(Boyd​​and​​Staetsky,​​2014;​
​Curtis,​​2019).​​Despite​​numerous​​initiatives​​in​​sports​​to​​combat​​inequality​​and​​discrimination,​
​it​ ​has​ ​been​ ​demonstrated​ ​that​​few​​have​​specifically​​targeted​​antisemitism.​​With​​the​​rise​​of​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK​ ​(CST,​ ​2023),​ ​it​ ​is​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​understand​ ​this​ ​issue​ ​better​ ​to​ ​develop​
​effective preventative measures.​


​To​ ​recap,​ ​this​ ​project​ ​undertook​ ​a​ ​comprehensive​ ​literature​ ​review​ ​followed​ ​by​ ​a​
​multi-phased approach, consisting of four phases:​


         ​● Phase 1: Interviews with anti-discrimination experts​
         ​● Phase 2: Creation of an educational resource through creative non-fiction​
         ​● Phase 3: Focus group interviews​
         ​● Phase 4: Expert book review​




                                                              ​273​
​Through​ ​these​ ​phases,​ ​a​ ​co-created​ ​educational​ ​resource​ ​for​ ​children​ ​was​ ​developed​ ​to​
​educate​ ​individuals​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​Judaism,​ ​using​ ​narratives​ ​and​ ​discussions​​centred​
​on​ ​football.​ ​This​ ​reflective​ ​chapter​ ​provides​ ​an​ ​in-depth​ ​critical​ ​analysis​ ​of​ ​key​ ​facets​
​underpinning​ ​the​ ​entirety​ ​of​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process,​ ​including​ ​an​ ​examination​ ​of​ ​relevant​
​theoretical​ ​frameworks​ ​integrated​ ​within​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​methodological​ ​considerations​ ​for​
​the project, and significant challenges encountered in the execution of the initiative.​


​Before​ ​engaging​ ​in​ ​any​ ​data​ ​collection,​ ​the​ ​first​ ​stage​ ​of​ ​the​ ​thesis​ ​process​ ​involved​
​engagement​ ​with​ ​key​ ​literature​ ​to​ ​develop​​a​​deeper​​understanding​​of​​the​​current​​research​
​conducted​ ​on​ ​antisemitism,​ ​specifically​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​football.​ ​As​ ​discussed​​in​​the​​literature​
​review​ ​(see​ ​p.32),​ ​scholars​ ​including​ ​Pavel​ ​Brunssen​ ​and​ ​Jasmin​ ​Seijbel​ ​have​ ​explored​
​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​European​ ​football​ ​(Brunssen,​ ​2022;​ ​2023;​ ​Brunssen​ ​and​
​Schüler-Springorum,​ ​2021;​ ​Seijbel​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2022;​ ​Seijbel​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2023).​ ​Additionally,​ ​Emma​
​Poulton​​has​​conducted​​considerable​​research​​on​​antisemitism​​in​​British​​football,​​with​​specific​
​reference​ ​to​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​and​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​word​ ​‘Yid’​ ​in​ ​British​ ​football​​(Poulton,​
​2013;​​2016;​​2020;​​2021;​​2023;​​2024).​​Other​​scholars,​​including​​Jon​​Dart,​​have​​also​​explored​
​antisemitism,​ ​but​ ​more​ ​broadly​ ​in​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​sport,​ ​as​ ​opposed​ ​to​ ​solely​ ​focusing​ ​on​
​football​​(Dart,​​2019;​​2021;​​Dart​​and​​Long,​​2021).​​A​​crucial​​stage​​of​​this​​literature​​review​​was​
​to​​engage​​with​​sociological​​theory,​​which​​was​​subsequently​​used​​to​​inform​​the​​later​​stages​​of​
​the​ ​project,​ ​including​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​and​ ​analysis;​ ​reflection​ ​on​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​theory​ ​will​ ​be​
​discussed​ ​later​ ​in​ ​this​ ​chapter.​ ​The​ ​literature​ ​review​ ​enabled​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​to​ ​identify​
​common​ ​challenges​ ​in​ ​addressing​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​both​ ​sport​ ​and​ ​society,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​to​
​critique the various theoretical approaches used in previous academic studies on this topic.​


​Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​of​ ​the​ ​research​ ​was​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​an​ ​evidence-based​ ​and​ ​co-created​
​educational​​initiative​​focused​​on​​reducing​​antisemitism​​in​​British​​football;​​therefore,​​a​​review​
​of​ ​literature​ ​relating​ ​to​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives​ ​was​ ​also​ ​conducted​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​the​
​strengths​​and​​limitations​​of​​similar​​initiatives​​to​​the​​one​​developed​​in​​this​​thesis.​​Initially,​​the​
​intention​ ​was​ ​to​ ​create​ ​an​ ​initiative​ ​for​ ​football​ ​fans;​ ​nevertheless,​ ​it​ ​became​ ​apparent​
​through​ ​both​ ​the​ ​literature​ ​review​ ​write-up​ ​and​ ​the​ ​later​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​stage,​ ​that​
​developing​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​for​ ​individuals​ ​who​ ​already​ ​have​ ​their​ ​preconceived​
​notions​ ​about​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​may​ ​not​ ​serve​​a​​purpose.​​This​​chapter​​will​​therefore​​critically​


                                                             ​274​
​reflect​ ​on​ ​the​ ​rationale​ ​behind​ ​the​ ​methodological​ ​decisions​ ​that​ ​led​ ​to​ ​the​ ​design​ ​of​ ​the​
​educational initiative in the form of a book.​

​Revisiting the research aim and objectives​

​To recap, the overarching aim of this study was:​


       ​To​ ​develop​ ​an​ ​evidence-based​ ​and​ ​co-created​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​focused​ ​on​
       ​eradicating​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​British​ ​Football,​ ​with​ ​input​ ​from​ ​anti-discrimination​
       ​experts and the Jewish community.​


​As​​discussed​​in​​the​​personal​​reflection,​​the​​primary​​goal​​was​​to​​create​​a​​resource​​or​​initiative​
​that​ ​could​ ​contribute​ ​to​ ​creating​​change​​for​​the​​Jewish​​community.​​However,​​it​​was​​crucial​
​that​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​was​ ​grounded​ ​in​ ​theory​ ​and​ ​shaped​ ​by​ ​the​ ​input​ ​of​ ​key​ ​stakeholders.​
​Therefore,​ ​this​ ​project's​ ​objectives​ ​were​ ​achieved​ ​through​ ​the​ ​application​ ​of​ ​various​
​theories,​ ​most​ ​notably​ ​CRT​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001)​ ​and​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020),​ ​to​
​identify​ ​key​ ​factors​ ​that​ ​should​ ​be​ ​considered​ ​when​ ​addressing​ ​inequalities​ ​and​
​discrimination,​ ​specifically​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​diverse​ ​data​ ​collection​
​methods​​facilitated​​engagement​​with​​key​​stakeholders,​​including​​anti-discrimination​​experts​
​and​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​allowing​​the​​researcher​​to​​amplify​​the​​voices​​of​​the​
​Jewish community.​


​The​ ​following​​research​​objectives​​played​​a​​pivotal​​role​​in​​providing​​a​​framework​​that​​would​
​support the completion of the aim:​


​Objective​ ​1​ ​-​ ​Investigate​ ​the​ ​perspectives​ ​of​ ​key​ ​stakeholders​ ​on​ ​antisemitism,​ ​religion,​
​ethnicity and identity within the football and wider social context.​


​Through​​an​​extensive​​review​​of​​the​​literature​​and​​the​​Phase​​1​​interviews​​with​​experts​​in​​the​
​fields​​of​​sport​​and​​discrimination,​​it​​was​​possible​​to​​explore​​and​​analyse​​the​​perspectives​​of​
​key​​stakeholders​​on​​issues​​such​​as​​antisemitism,​​religion,​​ethnicity,​​and​​identity,​​both​​within​
​the​​context​​of​​football​​and​​broader​​society.​​This​​process​​allowed​​for​​a​​deeper​​understanding​
​of​​how​​these​​interconnected​​issues​​exist​​within​​sport,​​particularly​​football,​​but​​also​​how​​they​


                                                            ​275​
​reflect​ ​and​ ​influence​ ​wider​ ​society.​​The​​literature​​and​​data​​gathered​​provided​​a​​foundation​
​that​ ​was​ ​critical​ ​for​ ​examining​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​in​ ​challenging​ ​discrimination,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​a​
​platform upon which to develop an educational initiative.​


​Objective​ ​2​ ​-​ ​Identify​ ​and​ ​evaluate​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives​ ​in​ ​football​ ​and​ ​sport​ ​to​
​identify good practice on how antisemitism may be tackled.​


​Through​​a​​comprehensive​​review​​of​​literature​​(Chapter​​2),​​current​​research​​on​​antisemitism​
​in​ ​sport​ ​(Brunssen,​ ​2022;​ ​2023;​ ​Dart,​ ​2021;​ ​Dart​ ​and​ ​Long,​ ​2021;​ ​Poulton,​ ​2016,​ ​2020;​
​Poulton​​and​​Durell,​​2016),​​has​​been​​explored​​providing​​a​​foundation​​for​​the​​development​​of​
​an​ ​educational​ ​initiative.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​initiatives​ ​that​ ​are​ ​being​ ​used​
​within​​sport​​to​​combat​​anti-discriminatory​​behaviours​​and​​attitudes​​in​​sport​​were​​identified​
​(Dixon​​et​​al.​,​​2016;​​Magrath​​and​​Stott,​​2019).​​The​​review​​of​​literature​​highlighted​​the​​gaps​​in​
​existing​​research,​​as​​well​​as​​the​​effectiveness​​of​​current​​initiatives​​in​​addressing​​these​​issues.​
​Alongside​ ​highlighting​ ​the​ ​key​ ​strengths​​of​​the​​work​​being​​conducted,​​the​​literature​​review​
​also​​addresses​​the​​limitations​​and​​challenges​​that​​are​​often​​overlooked​​in​​these​​campaigns,​
​such​​as​​the​​lack​​of​​funding​​and​​the​​difficulty​​in​​measuring​​the​​true​​impact​​of​​these​​initiatives​
​on changing attitudes and behaviours (Kilvington and Price, 2017)​


​In​ ​addition,​ ​this​ ​objective​ ​was​ ​met​ ​through​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​interviews​ ​with​ ​anti-discrimination​
​experts​​in​​the​​field​​of​​sport.​ ​These​​interviews​​facilitated​​a​​better​​understanding​​of​​the​​work​
​being​ ​done​ ​by​ ​experts​ ​in​ ​the​ ​field,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​specific​ ​elements​ ​and​ ​concepts​ ​applied​ ​to​
​produce​ ​successful​ ​initiatives.​ ​Through​ ​this​ ​process,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​been​ ​possible​ ​to​ ​identify​ ​good​
​practice​ ​and​ ​uncover​ ​potential​ ​areas​ ​for​ ​improvement​ ​for​ ​these​ ​initiatives,​ ​particularly​ ​in​
​terms​ ​of​ ​addressing​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​unique​ ​to​ ​their​ ​work,​ ​but​ ​also​ ​with​ ​regards​ ​to​ ​their​
​implementation and long-term sustainability.​


​Throughout​​both​​stages​​of​​the​​research,​​this​​objective​​was​​addressed​​by​​integrating​​insights​
​from​ ​the​ ​literature​ ​review​ ​with​ ​expert​ ​perspectives​ ​derived​ ​from​​original​​empirical​​data​​to​
​explore​​potential​​approaches​​to​​antisemitism.​​It​​is​​important​​to​​note​​that​​the​​term​​‘tackled’​
​was​ ​used​ ​in​ ​the​ ​objective.​ ​While​ ​this​ ​term​ ​is​ ​fitting​ ​within​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​a​ ​sports-related​
​thesis,​ ​it​ ​did​ ​not​ ​entirely​ ​capture​ ​the​​complexity​​of​​the​​issue,​​as​​‘tackled’​​suggests​​that​​the​


                                                              ​276​
​problem​ ​of​​antisemitism​​could​​be​​fully​​resolved.​​Upon​​reflection,​​terms​​such​​as​​‘addressed’​
​or ‘reduced’ may be more appropriate.​


​Objective​ ​3​ ​-​ ​Develop​ ​a​ ​theoretically-informed​ ​educational​​initiative​​which​​could​​be​​used​​to​
​decrease antisemitic behaviour in football.​


​It​​is​​important​​to​​note​​that​​whilst​​the​​third​​research​​objective​​was​​initially​​aimed​​at​​reducing​
​antisemitic​ ​behaviours​ ​in​ ​football,​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​shifted​ ​its​ ​focus​ ​to​ ​using​ ​football​ ​as​ ​a​
​narrative​ ​vehicle​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​younger​ ​individuals,​ ​some​ ​of​ ​whom​ ​might​ ​be​ ​fans​ ​already​
​attending​ ​games.​ ​The​ ​purpose​ ​of​ ​this​ ​shift​ ​comes​ ​from​ ​empirical​ ​data,​ ​from​ ​both​ ​the​
​research​​findings​​and​​secondary​​data,​​which​​discussed​​the​​challenge​​in​​tackling​​attitudes​​of​
​those​​individuals​​who​​already​​attend​​matches​​(Dixon​​et​​al.​,​​2016).​​The​​initiative​​now​​seeks​​to​
​teach​​these​​younger​​audiences​​about​​antisemitism​​and​​Judaism,​​with​​the​​goal​​of​​decreasing​
​antisemitic​ ​behaviour​ ​at​ ​football​ ​matches​ ​but​ ​also​ ​more​​broadly​​in​​society.​​As​​a​​result,​​the​
​initiative​ ​has​ ​evolved​ ​from​ ​being​ ​a​ ​tool​ ​to​ ​combat​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​to​ ​employing​ ​a​
​unique,​ ​football-based​ ​narrative​ ​approach​ ​that​ ​leverages​ ​the​ ​sport​ ​itself​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​and​
​address antisemitism.​


​The​ ​educational​ ​initiative​ ​was​ ​developed​ ​using​ ​CNF,​ ​grounded​ ​in​​the​​research​​findings​​and​
​informed​ ​by​ ​CRT,​ ​HebCrit,​ ​and​ ​bystander​ ​intervention​ ​theory.​ ​This​ ​theoretically-informed​
​initiative​​is​​designed​​to​​engage​​children​​BIM​​in​​primary​​schools,​​using​​football​​as​​a​​relatable​
​tool​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​students​ ​and​ ​deliver​ ​lessons​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​​and​​Judaism.​​Additionally,​​the​
​initiative​ ​aligns​ ​with​ ​key​ ​principles​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Personal,​ ​Social,​ ​Health​ ​and​ ​Economic​ ​(PSHE)​
​curriculum,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​it​ ​not​ ​only​ ​meets​ ​educational​ ​standards​ ​but​ ​also​ ​effectively​
​integrates​​with​​existing​​frameworks​​for​​teaching​​about​​diversity​​and​​social​​cohesion.​​Through​
​this​ ​approach,​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​aims​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​children​ ​aged​ ​10-11​ ​about​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​
​Judaism, using football to make the lessons both accessible and impactful.​


​Objective​ ​4​​-​​Explore​​how​​key​​stakeholders​​respond​​to​​an​​original​​educational​​initiative​​that​
​aims to decrease antisemitism in football.​




                                                           ​277​
​The​ ​key​ ​stakeholders​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​include​ ​the​​primary​​target​​audience,​​10-11​​year-olds,​
​alongside​ ​school​ ​educators,​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts,​ ​and​ ​members​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community.​ ​The​ ​original​​intention​​was​​to​​evaluate​​how​​this​​young​​audience​​would​​respond​
​to​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​as​ ​it​​would​​provide​​an​​opportunity​​to​​gather​​data​​into​​the​​effectiveness​​of​
​the​ ​educational​ ​content​ ​and​ ​its​ ​ability​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​and​ ​resonate​ ​with​ ​children​ ​of​ ​this​ ​age​
​group.​ ​However,​ ​due​ ​to​ ​uncontrollable​ ​extraneous​ ​circumstances​ ​outlined​ ​in​ ​the​ ​previous​
​chapter, this trial could not be conducted.​

​Despite​​these​​challenges,​​opportunities​​for​​feedback​​were​​still​​available​​during​​Phases​​3​​and​
​4​​of​​the​​research.​​Interviews​​and​​focus​​groups​​were​​conducted,​​enabling​​other​​stakeholders​
​to​​contribute​​valuable​​insights,​​each​​playing​​a​​vital​​role​​in​​refining​​the​​initiative.​​The​​feedback​
​suggested​​that​​the​​initiative​​shows​​significant​​potential​​in​​its​​current​​form,​​with​​participants​
​finding​​the​​use​​of​​sport​​as​​a​​conversational​​tool​​to​​be​​highly​​effective​​in​​engaging​​the​​target​
​audience​ ​and​ ​making​ ​complex​ ​topics​ ​more​ ​relatable.​ ​However,​ ​the​ ​final​ ​phase​ ​of​ ​data​
​collection​ ​also​ ​highlighted​ ​several​ ​essential​ ​steps​ ​that​ ​need​ ​to​ ​be​ ​taken​ ​-such​ ​as​ ​the​
​employment​ ​of​ ​a​ ​professional​ ​illustrator​​and​​a​​children's​​writer​​-​​to​​enhance​​the​​initiative’s​
​effectiveness and appeal in educational settings.​

​In​​the​​latter​​part​​of​​this​​chapter,​​future​​recommendations​​will​​be​​discussed,​​focusing​​on​​the​
​necessary​ ​steps​ ​to​ ​bring​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​to​ ​fruition.​ ​A​ ​primary​ ​recommendation​ ​is​ ​to​ ​secure​
​funding​ ​to​ ​finalise​ ​the​ ​educational​ ​resource,​ ​which​ ​would​ ​include​ ​hiring​ ​an​ ​editor​ ​and​
​illustrator​​to​​polish​​the​​content​​and​​presentation.​​Once​​these​​elements​​are​​in​​place,​​it​​would​
​be​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​pilot​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​in​ ​schools​ ​to​ ​evaluate​ ​its​ ​impact​ ​and​ ​effectiveness​ ​in​
​reducing​ ​antisemitic​ ​attitudes​ ​and​ ​educating​ ​individuals​ ​about​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​and​
​the​ ​challenges​ ​they​ ​often​ ​face.​ ​This​ ​trial​ ​phase​ ​would​ ​not​ ​only​ ​provide​ ​insights​ ​into​ ​the​
​initiative’s​​strengths​​and​​limitations​​but​​also​​offer​​an​​opportunity​​for​​further​​refinement​​and​
​broader implementation.​

​Theoretical reflections​


​The​​theoretical​​frameworks​​informing​​this​​research​​include​​HebCrit,​​CRT,​​BIM,​​and​​CNF​​each​
​offering​ ​unique​ ​insights.​ ​This​ ​chapter​ ​will​​focus​​on​​theoretical​​reflections​​regarding​​HebCrit​
​and​ ​CRT,​ ​while​ ​CNF,​ ​will​ ​be​ ​discussed​ ​in​ ​a​ ​later​ ​sub-chapter,​ ​where​ ​its​ ​roles​ ​in​ ​the​


                                                            ​278​
​methodological​ ​process​ ​will​ ​be​ ​explored.​ ​After​ ​reviewing​ ​the​ ​literature​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​
​football​ ​(see​ ​p.​​28)​​within​​the​​field​​of​​sport​​sociology,​​it​​was​​evident​​that​​there​​is​​a​​lack​​of​
​research​​that​​is​​theoretically​​informed.​​There​​are​​some​​researchers​​who​​have​​engaged​​with​
​frameworks​ ​relevant​ ​to​ ​the​ ​specific​ ​concept​ ​they​ ​are​ ​looking​ ​into;​ ​for​ ​example,​ ​Poulton’s​
​(2020)​​research​​on​​policies,​​using​​the​​multiple​​streams​​approach​​or​​linguistic​​reclamation​​to​
​explain​ ​how​ ​marginalised​ ​groups​ ​can​ ​reclaim​ ​derogatory​ ​terms​ ​(Poulton​​and​​Durell,​​2016).​
​Therefore,​ ​those​ ​who​ ​have​ ​engaged​ ​with​ ​theory,​ ​use​ ​theory​ ​that​ ​focuses​​more​​broadly​​on​
​general​ ​social​ ​dynamics,​ ​rather​ ​than​ ​on​ ​the​ ​specific​ ​nuances​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​identity​ ​or​
​antisemitism.​


​This​ ​highlighted​ ​a​ ​gap​ ​in​ ​applying​ ​a​ ​more​ ​specific​ ​theoretical​ ​approach,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​HebCrit​
​(Rubin,​​2020),​​to​​understanding​​the​​complexities​​of​​antisemitism​​in​​sport.​​With​​this​​in​​mind,​
​this​​research​​incorporated​​Rubin’s​​(2020)​​theory​​of​​HebCrit​​which​​more​​precisely​​addresses​
​the​ ​unique​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​ensuring​ ​a​ ​deeper​ ​and​ ​more​ ​specific​
​understanding​ ​of​ ​antisemitism,​ ​when​ ​applying​ ​it​ ​to​ ​the​ ​context​ ​of​ ​football.​ ​Given​ ​the​
​aforementioned​ ​theoretical​ ​underpinnings​ ​of​ ​past​ ​studies​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​sport​ ​and​
​society,​​it​​is​​also​​worth​​emphasising​​that​​Rubin’s​​(2020)​​theory​​of​​HebCrit​​has​​only​​been​​used​
​as​​a​​theoretical​​framework​​in​​a​​very​​limited​​range​​of​​academic​​research.​​As​​mentioned​​in​​the​
​review​ ​of​ ​literature​​(see​​p.​​81),​​as​​of​​November​​2024,​​Rubin’s​​(2020)​​theory​​of​​HebCrit​​had​
​eleven​​citations​​in​​Google​​Scholar.​​It​​was​​cited​​in​​nine​​pieces​​of​​peer​​reviewed​​literature,​​two​
​doctoral​​theses​​and​​one​​Masters​​dissertation.​​Therefore,​​its​​use​​in​​this​​thesis​​provides​​novel​
​contributions to knowledge in the field of sport sociology.​


​Alongside​ ​HebCrit,​ ​CRT​ ​was​ ​also​ ​used​ ​within​ ​the​ ​creation​ ​of​ ​the​ ​book​ ​for​ ​the​ ​educational​
​initiative,​ ​as​ ​the​​key​​tenets​​were​​embedded​​within​​the​​story.​​In​​the​​field​​of​​sport​​sociology,​
​CRT​ ​has​ ​been​ ​used​ ​frequently​​by​​scholars,​​including​​Kevin​​Hylton​​(2005;​​2009;​​2010;​​2021)​
​and​ ​Burdsey​ ​(2011),​ ​to​ ​analyse​ ​and​ ​critique​ ​racial​ ​inequities​ ​and​ ​power​ ​dynamics​ ​within​
​sports​ ​settings.​ ​Specifically,​​Hylton’s​​work​​has​​used​​CRT​​to​​challenge​​dominant​​narratives​​in​
​sport,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​racial​ ​stereotyping​ ​and​ ​examining​ ​how​ ​institutionalised​ ​racism​ ​exists​ ​within​
​sport,​​whilst​​advocating​​for​​social​​change​​by​​addressing​​how​​these​​inequalities​​in​​sport​​could​
​be​ ​challenged.​ ​Therefore,​ ​CRT's​​application​​in​​this​​thesis​​has​​proven​​valuable​​for​​examining​
​how​​racial​​identities​​impact​​discrimination​​in​​football,​​which​​evolved​​from​​CRT​​to​​address​​the​


                                                           ​279​
​specific​ ​needs​ ​and​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community,​ ​was​​deemed​​appropriate​​for​​this​
​project.​


​Research​ ​from​ ​Judaken​ ​(2018)​ ​emphasised​ ​that​ ​antisemitism​ ​is​ ​an​​under-theorised​​area​​of​
​research​​and​​advocated​​for​​the​​development​​of​​a​​new​​theoretical​​framework​​to​​better​​study​
​this​ ​issue.​ ​With​ ​this​ ​in​ ​mind,​ ​the​ ​development​ ​of​ ​HebCrit​ ​in​ ​2020,​ ​provided​ ​benefits​ ​in​
​bringing​ ​Jewish​ ​issues​ ​to​ ​the​ ​forefront​ ​of​ ​critical​ ​discussions​ ​on​ ​race,​ ​identity,​ ​and​
​discrimination​ ​(Muller,​ ​2024;​ ​Selznick​​and​​Greenes,​​2024).​​The​​framework​​can​​therefore​​be​
​used​​within​​both​​this​​thesis​​as​​well​​as​​further​​studies​​and/or​​policy​​to​​amplify​​the​​voices​​of​
​Jewish​​individuals,​​thus​​addressing​​issues​​unique​​to​​this​​population​​-​​as​​seen​​in​​the​​work​​of​
​Glauz-Todrank​ ​(2022)​ ​on​ ​court​ ​cases​ ​and​ ​Muller​ ​(2024)​ ​within​ ​educational​ ​settings.​
​Specifically,​ ​with​ ​its​​particularly​​strong​​focus​​on​​antisemitism,​​it​​offers​​a​​tool​​to​​analyse​​and​
​challenge​ ​this​ ​form​ ​of​ ​discrimination​ ​and​ ​prejudice.​ ​By​ ​doing​ ​so,​ ​HebCrit​ ​fills​ ​a​ ​gap​ ​in​
​traditional​ ​CRT​​frameworks​​(Rubin,​​2020),​​which​​understandably,​​may​​not​​explicitly​​address​
​antisemitism and the Jewish community (Hornsved, 2022).​


​However,​​similar​​to​​CRT,​​this​​theory​​provides​​five​​key​​tenets​​alongside​​explanations​​for​​these​
​crucial​​factors​​which​​can​​be​​used​​to​​provide​​a​​more​​nuanced​​understanding​​of​​the​​struggles​
​and​ ​challenges​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​After​ ​reviewing​​twelve​​recent​​pieces​​of​​literature​
​that​ ​reference​ ​Rubin's​ ​(2020)​ ​work,​ ​two​ ​particular​ ​tenets​ ​have​ ​gained​ ​more​ ​prominence:​
​"Jewish​ ​personal​ ​stories​ ​have​ ​value"​ ​and​ ​"Jews,​ ​and​ ​their​ ​perception​ ​as​ ​White,​ ​creates​
​invisibility​​and​​tension."​​It​​is​​important​​to​​note​​that​​this​​thesis​​has​​also​​emphasised​​the​​value​
​of​​stories,​​particularly​​when​​using​​CNF​​as​​a​​tool​​for​​advancing​​the​​initiative.​​Nevertheless,​​as​
​discussed​ ​in​ ​Chapter​​6,​​all​​five​​tenets​​of​​HebCrit​​were​​integrated​​into​​the​​narrative​​through​
​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​CNF,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​each​​theoretical​​concept​​highlighting​​the​​challenges​​faced​​by​
​the Jewish community was reinforced for the reader.​


​Although​ ​HebCrit​ ​adapts​ ​CRT​ ​by​ ​focusing​ ​on​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​experience,​ ​it,​ ​like​ ​any​​theoretical​
​framework,​ ​has​ ​its​ ​limitations​ ​and​​areas​​for​​development.​​The​​fact​​that​​this​​theory​​has​​not​
​been​ ​widely​ ​used​ ​in​ ​academic​ ​literature​ ​presents​ ​challenges,​ ​as​ ​there​ ​is​ ​limited​ ​critique​
​available.​ ​Of​ ​the​ ​twelve​ ​cited​ ​pieces​ ​of​ ​literature,​ ​none​ ​address​ ​any​ ​specific​ ​limitations​ ​of​
​HebCrit,​​other​​than​​Selznick​​and​​Greenes​​(2024)​​who​​alludes​​to​​the​​idea​​that​​addressing​​all​


                                                            ​280​
​five​ ​tenets​ ​and​ ​integrating​ ​them​ ​at​ ​the​ ​same​ ​time​ ​would​ ​be​ ​a​ ​challenge.​ ​Typically,​
​researchers​ ​are​ ​aware​ ​of​ ​such​ ​limitations​ ​and​ ​engage​ ​with​ ​the​ ​critiques​ ​while​ ​proceeding​
​with​ ​caution​ ​as​ ​needed.​ ​Consequently,​ ​this​ ​creates​ ​opportunities​ ​for​ ​further​ ​criticism​ ​and​
​refinement of the theory.​


​It​ ​is​ ​important​ ​to​ ​recognise​ ​that​ ​HebCrit,​ ​like​ ​CRT,​ ​is​ ​rooted​ ​in​​the​​American​​experience​​of​
​race,​ ​ethnicity,​ ​and​ ​religion​ ​(Burdsey,​ ​2011;​ ​Moffitt,​ ​Juang​ ​and​ ​Syed,​​2019).​​This​​focus​​may​
​limit​ ​its​ ​applicability​ ​to​ ​different​ ​geographical​​contexts,​​potentially​​affecting​​its​​relevance​​in​
​the​ ​English​ ​setting.​ ​Literature​​from​​Boyd​​and​​Staetsky​​(2014)​​reinforces​​that​​experiences​​of​
​the​​Jewish​​individuals​​differ​​in​​the​​USA​​compared​​to​​the​​UK,​​arguing​​that​​Jews​​in​​the​​UK​​tend​
​to​​feel​​more​​secure​​and​​experience​​lower​​levels​​of​​antisemitism​​compared​​to​​other​​Western​
​European​ ​countries,​ ​despite​ ​Orthodox​ ​Jews​ ​feeling​ ​more​ ​anxious​ ​and​ ​susceptible​ ​to​
​antisemitic​ ​incidents.​ ​Nonetheless,​ ​the​ ​principles​ ​of​ ​these​ ​theories​ ​are​ ​still​ ​pertinent​ ​and​
​effective​ ​in​ ​amplifying​ ​the​ ​voices​ ​of​ ​the​ ​English​​Jewish​​community.​​Similarly,​​this​​highlights​
​the​ ​potential​ ​for​ ​further​ ​research​ ​to​ ​adapt​ ​HebCrit​ ​to​ ​better​ ​reflect​ ​various​ ​geographical​
​contexts, including England.​


​Furthermore,​ ​similar​ ​to​ ​other​ ​theories​ ​that​ ​have​ ​evolved​​from​​CRT,​​such​​as​​LatCrit​​(Valdes,​
​1998)​ ​and​ ​TribalCrit​ ​(Brayboy,​ ​2001),​ ​HebCrit​ ​might​ ​be​ ​critiqued​ ​for​ ​its​ ​narrow​ ​focus​ ​on​
​Jewish​ ​experiences.​ ​However,​ ​given​ ​that​​different​​communities​​face​​unique​​challenges,​​it​​is​
​important​​to​​recognise​​that​​the​​specific​​nature​​of​​the​​theory​​provides​​valuable​​insights​​into​
​the​ ​distinct​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​(Muller,​ ​2024;​ ​Silverman,​ ​2024).​ ​While​
​HebCrit​ ​may​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​particular​ ​issues​ ​relevant​ ​to​ ​Jewish​ ​individuals,​ ​this​ ​nuanced​ ​focus​
​allows​​for​​a​​deeper​​understanding​​of​​how​​specific​​factors​​influence​​Jewish​​experiences,​​and​
​can​​serve​​as​​a​​tool​​to​​further​​explore​​and​​address​​the​​needs​​of​​the​​community​​(Selznick​​and​
​Greenes, 2024).​


​While​ ​the​ ​theory​ ​examines​ ​the​ ​interplay​ ​between​ ​race​ ​and​ ​economics,​ ​particularly​
​addressing​​issues​​like​​the​​perceived​​invisibility​​of​​Jews​​due​​to​​their​​perceived​​Whiteness​​and​
​the​ ​stereotypical​ ​claims​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​political​ ​and​ ​economic​ ​power​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020),​ ​it​ ​often​
​overlooks​ ​other​ ​intersecting​ ​identity​ ​factors​ ​that​ ​shape​ ​individuals'​ ​experience.​
​Intersectionality,​ ​as​ ​coined​ ​by​ ​Crenshaw​ ​(1989),​ ​is​ ​a​ ​concept​ ​which​ ​emphasises​ ​the​


                                                            ​281​
​multidimensionality​ ​of​ ​minority​ ​individuals'​ ​lived​ ​experiences.​ ​Although​ ​CRT​ ​incorporates​
​intersectionality​ ​as​ ​a​ ​core​ ​concept​ ​(Delgado​ ​and​ ​Stefancic,​ ​2001),​ ​HebCrit​ ​does​ ​not​ ​fully​
​address​​how​​Jewish​​identity​​intersects​​with​​other​​factors​​such​​as​​gender,​​race,​​sexuality,​​and​
​socioeconomic​ ​class.​ ​While​ ​HebCrit​ ​does​ ​touch​ ​upon​ ​economic​ ​stereotypes​ ​about​ ​Jewish​
​individuals,​ ​it​ ​fails​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​how​ ​an​ ​individual's​ ​socioeconomic​ ​status​ ​might​ ​affect​ ​their​
​experiences.​ ​Similarly,​​while​​the​​theory​​acknowledges​​the​​perception​​of​​Jews​​as​​White,​​this​
​discussion​ ​does​ ​not​ ​fully​ ​account​ ​for​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​individuals​ ​who​ ​are​ ​non-White​​or​
​from diverse racial backgrounds within the Jewish community.​


​Similarly,​ ​as​ ​noted​ ​in​ ​the​ ​literature​ ​review,​ ​Jewish​ ​cultures​ ​and​ ​traditions​ ​vary​ ​significantly​
​depending​ ​on​ ​the​ ​Jewish​​movement​​to​​which​​a​​person​​belongs,​​such​​as​​Orthodox,​​Reform,​
​or​​Liberal​​(Kahn-Harris,​​2018;​​Valins,​​2003).​​Consequently,​​some​​of​​Rubin’s​​key​​tenets​​may​​be​
​more​​relevant​​to​​certain​​movements​​than​​others.​​For​​instance,​​the​​experiences​​of​​individuals​
​in​ ​Orthodox​ ​communities​​can​​differ​​substantially​​from​​those​​in​​Reform​​communities​​due​​to​
​differing​ ​religious​ ​practices​ ​and​ ​social​ ​values​​(Kahn-Harris,​​2018;​​Vulkan,​​2012).​​As​​a​​result,​
​while​​HebCrit​​provides​​valuable​​insights,​​its​​applicability​​might​​vary,​​requiring​​adjustments​​to​
​address the diverse experiences and issues faced by different Jewish movements.​


​Lastly,​​HebCrit​​may​​need​​to​​incorporate​​specific​​contemporary​​issues​​and​​challenges​​faced​​by​
​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​For​ ​example,​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​in​ ​England​ ​has​ ​been​ ​notably​
​affected​​by​​the​​ongoing​​Israeli-Palestinian​​conflict,​​which​​escalated​​more​​recently​​on​​October​
​7,​​2023.​​This​​escalation​​has​​subsequently​​influenced​​perceptions​​and​​experiences​​within​​the​
​community​​(Freedman​​and​​Hirsh,​​2024;​​Seymour,​​2024).​​The​​complexities​​of​​this​​geopolitical​
​situation​​could​​prove​​challenging​​when​​incorporating​​it​​into​​theory​​due​​to​​the​​diverse​​and​​at​
​times,​ ​controversial​ ​viewpoints​ ​within​ ​the​ ​community.​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​HebCrit​ ​must​ ​be​
​adapted​​to​​address​​these​​evolving​​issues​​to​​ensure​​that​​it​​accurately​​reflects​​and​​responds​​to​
​the​ ​current​​realities​​faced​​by​​Jewish​​communities.​​Finally,​​it​​is​​worth​​noting​​that​​the​​lack​​of​
​research​​using​​HebCrit​​to​​date​​(as​​of​​writing​​in​​2024)​​makes​​these​​flaws​​inevitable​​and​​that​
​future research using HebCrit may address these limitations going forward.​


​Although​ ​HebCrit​ ​has​ ​proved​ ​beneficial​ ​as​​a​​theory​​to​​guide​​the​​researcher​​and​​inform​​the​
​creation​​of​​the​​initiative,​​it​​is​​important​​to​​consider​​alternative​​theories​​that​​could​​have​​been​


                                                            ​282​
​utilised​ ​throughout​ ​this​ ​project.​ ​Initially,​ ​employing​ ​theories​ ​from​ ​Norbert​ ​Elias​ ​was​
​contemplated,​ ​given​ ​prior​ ​knowledge​ ​and​ ​experience​ ​with​ ​Eliasian​ ​theory​ ​(Lunn,​ ​2023).​
​Specifically,​ ​Elias's​ ​concept​ ​of​ ​‘established/outsiders’​ ​(Elias​ ​and​ ​Scotson,​ ​1965)​ ​was​
​considered,​ ​given​ ​that​ ​Biale​ ​et​ ​al.​ ​(1998,​ ​p.​ ​5)​ ​describes​ ​Jewish​ ​people​ ​as​ ​having​ ​an​
​insider/outsider​ ​status,​ ​“standing​ ​somewhere​ ​between​​the​​dominant​​position​​of​​the​​White​
​majority​ ​and​ ​the​ ​marginal​ ​position​ ​of​ ​people​ ​of​ ​colour.”​ ​Additionally,​ ​Elias​ ​has​ ​been​
​frequently​ ​referenced​ ​in​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​sociology​ ​to​ ​address​​complex​​issues,​​making​​his​
​work a valuable framework for this study (Waddington and Malcolm, 2006).​


​However,​ ​when​ ​comparing​ ​the​ ​work​ ​of​ ​Norbert​ ​Elias​ ​to​ ​HebCrit,​ ​his​ ​work​ ​has​ ​limited​
​discussion​ ​regarding​​religion,​​specifically​​Judaism.​​Elias’s​​work​​could​​have​​been​​beneficial​​in​
​earlier​ ​studies​ ​examining​ ​group​ ​identities,​ ​like​ ​Judaism​​or​​other​​marginalised​​communities.​
​Furthermore,​ ​HebCrit​ ​offers​ ​a​ ​chance​ ​for​ ​a​ ​more​ ​nuanced​ ​exploration​ ​of​ ​the​ ​specific​
​challenges​​faced​​by​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​which​​is​​a​​central​​focus​​of​​the​​research​​question.​
​Therefore,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​concluded​ ​that​​both​​CRT​​and​​HebCrit​​were​​the​​most​​suitable​​frameworks​
​due​ ​to​ ​the​ ​increasing​ ​use​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​in​ ​sports​ ​literature​ ​and​ ​HebCrit’s​ ​nuanced​ ​approach​ ​to​
​exploring​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​this​ ​research​ ​project​ ​began​ ​in​ ​2020,​
​coinciding​ ​with​ ​the​ ​publication​ ​of​ ​HebCrit​ ​in​ ​the​ ​same​ ​year.​ ​Although​ ​utilising​ ​HebCrit​
​presented​​a​​challenge,​​as​​the​​researcher​​was​​the​​first​​in​​sports​​academia​​to​​apply​​this​​theory,​
​it​ ​ultimately​ ​proved​ ​beneficial​ ​because​ ​the​ ​nuanced​ ​approach​ ​of​ ​the​ ​theory​ ​provided​ ​a​
​framework​​to​​critique​​and​​address​​antisemitism​​within​​the​​sports​​context,​​with​​specific​​focus​
​on​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse,​ ​thus​ ​using​ ​the​ ​theory​ ​to​ ​then​ ​amplifying​​marginalised​​Jewish​​voices.​
​Lastly,​​both​​CRT​​and​​HebCrit​​have​​been​​instrumental​​in​​shaping​​the​​thesis’​​narrative,​​as​​they​
​both emphasise the importance of storytelling.​


​Looking​​ahead,​​it​​would​​be​​beneficial​​for​​HebCrit​​to​​be​​explored​​within​​policy-making​​to​​help​
​voice​ ​the​ ​main​ ​concerns​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​The​ ​start​ ​of​ ​this​ ​has​ ​been​ ​seen​ ​in​
​Glauz-Todrank’s​ ​(2022)​ ​work​ ​in​ ​giving​ ​voice​ ​to​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​in​ ​court​ ​cases,​ ​and​
​Muller’s​ ​(2024)​ ​work​ ​on​ ​using​ ​the​ ​voices​ ​of​ ​Jews​ ​within​ ​an​ ​educational​ ​workshop.​ ​As​
​evidenced​​by​​Muller,​​integrating​​HebCrit​​within​​educational​​settings​​would​​be​​advantageous​
​as​ ​it​ ​highlights​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​face,​ ​which​ ​students​ ​can​ ​often​ ​be​




                                                          ​283​
​unaware​ ​of.​ ​Educating​ ​individuals​ ​on​ ​these​ ​matters​ ​would​ ​foster​ ​greater​ ​understanding,​
​awareness, and potentially lead to a more inclusive society.​


​Methodological reflections​


​As​ ​outlined​ ​in​ ​the​ ​introduction​ ​of​ ​this​ ​chapter,​ ​this​ ​project​ ​employed​ ​a​ ​multi-phased​
​approach,​ ​utilising​ ​various​​methods​​such​​as​​interviews,​​focus​​groups,​​and​​questionnaires​​to​
​gather​ ​data.​ ​This​ ​diverse​ ​methodology​ ​has​ ​enriched​ ​the​ ​depth​​of​​the​​research​​by​​ensuring​
​methodological​ ​triangulation,​ ​demonstrating​ ​that​ ​a​ ​rigorous​ ​approach​ ​has​ ​been​ ​taken​
​throughout​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process,​ ​thereby​ ​enhancing​ ​its​ ​credibility​ ​(Gray,​ ​2022).​​Therefore,​
​reflecting​ ​on​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​multiple​ ​research​ ​methods​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​in​ ​providing​ ​a​ ​critical​
​reflection.​


​The​ ​use​ ​of​ ​three​ ​different​ ​methods​ ​was​ ​intentional,​ ​as​ ​each​​addressed​​a​​specific​​aspect​​of​
​the​ ​research​ ​problem.​ ​Interviews​ ​were​ ​ideal​ ​for​ ​one-on-one​ ​discussions​ ​about​ ​individuals'​
​work​ ​on​ ​anti-discrimination​​initiatives.​​Focus​​groups,​​on​​the​​other​​hand,​​were​​better​​suited​
​for​​gathering​​insights​​on​​the​​strengths​​and​​limitations​​of​​the​​proposed​​children's​​book.​​Lastly,​
​questionnaires​ ​provided​ ​an​ ​effective​ ​means​ ​for​ ​implementing​ ​a​ '​book​ ​review.'​ ​This​
​multi-method​ ​approach​ ​enabled​ ​a​ ​deeper​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​diverse​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​tools,​
​from​ ​conducting​ ​in-depth​ ​semi-structured​ ​interviews​ ​and​ ​moderating​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​to​
​designing​ ​appropriate​ ​questionnaires.​ ​While​ ​the​ ​project​ ​has​ ​greatly​ ​benefited​ ​from​ ​the​
​diverse​ ​range​ ​of​ ​techniques​ ​used,​ ​it​ ​has​ ​also​ ​been​ ​advantageous​ ​for​ ​the​ ​researcher.​ ​This​
​approach​ ​has​ ​allowed​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​to​ ​become​ ​proficient​ ​in​ ​various​ ​qualitative​ ​methods,​
​enhancing​​their​​ability​​to​​triangulate​​data​​effectively​​and​​draw​​well-rounded​​conclusions.​​The​
​next​​stage​​of​​this​​chapter​​will​​offer​​some​​methodological​​reflections​​in​​a​​chronological​​order​
​reflecting​ ​on​ ​each​ ​phase​ ​of​ ​the​ ​project​ ​to​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​clear​ ​and​ ​structured​ ​analysis​ ​of​ ​the​
​research process.​


​Phase 1 methodological reflections​


​As​ ​outlined​ ​in​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​1​ ​methodology,​ ​the​ ​first​ ​phase​ ​of​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​involved​
​conducting​ ​expert​ ​interviews​ ​with​ ​specialists​ ​in​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​in​ ​sport.​ ​However,​ ​the​


                                                            ​284​
​researcher​ ​encountered​ ​some​ ​recruitment​ ​challenges​ ​during​ ​the​ ​preparation​ ​for​ ​these​
​interviews.​​Given​​the​​specific​​focus​​of​​this​​study,​​the​​researcher​​aimed​​to​​engage​​individuals​
​from​ ​certain​ ​organisations​ ​working​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​football​ ​to​ ​gain​ ​feedback​ ​on​ ​their​
​current​ ​initiatives.​ ​However,​ ​some​ ​organisations​​declined​​to​​participate​​in​​the​​research​​due​
​to​ ​lack​ ​of​ ​time​ ​and​ ​changes​ ​in​ ​their​​staffing.​​Additionally,​​some​​participants​​were​​happy​​to​
​talk​​about​​their​​work​​in​​an​​informal​​manner​​but​​not​​to​​take​​part​​within​​the​​research​​process​
​and​​for​​any​​comments​​not​​to​​be​​included​​in​​the​​research.​​Hennink​​et​​al​.​​(2020)​​explored​​how​
​participants​ ​may​ ​be​ ​hesitant​ ​to​ ​engage​ ​in​ ​certain​ ​contexts​ ​due​ ​to​ ​factors​ ​such​ ​as​ ​social​
​hierarchies​​and​​expectations.​​However,​​it​​is​​essential​​to​​emphasise​​that​​participation​​should​
​always​ ​be​ ​voluntary​ ​(Nelson​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2011).​ ​While​ ​research​ ​ethics​ ​mandate​ ​that​ ​all​
​participation​ ​must​ ​be​ ​voluntary,​ ​allowing​ ​these​ ​organisations​ ​the​ ​right​ ​to​ ​decline​
​involvement,​ ​their​ ​participation​ ​would​ ​have​ ​been​ ​especially​ ​valuable​ ​given​ ​the​ ​complex​
​nature​ ​of​ ​this​ ​topic.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​limited​ ​work​ ​being​ ​done​ ​in​ ​this​ ​area​ ​highlights​ ​the​
​importance​ ​of​ ​collaborating​ ​with​ ​key​​stakeholders,​​which​​would​​have​​strengthened​​specific​
​elements​ ​related​ ​to​ ​antisemitism​​in​​football.​​Despite​​these​​challenges,​​the​​experts​​who​​did​
​participate provided valuable support for developing the initiative.​


​Unfortunately,​​due​​to​​the​​Covid-19​​pandemic,​​interviews​​had​​to​​be​​conducted​​online​​(Brown,​
​2022;​ ​Sah,​ ​Singh​​and​​Sah,​​2020).​​This​​created​​some​​limitations,​​such​​as​​reducing​​the​​ability​
​to​ ​observe​ ​body​ ​language​ ​and​ ​tone,​ ​which​ ​are​ ​crucial​ ​elements​ ​in​ ​understanding​ ​the​ ​full​
​context​​of​​participants'​​responses​​(Brown,​​2022).​​The​​lack​​of​​in-person​​interaction​​may​​have​
​also​ ​affected​ ​the​ ​depth​ ​of​ ​rapport​ ​that​ ​could​ ​be​ ​established​ ​between​ ​the​ ​interviewer​ ​and​
​participants,​ ​potentially​ ​leading​ ​to​ ​more​ ​limited​ ​discussions​ ​(Keen,​ ​Lomeli-Rodriguez​ ​and​
​Joffe,​​2022).​​Additionally,​​technical​​problems,​​such​​as​​internet​​connection​​issues,​​could​​have​
​disrupted​ ​the​ ​flow​ ​of​ ​conversation,​ ​further​ ​limiting​ ​the​ ​quality​ ​of​ ​the​ ​data​ ​collected​ ​(Sah,​
​Singh​ ​and​ ​Sah,​ ​2020).​ ​Despite​ ​these​ ​challenges,​ ​efforts​ ​were​ ​made​ ​to​ ​mitigate​ ​these​
​limitations​ ​by​ ​encouraging​ ​participants​ ​to​ ​express​ ​themselves​ ​fully​ ​and​ ​by​ ​paying​ ​close​
​attention to verbal cues during the interviews.​


​Overall,​ ​conducting​ ​interviews​ ​with​ ​experts​ ​online​ ​proved​ ​beneficial,​ ​as​ ​virtual​ ​interviews​
​often​ ​help​ ​participants​ ​feel​ ​more​ ​relaxed​ ​and​ ​under​ ​less​ ​pressure​ ​to​ ​disclose​ ​personal​
​information.​ ​Reflecting​ ​on​ ​the​ ​process,​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​online​ ​platforms​ ​also​​contributed​​to​​the​


                                                            ​285​
​researcher's​ ​own​ ​comfort,​ ​as​ ​being​​in​​a​​familiar​​environment​​reduced​​stress​​and​​facilitated​
​better​​focus.​​Furthermore,​​scheduling​​interviews​​became​​more​​convenient​​since​​participants​
​only​ ​needed​ ​to​ ​be​ ​available​ ​during​ ​the​ ​interview​ ​itself,​ ​without​ ​the​​added​​commitment​​of​
​activities​ ​like​ ​travel.​ ​As​ ​a​ ​result,​ ​online​ ​interviews​ ​were​ ​less​ ​time-consuming​ ​for​ ​both​ ​the​
​interviewer and the interviewees and, ultimately, more cost-effective (Cleland​​et al.​, 2019).​


​Finally,​​a​​key​​strength​​of​​the​​project​​was​​the​​inclusion​​of​​those​​experts​​who​​took​​part​​in​​data​
​collection​ ​on​ ​numerous​ ​occasions.​ ​This​ ​is​ ​extremely​ ​important​ ​for​ ​the​ ​success​ ​of​ ​the​
​initiative​ ​were​ ​it​ ​to​ ​be​ ​implemented,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​is​ ​critical​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​relationships​ ​with​ ​key​
​stakeholders,​ ​as​ ​discussed​ ​in​​the​​sub-theme​​‘Sport​​and​​partnerships’​​in​​Phase​​1.​​Therefore,​
​throughout​ ​the​ ​three​ ​phases,​ ​some​ ​expert​ ​participants​ ​continued​​to​​take​​part​​in​​the​​study​
​and​​participated​​in​​multiple​​phases,​​which​​allowed​​the​​researcher​​to​​develop​​a​​professional​
​relationship​ ​with​ ​these​ ​individuals.​ ​Therefore,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​critical​ ​to​ ​make​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​with​
​these​ ​individuals​ ​as​ ​time-effective​ ​and​ ​cost-effective​​as​​possible​​to​​retain​​their​​input​​to​​the​
​process.​


​Phase 2 methodological reflections​


​As​ ​discussed​ ​in​ ​earlier​ ​chapters,​ ​data​ ​was​ ​collected​ ​through​ ​interviews,​ ​focus​ ​groups,​ ​and​
​questionnaires​​at​​different​​stages.​​This​​data​​was​​then​​incorporated​​into​​the​​book's​​narrative​
​in​​Phase​​2​​using​​CNF.​​Furthermore,​​CNF​​allowed​​the​​researcher​​to​​engage​​with​​two​​theories,​
​CRT​​and​​HebCrit,​​facilitating​​the​​development​​and​​expansion​​of​​these​​narratives.​​Therefore,​
​CNF​ ​offered​ ​a​ ​unique​ ​contribution​ ​to​ ​the​ ​research​ ​by​ ​integrating​ ​real-life​​experiences​​with​
​core​​tenets​​and​​insights​​from​​key​​theories​​to​​create​​a​​narrative​​designed​​to​​educate​​people​
​about​ ​discrimination​ ​(Kotišová,​ ​2019),​ ​specifically​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Additionally,​ ​using​ ​CNF​ ​to​
​integrate​​data​​and​​theory​​was​​essential​​because​​participants​​highlighted​​in​​the​​first​​round​​of​
​data​ ​collection​ ​the​ ​need​ ​to​ ​amplify​ ​the​ ​voices​​of​​marginalised​​communities,​​as​​seen​​in​​the​
​Phase​ ​1​ ​sub-theme​ ​‘First-Hand​ ​experience’.​ ​This​ ​theme​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​
​shaping​ ​initiatives​ ​based​ ​on​ ​the​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​those​ ​who​ ​have​ ​faced​ ​discrimination​ ​to​
​ensure they accurately reflect their realities.​




                                                            ​286​
​As​​discussed​​in​​Chapter​​6,​​titled​​‘Phase​​2:​​Creation​​of​​educational​​resource​​and​​focus​​groups’,​
​HebCrit​​(Rubin,​​2020),​​CRT​​(Delgado​​and​​Stefancic,​​2001),​​and​​BIM​​(Latané​​and​​Darley,​​1970)​
​were​ ​utilised​​as​​foundational​​frameworks​​for​​developing​​the​​narrative.​​These​​theories​​were​
​designed​ ​to​ ​reveal​ ​how​ ​racism​ ​and​ ​antisemitism​ ​are​ ​embedded​ ​within​ ​societal​ ​structures​
​and​​to​​challenge​​and​​deconstruct​​various​​dominant​​narratives.​​As​​CNF​​enables​​the​​reader​​to​
​viscerally​ ​enter​ ​the​ ​world​ ​of​ ​these​ ​individuals​ ​and​ ​their​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​(Clayton,​ ​2010),​
​these​ ​theories​ ​have​ ​been​ ​particularly​ ​effective​ ​in​ ​understanding​​the​​complexities​​of​​racism​
​and antisemitism in everyday life, thus amplifying the impact of the educational initiative.​


​Employing​​CNF​​also​​aligns​​with​​two​​key​​tenets​​of​​these​​theories.​​In​​CRT,​​a​​central​​tenet​​is​​the​
​use​ ​of​ ​storytelling​ ​and​ ​counter-storytelling,​ ​which​ ​are​ ​essential​ ​for​ ​teaching​ ​about​
​inequalities​ ​and​ ​everyday​ ​racism.​ ​Specifically,​ ​literature​ ​from​ ​Aguirre​ ​(2000,​ ​p.​ ​321)​ ​stated​
​that​ ​storytelling​ ​provides​ ​a​ ​valuable​ ​“methodological​ ​tool​ ​for​ ​giving​ ​voice​ ​to​ ​marginalised​
​persons​ ​and​ ​their​ ​communities”.​ ​These​ ​techniques​ ​have​ ​been​ ​argued​ ​to​ ​not​ ​only​ ​educate​
​and​ ​motivate,​ ​but​ ​to​ ​also​ ​document​ ​historical​ ​events​ ​and​ ​engage​ ​audiences​ ​(Collins​ ​and​
​Cooper,​​1997).​​Similarly,​​HebCrit​​emphasises​​the​​importance​​of​​storytelling​​as​​a​​core​​aspect​
​through​ ​the​ ​tenet​ ​‘Jewish​​personal​​stories​​have​​value’;​​this​​tenet​​reinforces​​the​​notion​​that​
​fully​ ​incorporating​ ​Jewish​ ​counter-stories​ ​will​ ​help​ ​to​​enhance​​the​​understanding​​of​​Jewish​
​people's​ ​lived​ ​experiences​ ​(Rubin,​ ​2020).​ ​As​ ​highlighted​ ​by​ ​both​ ​Delgado​ ​(1989)​ ​and​
​Solorzano​ ​and​ ​Yasso​ ​(2002),​ ​storytelling​​serves​​as​​a​​methodological​​approach​​that​​provides​
​rich,​ ​qualitative​​data​​articulated​​by​​members​​of​​marginalised​​groups​​who​​have​​experienced​
​racial​​discrimination​​and​​silencing.​​This​​approach​​allows​​these​​individuals​​to​​share​​their​​lived​
​experiences​​in​​their​​own​​voices.​​CNF​​enables​​researchers​​to​​incorporate​​dialogue​​and​​vividly​
​bring​​events​​to​​life​​(Clayton,​​2010).​​By​​utilising​​stories​​rooted​​in​​CRT​​and​​HebCrit,​​the​​use​​of​
​CNF​ ​transforms​ ​factual​ ​narratives​ ​into​ ​engaging​ ​and​ ​relatable​ ​accounts​ ​for​ ​the​ ​intended​
​audience.​ ​Using​ ​CNF​ ​to​ ​integrate​ ​theory​ ​into​ ​the​ ​narrative​ ​proved​ ​advantageous,​ ​as​ ​it​
​allowed​​the​​researcher​​to​​bring​​theoretical​​concepts​​to​​life.​​These​​concepts,​​derived​​from​​the​
​everyday​ ​experiences​ ​of​ ​marginalised​ ​communities,​ ​helped​ ​to​ ​illustrate​ ​and​ ​contextualise​
​complex​ ​issues​ ​of​ ​race​ ​and​ ​antisemitism.​ ​By​ ​telling​ ​stories​ ​that​ ​embody​​the​​core​​tenets​​of​
​both theories, CNF made these complex ideas more accessible and engaging.​




                                                           ​287​
​The​ ​key​ ​tenets​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​and​ ​HebCrit​ ​thus​ ​provided​ ​a​ ​framework​ ​for​ ​building​ ​narratives;​
​however,​​there​​were​​challenges​​associated​​with​​using​​these​​theories​​in​​educational​​settings​
​for​ ​children​ ​aged​ ​10-11​ ​years.​ ​Given​ ​that​ ​CRT​ ​and​ ​HebCrit​ ​were​ ​developed​ ​in​ ​higher​
​education​ ​contexts​ ​and​ ​contain​ ​complex​ ​concepts​ ​such​ ​as​ ​intersectionality,​ ​adapting​​these​
​theories​ ​to​ ​a​ ​younger​ ​audience​​required​​careful​​consideration.​​Consequently,​​not​​all​​tenets​
​of​​HebCrit​​and​​CRT​​could​​be​​fully​​incorporated​​into​​the​​initiative,​​as​​some​​concepts,​​such​​as​
​intersectionality,​ ​were​ ​considered​ ​too​ ​advanced​ ​or​ ​abstract​ ​for​ ​the​ ​intended​ ​age​ ​group.​
​Those​ ​tenets​ ​which​ ​were​​used​​have​​been​​outlined​​in​​Chapter​​6.​​Similarly,​​it​​is​​important​​to​
​note​​that​​throughout​​the​​process​​of​​this​​project​​the​​researcher​​did​​not​​adhere​​strictly​​to​​all​
​of​ ​the​ ​principles​ ​of​ ​CNF.​ ​Instead,​ ​the​ ​research​​was​​informed​​by​​key​​CNF​​principles,​​such​​as​
​integrating​ ​secondary​ ​data​ ​from​ ​past​ ​studies​ ​(Cheong,​ ​Lyons,​ ​Houghton​ ​and​ ​Majumdar,​
​2023)​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​​football​​to​​inform​​the​​initial​​draft​​of​​the​​book.​​Rather​​than​​basing​
​the​ ​narrative​ ​solely​ ​on​ ​empirical​ ​evidence​ ​collected​ ​during​ ​data​ ​gathering,​ ​the​ ​researcher​
​first​ ​used​ ​this​ ​secondary​ ​data​ ​to​ ​draft​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​and​ ​subsequently​ ​incorporated​ ​feedback​
​from​ ​the​ ​Jewish​​community​​and​​anti-discrimination​​experts​​through​​focus​​groups​​(Phase​​3)​
​and book reviews (Phase 4) to refine and enhance the content.​


​Having​ ​used​ ​secondary​ ​data,​ ​from​ ​both​ ​media​ ​articles​ ​and​ ​past​ ​studies​​on​​antisemitism​​in​
​society,​ ​sport,​ ​and​ ​football,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​built​ ​a​ ​foundation​ ​of​ ​existing​ ​knowledge​ ​to​
​develop​ ​a​ ​narrative​ ​around.​ ​Then,​ ​by​ ​engaging​ ​with​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​and​
​anti-discrimination​​experts,​​significant​​value​​was​​added​​to​​the​​research.​​This​​process​​helped​
​in​​refining​​and​​validating​​the​​content,​​making​​it​​more​​accurate​​and​​nuanced.​​The​​inclusion​​of​
​individual​ ​experiences​ ​ensures​ ​that​ ​the​ ​final​ ​work​ ​is​ ​representative​ ​and​ ​sensitive​ ​to​ ​the​
​experiences​ ​of​ ​those​ ​directly​ ​affected​ ​by​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Finally,​ ​by​ ​having​ ​an​ ​iterative​
​approach​​-​​through​​drafting​​the​​book​​first​​based​​on​​interview​​data​​and​​secondary​​data,​​and​
​then​​refining​​it​​with​​feedback​​from​​focus​​groups​​and​​book​​review​​-​​it​​enhanced​​the​​final​​draft​
​product’s​ ​quality.​ ​This​ ​method​ ​allows​ ​the​ ​researcher​​to​​incorporate​​a​​range​​of​​insights​​and​
​corrections, leading to a more comprehensive and polished work.​


​However,​ ​the​ ​project’s​ ​pragmatic​ ​alignment​ ​to​ ​certain​ ​CNF​ ​principles​ ​may​ ​have​ ​limited​ ​its​
​methodological​ ​rigour,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​did​ ​not​ ​adopt​ ​a​ ​‘purist’​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​CNF.​ ​CNF​
​emphasises​ ​grounding​ ​narratives​ ​in​ ​empirical​ ​evidence​ ​and​ ​constructing​ ​them​ ​through​


                                                          ​288​
​rigorous​ ​processes;​ ​by​ ​deviating​ ​from​ ​these​ ​principles,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​might​ ​have​ ​missed​
​capturing​​the​​most​​authentic​​and​​contextually​​grounded​​narratives.​​Additionally,​​the​​reliance​
​on​​secondary​​data​​-​​especially​​from​​media​​sources​​-​​could​​introduce​​biases​​or​​limitations​​that​
​might​ ​be​ ​perpetuated​ ​in​ ​the​ ​book​ ​if​ ​not​ ​carefully​ ​addressed​ ​during​ ​the​ ​revision​ ​process.​
​Finally,​ ​the​ ​delay​ ​in​ ​gathering​ ​feedback​ ​from​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​(Phases​ ​3​ ​and​ ​4)​ ​may​
​have​ ​constrained​ ​the​ ​accuracy​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initial​ ​narrative.​ ​Ideally,​ ​engaging​ ​these​ ​participants​
​from​​the​​outset​​would​​have​​ensured​​that​​the​​narrative​​was​​more​​directly​​informed​​by​​lived​
​experiences, thereby reducing the risk of misrepresentation.​


​Phase 3 methodological reflections​


​During​ ​Phase​ ​3,​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​were​ ​conducted​ ​to​ ​gather​ ​feedback​ ​on​ ​the​ ​first​ ​draft​ ​of​ ​the​
​initiative.​ ​This​ ​was​ ​particularly​ ​beneficial​ ​as​ ​it​ ​allowed​ ​the​ ​generation​ ​of​ ​constructive​
​feedback​ ​(Gray,​ ​2022)​ ​in​ ​order​ ​to​ ​make​ ​appropriate​ ​revisions.​ ​Most​ ​importantly,​ ​the​ ​focus​
​groups​ ​highlighted​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​a​ ​resource​ ​pack​ ​to​ ​accompany​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​which​ ​was​
​especially​ ​valuable​ ​as​ ​it​ ​provided​ ​additional​ ​support​ ​and​ ​context​ ​for​ ​staff​ ​using​ ​the​ ​book.​
​Overall,​ ​this​ ​phase​ ​of​ ​the​ ​project​ ​was​ ​highly​ ​advantageous​ ​as​ ​it​ ​facilitated​ ​meaningful​
​improvements​​based​​on​​direct​​input​​from​​participants.​​Additionally,​​this​​was​​the​​first​​phase​
​in​​which​​the​​researcher​​interacted​​extensively​​with​​members​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community,​​some​
​Jewish​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts​ ​who​ ​participated​ ​in​ ​Phase​ ​1.​ ​This​ ​was​ ​particularly​
​valuable,​​as​​incorporating​​the​​voices​​of​​the​​Jewish​​community​​ensured​​that​​the​​resource​​was​
​informed by those it aimed to represent and added authenticity to the narrative.​


​However,​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​also​ ​presented​ ​challenges,​ ​as​ ​participants​ ​had​ ​differing​
​opinions​​on​​some​​part​​of​​the​​initiative,​​leading​​to​​conflicting​​messages​​in​​the​​data.​​Notably,​
​there​ ​were​ ​disagreements​ ​about​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​the​ ​term​ ​‘Yid’​ ​in​ ​the​ ​book,​ ​reflecting​ ​broader​
​societal​​debates​​on​​the​​topic​​(Poulton​​and​​Durell,​​2016).​​Although​​this​​development​​created​
​challenges,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​was​ ​able​ ​to​ ​make​ ​judgement​ ​calls​ ​through​ ​the​ ​support​ ​of​ ​their​
​supervisory​​team​​who​​facilitated​​through​​the​​role​​of​​‘critical​​friends’​​(Richards​​and​​Fletcher,​
​2020).​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​looking​ ​forward​ ​it​ ​may​ ​be​ ​that​ ​sensitive​ ​topics​​such​​as​​the​​use​​of​​the​
​term ‘Yid’ are re-addressed if the book were to be published for wider distribution.​




                                                            ​289​
​Another​ ​outcome​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​was​ ​the​ ​need​ ​for​ ​images.​ ​However,​ ​as​ ​a​
​self-funded​ ​researcher,​ ​one​ ​of​ ​the​ ​most​ ​significant​ ​challenges​ ​encountered​​was​​the​​lack​​of​
​funding​ ​(Cornell,​ ​2020).​ ​This​ ​shortage​ ​of​ ​funds​ ​meant​ ​that​ ​the​ ​project​ ​could​​not​​meet​​the​
​desired​​standards,​​as​​the​​researcher​​could​​not​​afford​​to​​hire​​a​​professional​​editor,​​illustrator,​
​or​​publisher.​​These​​financial​​constraints​​created​​some​​difficulties​​throughout​​the​​duration​​of​
​the​​project.​​Therefore,​​due​​to​​limited​​funding,​​the​​researcher​​turned​​to​​artificial​​intelligence​
​(AI)​​software​​to​​generate​​the​​images​​for​​‘Joe’s​​Footballing​​Journey’.​​This​​approach,​​however,​
​came​ ​with​ ​its​ ​own​ ​set​ ​of​ ​challenges,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​reinforcing​ ​existing​ ​stereotypes,​ ​which​ ​were​
​detailed​ ​in​​the​​previous​​chapter.​​This​​was​​especially​​problematic​​given​​that​​the​​book​​aimed​
​to​ ​educate​ ​individuals​ ​about​ ​discrimination,​ ​specifically​ ​antisemitism.​ ​Using​ ​images​ ​that​
​perpetuated​ ​these​ ​biases​ ​and​ ​stereotypes​ ​would​ ​simply​ ​undermine​ ​the​ ​book's​ ​purpose​
​(Kong,​ ​2022;​ ​Naudts,​ ​2024).​ ​Nevertheless,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​pivotal​ ​that​ ​images​ ​were​ ​included,​ ​as​
​feedback​ ​from​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​3​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​emphasised​ ​the​ ​necessity​ ​of​ ​including​​imagery​​in​
​the​ ​book​ ​under​ ​the​ ​sub-theme​ ​‘Pedagogical​ ​Additions’,​ ​making​ ​the​ ​inclusion​ ​of​ ​images​
​essential.​


​Given​ ​the​ ​limited​ ​funding​ ​available,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​and​ ​their​ ​supervisory​ ​team​ ​carefully​
​weighed​​the​​strengths​​and​​limitations​​of​​using​​AI​​for​​the​​images.​​The​​primary​​advantage​​was​
​the​ ​cost-effectiveness​ ​of​ ​AI,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​either​ ​free​ ​or​ ​available​ ​at​ ​a​ ​minimal​ ​annual​ ​fee,​
​compared​ ​to​ ​the​ ​high​​costs​​quoted​​by​​illustrators.​​Therefore,​​to​​overcome​​some​​challenges​
​(e.g.​ ​biases),​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​invested​ ​considerable​ ​time​ ​in​ ​selecting​ ​the​ ​most​ ​suitable​ ​AI​
​software​​(through​​which​​Canva​​Pro​​was​​selected)​​and​​edited​​specific​​images​​to​​ensure​​they​
​were​​appropriate​​for​​the​​book.​​Despite​​this,​​it​​is​​worth​​noting​​that​​during​​the​​final​​phase​​of​
​data​ ​collection​ ​in​ ​the​ ​Phase​ ​4​ ​book​ ​review,​ ​a​ ​participant​ ​suggested​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​
​“finding​ ​an​ ​illustrator​ ​or​ ​graphic​ ​artist​ ​who​ ​can​ ​produce​ ​images​ ​that​​bring​​the​​narrative​​to​
​life,”​ ​while​ ​acknowledging​ ​that​ ​“I​ ​realise​ ​that​​all​​this​​might​​have​​funding​​implications”.​​This​
​comment​ ​underscores​ ​the​ ​financial​ ​constraints​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​faced​ ​and​ ​the​ ​limitations​
​imposed on realising the full potential of the project.​


​Despite​ ​these​ ​challenges,​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​has​ ​initiated​ ​several​ ​conversations​ ​with​
​organisations​ ​that​ ​showed​ ​substantial​ ​interest​ ​in​ ​developing​ ​a​ ​partnership;​ ​these​ ​included​
​experts​ ​who​ ​took​ ​part​ ​in​ ​both​ ​the​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​and​ ​‘book​ ​review’.​ ​However,​ ​these​


                                                           ​290​
​organisations​ ​required​ ​a​ ​finalised​ ​product,​ ​which​ ​had​ ​been​ ​trialled​ ​and​ ​tested,​ ​before​
​committing​ ​to​ ​any​ ​investment.​ ​Therefore,​ ​trialling​ ​and​ ​testing​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​will​ ​likely​ ​form​
​part​ ​of​ ​a​ ​future​ ​research​ ​plan​ ​for​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​in​ ​order​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​this​ ​work.​ ​Looking​
​ahead,​ ​securing​ ​funding​ ​would​ ​greatly​ ​enhance​​the​​initiative's​​success.​​It​​would​​enable​​the​
​researcher​​to​​hire​​a​​professional​​proofreader​​and​​editor,​​or​​an​​illustrator,​​to​​ensure​​the​​final​
​product​​meets​​the​​highest​​standards,​​as​​highlighted​​by​​participants​​in​​the​​final​​phase​​of​​data​
​collection.​


​Phase 4 methodological reflections​


​In​ ​the​ ​previous​ ​methodology​ ​section​ ​(Phase​ ​4),​ ​it​​was​​discussed​​that​​the​​final​​stage​​of​​this​
​project​ ​was​ ​to​ ​trial​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​in​ ​schools​ ​in​ ​May​ ​2024.​ ​During​ ​the​ ​initial​ ​data​ ​collection​
​under​​the​​sub-theme​​‘recommendations’​​in​​Phase​​1,​​it​​was​​suggested​​that​​a​​trial​​or​​pilot​​of​
​the​ ​initiative,​ ​including​ ​the​ ​children's​​book​​and​​resource​​pack,​​was​​necessary.​​A​​trial​​would​
​have​ ​been​ ​particularly​ ​beneficial​ ​during​ ​the​ ​PhD​ ​process,​ ​providing​ ​an​ ​opportunity​ ​to​
​evaluate​ ​the​ ​initiative's​​success​​and​​make​​any​​necessary​​adjustments​​based​​on​​the​​findings​
​(Lendrum and Humphrey, 2012).​


​However,​ ​in​ ​October​ ​2023,​ ​when​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​attempted​ ​to​ ​arrange​ ​this​ ​final​​stage,​​the​
​schools​ ​that​ ​had​ ​initially​ ​shown​ ​interest​ ​indicated​ ​they​ ​could​ ​not​ ​proceed​ ​due​ ​to​ ​the​
​geopolitical​ ​situation,​ ​particularly​ ​the​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​ ​conflict.​ ​This​ ​development​ ​posed​
​significant​​challenges​​for​​the​​progression​​of​​this​​research​​project.​​Firstly,​​the​​researcher​​faced​
​a​ ​significant​ ​challenge​ ​as​ ​they​ ​were​ ​unable​ ​to​ ​complete​ ​a​ ​trial,​ ​which​ ​would​​have​​allowed​
​them​​to​​observe​​the​​initiative​​in​​practice​​and​​measure​​its​​impact.​​Additionally,​​it​​limited​​the​
​scope​​of​​the​​research,​​preventing​​the​​collection​​of​​crucial​​feedback​​that​​could​​inform​​future​
​iterations of the initiative.​


​Although​ ​the​ ​trial​ ​could​ ​not​ ​proceed,​ ​the​ ​supervisory​ ​team​ ​and​ ​the​ ​researcher​​decided​​to​
​gather​ ​a​ ​final​​portion​​of​​data​​to​​gain​​further​​feedback​​on​​the​​amended​​children's​​book​​and​
​the​ ​newly​ ​created​ ​resource​ ​pack.​ ​They​ ​decided​ ​the​ ​best​ ​option​ ​would​ ​be​ ​to​ ​gain​ ​further​
​feedback​ ​from​ ​specialist​ ​experts​ ​to​ ​gain​ ​greater​ ​insights.​ ​Although​ ​this​ ​was​ ​not​ ​what​ ​was​




                                                               ​291​
​envisioned​ ​for​ ​Phase​ ​4,​ ​it​ ​still​ ​provided​​valuable​​insights​​into​​various​​aspects,​​including​​the​
​publishability, practicality, structure, and layout of the materials.​


​Despite​ ​having​ ​an​ ​alternative​ ​plan,​ ​the​ ​withdrawal​ ​of​ ​school​ ​participation​ ​reinforced​ ​the​
​greater​ ​need​ ​for​ ​such​ ​initiatives.​ ​Data​ ​from​ ​CST​ ​(2023)​ ​has​ ​shown​ ​that​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​
​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​rose​ ​by​ ​589%​ ​following​ ​the​ ​Hamas​ ​terror​ ​attack​ ​on​ ​Israel​ ​on​ ​October​ ​7.​
​This​ ​highlights​ ​how​ ​the​ ​Israeli-Palestinian​ ​conflict​ ​had​ ​increased​ ​prejudice​ ​and​ ​hostility​
