​towards​ ​Jewish​ ​individuals,​ ​reinforcing​ ​the​ ​persistent​ ​issue​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​the​ ​UK.​ ​As​
​discussed​ ​previously,​ ​the​​IHRA’s​​(2016)​​definition​​of​​antisemitism​​includes​​examples​​related​
​to Israel that are considered antisemitic:​


    ​●​ ​Accusing​ ​Jewish​ ​citizens​ ​of​ ​being​ ​more​ ​loyal​ ​to​ ​Israel,​ ​or​ ​to​​the​​alleged​​priorities​​of​
         ​Jews worldwide, than to the interests of their own nations.​
    ​●​ ​Using​ ​the​ ​symbols​ ​and​ ​images​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​classic​ ​antisemitism​ ​(e.g.,​ ​claims​ ​of​
         ​Jews killing Jesus or blood libel) to characterise Israel or Israelis.​
    ​●​ ​Drawing comparisons of contemporary Israeli policy to that of the Nazis.​
    ​●​ ​Holding Jews collectively responsible for actions of the state of Israel.​


​As​ ​previously​ ​mentioned,​ ​antisemitism​ ​and​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​increased​ ​by​ ​589%​ ​since​
​October​ ​7th​ ​2023,​ ​with​ ​these​ ​four​ ​examples​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​becoming​ ​more​ ​prevalent​
​during​ ​this​ ​period.​ ​This​ ​is​ ​supported​ ​by​ ​reports​ ​from​ ​CST​ ​(2023),​ ​which​ ​found​ ​that​ ​of​ ​the​
​4,103​ ​instances​ ​of​ ​anti-Jewish​ ​hate​ ​reported​ ​in​ ​2023,​ ​2,699​ ​(66%)​ ​occurred​ ​on​ ​or​ ​after​
​October​ ​7th.​ ​The​ ​most​ ​common​ ​form​ ​of​ ​antisemitic​ ​abuse​ ​was​ ​related​​to​​Israel,​​Palestine,​
​the​​Hamas​​terror​​attack,​​or​​the​​subsequent​​war.​​Additionally,​​incidents​​involving​​damage​​and​
​desecration​​of​​Jewish​​property,​​including​​schools,​​synagogues,​​and​​cemeteries,​​increased​​by​
​146%,​ ​often​ ​accompanied​ ​by​ ​language​ ​referencing​ ​Israel,​ ​Palestine,​ ​and​ ​anti-Jewish​
​sentiments.​


​Within​ ​the​ ​book​ ​‘Joe’s​ ​Footballing​ ​Journey,’​ ​there​ ​is​ ​no​ ​discussion​ ​of​ ​the​​Israeli-Palestinian​
​conflict;​​it​​solely​​focuses​​on​​Judaism​​and​​antisemitism.​​Although​​the​​challenges​​schools​​face​
​in​ ​navigating​ ​the​ ​complexities​ ​of​ ​teaching​ ​about​ ​antisemitism​ ​are​ ​recognised,​ ​especially​ ​in​
​the​​context​​of​​the​​Israeli-Palestinian​​conflict​​(Bernstein,​​Grimm​​and​​Müller,​​2022),​​it​​is​​crucial​


                                                            ​292​
​for​ ​schools​ ​to​ ​recognise​ ​that​ ​antisemitism,​ ​as​ ​a​ ​form​ ​of​ ​prejudice​ ​and​ ​discrimination,​ ​can​
​exist​ ​independently​ ​of​ ​geopolitical​ ​events​ ​(Cohen​ ​et​ ​al.​,​ ​2009).​​Jewish​​education,​​including​
​the​ ​teaching​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​culture​ ​and​ ​religion,​ ​should​ ​not​ ​be​​diminished​​by​​political​​tensions.​
​Therefore,​ ​schools​ ​have​ ​a​ ​responsibility​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​students​ ​about​ ​all​ ​forms​ ​of​
​discrimination, including antisemitism, to foster a more inclusive society.​


​Before​ ​contacting​ ​the​ ​schools,​ ​there​ ​was​ ​an​ ​expectation​ ​that​ ​they​ ​might​ ​withdraw​ ​from​
​participation​ ​in​ ​light​ ​of​ ​the​ ​aforementioned​ ​concerns.​ ​Nonetheless,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​hoped​ ​that​ ​the​
​schools​ ​would​ ​recognise​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​especially​ ​given​ ​the​ ​rise​ ​in​
​antisemitism​​at​​that​​time.​​Nevertheless,​​one​​particular​​school​​consulted​​with​​their​​governors​
​and​​senior​​leadership​​team​​regarding​​the​​trial​​and​​feared​​it​​might​​create​​additional​​tensions​
​between​ ​parents.​ ​The​​‘role​​of​​the​​parent’​​(Phase​​3)​​was​​a​​significant​​finding​​from​​the​​focus​
​groups,​ ​highlighting​ ​that​ ​parental​ ​political​ ​or​ ​negative​ ​viewpoints​ ​can​ ​often​ ​hinder​ ​the​
​success​​of​​an​​initiative.​​This​​setback​​has​​shown​​that​​the​​role​​of​​parents​​significantly​​impacts​
​the​ ​success​ ​of​ ​such​ ​initiatives,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​prevents​​the​​initiative's​​growth.​​For​​example,​​literature​
​from​ ​Hermann-Wilmarth​ ​and​ ​Ryan​ ​(2019)​ ​found​ ​that​ ​the​ ​role​ ​of​ ​the​ ​parent​ ​can​ ​create​
​significant​ ​challenges​ ​within​ ​education​​for​​similarly​​sensitive​​topics,​​as​​their​​research​​found​
​that​ ​parents​ ​often​ ​objected​ ​to​ ​the​ ​teaching​ ​of​ ​same-sex​ ​relationships​ ​within​ ​primary​
​education.​​This​​situation​​highlighted​​a​​significant​​challenge​​going​​forward​​with​​the​​initiative,​
​emphasising​ ​the​ ​need​ ​to​ ​carefully​ ​navigate​ ​and​ ​address​ ​the​ ​concerns​ ​of​ ​all​ ​involved​
​individuals​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​successful​ ​implementation.​ ​Although​ ​this​ ​was​ ​an​ ​unfortunate​ ​matter​
​that​ ​impacted​​the​​final​​stage​​of​​the​​data​​collection,​​it​​does​​provide​​opportunities​​for​​future​
​research, which will be discussed within the later stages of this chapter.​

​Original contribution to knowledge​

​This​ ​thesis​ ​has​ ​made​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​contribution​ ​to​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​the​ ​sociology​ ​of​ ​sport​ ​by​
​engaging​ ​with​ ​HebCrit​ ​(Rubin,​​2020),​​a​​theoretical​​framework​​that,​​as​​previously​​discussed,​
​has​​not​​yet​​been​​applied​​to​​the​​study​​of​​sports,​​particularly​​within​​the​​context​​of​​the​​United​
​Kingdom.​ ​Given​ ​the​ ​recent​ ​development​ ​of​ ​HebCrit,​ ​navigating​ ​its​ ​application​ ​required​ ​a​
​cautious​ ​approach,​ ​as​ ​it​ ​presents​ ​certain​ ​limitations​ ​that​ ​are​ ​typically​ ​acknowledged​ ​and​
​addressed​ ​by​ ​researchers​ ​throughout​ ​the​ ​research​ ​process.​ ​This​ ​thesis​​thus​​represents​​the​
​first​​critical​​examination​​of​​Rubin's​​(2020)​​HebCrit​​theory​​in​​the​​field​​of​​the​​sociology​​of​​sport​


                                                            ​293​
​-​​and​​possibly​​beyond​​this​​field​​-​ ​providing​​a​​unique​​perspective​​that​​has​​yet​​to​​be​​offered​​in​
​existing​​literature​​to​​the​​best​​of​​my​​knowledge.​​As​​a​​result,​​this​​research​​not​​only​​adds​​to​​the​
​academic​ ​discussion​ ​on​ ​antisemitism​ ​in​ ​sport,​ ​but​ ​also​ ​opens​ ​the​ ​door​ ​for​​further​​critique​
​and refinement of Rubin's theory, encouraging ongoing scholarly debate and development.​

​Rubin​ ​(2020)​ ​emphasises​ ​the​ ​significance​ ​of​ ​Jewish​ ​personal​ ​stories,​ ​particularly​ ​when​
​framed​ ​through​ ​the​ ​lens​ ​of​ ​creative​ ​nonfiction​ ​(CNF),​ ​as​ ​it​ ​ensures​ ​the​​narratives​​are​​both​
​authentic​ ​and​ ​derived​ ​from​ ​the​ ​research​ ​data​ ​(Smith​ ​et​ ​al.,​ ​2015).​ ​By​ ​doing​ ​so,​ ​these​
​narratives​ ​go​ ​beyond​ ​storytelling​ ​to​ ​contribute​ ​meaningfully​ ​to​ ​academic​ ​discourse,​ ​by​
​presenting​ ​nuanced​ ​insights​ ​that​ ​amplify​ ​the​ ​voices​ ​of​ ​this​ ​marginalised​ ​community.​ ​This​
​approach​ ​not​ ​only​ ​presents​ ​and​ ​gives​ ​voice​ ​to​ ​individual​ ​experiences​ ​but​ ​also​ ​challenges​
​existing frameworks by integrating lived realities into scholarly research.​

​Furthermore,​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​CNF​ ​has​ ​demonstrated​ ​methodological​ ​innovation,​ ​particularly​ ​in​
​fields​​like​​the​​sociology​​of​​sport,​​where​​such​​approaches​​remain​​underutilised.​​As​​of​​now,​​no​
​known​ ​scholars​ ​within​ ​this​ ​discipline​ ​have​ ​employed​ ​CNF​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​initiatives​ ​addressing​
​racial​ ​or​ ​religious​ ​discrimination.​ ​Although​ ​similar​ ​projects​ ​have​ ​helped​ ​to​ ​inspire​ ​this​
​project,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Sense​ ​over​ ​Sectarianism​ ​(n.d.)​ ​who​ ​use​ ​storytelling​ ​to​ ​educate​ ​young​
​children​​about​​sectarianism,​​this​​is​​the​​first​​children's​​book​​on​​antisemitism​​in​​football​​which​
​has​​been​​informed​​by​​academic​​and​​sociological​​theory​​through​​the​​use​​of​​CNF.​​By​​bringing​
​to​ ​attention​ ​the​ ​personal,​ ​theoretically-informed,​ ​and​ ​research-grounded​ ​narratives,​ ​the​
​study​​not​​only​​enhances​​scholarly​​knowledge​​but​​also​​provides​​an​​avenue​​for​​future​​research​
​by using CNF as a transformative tool in other areas of sociological research.​

​As​ ​seen​ ​in​ ​part​ ​of​ ​‘Joe’s​​Footballing​​Journey’,​​CNF​​has​​not​​only​​been​​utilised​​to​​amplify​​the​
​voices​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​but​ ​has​ ​also​ ​incorporated​ ​media-based​ ​experiences​ ​and​
​survey​ ​data​ ​from​ ​organisations​ ​like​ ​Level​ ​Playing​ ​Field.​ ​Through​ ​CNF,​ ​these​ ​efforts​ ​aim​ ​to​
​highlight​​the​​match-day​​experiences​​of​​disabled​​sports​​fans,​​giving​​them​​a​​platform​​to​​share​
​their​ ​perspectives.​ ​As​ ​mentioned,​ ​the​ ​next​ ​section​ ​of​ ​this​ ​concluding​ ​chapter,​ ​a​ ​future​
​recommendation​ ​is​ ​to​ ​further​ ​encourage​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​CNF​ ​to​ ​give​ ​voice​ ​to​ ​other​
​underrepresented​​groups​​and​​to​​explore​​its​​potential​​in​​addressing​​broader​​social​​inequality​
​issues within sport.​




                                                           ​294​
​Future recommendations​

​As​ ​mentioned​ ​in​​the​​review​​of​​literature,​​there​​are​​current​​initiatives​​being​​implemented​​in​
​the​​field​​of​​sport​​and​​football​​to​​decrease​​antisemitism​​in​​England,​​such​​as​​Chelsea​​FC’s​​‘Say​
​No​​To​​Antisemitism’​​campaign.​​Nevertheless,​​as​​discussed​​previously,​​there​​is​​still​​much​​work​
​to​​be​​done​​to​​fully​​address​​this​​issue​​and​​these​​campaigns​​are​​not​​designed​​to​​be​​embedded​
​into​ ​traditional​ ​school​ ​curriculum;​ ​instead,​ ​they​ ​attempt​ ​to​ ​work​ ​with​ ​individuals​ ​already​
​attending​​matches,​​some​​of​​which​​are​​wishing​​to​​reduce​​their​​ban​​for​​antisemitic​​behaviours​
​(Chelsea FC, 2018).​

​As​​mentioned​​in​​the​​previous​​chapter,​​the​​plan​​was​​to​​conduct​​a​​feasibility​​trial​​as​​part​​of​​this​
​PhD.​ ​However,​ ​due​ ​to​ ​various​ ​factors,​ ​including​ ​the​ ​current​ ​political​ ​climate,​ ​funding​
​constraints,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​time​ ​needed​ ​for​​a​​full​​feasibility​​study,​​it​​was​​not​​possible​​to​​carry​​out​
​the​ ​trial.​ ​Therefore,​ ​looking​ ​forward,​ ​one​ ​recommendation​ ​would​​be​​to​​complete​​a​​trial​​of​
​the​ ​initiative​ ​to​ ​measure​ ​its​ ​success​ ​and​ ​effectiveness.​ ​This​ ​would​ ​involve​ ​another​
​multi-phased​ ​project​ ​including​ ​interviews,​ ​questionnaires,​ ​and​ ​observations​ ​in​ ​order​ ​to​
​collect​ ​data​ ​on​​the​​book’s​​utility​​in​​a​​real-world​​context.​​The​​intention​​behind​​the​​following​
​stages​​is​​to​​gather​​comprehensive​​data​​on​​the​​effectiveness​​of​​the​​initiative,​​assess​​its​​impact​
​on​ ​the​ ​target​ ​audience,​ ​and​ ​understand​ ​how​ ​it​ ​is​ ​received​ ​and​ ​implemented​ ​by​​educators​
​and students.​

​Pre-​ ​and​ ​post-trial​ ​interviews​ ​will​ ​be​ ​conducted​ ​with​ ​the​ ​class​​teacher​​to​​gain​​insights​​into​
​their​ ​perspectives​ ​before​ ​and​ ​after​ ​the​ ​initiative.​ ​The​ ​pre-trial​ ​interview​ ​establishes​ ​a​
​baseline​​understanding​​of​​the​​teacher’s​​expectations,​​while​​the​​post-trial​​interview​​explores​
​changes​ ​in​ ​perceptions,​ ​challenges​ ​faced,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​initiative's​ ​overall​ ​effectiveness.​
​Additionally,​ ​short,​ ​paper-based​ ​questionnaires​ ​will​ ​be​​administered​​to​​children​​before​​and​
​after​ ​the​ ​trial​ ​to​ ​measure​ ​their​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​the​ ​content,​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Judaism​ ​and​
​antisemitism,​ ​using​ ​Likert​ ​scales.​ ​Finally,​ ​researcher​ ​observations​ ​will​ ​focus​ ​on​ ​staff​ ​and​
​student​ ​engagement,​ ​assessing​ ​the​ ​teaching​ ​methods​ ​and​ ​the​ ​initiative’s​ ​reception​ ​in​ ​the​
​classroom.​

​Collectively,​ ​interviews,​ ​questionnaires​ ​and​ ​observations​ ​of​ ​this​ ​nature​ ​would​ ​provide​ ​a​
​holistic​​view,​​offering​​comprehensive​​insights​​into​​participants'​​perspectives​​and​​experiences​



                                                           ​295​
​(Gardner,​ ​2010;​ ​Koskei​ ​and​ ​Simiyu,​ ​2015)​ ​of​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​in​ ​practice.​ ​However,​ ​prior​ ​to​
​trialling​ ​the​ ​initiative,​ ​the​ ​aim​ ​would​ ​be​ ​to​ ​secure​ ​funding​ ​to​ ​enhance​ ​the​ ​book​ ​and​
​resources,​ ​potentially​ ​through​ ​the​ ​use​ ​of​ ​an​ ​illustrator​ ​or​ ​editor,​ ​as​ ​suggested​ ​in​ ​the​ ​final​
​round​​of​​data​​collection.​​By​​trialling​​the​​initiative,​​valuable​​data​​could​​be​​gathered​​to​​confirm​
​whether​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​has​ ​scope​ ​in​ ​schools.​ ​If​ ​this​ ​proves​ ​successful,​ ​the​ ​goal​ ​would​​be​​to​
​collaborate​ ​with​ ​relevant​ ​organisations​ ​or​ ​individuals​ ​to​ ​facilitate​ ​its​ ​implementation​ ​in​
​schools.​ ​This​ ​might​ ​include​ ​participants​ ​from​ ​the​ ​research​ ​and​ ​data​ ​collection​ ​phases​​who​
​have shown interest and are well-equipped to contribute.​

​Having​​reflected​​upon​​this​​project​​in​​depth,​​there​​are​​several​​areas​​where​​further​​research​​is​
​needed.​​This​​includes​​exploring​​HebCrit​​in​​the​​context​​of​​England​​by​​engaging​​with​​members​
​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​to​ ​determine​ ​if​ ​the​ ​key​ ​tenets​ ​of​ ​HebCrit​ ​align​ ​with​ ​their​
​experiences.​ ​To​ ​ensure​ ​this​ ​process​ ​remains​ ​reflexive,​ ​it​ ​is​ ​essential​ ​to​ ​acknowledge​ ​the​
​researcher’s​ ​own​ ​positionality​ ​(Hadi​ ​and​ ​José,​ ​2016)​ ​and​ ​actively​​avoid​​projecting​​personal​
​assumptions​​onto​​the​​study.​​Engaging​​in​​dialogue​​with​​the​​Jewish​​community​​will​​allow​​their​
​lived​​experiences​​to​​shape​​the​​research​​(Rubin,​​2020).​​Additionally,​​there​​is​​scope​​to​​explore​
​how​ ​policy​ ​could​ ​implement​ ​HebCrit​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​the​ ​voices​ ​of​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community​ ​are​
​reflected in educational and societal frameworks.​

​Finally,​ ​sport​ ​has​ ​been​ ​recognised​ ​as​ ​a​ ​powerful​ ​tool​ ​to​​address​​and​​reduce​​discrimination​
​(Oliver,​ ​2014),​ ​supporting​ ​the​ ​argument​ ​that​ ​sport​ ​as​ ​a​ ​powerful​ ​tool​ ​in​ ​which​ ​to​ ​address​
​discrimination​ ​from​ ​organisations​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Kick​ ​It​ ​Out​ ​who​ ​have​ ​used​ ​their​ ​platform​ ​to​
​reinforce​ ​the​ ​importance​ ​of​ ​equality,​ ​inclusion,​ ​and​ ​diversity​ ​within​ ​football,​ ​while​ ​raising​
​awareness​ ​and​ ​challenging​ ​discriminatory​ ​behaviour​ ​across​ ​all​ ​levels​ ​of​ ​the​ ​sport.​ ​Looking​
​ahead,​ ​there​ ​are​ ​plans​ ​to​ ​collaborate​ ​with​ ​other​ ​scholars​ ​and​ ​academics​ ​to​ ​use​ ​creative​
​non-fiction​ ​to​ ​write​ ​a​ ​series​ ​of​ ​books​ ​that​ ​leverage​ ​various​ ​sporting​ ​contexts​ ​to​ ​address​
​challenging​ ​issues​ ​related​ ​to​ ​discrimination.​ ​For​ ​instance,​ ​narratives​ ​could​ ​be​ ​crafted​ ​to​
​discuss​ ​topics​ ​such​ ​as​ ​disability,​ ​gender,​ ​and​ ​sexuality,​ ​potentially​ ​being​ ​adapted​ ​to​ ​reach​
​different​ ​populations.​​For​​example,​​working​​with​​campaigns​​and​​organisations​​such​​as​​‘ This​
​Girl​​Can’​​or​​‘Women​​in​​Sport’​​and​​like-minded​​scholars​​whose​​work​​has​​explored​​challenges,​
​inequalities​ ​and​ ​discrimination​ ​would​​be​​beneficial​​for​​developing​​narratives​​in​​sport​​which​
​could amplify the voices and experiences of female athletes in sport.​



                                                             ​296​
​Personal reflection​

​Lastly,​ ​I​ ​wish​ ​to​ ​reflect​ ​personally​ ​on​ ​this​ ​project.​ ​In​ ​the​ ​reflexivity​ ​section​ ​(see​ ​p.​ ​102),​ ​I​
​discuss​ ​my​ ​religious​ ​upbringing​ ​and​ ​heritage,​ ​intending​ ​to​ ​share​ ​and​ ​reflect​ ​upon​ ​how​ ​my​
​personal​ ​experiences​ ​and​ ​beliefs​​may​​have​​impacted​​this​​project,​​and​​what​​measures​​were​
​put​​in​​place​​to​​ensure​​my​​biases​​wouldn't​​affect​​the​​research.​​Reflecting​​back​​on​​the​​process,​
​I​ ​have​ ​been​ ​able​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​an​ ​understanding​ ​of​ ​how​ ​my​ ​own​ ​upbringing,​ ​personal​
​experiences,​​and​​Jewish​​identity​​likely​​played​​a​​significant​​role​​in​​shaping​​the​​research​​topic,​
​and subsequently the aim and objectives.​

​Firstly,​ ​my​ ​upbringing​ ​has​ ​influenced​ ​the​ ​selection​ ​of​ ​research​ ​topics,​ ​as​ ​discussed​ ​in​ ​this​
​personal​ ​reflection​ ​as​ ​it​ ​may​ ​have​ ​made​ ​me​ ​more​ ​aware​ ​of​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​the​ ​Jewish​
​community​​face.​​Additionally,​​the​​proposed​​aim​​and​​objectives​​could​​have​​been​​shaped​​due​
​to​ ​my​ ​personal​ ​motivations,​ ​particularly​ ​being​ ​motivated​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​how​ ​antisemitism​ ​is​
​experienced​ ​and​ ​understood​ ​by​ ​various​ ​groups,​ ​not​ ​just​​my​​own​​experiences.​​Additionally,​
​my​​upbringing​​may​​have​​driven​​me​​to​​identify​​and​​highlight​​practices​​that​​could​​be​​effective​
​in​ ​combating​ ​antisemitism,​ ​as​ ​an​ ​individual​ ​who​ ​wishes​ ​to​ ​advocate​ ​for​ ​better​ ​solutions.​
​Lastly,​ ​my​ ​background​ ​might​ ​influence​ ​my​ ​abilities​ ​to​ ​ensure​ ​that​​the​​initiative​​is​​culturally​
​relevant​ ​and​ ​sensitive​ ​to​ ​Jewish​ ​experiences;​ ​nevertheless,​ ​it​ ​was​ ​crucial​ ​to​ ​inform​ ​this​
​through​​numerous​​Jewish​​voices,​​as​​opposed​​to​​only​​my​​experiences.​​Lastly,​​it​​was​​important​
​for​ ​me​ ​to​ ​consider​ ​how​ ​my​ ​perspectives​ ​and​ ​experiences​ ​could​ ​shape​ ​how​ ​I​ ​interpret​
​responses​ ​from​ ​stakeholders,​ ​particularly​ ​in​ ​understanding​ ​their​ ​feedback​ ​on​​how​​well​​the​
​initiative addresses antisemitism.​

​However,​​I​​have​​not​​yet​​addressed​​how​​my​​upbringing​​and​​heritage​​led​​me​​to​​pursue​​a​​PhD​
​exploring​​antisemitism​​in​​football.​​It​​all​​started​​with​​a​​conversation​​during​​my​​undergraduate​
​studies.​ ​My​ ​now​ ​father-in-law,​ ​a​ ​Tottenham​ ​Hotspur​ ​supporter,​ ​asked​ ​me​ ​"How​ ​do​ ​your​
​family​​feel​​about​​the​​use​​of​​the​​word​​‘Yid’?".​​He​​was​​referring​​to​​my​​uncle​​and​​cousins,​​who​
​are​ ​also​ ​passionate​ ​Tottenham​​Hotspur​​fans​​and​​also​​Jewish.​​At​​the​​time,​​I​​was​​unaware​​of​
​Tottenham​​Hotspur's​​connection​​to​​the​​Jewish​​religion​​and,​​more​​importantly,​​the​​term​​‘Yid’.​
​This​ ​prompted​ ​open​ ​conversations​ ​with​ ​my​ ​family​ ​about​ ​the​ ​use​​of​​the​​word​​‘Yid’,​​which​​I​



                                                                 ​297​
​found​​fascinating​​and​​decided​​to​​explore​​further​​in​​my​​university​​studies,​​when​​undertaking​
​a​ ​BA​ ​in​ ​Sport​ ​Studies​ ​and,​ ​later​​on,​​an​​MRes​​in​​Sport​​and​​Exercise​​Science.​​Throughout​​my​
​undergraduate​ ​and​ ​postgraduate​ ​studies​ ​at​ ​the​ ​University​ ​of​ ​Winchester,​ ​I​ ​continued​
​researching​ ​topics​ ​related​​to​​the​​term​​‘Yid’,​​religious​​identities​​in​​football,​​and​​antisemitism​
​in​ ​football.​ ​It​ ​was​ ​during​ ​this​ ​time​ ​that​ ​I​ ​began​ ​to​ ​discover​ ​myself​ ​as​ ​a​ ​researcher​ ​and​
​academic,​ ​finding​ ​a​ ​research​ ​area​ ​that​ ​I​​was​​passionate​​about​​and​​was​​encouraged​​to​​take​
​my research further through the completion of a PhD.​

​Alongside​​some​​personal​​motivations,​​my​​initial​​motivation​​for​​undertaking​​this​​PhD​​was​​not​
​only​ ​to​ ​delve​ ​deeper​ ​into​ ​a​ ​topic​ ​I​ ​was​ ​passionate​ ​about​ ​but​​also​​to​​create​​change​​for​​the​
​Jewish​​community,​​which,​​although​​I​​have​​not​​always​​felt​​connected​​to​​religiously,​​has​​always​
​supported​​me.​​When​​I​​first​​began​​developing​​the​​project​​in​​February​​of​​2019,​​I​​envisioned​​a​
​project​​that​​would​​ideally​​create​​measurable​​and​​meaningful​​change.​​Therefore,​​a​​significant​
​milestone​​in​​this​​project​​was​​the​​realisation​​that​​I​​was​​going​​to​​write​​a​​book.​​I​​proposed​​the​
​idea​​of​​writing​​a​​children's​​book​​to​​my​​supervisory​​team,​​expecting​​them​​to​​dismiss​​it​​as​​too​
​ambitious.​​Instead,​​they​​responded​​positively​​and​​supported​​me​​in​​pursuing​​it.​​Ironically,​​as​​a​
​child,​​my​​parents​​were​​always​​told​​I​​needed​​to​​read​​more.​​Given​​this,​​having​​written​​a​​book​
​that could potentially be read by children in schools feels like a full-circle moment.​

​Finally,​ ​within​ ​the​ ​introduction,​ ​I​ ​outlined​ ​how​ ​the​ ​context​ ​surrounding​ ​antisemitism​ ​has​
​shifted​​throughout​​my​​time​​as​​a​​researcher,​​particularly​​with​​the​​rise​​of​​populist​​and​​far-right​
​politics​ ​across​ ​Europe​ ​and​ ​the​ ​impact​ ​of​ ​Trump’s​ ​first​ ​term​ ​as​ ​U.S.​ ​President.​ ​These​
​developments,​ ​along​ ​with​ ​recurring​ ​tensions​ ​around​ ​Israel/Palestine,​ ​have​ ​influenced​ ​not​
​only​ ​the​ ​public​ ​visibility​ ​of​ ​antisemitism​ ​but​ ​also​ ​how​ ​it​ ​is​ ​perceived​ ​and​ ​discussed​
​(Freedman​ ​and​ ​Hirsh,​ ​2024;​ ​Seymour,​ ​2024).​ ​As​ ​these​ ​dynamics​ ​have​ ​unfolded,​ ​I​ ​have​
​reflected​ ​on​ ​my​ ​own​ ​position​ ​within​ ​this​ ​changing​ ​landscape.​ ​They​ ​have​ ​shaped​ ​my​
​approach,​ ​both​ ​in​ ​terms​ ​of​​research​​focus​​and​​my​​broader​​commitment​​to​​addressing​​how​
​antisemitism continues to manifest within football and society more widely.​

​Concluding thoughts​

​In​​summary,​​this​​chapter​​has​​provided​​an​​opportunity​​to​​critically​​assess​​the​​methodological​
​decisions​​made​​throughout​​the​​course​​of​​this​​project​​by​​examining​​each​​phase​​of​​the​​study​



                                                             ​298​
​in​ ​detail.​ ​This​ ​breakdown​ ​enabled​ ​the​ ​researcher​ ​to​ ​consider​ ​the​ ​key​ ​strengths​ ​and​
​limitations​ ​of​ ​the​ ​project,​ ​as​ ​well​ ​as​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​encountered​ ​during​ ​the​ ​process.​
​Analysing​ ​existing​ ​initiatives​ ​revealed​ ​that​ ​very​ ​little​ ​has​ ​been​ ​done​ ​to​ ​address​ ​or​ ​reduce​
​antisemitism​ ​through​ ​discussions​ ​related​ ​to​ ​sport.​ ​This​ ​reflection​ ​has​ ​also​ ​allowed​ ​the​
​researcher​ ​to​ ​identify​ ​the​ ​novel​ ​contributions​ ​this​ ​project​ ​brings​ ​to​ ​the​ ​field​ ​of​ ​sport​
​sociology,​​such​​as​​the​​innovative​​application​​of​​theory​​and​​the​​development​​of​​a​​co-created​
​initiative aimed at reducing antisemitism.​

​This​ ​PhD​ ​study​ ​has​ ​achieved​ ​its​ ​overarching​ ​aim​ ​to​ ​develop​ ​an​ ​evidence-based​ ​and​
​co-created​​educational​​initiative​​focused​​on​​eradicating​​antisemitism​​in​​British​​football,​​with​
​significant​ ​input​ ​from​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts​ ​and​ ​the​ ​Jewish​ ​community.​ ​Through​ ​the​
​application​ ​of​ ​CRT​ ​and​ ​HebCrit,​ ​the​ ​research​ ​identified​ ​key​ ​factors​ ​essential​​for​​addressing​
​inequalities​ ​and​ ​combating​ ​antisemitism​ ​within​ ​the​ ​football​ ​context.​ ​The​ ​diverse​ ​data​
​collection​ ​methods​ ​employed,​ ​including​ ​interviews,​ ​focus​ ​groups​ ​and​ ​questionnaires,​
​facilitated​ ​meaningful​ ​engagement​ ​with​ ​key​ ​stakeholders,​ ​ensuring​ ​that​ ​both​ ​experiences​
​and​ ​knowledge​ ​of​ ​the​ ​anti-discrimination​ ​experts​ ​and​ ​the​ ​voices​ ​of​ ​the​​Jewish​​community​
​were amplified throughout the process.​

​Hopefully,​ ​this​ ​project​ ​and​ ​its​ ​outcomes​ ​will​ ​be​ ​the​ ​start​ ​of​ ​some​ ​positive​ ​change​ ​for​ ​the​
​Jewish​​community.​​However,​​the​​discussion​​also​​acknowledges​​the​​significant​​challenges​​that​
​lie​ ​ahead​ ​in​ ​the​ ​implementation​ ​of​ ​such​ ​initiatives.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​clear​ ​that​ ​there​ ​is​ ​still​ ​substantial​
​scope​ ​for​​further​​research​​to​​be​​conducted​​in​​conjunction​​with​​the​​initiative,​​particularly​​to​
​assess​​its​​impact​​before​​implementation.​​Going​​into​​the​​project,​​the​​aim​​was​​to​​change​​the​
​attitudes​ ​of​ ​those​ ​sporting​ ​fans;​ ​nevertheless,​ ​with​ ​the​ ​way​ ​that​ ​the​ ​initiative​ ​has​ ​been​
​designed,​ ​it​ ​will​ ​hopefully​ ​create​ ​greater​ ​change​ ​within​ ​society​ ​as​ ​a​​whole,​​beginning​​with​
​educating​​children.​​By​​instilling​​awareness​​and​​understanding​​from​​a​​young​​age,​​the​​initiative​
​aspires​​to​​foster​​a​​more​​inclusive​​and​​respectful​​society.​​Despite​​the​​anticipated​​challenges,​
​the​ ​hope​ ​is​ ​that​ ​this​ ​project​ ​will​ ​mark​ ​the​ ​beginning​ ​of​ ​a​ ​significant​ ​and​ ​lasting​ ​positive​
​transformation in attitudes towards antisemitism.​

Dr Peter Wright,

Dear Dr Wright,

UREC Registration No: 201435
Study Title: Antisemitism in British Football: Examining Good Practice in
Anti-Discrimination Educational Initiatives – Phase One

Thank you for the email of 4th January 2021 outlining the response to the points raised in my
previous conditional approval letter regarding the PhD study of your research student, Bonita
Lunn and attaching the revised documents. I am pleased to inform you that, on this basis,
UREC is happy to grant full approval for this study.

The UREC approval period for the data collection phase of the study is two years from the date
of this letter, so until 5th January 2023. If you need the approval to be extended please do
contact me nearer the time of expiry.

Phase 1 information sheet
Antisemitism in British Football: Examining Good Practice in Anti-Discrimination
Educational Initiatives

You are being invited to take part in a research study. Before you decide whether or not to
take part, it is important for you to understand why the research is being done and what it
will involve. Please take time to read the following information carefully.

What is the purpose of the study?
The aim of this project is to develop an evidence-based and co-created educational
initiative focused on eradicating antisemitism in Britain. By discussing with organisations
and exploring previous initiatives, an initiative will be created. Then the initiative will be
trialled on football fans to finalise a plan that can be used to tackle antisemitic behaviours
in football.

Why have I been invited to participate?
You were chosen to participate as you have previous experience in developing
anti-discrimination educational initiatives in sport.

Do I have to take part?
Participation is completely voluntary and therefore, it is up to you to decide whether or not
to take part in this study. If you do decide to take part, you will be given this information
sheet along with a privacy notice that will explain how your data will be collected and used
and be asked to give your consent. If you decide to take part, you are still free to withdraw
at any time and without giving a reason.

What will happen to me if I take part?
If you decide to participate in this study, you will take part in a one-to-one interview with
Bonita Lunn, the researcher. This interview will last approximately 30-45 minutes and will
be audio recorded. The interview will explore anti-discrimination educational initiatives
and their impact.

What are the possible disadvantages and risks of taking part?
The risks associated with this research are no greater than risks in your day-to-day life.
However, some information and discussions could be deemed sensitive and may cause
some distress. Nevertheless, if the participant feels any psychological discomfort they have
the right to withdraw from the research at any given time. Furthermore, all participants
have the contact details for the primary researcher and are able to contact them in order
to be signposted to appropriate support.

For any further support, please contact:
Bonita Lunn (Primary Researcher) 19137379@brookes.ac.uk 07525 094 186 Dr Stuart
Whigham SWhigham@brookes.ac.uk 01865 483 857
What are the possible benefits of taking part?
By taking part in this research, you will be contributing towards a new educational initiative
which could be used to tackle antisemitic behaviours. By being involved in the discussions
of this educational initiative you will be potentially improving the lives of members of the
Jewish community, if this initiative is used by sporting professionals or members of
National Governing Bodies.

Will what I say in this study be kept confidential?
All personal information and data collected will be kept strictly confidential. To ensure this,
pseudonyms, chosen by the participants, will be ensured to provide anonymity. Any
information that could potentially compromise the participants anonymity, will be
removed to ensure the participant can not be recognised.

Individuals who will have access to this data are Bonita Lunn (researcher) and members of
the supervisory team (Dr Peter Wright, Dr Stuart Whigham and Dr Adam White). All data
will be stored on a password protected laptop and/or on the university's Google Drive,
which the University has a data security agreement with Google.

Data generated by the study must be retained in accordance with the University's policy on
Academic Integrity. The data generated by the research will be kept securely in electronic
form for a period of ten years after the completion of a research project. The
pseudonymised data could be published within an academic journal article or used for
conference presentations which would exceed the ten years.

What should I do if I want to take part?
If you would like to take part in this research, please contact the primary researcher, Bonita
Lunn. You will then be provided with a consent form, which you will then have 48 hours to
return via email. If you have any further questions, please do not hesitate to contact the
researcher.

What will happen to the results of the research study?
The results of this research will be used for the researcher's PhD thesis. There is also
potential that results may be used in journal publications and may be presented in
academic conferences. A summary of the findings will be available to participants, upon
request.

Who is organising and funding the research?
This research has been organised by Bonita Lunn, a PhD student in the Department of
Sport, Health Sciences and Social Work in the Faculty of Health and Life Sciences at Oxford
Brookes University.

Who has reviewed the study?
The University Research Ethics Committee at Oxford Brookes University has approved this
research.

This Privacy Notice provides information on how Oxford Brookes University (Oxford
Brookes) collects and uses participant’s personal information when you take part in one of
our research projects. Please refer to the research Participant Information Sheet for further
details about the study and what information will be collected about you and how it will be
used.

Oxford Brookes is the Data Controller of any data that you supply for this research. This
means that we are responsible for looking after your information and using it lawfully. We
will make the decisions on how your data is used and for what reasons.

Why do we need your data?

The aim of this project is to develop an evidence-based and co-created educational
initiative focused on eradicating antisemitism in British Football. By discussing with
organisations and exploring previous initiatives, the initiative will be trialled on members of
the Jewish community, teachers and experts to finalise a plan that can be used to tackle
antisemitic behaviours.

Oxford Brookes’ legal basis for collecting this data is:

Your consent is an ethical requirement.

Oxford Brookes University’s legal basis for processing your Personal Data (or information) is
set out in Art 6 UK GDPR.

The basis for processing data in this case is:

   ● Public task: your Personal Data will be used in academic research. Oxford Brookes
     University is a public body and staff and students carry out research in line with the
     University’s legal powers and constitution.

Special Category Data:

Oxford Brookes may ask you for sensitive data such as: racial or ethnic origin, political
opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade-union membership, data concerning
health or sexual life, genetic/biometric data. This is defined by law as Special Category
Data. If Oxford Brookes requests this data it can only be used because one of the following
processing exemptions applies as set out in Art 9 UK GDPR:

      ●       You have given OBU explicit consent to do so; and / or

      ●       Processing is necessary for scientific or research in the public interest.



What type of personal data will Oxford Brookes use?

                             3
4
                     Chapter 1
                   Introduction




T
   his is Joe Ford; he is eleven years old and is in his final year at
   Greenfields Primary School. Joe lives with his older sister Lorna,
and his Mum and Dad in the North of Bradstock, the capital city.

“Come on, Joe, we are going to miss kick off!” shouts Mrs Ford.
This is Joe’s mum, Mrs Ford. Both Mrs Ford and Joe are off to see
Bradstock Rovers FC play. She is a massive Bradstock Rovers fan
and has supported them since she was a young girl. Within the
Ford family, it is a tradition to support Bradstock Rovers, with
Grandpa Harry being the biggest supporter.

What is funny, though, is that Mr Ford supports Hadleigh City as
he grew up in Hadleigh who Joe’s sister Lorna supports too. They
don’t go to matches very often, though, as the stadium is nearly
4 hours away, but when they play away games against Bradstock
Rovers the whole family attends the matches and there is often
some tension within the Ford household.


                                  5
“Sorry, Mum, I couldn’t find my scarf!” Joe yells. When his beloved
team plays, Joe must always wear his lucky scarf. When Bradstock
Rovers played in the FA Cup semi-finals, Mrs Ford accidently put
Joe’s scarf in the wash and they lost. Joe claims it was because he
didn’t have his lucky scarf. Joe refuses to have his scarf washed
now!

“Make sure to wrap up warm and enjoy the game,” muttered Mr
Ford. Joe grabs his coat and runs out the door, slamming it behind
him. As soon as the door bangs, Joe and Mrs Ford dash in a hurry.

“We are going to miss the train,” Mrs Ford exclaimed as they ran
down the road to the train station. Frantically, they sprint down the
long, narrow road. The Ford family only live a short distance from
the station, and luckily only one stop from Bradstock stadium. With
seconds to spare, Joe and Mrs Ford dive onto the train. Gasping to
catch their breath, they hear a familiar voice coming from behind
them.

“Where have you been? You only just made it!” asks a voice on the
train. “Sorry, Grandad, I couldn’t find my lucky scarf!” says Joe.
This is Joe’s Grandpa, Harry. He has supported Bradstock Rovers
since he was a young boy. Every year, Grandpa Harry buys Joe and
Mrs Ford season tickets to Bradstock Rovers for their Christmas
present, and every week all three of them attend the matches
together. One year for Christmas, he even bought Lorna tickets
to watch them play in hope that she would come to matches with
them, and become a Bradstock Rovers fan too, but she didn’t.



                                   6
T
   he train journey was only short, and within a few minutes they
   had arrived at their stop. Joe’s enthusiasm rose as he, Grandpa
Harry and Mrs Ford leapt off the train. Masses of people clambered
off the train and began walking to the stadium. Joe always
enjoyed walking to the ground because he felt a strong sense of
togetherness with all the other Bradstock supporters. He could also
see the stadium from afar, and, with each step he took, he knew he
was moving closer and closer to the ground. Bradstock Stadium
was one of the most remarkable football stadiums, both in terms
of size and the beauty of its gigantic structure. As they approached
the stadium, Joe felt anxious yet excited. As Joe reached his regular
seat, he noticed a large number of fans; most of whom were
dressed in their blue and white Bradstock Rovers kit.

The football players came onto the pitch and as more fans arrived,
the noise level increased, becoming more and more thunderous.
Booming sounds echoed within the stadium; as the whistle blew,
fans looked down onto the pitch to see the players kneeling.
When the players began kneeling, the stadium went silent and an
announcement was made to the stadium: “Please, remain silent as
players take the knee, in the campaign to eradicate Racism from
football.” As the crowd remained silent, Joe began to think about
why players take the knee.




                                  7
A few seconds passed, and, as the players rose to their feet, the
whistle blew and the game began as Bradstock Rovers star player,
Kahn, made the first pass. The game continues with Bradstock
Rovers taking the lead at half time and then winning the game 2-0
at the end of the evening. “I told you my scarf was lucky,’’ Joe says
to his mum as they leave the stadium. Mrs Ford replies, “You keep
telling yourself that! Bring on the next game!”




      (IMAGE OF JOE, GRANDPA HARRY AND MRS FORD
             IN THE CROWD WITH LGBT+ FLAG Etc.)

                 Chapter 2
              The Final Match




T
   his week was Joe’s final week at Greenfields Primary School. Joe
   had been to this school since he was four years old, so he was
feeling a range of emotions about leaving. He knew he would miss
his friends but was also excited to meet some new people. Luckily,
two of his friends, Zara and Alex, were going to Thorndon High
School with him.

It was a busy week at school as there were going to be lots of final
events for the Year 6 children, including their sports day and
school play. Joe was most excited about his last day, as the parents
and staff had organised for the children to go to a theme park. Joe
had never been to a theme park before and was looking forward to
riding one of the world’s biggest roller coasters.



                                  11
“Okay, Year 6, have we all got our football kits?” asked Joe’s teacher.
Today was the final football match for the Year 6 team, they were
playing against another local school. Joe already knew some of
the players from the other school, as they were going to Thorndon
High School too. “Make sure you don’t forget your boots, it’s
muddy out there!” said Joe’s teacher.



N
     ot only does Joe enjoy watching football, but he loves playing
     the game. When Joe plays football, he gains a sense of
accomplishment and pride, and when Joe is experiencing a difficult
day, he knows that he will feel much better when he plays a game
of football since it makes him happier and more relaxed. He also
likes spending time with his friends, some of his closest friends are
those he has played football with, either at school or his local club.

As it was their last game, some of the parents and guardians were
there to watch. The game gets underway, with Greenfields kicking
from left to right. Alex heads forward, with the defence heading
towards him. There is a tumble for the ball, and it is booted off the
pitch by the opposition. One of Joe’s teammates steps in to take the
throw, he tries to throw the ball over the defender, but they manage
to head it towards their teammate. The opposition start to attack,
successfully sending it towards the goal, but Joe’s team work
together to defend the ball. Alex receives a long ball down field and
makes the break to get behind the defence. He takes a shot, but the
goalkeeper makes a superb save.




                                  12
A
     s the game continues, the score remains 0-0. Joe gains
     possession of the ball and dribbles it past the defenders.
He could hear Mrs Ford cheering from the side-lines, “Go on, Joe,
shoot!”. Joe scored and ran up to his teammates, giving them all a
high five. He ran past his mum and gave her a high five too.

It was half-time, and as Joe’s teacher was discussing tactics with
the players, Mrs Ford came over and handed them a box of orange
segments to enjoy. As the children devoured their oranges, Joe’s
teacher continued to motivate the children, they finished by saying,
“This is your last match as a group, so go out and enjoy yourselves.”
All the players huddled in a circle. put their arms in and, after the
count of three, lifted their arms together, “1, 2, 3 GREENFIELDS,”
they exclaimed!

The players got into their starting positions, the whistle blew and
the second half began. Although the other team scored a goal
within the first 5 minutes of the second half, the second half went
well for Joe’s team. One of his closest friends, Zara, scored an
outstanding goal in the top left corner. The game finished, and it
was a great way to end their final game. Joe’s team won 5-1, with
Joe scoring two of the goals. As they headed back to school, Joe
wondered what playing football would be like at high school. Will
he still have the time to play football in his new school due to an
increase in school work? Will he make the school team if there are
more students to be selected from?

                Chapter 3
              A New Day at
            Secondary School


I
 t was just before 9 o’clock, and the sun was shining brightly on
 the morning of Joe’s first day at secondary school. He eagerly
awaits outside the gates with two of his close friends, Zara and Alex,
who used to go to Greenfields Primary with him. Joe, Zara and Alex
all have two things in common: they love football and they also
support Bradstock Rovers. “Tough game on the weekend, Kahn was
on top form though!” said Zara. Kahn is Zara’s favourite Bradstock
Rovers player, she has always looked up to him as a role model
because he is a Muslim and so is she. She has also met him at her
Mosque, when he came to encourage young Muslim boys and girls
to take up football.

“If only we weren’t offside in the second half. We would have won!”
chipped in Alex. Alex has two older brothers and they play football
in their garden, even when it’s raining! Zara plays for her local
team every Saturday; she is their leading goalscorer. Today is their
first day of secondary school. Alex and Zara also go to Thorndon


                                 15
High School but are in different form groups. Once they arrived
at the front door, they parted ways and agreed to meet up at
lunchtime.

“See you both on the field at lunchtime for a kickabout” shouts
Joe. Joe felt a range of emotions, including excitement and
nervousness, a similar feeling to when he arrived at football
matches. Joe walks hastily down the corridor searching for his
classroom, he turns around and sees a teacher. “Excuse me, I
think I am lost,” mumbled Joe. He recited the room number as the
teacher explained where to go.



A
     s he approaches the classroom, his teacher welcomes him
     in, “I’m Miss Cooper, do come in and take a seat”. As Joe
sat down, he noticed a class full of faces, some looked nervous
and others looked eager to learn. “Welcome to Thorndon High,
I am Miss Cooper, your form teacher this year.” As Miss Cooper
introduced herself, some students gazed around the room with
apprehensive faces. “To start, I would like us to introduce ourselves
to the rest of the class. I am Miss Cooper, and I am a teacher of
Religious Studies and History.”

Each student took it in turn to say their name and something
interesting about themselves; Joe was frantically trying to think
of something fascinating to say about himself. However, before it
was his turn a boy, in the front row said, “My name is Noah and I
support Bradstock Rovers,” just hearing the name of his beloved
club filled Joe with happiness. Next, it was Joe’s turn to introduce
himself.


                                  16
“Hi, I am Joe and over the summer holidays I went to Spain and
visited the FC Barcelona Stadium.” Miss Cooper thought Joe’s
fact was interesting and encouraged the rest of the class to share
something they did over the summer holiday with the student
sitting next to them. As the children were talking, the bell for
breaktime rang.

“Please, just let me finish up before you head off,” yelled Miss
Cooper, so the students could hear her voice over the noisy bell.
Miss Cooper continued to speak as she explained what the plan for
their first day was, but Joe was hardly listening as he was thinking
about the next coming match at the Bradstock stadium. It was the
big derby against their rival club, Kingswood City. As Miss Cooper
allowed the class to leave, he picked up his drink and headed to the
field to meet Zara and Alex.

“Alex!” yelled Joe.

“Oh, Hi…How was your lesson?” asked Alex.

“It was okay, have you seen Zara?” as he asks, they notice her
walking towards them. Alex, Joe, and Zara sat down on the
grass, began having a snack and chatted about the upcoming
match against their rivals. While they ate their lunch, Joe spotted
one of his classmates sitting alone. It was Noah, the Bradstock
Rovers supporter. He decided to approach him, “Hey, you support
Bradstock Rovers don’t you?”.

The boy mumbled “yes, I do!”.



                                  17
“So do we. Did you see the game this weekend?” asks Alex. The
group immediately started talking about Saturday’s game. As their
football-related discussions continued, the group decided to play a
brief game before returning to their class. Joe was pleased that he
had spoken to someone in his class, and this marked the beginning
of a new friendship between Joe and Noah.

F
   inally, the big derby between Bradstock Rovers and Kingswood
   City arrived. Because they were so close to one another, these
teams were fierce rivals. Joe is attending a game versus Kingswood
City for the first time. Mrs Ford didn’t want Joe to go ‘til he was

T
   hat weekend, Mrs Ford, Grandpa Harry and Joe went to their
   weekly Bradstock Rovers match. This week, they were playing
the current champions for their league, Alport Forest. The Ford
family knew this was going to be a tough game for Bradstock
Rovers as they had their finest players on the pitch. Like the
previous matches Joe had attended, it started with a player taking
the knee. However, this time one of the opposing team members
did not kneel. Joe heard a voice behind him say, “I read online that
he wasn’t going to take the knee, he doesn’t think he should kneel
to show that his community matters.”

The game began, and from the offset the opposing team were
chanting and singing songs, both to show pride in their club, but to
also wind up the opposition. Even some of those songs and chants
contained some discriminatory words.

Opposing teams continue to chant, sing and shout:

What Joe came to realise was that the chanting from Bradstock
Rovers did silence the abuse from other teams. However, as Joe
continued to hear his fellow Bradstock Rovers fans chant the word
Yid, he wondered what he could do to get everyone to stop, not just
the Bradstock Rovers fans but also the other teams. Why did they
have to say such horrible things?

Bradstock Rovers were unfortunate to lose 1-0 that night. Despite
playing stronger football and having several chances to equalise,
Bradstock Rovers were unable to get past their defence. However, as
Joe walked home, it wasn’t football that was on his mind: all he was
thinking was, what could he do to make a difference?

                 Chapter 8
               The Synagogue


I
 t was the day of the school trip to the synagogue. As the children
 stepped off the bus, they were greeted by a friendly face, Noah’s
Grandma. “Hello, and welcome to the synagogue, please follow
me.” She led them through the reception of the building and into
the prayer hall. As they entered some were amazed to see such a
magnificent building, standing tall with beautiful detailing.

“Wow, is this where you come to pray?” enquired Tom, one of their
classmates. The synagogue that the children were seated in was
very grand, decorated with patterns and bible stories.

Noah was delighted that one of his peers had asked a question
“I come here on Saturdays, for Shabbat,” answers Noah.

“Hello, Year 7. I am Noah’s Grandma, you can call me Naomi,” she
said, whilst introducing herself to the group. “Please come in and
please take a seat in our synagogue.” The children scrambled to
find themselves a seat next to their friend. Joe takes a seat next to
Noah. “I am excited to be talking to you today and showing you
around our synagogue. A synagogue is a building where Jewish
people go to pray. It is like a church, where Christians go to or a

                                  41
Mosque, where Muslims go to or even a Temple, for Hindus. We
don’t only come here to pray, as sometimes the synagogue is used
for various other communal activities, like this visit today.”



A
     s the students settled down, Grandma Naomi approached a
     table holding a very large scroll, “firstly, I am going to start
by showing you this. This is the Torah; this is the first 5 books of
the Old Testament,” says Grandma Naomi whilst pointing to the
Torah on the table. “The Torah is so special that most people are not
allowed to touch it. It is usually kept in a safe place called an Ark.
This is our Ark.” Although all synagogues look different from one
another, they all have an Ark with an everlasting light on, which is
lit all the time. The children look towards the Ark, amazed to see a
range of large scrolls.

“So when we read from the Torah, we use a special pointer stick
to follow the words. This is called Yad, we do this so that we don’t
make the parchment dirty.” Naomi holds the shining Yad up to her
face, and then passes it to Noah and tells him to pass it around so
all the children can see it. “We also read in the opposite direction,
from right to left.”

“Why do you read the Torah?” asks Arlo.

“The Torah contains 613 commandments known as mitzvah. They
are the rules that Jews strive to adhere to. The Ten Commandments
are the most important,” she explained, “We read the Torah on
religious holidays, on special occasions for example on Shabbat.
Shabbat is when I come to synagogue on Saturdays to attend
services.”

                                   42
“Shabbat begins on Friday evenings and finishes on Saturdays at
sundown. This is the day of rest, and we shouldn’t do any work. This
would mean no homework too!” she explains. “On Friday nights
families gather and light the candles.” Naomi begins to bring out
some candles, a loaf of bread and a cup.



W
       hilst placing the items on the table, Grandma Naomi invites
       the children to do Shabbat with her. Whilst listening to
Grandma Naomi, they stand up quietly and place themselves
around a large circle. Grandma Naomi asks if Noah wanted to
come up to recite the blessing of the candles. As he approaches, he
places a small cap on his head. This brimless cap is called a kippah.
Noah says the prayer as his grandmother lights two candles. After
the candles, the students were all given a glass of grape juice, to
represent the wine, and a piece of Challah which is like a loaf of
bread plaited in an oval shape.

“So, why do you do this?” asks a student in Noah’s class.

“Another wonderful question. During this time, we remember that
God created the world and rested on the seventh day. Saturday
is considered to be God’s Day of rest by Jews, so we rest too on a
Saturday. So we all come here, and our Shabbat services are usually
led by a Rabbi, which in Hebrew means teacher. Sometimes, the
service can be led by a Jewish person, and it doesn’t always have
to be the Rabbi. Rabbi means ‘teacher’ in Hebrew. Hebrew is the
language we speak. Our Rabbi is called Simon, both men and
women can be Rabbi.”



                                  43
“Who here likes Christmas?” questioned Grandma Naomi. Many
of the children raise their arms quickly. “Does anyone else follow
any other religious holidays?” she asks. Zara raises her hand slowly.
“That’s great, would you like to share which holidays you enjoy?”
Zara begins to tell the other students about Ramadan, a religious
holiday whereby her family won’t eat or drink during the hours of
daylight. “Thank you for sharing that with us,” remarked Grandma
Naomi. “Just like Christmas and Ramadan, we celebrate holidays.
Hanukkah, Passover, Yom Kippur are amongst some of the holidays
we celebrate.”

As the children were leaving the synagogue and getting onto the
bus, they thanked Naomi for the wonderful day they had and for
teaching them about the Jewish religion. At the start of the day
Noah was nervous about what his peers would think but by the
end, he was glad that his classmates learnt more about his religion.



                    Discussion Points

Phase 3 vignettes of participants
   1) Keagan - interview

      Keagan is an Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Manager. He has worked for a range of
      organisations, but predominantly is focused on sport, whereby he has designed and
      delivered inclusion projects within the sport sector. For confidentiality reasons, this
      interview was conducted alone. Keagan previously part in the Phase 1, expert
      interviews.

   2) Matthew - interview

      Matthew is the Development Officer for the council, whereby his role involves
      developing and supporting initiatives to combat and decrease religious prejudice.
      Likewise, For confidentiality reasons, this interview was conducted alone and for
      practicality purposes, it was done online. Matthew also took part in the Phase 1,
      expert interviews.

   3) Nate - Email interview

      Nate is the Head of Education at a Jewish Charity, with a wealth of experience in
      education and project management. Nate took part in the initial expert interview, in
      Phase 1. When providing feedback on the book, it should be noted that his
      responses were provided via email, due to time constraints.

Educators

   1) SH School focus group

      The first focus group that took place with educators was at SH School. This consisted
      of six, female members of staff. The following job titles were held: Head of SENCO
      (Carly), Year 6 teacher and Head of English (Lauren), Head of Mathematics
      (Charlotte), Year 3 Teacher (Rachel), Teacher of Languages and Religious Studies
      (Jasmine), Deputy Headteacher and Head of Early Years (Sophia). It should be noted
      that, SH School is an all girls, private, primary school. This focus group was
      conducted face-to-face.

   2) CH School - Pair interview

      The second focus group that took place was with educators at CH School. This
      consisted of two educators; one male primary school teacher and one, female,
      learning support assistant, with experience in supporting SEN students,
      predominantly in secondary schools. This focus group was conducted face-to-face.

   3) LB School focus group

      The final focus group that took place was with educators at LB School. This
      consisted of three, female members of staff. These individuals were recruited via
      the social media advert. Two members of staff were class teachers, and the other
      was a teaching assistant. It should be noted that all three teachers, at current,
      primarily work with students with Special Educational Needs but have experience in
      working with students in a mainstream setting. This focus group was conducted
      face-to-face.

   4) Nancy- interview

      Nancy is currently the Head Teacher of a Jewish School in North London. Given this,
      she responded to questions designed for both Educators and Members of the
      Jewish community. She has been Head Teacher for four years, but had twelve years
      of teaching experience. This interview was conducted online, and for confidentiality
      reasons was conducted alone.

Members of the Jewish Community

   1) Brian - interview

      Brian was recruited through a synagogue to take part in the research process, to
      gain feedback on whether the book was reflective of the Jewish community. Brian
      had also some experience working for a company that aims to combat all forms of
   discrimination within sport. With that in mind, an individual interview was done
   with Brian so that he could also discuss his experiences when working in the field of
   anti-discrimination.

2) Simon and Leah - Pair interview

   A pair interview was completed with Simon and Leah, who both belonged to the
   same synagogue. Both Simon and Leah belong to the Jewish community, however,
   Leah also fell into the category of Educator, as she was a Year 4 teacher in a mixed,
   state, primary school. It is important to take this into account considering a range of
   her answers focused around using it within a teaching context.

3) Chris - interview

   Chris was recruited through a synagogue to take part in the research process, to
   gain feedback on whether the book was reflective of the Jewish community. Due to
   Chris’ limited time, this interview was conducted online and individually.

4) Patrick - interview

   Patrick was recruited through a synagogue to take part in the research process, to
   gain feedback on whether the book was reflective of the Jewish community. Due to
   Patricks limited time, this interview was conducted online and individually.

5) Iris - interview

   Iris was recruited through a synagogue to take part in the research process, to gain
   feedback on whether the book was reflective of the Jewish community. Due to Iris'
   limited time, this interview was conducted online and individually.

6) KH Synagogue - focus group

   The final focus group that took place with members of the Jewish community took
   place at KH Synagogue. This consisted of two, male members and one female. One
   of these participants was recruited through a social media advertisement and then
referred to additional participants using a snowball sampling method. One member
of staff was also a volunteer in delivering holocaust workshops to primary school
students. This focus group was conducted face-to-face.

Phase 3 information sheet
                             Participant Information Sheet


Antisemitism in British Football: Examining Good Practice in Anti-Discrimination
Educational Initiatives

You are being invited to take part in a research study. Before you decide whether to take
part, it is important for you to understand why the research is being done and what it will
involve. Please take time to read the following information carefully.

What is the purpose of the study?
The aim of this project is to develop an evidence-based and co-created educational
initiative focused on eradicating antisemitism in British football. By discussing with
organisations and exploring previous initiatives, an initiative has been created. The
initiative will be given to Members of the Jewish Community, Teachers and Experts to gain
their feedback, which can be utilised to produce a finalised initiative that can be used to
tackle antisemitic behaviours.

Why have I been invited to participate?

You have been asked to participate in this study, as you are either a member of the Jewish
community, a teacher or an anti-discrimination expert. Your feedback and opinions on the
planned initiative is essential when implementing this project into school settings.

Do I have to take part?

Participation is completely voluntary and therefore, it is up to you to decide whether or not
to take part in this study. If you do decide to take part, you will be given this information
sheet along with a privacy notice that will explain how your data will be collected and used
and be asked to give your consent. If you decide to take part, you are still free to withdraw
up to the point of analysis, without giving a reason.

What will happen to me if I take part?

If you decide to participate in this study, you will be given a draft copy of the initiative to
read over prior to taking part in a focus group with the researcher. This might take 15-45
minutes, depending on your level of engagement. The focus group will last approximately
40-60 minutes and will be audio recorded. If you agree to take part in the later focus group,
you will take part in reviewing the proposed initiative with 4-8 other individuals who share
the same demographic as yourself (Jewish, Teacher or Expert). You will be asked a range of
questions about an initiative which you would have seen previously to gain your feedback
on it.

What are the possible disadvantages and risks of taking part?

The risks associated with this research are no greater than risks in your day-to-day life.
However, some information and discussions could be deemed sensitive and may cause
some distress. Nevertheless, if the participant feels any psychological discomfort, they have
the right to withdraw from the research at any given time. Furthermore, all participants
have the contact details for the primary researcher and are able to contact them in order to
be signposted to appropriate support.

For any further support, please contact:
Samaritans           116 123                          www.samaritans.org
Mind                 020 8215 2243                    www.mind.org
Jami                 020 8458 2223                    www.jamiuk.org
Jewish Care          020 8922 2222                    www.jewishcare.org


What are the possible benefits of taking part?

By taking part in this research, you will be contributing towards a new educational initiative
which will be used to tackle antisemitic behaviours and hopefully reduce antisemitic
attitudes for future generations.

Will what I say in this study be kept confidential?

All personal information and data collected will be kept strictly confidential. To ensure this,
pseudonyms, chosen by the participants, will be ensured to provide anonymity. Any
information that could potentially compromise the participants anonymity, will be removed
to ensure the participant cannot be recognised.

Individuals who will have access to this data are Bonita Lunn (researcher) and members of
the supervisory team (Dr Peter Wright, Dr Stuart Whigham and Dr Adam White). All data
will be stored on a password protected laptop and/or on the university's Google Drive,
which the University has a data security agreement with Google.

Data generated by the study must be retained in accordance with the University's policy on
Academic Integrity. The data generated by the research will be kept securely in electronic
form for a period of ten years after the completion of a research project. The
pseudonymised data could be published within an academic journal article or used for
conference presentations which would exceed the ten years.

What should I do if I want to take part?

If you would like to take part in this research, please contact the primary researcher, Bonita
Lunn. You will then be provided with a consent form. Please ensure that you have returned
this consent form at least 48 hours before the focus group/interview via email. If you have
any further questions, please do not hesitate to contact the researcher.

What will happen to the results of the research study?
The results of this research will be used for the researcher’s PhD thesis. There is also
potential that results may be used in journal publications and may be presented in
academic conferences. A summary of the findings will be available to participants, upon
request.

Who is organising and funding the research?
This research has been organised and funded by Bonita Lunn, a PhD student in the
Department of Sport, Health Sciences and Social Work in the Faculty of Health and Life
Sciences at Oxford Brookes University.

Who has reviewed the study?
The University Research Ethics Committee at Oxford Brookes University has approved this
research.

Who has reviewed the study?

You should state that the research has been approved by the University Research Ethics
Committee, Oxford Brookes University and you must give the UREC registration number.

the Chair of the University Research Ethics Committee on ethics@brookes.ac.uk.


Thank you for your consideration in taking part in this research project. I look forward to
hearing from you in the near future.

                Chapter 1
              Introduction

  his is Joe Ford; he is eleven years old and is in his
  final year at Greenfields Primary School. Joe
  lives with his older sister, Lorna,
and his mum and dad in a town called Bradstock.

This is Joe’s mum, Mrs Ford. “Come on, Joe, we
are going to miss kick off!” shouted Mrs Ford.
Both Mrs Ford and Joe are off to see Bradstock
Rovers FC play. She is a massive Bradstock
Rovers fan and has supported them since she
was a young girl. Within the Ford family, it is a
tradition to support Bradstock Rovers, with
Grandpa Harry being the biggest supporter.

What is funny, though, is that Mr Ford supports
Hadleigh City, as he grew up in a town called
Hadleigh, who Joe’s sister, Lorna, supports too.
They don’t go to matches very often, though, as
the stadium is nearly 4 hours away, but when
they play away games against Bradstock Rovers
the whole family attends the matches and there

                                                          1
is often some tension within the Ford household.

“Sorry, Mum, I couldn’t find my scarf!” Joe
yelled. When his beloved team played, Joe would
always wear his lucky scarf. When Bradstock
Rovers played in the FA Cup semi-finals, Mrs Ford
accidently put Joe’s scarf in the wash and they
lost. Joe claimed it was because he didn’t have
his lucky scarf. Joe refused to have his scarf
washed now!

“Make sure to wrap up warm and enjoy the game,”
muttered Mr Ford. Joe grabbed his coat and ran out
the door and slammed it behind him. Joe and Mrs
Ford dashed off in a hurry.

“We are going to miss the train,” Mrs Ford
exclaimed as they ran down the road to the train
station. Frantically, they sprinted down the long,
narrow road. The Ford family only lived a short
distance from the station, and luckily only one stop
from Bradstock stadium. With seconds to spare, Joe
and Mrs Ford dived onto the train. They gasped to
catch their breath and heard a familiar voice
coming from behind them.

“Where have you been? You only just made it!”
asked a voice on the train. “Sorry, Grandad, I
couldn’t find my lucky scarf!” said Joe.




                                                       2
This is Joe’s Grandpa, Harry. He has supported
Bradstock Rovers since he was a young boy. Every
year, Grandpa Harry bought Joe and Mrs Ford
season tickets to Bradstock Rovers for their
Christmas presents, and every other week all three
of them attended the home matches together. One
year for Christmas, he even bought Lorna tickets
to watch them play in the hope that she would
come to matches with them, and become a
Bradstock Rovers fan too, but she didn’t.


  he train journey was only short, and within a
few minutes they had arrived at their stop. Joe’s
enthusiasm rose as he, Grandpa Harry and Mrs
Ford leapt off the train. Masses of people also
clambered off and began walking to the stadium.
Joe always enjoyed walking to the ground
because he felt a strong sense of
togetherness with all the other Bradstock
supporters. He could also see the stadium in the
distance, and, with each step he took, he knew he
was moving closer and closer to the ground.
Bradstock Stadium was one of the most
remarkable football stadiums, both in terms
of size and the beauty of its gigantic structure. As
they approached the stadium, Joe felt anxious yet
excited. As Joe reached his regular seat, he noticed
a large number of fans; most of whom were


                                                       3
dressed in their blue and white Bradstock Rovers
kit.

Before the game began, Joe skimmed his
programme; as he flicked through, he stopped to
read about Bradstock Rovers Women's team. "They
are top of the league", Joe exclaimed to his
Grandad.


Grandpa Harry said, "That's because we have
Williams. She scored the winning goal at the
Euro's.” The football players came onto the pitch
and as more fans arrived, the noise level
increased, becoming more and more thunderous.
Booming sounds echoed within the stadium; as
the whistle blew, fans looked down onto the pitch
and saw the players kneeling.


When the players began kneeling, the stadium
went silent and an announcement was made,
“Please, remain silent as players take the knee, in
the campaign to eradicate racism and
discrimination from football.” As the crowd
remained silent, Joe began to think about why
players take the knee. A few seconds passed, and,
when the players rose to their feet, the whistle
blew and the game began as Bradstock Rovers
star player, Khan, made the first pass. The game


                                                      4
continued with Bradstock Rovers taking the lead
before half time and then winning the game 2-0 at
the end of the evening. “I told you my scarf was
lucky,’’ Joe said to his mum as they left the
stadium. Mrs Ford replied, “You keep telling
yourself that! Bring on the next game!”

              Chapter 2
           The Final Match
  his week was Joe’s final week at Greenfields
  Primary School. Joe had been to this school since
  he was four years old, so he was
feeling a range of emotions about leaving. He
knew he would miss his friends but was also
excited to meet some new people. Luckily, two of
his friends, Zara and Alex, were going to Thorndon
High School with him.

It was a busy week at school as there were going
to be lots of final events for the Year 6 children,
including their sports day and school play. Joe
was most excited about his last day, as the
parents and staff had organised for the children to
go to a theme park. Joe had never been to a theme
park before and was looking forward to riding one
of the world’s biggest roller coasters.

“Okay, Year 6, have we all got our football kits?”
asked Joe’s teacher. Today was the final football
match for the Year 6 team; they were playing
against another local school. Joe already knew
some of the players from the other school, as they
were going to Thorndon High School too. “Make
sure you don’t forget your boots, it’s muddy out
there!” said Joe’s teacher.

                                                      7
    ot only did Joe enjoy watching football, but he
    loved playing the game. When Joe played
    football, he gained a sense of
accomplishment and pride, and when Joe
experienced a difficult day, he knew that he would
feel much better when he played a game of
football since it made him happier and more
relaxed. He also liked spending time with his
friends, some of his closest friends were those he
had played football with, either at school or his
local club.

As it was their last game, some of the parents and
guardians were there to watch. The game got
underway, with Greenfields kicking from left to
right. Alex headed forward, with the defence
heading towards him. There was a tumble for the
ball, and it was booted off the pitch by the
opposition. One of Joe’s teammates stepped in to
take the throw, he tried to throw the ball over the
defender, but they managed to head it towards
their teammate. The opposition started to attack,
successfully sending it towards the goal, but Joe’s
team worked together to defend the ball. Alex
received a long ball down field and made the break
to get behind the defence. He took a shot, but the
goalkeeper made a superb save.




                                                      8
As the game continued, the score remained
0-0. Joe gained possession of the ball and
dribbled it past the defenders. He could hear Mrs
Ford cheering from the side-lines, “Go on, Joe,
shoot!”. Joe scored and ran up to his teammates,
giving them all a high five. He ran past his mum
and gave her a high five too.

It was half-time, and as Joe’s teacher was
discussing tactics with the players, Mrs Ford
came over and handed them a box of orange
segments to enjoy. As the children devoured their
oranges, Joe’s teacher continued to motivate the
children; they finished by saying, “This is your
last match as a group, so go out and enjoy
yourselves.” All the players huddled in a circle.
put their arms in and, after the count of three,
lifted their arms together, “1, 2, 3 GREENFIELDS,”
they chanted!

The players got into their starting positions, the
whistle blew and the second half began. Although
the other team scored a goal within the first five
minutes of the second half, the second half went
well for Joe’s team. One of his closest friends, Zara,
scored an outstanding goal in the top left corner.
The game finished, and it was a great way to end
their final match. Joe’s team won 5-1, with Joe
scoring two of the goals.


                                                         9
As they headed back to school, Joe wondered what
playing football would be like at high school.
Would he still have the time to play football in his
new school due to an increase in school work?
Would he make the school team if there are more
students to be selected from?

             Chapter 3
           A New Day at
         Secondary School

 t was just before 9 o’clock, and the sun was
 shining brightly on the morning of Joe’s first
 day at secondary school. He eagerly
waited outside the gates with two of his close
friends, Zara and Alex, who used to go to
Greenfields Primary with him. Joe, Zara and Alex all
had two things in common: they loved football and
they also supported Bradstock Rovers. “Tough
game on the weekend, Khan was on top form
though!” said Zara.


Alongside Williams, the leading goal scorer for
Bradstock Rovers Women's team, Khan was Zara’s
favourite Bradstock Rovers player, she had always
looked up to him as a role model because he was a
Muslim and so is she. She had also met him at her
Mosque, when he came to encourage young Muslim
children to take up football.



                                                       12
“If only we weren’t offside in the second half. We
would have won!” chipped in Alex. Alex has two
older brothers and they played football in their
garden, even when it was raining! Zara played for
her local team every Saturday; she was their
leading goalscorer. Although Alex and Zara attend
the same school as Joe, they were in different form
groups. Once they arrived at the main door, they
parted ways and agreed to meet up at lunchtime.

“See you both on the field at lunchtime for a
kickabout” shouted Joe. Joe felt a range of
emotions, including excitement and nervousness,
a similar feeling to when he arrived at football
matches. Joe walked hastily down the corridor
searching for his classroom, he turned around
and saw a teacher. “Excuse me, I think I am lost,”
mumbled Joe. He recited the room name and the
teacher explained where to go.

    s he approached the classroom, his teacher
    welcomed him in, “I’m Miss Cooper, do
    come in and take a seat”. As Joe
sat down, he noticed a class full of faces, some
looked nervous and others looked eager to
learn. “Welcome to Thorndon High, I am Miss
Cooper, your form teacher this year.” As Miss
Cooper   introduced   herself,   some   students
gazed around the room with
apprehensive faces. “To start, I would like us to

                                                      13
introduce ourselves to the rest of the class. I am
Miss Cooper, and I am a teacher of Religious
Studies and History.”

Each student took it in turn to say their name
and something interesting about themselves;
Joe was frantically trying to think of something
fascinating to say about himself. However,
before it was his turn a boy in the front row said,
“My name is Noah and I support Bradstock
Rovers,” just hearing the name of his beloved
club filled Joe with happiness. Next, it was Joe’s
turn.

“Hi, I am Joe and over the summer holidays I
went to Spain and visited the FC Barcelona
Stadium.” Miss Cooper thought Joe’s fact was
interesting and encouraged the rest of the class
to share something they did over the summer
holiday with the student sitting next to them. As
the children were talking, the bell for breaktime
rang.

“Please, just let me finish up before you head off,”
yelled Miss Cooper, so the students could hear her
voice over the noisy bell. Miss Cooper explained
what the plan for their first day was, but Joe was
hardly listening as he was thinking about the
upcoming match at the Bradstock stadium. It was
the big derby against their rival club, Kingswood

                                                       14
City. As Miss Cooper allowed the class to leave, he
picked up his drink and headed to the field to meet
Zara and Alex.

“Alex!” yelled Joe.

“Oh, Hi…How was your lesson?” asked Alex.

“It was okay, have you seen Zara?” as he asked,
they noticed her walking towards them. Alex,
Joe, and Zara sat down on the grass, began
having a snack and chatted about the upcoming
match against their rivals. While they ate their
lunch, Joe spotted one of his classmates sitting
alone. It was Noah, the Bradstock
Rovers supporter. He decided to approach him,
“Hey, you support Bradstock Rovers don’t you?”.

The boy mumbled “yes, I do!”.

“So do we. Did you see the game this weekend?”
asked Alex. The group immediately started talking
about Saturday’s game. As their football-related
discussions continued, they all decided to play a
brief game before returning to their class. Joe was
pleased that he had spoken to someone in his class,
and this marked the beginning of a new friendship
between Joe and Noah.

    s Mrs Ford continued her discussion, Joe gazed

  hat weekend, Mrs Ford, Grandpa Harry and Joe

kneel to show that his community matters.”

The game began, and from the offset the opposing
team were chanting and singing songs, both to

Army! Yid Army!” This caused much confusion for

Why does she not realise this word is offensive
and upsetting for the Jewish community? A funny

so that she could hear him over the chanting of

What Joe came to realise was that the chanting
from Bradstock Rovers did silence the abuse from

wondered what he could do to get everyone to stop,
not just the Bradstock Rovers fans but also the
other teams. Why did they have to say such horrible
things?

Bradstock Rovers were unfortunate to lose 1-0 that

several chances to equalise, Bradstock Rovers were
unable to get past Alport Forest’s defence. However,
as Joe walked home, it wasn’t football that was on
his mind: all he was thinking was, what could he do
to make a difference?

                                                       40
here to pray, as sometimes the synagogue is used

As the students settled down, Grandma Naomi

This is our Ark.” Although all synagogues look

with an everlasting light on, which is lit all the
time. The children looked towards the Ark, amazed
to see a range of large scrolls.

“So when we read from the Torah, we use a
special pointer stick to follow the words. This is
called a Yad. We do this so that we don’t make the
parchment dirty.” Naomi held the shining Yad up
to her face, and then passed it to Noah and told
him to pass it around so all the children could see
it. “We also read in the opposite direction, from
right to left.”

“Why do you read the Torah?” asked Arlo.

“The Torah contains 613 commandments known as
mitzvah. They are the rules that Jews strive to

important,” she explained. “We read the Torah on

Shabbat is when I come to synagogue on Saturdays
to attend services.”


“Shabbat begins on Friday evenings and finishes on
Saturdays at sundown. This is the day of rest, and
we shouldn’t do any work. This would mean no
homework too!” she explained. “On Friday nights
families gather and light the candles.” Naomi
began to bring out some candles, a loaf of bread
and a cup.

     hilst placing the items on the table, Grandma

“So, why do you do this?” asked a student in Noah’s

                                                      42
“Another wonderful question. During this time, we

Sometimes, the service can be led by a Jewish
